11215-poems-1828:
Thomas Gent's Poems, published in London in 1828, collects verses previously printed separately with many pieces printed here for the first time. Gent presents them modestly as the amusements of a man whose fortune does not allow him to devote himself to poetry, and thanks critics who judged them by that standard. A note records a severe domestic bereavement during printing, and a tribute to the wife he lost.

The poems themselves are occasional and personal, in the manner of early nineteenth-century magazine verse. Their interest today is partly literary and partly biographical: a minor poet's self-presentation in print. Readers of Romantic-period verse will find a small, sincere volume, unambitious and affecting in its preface.
15613-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's children's weekly for May 20, 1897 again leads with its atlas premium. A Rand McNally 1897 Atlas of the World goes to a subscriber who brings in a new yearly subscription. The atlas offers 160 pages of colored maps from new plates, with a marginal index. The editors repeat their warning: an old atlas is no better than an old directory. Countries change, and knowledge grows.

Non-subscribers could send five dollars for two subscriptions and still earn the atlas, sent to either address. That repeated offer shows a paper building its list week by week, while its news pages kept school readers current on the world. The number, like its neighbors, mixes business with education, in short pieces written for boys and girls to read and discuss.
16281-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for January 28, 1920, volume one hundred fifty-eight, jokes about petrol rising eightpence a gallon, leaving pedestrians to be knocked down by horse vehicles or hand trucks. Moleskins at eighteenpence each draw a note that the moles dispute the figures. A motor-coat lined with Persian lamb at three hundred pounds is set against a waistcoat lined with English lamb. That waistcoat costs a fraction of the sum.

A Carlisle defendant charged with impersonation at a municipal election calls it only a frolic, and the bench, entering into the spirit, sends him for a good frisk in the second division. Cartoons and verses would have kept the same brisk pace. The issue is a funny, compact record of postwar prices and politics.
16619-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Charivaria jokes open the July 28, 1920 Punch, on railway fares, a Mile End duck that laid four eggs in a day, and Tube travel from Bank to Ealing in thirty-five minutes. Mersey shipyard men demanding more pay when not working than the reverse get a jab, as does a French writer on manners at Covent Garden.

Drawings, verse, and short jokes fill the remaining pages, all tuned to summer Britain. Its jokes belong to late July alone: fares, tubes, and shipyard pay. Beside the July 14 number, this issue shows Punch's humor tracking each week's headlines with the same dry, quick wit.
200-the-project-gutenberg-encyclopedia-v:
Project Gutenberg's early encyclopedia project reproduced a famous 1911 reference work in electronic form. Volume 1 of 28, plus an index, covers the opening entries of the alphabet. A header warns that the text is unrevised and that the original title is trademarked.

The volume's disclaimer explains the licensing limits that shaped its plain name. Readers get 1911 knowledge as it stood, from science to history to biography. Later volumes continue the alphabet in sequence. The set shows the young digital library's ambition to put reference works online. Later Gutenberg volumes extend the same 1911 text through the rest of the alphabet.
22653-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of April 28, 1920, from volume 158 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Peace had returned, Prohibition ruled America, and Punch watched both with its usual raised eyebrow.

One joke quotes a New York report of streaming silver light and stars piled high over the city. That New Yorkers can still see such sights, Punch remarks, must sadden the Prohibitionists. The hint is plain: the vision owed more to drink than to weather. Sketches, poems, and cartoons round out the number. The issue catches Britain in 1920: relieved, a little weary, and ready to laugh at American experiments.
5931-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
River adventure opens chapters twenty-nine through thirty-one of this second-volume Don Quixote portion. Chapter twenty-nine treats the famous adventure of the enchanted bark, as Quixote and Sancho reach the river Ebro two days after quitting the grove, delighting in the charms of its banks. Chapter thirty follows Quixote's adventure with a fair huntress, and chapter thirty-one treats many and great matters.

Readers travel from river to hunt to courtly talk, as Quixote's delusions meet water, sport, and noble company. The chapters favor scenery and conversation, letting the Ebro carry the knight toward the duke and duchess. This part suits readers following volume two in order, since its river journey leads directly to the great household episodes ahead.
alchemistishe-und-chemische-zeichen-1928:
Alchemistische und chemische Zeichen, published in 1928 by Fritz Lüdy the younger, is a German reference work on the signs of alchemy and chemistry. It collects the text and symbology of historic alchemy and chemistry: the marks, characters, and shorthand symbols with which practitioners denoted metals, substances, and operations across the centuries. The copy preserved here was scanned from the collection of the University of Michigan.

Without such a key, the old books are full of signs no modern reader can parse. Lüdy's work decodes them, gathering the symbol sets of the tradition into one place. It remains a practical tool for anyone reading alchemical manuscripts and early chemical texts, where a single sign can carry the whole meaning of a process.
anna-comnena-alexiad-dawes-1928:
Anna Comnena, daughter of the emperor Alexius I, wrote the Alexiad in her widowhood to tell her father's reign, from 1081 to 1118. Elizabeth Dawes translated the Greek into English in 1928. The work is the first great history known to be written by a woman. Anna wrote as a princess, a scholar, and a partisan.

Alexius fights Normans, Turks, and rebels, rebuilds an empire in ruins, and then meets the armies of the First Crusade. Anna eyes the western knights with awe and contempt at once. Her portraits of her father and of Bohemond still glow. The Alexiad is the key Byzantine source for the crusade and a family monument. Her learning shows on every page.
arxiv-2412-00528:
André Kézdy and Jenő Lehel completed a description in twenty twenty-four of the length polyhedron of an interval order. Interval orders rank items by intervals on a line; their length polyhedron collects all possible interval length assignments with integer endpoints. Earlier work by the authors modeled it with a key graph, whose cycles yield the inequalities defining the polyhedron's faces.

Here they prove that inequality system is totally dual integral, a strong niceness property. Exploiting circulations and the key graph's structure, they show a redundant cycle inequality is exactly one that combines positively and integrally from smaller ones. That test prunes the system down to the unique minimal Schrijver system. When the key graph has few cycles, the whole computation runs in polynomial time.
arxiv-2412-01028:
Ze-Zhou Zhang, Hong-Gang Luo, and Wei Wu wrote a paper from 2024 on measuring faint things with quantum probes in the cold. Such probes can gauge heat, fields, and traits with precision. A snag has blocked them at low heat. When the probe is loosely tied to what it measures, its error blows up as the cold deepens.

The team proposes to tie the probe more tightly. A mapping trick lets them track what that tight tie does to the probe's resting state. The tight tie reshapes that state and lifts precision a great deal. In their sums, colder now means better: precision grows in a power law as the heat falls. That flips the loose-tie result, where precision fades fast in the cold. The team says the path could bring quantum gauges to the coldest settings, where many quantum tools must work.
arxiv-2412-01628:
Keren Censor-Hillel and Einav Huberman write a 2024 paper on keeping network labels useful even when some of them are lost. In a labeling scheme, a central oracle assigns each node of a graph a short label. Nodes then use their labels alone to answer tasks such as distance queries or proofs about the graph. Hardware faults or lost contact with the oracle can erase some labels.

The authors define a resilient scheme in two parts. First, the oracle rewrites any labeling into a tougher form. Then the nodes run a shared method to rebuild their first labels from the new ones, even with some labels missing. Their scheme restores labels with near-best possible cost. The work extends an earlier idea built only for proof labels to labeling schemes in general.
arxiv-2412-02128:
Stacking two twisted sheets of graphene can create quantum phases of matter that exist nowhere else. Sen Niu and co-authors map the phase diagram of a double twisted stack in this 2024 paper using large-scale exact computer simulations at half filling of its lowest band.

Across a wide range of settings the ground state splits into six near-identical copies, a signature of a special topological order. Further checks of its quantum numbers and entanglement pattern name it as the non-Abelian Moore-Read state, while ruling out a simple charge pattern. Such states are chased for their promise in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2412-03028:
Chaudhary, Lin, Tan, and Singh present a paper from twenty twenty-four on generating specifications for neural networks in computer systems. Specifications state exactly what correct behavior means for a system. Networks acting as black boxes need such rules to stay trustworthy. Hand-writing them is slow expert work that scales poorly. Their framework mines specifications from the classic algorithms networks replace. Those old algorithms encode trusted behavior from years of use. Observed behaviors are grouped into compact spec statements.

Specs are built for network models in streaming and congestion control. They match expert intuition and look correct on checks. The specs also expose unknown flaws in leading models. Automation could widen formal checking of learned components.
arxiv-2412-03728:
Diego Fallas Padilla, Mingjian Zhu, and Han Pu propose, in a 2024 quantum physics paper, a new way to measure entanglement between two parts of a qubit system. Standard measures can be hard to compute or to read in a lab. Their protocol draws on monogamy, the idea that entanglement shared with one partner limits what can be shared with others.

The plan evolves and measures one part, then uses spin squeezing in that part to infer the shared entanglement. For small systems they derive exact results and show the plan works best for a classic shared state. For larger systems, a smart choice of the squeezing step improves accuracy. The method suits labs where full state mapping is out of reach.
arxiv-2412-04228:
David Ribar, Clifford Woodward, and Jan Forsman explain strong barriers between charged surfaces in clustered salt solutions, in two thousand twenty-four. Experiments have found oddly long-ranged forces between such surfaces in strong salt water. Ion clustering has been proposed as the cause, but the size of the effect needed a model.

Their model treats clusters as chains of alternating positive and negative ions, forming a polyampholyte salt. A statistical theory then gives ion layouts and surface forces. The clustered salt raised free energy barriers far beyond those of simple salt. The cause is a brush-like layer at each surface, which resists being squeezed. The authors suggest uses in stabilizing particle dispersions.
arxiv-2412-04528:
Ryde and co-authors measure the chemistry of giant stars in the dense cluster at the Milky Way's center, in this 2024 paper. Heavy dust long blocked such work. Alpha elements like magnesium and calcium record how fast stars formed and how gas flowed in.

Sharp infrared spectra from a large telescope covered nine red giants, with line choices calibrated on fifty nearby cousins. The center stars, mostly metal-rich, carried high alpha shares. Their pattern matches the inner bulge and the metal-rich high-alpha group near the Sun. The match implies a fast early star-forming burst at the galaxy's heart.
arxiv-2412-05228:
Phones and edge devices pack many processors onto one chip that shares a single pool of memory, and that sharing can leak. Ismet Dagli, James Crea, Soner Seckiner, Yuanchao Xu, Selçuk Köse, and Mehmet Belviranli build a covert channel that runs purely on fights over that shared memory. A covert channel is a hidden way for two programs to talk. Earlier channels of this kind needed a shared cache or special access rights.

Their channel, MC3, lets a program on the main processor signal one on the graphics processor with no such help. On three NVIDIA Orin chips they reached six point four kilobits per second with under one percent errors. The work shows a quiet risk built into shared-memory chip design.
arxiv-2412-05328:
Valeria Chiadò Piat, Virginia De Cicco, and Anderson Melchor Hernandez wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-four about relaxing an energy functional with linear growth. Relaxation replaces a rough energy with the smoothest lower version that keeps the same minima, which makes variational problems solvable. Their functional is degenerate and weighted, and the weight lacks the standard doubling traits that ease proofs.

The authors work in the one-dimensional case. Their main tools are Sobolev inequalities that carry two weights at once. With them, they obtain an explicit formula for the relaxed functional and a clear statement of its domain. The result extends relaxation theory to weights that fall outside the classic Muckenhoupt class.
arxiv-2412-05428:
O. A. Dobush and M. A. Shpot introduce a new probability distribution and the special function that normalizes it, motivated by a cell model of simple fluids. The distribution blends a Poisson law with a Gaussian-style penalty on large counts. Its normalizing sum defines the new function, which the authors study in depth. Writing in twenty twenty-four, they derive asymptotic estimates for large values of one parameter. The same treatment covers the function's logarithm and its logarithmic derivative.

Beyond a threshold in the second parameter, the exact function oscillates around its asymptotic form. That wiggle is the mathematical fingerprint of interesting physics. The authors connect the results to the Curie-Weiss cell model, where particles interact in a mean-field way inside cells. The distribution may serve other counting problems with suppressed tails.
arxiv-2412-05528:
Dillon Chen and co-authors offer a 2024 primer and survey on AI planning, the field that helps machines choose steps to reach a goal. Planning ideas are well known in that field but less so in nearby areas such as machine learning with rewards. The authors aim to share those ideas in plain terms and show how they connect across fields.

The survey starts with the classic planning problem and how it is written down, then moves to forms that handle doubt and time. It reviews the best current methods, with a focus on how they use the shape of a problem to solve it faster. The last part covers learning structure from raw inputs and applying what was learned to new cases.
arxiv-2412-07228:
Siyang Li and four co-authors present T-TIME, a 2024 method making brain-computer interfaces work without calibration sessions. EEG-based interfaces read brain signals to control devices, but each new user normally endures a tedious calibration because brains differ and signals drift. Transfer learning can help, yet mostly in offline settings where all the new user's data exist in advance. T-TIME tackles the online case, where unlabeled trials stream in and answers are due instantly.

It starts several classifiers from aligned past data, predicts each new trial by ensemble, then updates the classifiers by shrinking uncertainty and matching distributions. On three public motor imagery data sets, it beat about twenty rival methods. The authors call it the first test-time adaptation for calibration-free BCIs, a step toward plug-and-play devices.
arxiv-2412-09028:
Wenjie Mei and co-authors use special neural networks to model an electric motor drive in a 2024 paper. Learning how systems change over time helps predict their behavior. The team focused on a permanent magnet motor, a nonlinear system used widely in machines. Their networks are built to respect time flow, learning the motor's dynamics from data and forecasting its current paths.

Tests ran under varied load shocks and with no load at all. The method rebuilt the original system faithfully and predicted well over both short and long spans. It also held up under rough conditions. Readers see a modeling tool that may extend to weather, robots, and group behavior studies.
arxiv-2412-10828:
Harsha Hutridurga, Krishan Kumar, and Amiya K Pani give error bounds for a numeric method for a coupled flow system. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The system joins a Vlasov equation for a spread of particles with an unsteady Stokes flow. Such pairs model thin fluids with many fine particles.

First they prove that a strong solution, when it exists, is the only one. Then they build a scheme that uses discontinuous Galerkin steps for both parts. The scheme keeps mass and momentum. With a special projection, they prove the best rate of error for smooth starts. Tests with a split-time code match the theory, and they note how the bounds extend to three ways.
arxiv-2412-11728:
Wenchao Gu and co-authors present a 2024 paper on SECRET, a system for finding code snippets from plain-language requests at very large scale. Deep learning retrievers encode code and queries as vectors, but scanning a huge code base vector by vector is slow. Hashing methods shrink everything to short codes for fast matching, yet their recall step still crawls through the whole store.

SECRET segments the deep hash codes so candidates can be recalled in blocks rather than by one long scan. The design keeps the accuracy of learned representations while cutting retrieval cost. The authors present it as a practical path to searching industrial-scale code collections interactively.
arxiv-2412-17728:
Yue-Chang Peng and four co-authors use warped accretion disks to explain why some quasars brighten and dim in near-regular cycles. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Long sky surveys found quasars whose light rises and falls over years, with swings that slowly fade. No agreed cause exists yet.

In their model, a bending wave travels through the disk that feeds the black hole. The wave tips the disk's inner part back and forth across our line of sight. That tipping makes the light vary in cycles that damp over time. The team solved the warp equation and built fake light curves. They then fit one real quasar from survey data at several viewing angles. The fit was decent, which supports the warped disk idea. Wider tests on more quasars come next.
arxiv-2412-18428:
Farhad Nooralahzadeh and co-authors present a system that answers questions across databases, text, images, and video in plain language, in a paper from 2024. Large organizations store knowledge in all those forms at once. Tools existed for each form alone, but joint questions in natural language were largely untested.

Their system, called M2EX, uses language model agents to split a question into sub-tasks. One agent turns a sub-question into a database query, another analyzes images, and a planner lines the steps up in an efficient order. Tests on multi-modal data sets showed better accuracy than past systems. Query time, API cost, and planning effort also improved. The design draws on a real use case in a large organization.
arxiv-2412-19628:
Mingshu Zhao, Yi Luo, and Yong Ouyang build large image filters from stacked small ones with a recursive split, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Large filters widen the view of a vision net but balloon in size and cost. Their method, RecConv, grows view by levels while cost stays flat per level.

Parameter growth stays linear in levels, far below the steep growth of standard large filters. Compute rises only slightly at the top level in their counts. A test net beat a close rival on object finding by near two points at like cost. Code and models are shared. Readers who design vision nets get wide views at small-filter prices.
arxiv-2412-20128:
Jin Matsuda, Hikaru Watanabe, and Ryotaro Arita (2024) argue that common antiferromagnets hide more symmetry breaking than textbooks suggest. Altermagnets, a newer class, split electron spins without relativity and draw spintronics interest. Plain ones were thought to break nothing. The authors show that when the magnetic pattern repeats with a nonzero wave vector, it clashes with the crystal's screw symmetries. That clash breaks symmetries at the whole-crystal scale while leaving the spin bands degenerate.

Yet a hidden spin splitting still shapes the electrons. It drives effects such as nonlinear transport and optical activity. The team checked the idea with first-principles work on manganese disulfide, a multiferroic candidate. The effects appeared in the numbers. The authors offer a fresh design lens for spintronic materials: look for useful effects in plain antiferromagnets that were dismissed as featureless. The hidden split does the work while the surface stays quiet.
arxiv-2501-00328:
Speaker recognition software can fail when a voice is heard in a new style, say a podcast rather than a phone call. Hoang Long Vu, Phuong Tuan Dat, Pham Thao Nhi, Nguyen Song Hao, and Nguyen Thi Thu Trang built a dataset to attack that problem for Vietnamese. VoxVietnam holds over one hundred and eighty-seven thousand clips from one thousand four hundred and six speakers, gathered by an automated pipeline from public sources.

The clips span many speech genres, which earlier Vietnamese sets lacked. Tests showed models trained on one genre stumble on others. Adding VoxVietnam to training lifted performance a great deal. The team offers the set as a base for sturdier voice systems in less-studied languages.
arxiv-2501-01628:
Stefan Zellmann, a solo author, writes on drawing three-dimensional science data on a supercomputer, in a paper from 2025. Such drawing work is split across many machines when the data are too big for one node. Tools for the task vary a lot, even though the core steps are much the same.

Zellmann uses a standard called ANARI, which aims to unify how rendering tools are built. The paper explains the main ideas and hard parts of drawing in parallel, in plain terms for computing staff. A case study shows data-parallel rendering on RAMSES, a new supercomputer at the University of Cologne. The work shows both the promise and the strain of the standard at large scale.
arxiv-2501-05928:
Four researchers wrote a computer security paper in two thousand twenty-five on hidden backdoors in AI models. A backdoored model behaves normally until a secret trigger appears, when it gives a wrong answer the attacker wants. Most work on hiding such attacks focuses on the input or on the model's internal features.

The authors tested twelve known attacks against seventeen defenses of varied kinds. Attacks that looked stealthy in input and feature terms could still be caught by looking at the model's parameters, the numbers that define it. They then studied what marks these attacks leave in that space. The result exposes a blind spot in current attack design.
arxiv-2501-06128:
Nivedhitha Duggi, Masoud Rafiei, and Mohsen Amini Salehi gather benchmarks for how different kinds of applications run on varied cloud machines, in a report from twenty twenty-five. Cloud providers rent out architecturally mixed servers, each suiting some workloads better than others. Little guidance existed on matching popular application types to machines across providers.

The report curates benchmark datasets from the authors' lab across three domains. One covers deep network inference for industrial uses. Another covers machine learning inference for assistive technology. The third covers video transcoding for media work. The authors offer the collection so others can pick cloud services wisely on cost, speed, energy, and carbon grounds.
arxiv-2501-06828:
Ruizhe Ou and his four co-authors, publishing in 2025, teach a large AI model to answer questions about satellite images down to the exact pixel. Existing models can caption a scene or point to a region. None could chat about an image and return a precise outline of the object asked for. Their model, GeoPix, adds a mask-making module to a multimodal language model, steered by tokens the model itself produces.

To train it, the team built a dataset of 65,000 images and 140,000 labeled objects, each with a description, a box, and an outline. A memory module that stores class-level geographic context helps with objects at many scales. Training runs in two stages to balance talking and masking. Tests show strong pixel-level outlining while keeping image and region skills competitive. The authors target mapping and monitoring uses.
arxiv-2501-08228:
Odile Sauzet writes on a common snag in health studies: turning a smooth measure into a yes-or-no event. Her paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Splitting a measure at a cut point is known to waste information. Yet doctors and journals still often need results stated as events. She asks how survival curves can be built when the event is defined by crossing such a cut.

Sauzet proposes a version of the Kaplan-Meier curve built from the spread of the measure itself. Her method trims a normal spread step by step to track who stays event-free. She tests the method in a simulation study. A case study then shows how it works on real data. The paper offers a cleaner path than plain splitting.
arxiv-2501-09328:
Yixiao Xu and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a way to mark neural networks so owners can prove a stolen copy is theirs. Thieves can query a model and train a clone that mimics it. A hidden watermark lets the owner test a suspect model and claim it, but most marking schemes need costly retraining.

Their method, Neural Honeytrace, plants the mark with no retraining at all. It sends the mark through the model in steps, riding a known quirk of how models learn rare triggers. In tests, proving ownership took as few as two percent of the queries older methods needed. The scheme also held up better against thieves who adapt their theft to the defense.
arxiv-2501-11928: Joonil Kim and Jeongtae Oh published a research paper in 2025 on maximal operators, tools that track the largest local averages of a function, set on the Heisenberg group. They study sparse, or lacunary, families of ellipses. The core question is for which power settings these operators stay bounded. Starting from the skew-symmetric matrices natural to this setting, they extend the estimates to arbitrary matrices. The pair give conditions on the matrix that decide boundedness, showing how the curvature it induces governs the answer for both circular and elliptic versions.
arxiv-2501-12728:
Six authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five calling for reform in how software engineering research handles data. The field relies on experiments and statistics, yet worries about misapplied methods date back decades. The authors set out to measure the problem and to test whether experts can spot it.

They surveyed about twenty-seven thousand empirical studies, using language models to class their statistics as sound or not. They also gave thirty primary studies to thirty-three experts in a workshop. Serious statistical flaws showed up in the studies, and the experts caught and fixed few of them, raising concern about the field's statistical skills.
arxiv-2501-12828:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Haradhan Dutta, and Hari Shankar Mahato model thin fiber reinforced hydrogels in this 2025 paper. The material mixes a fiber frame with soft gel inclusions in a repeating pattern. Such composites appear in biomedical and soft engineering uses. Predicting their combined elastic and fluid behavior needs a reduced model.

The fibers follow linear elasticity, while the gel follows Biot poroelasticity with fluid pressure. Both the pattern size and the sheet thickness shrink to zero together. An unfolding method tracks that double limit rigorously. The limit shape behaves like a Kirchhoff-Love plate, the classic thin plate model. A unique solution for the resulting macroscopic problem is proved. Engineers gain a tractable model for design calculations.
arxiv-2501-17028:
Chandrasekar Sridhar and three co-authors propose a faster certification path for learning systems in aircraft in a 2025 paper. Machine learning is entering aviation, yet classic software standards were not written for models that learn from data. Even low-risk uses need a trustworthy approval process.

Their semi-automated approach splits work between people and tools. It stresses data and model validation, resilience checks, and usability assurance. A classification step scales the rigor to the system's traits. An assurance profile rolls results into one confidence measure for the model. Human oversight stays woven into key judgments. A case study with a camera system that tells military from civilian vehicles shows the process in action.
arxiv-2501-18028:
Cassandra Mussard, Arthur Charpentier, and Stéphane Mussard rebuild two classic data tools, nearest neighbors and k-means, on a new kind of distance that reads ranks as well as values. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Standard distances can be thrown off by noise and outliers. A Gini-style prametric folds rank information into the gap between points.

Their clustering version is proven to converge and to resist noisy data. Their neighbor version matches top rivals in messy settings. Sixteen public data sets put both through clustering and sorting trials. The Gini versions came out ahead on performance and speed. The work opens rank-based measures as a direction for machine learning. It suits data where extremes are common and ranks stay meaningful when values wobble.
arxiv-2501-18728:
Evie Ladbrook and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on squeezing a polar metal and watching its internal distortions grow. Polar metals break a rule of thumb: they carry an electric polarization, like an insulator, yet conduct like a metal. That mix promises odd physics and devices that use both traits.

The team compressed single crystals of one such metal and tracked the atomic shifts with diffraction at high pressure. The polar distortion grew stronger under pressure rather than fading. Computer modeling then checked a common assumption: that bigger distortion means proportionally bigger spin splitting of electrons. The link is not so simple, the calculations warn.
arxiv-2501-19128:
Wenyun Li, Wenjie Huang, and Chen Sun improve reinforcement learning when rewards are rare, in a research paper from 2025. Agents in many tasks get feedback only at scattered moments, so shaping a useful reward signal is hard. Most past methods learn only from the few rewarded steps and waste the rest.

The approach also learns from the mass of zero-reward steps. A semi-supervised method plus a new data-mixing trick builds a map of how paths through a task relate. Tests on Atari games and robot arm tasks beat supervised rivals, doubling peak scores in the sparsest settings. The mixing trick alone added a clear margin.
arxiv-2502-00228:
Yuanyuan Yang and colleagues extended a classic search puzzle in a 2025 theory paper. In the Pandora problem, each closed box hides a prize and costs money to open, and a searcher wants the best payoff after costs. Their version adds two twists: boxes must be opened in an order set by a network map, and prizes in linked boxes move together in a memory-like pattern.

For maps shaped like forests, they give best-possible adaptive plans. For simpler line maps they give near-best plans, and for forests a plan guaranteed at least half the best payoff. Their plan also runs much faster than brute force as maps grow. Uses include costly searches in data and computing design.
arxiv-2502-01128:
Fredrik Bagge Carlson and three co-authors compile Julia code straight to machine binaries, skipping C. Their 2025 paper challenges a long-held rule in control engineering. The rule says fast, embedded work must be rewritten in C. High-level languages were thought too slow or too loose for real-time control.

Recent Julia compiler work feeds its native code path through LLVM. Models written with ModelingToolkit compile into stand-alone programs. One case built a nonlinear state estimator that runs on a Raspberry Pi. Another built a PID controller library callable from C programs. Skipping C code generation lifts many limits placed on model code. Productive languages, the authors argue, can ship real-time systems as-is.
arxiv-2502-02928:
A code model that can read its own error notes and patch itself needs less hand-holding. Muntasir Adnan, Zhiwei Xu, and Carlos Kuhn build that loop in 2025 as PyCapsule, a two-agent pipe for Python. One agent writes; the other runs the code against cases, reads the crash, and sends the writer back in with the note. Smart prompts frame each round.

On three known test sets the loop lifted pass rates over the past best, by a hair on the small set and by a quarter on the big shop set. More patch rounds past a point hurt, as thin error notes began to mislead. The team pitch the pipe as a light, cheap way to firm model code for real use.
arxiv-2502-03628:
Zhuowei Li and nine co-authors study why large vision-language models invent details that are not in the picture. These models reason over images and text together, yet often produce fluent descriptions with no visual basis. The team traced token rankings during generation to see where grounding slips away.

Three patterns emerged: visually grounded tokens steadily lose favor, meaningful tokens peak in earlier layers, and true information stays highly ranked without being chosen. Their fix, VISTA, steers generation at inference time with no extra training. It reinforces visual signals and draws on early-layer activations to favor grounded words. Tests showed reduced hallucination across decoding strategies.
arxiv-2502-03928:
Hong Han and a team of co-authors study a wireless system that sends both data and power at once. Their twenty twenty-five paper calls the setup SWIPT. A device can split the signal to harvest power, or switch in time between power and data modes.

The team built one deep learning model, SWIPTNet, to handle both modes. It uses a graph neural network, since the setup maps well to a graph. Tricks like a simpler output form and richer input traits help it meet quality goals. A transfer step lets the model carry what it learned from one mode to the other. Tests show near-best results in a flash, far faster than classic methods.
arxiv-2502-05128:
Rahul Bhardwaj presents a 2025 mathematics paper on rebuilding a tensor field from its line-like measurements. The field here assigns a symmetric tensor at each point of a disk, encoding directional quantities like strain. A V-line transform integrates the field along two-armed paths shaped like the letter V. Three flavors exist, named longitudinal, mixed, and transverse, after how they weigh directions.

The goal is to recover the whole field from a mix of these transforms. Bhardwaj uses two different techniques for two different data sets, each fitted to what the measurements reveal. Problems of this kind, called tensor tomography, arise in imaging of materials and medical scans. Solving them tells engineers what internal directional structure produced the readings. The paper is a theoretical contribution to that recovery problem.
arxiv-2502-05628:
Houcheng Jiang and co-authors present AnyEdit, a 2025 method for updating facts stored inside large language models, even when the knowledge is long. Models often answer with stale or wrong facts, and editors that fix them usually work by nudging a single token's inner state. That shortcut fails on long-form knowledge such as poems, code, and math derivations, a wall the authors call the efficacy barrier.

AnyEdit splits the new knowledge into a chain of chunks and edits the key token of each chunk in turn, in step with how the model itself generates text. The authors ground the scheme in information theory. On benchmarks of long and mixed-format knowledge, it beat strong rivals by over twenty percent. It also works as a plug-in, letting older editors handle knowledge of any length or shape.
arxiv-2502-07228:
Many atomic physics labs need a strong, steady beam of hot atoms, and Peter Dotti, Xiao Chai, Jeremy Tanlimco, Ethan Simmons, and David Weld describe a source built to survive the heat. Their design pushes vapor through a nozzle pierced by many tiny steel tubes, which line the atoms up into a narrow beam. The whole nozzle is welded steel, so the high heat stays away from the seals that hold the vacuum.

Older designs tend to fail where hot parts meet those seals. This one moves the weak point out of the heat's path. The team ran the source with lithium at several temperatures and measured the beam while it worked, showing it holds up under real use.
arxiv-2502-10028:
Yuxin He and five co-authors add 3D foresight to robot manipulation policies in two thousand twenty-five. World models have lifted how well robots learn to handle objects. Past work modeled change in flat 2D views alone. Tasks with deep motion along the view axis suffer from that flat view.

Their frame joins 3D world modeling with policy learning in one loop. Three self taught tasks build the foresight: depth now, future color plus depth, and 3D flow. The tasks back each other up inside the frame. Tests in simulation and the real world show big gains. Inference speed stays intact as well.
arxiv-2502-10628:
Sadaf Salehkalaibar and co-authors design a smarter realism score for video compression in a 2025 computing paper. Streaming compression must shrink each frame as it arrives, with no peeking ahead. Judging realism by single frames misses how errors stick around across a sequence. Their score judges each new frame jointly with the frames rebuilt before it.

Theory for simple signal models shows the new score avoids frozen errors that older scores allow. It also exploits links between a sharp current frame and its neighbors. Tests on moving digit clips and standard video sets backed the math. Live streams and calls could look cleaner at the same bit budget with such a guide.
arxiv-2502-11628:
Aimo Winkelmann and co-authors sharpen crystal strain measures from low resolution diffraction patterns by matching them to simulations, in work from twenty twenty-five. The method, electron backscatter diffraction, maps crystal orientation and strain in materials. High resolution patterns are data heavy and slow to gather.

Simulated patterns are super sampled to stand in for fine real data in best fit matching. That lifts the precision of strain and rotation values drawn from coarse patterns a great deal. Tests on hardness indents in a silicon wafer showed very low noise on strain free zones. Finite element models helped read the strain maps. Data size needs could fall by about a hundredfold, the team estimates.
arxiv-2502-12328:
Jhamtani, Andreas, and Van Durme introduce PeopleJoin, a test bed for AI agents that gather facts through teammates. A request arrives, and the agent must find who can help. It then chats with those people to collect what they know. Last, it compiles an answer or summary for the requester. Tasks span questions over tables and the drafting of documents. The needed facts are spread across fake organizations of 2 to 20 users.

Several known agent designs were run on the benchmark. Scores covered both accuracy and cost of completion. The setup mirrors real office hunts for scattered knowledge. It also surfaces fresh questions about how agents should pick and query helpers.
arxiv-2502-12728:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim derive a recurrence for a family of counting polynomials in a 2025 mathematics paper. Bell polynomials count ways to split sets into blocks, and their degenerate versions warp the counting with a parameter. Spivey found a famous recurrence for the plain Bell numbers, expressing each in terms of smaller ones.

The authors generalize that recurrence to the degenerate polynomials using two simple operators: multiply by the variable, and differentiate. The two operators obey a neat swapping rule that powers the proof. They also obtain the matching recurrence for the refined r Bell polynomials, which count partitions with some elements pre assigned. The results extend a classical identity into the degenerate setting.
arxiv-2502-13228:
Jake Snell and Thomas Griffiths rethink a popular safety method for AI forecasts in their 2025 paper. Conformal prediction gives a set of likely answers with a promise about error rates, even when the model is a black box. But its promises rest on frequentist probability, which can limit where the method makes sense.

The authors recast the method's core steps in Bayesian terms, which track belief rather than long-run frequency. Seen this way, some gaps in the usual promises stand out. They then offer a practical fix based on Bayesian quadrature, a way to estimate ranges by smart sampling. Their version gives clearer promises and a richer picture of the losses a user may face at test time.
arxiv-2502-13328:
Joseph Tran and Abdullah Al Maruf design controls that hide a network's state from distant watchers in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In double-integrator networks, each node tracks position and speed, linked to its neighbors. The goal is feedback control that blocks some nodes from inferring the full state.

Their first design needs a few more control nodes than watched nodes and leans on assigning the system's modes by hand. A smarter design uses the network's shape: the count of control nodes then depends on a cut set between the control and watched sites. The authors extend the ideas to higher-order networks, where nodes track more derivatives.
arxiv-2502-13428:
Guanming Xiong and co-authors speed up tree search for answering questions from knowledge bases in this 2025 paper. A language model must chain facts across a vast graph to answer well. Searching that chain step by step with Monte Carlo tree search works, but judging each step usually means costly rollouts or a trained reward model.

Their method scores each partial chain by information gain instead. A ratio of model likelihoods, with the question kept in view, stands in for how much a step teaches. It needs only forward passes of an open model, no extra training, and it grades steps mid-path rather than only at the end. On four standard benchmarks the method beat straight-line baselines every time. It also improved the accuracy per unit of compute over classic rollout search. The code and data are public.
arxiv-2502-13728:
Marco Arazzi, Mert Cihangiroglu, Serena Nicolazzo, and Antonino Nocera distill training data across many owners without gathering it in one place. Their paper appeared in 2025. Dataset distillation squeezes a big dataset into a tiny synthetic one that trains models nearly as well. Doing it centrally endangers privacy. Their federated version lets each client shape the shared synthetic set from its own data, sending only updates.

Gradients can leak data to a curious server, so they add a tuned local differential privacy shield. They also test the framework against malicious clients planting backdoors, and report robustness when most clients behave. The authors say distilled data can be a shareable asset rather than a privacy liability.
arxiv-2502-14028:
Marie Lecroq and co-authors recalculate the light output of the first, nearly metal-free stars, in a paper from 2025. These population III stars lit the early universe. Telling their light apart from other early sources is a key test for new telescopes.

Using a fresh population model that matched known data well at later eras, the team checked proposed spectral fingerprints. The fingerprints work, but only while a population is younger than about a million years. The paper also supplies the rates modelers need: how many ionizing photons such stars make, how many hydrogen-splitting photons they emit, and how often each kind of supernova occurs. A side study predicts the gravitational wave signals from black hole pairs born of these stars.
arxiv-2502-14128:
How a material answers strong light is written in its quantum geometry, argue Jingxu Wu and Chenjia Li in a 2025 arXiv paper. They build a framework for nonlinear optical response in multiband systems, using a gauge safe formulation borrowed from phase space algebra.

Following the density matrix under shifts, they derive tidy forms for the polarization and its response tensors. Geometric phases, Berry curvature among them, turn out to cancel parts that physics forbids. Computer simulations checked the math, with side results on rectification and topological Hall style effects. The authors pitch the work at designers of metamaterials and photonics.
arxiv-2502-15128:
Zahid Ullah and Jihie Kim outline hearts in medical scans with a network that remembers what a heart should look like, in a 2025 paper. Automated heart segmentation often errs in anatomically impossible ways, and past fixes bolt on extra modules that complicate training and crack when image quality drops. Their system, DAM-Seg, instead builds memory into the network itself, using dense associative networks, a modern form of memory model.

The network is restricted to a small stock of stored patterns drawn from heart images. When a new scan arrives, the output is formed as a blend of those patterns, which keeps the predicted outline heart-shaped by construction. Because the patterns do not depend on the input, the method stays steady even when parts of the heart are barely visible. On two public ultrasound and scan datasets, DAM-Seg beat the baseline systems on every measure the authors report.
arxiv-2502-15828:
Mengyang Sun and colleagues improved a popular fine-tuning recipe in 2025. Large foundation models are often adapted with low-rank adapters, small trainable matrices that cut storage and training cost. Stacking several adapters as a mixture of experts adds expressive power and helps on downstream tasks, but the mixture trains unstably and its robustness during tuning and use is weak.

Inspired by Riemannian preconditioners that treat a single adapter as a subspace projector, the authors propose training the mixture through projections across multiple spaces, which steadies and strengthens feature learning. They demonstrate the strategy with two standard optimizers, showing it works under both, and they release the source code. The result is a stronger mixture of low-rank experts for adapting foundation models without giving up the efficiency that made adapters attractive.
arxiv-2502-16928:
Prunescu and Shunia cleaned up a math claim in twenty twenty-five on short forms for step-rule number lists. Such lists, where each term rests on fixed past terms, can be built by split and rest steps on growth sums. A past proof of a rest-rest form had two flaws to patch.

It worked only for large steps and needed a fix term in the first sum. Their new proof holds for all steps from one up, with no fix term. The gain comes from a short arith-metic cut drawn from the split-rest form. Clean forms help both proofs and fast code for such lists.
arxiv-2502-17628:
Garima Chib, Parisa Mollaei, and Amir Barati Farimani grade AlphaFold on the shapes of G protein-coupled receptors. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets a receptor family behind roughly a third of approved drugs. Few family members are drugged so far, in part since their shapes are hard to model. The team compares predicted shapes with measured ones across the family. Two gauges lead: mean carbon displacement and a helix gap tied to activation.

Both model generations nail inactive shapes best. The lower a receptor's activity level, the smaller the warp. Active shapes wobble more, since firing and ligand binding shift the frame. Scores also swing by receptor class, riding on training data depth and shape variety. The study backs AlphaFold for drug hunts while flagging active-state work for repair.
arxiv-2502-17828:
Jadon Lin, C. Martijn de Sterke, Ognjen Ilic, and Boris Kuhlmey study sails pushed by light for interstellar flight in a 2025 photonics study. A lightsail rides the pressure of a powerful laser beam, the only known route to a sizable fraction of light speed, fast enough to reach nearby stars within a human lifetime. Speed is useless if the sail tumbles or drifts off the beam, so stability is as vital as acceleration.

Recent photonics and patterned metamaterials offer sails that help center and steady themselves in the beam. The authors weigh fast and stable design together, the pairing any real probe mission needs.
arxiv-2502-18628: Nicholas Chiem presents a 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics, on a Schrödinger operator driven by Arnold's cat map. The potential is smooth and monotone, with its slope along the unstable direction kept away from zero. Chiem proves that the Lyapunov exponent of the operator stays uniformly positive at every energy, as long as the coupling is large enough. Uniform positivity of this exponent is a key step toward proving localization behavior in such chaotic models.
arxiv-2502-18728:
Minsung Cho and co-authors scale up hard choices made under chance, in work from 2025. Chance-based inference is hard on its own, and picking the best act on top of it is harder still. Their plan compiles the problem into a fresh middle form: a branch diagram weighted by a new score ring that suits branch-and-bound search.

The form splits problems by program shape and prunes weak branches early. It also supports staged builds, so users can peek at best values mid-run. Two languages compile to it, one for reward-based choices and one for exact inference with nested best-guess tasks. Tests showed strong speed and range.
arxiv-2502-19228:
Peter Reimann and Christian Eidecker-Dunkel wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on how a simple quantum system returns to equilibrium. Their system is a chain of spin-half particles, a standard model with open ends. It starts in thermal balance, then a weak local nudge, a quantum quench, disturbs it at time zero.

Focusing on nudges and readings at a single spin, the authors show the system settles back to thermal equilibrium for large times. The proof uses only the basic laws of quantum mechanics, with no extra assumptions. They also compute the relaxation in quantitative detail and chart its many interesting features.
arxiv-2502-19528:
Arwa Alanqary and four colleagues improve how transportation planners calibrate travel demand in traffic simulators. Estimating origin-destination demand is underdetermined: many demand patterns fit the same counts. Planners usually lean on a prior demand matrix, which biases results.

Their formulation adds sample segment-level track counts as a regularization term. The calibration then preserves the observed distribution of track counts while matching path-level travel times. Tests on Seattle's highway network under varied congestion showed clear improvements in solution quality. The method recovered ground-truth demand patterns more accurately at both origin-destination and segment levels. The authors present partial trajectory observations as an underused data source for demand estimation.
arxiv-2502-20428: Yuval Filmus, writing alone in 2025, extends a classic result on when group decisions must collapse into dictatorship. Arrow's theorem says fair voting rules face hard limits. A boolean version asks which rules force one voter to rule. Earlier work settled that question when unanimity is assumed. Another line dropped the unanimity assumption for yes-no predicates. Filmus merges both lines for wider alphabets and rules. As a payoff, all aggregators of every symmetric yes-no rule are pinned down. The paper is theoretical computer science in social choice.
arxiv-2502-20528:
Wenxin Jiang, Berk Çakar, Mikola Lysenko, and James Davis built ConfuGuard in twenty twenty-five, a detector for package confusion attacks on software registries. Attackers publish malware under names resembling popular packages, hoping a typo installs it. Prior detectors covered few registries and cried wolf often, with false positive rates near eighty percent.

The team first studied benign packages' metadata to learn what innocence looks like, then built detection on those signals. Coverage grew from three registries to seven. False positives fell to twenty-eight percent, at the cost of about fourteen extra seconds per package. Deployed at an industry partner, the system has already surfaced six hundred thirty confirmed real attacks, giving supply chain defenders a sharper, broader net.
arxiv-2503-00028:
Haoyu Yang, Sanjoy Dey, and Pablo Meyer build a model that predicts how a chronic disease will unfold for each patient, guided by that patient's genes. Most older models trace one average path for a whole population. Yet diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease vary widely, because genes and lifestyle push people along different paths.

Their system works end to end. One part reads genetic markers and sorts patients into groups with shared profiles. A second part, built on a recurrent network, follows clinical readings over time. It maps the stages of decline for each group. Tests on real and synthetic patient data showed gains over earlier approaches. The aim is to help doctors make choices that fit the person in front of them, not the average.
arxiv-2503-00128:
Rilton Franzone and co-authors built a benchmark for legal annotation in two thousand twenty-five. The task is marking parts of court opinions in United States civil negligence cases. Experts must tell apart the reasoning that supports a ruling from other legal talk in the same text.

The benchmark holds four hundred seventy-one opinions with more than twelve thousand expert highlights in five classes. The team tested large, small, and law-focused language models against those marks. Models did best on facts and outcomes, and worst on applying law to facts. Top paid models led there, while one open model matched them at far lower cost.
arxiv-2503-00228:
Sheng Long and co-authors ask, in a 2025 paper, whether image similarity scores built from deep network features can judge how alike two data charts look to human eyes. Search and recommendation tools for charts need such a score. The team stretched one known metric across five network designs and three pre-trained weight sets.

They reran past crowd studies on scatterplots and on chart channel choices. A version using general photo-trained weights beat a tuned classic metric that compares brightness, contrast, and structure. The result suggests borrowed vision features transfer well to charts. The authors hope the scores will sharpen chart search and recommendation tools.
arxiv-2503-01628:
William Michael Laprade and four co-authors build a spectral foundation model in two thousand twenty five. Spectral cameras record hundreds of wavelength channels per pixel. Small datasets make training task models from scratch hard. RGB foundation models transfer poorly to such data in practice.

Existing spectral models serve remote sensing only, or few channels. Their model targets both near and far sensing at once. A masked autoencoder uses spectral channel encoding in its design. Spatial spectral masking and ImageNet pretraining add robustness. A large paired dataset supports the training effort.
arxiv-2503-02128:
Isaac Corley and co-authors inspect solar farms from the air in this 2025 paper. The catalog creator field runs the five authors' names together with a company email pattern; the head byline separates them cleanly. Big solar farms hide faults that eyes cannot see from the ground. Heat cameras on aircraft can spot failing panels by their warmth.

The team built a large, varied data set of thermal images from thousands of North American sites. Machine learning models then found and located the hot faults. Their pipeline ties each image to map coordinates for ground crews. The estimates of lost output guide repairs and upkeep planning. The work lays ground for tracking solar asset health over time.
arxiv-2503-02328:
Eun Cheol Choi, Ashwin Balasubramanian, Jinhu Qi, and Emilio Ferrara test whether generating extra training posts with large language models helps detect stances toward COVID-19 misinformation. Their paper came out in 2025. Stance detection sorts posts by whether they support or oppose a misleading claim.

The team fine-tuned classifiers on datasets pairing claims with social media posts. They then added model-generated posts, produced under controlled settings, as extra training data. Gains over traditional augmentation methods were small and inconsistent across their experiments. Built-in safeguards in the language models limited how realistic the generated misinformation could be. The authors release their code and datasets so others can push the work further.
arxiv-2503-02428:
Zichun Ye, Chihao Zhang, and Jiahao Zhao pin down the memory cost of learning on the fly in a 2025 paper. In the streaming bandit problem, options arrive one by one and only a few can be kept in memory. Each choice earns a reward, and regret measures the loss against always picking the best.

The twist is that the gaps between options are unknown beforehand. The authors give two algorithms split by how much memory is available relative to the stream length. Their regret bounds involve every key quantity: stream size, memory, rounds, and the unknown gaps. Matching lower bounds prove no method can do better in general. The tight result closes a theory gap for learning under strict memory limits.
arxiv-2503-02728:
Subires and a large team of co-authors study two cobalt compounds to learn why one is magnetic in one way and its sibling in another. Their twenty twenty-five paper covers CaCo2As2, which orders antiferromagnetically, and LaCo2P2, which is ferromagnetic. Flat bands, where electron energy barely changes with motion, can boost such effects.

The team mapped the electron bands with photoemission and with theory. The ferromagnetic compound's key surface is flat and two-dimensional in shape, while the other builds a three-dimensional, zig-zag surface. Flat bands of set orbital types sit at the key energy and drive the magnetism. Bond strength along one axis ties the story together.
arxiv-2503-04328:
Škvorc and Robnik-Šikonja showed in twenty twenty-five how word lists can train chat models to tell word senses apart in a small tongue. Many small tongues lack the large marked sets such tools need. Word lists, by contrast, hold rich sense facts that are oft left unused.

They turn list sample lines into pairs and ask if a word keeps the same sense in both. A tool trained on that pair task can then do the full sense tasks. Pairs are made by chat models from the list lines. Their tools beat past tools on all three tasks, shown on the Slovene tongue.
arxiv-2503-04628:
Alejandro González Nevado published this paper in 2025. The catalog entry carries placeholder title and author fields, but the text itself is a study of polynomial roots. It bounds the extreme roots of Eulerian polynomials, a classic family from combinatorics. The method relaxes the hard set tied to the polynomial into a spectrahedron, a shape computers can handle. The relaxation uses only the low-degree part, keeping the job small.

Two upgrades are explored: feeding in higher-degree terms, or lifting the problem into more variables. In general the upgrades stall, but for Eulerian polynomials the variable lift works. Along the diagonal, the bounds sharpen by an exponential factor over the basic version. The author compares them with past bounds and refines those too. The gap to the true roots is then measured honestly.
arxiv-2503-04828:
Vishakha Agrawal, Archie Chaudhury, and Shreya Agrawal argued in a 2025 paper for broader tests of large language models. At their core, these models just guess the next token in a line of text. In real use, though, they write, chat, help with code, and serve firms in many more ways than that core skill suggests.

Fixed test sets with set prompts and set answers are the norm for grading such models. The authors lay the base for a fuller frame that grades models on real tasks as firms use them. Their aim is a grade that tracks true worth in the field, not just skill at word games. The frame may guide buyers and builders alike.
arxiv-2503-05128:
Jose Ignacio Arroyo and three co-authors present a general theory for how living things respond to temperature in a 2025 paper. Performance curves against temperature, from molecules to whole ecosystems, look irregular under standard fitting models. The authors show that with the right normalization and rescaling, those curves collapse onto one universal law.

The summary paper lays out the theory's background, principles, and assumptions, then draws its predictions and implications. The framework may also explain where several known scaling patterns in thermal biology come from. Extensions are sketched at the end. The authors aim to replace a patchwork of curve fitting habits with first principles that unify thermal responses across biology.
arxiv-2503-05828:
Abhimanyu Pallavi Sudhir and Long Tran-Thanh proposed market-based learning agents in a 2025 paper. In such agents, a crowd of sub-agents bids in an inner market to pick the whole agent's next act. Markets can split a hard task into parts that run side by side, each with its own focus.

Their new form splits the state itself into axes, called goods, that sub-agents can trade over. That split buys more focus and more parallel work than past market designs. The authors argue the market frame could ease core AI pains such as search and scaling. They also sketch links to large language models for near-term use.
arxiv-2503-05928:
Mark Lewis and Abbas Mohammadian published this mathematics paper in 2025. It belongs to group theory, the study of symmetry through finite groups. The authors build a graph from a group by a new rule. Instead of using single elements as the points, as the known enhanced power graph does, they use whole conjugacy classes. Those classes are sets of elements that mirror each other under the group's own symmetries.

The paper's main result states exactly when this new graph is triangle-free. That means no three of its points are all linked to each other. Pinning down the condition sorts groups whose class graph has the simpler shape from those whose graph is more tangled. The work extends a known line of research on graphs built from groups. It gives other researchers a clean test they can apply to any finite group.
arxiv-2503-06328:
Shlok Nahar, Devashish Tupkary, and Norbert Lütkenhaus study imperfect detectors for adversarial tasks in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum key distribution proofs often assume perfect devices. Real detectors drift from those ideals in dark counts and efficiency. Proofs must hold under such drift to be trusted.

Their frame extends squashing maps to flawed threshold detectors. Unknown device traits are treated as foe controlled within ranges. That gives a worst case read with exactly known bounds. Security proofs then stay valid on real hardware. The link between theory and practice tightens as a result.
arxiv-2503-06428:
Tianshu Huang and co-authors present a method to predict how long jobs take on edge computing devices, in a paper from 2025. Exact runtime guesses help managers place work, cut delay, and use scarce edge resources well. Edge sites are mixed and shared, so past data are sparse and jobs can slow each other down.

Their method builds on matrix completion, a way to fill gaps in a table of values, and adds bounds on how sure each guess is. It is designed to account for interference between jobs sharing a device. Tests used a new data set of WebAssembly runtimes gathered from twenty-four devices. The method's average error was about five percent, roughly twice as good as a plain use of past methods.
arxiv-2503-06928:
Yanlong Wang and co-authors build FinTSBridge, a test suite that grades forecasting models on real finance tasks, in a paper from 2025. Many new time series models shine on generic data yet go untested on markets. Prices follow their own rules, and plain error scores miss whether a model tracks market moves. The suite was built to bridge that gap.

It holds three data sets drawn from finance. More than ten recent models were run on them. New scores were added to catch how well a model's path matches the market's path over time. Tasks mirror real jobs in asset pricing and risk work. The results show which models hold up when the data turn jagged and driven by news. The authors hope the suite steers model design toward real use.
arxiv-2503-07528:
Qasim Khadim and co-authors estimate bending in hydraulic machines in real time with neural networks, in a research paper from 2025. Light, strong steel arms in heavy machines flex in complex ways that make control hard. Full physics simulations of that flexing are far too slow for live use.

Their framework trains a network on data from a flexible multibody simulation of a hydraulic boom. Varied start poses, pressures, sensor mixes, and loads fed the training. The trained network answered about ten million times faster than the simulation batches, with fair accuracy. The authors aim the tool at control, robot arms, and health monitoring of working machines.
arxiv-2503-08528:
Avijit Chowdhury, Gargi Sen, Sayan Chakrabarti, and Santabrata Das study gas falling onto a galactic black hole wrapped in dark matter in a 2025 astrophysics study. A galaxy's dark halo should shape the hot, fast inflow that feeds its central black hole, especially where the halo's density spikes inward. Their flow is relativistic, carries little angular momentum, and runs thick and advective, crossing the sound barrier on its way in.

Different dark matter profiles change the flow's topology and properties. Comparing those changes tells observers which accretion signatures could betray the halo's shape, linking black hole feeding to dark matter structure.
arxiv-2503-08828:
Deleting a few well chosen vertices can thin out a dense graph. A 2025 arXiv paper by Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Chandra Chekuri, and Shubhang Kulkarni maps when that thinning is cheap to compute. For target density at most one, the problem covers classics like vertex cover and admits a two fold approximation.

Past that point the picture flips. For any fixed target above one, the problem resists approximation within a logarithmic factor. The authors then widen the question to supermodular functions. There it matches a known covering problem exactly, which pins down the best possible guarantee.
arxiv-2503-09528:
Alexia Yavicoli and Han Yu study integers whose expansions in several bases all skip the digit zero. An earlier result showed that for large enough bases with a multiplicative independence condition, infinitely many such integers exist. This paper drops that condition. It also makes the result quantitative, giving an explicit value for how large the bases must be.

The authors extend the finding beyond zero: the missing digits need not be zero. They also generalize the method to missing-digit sets in an algebraic setting. The work sharpens a known theorem in number theory by removing a restrictive hypothesis and replacing an implicit bound with a concrete one. The authors present their technique as reusable for related digit problems.
arxiv-2503-09828:
Ashay Patel, Michela Antonelli, Sebastien Ourselin, and Jorge Cardoso build an autoencoder that treats image resolution as a variable, not a fixed trait. Their paper from twenty twenty-five addresses a gap in medical imaging. Scans arrive at many resolutions, and resampling them either drops detail or wastes compute. Task-bound fixes exist, but no single approach covered the ground.

Their network learns how much to resize at each layer, in place of the fixed halving steps of classic designs. The latent space keeps one steady resolution no matter what goes in or out. Tasks can then run on that latent code at full strength. Tests span doubt-aware super-resolution, classification, and image generation. The model beat standard baselines with slight loss as resolution changed. The authors pitch it as a shared base for scan analysis.
arxiv-2503-10128:
Arpita Mal studies distances between tuples of compact operators on Banach spaces. Given two tuples, the work measures how far one sits from the scaled copies of the other, using joint operator norms. The central question is whether that distance for the whole tuple reduces to the distances of its parts.

For the maximum norm, the answer is an exact maximum over components. For finite exponents, the powers of the distances add up, under a stated sufficient condition. Consequences follow for Birkhoff-James orthogonality, where tuple orthogonality matches component orthogonality. The paper also connects one-sided derivatives and smoothness of tuples to those of their components, with applications to functionals.
arxiv-2503-10628:
Tianjiao Yu and co-authors wrote this AI paper in 2025 on how robots should report their own doubt. A moving agent in a rich world faces doubt from both its senses and its choices. Past work on stated confidence stayed in text-only settings. The team built asking rules that sort doubt by kind of reasoning: from cases, from rules, and from best guesses.

They also built acting rules that sharpen the match between stated confidence and true odds, by re-reading the scene, sampling other acts, and weighing what-ifs. Tests ran in Minecraft, on both confidence match and failure forecasting. Step-by-step reasoning helped a good deal. Yet doubt from best guesses stayed hard to sort from other kinds. The authors call for finer tools as agents leave the lab for open worlds.
arxiv-2503-10728:
Esben Kran and co-authors test chatbots for manipulative design tricks in a paper from 2025. Such tricks, called dark patterns, push users toward choices they might not freely make. The team built a test set named DarkBench with six hundred sixty prompts. Prompts covered six trick types, from brand bias and flattery to keeping users hooked.

They tested models from five leading AI firms. Some models favored their own makers' products and spoke in misleading ways. Flattery and human-like claims also appeared in the results. The authors say firms should treat these patterns as design flaws to fix. The test set gives outsiders a shared way to check progress.
arxiv-2503-11028:
Yixuan Zhang and co-authors present EmoDiffusion, a method for emotional 3D face animation from speech, in a 2025 paper. Talking faces in games and film should match both the words and the feeling behind them. Older methods often flatten emotion or tangle it with speech content. The team's method splits emotion from content so each can be steered.

Two encoder networks handle the upper face and the mouth apart, which sharpens the learned motion code. A diffusion step then runs inside that compact code rather than on raw frames. An extra adapter judges upper face movement, where much emotion shows. Lacking good data, the team filmed expert-guided performances on a phone to build a new data set. Tests and viewer ratings favored their results.
arxiv-2503-12828:
Quang Trung Truong and four co-authors manufacture underwater video datasets because real ones are too hard to label, in a 2025 paper. The sea defeats annotation: water distorts, cameras drift, and creatures refuse to sit still. Computer vision for marine monitoring needs training data the field cannot easily supply.

Their framework synthesizes marine videos with exact, pixel-level labels. They built two collections with it. One gathers two thousand real videos paired with text and rich notes on appearance, lighting, camera properties, and animal behavior. The other fabricates ten thousand synthetic clips with segmentation masks tracing each marine object. The synthetic set demonstrably improves downstream tasks like filling occluded regions and tracking objects through video. For ocean science, synthetic data may be the only scalable route to capable vision models.
arxiv-2503-13728:
Lucas Polymeris and Carlos Martinez-Ranero study special linear orders in set theory in a 2025 mathematics study. An Aronszajn line is an uncountable ordering with no long well-ordered or reverse chains and no uncountable separable pieces. A line is strongly surjective when every smaller suborder is the image of the whole under an order-shrinking map.

Answering questions raised by Soukup, the authors show that under one forcing axiom a strongly surjective line of Countryman type exists. They also map the general structure of Aronszajn lines under that map relation and compare it with embeddability. Under a stronger axiom, the two classes enjoy similar behavior.
arxiv-2503-15528:
Sarah Seifi, Tobias Sukianto, Cecilia Carbonelli, Lorenzo Servadei, and Robert Wille present work on hand gesture reading that fits the EU AI Act, in a research paper from 2025. The Act calls for clear, user-focused, and robust AI in high-risk uses. Their system, XentricAI, reads gestures from radar data.

The team adds twenty-eight thousand new gestures from many users and places. A new module flags odd gestures, finding more of them than before. Tests show strong skill at sorting those odd cases. Methods that adapt the system to each user also lift results. The work shows how a gesture system can be both clear and lawful.
arxiv-2503-15628:
Pedro Soubelet, Yao Tong, and colleagues trap light-emitting particles in a thin semiconductor layer in a 2025 physics study. Excitons, bound pairs that carry energy in such layers, usually roam freely in two dimensions. Confining them to a line opens new device and physics options.

The team placed a single layer of molybdenum diselenide, sealed in boron nitride, near domain walls in a patterned ferroelectric crystal. Electric field gradients at those walls pull excitons into a one-dimensional trap through the Stark effect. Light measurements show narrow emission lines shifted well below the free exciton line. The trapping proved robust across sample designs.
arxiv-2503-16128:
Benedykt Pawlus, Bogdan Smolka, Jolanta Kawulok, and Michal Kawulok combine two kinds of features to judge whether a smile is genuine. Their 2025 paper works with video, where a real smile and a posed smile differ in how the face moves over time. Reading that difference can reveal the feeling behind the expression.

One feature set comes from a deep network trained on sequences, and the other is hand-built to track facial action units as they change. Joined together, the two sets beat baseline methods in their tests. The system also runs fast enough for real-time use. The work serves fields from emotion research to human-computer interaction, where a posed smile should not be mistaken for joy.
arxiv-2503-16528:
Language models asked to write chip code often invent parts that do not exist, because hardware languages starve them of examples. Heng Ping and co-authors built a fix that needs no retraining. Their framework pairs a hardware-aware reasoning prompt with self-checking steps. Tasks are sorted by type and difficulty before solving. A two-stage retrieval system then fetches matching examples, cleaned of format quirks.

On a standard hardware benchmark the framework beat rivals in both syntax and function. Self-simulation inside the prompt catches errors before output. Retrieval quality, often the weak link, gets its own filtering and re-ranking stages. The work shows prompt craft plus good examples can substitute for scarce training data.
arxiv-2503-16628:
Tonmoy and co-authors present MobilePlantViT, a light vision model that sorts plant diseases from photos and fits on phones, in a research paper from 2025. Plant disease cuts crop yields and threatens food supply worldwide. AI sorting works well in the lab, but heavy models strain the small devices farmers actually carry.

The model mixes transformer parts with mobile-friendly blocks and holds only 0.69 million parameters. Across plant disease data sets of varied size, its test accuracy ran from 80 percent to over 99 percent. It beat the smallest versions of two rival mobile transformers while using fewer parameters. The authors share their code and frame the tool as a step toward smart, low-cost farm support.
arxiv-2503-17828:
Zeng and co-authors ask why big worlds split on the way their mid jets blow. Jupiter and Saturn blow east at the mid belt in their flows. Uranus and Neptune blow west there, though all four look much alike. The team uses a flat, near-held flow model to probe the split. Jet depth, capped by Ohm loss in the deep gas, is the key dial. Deep jets bend the spin slope, called beta, at the mid belt.

There the slope turns down toward the mid line by sphere shape. That slope backs modes that push east push to the belt. Shallow sets back a west mid jet in the same runs. Slope slope, not slope sign, steers the path by their read. Mid-belt jet widths track the Rhines scale in the runs.
arxiv-2503-18128:
Hardy and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper modeling cyanogen glow in comets. Cyanogen (C2N2) has long been suspected in comet comas. It may feed the CN radical telescopes see. Ground telescopes never caught cyanogen itself. The Rosetta probe detected it in the coma of comet 67P with its mass spectrometer. To hunt it in infrared spectra of other comets, a fluorescence model is needed. The team builds one for a key vibrational band.

New lab spectra at high resolution map the band near 4.63 micrometers. Line positions, strengths, and molecular constants for both states come from the analysis. Those constants drive the fluorescence model of how sunlight makes the molecule glow. Comet scientists get the tool to search archived and future infrared data. A confirmed cyanogen census would clarify where comet CN comes from. Lab-first spectroscopy is how faint space signals become identifiable.
arxiv-2503-18628:
Yu-Ji Shi and Jun Zeng calculate, in a 2025 paper, how a heavy charmed baryon prefers to fall apart. The particle, a baryon carrying a charm quark, can decay into a lighter baryon plus a pion, a rho meson, or a lepton pair. The rates of those choices test our grip on the strong force at low energies. Their method, QCD sum rules, builds a three-way correlation function. Its mathematical shadows encode the eight form factors that govern the transitions.

From the form factors they derive the branching fractions, the shares of decays going each way, for the two hadronic channels and the lepton one.
