The results are compared with other theories and with measurements. The authors offer the numbers as benchmarks for experiments hunting these rare decays. They are one more check on whether sum-rule machinery still tracks reality in the charm sector.
arxiv-2503-20028:
Pengfei Du wrote this 2025 paper presenting OmniNova, a framework for teams of language-model agents that divide complex work among themselves. Single models with tools can automate tasks, but several agents together stumble over coordination, wasted resources, and garbled hand-offs. OmniNova organizes them into a hierarchy: coordinator, planner, supervisor, and specialist agents, each with a defined remit.

Tasks route dynamically to agents matched to their complexity, and different cognitive jobs draw on different sizes of model, so cheap thinking is not billed at premium rates. Across fifty tasks in research, data analysis, and web interaction, the framework beat a baseline on completion, 87 percent against 62, while using 41 percent fewer tokens. Human judges also scored its results higher. Du offers the design, plus an open-source implementation, as a template for automation systems.
arxiv-2503-20128:
F. Adersh, M. Muhsin, and M. Sahoo analyzed a tiny spinning heat machine in a 2025 theory paper. Their device is a charged, self-propelled particle trapped in an uneven bowl-shaped potential, touching two heat baths at different temperatures, with a steady magnetic field through the plane. Asymmetry plus heat difference makes the particle gyrate and push a torque on its trap, so the setup can work as an engine or a heat pump.

Self-propulsion changed performance only when the magnetic field was present. With a load opposing the torque, the same setting could act as engine or pump depending on load strength. With the load aiding the torque, only pumping was possible. The study maps a tunable nanoscale energy converter.
arxiv-2503-20628:
Xu Zhu, Wenwen Zhou, and Bin Wu proved a Carleman estimate in twenty twenty-five for a fully discrete version of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. This equation models systems from superconductivity to fluid patterns, and here it carries dynamic boundary conditions, where the boundary itself evolves. Carleman estimates are weighted energy bounds that power results about control and observability.

Working on a fully discrete scheme — a grid in both space and time — the authors first prove the estimate for the adjoint system. From it they derive a relaxed observability inequality, saying the whole state can be partly recovered from boundary readings. That yields a controllability result for the discrete equation. Such results matter when control must be designed on the same grid a computer will use.
arxiv-2503-20728:
Joona Pankkonen, Lauri Ylinen, Matti Raasakka, and Ilkka Tittonen tune quantum circuits better by teaming two optimizers. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Variational circuits are the workhorse of today's noisy quantum machines. They serve chemistry, learning, and optimization tasks. Tuning their angles is often the bottleneck. Rotosolve, a gradient-free tuner, is a favorite for the job.

The authors improve Rotosolve and marry it to a quaternion-based selector. Random axis initialization rounds out the package. Simulations show higher accuracy across circuit sizes and cost functions. Average performance beats either parent method alone. Shallow circuits show a trade-off worth noting. Near-term quantum software gains a steadier tuner.
arxiv-2503-21128:
Russell Tsuchida, Jiawei Liu, Cheng Soon Ong, and Dino Sejdinovic introduce a new family of probability models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Squared families build densities by squaring a shifted summary of the data. They start out singular, but the snag is easy to fix.

Once fixed, the family is unusually tidy. One kernel integral feeds the information measure, the divergence, and the normalizing constant alike. That constant splits into a part computed once for all settings. The authors place the family among a wider class built by warping statistics. Only two other kinds share its neat geometry. Tests of fitting show the models learn target densities at solid rates, even when misspecified.
arxiv-2503-21328:
Koczor-Benda and co-authors ask whether a molecule-generating model truly learns the mix of chemistry in its training data. Models that build three-dimensional molecules feed drug and materials design. Success is usually scored on novelty and validity alone.

Their audit of the G-SchNet model compares generated molecules against training sets of large organic molecules. The model skewed its output toward unsaturated molecules rich in heteroatoms, whatever the training mix or settings. Plain carbon-chain molecules came out too rarely. The authors argue generation bias deserves routine measurement beside novelty. A model that misreads its training space, they warn, misleads design pipelines downstream.
arxiv-2503-21928:
Ding Zhu, Zhiqun Zuo, and Mohammad Mahdi Khalili present a computing paper from 2025 on training lean models. Big learning models cost much to train and run. Making most weights zero cuts that cost, and block patterns of zeros suit fast chips best. Yet training a block-sparse model from scratch had no efficient method.

Past methods started from a full dense model, which wastes the very savings sought. The team's method trains the sparse model directly, block by block. It also finds the right block size during training, rather than fixing it in advance. Tests and theory both showed large cuts in compute and memory costs. Accuracy held level with the dense baselines. The authors say block-sparse training can now start lean from step one.
arxiv-2503-22528:
Neural networks that solve differential equations often need huge numbers of parameters and stay hard to interpret. Tiago de Souza Farias and co-authors introduce MixFunn in this 2025 paper, a leaner network built from two new neuron types.

One neuron blends several shaped curves for flexibility, and the other adds a squared term that captures how inputs interact. Together they match or beat standard models with a tiny fraction of the parts. Tested on problems from mechanics, quantum physics, and fluid flow, the network stayed accurate and stretched better to new regions. Its solutions can also be read back as plain formulas.
arxiv-2503-23328:
Haricharan Balasundaram and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on matching people to programs with limited seats. The hospital-residents model covers real problems like school choice and placing students into degree programs. Each program has a quota, and the authors ask what happens when every applicant must be placed, even past a quota, at a cost.

They study two cost goals. Keeping costs low for each program on its own can be solved fast, in polynomial time. Keeping the total cost low across all programs is NP-hard, meaning no fast exact method is expected. For that hard case, the team give approximation methods with proven guarantees, so planners still get usable answers.
arxiv-2503-23428:
Qiang Zhai and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how a free surface speeds up the depths of a glassy film. Glass formers move faster near a free face. The team uses a lattice model with marked particles and no elastic effects. That clean setup lets them test if stretch alone can explain the deep tail of fast layers.

The mobile layer's depth shifts with how it is defined, though all gauges rest on local relax rates. Rates fit a double exponential form with a long tail. Their fit rules out stretch as the sole cause of the tail. Hop rates by layer show a far more shallow surface effect.
arxiv-2503-24128: Giovanni Italiano and Matteo Migliorini wrote a paper from 2025 building the first hyperbolic six-dimensional space with a special kind of circle-valued height function. A perfect such function has the fewest critical points, and it is a fibration over a circle for spaces whose Euler count does not vanish. From this example the authors extract a subgroup of a hyperbolic group with a sharp finiteness profile: it meets the second finiteness level but not the third. Such examples are prized tests for conjectures about group structure.
arxiv-2504-00128:
Timely warnings for storm gusts save lives and property, but gusts are hard to forecast at a single place. Neural weather models now predict the broad atmosphere cheaply on a global grid. The five authors post-process the Pangu-Weather model's output to predict hourly gust distributions up to three days ahead over five Swiss regions. They test a hierarchy of statistical and deep learning methods and pin the forecasts with generalized extreme value distributions.

A convolutional network that reads the spatial pattern of the predicted environment did best, beating direct forecasts at every lead time and gust speed. The authors conclude that neural weather models add real value for extreme wind forecasting and could power more responsive early warning systems.
arxiv-2504-02428:
Callum Barber and Nik Ruškuc published a research paper in 2025 on a rare trait in the algebra of semigroups, structures that model combining operations. Some semigroups force every substructure of their square that contains the diagonal to be a congruence, a tidy equivalence. The authors call such semigroups DSC and ask which ones exist.

All finite groups have the trait, and any such semigroup must be simple. For wide classes, from periodic to inverse semigroups, the pair prove only groups qualify. Yet odd non-group examples do exist, built with an older construction made for congruence-free cases. Some of those examples are also regular or bisimple. The paper maps where the trait can and cannot live.
arxiv-2504-02528:
Ned Thaddeus Taylor and co-authors present a software package that predicts how atoms arrange at the boundary between two crystals, in a paper from 2025. Interfaces control how most devices perform, yet their structure is hard to guess. The number of possible layouts is vast, and each one is costly to score.

The package, called RAFFLE, samples that space with rules drawn from physics and a genetic search. It describes structures with evolving patterns of two, three, and four atom groups, updated by active learning as results come in. Those patterns guide where new atoms are placed. Tests on pure metals and layered compounds recovered known stable phases. On silicon-germanium boundaries, it found that mixing atoms across the join lowers strain and beats a sharp join.
arxiv-2504-02728:
Eoin Mackall and Cameron Ruether study how Azumaya algebras with a quadratic pair deform. Their paper from twenty twenty-five builds a tangent-obstruction theory for these paired objects. The question is when small warps of the pair stay unblocked. Two settings split the tale. When two is a unit, or the algebra has degree two, the pair's theory collapses to the algebra's own.

In those cases, free deformation of the algebra lifts to the pair. Pure characteristic two breaks the peace. The authors build a biquaternion example on an Igusa surface where the algebra deforms freely but the triple does not. A new obstruction, special to characteristic two, sits between the known strong and weak ones. It decides when a canonical Lie algebra extension splits.
arxiv-2504-02928:
Vinh Tran and co-authors simulate how dark matter halos collapse when their self-interactions spike at certain speeds, in this 2025 paper. In self-interacting models, halo cores can densify hugely over time, changing dwarf galaxies and lensing signals. Resonant models add a twist: the interaction strength peaks near set relative velocities. The team ran clean simulations of lone halos across a wide mass range under two such models.

As a halo's core forms, its particle speeds drift across the resonance, so the collapse path bends away from the tidy self-similar track by up to a fifth. Halos of different masses land at different collapse stages after the same time, with varied profiles and rotation curves. Alignment with the resonance sets the pace. The authors map that interplay for observers.
arxiv-2504-04028: Paresh Singh Arora, writing alone, computes the local zeta function of the Klein quartic curve, a classic curve given by a short cubic equation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Zeta functions tally a shape's points over finite fields and encode deep facts about it. Arora reaches the curve by viewing it as a quotient of the degree-seven Fermat curve, where the counting is more tractable. He closes by naming the modular forms attached to the curve through its Galois representations.
arxiv-2504-06528:
Dadpour and co-authors build a fast drive kit for light-tweezer atom grids. Tweezer grids trap atoms and bits in rows for lab tests. Fast back-feed lets tests bend as shots come back live. Their kit is part-built and free for peers to copy and tweak. A main board plus side cards form its cheap core frame. Fast pipes move data to and from GPU chips in the kit.

Those pipes skip the CPU, which cuts wait on each loop. GPU skill at grid math and twin work drives the gain. The team times runs that build clean chains and grids of atoms. Set fix plans run in the kit for those time checks. Bottleneck spots and ways to trim wait get care next. The kit can also run bend and lead plans for tests.
arxiv-2504-07028:
Uthman Olawoye and Jason Gross wrote a 2025 paper on locating a drone from a ground robot when GPS is unavailable. The ground vehicle carries a LiDAR sensor, which maps its surroundings with laser pulses. The team tested whether a deep learning method for spotting objects in 3D could find the drone in that laser data and report its position.

The method they used, PointPillars, stacks the laser points into columns and feeds them to a neural network built for images. It then draws a 3D box around the object it finds, here the drone. The authors compared its position reports against the older approach: cutting the point cloud into clusters by distance and applying hand-written rules. Both were checked against a known true position. The study weighs whether learned detection can replace hand-tuned geometry for drone tracking in places where satellite signals cannot reach.
arxiv-2504-08828:
Mazyar Dawoodian and Ould el Moctar sharpen the theory that predicts when a liquid tears open into vapor bubbles, in a 2025 paper. Such cavitation chews up propellers and pumps, so its starting pressure matters. Classic theory treats bubble birth in pure liquid, but real liquids hide nanoscale gas pockets. Their enhanced model folds those pockets in and is checked against molecular dynamics simulations.

Gas nuclei, they find, lower the stretch a liquid can bear before cavitating. The new model predicts lower inception pressures than the classic Blake threshold and lands close to the simulations. The choice of gas law matters most for small nuclei at low temperatures. The authors say engineers should reckon with hidden gas when setting cavitation margins.
arxiv-2504-09128:
Nation and Paolini settled two open problems in twenty twenty-five about the logic of free lattices. A lattice has meet and join operations. A free lattice is the least constrained kind. Their first work mapped which statements hold across all free lattices. That map was still far from full.

The main result is that the universal theory of infinite free lattices is decidable. A set procedure can always settle such statements. Next, free lattices built from a finite set can be told apart. A positive sentence does this for each size. Free lattices are also rigid among projective lattices built from a finite set. A projective lattice shares the same theory as an infinite free lattice just when its breadth tops four. The work goes on from a long line of work in universal algebra.
arxiv-2504-09328:
Sonia Laguna and co-authors build a system that turns text prompts into full indoor scenes for training vision models, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Scene tools need large, true-to-life data sets, but hand-made scenes are slow and scarce. The pipeline joins text-to-image and multi-view generators with a field-based meshing step to make solid objects.

Made objects drop into preset floor plans through a rendering tool. New loss rules and training tweaks lift the quality of the made assets. Scenes can be built on demand and reshaped to order. Readers who train depth or tracking models get a scalable source of stand-in data.
arxiv-2504-09928: Obradović and Tuneski present a 2025 note in geometric function theory. The topic is the Bazilevič class of univalent functions. These map the unit disc one-to-one with a special twisting property. The authors find sharp bounds on the gap between the sizes of the second and first logarithmic coefficients. Sharp means no better bound is possible. The result adds a precise entry to the long study of coefficient problems for univalent functions.
arxiv-2504-10028:
Rick den Otter and co-authors present a method for reading thinking steps from brain data in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Group averages can hide how a person's strategy changes from trial to trial. The team combines pattern analysis with a sequence model to decode strategy on each single trial.

They test the method on a decision task where people were told to favor speed or accuracy. The model found an extra step, which they call Confirmation, that appeared mostly under accuracy instructions but often under speed ones too. When this step was likely, answers were more often correct and minds changed more. The authors say the method shows strategy varies within a task, against older assumptions.
arxiv-2504-12328:
Jialun Zhong and co-authors survey reward models in two thousand twenty-five, the scoring systems that steer large language models toward answers people prefer. A reward model stands in for human judgment, giving training signals that shape model behavior across tasks.

The survey organizes the field in three parts: how preference data is collected, how the models are built and trained, and how they are used in practice. It then maps the applications of reward models and the benchmarks used to test them. Open problems get a close look, from gaming the score to weak coverage of real tastes. The authors also chart future directions and share a public resource list for newcomers to the field.
arxiv-2504-12528:
Carlos Madrid Padilla, Shitao Fan, and Lizhen Lin propose, in a 2025 preprint, a tougher form of variational Bayes for messy, huge datasets. Variational Bayes speeds up Bayesian inference by fitting a simple stand-in for the true posterior. Outliers and contaminated data can poison that fit. Their method splits the data into disjoint chunks and infers a posterior for each chunk on its own. The chunk answers are then merged by a geometric median under a distance between distributions. The merged result is called the Variational Median Posterior.

Because a median shrugs off a few bad inputs, one poisoned chunk cannot wreck the whole. The authors prove the merged posterior still shrinks toward the truth like the real one. They also prove a robustness guarantee and a limit theorem for two common model families. Practical algorithms are adapted for computing it. Numerical tests back the claims of strength and scale.
arxiv-2504-13128:
Nandan Thakur and five co-authors build retrieval benchmarks in twenty twenty-five. Testing search systems needs hard, realistic questions over real documents. Their framework, FreshStack, builds such benchmarks automatically. It starts by collecting corpora from code and technical documentation.

Next it generates nuggets, the key facts inside community questions and answers. It then checks nugget-level support by retrieving documents with fused techniques. The team built five data sets on fast-growing, recent, niche topics. Those choices keep the tasks genuinely challenging. Existing retrieval models, used out of the box, fell well short of oracle performance on all five. Rerankers sometimes failed to help first-stage retrieval at all. Readers get headroom measured honestly for technical search.
arxiv-2504-13928:
Li Song presents a prototype system that lets game characters powered by large language models talk with players across platforms. Non-player characters in traditional games are limited by static dialogue trees. They also interact on a single platform only.

The prototype connects a Unity game environment with the social platform Discord, so the same character can converse in both places. Dialogue logs are stored in a cloud database, which lets the system synchronize memory between platforms and keep conversations coherent. Initial experiments show that cross-platform interaction is technically feasible. Song points to future work on emotional modeling and persistent memory support. The study offers game developers a foundation for characters who maintain one continuing relationship with a player, wherever the player meets them.
arxiv-2504-14128:
Christopher Zhang Cui and co-authors build a suite of text adventure games to test machine reasoning, in work from 2025. The suite, called TALES, mixes machine-made and human-written games. Text games force step-by-step choices based on a long story history, which makes them a stern test of planning.

The team ran a range of open and closed language models through the games. Agents did well on the synthetic set. On games made for human fun, even the best fell short of fifteen percent success. Close reads of top runs show where their plans break. Code and charts are shared online.
arxiv-2504-14328:
Diptendu Chatterjee, Avishek Majumder, and Subhra Mazumdar present ScaloWork, a scheme to make blockchain mining do useful work. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that Bitcoin's hash-based proof of work burns vast power on sums with no other use. Prior swaps of the hash task had flaws in speed and answer quality. ScaloWork picks block winners by a graph task instead.

The task is to find a minimum dominating set in a real network graph. A graph symmetry trait keeps answers checkable and hard to fake. Miners can pool their search, which lets the scheme face large real graphs. The design blocks free riders who take rewards without work. A full security study says the scheme is as safe as hash-based work. A test build beat the prior scheme on all fronts.
arxiv-2504-14628:
Shunxin Guo and colleagues proposed a leaner way in 2025 to train AI models across many separate devices. In federated learning, phones or hospitals train locally and share updates, but real clients join and leave, and their data differ wildly. Sending full models back and forth wastes bandwidth and slows the start for each newcomer.

Their framework borrows a gene metaphor: small knowledge fragments, called learngenes, carry the core skill of a big model. Local training protects the most informative weights, squeezes the fragment down by sensitivity checks, and the server merges fragments into a stronger one. New clients can then start fast from the shared fragment instead of from scratch.
arxiv-2504-15628:
Zeyin Wang, Di Zhang, and colleagues balance security and delay for short-packet links used at low altitude in a 2025 study. Drone and air-taxi links send brief packets and cannot wait long, yet an eavesdropper may sit close to the receiver. Standard security analysis rarely prices the delay that protection adds.

The authors define a secure latency measure and derive formulas for the chance of secure delivery and the average secure delay. Signal strength and packet length both feed the trade-off. Optimizing those settings gives the lowest delay for each design. Numerical checks confirm the analysis, offering guidance for safe low-altitude communication systems.
arxiv-2504-16528:
Ashwani Anand, Satya Prakash Nayak, Ritam Raha, Irmak Sağlam, and Anne-Kathrin Schmuck extend strategy templates to games with numeric payoffs. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on two-player energy and mean-payoff games. A template stands for infinitely many winning strategies at once. Qualitative templates for omega-regular games came first. Their QaSTels carry the idea to quantity.

Foundations cover how to build such templates and how to merge them with the qualitative kind. Mixed goals, part numeric and part logical, then fit one frame. A prototype tool runs the synthesis. Tests show the perks hold: runtime flexibility beats a single fixed strategy, and templates compose as new goals arrive. Control-style cases show the gains in action. The work serves cyber-physical system design.
arxiv-2504-16928:
Troß and five co-authors weigh two-tone laser drives to boost high wave bursts from argon in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such bursts turn soft light into hard rays in short, bright pops. Which drive mix wins can shift with the ray force in scope.

Inside, two-tone drives beat the best lone-tone drive by wide gaps in most test bands. Gains ran from small to vast, set by ray force and by which tones were paired. The team maps which scheme wins at each ray force band in their runs. One tone pair also threw a tighter ray beam than the rest. That hints it lines up the short paths of freed charges best on their return.
arxiv-2504-17728:
Rebuilding a 3D scene from video works best with sharp, well-lit frames, but casual phone clips are blurry and unevenly exposed. Shucheng Gong, Lingzhe Zhao, Wenpu Li, Hong Xie, Yin Zhang, Shiyu Zhao, and Peidong Liu tackle that mess head-on. Their method rebuilds wide-range 3D scenes, holding both bright and dark detail, from auto-exposure videos shot on the move.

One model handles the whole chain: the camera's path through time, the shifting exposure, and how the sensor turns light into pixels. All are fitted together in a single stage. On made-up and real datasets the method beat rivals in both toughness and image quality. The team promises to release the code and data.
arxiv-2504-17828:
Bozheng Li and co-authors build a benchmark that tests how well video models grasp editing, in a research paper from 2025. Most shared videos are edited, yet large video models are rarely tested on editing choices. Their new test set, VEU-Bench, sorts editing parts from single-frame traits like shot size to links between shots like cuts and transitions.

The benchmark holds 19 fine-grained tasks in three stages: naming what is present, reasoning about it, and judging it. The team built an automatic labeling pipeline backed by a knowledge base to mark the videos. Tests of 11 leading video models showed weak results, some below random choice. A tuned expert model named Oscars beat open models by a wide margin and matched strong commercial systems.
arxiv-2504-18128:
Tatsunori Tanaka and co-authors teach clinical language models to reason over time in patient records in two thousand twenty-five. Models trained on hospital notes treat each record as a still page. Real care unfolds in order, with later states growing out of earlier ones.

Their pretraining task pairs an earlier note segment with a later one and asks: does the later state follow from, clash with, or sit neutral to the earlier? Learning that judgment builds quiet time sense into the model. Trained on a large corpus drawn from the MIMIC-IV records, the model topped tests in time-aware question answering, early warning prediction, and disease course modeling. The task is offered as a general add-on for clinical models.
arxiv-2504-19328:
Arshdeep Singh, Abhishek Santra, and Sharma Chakravarthy build a scalable way to find repeating patterns inside multilayer networks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such networks stack several layers of links, which suits data with many kinds of ties.

Their method splits the problem by layer. Each layer is mined on its own, and the results are then composed into patterns for the whole network. They prove the composition step is correct. The system runs on a distributed framework, so it grows with data size. Tests on large made-up and real networks measure speed and response time. The authors argue the split approach stays both accurate and efficient where whole-network mining bogs down.
arxiv-2504-19828:
Zhiming Hu, Daniel Haeufle, Syn Schmitt, and Andreas Bulling presented HOIGaze in twenty twenty-five, for estimating where a person looks during hand-object interactions in extended reality. Gaze drives interfaces and activity understanding, but training data for this setting are noisy. Their insight: eyes, hands, and head move in coordination during manipulation, and that coordination flags which training samples are trustworthy.

The system first recognizes which hand is being watched, then estimates gaze with transformers fusing head and hand-object features. A coordination loss upweights well-coordinated samples during training. On two benchmark data sets it cut mean angular error by about fifteen and six percent respectively over prior methods. It also boosted a downstream activity recognition task, showing the cleaned gaze signal's broader value.
arxiv-2504-20228:
Girish Agarwal shows that one simple output read can hit the quantum limit for sensing spread across a network, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Beating the standard quantum limit at many spots at once is a prized goal. Squeezed probes and linked states set the stage.

A mixed device web spreads the linked probe across nodes. Error feel at just one exit port then meets or nears the best bound math allows. Top-grade network sensing follows from that plain read. Past work proved the point for single traits like phase and loss. Readers get a simple gauge for a hard network task.
arxiv-2504-20828:
Azam Ikram, Xiang Li, Sameh Elnikety, and Saurabh Bagchi present a serving system that keeps large language model replies fast and steady, in work from twenty twenty-five. Hosts must meet two goals at once: a quick first word and a steady stream after. Most systems trade one goal for the other.

Their system, called Ascendra, splits hardware into low and high priority groups. The low group runs requests out of order for max output, with a risk of starvation. A model spots requests near their deadline and moves them to the high group, which is tuned for low delay. Tests beat two known serving systems on throughput by up to about seventy parts in a hundred. Both speed goals held at the same time.
arxiv-2504-21628:
Zan-Bo Zhang, Wenhao Wu, and Weihua He present a 2025 math paper on directed graphs. A directed graph has edges with a set direction. The authors study rules on vertex degree that force cycles of set lengths. Their rule class extends an older type for plain graphs. It also widens a class of dense directed graphs studied since the 1990s.

Under their new rule, the graph holds more than a full tour cycle. It also holds a short cycle of length three and a near-full cycle one step short. Odd graphs that break the pattern are fully described. The authors guess the rule may force cycles of every length. The paper is proof-based and suits readers in graph theory. It sharpens what degree rules alone can promise about cycles in directed graphs.
arxiv-2505-00328:
Jie Cao and Zhenyu Yu present a study from twenty twenty-five on the spectrum of a Sturm Hamiltonian with a pattern that turns periodic at large scales. Such operators model electrons in one dimensional chains with a twist in their layout. The team works in the strong coupling case. They study four marks of the spectrum and of how states spread.

They prove strict gaps between these four marks. The marks are a smoothness rate for the density of states, two size measures, and a spread rate for motion. Their tool is a pressure function from the theory of heat and order. They also give how each mark behaves as coupling grows large. The results sharpen what is known about how these spectra are built.
arxiv-2505-01228:
Sira Gratz and Christian Korff work on cluster algebras, a branch of algebra tied to geometry, in a 2025 paper. A well-known case comes from Grassmannians, spaces that collect all flat slices of a fixed size inside a bigger space. On such a space, special coordinates can be swapped step by step through moves called mutations.

Earlier work built a limit object by stacking larger and larger finite cases, linking it to an infinite version used in the study of wave equations. Gratz and Korff prove that this limit ring is itself a cluster algebra, now of infinite rank. More broadly, they show that infinite-rank cluster algebras are exactly the limit objects of a natural class. The result gives a firm frame for infinite algebraic structures.
arxiv-2505-01528:
Robbie King and four co-authors present a framework to speed quantum simulation in a 2025 paper. Their method amplifies the part of a system's spectrum that matters for low-energy problems. That focus sharpens tasks like estimating a system's energy or phase, which sit at the heart of quantum chemistry and materials work. They show the method yields faster algorithms than prior art for these tasks.

As a showcase, they apply it to a famously hard model of strongly linked particles. There it beats generic simulation methods by a factor tied to the square root of the system size. The results match a companion study that set record gate costs for real chemistry problems.
arxiv-2505-04328:
Jan Bartsch, Alfio Borzi, Gabriele Ciaramella, and Jan Reichle wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It develops a way to steer processes that evolve randomly and also jump suddenly, as many natural and financial systems do.

Such processes mix steady random drift with abrupt jumps. Rather than lifting the problem into a much larger equation, the method works at the small-scale level. That keeps computing costs down and lets calculations run in parallel. The authors derive a companion process that shows how to adjust the controls. They then solve the system with random sampling methods. Numerical tests confirm the approach works. A variant also avoids storing the whole forward run, which saves memory.
arxiv-2505-05528:
Hanxun Huang and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on a universal attack against CLIP vision-language models. A single crafted noise pattern, they show, can fool many CLIP encoders and the larger systems built on them, across images, tasks, and domains at once, a trait they call super transferability.

The trick is surrogate scaling: instead of a few fixed stand-in models, the attack picks a small, well-chosen subset from a large pool on the fly, keeping costs down. Benchmarks show the method beating earlier universal attacks by a wide margin. The authors release their code and frame the result as a warning for deployed systems.
arxiv-2505-05728:
Rong-Hua Wang and Michael Zhong prove new remainder rules for sums built from Delannoy numbers in this 2025 paper. Those numbers count lattice paths and show up in many counting problems. The pair study sums that mix the numbers with powers and with a polynomial form. Their tool is a reduction method that strips a sum down step by step. For prime moduli, they give exact remainder formulas for two families of sums.

The formulas involve symbols that track whether a value is a square modulo the prime. For sums up to a power of two, they find clean patterns tied to fixed whole numbers. One case settles a guess made by Guo and Zeng in 2012. The numbers in their formulas can be found by a fixed routine. The work adds to the arithmetic theory of these classic counting numbers.
arxiv-2505-06028:
Caizergues and four co-authors worked out the odds that a huge vote has a Condorcet winner in twenty twenty-five. A Condorcet winner is a candidate who beats each rival head-to-head. Their broader question asks for a candidate backed over each rival by a set share of voters.

The team assumes voters rank choices on their own. They show the method on two known models, Impartial Culture and Mallows. In place of plain chance arguments, they use analytic combinatorics. That toolkit gives not just the limiting odds but how fast the odds settle, plus higher-order fix-up terms. For Impartial Culture they give the constant term and the first fix-up in full. The fix-up hinges only on whether the voter count is even or odd. Side results in multivariate analytic combinatorics may serve other researchers too, the authors note.
arxiv-2505-06128:
Tauqir Shinwari and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, the large-area growth of a magnetic layered material stacked on graphene. The material, an iron gallium telluride, stays magnetic well above room temperature and points its magnetism straight out of the sheet, a prized mix for future memory and logic devices. Until now it existed only as small crystals or peeled flakes, too tiny and uneven for real processing.

Using molecular beam epitaxy, the team grew smooth, continuous films over large areas on graphene templates. Checks of the crystal structure confirmed high quality. Magnetism measures showed the out-of-plane preference intact, with the ordering temperature pushed up to about 400 kelvin. X-ray probes of the atoms' spin and orbital moments backed the picture. The authors present the stack as a workable platform for two-dimensional spintronic devices.
arxiv-2505-06828:
Jingyang Zhao and Mingyu Xiao improve an approximation algorithm for sports scheduling in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The bipartite traveling tournament problem designs a tournament between two leagues of n teams each, under feasibility constraints, minimizing total travel distance. It models real interleague schedules such as those in professional basketball and baseball leagues. Previously, a guarantee slightly above a factor of two was known only when n was divisible by three.

Open cases remained when n left remainders one or two on division by three. The authors answer the question positively with an algorithm guaranteeing within a factor of about one and a half of optimal, for any n. That bound also improves the earlier result for the divisible-by-three case. The work closes a gap in the problem's approximation theory.
arxiv-2505-08228:
Unai Gurbindo, Axel Brando, Jaume Abella, and Caroline König teach object detectors to cope with bad weather, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Rain, fog, and snow degrade the cameras self-driving cars rely on. Collecting real training images in every storm is impractical.

Their method uses an image-editing diffusion model to restyle clear images into realistic bad-weather versions. Detectors trained with these additions were tested first in a driving simulator, then on real photo sets known for hard conditions. The gap in detector performance under bad weather was measured and then narrowed by the tailored augmentation. The authors offer the recipe as a base for hardier perception in demanding settings.
arxiv-2505-09428:
Eric Switzer and six co-authors show how to entangle single atoms with quantum gates in a 2025 paper. Entanglement is a core resource for quantum computing, but making it on demand in solid devices stays hard. Their platform pairs a scanning tunneling microscope with electron spin resonance.

Two titanium atoms on a thin surface layer form the two-qubit test system. Carefully timed microwave pulses run a standard gate pair that creates a Bell state. A master equation code tracks how faithful and how entangled the result is. The simulations show strong entangled states from this atom-scale setup. The work supports microscope-based tools as a path toward small quantum circuits.
arxiv-2505-10728:
Boshun Yang, Nikolaus Vogt, and Susanne M Hoffmann revisit a bright guest star seen in China in fourteen oh eight. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses Ming dynasty court records. One record is a newly found note from the royal court. The object stayed still for more than ten days and shone yellow.

That stillness rules out a comet or meteor. The team places it in the Milky Way, in a part of the sky now split between two star groups. Its brightness fits a slow nova or a supernova. One known remnant, from a bright red nova in the late sixteen hundreds, sits in the search zone and stands out as a lead.
arxiv-2505-11228:
Derrick Gilchrist Edward Manoharan, Anubha Goel, and colleagues learn how hidden cascades spread through social networks in a 2025 study. Classic spread models assume everyone's state, informed or infected, can be seen. In reality the state that decides whether someone spreads further is often hidden, while side signals, like symptoms, are visible and carry information about the hidden process.

Their classification approach reads those intermediate indicators to infer the underlying diffusion. Framing the problem as classification lets standard learning tools work on partial views. Better inference from symptoms alone could guide interventions during outbreaks when direct testing lags.
arxiv-2505-11928:
Stanisław Piestrak and Piotr Patronik design, in a 2025 engineering paper, cheap circuits that convert numbers into a residue form used by fast arithmetic systems. Such systems split a number into remainders against several moduli. One favored modulus, one more than a power of two, works best in a shifted representation that the converter should output directly.

Their generator design splits into a flexible head that fits any input size and a fixed tail block that adds four values under the modulus. When both twin moduli are used, the design shares adders between the two generators and saves hardware. The shifted output comes for free. The paper targets low-cost, high-speed number systems.
arxiv-2505-12028:
Yupei Ren and co-authors build, in a 2025 education paper, a richer way to map the structure of student arguments. Standard argument mining uses a few plain link types, which miss the fine weave of real essays. The team defines fourteen link types along two axes, covering how parts support, attack, and qualify each other.

They test the scheme on three tasks: spotting argument parts, predicting the links between them, and grading whole essays. Writing quality itself changed how well parts and links could be found. Discourse links also tracked argument traits in useful ways. The authors argue that fine-grained maps give fairer, deeper scores of student writing and better feedback.
arxiv-2505-12328:
Li, Wan, and Sui present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a shared task entry testing language models at structural reasoning. The task demands listing all problem conditions before reasoning. Each reasoning step must pair a claim with its evidence. Logical validity of every pair gets checked at the end. Their system uses one off-the-shelf model with a crafted multi-turn prompt. A light cleanup step enforces the required output format. No fine-tuning, outside search, or model combining is used.

The entry ranks fifth overall in the shared task. Scores match far heavier rival pipelines. Strengths and limits of the lean approach are analyzed. Future steps for structural reasoning work are outlined.
arxiv-2505-14028:
Ye Wang and co-authors build a large data set for image style transfer in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Style transfer repaints a photo in the look of another image or a text prompt. Training good models needs many high quality examples, which are hard to gather at scale.

Their data set holds over one million triplets of content image, style, and styled result, across one thousand style categories, with text descriptions. A filtering framework scores each triplet on content preservation, style match, and aesthetic appeal. On this base they train a transformer model that follows either text or image guidance and outputs detailed high-resolution results. Tests showed it beat existing approaches.
arxiv-2505-15228:
Mathew Vanherreweghe, Lirandë Pira, and Patrick Rebentrost tune a polynomial neural network by turning its design choices into a puzzle for quantum-style optimizers, in a 2025 paper. Their networks build each neuron from Chebyshev polynomials, whose degrees must be chosen per neuron. Brute force over all choices explodes. Recasting degree choice as a binary optimization problem collapses it to one solve per layer.

The design shines on small datasets, shrugs off input scaling, and regularizes itself through its polynomial bones. Theory ties its behavior to traits of financial time series. Across several domains it matched or beat traditional architectures where data were scarce and stability mattered. Code and overhead tricks are published.
arxiv-2505-16328:
Anupam Ghosh, Partha Konar, Tousik Samui, and Ritesh Singh studied how to tell two leptoquark models apart at a future collider in twenty twenty-five. Leptoquarks are hypothetical particles linking quarks and leptons. Two scalar versions, named S3 and R2, couple to top quarks with different handedness, leaving distinct patterns in how top quarks come out polarized.

The team probes those patterns through jet substructure: the inner shape of particle sprays. Tools like Soft Drop and subjettiness measures, plus a custom heavy-flavor tag, feed a boosted decision tree that separates signal from background. For a leptoquark of a set mass, the analysis reaches strong significance at the high-luminosity LHC. A second classifier separates the two models from each other better than classic single variables.
arxiv-2505-16528:
Junichi Baba runs a galaxy simulation to see how the birth of a central bar reshapes star birth and star drift. It also tracks the age spread of disk stars in a Milky Way like galaxy. Bars drive gas inward and stir orbits. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Star birth in the inner disk peaks sharply as the bar forms. Strong spiral arms feed birth first, then the bar chokes it off. Birth in the outer disk goes on at low levels, while inner stars drift outward in bulk. That drift stamps a peak in outer disk ages at the bar birth era. Those stars also carry higher metal levels from their inner birth place.
arxiv-2505-16928:
Bosung Kim and Prithviraj Ammanabrolu present a 2025 arXiv paper on long-memory reasoning for embodied AI agents. Finding one clue in a long video is a start; their benchmark hides several clues across hundreds of household task steps. The framework generates endless reproducible long trajectories in a simulated home, each with ground-truth actions.

The team tests ways to stretch language model agents for the long haul: interleaving goal, state, and action, plus context extension and parallelism tricks. Results map where agents lose the thread and which training choices help. The authors offer the suite as a foundation for home robots that must plan over very long horizons.
arxiv-2505-17028:
Nikolas Aksamit and co-authors build simpler models for how wind moves snow and where it piles up, in a research paper from 2025. Snow transport shifts with gusts and eddies, and single grains add their own lag and drift. Even with perfect wind maps, forecasts rest on rough rules that can turn unstable in the math.

The team pairs a modern model of snow grain drag with tools that shrink complex systems to their main patterns. They add new measures for tracking buildup, so the small models keep a clear physical sense. Each simplification carries a stated error bound rather than a hidden guess. The authors aim the framework at snow scientists, water experts, and glacier researchers.
arxiv-2505-18728:
Andrea Ceni and five co-authors fuse two machine learning traditions in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Graph networks learn by passing messages between linked nodes. State-space models, stars of recent sequence learning, track long histories fast. Earlier blends ran the sequence tools on paths pulled out of graphs, breaking key symmetries. The authors instead wire state-space computation straight into message passing.

Their model, MP-SSM, works on still and changing graphs alike. It keeps the fairness property that node order cannot matter. It spreads information across long distances cheaply. An exact sensitivity analysis shows what the model responds to. The work serves researchers learning from networks, from molecules to social graphs.
arxiv-2505-19228:
Astrid Veronig and twelve co-authors review coronal dimmings in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. When the Sun erupts, patches of its corona suddenly darken in ultraviolet and X-ray images. These dimmings are footprints of the departing mass ejection and signs of lost coronal mass.

The review gathers what is known about how dimmings form and fade. They reveal the eruption's trigger, the magnetic reshaping it causes, and how the corona refills afterward. The authors add a new sorting scheme based on which magnetic systems join the eruption. Work on other stars is covered too: dimmings there may betray stellar eruptions we cannot image directly. The synthesis turns a side effect into a diagnostic tool.
arxiv-2505-19828:
Md Basim Uddin Ahmed and four co-authors built a benchmark for hunting code flaws in real C and C++ work, in a paper published in 2025. Earlier benchmarks label whole functions as flawed or clean, which hides where the flaw sits. Real flaws turn on specific lines and on the web of calls and data around them. Their benchmark holds more than 25,000 function samples drawn from nearly 6,000 known flaws, from 1999 to 2024.

The tests run line by line, with the full context in view. Top models still did poorly. The best scored under a quarter on the main scale for flawed lines identified with the right reasons. The authors read the outputs to map where models go wrong. They present the benchmark as a new standard for flaw detection in real code, and as a push to build sharper tools.
arxiv-2505-20328:
J.-F. Wang and G. Qin proposed a fresh way to accelerate cosmic rays in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Cosmic rays, charged particles at extreme energies, famously follow a power-law energy spectrum, and shocks are the textbook accelerator. The authors start from the focusing equation for particle diffusion and add a neglected ingredient: the background flow speed varies from place to place, as it does across real astrophysical plasmas.

Pitch-angle scattering plus those flow variations together pump particle momentum. Solving the averaged distribution gives power-law spectra directly, and for particles crossing compressible waves the predicted index range covers the values observed for galactic cosmic rays. A second accelerator beside shocks could explain spectra shocks alone strain to fit.
arxiv-2505-20528:
Soo Go and Victor Y Pan present a 2025 paper on very fast ways to estimate the 1-norm of a matrix, a size measure used across computing. An algorithm counts as superfast when it touches far fewer numbers than the matrix holds. Such methods are prized for structured matrices but can fail badly on hard inputs in some uses.

The authors devise new superfast methods that, in their tests, give accurate norm estimates for real-world matrices again and again. The tricks behind them are surprisingly simple, they note. With more testing and polish, they argue, the methods could be taken up in everyday computation. The paper is dedicated to the memory of Nicholas J Higham.
arxiv-2505-21728:
Amir Said, Xin Zhao, Marta Karczewicz, Hilmi Egilmez, Vadim Seregin, and Jianle Chen wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It seeks cheaper transforms for squeezing video, where matrix-based transforms tuned to the signal have long been too costly to run.

Rather than hunt for full matrices that squeeze best, the team hunts for a few parameters that define a new class of transforms, called HyGTs. These have cheap forms that run well in parallel. Built as an add-on to the HEVC standard, they cut bit rate by a clear margin in tests. They also use far less memory than the classic optimal matrices. The gain points a way for next-round video standards.
arxiv-2505-21828:
Chen Yueh-Han, Guy Davidson, and Brenden Lake test whether language models apply basic safety facts to new situations, in this 2025 paper. A model that knows melon balls can choke a baby should warn about them even when the user only asks for lunch ideas. Missing such warnings in naive questions can lead to real harm.

Their benchmark, SAGE-Eval, holds 104 safety facts drawn from trusted bodies such as health agencies. The facts were expanded into more than ten thousand test scenes across seven everyday areas, from outdoor activity to medicine. Even the best model passed only fifty-eight percent of the facts. Bigger models and more training did not track success closely, so scale alone will not fix the gap. The authors urge developers to run the benchmark before release, and they publish it freely for that use.
arxiv-2505-22128:
Alejandro Mousist tackles blurred Earth observation images in a solo 2025 paper on the IMAGIN-e mission, which flies aboard the International Space Station. A mechanical defocus in the camera softens the images the mission captures. His method must work on board the spacecraft, with no clean reference image to learn from and only limited computing power.

The method first estimates the defocus kernel, the shape of the blur, and then trains a restoration model within a GAN framework. On Sentinel-2 images with synthetic blur added, image quality improved sharply, with SSIM rising by 72.47% and PSNR by 25.00%. On real IMAGIN-e images, where no reference exists, perceptual quality scores also improved greatly. The approach is now deployed on the mission itself. It supports tasks such as water body segmentation and contour detection within the limits of onboard computing.
arxiv-2505-22828:
Yisca Kares studies a counting measure on rearrangements in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is the symmetric group, the set of all ways to shuffle a fixed list of items. Items are grouped into conjugacy classes by their cycle shape. The measure, called the des statistic, counts falls in a rearrangement when read in order.

Kares pins down the full range of that measure inside every class. The lowest value is one for every class except the identity, where nothing moves. Every value between that floor and the top of the range really occurs, with no gaps. The paper also gives a hands-on method to build a rearrangement hitting any chosen value, and draws out what the result means for counting problems.
arxiv-2505-23328:
Roberta Vieliute, Juan Hernández Santisteban, Keith Horne, and Hannah Cornfield present a tool that aligns brightness records of active galaxies taken by many telescopes, in work from 2025. Long watch campaigns mix data from scopes with small offsets between them. Aligning those records well is key to measuring how the galaxy varies.

Their program, PyTICS, uses hundreds of steady stars in the same frames to set per-scope and per-night fixes. It also builds a noise model from the star scatter, which flags bad nights, scopes, and stars. No guess about the galaxy's own variation shape is needed. Runs on ten one-meter robotic scopes showed tighter error bars than rival tools. Extra fixes handle very blue galaxies.
arxiv-2505-24828: Douglas Wright and Udoh Akpan study solitary waves in long-range versions of a classic lattice model, in part one of a 2025 series. In the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou lattice, particles link along a chain, and the long-range variants let them interact over any distance. The authors develop conditions strong enough to guarantee that solitary wave solutions, waves that hold their shape as they travel, can be built in these lattices.
arxiv-2506-00128:
Gabriel Aracena and four co-authors present a 2025 paper revisiting whether language models can sort software issue reports automatically. Open source teams drown in bug reports and feature requests, and sorting them by hand eats maintainer time. Older machine learning sorters needed big labeled data sets to do well.

The team reran the question with more data and newer models. Their system reads an issue's text and assigns its class, helping teams route work and recover information faster. The study compares model generations and training sizes to see what actually moves accuracy. Findings speak to how much curated data a project still needs when a strong general model is on hand.
arxiv-2506-00228: Rebekah Gelpí and six co-authors built Sorrel, a simple Python frame for multi-agent reinforcement learning, in a short paper from twenty twenty-five. It lets users make and test new worlds where many agents learn at once. Ease of use comes first, and its core loop is shaped to feel natural to those who study minds and groups. Social scientists can use it to probe how learning and contact shape group dynamics.
arxiv-2506-00928:
People watching an action can tell at a glance whether it is finished or still unfolding, and Olga Loginova and Sofía Ortega Loguinova test whether video-language models can do the same. They built a benchmark called Perfect Times: short clips of daily activities paired with questions about duration and completion. The questions come in four languages, English, Italian, Russian, and Japanese, with wrong answers crafted to bait shallow reading.

Top models, strong on text tests, fell short of human-like judgment on the clips. They leaned on surface cues rather than the flow of the event itself. The team argues that real time sense needs deeper fusion of sight and language, and offers the set as a new bar for that skill.
arxiv-2506-01028:
Harvey Friedman and Albert Visser ask when two formal theories that can interpret each other are really the same theory in a 2025 paper. Logic offers two grades of sameness: bi-interpretability, the looser one, and synonymy, also called definitional equivalence, the strictest. When the first implies the second was open for an important class of cases.

For sequential theories, they prove the implication holds when both interpretations are one-dimensional and preserve identity. The proof leans on a Schröder-Bernstein style result proved under very weak assumptions, which they note has interest of its own. A counterexample shows the identity condition cannot be dropped, so the theorem is exactly as strong as possible.
arxiv-2506-01728:
Chendi Qian and Christopher Morris improve machine learning solvers for quadratic programming in a 2025 paper. Quadratic programs sit inside many tasks, from training models to planning. Neural networks that pass messages on graphs can learn to solve them fast, but training data are scarce, above all for hard cases.

The pair design data augmentation that creates new training problems while keeping the best answer unchanged. Theory backs the safety of these changes. They fold the trick into a self-supervised method that pre-trains the network by contrast. Tests show better accuracy on held-out problems in supervised use. The pre-training also carried over to related problem types. The authors say principled augmentation is the key step for data-poor solver learning.
arxiv-2506-03128:
Andreas Auer and co-authors teach a forecasting model to use side information it has never been trained on, in this 2025 paper. Pretrained time series models can forecast new series cold, but most ignore helpful covariates like weather or prices. Data that pairs series with covariates is scarce. Their model, COSMIC, reads covariates through in-context learning, treating past stretches as worked examples.

A trick called informative covariate augmentation fakes the missing training material, so no covariate datasets are needed at all. In tests, COSMIC topped zero-shot forecasting charts with and without covariates in play. Checks confirmed the model truly leans on the side signals rather than ignoring them. The authors pitch it as a step toward forecast tools that use everything a user knows.
arxiv-2506-03228: Jose Garre Rubio presents a simple mechanism producing unstable degeneracies in local Hamiltonians, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The starting observation is elementary: if local operators commuting with a Hamiltonian's terms map one eigenstate to another, the second is also an eigenstate. From this, a no-go result follows. A state cannot be both a unique ground state and part of a degeneracy protected against local perturbations. The short abstract states the mechanism and the obstruction plainly.
arxiv-2506-03828:
Dhaval Patel, Shuxin Lin, James Rayfield, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It introduces AssetOpsBench, a test ground for AI agents that would run and maintain industrial equipment.

Factories want software that can watch machine health and plan upkeep on its own, cutting downtime. The bench offers four specialist agents, more than one hundred forty questions written by people from real plant scenarios, and a simulated sensor-data environment. Its scoring system weighs two designs: agents that act directly with tools, and agents that plan first and then execute. The system also hunts for new failure patterns on its own. The authors report a public platform with hundreds of users and agent entries, aimed at making results easy to repeat and compare.
arxiv-2506-04828:
Artem Latyshev, Gregory Gorbov, and Aleksandr Panov present a learning framework for control tasks where a wrong move can cause real harm, in a 2025 paper. Model-based reinforcement learning plans ahead with a learned model of the world, but model errors can turn plans dangerous. The team aims to gain the speed of planning without trusting the model blindly.

Their method switches on the fly between acting on the plan and acting on a direct policy, based on how reliable the model looks. Safety limits also shift as the agent grows more capable, rather than staying fixed. The goal at each step is to beat the safe fallback choice on both safety and performance, not merely to clear a bar. On a range of hard continuous control tasks with safety rules, the method beat non-adaptive rivals.
arxiv-2506-06428:
A string moving through anti-de Sitter space casts a shadow made of causal diamonds on the space's boundary, show Bercel Boldis and Péter Lévay in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their bridge is projective geometry: certain lines in a projective space organize the bulk, the boundary, and the space of diamonds at once.

Under the map, each point of the string lands on the two tips of one boundary diamond, and the string's equations turn into equations for how diamonds move. The authors also give the reverse lift, from diamond back to string. The two dimensional case, worked out fully, ties the construction together.
arxiv-2506-07928:
Austin Pollok wrote a 2025 finance paper on forecasting realized variance out of sample. The gap between market implied swings and real swings can predict stock option gains at the monthly scale. Whether that power rides on firm level swing forecasts was not clear.

Pollok moves the test to daily data and pits big machine learning models against lean factor models. Small gains in standard forecast error scores turned into clear gains in portfolio profit. That split suggests scores miss what portfolio builders care about most. He argues for training models with portfolio aims in mind, not pure error aims. The work speaks to traders who build option books from swing forecasts.
arxiv-2506-08328:
Junoh Heo and co-authors published this statistics paper in 2025. Engineers often run the same simulation at several fidelity levels: cheap rough runs and costly fine ones. Combining them raises accuracy. But some problems need answers finer than the finest run available. In those cases a tuning dial controls accuracy, and the exact answer sits at a dial setting no one can afford. The team proposes a model that learns across fidelity levels and extrapolates to that exact limit.

Borrowing ideas from diffusion models in machine learning, their Diffusion Non-Additive model allows tangled, non-additive links between levels. It supplies formulas for its predictions and their uncertainty, plus proven bounds on its error. Those bounds feed a strategy for choosing which runs to perform. Tests on numerical problems and real cases supported the method, and an R software package accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2506-08628:
Klimek and Witek present a paper from twenty twenty-five on mining logic rules from process logs. Formal specs guide checking how systems behave. Writing them by hand in complex systems is slow and error-prone. Their method turns mined process models into logic statements by patterns. Automated provers then test the statements for consistency. Both general and real event logs feed the evaluation. Noise in the data shapes how testable the specs become.

Properties like satisfiability and requirement fit are checked automatically. Results support use in realistic software settings. The authors aim at empirical software engineering practice. Automation could steady spec quality across projects.
arxiv-2506-09628:
Lin Huang and six co-authors show that a slope in heat can push magnetic zones across a stacked metal film, by force from disorder. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The film is a stack of thin layers, made in a lab track, with tiny heaters and heat gauges built in. The team read the zones' moves with a force scope. They stripped out the pull of the heater's own magnetic field. The pure heat pull always drove zones toward the heater. Steeper slopes gave larger shifts, up to a slow top speed. Counts of each force's strength showed the disorder force beat its two spin-based kin.
arxiv-2506-10328:
Sadia Kamal, Tim Oates, and Joy Wan built a system in twenty twenty-five that drafts clinical SOAP notes for skin cancer visits. SOAP notes — subjective, objective, assessment, and plan — are the standard record of a patient visit, but writing them by hand eats clinician time and feeds burnout. Skin cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, so the note load is huge.

Their framework learns from weak supervision, needing few hand-labeled examples. It takes a lesion image plus sparse clinical text and produces a structured note. Scores on clinical relevance metrics matched those of top commercial models. The authors add two new metrics of their own, checking alignment with expert medical concepts and coherence with the input. The goal is documentation that scales without draining clinicians.
arxiv-2506-10728:
Priyanka Kargupta, Runchu Tian, and Jiawei Han tackle fact-checking for claims that resist a simple true or false label, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Scientific and political claims usually bundle several aspects together. Judging each aspect separately is easier and more informative.

Their framework, ClaimSpect, builds a hierarchy of aspects for a given claim. Retrieval over an input corpus finds segments relevant to each aspect. Those segments reveal new sub-aspects and the perspectives people take on them. Perspectives are labeled as support, neutral, or oppose, with their prevalence measured. The output gives readers a structured, well-rounded view. Readers can also focus on the angles they care about, such as safety for children.
arxiv-2506-12928:
King Zhu and Hanhao Li lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, though the catalog names no creator for it. It gives the first planned study of scaling test-time compute for language model agents, programs that act in steps.

Four levers are tried: drawing many tries at once, revising in sequence, checking and merging tries, and spreading the tries apart. The team ablates each part to see what does the work. More compute does lift agent scores. Knowing when to pause and reflect counts for much. A list-wise way of merging checks best. Wider spread in the tries also helps. The paper maps how the test-time gains seen in plain reasoning carry to agents.
arxiv-2506-14528:
Schoemann pins down the kernel of the Gysin map for curves cut from a surface in twenty twenty-five. A smooth surface sits in projective space, and plane slices give a family of curves. For smooth slices, the kernel inside the curve's Jacobian was known to be shifts of one subvariety. Her result decides which subvariety it must be.

Either it is the one from vanishing cohomology, or it is zero and the kernel is merely countable. Stack language and a rising chain of open parts carry the proof. Two ground fields from past work are now covered, and the frame is general.
arxiv-2506-16028:
Yogesh Mehta, Anirban Roy, Simon Foreman, Alexander van Engelen, and Nick Battaglia wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gauges how shaky models of carbon monoxide glow from far galaxies could skew surveys of the cosmic microwave background.

The team built a suite of fake skies from varied star formation and brightness rules, across cosmic time, with the infrared background glow in place. The carbon monoxide power they find spans a hundredfold range. The gas alone is too faint for today's surveys, but its cross-talk with the infrared glow will count as a foreground in future ones. Skipping it would bias key gauges by more than future error bars allow. A three-part summary can still catch the spread.
arxiv-2506-17028:
Lorenzo Carletti and Frédéric Robert ask when the sharpest form of a higher-order Sobolev inequality survives on curved spaces, in a 2025 paper. Sobolev inequalities bound a function's size by its derivatives, and the optimal versions anchor analysis on manifolds. For first-order derivatives the optimal inequality with a simple remainder term holds broadly. For higher orders, the authors show, it does not hold in general.

They prove conditions for success and failure that depend on the manifold's geometry, and the conditions are sharp in the second-order case and in small dimensions. The geometry of the space itself decides whether the best constant is attainable. Such results guide analysts choosing function spaces for equations in physics and geometry.
arxiv-2506-17628: Changjiang Bu, Lixiang Chen, and Ge Lin study the characteristic polynomial of sunflowers, a special family of uniform hypergraphs. A sunflower is a hypergraph whose edges all intersect in exactly the same shared set of vertices. The authors determine the eigenvalues of these structures and work out their spectral moments. From those results they derive an explicit formula for the characteristic polynomial. The result gives spectral graph theory a closed-form handle on a structured hypergraph family.
arxiv-2506-18628:
Piotr Matys and six co-authors present a method in 2025 to catch false statements by large language models, even when source text is supplied. Such errors, called contextual hallucinations, are a barrier to safe use. Their method, named AggTruth, watches the model's internal attention scores across the supplied passage.

The method sums attention in four different ways and flags outputs whose pattern looks like a hallucination. Across several models, it held steady on both familiar and new tasks, and beat the prior best method in many settings. The authors also show that picking which attention heads to use matters a great deal. Careful selection was key to the strongest results.
arxiv-2506-18728:
Steven Kolawole and co-authors introduce a benchmark for finding hidden parallelism inside single language model prompts, in work from 2025. Serving systems usually treat each prompt as one block. Yet many real prompts contain subtasks that could run side by side, such as translating several passages, cutting total wait time.

The dataset holds over 37,000 real user prompts from public chat logs. Each prompt carries a structured schema marking its task template, shared context, and repeated inputs. The schemas were extracted with model help and checked by multilingual rules. A test suite then runs prompts serially and in parallel, measuring speed, structure, and meaning. Parallel structure could be parsed in most curated sets, with speedups up to five times on some tasks and little quality loss.
arxiv-2506-19928:
Fatemeh Davoudi, Benjamin Rackham, and colleagues measure gravity-sensitive clues in the spectra of the smallest stars and brown dwarfs in a 2025 astronomy study. Ultracool dwarfs blur the line between stars and planets, and surface gravity helps tell young, puffy objects from old, compact ones. The team gathered near-infrared spectra for dozens of these dwarfs, including several known planet hosts.

Iron hydride and vanadium oxide bands, among other features, respond to gravity in known ways. The authors test how those indices track metal content and whether planet-hosting dwarfs stand out. Reliable gravity markers sharpen age and mass estimates for the faintest neighbors of the Sun.
arxiv-2506-20528:
Shoichiro Miyashita reconsiders gravitational thermodynamics in a simplified universe in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The setting is three-dimensional gravity with an Einstein-Maxwell-scalar system and no cosmological constant. Earlier work by Krishnan, Shekhar, and Bala Subramanian argued this system has no black hole solutions among its thermodynamic saddles, only empty flat space and boson stars. That would make its phase structure much simpler than in higher dimensions.

Miyashita shows the census was incomplete. Beyond the known empty and boson star saddles, three more exist: a BG saddle, its hairy generalization with scalar field attached, and a new configuration dubbed the boson star-PL saddle. With five saddle types, the thermodynamic phase space is far richer than expected. It closely resembles the higher-dimensional picture the earlier work had ruled out, revising how physicists should think about three-dimensional gravity as a model system.
arxiv-2506-20928:
Yuanxing Cheng and co-authors make a learning method choose its own training data wisely in a 2025 computing paper. Gaussian process regression predicts smooth functions but struggles when inputs live on a curved manifold inside high-dimensional space. Their framework trains a neural network to flatten the manifold into a small latent space while a Gaussian process learns there. An active learning rule picks which new points to label next.

The selection rule aims to shrink total prediction error across the whole space, not just at easy points. On synthetic tests the method beat random sequential sampling, even for jagged, discontinuous functions. Smart sampling matters wherever each label costs a lab run or a simulation.
arxiv-2506-21128:
Sara Kališnik and Davorin Lešnik present a 2025 paper in pure math on magnitude, a number that sums up the size of a space of points. Magnitude links to many fields, from shape theory to machine learning. A known flaw is that the number can jump wildly when points shift a bit. The pair ask where the number behaves well instead.

They define a class of tame spaces, called tractable, and pin down what makes a space belong. Inside that class, they prove magnitude changes smoothly as the space shifts. One result gives a fresh proof that magnitude is smooth on compact sets of the number line. They also show the change rate stays bounded on bounded parts of the line. Tame cases give users of magnitude a safe ground for real data work.
arxiv-2506-21228:
Trevor Vrckovnik, Dennis Arslan, Falk Eilenberger, and Sebastian Schmitt design chip-based sources of entangled photon pairs, in a paper from 2025. The catalog record leaves the creator field blank; the text names the four authors. Quantum links and computers need such pair sources on chip, small and cheap to make. Most designs force the match between light waves with fussy patterning steps.

Their scheme leans on traits the crystal already has. They derive rules for when a single-material waveguide can emit pairs with crossed polarization. Then they sort all candidate crystal classes by those rules. Two materials get a full numerical workup. One, barium titanate, beat the classic lithium niobate on both output and range of colors. The route promises sources that are simple to build and easy to scale.
arxiv-2506-22028:
Ossi Parikka and Roel Pieters built voice control for industrial robots on code-generating text models in a 2025 paper. Small-batch manufacturing needs humans in the loop, and speaking to the robot beats teaching pendants for speed, if the interpretation can be trusted. Their LMPVC design turns spoken commands into robot programs for the standard ROS2 ecosystem, following earlier code-making approaches. Then adds a Policy Bank: a library of reusable, teachable Python policies the system can store and recombine.

The bank compensates for the underlying model's limits, since a once-taught routine can be recalled exactly instead of regenerated hopefully. The prototype targets collaborative cells where tasks change faster than automation budgets.
arxiv-2506-22628:
Sound designers shape a synthesizer by ear: play a sound, compare it with a target in mind, adjust, and repeat. Amir Salimi, Abram Hindle, and Osmar Zaïane study automating that loop, where a loss function scores how close the made sound is to the target and guides each adjustment. Earlier studies compared loss functions only in narrow setups, leaving open whether one best choice exists.

The authors built four loss functions, mixing new and known ones, and paired each with three kinds of software synthesizers, giving sixteen combinations. For each they ran 300 randomized matching trials and scored the results by parameter error, sound-spectrum distance, and human listening scores. The three scores agreed fairly well, but which loss worked best depended strongly on the synthesizer. They conclude that new similarity measures should be tailored to each synthesis method rather than one measure for all.
arxiv-2506-24128:
Rychard Bouwens and a large team of co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on quasars in the early universe. Quasars are brilliant beacons lit by feeding black holes, but many may hide in dim, dusty host galaxies.

The team ranked one hundred ninety quasars from the universe's first billion years by a carbon emission line that traces the gas mass of the host. Quasars in the most massive hosts were then split by how bright they look in ultraviolet light. Only about three percent of them are UV-bright. More than eighty-five percent are UV-faint, far dimmer than their host mass would suggest. Black hole mass, more than dust or feeding rate, seems to drive the spread. The authors say most early giants are easy to miss in plain light surveys.
arxiv-2507-00128:
Haining Pan and Sankar Das Sarma wrote a 2025 physics paper on Majorana zero modes, exotic quasiparticles pursued as building blocks for quantum computers. These modes appear at the ends of a one-dimensional topological superconductor, and they always come in pairs. If the pair is well separated, the modes behave as non-Abelian anyons that can be braided to perform fault-tolerant quantum computation.

The protection depends on the overlap between the two modes being exponentially small, which keeps their energy splitting tiny. Real devices, however, use short and disordered nanowires, where the ideal picture blurs. Pan and Sarma use the Majorana splitting itself to define when such imperfect wires are truly in the topological regime. The criterion helps experimentalists judge whether their devices host genuine Majorana modes.
arxiv-2507-00428:
Mohammad Sada and co-authors run machine learning inside the network itself, on programmable smart network cards, in a 2025 paper. Tasks like quality prediction and anomaly spotting need answers in microseconds, before packets leave the edge. The cards speak a packet-processing language and can be retuned from the control plane.
