The team stores model weights in lookup tables the card consults at line speed.

Both neural networks and regression models were mapped this way. Retraining means rewriting table entries, not rebuilding hardware. The design keeps inference at the network's edge, away from the core. The authors present the work as a proof that programmable cards can host flexible, live learning where the traffic actually flows.
arxiv-2507-00828:
Alexander Hoyle and three co-authors build a fairer way to judge topic models. Their 2025 paper presents ProxAnn, an evaluation method grounded in real use. Automated scores for topic models track human taste poorly. Expert labels match better but cannot scale. The team wanted a test that mirrors how practitioners actually use these models.

In their protocol, a judge reads a topic's texts, names the category, then applies that name to new texts. Crowd workers ran the protocol on many models across two datasets. The team then checked whether language models could stand in for the humans. The best stand-ins matched a human judge closely enough to serve. Software, a web tool, and the data are shared freely.
arxiv-2507-01628:
Zilong He and co-authors present DaiFu, a framework that lets deep learning systems recover from crashes in place, in a 2025 paper. Crashes are common in these systems because their software stacks are complex, and each crash wastes computing time. The standard fix, restarting from a checkpoint, is heavy and slow for small coding slips or brief glitches.

DaiFu adds a light code change that lets a running program catch its own crash. It can then patch code, settings, or data on the fly and resume at once. In tests it cut recovery time by a factor of more than a thousand against top rivals, with overhead under half a percent. A new benchmark covers seven crash types.
arxiv-2507-02928:
Yang and five co-authors filled in hidden confounders with language models in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Estimating a treatment's effect from records fails when an unmeasured factor steers both treatment and outcome. Their framework, ProCI, asks a language model to propose such hidden factors. It then generates, fills, and checks them in rounds.

The model's grasp of meaning helps it find plausible confounders in text and tables alike. Its world knowledge supports what-if reasoning about the missing pieces. To avoid flat, collapsed guesses, the method reasons over distributions rather than single values. Tests across datasets and models showed clearer confounders and better effect estimates. The authors call it a first use of language models against hidden confounding.
arxiv-2507-04728: Qi Wu and Yong Lu improve bounds on the rank of a mixed graph in twenty twenty-five. A mixed graph is made by giving directions to some edges of a plain graph. Its H-rank is a quantity tied to an associated matrix. Earlier work bounded the rank of the underlying graph using its matching number and counts of even and odd cycles. Wu and Lu extend those bounds to mixed graphs. They also characterize classes of mixed graphs where the bounds are met exactly.
arxiv-2507-04828:
Samira Ahmadifarsani, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, and Ulf Schlichtmann ease the path for plugging custom AI chips into a major compiler in a 2025 paper. Edge devices increasingly run deep learning on dedicated accelerators, which are fast and frugal. But wiring a new chip into a modern learning compiler demands deep changes and expert knowledge of the compiler's guts.

Their approach builds on the TVM compiler and targets accelerators built around matrix multiplication, the core of deep networks. A high-level layer hides the compiler detail, so a chip team can integrate its hardware without mastering the internals. They also fold in a design space exploration tool that tunes the mapping of a network onto the chip on its own. The work aims to shorten the road from new silicon to running models.
arxiv-2507-05528:
Jiahuan Pei and co-authors build a multi-agent workflow that stages teaching chats between language models and grades their quality, in a paper from 2025. Virtual teachers and learners have grown fast, but work so far rarely spans large, varied course content or checks teaching quality with care.

Their system, WikiHowAgent, casts models as teacher and learner, with a manager running the exchange and an evaluator scoring it. The focus is step-by-step skills drawn from how-to guides. The team built a dataset of over one hundred thousand chats grounded in thousands of tutorials across many domains. Scoring mixes automatic metrics, rubric judgments, and human checks. Results across setups show the workflow works and reveal where model teaching is strong or weak.
arxiv-2507-06128:
Christopher Wilson and co-authors report a fixed rule for how well quantum states can be measured, in a physics paper from 2025. In quantum metrology, scientists use quantum states to measure things with great care. A math object called the Quantum Fisher Information Matrix tracks how much a state can tell about a value.

The team shows that when the measures used form a closed set under a math rule, the core values of that matrix do not change over time. In plain terms, each such set gives a state a fixed budget of sensing power. Moves that respect the same rules cannot raise that budget. A linked measure of how measures clash is fixed in the same way. The result can help sort useful states by group.
arxiv-2507-06328:
Ronak Mehta, Jelena Diakonikolas, and Zaid Harchaoui study min-max optimization problems where the coupling between the two sides is linear in at least one of them, in a 2025 paper. Such problems sit between fully bilinear and fully general ones, and they arise in robust optimization and in optimization under constraints. The authors build a general algorithmic framework around that middle structure.

Their bounds exploit any separability the problem offers, and in several settings they improve on the best known scaling in the dual dimension. The methods mix randomization with extrapolation and multi-point anchoring inside mirror descent updates. The authors hope the update strategies will transfer to related problem classes.
arxiv-2507-07128:
Richard J Cartwright and co-authors lay out, in a 2025 paper, how a planned space telescope could probe the habitability of icy ocean worlds in our own solar system. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is being built mainly to study Earth-like planets around other stars. Its tools will also cover ultraviolet light, which the ground can barely reach, and that range suits worlds such as Europa, Enceladus, Ceres, Ariel, and Triton.

The paper sets out what a key instrument, an integral field spectrograph, would need: wavelength reach, sharpness, and field size. The goals include catching geyser bursts as they happen and reading the light signatures of water, salts, and carbon compounds tied to life. The authors sort possible findings into steps, from steady gains to breakthroughs, and judge the telescope fit for long-term watching of these worlds.
arxiv-2507-07428:
Felipe Atenas and three co-authors build a convergence theory for algorithms whose target moves at every step. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Many optimization routines chase a fixed point, but real methods often swap operators as they go, leaving no single point that fits all steps.

Their trick adds a relocation step after each main update, carrying the current fixed point onto the next operator's ground. A widened version of a classic demiclosedness principle powers the proof. The payoff is a graph-based Douglas-Rachford method for splitting problems into many operators. Its step size may now vary between iterations, a freedom earlier versions lacked. The framework widens the design space for splitting algorithms generally.
arxiv-2507-08028:
Evgenii Rudakov, Jonathan Shock, Otto Lappi, and Benjamin Cowley split smooth human movement into its hidden sub-moves in real time, in work from 2025. A reach or a stroke is really a chain of small bursts. Reading the bursts informs motor control science, rehab, and interface design.

Older splitters are slow, imprecise, or starved of labeled data. Their learner trains on synthetic moves shaped by a least-jerk rule, then adapts to unlabeled human data in rounds. A convolutional net rebuilds the full move from its parts as a check. It beats prior methods on fake and real sets, even under heavy noise. Speed is under a millisecond per second of motion.
arxiv-2507-08128:
Arushi Goel and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper on Audio Flamingo 3, a fully open model that reasons over speech, sound, and music. A single new encoder, AF-Whisper, learns shared representations across all three audio types. The system can think step by step on demand, hold multi-turn chats with several clips, and handle audio up to ten minutes long.

The team built several large training sets with fresh curation methods and trained the model in five stages. Trained only on open data, the model set new best scores on more than twenty audio benchmarks. It passed both open and closed rivals trained on far larger datasets.
arxiv-2507-08828:
Tarek Berghout, writing alone in 2025, proposes a new learning paradigm in a brief technical note. Standard deep learning trains on fixed data and stops. His idea, Recurrent Expansion, adds a second loop: models learn from the behavior of earlier versions of themselves, tracked through inner feature maps and loss signals.

Variants run many model copies in parallel and pool their signals, even mixing unlike designs. A selective, scale-aware version targets real deployment. The note argues this shift could yield systems that improve themselves and reason about their own learning. A simple code example is included for beginners. The paper is a proposal and roadmap, not a benchmark study, and it invites the field to test the idea.
arxiv-2507-09128:
Ronak Mehta and Zaid Harchaoui published this paper in 2025. It builds theory for zero-shot prediction, the trick behind foundation models: pre-train one model, then apply it to new tasks with no labeled examples. The practice works well, and this paper asks what makes it work.

The authors define what quantities a zero-shot predictor must implicitly learn during pre-training. Generalization, they show, hinges on conditional independence relationships: the pre-training data must tie inputs, outputs, and task descriptions in the right pattern. When those relationships hold, knowledge transfers to unseen tasks; when they break, it should not. The framework covers the self-supervised and multimodal contrastive methods used to build foundation models. By naming the load-bearing assumptions, the theory tells practitioners what to check in their data. The authors frame it as a first map of a common but poorly understood method.
arxiv-2507-09328:
Achraf Zinihi, Matthias Ehrhardt, and Moulay Rchid Sidi Ammi build a space-and-time model of epidemic spread with built-in control choices, in a paper from 2025. Their model sorts people into groups from healthy to ill, quarantined, and recovered. Spread unfolds across a map as well as over time. Three controls can be tuned: prevention, quarantine, and treatment.

The paper first proves the model has one sound answer that stays positive. It then shows that a best control plan exists and works out the rules such a plan must obey. Computer runs test mixes of the three controls. Blends of drug and non-drug steps cut both illness and cost the most. The math gives health planners a frame for weighing vaccine, testing, and social steps together.
arxiv-2507-10028:
Shao-Wen Wei, Shan-Ping Wu, Yu-Peng Zhang, and Yu-Xiao Liu study black hole phase changes near absolute zero. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, asks if set rules govern these changes far below the hot point. Phase changes here mean shifts between states of a black hole. The authors use a classic equal-area rule on the curve where two states coexist.

They derive three fixed numbers that mark how the change behaves. One number stays the same no matter the black hole's charge or spin. The space size also sets one of the numbers. The result may help link black hole heat rules to the deeper theory of quantum gravity.
arxiv-2507-10128:
Anita Ziegler and five co-authors argued in twenty twenty-five that microbes and their bioreactors should be designed together, not in sequence. Standard bioprocess development engineers the organism first, tunes fermentation in the lab second, and scales up last. That relay wastes time and can strand a strain that no reactor serves well. Their formulation, SimulKnockReactor, optimizes both levels at once.

The upper level chooses reactor size and operating conditions to minimize investment and running costs for stirring, aeration, and pH control. The lower level picks gene knockouts in the microbe via flux balance analysis, implementing what the upper level requires. Tested on bacterial models up to genome scale, the joint approach matched or beat sequential design on cost. It also never proposed a strain unable to meet production capacity.
arxiv-2507-10228:
Hugo Villamizar, Daniel Mendez, and Marcos Kalinowski propose a framework for writing requirements for trustworthy artificial intelligence in a 2025 vision study. Worries about fairness, safety, and reliability are hard to turn into concrete system requirements. Such qualities depend on context and emerge in use, so engineers need structured help to pin them down.

The authors combine two existing approaches. One is artifact based and supplies templates that keep results consistent and traceable, though aimed at deterministic systems. The other uses multiple perspectives to surface concerns tied to data and learning. Joining them should help teams specify trust needs for learning systems more completely.
arxiv-2507-10328:
Sanino, D'Amico, França, and Carvalho show that facts read at a single site in a quantum system can betray long-range order that spans the whole system. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such order was long thought to hide from single-site probes, which are all that most lab tests can reach. The team studies a chain model at half fill, with both charge and spin parts. They find that local facts — charge and spin swings, odds of each state, and a link measure — show clear marks of the shift into a paired state. A prior soft break of a balance sets the stage. The work gives labs a way to see a hard state with plain tools.
arxiv-2507-12528:
Asiyeh Yaghoobi and her five co-authors, publishing in 2025, simulate how magnetic fields shape the second wave of star birth inside young globular clusters. The standard story has gas shed by old giant stars pooling in the cluster and forming new stars, but earlier simulations mostly ignored magnetism. The team runs three-dimensional models that add fields, radiation from hot young stars, and the old stars' winds as the cluster plows through thin gas.

They find the fields confine new star formation to the cluster's very center and make the new group more compact. A weak or medium field barely changes how much mass forms, while a strong one can raise or cut the total by a lot depending on its alignment with the motion. Strong fields also change how much of the gas is recycled star-stuff versus fresh outside gas, which alters the new stars' helium mix.
arxiv-2507-13328:
Yulu Qin, Dheeraj Varghese, Adam Dahlgren Lindström, Lucia Donatelli, Kanishka Misra, and Najoung Kim ask whether adding vision training changes what language models know about word kinds, in work from 2025. Word kinds form a tree, such as animal over dog over poodle. Past results on vision training effects were mixed.

The team compared matched pairs of text-only models and their vision-trained twins. On a text quiz needing kind knowledge, the vision-trained models often scored better. Yet deep checks showed the kind knowledge itself barely differed. What changed was how the models handled questions that held kind-linked pairs. The authors conclude vision training helps models use knowledge, rather than rebuild it.
arxiv-2507-13628:
Masahiro Ogawa, Qi An, and Atsushi Yamashita split moving from still objects in video shot from a moving camera, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Flow-only methods falter in rich scenes with turning or side-by-side motion. Their method starts from where the flow field seems to expand.

Odd flow points give a first motion score, then a segmentation prior sharpens it. The blend holds up under spin, parallel drift, and crowded street scenes. Tests on two public sets plus real traffic clips hit top marks. Robots and mapping tools need this split to read scenes right. Readers get a robust recipe for motion spotting on the move.
arxiv-2507-14728:
Maryam Salamatmoghadasi, Metin Ozturk, and Halim Yanikomeroglu tackle an energy-saving puzzle for future 6G networks, in a 2025 paper. Networks can switch off small base stations when traffic is light, but a sleeping station cannot report its own load. Planners must guess that load, and guesses carry error.

Their network model adds a high-flying platform station that acts as a super base station above the rest. Rather than propose yet another switching rule, the authors compare ways to estimate hidden loads. They try map-based guesses from neighbors and clusters, plus a memory-based deep learning method that reads load history. The study targets the missing-data problem that makes many saving schemes fail in practice.
arxiv-2507-15128:
Huw Price and Ken Wharton propose that quantum entanglement links, the EPR and Bell patterns, are artefacts of how the starting state is picked. In stats and cause modeling, a pick process can breed links in a subset drawn from an unlinked pool. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Here the pick is the setup of the first state in the tests. That choice pre picks a subset of a larger virtual pool of paths with no links. Since the pick comes first, not last, the links still back the what-if thoughts at the heart of the EPR case. The authors end with fresh lessons for cause modeling.
arxiv-2507-15428:
Jiaao Li and four co-authors present EgoPrune, a way to cut tokens in first person video in two thousand twenty-five. First person video shifts all the time as the wearer moves. It is the main visual input for embodied agents, so fast work on it matters. Vision and language models are strong but cost too much on long video.

EgoPrune picks key frames, drops tokens that repeat after a shift in view, and keeps a mix of apt and varied tokens. It needs no training. Tests on two bench sets beat prior training free methods and cut compute, memory, and wait. The team also ran it on a small edge device in a real agent.
arxiv-2507-15628:
Tang, Huang, Luo, Wang, Yu, Li, Fu, Sun, and Xiao survey in twenty twenty-five ways to make deep-learning video analysis faster and cheaper. Video data is exploding, and neural networks give the accuracy users want, but their running cost stays high. Most past surveys stressed accuracy gains, so this one organises efficiency methods from the ground up instead.

The review spans hardware support, data handling, model tweaks, and deployment choices. It frames these layers as one optimisation framework and maps known methods onto it. The authors then discuss standing problems, such as balancing speed against accuracy in live settings. They close with challenges meant to guide future work on efficient video systems.
arxiv-2507-16828:
Jialai She proves that a certain family of consecutive powerful numbers cannot exist. A powerful integer is one where every prime factor appears with exponent at least two. The Erdős-Mollin-Walsh conjecture asserts that no three consecutive powerful integers exist at all, and it remains a celebrated open problem in number theory.

Following recent work, She investigates potential counterexamples centered on perfect cubes, which are themselves powerful. The paper establishes a nonexistence result for triplets around cubes whose factors obey distinct structural constraints, specifically involving prime-square factors. The proof combines techniques from modular arithmetic and p-adic valuation with Thue equations and the theory of elliptic curves. Each family of near-misses ruled out narrows the search space for the full conjecture. The result is a brick in a wall number theorists have been building around a deceptively simple question.
arxiv-2507-17328:
Rui Wu, Nikola Kovachki, and Burigede Liu split hard engineering problems for a neural solver in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Finite element tools are reliable but slow on large, intricate structures. Neural methods are fast, yet they mostly handle simple shapes.

Their learning-based domain decomposition uses one pretrained neural operator, trained on easy domains, as the solver inside each piece of a split domain. A general theorem backs the approach for abstract equations. Tests on elliptic problems with patchy microstructures in complex shapes beat current state-of-the-art methods. The solver kept its accuracy at new resolutions and on micro patterns it had never seen. The authors aim to bring neural speed to real-world geometry.
arxiv-2507-17828:
Aigner and Dür show how reshaping a quantum system's energy levels can sharpen sensing. Parameter guessing depends on the spectrum of the Hamiltonian that stamps the signal. Unitary control can redesign that effective spectrum before measurement starts.

For Hamiltonians that commute, the control problem shrinks to a finite run of simple switches. Any target spacing of levels can be reached, though the total range may shrink. Each new spectrum is a weighted mix of the old levels, with weights forming a doubly stochastic matrix. Worked examples of single-parameter sensing show large gains in accuracy from this spectral design.
arxiv-2507-18128:
Zilu Yang and co-authors re-audit the pulsation frequencies of 68 Delta Scuti stars measured by the Kepler telescope, hunting for impostor signals. Their paper appeared in 2025. Kepler's slow cadence folds very fast vibrations down into the measured range, where they masquerade as real modes. A sliding periodogram method can tell true notes from reflections. The team re-examined 1,406 published frequencies with it.

Six frequencies in four stars turned out to be previously missed reflections of super-Nyquist signals. The authors say cleaning such artifacts sharpens the starquake models built on these stars. The method itself is the wider product: any long-cadence survey can use it to keep its frequency lists honest.
arxiv-2507-18428:
Lena Cibulski and Stefan Bruckner propose a scheme for describing decision problems precisely, aimed at visualization researchers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Decision-making is a stated goal of much visualization work, yet the term stays loosely defined. Existing task models describe decision processes but skip the conditions that frame a choice.

Their characterization spells out a decision problem through key properties of its data, its users, and its context. Designers can then state their decision-support claims exactly and pick encodings and interactions that fit. The authors test the scheme on decision tasks from published design studies. They use the gaps it exposes to chart future work on decision-centered visualization.
arxiv-2507-20628:
Detinko and Flannery write a short mathematics paper from 2025 on special subgroups of matrix groups over finite fields. The groups are nilpotent, a class with a strong internal order. They are also primitive, meaning they preserve no finer split of the space they act on.

The pair give a detailed account of how such groups are built. Their structure results sort the groups by the shape of their parts and the field they sit over. Results of this kind feed work in group theory and in computer algebra systems that handle matrix groups. The paper adds a full reference case for teams who classify finite matrix groups.
arxiv-2507-20728:
Andrés Holgado-Sánchez, Holger Billhardt, Sascha Ossowski, and Sara Degli-Esposti tackle how to learn the values of a whole society in a 2025 paper. AI systems that act on values need clear models of what people hold dear. Learning one person's values from their choices is hard enough. A society, though, is better seen as many groups with shared but distinct value sets.

The authors define this learning problem in formal terms and propose a method based on deep grouping of data. The method watches the stated choices of a sample of people and learns both shared value grounds and a set of group value systems. They test it on real data about travel choices. The approach could help build AI that respects the mix of values in a community.
arxiv-2507-20928:
Rudra Prosad Sarkar, Arnab Mukherjee, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay build a heat engine out of a single qubit whirled in circles near light speed. The motion makes the quantum vacuum act like a hot bath through the circular Unruh effect. That bath drives an Otto cycle, the quantum analogue of a classical engine loop.

Two half-circular rotations at ultra-relativistic speeds form the cycle's moving parts. The qubit's response depends strongly on its trajectory, and its transition probability settles to a constant at high acceleration. Extracted work grows with acceleration before leveling off. Efficiency, though, is untouched by the circular motion and matches earlier models. The study links relativistic motion to quantum thermodynamics in a clean test system.
arxiv-2507-21428:
Elias Lumer and co-authors present a memory manager that lets language model agents swap tools in and out across long conversations, in a paper from 2025. Agents fetch tools and data services per question, but the context window is fixed. Across many turns, stale tools crowd out fresh ones.

Their system, MemTool, comes in three modes: a fully autonomous mode where the agent manages its own tools, a fixed workflow mode, and a hybrid. Tests ran over one hundred straight user exchanges on a tool benchmark across many models. Reasoning models cleared stale tools well on their own; mid-sized models lagged badly. Workflow and hybrid modes kept memory tidy for all, while autonomous and hybrid modes finished tasks best. Trade-offs per mode are spelled out.
arxiv-2507-22028:
Honglin He and co-authors present a learning framework for navigation models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Navigation foundation models learn from huge video collections and generalize across settings. Yet offline training alone leaves them blind to the effects of their own actions.

Their Seeing-to-Experiencing framework adds reinforcement learning in simulation after video pretraining. One innovation steadies offline learning with anchor-based matching of motion patterns. A second, a residual-attention module, adds reactive behavior without erasing pretrained knowledge. The goal is safe, interactive movement in real city settings, such as dodging obstacles and pedestrians. The team also builds a full end-to-end evaluation.
arxiv-2507-22128:
Radio telescopes of the SKA generation will pour out more data than one machine can process, so image building must be shared across computers. Wang and co-authors propose a decentralized framework that splits the work by spatial frequency. Each node holds part of the visibility data, the raw measurements, and rebuilds a near-full-resolution image by borrowing the major-cycle images already made by the other nodes.

They plug the scheme into two established reconstruction methods, multiscale CLEAN and a sparsity-based convex approach, and test it on four datasets with two ways of splitting the data. Image quality matched the serial versions while runtimes fell, most sharply on the larger datasets, where speedups approached the ideal twofold. The authors present the framework as one piece of the scalable pipeline the new telescopes demand.
arxiv-2507-22228:
Damian Swift builds a strength model for rhenium, a dense metal used as an x-ray shield in laser-driven tests. The paper appeared in 2025. In such tests, the metal is crushed at extreme pressure, and its strength affects how results are read. Swift fits a standard model, called the Steinberg-Guinan model, to data from computer estimates and from tests on rolled bars.

The fit tracks how the metal hardens as it is worked and how it softens with heat. It matches hardness tests well at normal pressures. At very high pressures, though, the model gives lower strength than some diamond-cell tests suggest. Swift notes that rhenium may in fact grow stronger under crushing than the model says. The work gives test designers a firmer base for planning and reading high-pressure shots.
arxiv-2507-22728:
Bing-Bing Liu and Shi-Lei Su propose a way to gain true gain on the ground state of a parity time symmetric quantum system. Such systems pair a loss term on one state with a gain term on the other. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past dilation tricks build these systems inside larger plain ones, yet the pure gain term stayed out of reach. Systems without it show a shifted spectrum but miss the full physics. The new method blends an effective operator trick with a master equation for steady measurement. Averaged over paths, true ground state gain emerges, the authors argue.
arxiv-2507-23628:
Matéo Spriet's paper from 2025 builds a quasiprobability picture of quantum mechanics for a broad family of groups. The Kirkwood-Dirac picture assigns values that can dip below zero, a sign of true quantum behavior. Spriet sets it up over locally compact abelian groups that can be counted in stages, using the Fourier transform. He links it to a known phase-space method and shows a rival picture keeps its symmetric reading there.

He then finds every pure state, in a broad sense, whose values stay positive: they are, up to group moves, flat measures on closed subgroups. The quantum-classical border in this picture is real exactly when the group has a compact core part. For round, connected groups he gives a full shape-based account of that border. The work unifies results first seen for finite groups.
arxiv-2508-01028:
Courtney Kunselman, Siya Zhu, Doğuhan Sarıtürk, and Raymundo Arróyave present a software flow for building heat-and-phase models of metal mixes, in work from 2025. Their test case is a mix of platinum and tungsten. The flow joins machine-learned models of atom forces with a standard toolkit for alloy work.

The learned models yield energy accounts that rest on real physics and need only slight tuning. That tuning is done with a slope-based method matched to lab data, which makes the fit fast and stable. The result is a phase chart that matches what is known of the mix. The whole flow is shared in the open, so other teams can build models for other metal pairs the same way.
arxiv-2508-01428:
Liping Li and a large team of co-authors dissect the light of supernova SN 2024gy, in a 2025 preprint, to read how the star exploded. It is a Type Ia event, the kind used as cosmic distance markers. Early spectra showed unusually fast-moving material. The team tracked the event's brightness and took spectra at many epochs. Its peak brightness and fade rate fit the normal pattern for its class. From the heat output they estimate the mass of radioactive nickel forged in the blast.

Calcium lines raced outward far faster than silicon lines at the same moment. That split hints at layered ionization in the outer debris. The strong fast calcium may signal little hydrogen mixing in the fastest layers. Both clues point to a delayed detonation, where a slow burn turns into a blast. A nickel-to-iron ratio from the late spectrum backs the same story.
arxiv-2508-03428:
Bojan Derajić, Mohamed-Khalil Bouzidi, Sebastian Bernhard, and Wolfgang Hönig combine learning with model predictive control for robot collision avoidance in a 2025 paper. A predictive controller steers by planning ahead, but it needs a safe end state for each plan. The truly safe set shifts as obstacles move and is too costly to compute live.

Their method approximates that set with a distance measure minus a learned correction. A neural network supplies the correction, shaped so the estimate never claims more safety than the distance alone. A second network adapts the correction to each scene. In simulations and on real hardware, success rates rose up to 30 percent over the best rival method.
arxiv-2508-03728:
Revanth Gangi Reddy and co-authors (2025) present WiNELL, software agents that keep Wikipedia current. The encyclopedia depends on human editors, and pages age fast. Inspired by an older never-ending learning system, the authors built agents that gather fresh information online. They pick what is new and important for a target entry. They draft precise edits for human review, rather than publishing directly.

The editing models learned from Wikipedia's history of human edits. That training makes their suggestions match house style. In tests, they beat open instruction-following models and GPT-4o on coverage of key facts and editing efficiency. On busy, fast-changing pages the full system found and proposed timely factual updates. The authors frame the work as a research direction: agents that maintain knowledge bases forever, with people approving the changes. Wikipedia is the proving ground, not the limit.
arxiv-2508-04628:
Kehan Cai, Chunyi Zhang, and Xifan Wu work out the dielectric permittivity of water with machine-learned potentials, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. This trait lies behind much of water's behavior in physics, biology, and chemistry. Their method takes in, in a set way, distinct electric boundary conditions. Long-range Coulomb forces are built into the potential.

The potential is a deep model with long-range effects. It was trained on data from hybrid density functional theory. A second neural network predicts the centers of maximally localized Wannier functions. Those centers let the team judge the dielectric response. The authors compare three boundary conditions: metallic, insulating, and Kirkwood-Fröhlich. Each shapes linked dipole fluctuations and dielectric relaxation in its own way. They also give a consistent way to get the Kirkwood correlation factor and length. The frame should extend to other polar liquids.
arxiv-2508-05528:
James Lutsko looks at open boundary conditions in stochastic hydrodynamic models of nucleation, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Stochastic hydrodynamics is a central tool for the study of first-order phase transitions at a basic level. Mixed with free energy models from density functional theory, it can model crystallization. It yields free energy barriers, nucleation pathways, and key eigenvalues.

Limits on computing, though, restrict the sizes that can be modeled. Real tests in effect involve endless volume, which small simulations cannot match. Open boundaries bring the math closer to test conditions. They also raise hard questions for the model. Lutsko asks whether the fluctuation-dissipation relation survives open boundaries. He also asks whether still points of the free energy surface stay still points of the dynamics. The paper works through what open systems mean for nucleation theory.
arxiv-2508-05728:
Santiago Casas and four co-authors introduce CLAPP, a chat assistant that pair-programs with researchers using a major cosmology solver. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The solver, CLASS, computes the early universe's history but has a steep learning curve. New users often stall on setup, code, and cryptic errors.

CLAPP wraps a language model around the solver's documentation. It answers questions, writes code, debugs errors, and makes plots in conversation. Several agent roles share the work, a search engine finds the right docs, and a live Python sandbox runs the code. The tool runs as a friendly web app. It lowers the entry barrier for scientists new to AI helpers. The authors aim to make human-AI teamwork normal in numerical cosmology.
arxiv-2508-05828: Danielle Bowerman and Matt Insall prove new shape results for extension monads, a tool first set out in the nineteen nineties by Insall. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. The work looks at how these monads act on wide sets of finite-step operations and on standard builds in algebra. One result says the monad step swaps cleanly with direct products for finite groups of algebras that share a signature. A second result says the only maps back from an enlargement are plain ones.
arxiv-2508-06328:
Zhiyou Xiao led a team building a system that both reads and produces mixed media in a 2025 paper. Retrieval-augmented systems can take in text and images together, but they usually answer in one form only. Real tasks often need answers that mix forms too, such as text with well-placed images. Their framework adds a learned inserter that picks images and places them in the output.

The inserter was trained with reinforcement learning to align image choice with meaning and context. Though small, it reasoned strongly and ran with low delay. Tests showed it beat baselines on both quality and speed for this new kind of generation task.
arxiv-2508-07128:
Gregory Schuit, Denis Parra, and Cecilia Besa judge fake chest X-rays by eye in two thousand twenty-five. Image generators could ease data scarcity in medical imaging. Rare ills are hard to learn from without more cases. But poor fakes can harm trust and model skill.

The team made X-rays for four chest ills with two model types. Real images came from a known hospital data set. Three radiologists tried to spot fakes and check if traits fit the named ill. Diffusion models made more real looking images on the whole. The rival type won on some traits. Cues the doctors used expose gaps in both.
arxiv-2508-07828:
Yu and Diaferio apply a tree based finder to clusters of galaxies around the cluster A2029 in twenty twenty-five. The finder groups galaxies by how strongly gravity binds them, building a family tree of structures. They ran it on a wide field of galaxy distance data centered on A2029. It found all the bright X ray clusters known there and most optical ones.

The tool also mapped groups and the thread like filaments that link clusters. At a lower threshold, it picked out three superclusters in the field. Its tree orders each supercluster's parts by binding energy. That order hints at how each supercluster grew and may evolve. The authors call the tool key for studying cosmic structure growth.
arxiv-2508-08628:
Benjamin Fields and Jason Goodman search starlight records for laser flashes that could come from alien tech, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The data come from a fine spectrograph in Chile that split the light of 2,821 stars for planet hunts. A laser would show as a lone bright line too narrow for nature.

One pass per star flagged 285 peaks. Most fell to known tricks: cosmic rays, gear flaws, and glow from Earth's own air. Eight sources passed, and the team checked all extra records of those stars. No spike ever came back at the same color. Four of the last seven shared their spike with other stars that night, which marks an Earth source not yet named. Three still defy all checks and merit a fresh look.
arxiv-2508-09228:
Saif and co-authors train one speech model for many tongues and tasks without letting the goals fight, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Hearing and translation goals pull against each other, and flat joint training stalls as tasks pile up. Three layered recipes split the goals at unlike depths.

A light layer picker builds clash-free steps from only the worst layers, saving cost. Tests on three speech sets show a two-level split of hearing from translation wins. The split beats flat training across the board. Code is shared openly. Readers who build speech stacks get a recipe book for peace among goals.
arxiv-2508-10428:
Pengbo Shen and co-authors present a 2025 benchmark and training framework for language models playing StarCraft II, a complex strategy game. Older benchmarks trim the game down, dropping races, actions, or context, so scores overstate real skill. Their benchmark, SC2Arena, keeps all playable races and the full low-level action space. It also reshapes the text view of the game to ease spatial reasoning.

The companion framework, StarEvolve, splits play among a planner, an executor, and a verifier that checks and corrects moves. It improves by fine-tuning on high-scoring games it played itself. In tests on the new benchmark, StarEvolve outplayed rivals on strategic planning. The authors release their code and tools, hoping to push general agents that plan and adapt in real time.
arxiv-2508-10528:
Ziye Deng and co-authors build the data and the model for a core medical AI task: pointing to the exact spot in a scan that a doctor's words describe. Such grounding feeds diagnosis help, question answering, and automatic report writing, but past work used few scan types and coarse labels. The team assembled Med-GLIP-5M, a data set of more than 5.3 million region labels across seven imaging types.

Labels run in layers, from whole organs down to small lesions. Their model learns from that variety without hand-built expert parts, and it picks up the layering on its own, telling a lung from a pneumonia patch inside it. It beat leading rivals on grounding benchmarks, and feeding its spatial output into question answering and report writing lifted both. The data set is set for public release.
arxiv-2508-10828:
Henry Powell, Guy Laban, and Emily Cross build a network that can tell when a person is sharing deep, personal facts with a social robot. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such sharing is a key part of how people bond. Past work in mind and social fields mapped its traits and effects in depth. But few tools can spot it as it goes, and fewer still for talk with robots. As robots join more social scenes, that skill grows in need. The team's network reads more than one channel at once, such as voice and face. Its build draws on tools made to read feelings. It learns from real talks with robots.
arxiv-2508-11128:
Christof Jung and Francisco Gonzalez Montoya charted a chaotic borderland in a 2025 dynamics study. Their model follows a lone particle pulled by two dwarf galaxies that orbit and tug on each other, a cousin of the classic restricted three-body problem. Special ridge-like surfaces in the motion space, called NHIMs, organize which paths stay nearby and which escape.

Three such surfaces anchor the system, with stable and unstable sheets that tangle around them. As the disturbance grows, the surfaces lose their grip and their orderly tori break, opening patches of temporary chaos. The breakups across the three surfaces seem coordinated. Maps and delay-time plots reveal the pattern in detail.
arxiv-2508-11228:
Sinha studies a thin sheet of charged grains with strong spin-orbit links, lit by round-spun light. The work uses the Floquet frame to track how light and matter reshape the bands. Light can open a Hall response that takes set values, with phase marks of 0, 1, and 3. Shifts in light strength and photon size drive the phase changes. Gaps close at set points in the zone as the shift takes place.

A weak straight Rashba term moves the Dirac points but leaves the phase marks the same. A pure straight Rashba sheet stays plain, with a mark of 0. When both terms act, the pure zones shrink to thin bands. A Dresselhaus term can start phase shifts even when it is small.
arxiv-2508-12128:
Taro Kimura and Go Noshita give a new integral formula for a counting object in geometry, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The object is the four-fold Pandharipande-Thomas vertex, used to count curves and surfaces inside four-dimensional spaces. Their method writes it as a contour integral handled by the Jeffrey-Kirwan residue, a rule for picking the right poles. The same integrand also yields the better-known Donaldson-Thomas vertex when a different reference vector is chosen.

Worked examples on curves and surfaces inside the four-fold show the machinery in action. The authors then examine the correspondence between the two counting theories in this setting, including higher-rank and supergroup-like versions. A shared integral behind both theories may simplify a correspondence that enumerative geometers have chased for years.
arxiv-2508-12228:
Haishan Ye and Xiangyu Chang present a 2025 theory paper on derivative-free optimization with the stingiest possible feedback. In the one-point setting, each query returns a single noisy function value, with no gradient and no paired comparison. Known methods of this kind need sample counts that grow quadratically or worse with the problem's dimension, while two-point methods reach the ideal linear growth. Whether one-point methods could match that rate was an open question.

The authors answer yes. Their algorithm reaches sample complexity that grows only linearly with dimension. The result closes a standing gap between the one-point and two-point theories. It matters for tuning and control problems where each test is costly and only one measurement per try is available. The title poses the question, and the paper resolves it.
arxiv-2508-12328:
Masanori Kobayashi asks whether a sender gains by persuading in stages rather than all at once. Persuasion games pit a sender's staged evidence against a receiver's belief updates. Receivers here update by rules that need not follow Bayes. Kobayashi studies a broad class of such non-Bayesian rules.

A property called divisibility decides the whole question. Under divisible rules, staged and one-shot persuasion pay the sender the same in any setting. Under other rules, staging can change the sender's take. So static persuasion loses nothing exactly when the receiver's rule is divisible. The result pins down when simple one-step designs suffice.
arxiv-2508-13028:
Li and six co-authors teach a speech synthesizer to sound sarcastic, a tone machines usually miss. Sarcasm lives in subtle melody and timing, and labeled sarcastic speech is scarce. Their method borrows feedback from a detector that judges sarcasm from both sound and text.

The detector's score becomes an extra training loss, pushing the synthesizer toward clearer sarcasm. A two-stage tune-up first exposes the model to many speech styles, then narrows to sarcastic speech. Listening tests and objective measures showed gains in quality, naturalness, and sarcasm strength. The authors aim at livelier entertainment and human-computer interaction.
arxiv-2508-14128:
Hu and three co-authors present a shield for large language models against jailbreak prompts in this twenty twenty-five paper. Jailbreak prompts try to trick a model into unsafe replies by hiding the true ask or by adding noise. The shield works at the prompt stage, before the model writes its reply.

Inside, the method first pulls out the core ask from a user prompt. It then checks that core alone and also checks the full prompt in a wrapped form. A final step picks the reply only when both checks agree it is safe. Tests show the shield cuts attack wins by half or more against strong attacks, while normal prompts still get good replies.
arxiv-2508-15128:
Mahadevan sets out a far wider frame for reinforcement learning, built on coalgebras and proof by coinduction, in work from twenty twenty-five. Math built on categories and functors already yields sharp takes on plain reinforcement learning. One known model of work spread across machines, not in lockstep, comes from Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis. Their settling theorem lines up with how coinductive proof works, step by step.

Markov chains, models that guess the next state, and straight-line systems all count as coalgebras of the right functors. Universal coalgebras stretch that kin far past the old cast of moving systems. The core fixed-point task grows too: find the final coalgebra while the work runs out of lockstep. Side-by-side work in topos-shaped functor categories frames the whole. The aim is one shared base for learning as a field.
arxiv-2508-15628:
Alan Guimarães surveys how two-fold symmetries and order-two symmetries intertwine inside the Grassmann algebra. That algebra, built on an infinite-dimensional vector space, is a cornerstone of superalgebra. A grading by parity splits it into even and odd parts; automorphisms of order two induce such superalgebra structures. Recent years have clarified how the two notions constrain each other.

The survey gathers those results over fields whose characteristic is not two. Concrete examples of non-homogeneous automorphisms, drawn from the cited literature, show the theory's sharper edges. Such automorphisms refuse to respect the grading one might expect. The paper closes with a conjecture on classifying all superalgebra structures the Grassmann algebra admits. As a survey, it maps a small field completely: what is known, what the examples teach, and what remains open.
arxiv-2508-16228:
Tymon Kilich and Krzysztof Pachucki compute a tiny magnetic effect in the hydrogen anion in a 2025 physics paper. The anion, a hydrogen atom with an extra electron, is the lightest stable negative ion. Physicists plan to compare it against the antiproton in a Penning trap, and magnetic shielding inside the ion affects that test.

The authors calculate how strongly the ion's electrons shield its nucleus from an outside magnetic field. They add corrections for the nucleus's finite mass, for relativity, and for quantum electrodynamics. The mass correction turns out surprisingly large, about a tenth of a percent. Their final value is accurate to nine parts per trillion, clearing the way for the antiproton comparison.
arxiv-2508-17028:
Thi-Nhung Nguyen, Hoang Ngo, Dinh Phung, Thuy-Trang Vu, and Dat Quoc Nguyen wrote this paper in 2025. It helps large language models answer questions about tables. Their method searches by entities. It does not rely on heavy clean-up of the table. It does not rely on matching keywords.

Tables are hard to work with. Their layouts vary a lot. They often lack clear context. That makes it hard for models to reason over them. The new method matches a question to table entities by meaning. It also follows the hidden links between cells. Each cell stays tied to the thing it names. The team also uses a graph query language for this task. They say this is a first. On two standard tests, WikiTableQuestions and TabFact, the method set new best scores.
arxiv-2508-17228:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim wrote a math paper in 2025 on Bell polynomials. Bell numbers count the ways to split a set into groups, a classic topic in counting math. A result by Spivey gave a rule to build each Bell value from smaller ones.

Later work stretched that rule to worn, degenerate versions of the numbers. The pair now stretch it further using chance. Their new rules cover both the degenerate Bell family and a wider r-Bell family. Random variables drive the proofs, which tie counting rules to expected values. The work adds a probability lens to a busy line of counting research.
arxiv-2508-17928:
Partitions count the ways a number can be split into pieces, and overpartitions loosen the rules by letting some pieces be marked. Mohammed Nadji and co-authors study a fresh family of these counts in this 2025 paper, built by stretching a classic Schur-style rule across a parameter.

They prove number-pattern results, called congruences, for several settings of that parameter: the small cases three and nine, and any power of two or three. Such patterns reveal hidden regularity in how the counts land across the number line. The work extends a line of research the first author helped start on this family.
arxiv-2508-18228:
Marianna Csornyei and her co-author Stull prove a new result in pure mathematics in a 2025 paper. Their topic is radial projection, which means looking at a set of points in the plane from one chosen point and asking how large the view of the set appears. They measure size using a notion of dimension suited to rough, scattered sets.

The authors improve the best known lower bound for that projected size. Their bound depends on the sizes of both the viewing set and the set being viewed, as long as the first set does not lie on a single line. The result sharpens what mathematicians can guarantee about how much of a set must remain visible from at least one viewpoint.
arxiv-2508-18328:
Masudul Hasan Masud Bhuiyan, Matteo Varvello, Yasir Zaki, and Cristian-Alexandru Staicu present a 2025 measurement study of the multilingual web and its barriers for blind users. Nearly half of top websites run in English, yet many mix English with local languages. Screen readers often handle non-Latin scripts poorly, misreading or mispronouncing text. To study the problem at scale, the team built LangCrUX, a data set of 120,000 popular sites across 12 languages that mainly use non-Latin scripts.

Their analysis found that accessibility hints on pages often fail to match the languages actually shown. That mismatch weakens screen readers and shuts out users who are not bilingual. The team also built Kizuki, a browser tool that tests pages with language awareness. The work gives developers a way to catch these barriers.
arxiv-2508-19228:
Zayd M K Zuhri, Erland Hilman Fuadi, and Alham Fikri Aji propose a gentler training goal for language models: predict the order of coming words rather than their exact identity. Their 2025 paper notes that guessing several future words exactly, a recently popular side goal, helps only inconsistently. Ordering those words by closeness in the text is an easier signal that still teaches foresight.

The method needs just one extra output layer. Models of three sizes trained this way beat the plain next-word baseline and both exact-prediction variants across nine standard benchmarks. Extra training on math and code kept the edge there too. On a graph path-finding task, only the order-trained models succeeded. A cheaper side goal may teach planning better than a harder one.
arxiv-2508-19628:
Yuichiro Kamada, Fuhito Kojima, and Akira Matsushita wrote this 2025 lecture paper on the costs of splitting matching markets into fragments. School choice, medical residency, and daycare placement all run as local markets, and walls between regions waste matches. The authors survey real cases, then test integration on Japanese daycare data.

Estimating family preferences, they simulate merging regional markets two ways: fully, or partially under a fairness rule that inflow equals outflow for each region. Partial integration recovered 39 to 60 percent of the welfare gain of full merging, worth a 3.3 to 4.9 percent cut in travel time. Unmatched children fell by a similar share. Even imperfect integration, they argue, claws back real losses.
arxiv-2508-19928:
Peter Hilgers and Anton Shutov published this mathematics overview in 2025 on the growth forms of tilings. A tiling covers a surface with shapes that fit without gaps. Around any chosen tile, other tiles sit in shells at fixed step distances from it. As those shells grow, their outline settles toward a limiting shape, which mathematicians call the growth form or corona limit.

The paper surveys what is known about these limit shapes across several families of tilings. It covers regular periodic tilings, multigrid tilings built from overlapping grids, substitution tilings that grow by repeated replacement, and the recently famous hat tiling. Along the way the authors collect proven results, open guesses, and questions nobody has settled yet. The overview serves as a map of a small but active corner of tiling theory.
arxiv-2508-20128:
Yue-Liang Wu presents the theoretical foundations of the General Standard Model, a framework unifying particle physics and cosmology inside Gravitational Quantum Field Theory. The paper from twenty twenty-five builds the model from first principles, starting only from the intrinsic properties of leptons and quarks. Its gauge symmetry enlarges the Standard Model's familiar trio with conformal inhomogeneous spin gauge structure. All four known interactions, plus the Higgs interaction, sit inside.

Novel forces are predicted alongside: spin gauge, chirality boost-spin gauge, and scaling gauge interactions among them. The framework claims fresh leverage on gravity, spacetime, dark matter origins, dark energy dynamics, and the inflationary epoch. The paper is a comprehensive analysis meant as a bridge between quantum field theory and general relativity.
arxiv-2508-21528:
Nick Laskin solves a textbook problem inside a new theory in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The theory is fractional quantum mechanics, which swaps the usual wave equation for one with fractional derivatives. The problem is a particle trapped in a finite square well, a standard model of confinement. Laskin finds the exact energy spectrum for that trap. He also gives a simple graphical method to count the bound levels and read off their energies.

The method turns a hard equation into a picture-based recipe. Such exact results are rare in the fractional theory and serve as benchmarks. They also suggest a practical path: real quantum wells might mimic fractional behavior. Physicists who test new quantum frameworks are the audience.
arxiv-2508-21628:
Sarfaroz Yunusov, Kaige Chen, Kazi Nishat Anwar, and Ali Emami ask if a user's traits predict which large language model they like to work with. As models join daily work, results are shaped through talks that run for many turns. It was not known if distinct trait types tend to favor distinct models.

The team ran a study with 32 people, spread evenly across four Keirsey types. Each person worked with both GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 on four joint tasks. The tasks were data work, creative writing, search for facts, and writing help. Likes proved strongly tied to traits. Rational types strongly liked GPT-4, most of all for goal-based tasks. Idealists favored Claude 3.5, most of all for creative and data tasks. Help scores were alike across models.
arxiv-2509-00228:
Wenqi Shi and José R. Zubizarreta present a weighting framework in 2025 for evidence synthesis that is both personalized and transparent. Causal methods have advanced fast, but most work stays inside single studies, which limits broad conclusions. Thorough causal understanding needs integration across diverse designs and data sources, aimed at specific patient groups.

Their framework handles both individual-level and aggregate-level data and extends classic regression-based meta-analysis. Weights tailor the synthesis to the covariate profile of a target population, so results speak to the patients at hand. The approach also keeps the synthesis open to inspection. Personalized synthesis could guide treatment choices for defined groups rather than averages alone.
arxiv-2509-00328:
Bear Häon, Kaylene Stocking, Ian Chuang, and Claire Tomlin introduce a framework in 2025 for interpreting and steering vision-language-action models from inside. Such models promise generalist embodied agents that adapt fast to new tasks and settings. Classic robotics steers by explicit models of motion and control, while learned policies offer little insight into their choices.

Borrowing from mechanistic interpretability work on language models, the team projects internal activations onto the token embedding basis. Sparse semantic directions emerge, such as speed, that can be intervened on at inference time. Direct steering of behavior follows from those directions. The method aims to bring robustness and explainability to learned robot policies.
arxiv-2509-00628:
Zihan Yan, writing alone, summarizes recent progress on light-ray focusing and horizon thermodynamics in diffeomorphism-invariant theories of gravity, theories whose laws do not depend on the coordinates chosen. The setting is gravity coupled to bosonic matter, fields whose particles carry whole-number spin.

Yan explains how the gravity equation on a slightly disturbed Killing horizon, a steady black hole boundary, generalizes the Raychaudhuri equation, which tracks how light rays converge. A generalized expansion never increases under the null energy condition, proving a focusing theorem and defining an increasing horizon entropy, called Wall entropy. With higher-spin fields, the theorem holds subject to a higher-spin focusing condition Yan proposes as a consistency test.
arxiv-2509-00928:
Lukas Pertl, with two co-authors, studies superposition in graph neural networks. Superposition is the sharing of directions by multiple features. It makes these networks hard to interpret. Message passing mixes signals across the graph. Internal channels rarely align with human concepts as a result.

The team uses controlled experiments with unambiguous graph concepts. Features are extracted in two ways. One uses class-conditional centroids at graph level. The other uses linear-probe directions at node level. Simple basis-invariant diagnostics then analyze their geometry. Wider models show a phase pattern in feature overlap. Topology imprints overlap onto node features, which pooling partly remixes. Sharper pooling increases axis alignment and cuts channel sharing.
arxiv-2509-01028:
Zixin Zhu leads a team of six authors on CompSlider for image generation with many attributes. Text-to-image models struggle with fine control of attributes. Age and smile are examples given in the paper. Slider methods offer precise control of single attributes. Existing ones train an adapter per attribute, though. Entanglement among attributes is overlooked as a result.

CompSlider generates a conditional prior for the base model. It controls many attributes at once through that prior. New losses compose multiple changes while keeping image structure. The method works in the latent space of the prior. It does not require retraining the base model at all. That cuts the burden for training and inference both. Tests cover varied attributes and extend to video.
arxiv-2509-01428:
A conjecture from 1994, settled in 2022, says every graph without isolated vertices holds a large induced subgraph where all degrees are odd. Jiangdong Ai, with four co-authors, generalizes that result. Their graphs carry labels of zero or one on each vertex, and the subgraph must give even degree to zero-labeled vertices and odd degree to one-labeled ones.

The team sets a pointwise lower bound for the largest such subgraph under a given labeling, which yields a linear bound for the worst labeling. For connected graphs they obtain a sharp bound tied to a chromatic quantity of the graph's minors. Using known cases of Hadwiger's conjecture, they settle several ranges of a related parameter. The work sharpens a classic result in graph theory about parity and dense substructures.
arxiv-2509-01528: Ylli Andoni and Shanshuang Yang study conformal maps, angle-preserving maps, from the unit disk onto a bounded Jordan domain, a region enclosed by a simple closed curve. They prove such a map is asymptotically symmetric exactly when the domain is bounded by a symmetric quasicircle, a curve with a matching symmetry trait. The result ties a map's limiting behavior to the shape of its boundary.
arxiv-2509-02428:
Yongwei Yuan and four co-authors wrote a 2025 programming languages paper on proving that code can go wrong in specified ways. Their setting is functional programs that call effectful library interfaces whose internals stay hidden.

Behaviour is captured by traces, time-ordered lists of library calls. Symbolic regular expressions describe those traces, letting the authors specify incorrect abstract data type behaviour across function boundaries. Their type inference algorithm works modulo the stated faults and uses symbolic finite automata to reason about traces piece by piece. When inference succeeds, the resulting types witness that an implementation can show some of the listed faults. The authors call it the first systematic under-approximate method for trace-based incorrectness specs.
arxiv-2509-03228:
Siqi Xiang and 5 co-authors built NeurStore in 2025, a system for storing deep learning models inside databases. Analytics increasingly run AI models where the data lives, so databases must hold growing fleets of large models. Storing each model as one whole file wastes space, and generic compression ignores how models are structured.

NeurStore stores models as tensors, the multi-dimensional arrays that hold their weights, and indexes them with an enhanced graph structure. Near-duplicate tensors are kept once, with only their small differences saved. A custom quantization step, which stores numbers at lower precision, squeezes those differences further while controlling accuracy loss. Loading can even compute directly on compressed tensors. Tests showed better compression ratios than leading approaches with competitive loading speed.
arxiv-2509-03428:
Athul S. Rema, Adrián E. Rubio López, and Felipe Herrera studied single-photon creation by a dipole inside a plasmonic nanocavity in a 2025 physics paper. Stationary spectra of such emitters are well mapped, but the coherent dynamics of photon birth in the cavity's near field were not. Their tool is a Lorentzian kernel approximation solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the coupled system.

The nanocavity's broadband response enters through a non-Markovian memory kernel, meaning the present behavior depends on the recent past. For a two-level dipole near a metal nanosphere, the photon's frequency spread starts localized at the qubit frequency. It then evolves into a Rabi doublet, a split pair of peaks signaling strong coupling, while interference patterns form in frequency and time. Driving the cavity with narrow pulses can even remove that splitting.
arxiv-2509-03628:
Measuring how often muon neutrinos striking argon produce exactly one charged pion is what the MicroBooNE collaboration does in a 2025 research paper. MicroBooNE is a detector experiment using the Booster Neutrino Beam, and the events studied are charged-current interactions, where the neutrino converts into a muon. Final states hold one pion and no other hadrons besides nucleons.

Cross sections, the effective target areas for the process, are reported for the full event set and sliced by particle momenta and angles. Kinematic cuts require muons and pions above set momenta and a limited angle between them. One measurement, the cross section against pion momentum for pions that rest without scattering first, is reported on argon for the first time. Comparisons with several neutrino interaction generators agree well overall. Only where muons emerge at very forward angles do models and data part ways.
arxiv-2509-03728:
Wesley Hanwen Deng and six co-authors' 2025 research paper focuses on using personas to improve automated red-teaming of AI models. Red-teaming probes models with adversarial prompts to surface risks before release. Human red-teamers bring identities and backgrounds that shape which attacks they invent, but automated systems had ignored identity entirely.

PersonaTeaming mutates attack prompts through assigned personas, either red-teaming experts or regular AI users. A dynamic algorithm also invents new persona types tailored to each seed prompt. New metrics measure mutation distance, complementing existing diversity scores for adversarial prompts. Across experiments, persona mutation raised attack success rates substantially, more than doubling in the best case, while keeping prompts diverse. Gains are measured against RainbowPlus, a leading automated red-teaming method. The authors discuss which persona types and mutation styles work best, and where automated and human red-teaming might complement each other.
arxiv-2509-03928:
Prasanna Kumar Billa and two co-authors devote a 2025 experimental physics paper to a water-repelling sphere plunging into a deep pool. A superhydrophobic sphere drags an air cavity behind it on entry, and that cavity later pinches off in stages. Entry dynamics matter for projectiles and engineered coatings meeting water at speed.

Two aspects are new. Experiments span a large range of densities relative to water. Light spheres, buoyed by their cavity, rise after entry, while heavy ones keep sinking. Pinch-off times for the primary and secondary cavity closures correlate with impact Froude number, a ratio of inertia to gravity, and with dimensionless density. A semi-empirical formula for cavity volume after pinch-off matches measurements across all densities. A force balance predicts a drastic buoyancy drop at pinch-off, confirmed by the abrupt deceleration two cameras recorded. Trajectories are compared with water-loving spheres from earlier work.
arxiv-2509-04028:
Andrea Begnoni and one co-author turn to telling primordial black holes apart from their impersonators at future gravitational wave observatories in a 2025 research paper. Primordial black holes, formed in the universe rather than from collapsing stars, would be a major discovery for cosmology and dark matter. No known astrophysical process makes sub-solar-mass black holes, so finding one would signal new physics.

Exotic objects, from strange quark stars to boson stars, can mimic them with similar signatures. The authors use the Fisher formalism across parameter ranges: binary masses, spins, and equations of state for nuclear and quark matter. They compute how far the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer could confidently detect sub-solar masses and tidal effects. Their results indicate sub-solar black holes could be probed out to cosmological distances around redshift three. For heavier objects, up to about two solar masses, tidal signatures do the distinguishing.
arxiv-2509-04128:
Ainhize Barrainkua and three co-authors examine fairness in the advice given to people turned down by algorithms in a 2025 research paper. Laws increasingly require such systems to offer recourse: concrete steps a person can take to flip a negative decision. Equal step costs for everyone can still burden some groups more, the authors show. They link fairness in the original decisions with fairness in the recourse offered, and expose limits of the usual equal-cost rule.

Their alternative framework measures social burden, the real-world weight of the steps demanded. A practical method called MISOB then cuts that burden for every group in tests on real data. Decision accuracy stayed intact while burdens fell.
arxiv-2509-04328:
Amine Barrak and three co-authors secure the full delivery pipeline for serverless software in a 2025 research paper. Serverless platforms run small functions briefly on demand, shifting infrastructure work to providers. Open-source option OpenFaaS is their case study. Short-lived, finely scaled functions create security gaps that phase-by-phase tools miss. Their system, FaaSGuard, plants lightweight checks that fail closed, meaning they block progress on doubt, at every stage from planning and coding through building, deployment, and monitoring.

Twenty real functions from public GitHub repositories went through the pipeline. Hard-coded secrets, injection attacks, and resource exhaustion were among the threats targeted. Detection precision and recall scored high, with little disruption to normal continuous delivery habits.
arxiv-2509-04428:
Maicon Hespanha and one co-author, Renzo Scarpelli, analyze a system of fourth-order Schrödinger equations at the energy-critical threshold in a 2025 mathematics paper. Such equations model waves with stronger dispersion than the classic Schrödinger equation. The focusing, radial case with general power-type nonlinearities is studied here. Ground states, the lowest-energy steady solutions, anchor the whole analysis.

Local well-posedness is established first in a standard smoothness space, after laying hypotheses on the nonlinearities and proving what they imply. A virial argument, an energy bookkeeping identity, then forces blow-up for data with negative energy or excessive kinetic energy. Finally, the concentration-compactness and rigidity method yields scattering for data below the ground state's thresholds. The results generalize earlier treatments of such systems.
arxiv-2509-04528:
Juan Sapriza and thirteen co-authors present a fingernail-scale chip that measures the electrical impedance of body tissue in a 2025 engineering paper. Biological impedance reveals health and emotional signals without breaking the skin, yet research gear is usually bulky or single-purpose. Their system-on-chip, HEEPidermis, integrates everything needed: current generators, analog-to-digital converters based on oscillators, and a RISC-V processor for on-chip feature extraction toward closed-loop running.

An event-driven sub-sampler trims storage needs and saves energy during long recordings. The digital back-end and analog front-end models are open source, enabling fast simulation and reuse by other groups. The chip was fabricated in a TSMC 65-nanometer process. Wearable impedance research gains a versatile platform.
arxiv-2509-04928:
Economic factors behind many series may affect each series through an unknown, possibly nonlinear link. Tony Chernis, lead author with three co-authors, propose a Bayesian dynamic factor model with that flexibility in a 2025 econometrics paper. Gaussian process priors define the observation equation for each series, replacing a fixed linear link.

Factor dynamics follow a standard vector autoregression, which aids computation and interpretation. The authors describe an efficient estimation algorithm. In applications, the model improves forecasts of key United States series over linear benchmarks. It also extracts drivers of global inflation while capturing differences between countries.
arxiv-2509-05028:
Three numbers describe a solid's size from different angles: its diameter, its inradius, and its circumradius. René Brandenberg, lead author with two co-authors, present a complete system of inequalities linking those quantities in three-dimensional Euclidean space in a 2025 geometry paper. A complete system means the inequalities capture all relations among the three measures.

To build it, they prove quasiconcavity of the inradius over simplices that share a common facet. That result holds independently of the norm or gauge used to measure distance. The paper finishes a classical problem about how the three size measures constrain one another.
arxiv-2509-05228:
A voltage controlled phase shifter for particle accelerators is the subject of a 2025 engineering paper by Ilan Ben-Zvi and two co-authors. The device shifts the phase of a radio signal, meaning its timing within the wave, and it is built to handle very high average power.

The design uses ferroelectric capacitors, whose response changes with voltage, inside a resonant reflection circuit matched to its port. The authors report a very high ratio of phase shift to signal loss, a response under a millionth of a second, and power handling up to a megawatt. Better shifters of this kind could raise accelerator efficiency and cut both building and running costs.
arxiv-2509-05328:
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model without losing its toughness on unfamiliar data is the problem Xiang Yuan and three co-authors address in a 2025 machine learning paper. Earlier fixes guarded the model's weights, features, or outputs, yet those stand-ins do not always protect the actual function the model computes.

Their method limits how far the fine-tuned function drifts from the original, judged on simulated unfamiliar samples. A second rule keeps predictions stable when inputs are slightly perturbed, which further guards robustness. Across many vision-language backbones, the approach improved both the new task score and robustness to shifted data. It beat earlier regularisation methods on both measures.
arxiv-2509-06028:
How an isolated quantum system thermalizes, acting as its own heat bath, is tackled from first principles in a 2025 paper by Alexander Altland and two co-authors. Their quasiclassical Green function approach fuses several tools of many-body theory: the nonlinear sigma model of disordered systems, a strong-correlation formalism, and real-time path integrals. The result aims beyond earlier perturbation theory.

The theory follows thermalization from short scattering times through an effective Thouless time, when ergodicity sets in, out to the many-body Heisenberg time. Two case studies test it: a brickwork circuit model with and without conserved symmetries, and an array of capacitively coupled quantum dots. Using the spectral form factor as the check, agreement with numerical simulations is good. The authors present the formalism as a self-contained toolbox.
arxiv-2509-06628:
Three kinds of dark matter hunt are weighed together by Igor Reis and three co-authors in a 2025 astroparticle physics paper. The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory will watch the Galactic Center for light from dark matter annihilation. The authors forecast its reach inside two theory frameworks: effective field theory and simplified models with a mediator particle.

Their forecasts use an up-to-date instrument setup, current models of diffuse galactic glow, and fresh dark matter density profiles from the FIRE-2 cosmological simulations. Constraints from underground detectors and from ATLAS and CMS collider searches are updated with the same astrophysical inputs. Combined, the limits on the effective scale and on mediator mass improve on earlier studies. Scalar, pseudoscalar, vector, and axial-vector interactions are all covered, showing how the three search styles complement each other.
arxiv-2509-06828: Wobbles in a rotating black hole's spacetime are given curvature estimates by Gabriele Benomio and one co-author in a 2025 mathematical relativity paper. The setting is the linearized vacuum Einstein equations around a Kerr black hole exterior. Such estimates are steps toward proving that Kerr black holes are stable under small disturbances. The scheme uses a linearized system derived in the first author's doctoral thesis and covers the full sub-extremal range of Kerr spin values.
arxiv-2509-07328:
New Hampshire's legislative maps drew lawsuits after the 2020 census, with claims about fairness and gerrymandering. Atticus McWhorter and Daryl DeFord answer with an ensemble analysis in a 2025 research paper. They encode the state's redistricting rules, then generate a large collection of alternative maps by computer. The enacted maps can then be judged against that neutral baseline.

Their comparison shows how the chosen districts trade off geographic goals against partisan outcomes. The analysis also tests non-partisan justifications offered for the enacted plan. A further finding concerns the election data itself: how results are selected and combined changes measures of partisan symmetry. The work gives courts and the public a firmer mathematical footing for judging whether a map is an outlier.
arxiv-2509-07528:
Atoms excited to Rydberg states, with electrons pushed far from the nucleus, interact strongly over long distances. Suvechha Indu, Aniruddha Biswas, and Raka Dasgupta study such atoms trapped in an optical lattice in a 2025 research paper. Their system loses energy to its surroundings, making it dissipative and out of equilibrium. Several atoms may share one lattice site.

Depending on the on-site interaction strength, the excitation pattern settles uniformly or forms a density wave, alternating between sublattices like an antiferromagnet.
