A mean-field treatment also predicts an oscillating phase, though direct simulation in one dimension does not find it. The authors trace each phase through spatial correlations and fixed points of the dynamics. A starting population imbalance between sublattices strengthens the density-wave order. The study clarifies how driven quantum systems choose their patterns.
arxiv-2509-07728:
John Gouwar and 5 co-authors extend the Spack package manager in 2025 so it can mix pre-built binaries with source builds safely. Binary managers install fast but lock users into rigid compatibility, or ABI, requirements. Source managers like Spack, built for high-performance computing, allow deep customization but can force full rebuilds: swap one MPI library and an entire stack may recompile.

Their extension, splicing, adds a binary compatibility model to Spack's packaging language and dependency solver. Compatible binaries are reused where possible, while source builds stay available everywhere else. Installation-time overhead stays minimal in their tests, and rapid binary installation works even for ABI-sensitive dependencies such as MPI. The change targets computing centers where rebuild storms waste scarce supercomputer time.
arxiv-2509-08028:
Criminal networks change over time, and Daniel Catlin and 2 co-authors build that motion into network analysis in a 2025 criminology paper. Static maps can misidentify the key players in a drug trafficking organisation, because roles and relationships shift during an investigation. Data from court records also carry uncertainty about which links truly exist.

Using records from a two-year investigation, the team applies a dynamic version of Katz centrality to track each actor's importance across time. A new method adds possible missing edges through random Bernoulli trials, testing how robust the rankings are to data gaps. Police and analysts who target interventions at supposedly central figures need exactly this kind of time-aware, uncertainty-checked picture.
arxiv-2509-08128:
Why do some posts collect likes while similar ones draw replies instead? Yulin Yu and 3 co-authors decode mismatched engagement on Twitter in a 2025 social media study. Likes, retweets, and comments form a signalling system inside the attention economy, and the mix a post receives carries meaning beyond its total popularity.

An unexpectedness quotient quantifies how far each engagement type deviates from predictions. Analysis of over six hundred thousand tweets reveals distinct patterns behind the surprises, interpreted through signaling theory and attention economy ideas. Brands, campaigns, and researchers who read only total counts miss this structure; knowing which signal a post over-delivers helps explain what audiences actually valued about it.
arxiv-2509-08228:
Future cameras may shoot gigapixel video at a thousand frames per second, but today's sensors would melt the power budget. Miao Cao and 5 co-authors tackle that wall in a 2025 research paper. They work on video snapshot compressive imaging, which encodes many frames into one measurement at the sensor. Their ultra-sparse sampling sets exactly one sub-frame active at each pixel location.

Recovering the video from such sparse data is the hard part. The team built a real encoding system with a digital micromirror device to prove the sampling works. They then designed BSTFormer, a sparse transformer using block, global, and temporal attention. Tests on simulated and real data beat all previous methods clearly. The sampling strategy also offers a higher dynamic range than random sampling, and suits on-chip camera systems.
arxiv-2509-08328:
Car option-package pricing, a real automotive optimisation problem, becomes a test case for a quantum algorithm in a 2025 paper by Francesc Sabater and 8 co-authors. Decoded quantum interferometry has drawn attention as a promising quantum optimisation route. The authors walk the industrial problem through every step needed to run it.

The pricing problem is first written as an integer linear program, then converted into max-XORSAT instances, a form the quantum method consumes. A detailed circuit implements belief propagation, the decoding heuristic borrowed from error-correcting codes. End-to-end demonstrations on genuine industrial problems are how quantum optimisation earns credibility: they reveal the encoding costs and circuit depths that toy examples politely hide.
arxiv-2509-08428:
Bilayers of normal metal and ferromagnet can rectify radio signals through their own magnetisation, model Ulli Gems and 2 co-authors in a 2025 spintronics paper. Charge currents in the metal excite magnetic dynamics through the spin-Hall effect, and the inverse effect reads the motion back out. The response of interest is quadratic in the applied field, a diode-like rectification.

Near the frequencies of coherent magnetisation modes, that response is resonantly enhanced. A magneto-electric circuit theory captures the effect for magnetic insulators and magnetic metals alike, focusing on spin currents aligned with the equilibrium magnetisation. Spin-torque diodes already serve as sensitive microwave detectors; a circuit-level theory helps engineers design them deliberately instead of by trial fabrication.
arxiv-2509-08928:
Remy Mahfouf introduces an embedding deformation method for the near critical random bond Ising model in a 2025 paper. Ising models describe interacting spins, and s-embeddings give them a geometric form. Coupling constants vary across a family of models.

Differential equations continuously deform the embeddings as couplings change. That yields a geometric view of the critical scaling window on a large grid. Driving the deformation with Brownian motion on each edge creates random embeddings for random bond models. With high probability, conformal invariance survives in the scaling limit even for fairly large randomness. A slightly correlated version gets an even wider critical window.
arxiv-2509-09028:
Paolo Lipari and 1 co-author study the spatial distribution of cosmic rays and the galactic to extragalactic transition in a 2025 paper. Cosmic rays are high energy particles moving through the Milky Way. Their spread shapes the gamma ray and neutrino glow from interstellar gas.

Most models assume spectral shape is the same everywhere, with only intensity changing. New data from Fermi, Tibet, LHAASO, HAWC, and IceCube test that assumption. Results disfavor harder spectra in the inner galaxy and mildly favor softer inner spectra at very high energy. A growing confinement volume with energy could explain the pattern. An extragalactic share at the highest energies is another possible explanation.
arxiv-2509-10128:
Philip Arm and 5 co-authors develop energy-saving control for legged robots in this 2025 paper. Legged machines are strong candidates for exploring the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, where ground is rough. Their power and cooling budgets are tight, so controllers must waste little energy and must work under very different gravity.

The team trained reinforcement learning controllers with reward functions scaled by gravity and tuned to reward low power use. The same approach produced walking and body-pose controllers from lunar gravity up to a heavy super-Earth case. On a real robot under Earth gravity, the walking controller used about a fifth less power than a baseline. A spring offload rig let them test in simulated lunar gravity, where savings grew larger still.
arxiv-2509-10528:
City data arrives as a tangle of places and times, and Amirhossein Ghaffari with three co-authors release STM-Graph to tame it in this 2025 software paper. Their open-source Python framework converts raw urban event records into graph form, the format graph neural networks need for prediction tasks like forecasting demand or incidents across a city.

The package bundles several spatial mapping methods, pulls urban features from OpenStreetMap, and ships with multiple graph network models ready to train. Visualization tools and a graphical interface aim the tool at practitioners as well as researchers, including users who do not code. The design is modular, so new mapping methods and custom models slot in easily. For urban computing teams, the value is speed: faster experiments and cleaner benchmarks on messy real-world data.
arxiv-2509-11128:
Yibo Zhang and Liang Lin present ERIS in this 2025 paper on the security of audio large models, systems that take spoken input. Safety training for these models is usually tested on clean recordings, not on the messy sound of real places.

ERIS turns everyday background interference into a carrier for hidden spoken instructions. A genetic algorithm breeds and mixes naturalistic sounds, joining harmful requests with ordinary noise until the result sounds harmless to people and to safety filters yet still slips past the model's defenses. Tested on several audio models, the evolved clips beat both text-based and earlier audio attacks. The findings warn builders that real-world noise is an attack surface worth defending.
arxiv-2509-11228:
Rocks squeezed gently behave in a nonlinear way. This 2025 geomechanics paper by Rui Li and four co-authors simulates that behavior from images. At low stress, tiny cracks and grain contacts close up. The rock stiffens before settling into ordinary elastic response.

Image-based models usually miss this effect. Single image voxels are bigger than the cracks. Each voxel mixes pore space with solid. The authors treat mixed voxels as a transitional material. Its stiffness is middling. Its pore part deforms first. Finite element simulations then run on the digital rock. Two Bentheimer sandstone models served as tests. The method reproduced how porosity changes as stress rises. It also reproduced the elastic property changes.
arxiv-2509-11728:
Lauri Seppäläinen and three co-authors show a humble algorithm doing elite chemistry. This 2025 atmospheric science paper treats molecular clusters in air. How clusters form and grow seeds new aerosol particles. That process is a big climate uncertainty. Quantum chemistry is too slow to map it at scale.

Their tool is k-nearest neighbor regression. Chemically informed distance measures arm it. One measure is learned by metric learning. On molecular benchmarks, the simple models rivaled kernel ridge regression. Large cluster datasets told the same story. Sulfuric acid with water was one. Sulfuric acid with many bases was another. The models scaled past a quarter million entries. Errors on unseen larger clusters often neared one kilocalorie per mole.
arxiv-2509-12028:
Networks where a link can join three or more nodes at once, like co-authors on one paper, need hypergraphs rather than ordinary graphs. Yichao Chen, with two co-authors, proposes a new statistical model for such data in 2025, built on non-symmetric determinantal point processes.

Older hypergraph models mostly force every edge to the same size or lean only on node variety. A determinantal process naturally balances similarity and diversity among a hyperedge's members, allows edges of any size, and still yields a probability formula one can actually compute. Fitting runs through likelihood maximization with a projected adaptive gradient method. The authors prove the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, support it with simulations, and test edge prediction on several real datasets.
arxiv-2509-12128:
Star formation in the Milky Way's disk, regulated by plain pressure, is modeled analytically by José Franco and three co-authors in 2025. Their steady-state picture links the midplane interstellar pressure and metallicity to how molecular clouds are born and how quickly they turn into stars.

Beyond about five kiloparsecs from the center, pressure tracks the molecular gas surface density almost linearly. Cold neutral gas turns molecular once dust grains shield a cloud's core from dissociating radiation, and self-gravity takes over at a threshold column that grows with the square root of pressure. Following that two-step track across the disk, the authors derive the star formation rate at each radius. The final efficiency lands at only a few percent. That matches the galaxy's famously lazy pace.
arxiv-2509-12228:
Splitting a simulation across subdomains only works if the pieces agree at their shared borders. Cameron Rodriguez and five co-authors study that border problem in 2025 for the non-overlapping Schwarz method, which passes information between neighboring regions that do not overlap at all.

Two styles of border condition are compared, alternating Dirichlet-Neumann and Robin-Robin, across couplings of full physics models with fast reduced models built by operator inference. On a one-dimensional elastic wave test, Robin-Robin often converges faster, though poor tuning adds ripples at the seams. Richer reduced bases can beat even the full-model pairing in both accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2509-12328:
Do giant planets far from a star inflate smaller planets closer in? Dolev Bashi examines that question in a 2025 paper on Neptune-sized planets with short orbits. He compares planets whose stars host a confirmed outer giant with similar planets in systems with no giant.

On a mass-radius diagram, the two groups diverge modestly: inner planets with an outer giant cluster at larger radii for the same mass. Bayesian modeling put the average radius enhancement at roughly a sixth, after controlling for planet and star properties. Alternative cuts using a uniform set of parameters supported the signal, though the sample is small. Possible explanations include a longer supply of inner-disk gas that boosted envelope growth, among other mechanisms the author discusses.
arxiv-2509-12428:
Rye Howard-Stone and Ion Mandoiu describe MHASS, a simulator for microbiome sequencing data, in a 2025 paper. Microbiome studies often use PacBio HiFi amplicon sequencing, a long-read method that reads marker genes from many microbes at once. Testing study workflows for such data needs real-life synthetic data sets with known contents.

MHASS builds those data sets by combining genome-aware abundance modeling, how common each microbe is set from its genome, real-life dual-barcoding methods, and pass-number spreads taken from actual sequencing runs. The result is tailored data for benchmarking tasks such as grouping series into variants and assigning taxonomic names. The software is written in Python and is freely available, with supplementary evaluation material online.
arxiv-2509-13128:
Raphael Monat shrinks the Mopsa static checker to run in a browser alone in 2025. Static checkers prove facts about code without running it. Full tools carry heavy parts and hard installs, which block students and new users.

Try-Mopsa is compiled to JavaScript and needs no server. Its screen responds well on desktop and phone screens. All core Mopsa parts remain, with relational number domains kept in full. Changes needed for pure browser run are set out. The tool is pitched for first contact and teaching, where a pocket checker lowers the entry bar by much.
arxiv-2509-13328:
Danish Rizvi and David Boyle jointly tune in 2025 a drone-carried STAR surface, base beams, and flight path for multi-user downlinks. Past work treats transmit and reflect factors as free, which overstates gains. A coupled phase model is more honest.

A dual-actor deep learner handles mixed discrete and continuous acts. Two actor nets split the hybrid space. A harmonic fairness reward guards user equity. Surface size drag on flight energy is counted too. Gains top standard learners by large shares. Mobile beats fixed, and coupled beats split surfaces.
arxiv-2509-13628:
Mert Gürbüzbalaban, Yasa Syed, and Necdet Serhat Aybat study a trade-off in optimization in a 2025 paper: faster gradient methods tend to suffer more when gradient estimates are biased or adversarial. They examine generalized momentum methods, a family covering plain gradient descent, heavy-ball, and Nesterov acceleration, on smooth strongly convex problems.

For quadratic problems with Gaussian noise, they compute a risk-sensitive index from robust control theory in closed form, exposing a Pareto frontier between speed and robustness as step size and momentum vary. A large-deviation principle then links that index to how rarely the averaged iterates stay badly suboptimal. Beyond quadratics, they prove finite-time, high-probability guarantees under biased noise, the first such results for this method family.
arxiv-2509-13728:
K. Larbaoui, A. Lakdja, and G. Bassou study a novel ferromagnetic alloy from first principles in a 2025 paper. The alloy mixes potassium and calcium with nitrogen in varying proportions. Predicting whether such a mixture stays blended or separates into phases matters for any future use of the material.

The authors study structural traits and phase stability using a regular-answer model based on the total energy of mixing. A pseudopotential approach was used with a standard density functional. They investigated the bond-length spread as a function of composition and predicted phase separation of the two partially miscible parts, calculating the mixing enthalpy using an contact setting. Asymmetry about a mid-range composition appeared in the phase diagram due to the composition-dependent contact setting. The equilibrium solubility limit, the miscibility gap, was estimated at a very high temperature.
arxiv-2509-13828:
Nick Evans and Wanxiang Fan study chiral symmetry in a holographic model in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Chiral symmetry is the near-equivalence of left and right-handed quarks. It breaks spontaneously in strong magnetic fields. A helical field twists as it goes. Its wave vector can dial the breaking effect up or down.

The pair work in a bottom-up AdS/CFT model. Such a model maps a hard quantum problem to an easier gravitational one. In the helical field, the symmetric solution first loses stability. As the wave vector grows, stability returns, through a first-order transition. Seen from low energies, the twist averages away and the field drops out of sight. Both magnetic catalysis and its inverse show up. Each switches off when the wave vector grows large.
arxiv-2509-13928:
Belliard and Hutsalyuk compute full counting statistics for a quantum spin chain in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. The system is the twisted XXX chain. It is a ring of interacting spin one-half particles with a twist in its boundary conditions. It is also one of the classic exactly solvable models of quantum magnetism. Full counting statistics means the complete probability distribution of a measured spin quantity, not just its average.

The authors work with the quantum inverse scattering formalism and the modified algebraic Bethe ansatz. Those are the tools that make this model solvable. They construct an explicit formula for the statistics of an arbitrary spin operator. The formula takes the form of a form factor expansion, a sum over the chain's excited states. An abstract distribution becomes something computable term by term.
arxiv-2509-14128:
Monica Sekoyan and seven co-authors release two speech models in a 2025 technical report from the NVIDIA speech team. Canary-1B-v2 handles automatic speech recognition and speech-to-text translation across twenty-five mostly European languages, pairing a FastConformer encoder with a Transformer decoder, and a smaller companion, Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3, covers the same languages for recognition alone.

Training used well over a million hours of audio, with non-speech material mixed in to suppress hallucinated transcripts, and a two-stage pretraining then fine-tuning recipe with dynamic data balancing. A forced aligner with an auxiliary model supplies segment-level timestamps. Canary beats Whisper-large-v3 on English recognition while running about ten times faster, and stays competitive with much larger multilingual systems on translation.
arxiv-2509-14228:
Benjamin Shaffer and four co-authors consider robot teams hunting for the source of a leak or spill in moving water or air in 2025. Flow can shift and churn, so sensor readings come in bursts. The shape of the space also makes spread hard to predict.

Each robot in their system carries a learned physics based model of its surroundings on board. The robots use that model to pick sensing spots expected to give the most useful information about the source, a strategy called infotaxis. Compared with standard sensing plans, their approach cut error faster. It also located sources more accurately than plain machine learning baselines, even with limited computing on each robot.
arxiv-2509-14428:
Haolin Zou, Heyuan Yao and Victor de la Peña derive a scalable formula in 2025 for moments of self normalised statistics. Such statistics divide a quantity by a power of the sample mean, following the pattern of the classic t-statistic. Their chance behaviour was largely unknown.

The unified formula gives closed form moments for several important cases with nonnegative data. Its complexity does not grow with sample size, which keeps it usable for large samples. Numerical tests back the theory and reveal new facts about bias and variance. A debiasing method follows, illustrated on the odds ratio, the Gini coefficient and the squared coefficient of variation. Those measures appear across economics, ecology and machine learning.
arxiv-2509-14528:
Pradyumna Shome, Sashreek Krishnan and Sauvik Das examine AI agents in 2025 through the gap between industry marketing and user reality. Agent is used loosely, blurring what systems can do and how usable they are. Two questions structure the study.

A systematic review of marketed uses for over a hundred commercial agents finds three buckets: orchestration, creation and insight. A usability study then had thirty one participants attempt representative tasks on two popular agent tools. Many advertised capabilities proved hard to realise in practice. Failures clustered around setup, control and recovery from agent mistakes. The authors argue honest capability language and usability testing matter as much as model gains for everyday users.
arxiv-2509-15228:
Vasily Tarasov builds fractional dynamics where scaling is not local in time, in a solo 2025 paper. Plain scaling stretches a system in a uniform way. Non-local scaling lets the stretch hinge on the system's past. His tools are integro-differential operators of non-integer order, of Hadamard type, which extend the scaling operator.

Nonlinear problems with these operators and a timed chain of kicks have exact answers found with no approximation tricks. Reading those answers at set time points gives maps with non-local scaling in time, again exact. The build works for any positive order of the operators, and a worked case is given. Since no shortcuts sneak in, the maps track the smooth dynamics with care.
arxiv-2509-15428:
Michael Dritschel, Alejandra Maestripieri, and James Rovnyak continue a study of sums inside Krein spaces. A Krein space is like a standard inner product space, but some lengths can be negative. Part one of their work dealt with sums of well behaved parts of such a space. Here they turn to a wider class of parts, called quasi-pseudo-regular.

Such a part splits into a well behaved piece and a neutral piece, where all lengths are zero. The trio give new ways to tell when a part has this form. They study endless sums of these parts with a flexible sum notion based on ranges of operators. The paper is dense and aimed at experts in operator theory.
arxiv-2509-15528:
Hemansh Alkesh Shah and Kolahal Bhattacharya write a teaching study on a magnet near a superconducting ball. Students worldwide learn the method of images for electric charges near metal balls. The same trick can solve magnet problems, but textbooks rarely show it. A magnetic dipole near such a ball is a good case: the source has direction, unlike a point charge.

The pair solve the case where the dipole points straight at the ball with a single image dipole. For the sideways case, they model the dipole as a loop of current. They find images for the loop's parts that meet the edge rules. From those parts they deduce the image dipoles for the sideways case. The study suits class use.
arxiv-2509-15728: Chuyu Zhou, writing alone, proves a finiteness result about moduli spaces in algebraic geometry. These spaces, called K-moduli, collect stable pairs of shapes and divisors. The note shows that stability splits the space into finitely many chambers with a clean algebraic form. The proof rests on one assumption: that the degenerations of semistable pairs stay within a bounded family. The hope that such spaces turn out finite is what motivates that assumption. The result is a short, technical note for specialists in K-stability.
arxiv-2509-15828:
Ning Xu leads a team that speeds up hard planning problems with integer choices. Such problems, called integer linear programs, are slow for classic solvers at large scale. A search method that fixes most choices and redoes a neighborhood can help, but weak neighborhoods cap its gains. The team wanted stronger neighborhoods, picked on the fly.

Their frame mixes a hand built formula with a learning policy. The formula scores each variable's chance of joining the neighborhood, based on known feasible plans. The policy network picks the neighborhood size. Across tests, the frame beats past search based rivals by a wide margin. It stays light and scales well. The work targets very large planning problems.
arxiv-2509-16028:
Spoken chat systems that think with large language models often sound stiff, since good written text differs from good speech. Sang Hoon Woo and three co-authors split the job into three steps: think, put thoughts into speech-ready words, then speak. A fast tool called ReVerT does the middle step bit by bit, without waiting for the full reply.

Across several test sets, the split keeps the quality of the reasoning while speech sounds more natural and brief. The method shows that a short rewording stage can bridge deep thought and clear talk. Code and data for the work are shared in public.
arxiv-2509-16128:
Writing help from AI often arrives in a chat box, far from the lines it talks about, and writers may follow it too blindly. Martin Lou and three co-authors build AnchoredAI, a tool that pins each AI comment to the exact span of text it concerns. The tool keeps a rich link for each comment and updates that link when the draft changes.

In a controlled study against a chat-based tool, writers using the anchored version made more focused edits. They also reported a stronger sense of control and ownership of their work. The study shows that where feedback sits shapes how writers use it.
arxiv-2509-16328:
Language models that read medical scans and draft reports need both sharp accuracy and fast replies in the clinic. Jyun-Ping Kao reviews the graphics chips that supply the raw power for such work, from leading vendors' current lines. Key traits include raw compute speed, memory bandwidth, and onboard memory size.

Studies on chest image sets show the right chips cut wait times and raise throughput for report drafting and finding detection. The review also weighs privacy, cost, and power, plus tricks like lower precision math and model compression. Future chip traits should ease local and shared hospital use.
arxiv-2509-16428:
Rare isotopes live for a blink, so weighing them precisely and sorting them from near twins takes a nimble trap. F. M. Maier and nine co-authors design a multi-reflection time-of-flight device for a rare isotope facility, where ions bounce between mirrors to stretch their flight path. It stores ions at higher energy than usual, which boosts throughput while keeping sharp mass resolution.

The device would sharpen mass measures of short-lived isotopes, improve beam checks, and deliver purified beams to later stations. Simulations in the design study show the expected performance. The upgrade would widen the science reach of stopped and reaccelerated beam programs.
arxiv-2509-16628:
Janak Kapuriya and co-authors help small vision models answer science questions in a 2025 paper. The questions pair images, like charts or diagrams, with text. Small models often lag large ones on such tasks. The team use image captions as extra prompts during training. Captions tell the model what the image shows in words.

Training with captions lifted scores by a clear margin. The team also built a new test set for high-school science questions. A large model grades answers in their new scoring scheme, going past simple word matching. Code and data are shared in public. Smaller models that do well could run cheaply in classrooms.
arxiv-2509-16728:
Yassine Sekhmani and co-authors build exotic black hole solutions in a 2025 theory paper. Their holes live in higher dimensions and carry several extras at once. A global defect threads the space. A non-linear gauge field adds hair. A surrounding gas follows a generalized rule that links its pressure and density.

The field equations yield closed forms for the density and for a key shape function. Varying charges and couplings gives rich phase behavior. Maps of the defect shift in topology as settings change. The work shows how gauge quirks, defects, and odd matter jointly reshape heat traits of black holes. It is pure theory, aimed at deep gravity questions.
arxiv-2509-16828:
Sergio I. López, Juan C. Pardo, and Leandro P. R. Pimentel study sudden memory loss in random systems in a 2025 probability paper. A system can hold a trace of its starting state for a long while. The team define abrupt decorrelation: a sharp, sudden drop in that trace. They ask when such a drop occurs in linear random equations.

Their main case is a multi-variable process that pulls back toward a center. In one dimension, they extend results to drifts that change over time. The pattern echoes the cut-off effect known in Markov chains. Knowing when memory snaps off helps statisticians judge how long to run simulations before trusting them.
arxiv-2509-17428:
Hyesung Jeon, Seojune Lee, Beomseok Kang, Yulhwa Kim, and Jae-Joon Kim shrink language models for cheap fine-tuning. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins two trends: quantization, which cuts inference cost by storing weights in fewer bits, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which cuts training cost. In a quantized model, trimming the quantization error before fine-tuning is the key to accuracy.

Plain low-rank adapters lack the expressive range for that job. Fourier-style adapters are stronger, but bolting them onto quantized models can waste compute and miss the error. Their method, QWHA, uses the Walsh-Hadamard transform as its kernel and adds a careful adapter start, with adaptive parameter choice and value refinement. Tests show the method cuts quantization error while letting fine-tuning proceed. The result is a route to accurate quantized models that stay cheap to adapt.
arxiv-2509-17528:
Chen'guang Su and seven co-authors built a cold detector for rare particle events. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes a system of two large pure cesium iodide crystals, each a few kilograms, cooled to near ninety-five kelvin. Such detectors hunt faint signals, from coherent neutrino scattering to other low-energy rarities, where a bright, quiet crystal is gold.

Each wedge-shaped crystal is read at both ends by photomultiplier tubes that catch its scintillation light. The measured light yield came out high, with sharp energy resolution at low energy. The system showed even response across its volume, low inbuilt radioactivity, and stable running over a full month. Geant4 simulations of the light matched the observed trends and now guide design tweaks. The authors conclude that cryogenic pure CsI can scale up for low-threshold searches.
arxiv-2509-17628:
Yuzhen Lei, Hongbin Xie, Jiaxing Zhao, Shuangxue Liu, and Xuan Song built a benchmark for agents that must reason in stages. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that language models shine at single-domain questions, yet real work chains tasks across stages. Current benchmarks test isolated skills and miss how agents coordinate and optimize over a long job with no outside guidance.

Their benchmark, MSCoRe, holds a large set of domain question-answer items from the automotive, pharmaceutical, electronics, and energy sectors. A three-phase pipeline samples items, generates pairs, and grades quality at several levels. Tasks sort into three difficulty tiers by stage coverage and complexity. Tests of leading agents show commercial models ahead on all fronts. A clear gap in matching scores still splits simple tasks from complex ones, which is the headroom the benchmark was built to expose.
arxiv-2509-17828:
Stefan Kettemann extends a maths tool for messy spin chains to hot and excited states. His 2025 paper works on chains where bond strengths vary at random and spins pull on each other. The tool, a strong disorder method, zooms out step by step to a simple form.

For near-neighbour chains, link sizes settle into a known wild spread, while signs spread and grow more mixed with heat. For long-range links, he derives a master rule for all pairs. From it he gets heat traits such as response to a magnet field, pair links, and shared entropy.
arxiv-2509-18328:
Distant galaxies are hard to read: their gas motion shows up blurred and faint. M. Yttergren and six co-authors test how well three software tools recover that motion. Their 2025 paper builds fake galaxies that spin like disks, then makes fake telescope data from them. The fake data mimics what the ALMA telescope would record.

The tools, 3DBarolo, GalPaK3D, and Qubefit, each fit a 3D model to the fake data. On average all three were sound for group studies, with small over- or under-estimates of how cold and orderly the spin is. For single galaxies, though, the range of answers was wide. That range grows for galaxies that are not clean spinners. The authors urge readers to use their listed offsets and ranges when reading real distant galaxies. They also note a quick check that can be pulled from the data cube itself.
arxiv-2509-18528:
Carbon dioxide pushed past its critical point acts like both gas and liquid, and engineers want to use it for power and carbon storage. Julia Ream and five co-authors simulate turbulent jets of this supercritical fluid in this 2025 paper. Odd shifts in its properties near a pseudo-boiling point can change how a jet mixes and breaks up. The team asks how much of that change comes from heat effects alone.

They ran large eddy simulations of three jets with a flow solver and an equation of state for non-ideal gas behavior. The uniform-temperature jet behaved much like a normal gas jet, with small shifts in decay and spread. A heated jet that stayed off the pseudo-boiling point differed only slightly. Crossing that point changed things a lot: stronger shear instabilities appeared and the jet fell apart much faster. That faster breakup boosts mixing.
arxiv-2509-18628: Some algebras split one operation into two linked parts, and others merge parts in a set order. H. Alhussein proposes a new way to build the graded chains used to study such algebras, called dendriform algebras and pre-Lie algebras, in this 2025 paper. The chains give a steady route to their cohomology, the tool that sorts their hidden traits, by way of the classical case. That route makes the sums simpler and lets known methods carry over.
arxiv-2509-18728:
Some galaxies stop forming stars from the inside out, and gas maps can reveal why. S. Veronese and seven co-authors present the deepest hydrogen views yet of the nearby spiral NGC 1371 in this 2025 paper. The data come from the MeerKAT telescope's MHONGOOSE survey. They pair the 21-centimeter hydrogen line with radio continuum maps.

The hydrogen sits in a neat rotating disc with a hole about five kiloparsecs wide at the center. Inside that hole, the continuum maps show a very faint active nucleus and two wide bipolar bubbles, never seen before in this galaxy. The bubbles may come from a low-power jet running inside the disc plane. Signs of jet-driven outflows appear, but no molecular gas is detected. The picture: the bar or the small nucleus cleared and heated the center. That inside-out clearing is quenching the galaxy's star birth.
arxiv-2509-18828:
How a material answers a poke reveals its inner quantum life. Zhesen Yang, Zihan Wang, Juntao Huang, Zijian Zheng, and Jiangping Hu build a fingerprint from those answers in this 2025 paper. Response functions define a response Hamiltonian, a stand-in operator that is non-Hermitian by nature. Its eigenvalues and states form what they call the complex frequency fingerprint.

Within that frame, they show interactions alone can create point-gap topology and the non-Hermitian skin effect, a piling of states at a boundary. Unlike the loss-driven version, this interaction-driven skin effect depends strongly on frequency. A density of states in the complex frequency plane then separates skin modes from topological edge modes cleanly. The framework gives one lens for driven, interacting quantum matter. It may help read experiments where response spectra are the main data.
arxiv-2509-18928:
Zhijun Liu and six co-authors work on speech that a computer builds from text. Recent models build speech sound step by step, with each new piece of sound spread out by a diffusion process. These models reach top results in zero-shot text-to-speech, where the voice is copied from a short sample. Little work had yet tuned them with feedback on which outputs people prefer.

The team applies direct preference optimization, a feedback method, to the DiTAR speech model. They call the result ARDM-DPO. Fine-tuning with paired good and bad outputs makes the speech more expressive, meaning it sounds less flat and more human. It also holds up better on long texts, where weaker models often break down or lose the thread.
arxiv-2509-19128:
Training large language models with reinforcement learning is slow because generating fresh text idles the hardware or goes stale. Alexandre Piché and four co-authors present PipelineRL, a system built to keep accelerators busy without feeding the learner old data. Stale, off-policy data harms common learning algorithms, so freshness matters. Their design runs text generation and model training at the same time, side by side.

The key trick is in-flight weight updates: the generating model receives fresh weights mid-stream, with minimal interruption to the sequences it is writing. Experiments on long-form reasoning tasks used 128 top-end graphics processors. Learning ran about twice as fast as with conventional setups, while the training data stayed highly on-policy. The team also releases a scalable, modular open-source version of the system as a contribution.
arxiv-2509-19328:
Heart signals alone may reveal what a person is doing, according to Sina Montazeri and three co-authors. Activity recognition usually needs motion sensors, which cost power and need calibration. Electrocardiogram data, already collected by health wearables, could do double duty. Earlier ECG methods only backed up motion sensors or sorted broad states like active versus resting. This team aims for six distinct activities, recognized from ECG only.

They design three deep learning models: a convolutional net with channel-recalibration blocks, a residual net with stretched convolutions for longer patterns, and a hybrid mixing convolution with attention. On data from 54 subjects, all three topped ninety-four percent accuracy for people seen in training. For unseen people the hybrid led at about seventy-two percent, and the authors expect more training subjects to lift that. The work points to wearables that monitor heart and activity together.
arxiv-2509-19428:
Gordan Krnjaic and five co-authors work out how telescopes could spot a particular kind of dark matter. The target is an inelastic pair of states, made in the early universe by freeze-in through a light mediator. The two states differ in mass by less than the electron-positron threshold. That small gap makes the heavier state live longer than the universe itself, slowly decaying into its lighter partner plus photons. With a light mediator, the cosmic abundance fixes the decay rate directly.

Photons from the galactic center, the authors show, can effectively probe this scenario. The mediator sits near a hundred mega-electronvolts in mass and the dark matter near a giga-electronvolt. Those are ranges other searches struggle to reach. The paper ties a cosmological production mechanism to a concrete observational signal, giving X-ray astronomers a specific target.
arxiv-2509-19528:
Matrix multiplication sits under much of fast computing, and its speed limit shapes many other tasks. Kyle Doney and Cameron Musco show that, on quantum computers, several core matrix tasks share that same limit. Computing a determinant, or traces of powers and inverses of a matrix, can each be turned into multiplication with little extra cost. Their chain starts from a known quantum trick that links multiplication to the trace of a triple product.

From there, short reductions reach each target task. The fastest known methods for those tasks all run at the multiplication speed. Any real breakthrough on one would thus speed up multiplication itself on quantum hardware. The note tightens the map of which problems are truly hard. It also warns algorithm hunters where effort is most likely to pay off.
arxiv-2509-19828:
Cells that crawl toward chemical cues can build vessel-like webs, as seen in lab dishes. Nangao Zhang studies the math model of that process on a half-line, where an edge shapes all that follows. Two kinds of edge rules are treated one by one. He first shows the wave form that solutions should near, and that it is the only one of its kind.

He then shows the true solution settles toward that wave as time grows. He gives the rate of that settling for both edge rules. The edge is no small detail here: it picks the end state itself. Firm rates help users trust that patterns in simulations come from the model, not from the code.
arxiv-2509-19928:
Synthetic speech that reads every sentence in the same rhythm sounds robotic, yet measuring rhythm variety has lacked a good yardstick. Yifan Yang and seven co-authors build ProsodyEval, a dataset of one thousand samples from seven mainstream zero-shot speech systems. Two thousand human ratings grade how varied the prosody sounds. Standard acoustic measures sit beside those judgments for comparison.

Their new metric scores diversity as a weighted edit distance over discrete speech tokens. It tracks human judgment far better than the acoustic measures. Prosody covers pitch, timing, and stress, the music of speech. A metric that agrees with listeners lets builders tune for naturalness honestly. The benchmark and metric together give the field a shared target.
arxiv-2509-20228:
Jatin Agarwala and three co-authors present a research tool in this 2025 arXiv paper on music and social media. People talk about music online in ways that reveal taste, identity, and social ties. Reddit offers a rich record of such talk, since anonymity encourages open posting. The scale of that record defeats manual study.

Their platform, Muse-it, gathers Reddit posts around user-chosen queries across many communities. It supports topic modeling, trend tracking over time, and clustering of related posts. It also spots links to music services and pulls track details like artist, album, and genre. Those details are tied back to the discussions that mention them. An interactive interface displays the results as dynamic charts. The tool aims to make large-scale study of everyday music talk practical for researchers.
arxiv-2509-20628:
After a hurricane, crews must know which homes are lived in before they can target help. Yiming Xiao and seven co-authors judge occupancy from street video in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, Recov-Vision with its FacadeTrack core, ties street panoramas to land parcels. Each facade is squared up so a vision-language model can read it well.

The model lists plain signs of life or loss: blocked doors, tarps, and piles of debris. Two rule sets turn those signs into calls. One decides in a single open step. The other splits seeing from judging, with the judge set to play safe. In two surveys after Hurricane Helene, the split design gave up a bit of precision but found more occupied homes and scored best overall. Maps of the errors show where the misses cluster, which helps crews check the weak spots.
arxiv-2509-21028:
Answering a question that needs arithmetic over dozens of full scientific papers is a stern test for language models. Miao Li and three co-authors build SciTrek, a 2025 dataset for long-context numerical reasoning. Existing long-context tests mostly check simple retrieval or use artificial contexts.

SciTrek questions require counting, sorting, aggregation, and comparison over collections of real articles. The questions are generated automatically by turning them into database queries over article metadata, such as titles, authors, and references. Ground-truth answers come from executing those queries, so they are exact. Inputs exceed sixty-four thousand tokens. The dataset both evaluates current models and supplies training material to improve their numerical reasoning over long documents.
arxiv-2509-21128:
Two standard recipes improve a language model's reasoning, and they reshape its thinking in opposite ways. Kohsei Matsutani and five co-authors compare them in a 2025 study accepted for ICLR 2026. The recipes are reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces.

Beyond accuracy, the authors build a framework that quantifies reasoning paths themselves. They examine complete trajectories and their finer internal steps, across models of three sizes on mathematical tasks. Reinforcement learning squeezes the path distribution, concentrating on reliable routes. Supervised fine-tuning expands it, widening the variety of attempted paths. The contrast, captured in the paper's title, helps practitioners choose a training mix based on whether they need reliability or diversity of thought.
arxiv-2509-21328:
A buckled elastic strip can snap suddenly to a new shape when its clamped ends rotate. Authorship belongs to Chiraprabha Bhattacharyya and Ramsharan Rangarajan. An elastica is a thin elastic rod that bends. Clamping and rotating its ends can force a sudden snap to a new shape. Static limit points are routine to compute. The snap itself is fast and violent, and harder to model.

The authors propose a nonlinear model with a single degree of freedom that preserves energy. It rests on a surprising observation about strip profiles during the snap. Those profiles match a sequence of energy minimizing shapes under geometric constraints. Experiments and finite element simulations support the observation across many arch depths. The model avoids modal expansions and linearization.
arxiv-2509-21428:
Golden triangles offer a new map of musical scales in a 2025 paper by Yusuke Imai. The Tonnetz is a classic lattice that shows relations among harmonies. Recent work placed tones on an icosahedron through the golden ratio. Imai finds another link between music and that ratio. Seven tones sit on a golden triangle to represent a full scale.

The arrangement captures a major or minor scale and its tonic, dominant, and subdominant chords. Each chord appears as a golden triangle. Imai proposes a golden Tonnetz built from such triangles and gnomons. It represents all major and minor scales and triads. Transformations from Neo-Riemannian theory, such as relative and parallel exchanges, appear as moves among the golden shapes.
arxiv-2509-21528:
Safety training shapes language models before release, but unsafe continuations can still appear at inference time. Sathwik Karnik and Somil Bansal propose an inference time defence in a 2025 paper. Their framework, BRT-Align, borrows reachability tools from control theory. Autoregressive generation is modelled as a dynamical system in latent space. A safety value function is learned through backward reachability.

The value function estimates the worst case evolution of a generation trajectory. Two mechanisms build on it. A runtime monitor forecasts unsafe completions several tokens ahead. A steering filter perturbs latent states minimally to redirect generation away from unsafe regions. The filter is least restrictive by design, changing only what safety requires. Experiments support both mechanisms.
arxiv-2509-21628:
Whether two neural systems use equivalent internal representations is measured in many incompatible ways. Jialin Wu and 3 co-authors compare those similarity metrics in a 2025 paper. Single metric studies dominate prior work, though each metric stresses a distinct facet of correspondence. Artificial vision models and real neural recordings both serve as test beds. Known structure supplies the ground truth for scoring metrics.

For models, procedurally matched pairs should score higher than dissimilar pairs. For neural data, same region responses should align across subjects while distinct regions separate. Metrics preserving representational geometry performed strongly in their tests. Tuning sensitive measures also featured. The study guides how to pick a similarity metric for biological and artificial systems alike.
arxiv-2509-21728:
Audio deepfake detectors trained on fixed data go stale as synthesis methods evolve. Xin Wang and 3 co-authors test a retrieval augmented detector in a 2025 paper. At inference, the detector queries an external knowledge database, much like retrieval augmented generation in large language models. The database can update continuously during operation. When that helps, and when it does not, was not well characterized before.

That added lookup helps most when database content differs from the fine tuning data of the underlying self supervised model. The content must still align with the test domain. Purely model only baselines win in other conditions. Knowledge cutoff issues in detection motivate the design. The study maps optimal use scenarios for external sources in zero day deepfake detection. Fresh external data, used in the right conditions, can extend a detector life past its training cut off. It stays live as new fakes appear.
arxiv-2509-22128:
Giorgio Cartechini, Francesco Giuseppe Cordoni, Mirko Unipan, and Ilaria Rinaldi build the first machine learning model that predicts beam delivery time for a specific proton therapy machine. Knowing delivery time matters for running a treatment center well, for four-dimensional dose calculations, and for newer therapy techniques. Their 2025 paper targets the Mevion S250i system with Hyperscan technology, for which no machine-specific model existed.

The team mined machine log files from eleven patients, over a thousand files in all, extracting features like spot position, energy layer changes, aperture movements, and spot charge. An explanation method then ranked what drives the gaps: aperture movements dominate longer gaps, while spot position and charge matter for short ones. In two clinical uses, checking repainting and recalculating dose, predicted delivery times landed very close to the machine's own logs, and dose measures stayed within normal variation.
arxiv-2509-22428:
Leonhard Grosse and 3 co-authors design privacy tools when the true data distribution is only estimated. Their measure, pointwise maximal leakage, scores how much one outcome can reveal about a secret. Its guarantees depend on knowing how the private data was generated, which in practice is a guess from samples. The team widened the framework to sets of plausible distributions.

Within a set, they bound the worst-case leakage. Large-deviation bounds then give distribution-free guarantees with a small failure chance. For binary data, they derive an optimal mechanism, and the design task becomes a convex program with linear limits. Tests on Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms showed better utility than local differential privacy at like privacy levels.
arxiv-2509-22528:
Bruno Bentzen, Flavio Del Santo, and Nicolas Gisin examine the philosophy behind a new take on physics foundations. Gisin and Del Santo have rebuilt parts of physics on intuitionistic logic, guided by naturalism. Intuitionism treats truth as tied to what can be constructed or known in time. The authors ask how this stance differs from Brouwer's original defense of intuitionistic mathematics.

They recast Brouwer's two acts of intuitionism as a self-contained frame for the physics version. The paper then traces how the naturalistic view handles logic, language, time, ontology, meaning, and truth. Each topic gets a treatment that sets it apart from the classical picture.
arxiv-2509-22828:
Arman Barghi and 4 co-authors add a movable stack as a new primitive for tidying tabletops. Rearranging cluttered objects is a long-standing robotics problem. Classic planners move items one by one into fixed buffers, which wastes travel and can block later moves. Stacking adds buffer space, but a loaded base object normally cannot move. Their dynamic buffer forms temporary stacks that travel as a unit, like a human carrying a small pile.

Against a leading rearrangement planner, travel cost fell in both dense scenes with a fixed arm and large sparse scenes with a mobile one. A Delta robot with a parallel-jaw gripper executed the plans in practice. Dynamic buffering thus adds feasibility and efficiency at once.
arxiv-2509-22928:
Jake S Rhodes, Scott D Brown, and J Riley Wilkinson add local uncertainty scores to random forests. Knowing how sure a model is matters most in high-stakes work. Common tools use quantile models or Monte Carlo runs. Their method instead uses the test points and closeness scores that a random forest already produces.

They build local error spreads from out-of-bag errors of nearby points. Those spreads give ranges for numeric forecasts and trust scores for class calls. Changing the count of nearby points tunes coverage to a target level. For classification, dropping points flagged as unclassifiable raised accuracy. Their accuracy-rejection scores beat rival methods in tests.
arxiv-2509-23028:
Merging neutron stars could reveal the state of ultra-dense nuclear matter, if waveform models are exact enough. Sarah Habib and 13 co-authors compare two numerical relativity codes head to head. The codes, FIL and SpEC, differ in methods, grids, and equations solved. Models must be calibrated against such simulations before data can be read.

Despite their contrasts, the two codes agree within current resolution limits. Their costs for a set accuracy level are broadly alike. Error in the waveforms comes mostly from the fluid evolution step. The team also weigh what it would cost to reach the accuracy next-generation detectors demand.
arxiv-2509-23128:
Risk choices often hinge on side data, like a stressed market or a client profile. Xinqiao Xie and Jonathan Yu-Meng Li build one framework for robust conditional risk tasks. Prior optimal transport methods each carry narrow limits. Some need point estimates, some fit only few risk measures. Their union-ball formulation in optimal transport unifies the field.

Known methods fall out as special cases, which exposes their shared structure. Convex reformulations cover nearly all major risk functionals. Cutting-plane algorithms scale the approach to large problems. A portfolio test with rank-dependent utility shows the payoff. Conditional models reached optima that unconditional ones clearly missed.
arxiv-2509-23228:
Hessian structures on a flat two-dimensional space get a quantum twist in this study. Herguey Mopeng and 3 co-authors deform those structures into quantum ones. The frame is the algebra theory of Koszul-Vinberg structures, tied to the KV-Poisson work in this field. The team track which geometric and algebraic traits survive the deformation. Step by step, the deformation turns a classical Hessian setup into a quantum structure.

The aim is to link two areas that rarely meet. Deformation theory supplies the quantum passage, and Hessian geometry supplies the shapes. The paper is a short theory piece. It sets up the quantization and its preserved traits more than it applies them.
arxiv-2509-23428:
A tiny curve with a very rigid symmetry group sits at the heart of Rin Ray's paper. The sole author starts from a finite group inside the Morava stabilizer group at height p minus one. Inverse Galois theory then yields one curve of smallest genus whose symmetry group is exactly that group. Its shape, field, and equation all follow from the group itself, with no free choices.

Ray proves that deforming this curve matches Lubin-Tate space, the standard setting for such symmetries. The proof uses a coordinate-free argument that reduces to counting one character. The action becomes concrete: the group shifts and scales a small set of points on a line. Cohomology groups for the action are then computed.
arxiv-2509-23528:
Radio networks that learn from simulations often stumble in the real world, where signals behave differently. Russell Ford and 19 co-authors present Sim2Field, a path for taking AI into live radio access networks for 6G. Their method trains site-specific physical-layer functions on detailed digital twin simulations of each site. A testbed then supports fast prototyping, field trials, and data collection.

The team ran an AI channel estimation method over the air with a commercial user device. Throughput rose by up to forty percent when AI joined the physical layer. The paper frames the pipeline as a fix for both the reality gap and the cost of building proof-of-concept systems.
arxiv-2509-23628:
Light that loops once around a black hole forms a photon ring whose size can betray the hole's spin. Joseph R. Farah and 3 co-authors define a new interferometric observable for that ring ahead of the proposed Black Hole Explorer. The observable ties directly to the ring's brightness profile around its circle. In their survey of emission models, the brightness pattern shifts with the source's physics, while the ring's width stays nearly fixed.

That steadiness makes width a probe of the space-time itself, like the ring's shape. Diameter plus width could pin spin and tilt to within about twenty percent for a hole with known mass and distance. Large simulations back the claim.
arxiv-2509-24128:
Comparing image generation models can demand heavy compute, which shuts out students and small labs. Chandon Hamel and Mike Busch built GANji, a light framework that benchmarks three classic methods on a data set of over ten thousand Japanese kanji characters. The three methods are a variational autoencoder, a generative adversarial network, and a denoising diffusion model.

The diffusion model made the sharpest images by a standard fidelity score. It was also over two thousand times slower to sample than the other two. GANji lays out that trade-off between image quality, model type, and cost in a form cheap enough for teaching. The authors offer it for both classroom and research use.
arxiv-2509-24628:
In the first instants of a heavy-ion collision, before the quark-gluon plasma forms, a field state called the glasma fills the system. Dana Avramescu and 4 co-authors study how those fields steer heavy quark-antiquark pairs born back-to-back. Pairs with moderate sideways momentum, moving through glasma with a large enough saturation scale, lose their angular correlation quickly.

The team compares the broadening of that correlation across phases. The decorrelation width built up during the glasma phase is comparable to the width from the plasma phase that follows. Heavy flavor pairs thus carry information about the earliest stage, not just the plasma, a point for future probes.
arxiv-2509-25228:
Ahmad Ayaz Amin and co-authors introduce Random Projection Flows for density estimation on curved data in two thousand twenty-five. Many data sets live near a low-dimensional curved sheet inside a large space. Guessing the density there is hard, since most of the space is empty.

Random projections shrink the space while roughly keeping shape, which suits the task. The new flows use random near-orthogonal matrices to project data down before a standard flow runs. Unlike learned maps, the method needs no training of the projection and gives a closed form for the volume fix. Random matrix theory backs the design. The authors offer it as a fast, strong baseline for building data generators.
arxiv-2509-25828:
Dusit Niyato, Octavia Dobre, Trung Duong, George Karagiannidis, and Robert Schober wrote this two thousand twenty-five guide to writing survey papers in communications research. The field grows fast, making a strong call for surveys that pull sets of past work into clear sense. But a good one takes much more than summing up papers. The team draws on wide work as editors at top venues, one being IEEE Communications Surveys and Tutorials.

Their road map covers seven points. It starts with how to pick a new, key topic. It goes on to gathering past work in a set way and shaping the text well. Next comes writing reviews that judge, not just describe. It adds building tutorial parts round case studies. It ends with clear figures and with spotting paths for work to come. The guide aims at new researchers. It hopes their surveys will speed up new finds.
arxiv-2509-26028:
Michael Anastos and co-authors improve a strategy for building a target graph quickly in a semirandom process, in a 2025 paper. In each round of the process, a random vertex is offered, and the player adds one edge at that vertex. The aim is to force the growing graph to contain a given pattern graph with bounded degree.

A 2021 result built the pattern in a number of rounds set by a constant times the degree and the vertex count. The new work cuts that constant by two-thirds, and the authors show the new rate is best possible as the degree grows. The same bound holds for a tree-based variant of the process.
arxiv-2510-00128:
Connor Jerzak of the University of Texas at Austin wrote this 2025 paper on checking field experiments from space. Randomized trials are the gold standard for testing policies, yet their random assignment can drift in the field. Jerzak proposes a remote audit that uses only satellite images taken before treatment began. The images test whether assignment still looks random against local conditions.

The audit asks whether treatment status can be predicted from the images better than chance allows. It stays valid in small samples and respects blocked or clustered designs. Applied to a Ugandan youth jobs program, the audit confirmed the reported randomization. Applied to a school experiment in Bangladesh, it flagged assignment patterns that matched outside concerns. Jerzak notes the audit catches only image-visible problems, but it is cheap, fast, and can run before costly data collection starts.
arxiv-2510-00328:
Ahmed Fawzy, Amjed Tahir, and Kelly Blincoe published this 2025 review of vibe coding, the practice of building software by prompting AI tools. Practitioners, many with little coding background, describe the appeal as speed and instant flow. No prior study had gathered those firsthand accounts in one place. The authors run a systematic review of grey literature, meaning blogs, posts, and practitioner writing.

A paradox anchors their findings: users chase speed, yet judge the output fast but flawed. Quality checks are skipped often, or handed back to the same AI that wrote the code. Many users accept tool output with no changes at all. The authors warn of a new class of vulnerable developers who can build a product but cannot debug it. They urge tool designers and teams to invest in quality practice before a broader crisis forms.
arxiv-2510-00628:
Lin and five co-authors at National Taiwan University investigate selection bias in large audio-language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multiple-choice tests are a standard way to grade these models, but answers may shift with the order of the options rather than their content. That flaw, known in text and vision models, had never been studied systematically for audio models, where choices may also be spoken aloud.

The team tested six audio-language models on three benchmarks and their spoken versions. Every model showed the bias, and shuffling option order swung scores by up to twenty-four points in the worst cases. Rankings between models even flipped under reordering, which undermines trust in published comparisons. Permutation-based fixes, which average over several orderings, reduced the bias in most cases at extra computing cost.
arxiv-2510-00728:
Kim, Kim, and Ye, at KAIST AI, tackle extreme blind image restoration in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer vision. Restoration models recover clean images from degraded ones, but extreme cases stack severe damage beyond anything in training. Learning a direct map from extremely low quality to high quality spans too wide a gap, which produces artifacts and lost detail. The authors split the jump into two ones.

A projector first moves the ruined image onto a mildly degraded manifold, and a frozen restoration model finishes the job. The training objective comes from information bottleneck theory, balancing reconstruction of the degraded input against matching a high-quality prior. A Look Forward Once step refines the prompt once for better results. Models such as SeeSR and S3Diff improved in plug-and-play fashion, with no fine-tuning of the backbone. Experiments under degradation regimes backed the design.
arxiv-2510-00828:
Hsu and a large collaboration analyse how the ATLAS experiment's workload and data systems interact, in this paper for the SC Workshops 2025. ATLAS at CERN moves enormous datasets around a global computing grid. Its PanDA system schedules jobs, while Rucio manages the data itself, and each was optimized on its own terms. Running them together creates hidden inefficiencies, from idle resources to transfers nobody needed.

The team built a metadata-matching algorithm that links individual PanDA jobs to Rucio datasets at file level. That fine-grained view exposed transfer activity badly imbalanced across sites and times. Some anomalous jobs spent over three quarters of their runtime on transfers and correlated strongly with failures. The authors propose tighter coordination, shared performance awareness, and automated anomaly detection between the two systems.
arxiv-2510-01128:
Virally and four co-authors bound how many independent channels a photonic device can support, in this 2025 arXiv paper on optics theory. Engineers want optical systems to carry more distinguishable signals, and the singular values of the electromagnetic Green function count exactly those usable channels. Before this work, predicting how the channel strengths fall off for an arbitrarily shaped device was hard. The authors build a general method that bounds each ordered singular value directly.

Applied to three-dimensional volumes up to sixty-four cubic wavelengths, their indexed bounds stay quantitatively predictive rather than merely asymptotic. They work the results through application classes such as waveguides, metasurfaces, and planewave detection. The bounds feed straight into information-theoretic quantities like Shannon capacity and Fisher information. Designers can now check, before optimizing any structure, whether a hoped-for number of strong channels is physically possible at all.
arxiv-2510-01328:
Aarts and co-authors teach generative diffusion models to describe the mysterious distributions that complex Langevin dynamics samples. Some quantum theories carry complex weights that break ordinary simulation, a famous sign problem. Complex Langevin sidesteps it by wandering into complexified space, but nobody knows its sampled distribution directly.

Score-based and energy-based diffusion models learn that distribution from the process's own output. The comparison shows what each learner captures and misses. Success would let researchers audit a powerful but opaque simulation method. Dense-matter physics, where the sign problem bites hardest, motivates the whole exercise. Quark matter at high density is the flagship sign-problem victim. Learning a sampled distribution differs from sampling it directly. Score learners track gradients while energy learners track the density itself. Error budgets separate statistical noise from systematic drift. Trust in opaque simulators is the prize.
arxiv-2510-01428:
Tsou and co-authors weld specialized biomedical models onto a language model so one system can reason across genes, molecules, and proteins. Foundation models for each data type live in separate embedding spaces that cannot talk. Their framework, BioVERSE, repairs the isolation with light projection layers.

Each modality first aligns independently into the language model's shared space. Instruction tuning on mixed data then teaches joint reasoning across the aligned channels. Compact configurations beat larger language-model baselines on annotation and function tasks. The system also explains its labels in words, a generative edge pure encoders lack. Cell-type annotation, molecule description, and protein function headline the task list. Zero-shot annotation works because the spaces finally agree. Projection layers stay lightweight by design, not by accident. Interactive dialogue with the data becomes possible afterward. Silos were the real bottleneck all along.
arxiv-2510-01628:
Schürmann proves a Heisenberg-style uncertainty floor for quantum states trapped inside a ball on a slice of curved spacetime, using only the slice's own geometry. Textbook uncertainty assumes flat space and fixed coordinates, neither of which general relativity guarantees. His bound controls momentum spread through the first eigenvalue of the slice's Laplacian.

Nothing about lapse, shift, or extrinsic curvature enters the estimate. On weakly mean-convex balls a universal product bound holds with the familiar constant. A vector-field argument then sharpens the floor by a factor of pi. Curvature-sensitive refinements sit above the universal baseline as a second tier. Spectral geometry supplies the eigenvalue that does the controlling. Strict localization inside geodesic balls defines the state class. Measurement-theoretic formulations are the announced extension path. Anisotropic comparisons could tailor bounds to symmetric slices. Sharper constants demand curvature information, honestly stated.
arxiv-2510-01728:
Kowalski and Shan prove decay estimates for a classic wave equation in this 2025 mathematics paper. The equation is the generalized Korteweg-de Vries model, used for shallow water waves and related systems. Solutions spread out and shrink over time, a behavior called dispersive decay. The authors ask how weak the assumptions on the starting wave can be while decay still holds.

For the mass-critical case, they show the peak size of the solution falls off like the inverse cube root of time. That rate matches the simpler linear Airy model. Their proof needs only mild smoothness conditions on the initial data. Two new tools make the argument work. One shows that negative regularity persists as the solution evolves. The other extends Lorentz-Strichartz estimates to mixed norms. For stronger nonlinearities, their result needs no assumptions beyond the natural critical space.
arxiv-2510-02028:
Resino and four co-authors compress LiDAR scans with a lean autoencoder in this 2025 paper. Self-driving cars read their surroundings as dense three-dimensional point clouds. Those clouds are heavy to store and transmit, so a compact latent code is valuable. Heavyweight autoencoders defeat the purpose on vehicle hardware.

Their network, LiLa-Net, was trained on real traffic data from a semi-autonomous vehicle with a Velodyne sensor. The design trims encoder layers and simplifies the skip connections that carry detail past the bottleneck. Balancing skip information against the latent code proved key to reconstruction quality. The model scored well on Chamfer distance, Earth mover's distance, and accuracy metrics. It also generalized to objects unlike anything in the traffic training scenes. Diverse datasets and point cloud formats confirmed the approach's reliability. The result is a lightweight codec that keeps the detail drivers of later perception stages need.
arxiv-2510-02228:
Beck, Schweighofer, Böck, Lehner, and Hochreiter map the scaling laws of an LSTM revival in this 2025 machine learning paper. The xLSTM architecture promises transformer-level quality with cost growing only linearly in context length. Whether it scales predictably was unknown. The team trained models from eighty million to seven billion parameters on up to two trillion tokens.

Both IsoFLOP profiles and parametric fits chart compute-optimal and over-training regimes. For a fixed training budget, compute-optimal xLSTM models turn out larger than compute-optimal transformers. At inference, xLSTMs run faster than same-sized transformers. Their performance edge widens with context length, where transformer costs grow quadratically. The study also tracks how optimal model size shifts with context length. Designers can now budget xLSTM deployments with the same confidence as transformer ones. Linear-time sequence modeling graduates from curiosity to a plannable alternative.
arxiv-2510-02428:
Lin, Gharibyan, and Su train quantum circuits on classical computers at utility scale. Their 2025 physics paper uses a method called Pauli Path simulation. Preparing ground states is a core task for quantum machines. Exact classical simulation collapses beyond a few dozen qubits. Their method optimizes circuit parameters without a quantum device. Test systems included Ising models in one and two dimensions. A Kitaev honeycomb model joined the test set. System sizes passed one hundred qubits in these runs. Results matched exact energies and trusted tensor methods closely.

The team also checked physical fingerprints of the states. Magnetization and topological entanglement entropy both looked right. They then ran trained circuits on real quantum hardware. A forty eight qubit honeycomb state ran on a Quantinuum machine. Its energy error landed near five percent. Classical pretraining can hand quantum hardware a head start.
arxiv-2510-02528:
Fu and co-authors locate the attention heads that carry spatial relations inside a vision-language model. Their 2025 paper studies OpenFlamingo, a multimodal model. Such models learn tasks from a few shown examples. How they carry a relation like left-of stays hidden. The team runs causal mediation tests on model internals. A small subset of heads proves responsible for relations. Their activations form what the authors call function vectors. Injecting those vectors improves zero-shot relational answers. Fine-tuning only the vectors, with the model frozen, does even better.

Combined vectors solved analogies with untrained relations. Two relation vectors can add into a working third. Synthetic and real image sets both supported the claims. The fine-tuned vectors beat in-context learning baselines clearly. Models may store skills as portable activation packets. Finding those packets opens models to direct editing. Interpretability gains a concrete handle here.
arxiv-2510-02628:
Xu, Ferreira, and Tegge compare ways to choose which variables belong in a regression model. Their 2025 statistics paper benchmarks selection criteria against search strategies. Scientists select variables to expose underlying mechanisms. Each method pairs a scoring criterion with a search routine. The study crosses two criteria with four search styles. LASSO variants join the comparison as well. Simulations swept sample sizes, effect sizes, and correlations. Model spaces ranged from small to fairly large. Scores tracked correct identification, recall, and false discoveries.

Two combinations stood clearly above the rest. Exhaustive search with BIC and stochastic search with BIC won. Genetic and LASSO paths with BIC neared perfect identification under kind conditions. Harsh correlations hurt the LASSO path most. Thousands of samples were needed for small effects. Applied researchers get a concrete pecking order. Search effort pays when the criterion is BIC.
arxiv-2510-02728:
Zhang and the Xiaomi EV-AD VLA team match text descriptions to aerial images for drone navigation. Their 2025 technical report covers a RoboSense challenge entry. Drones must find places described in plain language. Databases mix drone, satellite, and ground camera views. Baseline retrievers miss fine grained semantic matches. The team's system works in two stages. A fast baseline first filters candidates coarsely. A vision language model then writes rich captions for images. Reranking compares the query against those captions. Language becomes the bridge between views.

Recall improved by roughly five to eight percent over the baseline. The gains held across every recall metric. The team placed second among eight challenge entries. Captions make cross-view matching auditable by humans. Spatially complex scenes benefit most from the refinement. Real rescue and inspection flights need this reliability. Explicit language intermediates beat raw embedding similarity here.
arxiv-2510-03128:
Davis and Dumitrescu classify a loosened form of two-dimensional field theory. Classic two-dimensional TQFTs match up with Frobenius algebras. Those algebras must stay finite in size, a real limit. Nearly Frobenius structures relax that rule for endless spaces. Their matching theories are called Almost TQFTs. A prior work proved the two sides mirror each other. This paper reframes the whole theory in geometric terms.

Colored ribbon graphs supply the new language. Their edge contraction and construction rules encode the theory's moves. The authors prove those graph rules match the functorial axioms exactly. A classification of Almost TQFTs in dimension two follows. Cobordisms split into pants pieces in a normal form. That form makes the graph translation plain to see. The bridge links algebra with enumerative geometry and topological recursion. Quantization can then be read as a rebuilding process.
arxiv-2510-03228:
Fares and Ribas build a texture recognizer around random embeddings pinned to a sphere. Randomized networks have long excelled at texture description. Past gains came mostly from better cross-information prediction tricks. Their MIXER redesigns the randomized architecture itself. Image patches are encoded by random projections first. The codes are forced onto a unit hypersphere's surface. Direction, not magnitude, carries the texture signal that way.

Two learning branches then decode from those codes. The Direct branch rebuilds each patch from its own code. The Mixed branch rebuilds one channel using all channels jointly. Each branch trains under its own optimization objective. The learned decoder weights become the texture descriptor. Several pure texture benchmarks tested the approach. Each benchmark stresses different traits like scale or lighting. MIXER took the highest average accuracy across them. Robustness and efficiency arrived together in the design. The authors flag richer patch constructions as future work.
arxiv-2510-03328:
Jothiraj, Karunanidhi, and Eichmeyer present a 2025 arXiv paper on grouping chip wafer defects without hand labels.
