Using system dynamics modeling with experimental simulations, they separate the forces at play and trace how bias activates and reinforces itself. Inductive bias, the tilt built into the learning machinery itself, turns out to matter more than the bias users bring. Standard remedies, rebalancing data and regularizing algorithms, help only partly. The authors call for stronger strategies and wider system boundaries that include demographics and item diversity.
arxiv-2510-22028:
Yilin Zhang, Wenda Xu, Zhongtao Liu, Tetsuji Nakagawa, and Markus Freitag audit the judges used to grade machine translation when no reference translation exists. Quality estimation scores guide data filtering and candidate ranking, so a hidden bias inside the judge quietly reshapes everything downstream.

Across ten language pairs, the team found two length effects. The metrics steadily predict more errors as translations grow longer, even for flawless texts. And when rival translations are equally good, learned metrics tend to prefer the shorter one, while language-model judges range from neutral to favoring longer output. Tracing one leading metric's behavior exposed a built-in penalty that grows with length. The findings warn that pipelines trusting these scores may be optimizing for brevity, not quality.
arxiv-2510-22328:
Kyle A. Oman presents a software package for working with galaxies from SWIFT simulations. After a run finishes, astronomers need the particles of one galaxy, not the whole volume. SWIFTGalaxy extends the SWIFT data reader for exactly that job. It focuses on particle groups listed in halo catalogs.

The package knows which particles form a galaxy. It also knows the galaxy's bulk properties. One shared frame is enforced for positions. Particles loaded later match rotations and shifts already applied in memory. Masking particle datasets is made simple. Helpers cover round and ball-shaped coordinates, the frames galaxy work uses most. Tools sweep across many galaxies at once. The code is open-source infrastructure. Simulation science quietly depends on such unglamorous tools.
arxiv-2510-22428:
Vincent E Coll and co-author Lee B Whitt revisit a basic calculus computation, the centroid of the region under a curve, and show it hides a rigid rule. They track the average point of that region as the interval grows and ask when a simple scaling identity holds for the height at the centroid. The condition they study is called the Geometric Scaling Property.

They prove the identity holds for all interval ends exactly when the function is a power law. For those laws they also give the best constant in the identity. Their proof turns the region into a probability distribution and uses how averages change with scale.
arxiv-2510-22528:
Cropping a photo well depends on composition, the deliberate placement of elements in the frame. Yen-Hong Wong and Lai-Kuan Wong present AesCrop in 2025, a model that suggests attractive crops for uses like thumbnails and view recommendations.

Older methods either scored crops without seeing the whole picture or predicted one crop with little variety. AesCrop combines both ideas and adds guidance about photographic composition inside its attention step, which directs focus toward key regions. It outputs several ranked crops with quality scores. Extensive tests show it beats current leading methods, suggesting explicit composition cues help a model find visually strong regions.
arxiv-2510-22728:
Medical image models must show their work, not just give answers. Khai Le-Duc leads a large team with twenty three co-authors. In 2025 they release S-Chain. It is a dataset for medical visual question answering. Each case links reasoning steps to image regions.

The set holds twelve thousand expert marked medical images. Boxes mark the exact regions used in each step. It supports sixteen languages. Total question pairs pass seven hundred thousand. Tests show this training improves grounding and robustness. The team also studies how retrieval interacts with visual proof. A new mechanism tightens the link between proof and reasoning.
arxiv-2510-22928:
Mingze Gong, Juan Du, and Jianbang You address the hard task of spotting faults in complex sensor data, such as readings from drones. Odd readings can warn of danger, but older methods miss subtle faults and scale poorly. Their framework, called Diffuse to Detect, borrows diffusion models in a new way.

Rather than rebuild data slowly, the method predicts noise in one step to flag values that do not fit. A graph network links sensors that affect each other, which sharpens the search. The authors link the method to the shape of the data itself and test it on drone data and beyond.
arxiv-2510-23028:
Hongyu Wu, Xuhui Fan, Zhangkai Wu, and Longbing Cao propose NestAR, a nested autoregressive model for making images. Autoregressive image models build pictures token by token, which gives good quality but costs much compute. A prior fix, VAR, sped things up yet narrowed the variety of samples.

NestAR stacks modules at several scales in a hierarchy, where each larger-scale module conditions the next stage. The nested design aims to keep the speed gains while restoring diverse outputs. For image teams, the model offers a path to fast generation that does not collapse to a few safe patterns.
arxiv-2510-23228:
Richard J Murchie and John Jeffers extend quantum illumination lidar so it can resist spoofing as well as jamming. Weak-light detection is vulnerable to an intruder who fakes returns or floods the receiver. Quantum illumination with delayed coincidence counts already beats classical light against jamming.

The authors add spoofing resilience to an experimentally feasible detection and ranging protocol. Their approach characterizes the system by its real experimental parameters and quantum states, not just detector data. Verified returns would let quantum lidar trust its ranges even when an adversary actively tries to deceive it.
arxiv-2510-23428:
Michael L Parker and six co-authors improve prediction of molecular properties by combining graph neural network features with classic descriptors and a mixed ensemble. Learned descriptors from a graph network capture structure well, while general-purpose descriptors add proven chemical information. Their MetaModel framework aggregates predictions from a diverse set of leading machine learning models.

The combined featurisation beats the cutting-edge ChemProp model on all regression data sets tested and on six of nine classification data sets. A best-of-both approach like this helps drug and materials teams screen compounds more accurately before costly experiments.
arxiv-2510-23628:
Amit Kumar and a co-author study fairness in matching markets. Two institutions rank candidates from two groups using signals that are biased and only partly aligned. Think shared test scores or AI assessments that each school processes on its own. One parameter measures the bias against the weaker group; another measures how closely the two rankings line up.

Earlier work assumed both schools judge in the same way, and found the chosen share of the weaker group tracks the bias in direct proportion. The new study focuses on markets where all candidates prefer the same school, and the story sharpens. The chosen share reacts in a curved way to how aligned the schools are: small drops in alignment can cause steep falls. The authors find threshold values where selection behavior flips. Their formulas show when better alignment beats bias cuts, and when the reverse holds, for fairer selection design.
arxiv-2510-23828:
Mena Attia and four co-authors test whether large language models truly grasp culturally grounded figurative language, in Arabic and in English. Idioms and proverbs pack local knowledge into few words, making them a sharp probe of cultural reasoning. The team built tasks on Egyptian Arabic idioms, proverbs from many Arabic dialects, and English proverbs, checking understanding, practical use, and connotation separately.

Across twenty-two models, a steady hierarchy appeared. Scores on Arabic proverbs trailed English proverbs by about four percent, and Egyptian idioms trailed Arabic proverbs by about ten percent. Using expressions appropriately in context proved harder than understanding them, with accuracy dropping about fourteen percent, though example sentences recovered much of the loss. Models also wobbled on connotation, agreeing with human judges at best about eighty-six percent of the time. The authors release Kinayat, the first Egyptian idiom dataset for both skills.
arxiv-2510-23928:
Raman Jha and two co-authors propose an adaptive way to choose keyframes for rebuilding 3D scenes from video in moving, changing environments. Reconstruction systems cannot use every frame, so the frames kept matter enormously. Fixed rules — every tenth frame, say — waste slots on dull stretches and miss the informative moments when the scene shifts.

Their method pairs two modules. One scores frames by photometric error and structural similarity, favoring shots the current model gets wrong. The other, a momentum-based rule, slides the selection threshold up or down with the pace of scene motion. The result is a compact stream of the most useful frames, easing the data bottleneck for real-time robot perception. Tested inside two recent reconstruction networks, Spann3r and CUT3R, the selector improved quality consistently. An ablation study confirms each module earns its place in the gains.
arxiv-2510-24128:
Yuchao Dong and Harry Zheng study when to stop a process under a mean variance goal, a problem where the best plan can change with time. Because the goal is time inconsistent, they treat stopping as a game and look for equilibrium strategies. Direct analysis of that game is mathematically hard to handle.

They add a small entropy based penalty term that fades to zero, modeling mixed stopping through the rate of a Cox process. For this smoothed problem, they derive a coupled equation system, prove a verification result, and show solutions exist for short time spans. Letting the penalty vanish formally gives a set of inequalities that should describe the true equilibrium stopping rule.
arxiv-2510-24528:
Zihan Chen and six co-authors present a graph based pseudo-labeling framework that makes in context learning cheaper for new tasks. Language models can learn a task from a few examples in the prompt, but collecting quality examples for hard or novel tasks is costly. Their two stage pipeline reduces reliance on the model for labeling.

First, readily available examples from other tasks prompt the model to pseudo-label a small set of target instances. Then a graph based label propagation spreads those labels to the remaining target examples with no further model queries. The fully pseudo-labeled set becomes in task prompts, cutting labeling cost while supporting in context learning.
arxiv-2510-24628:
Anh Ngo, Nicolas Rollet, Catherine Pelachaud, and Chloe Clavel study small signs that a talk has gone wrong. In Dutch chats, one speaker may hint that they missed what was said, and ask the other to fix it. Chat bots often miss these hints and lose the user.

The team built a model that joins word cues with tone of voice cues. Tone cues added clear gains over text and sound scores used on their own. Their work also shows how the two cue types work as a pair. Next steps may add face cues and tests in more tongues.
arxiv-2510-25128:
Uzair Akbar, Niki Kilbertus, Hao Shen, Krikamol Muandet, and Bo Dai recast data boosts, a trick to grow training sets, as acts on a cause web. Boosts help models in like data cases, but the team asks if they can help when the world is poked, not just sampled. Their claim turns on when the end rule stays fixed as boosts change.

When that holds, a boost acts like a poke to how cure picks are made. That can cut bias from hid traits that sway both cure and end. Known strong var tools can then be tuned with boost aware rules, in place of hard to find poke sources. The frame gives a new use for a cheap trick.
arxiv-2510-25228:
Chihiro Nagashima, Akira Takahashi, Zhi Zhong, Shusuke Takahashi, and Yuki Mitsufuji report a sound art work made with the artist Evala, where an AI makes fresh sound live for months. The work, Studies for, plays on eight channels at once in a show space. Its model was trained on more than two hundred hours of the artist's past sound works.

The team frames the work as a new form of archive: it keeps an artist's style, yet makes new parts past the old works. Their model is light yet of high grade. Needs drawn from the build stress the artist's voice in the loop, not just the tech. The show ran for three months.
arxiv-2510-25428: Thang-Long Nguyen-Ho, Minh-Khoi Pham, and Hoang-Bao Le report a competition solution. Their 2025 report covers multilingual e-commerce product search for Alibaba International. The task matches user queries to product items across languages. Their team, DcuRAGONs, used a data-centric method built on large language models. That method achieved the highest score among competing solutions. The short report details their methodology and results, and the team published its source code online for readers to inspect.
arxiv-2510-25528:
Yuyuan Zeng led seven co-authors on zero reinforcement learning. Yufei Huang, Can Xu, and Qingfeng Sun helped. Jianfeng Yan, Guanghui Xu, and Tao Yang joined. Fengzong Lian closes the eight-author team. Their 2025 paper improves thinking across general domains. Zero reinforcement learning trains pretrained models directly with rewards.

No supervised fine-tuning phase is needed beforehand. Current research focuses on easily verifiable domains mainly. Math and programming offer clear reward signals there. Diverse scenarios lack straightforward verification, though. Their paradigm mixes verifiable rewards with generative rewards. A generative reward model judges non-verifiable tasks. Multi-task training transfers thinking between domain types. A smooth length penalty mitigates reward hacking risks. It encourages more full thinking tokens in general domains. Tests used Qwen3 base models at two sizes. Superior thinking results appeared on extensive thinking tasks. General tasks also better under their method.
arxiv-2510-25828:
Mitrajyoti Ghosh, Kevin Liguori, Takemichi Okui, and Kohsaku Tobioka calculate a background that could fake a rare particle change. The change is muonium turning into antimuonium, where muonium is a short lived atom made of a muon and an electron. Experiments such as MACS and the planned MACE look for the change by measuring the energies of the final electrons and positrons.

Ghosh and the team show that hard Bhabha scattering, a clash between electrons and positrons, can swap those energies and mimic the signal. They find the effect is tiny for MACE, but it would beat a very weak true signal. Measuring the spin direction of the electron would cut the background far more.
arxiv-2510-26128:
Klaus Ziegler, working alone, investigates topological phases in a two dimensional superconductor whose order parameter varies smoothly in a periodic pattern. The order parameter, which sets the superconducting state, is modulated along one direction and uniform along the other, giving a spatially periodic phase. He works with the Bogoliubov de Gennes Hamiltonian, the standard equation for quasiparticles in a superconductor.

Ziegler shows that the periodicity of the order parameter fixes the winding number of the eigenfunctions, a topological count of how a phase twists. An invariant links that winding number to the Bloch vector. Solving the equation gives both bulk plane wave states and exponentially localized edge modes, and the analytic bulk edge link shows when edge states emerge from the bulk spectrum.
arxiv-2510-26428:
Gregoire Maire and Thomas Genet work on proving that certain logic programs are satisfiable, meaning they have a model and do not contradict themselves. Their target is constrained Horn clauses over algebraic data types, a format widely used to state program checks. One route is to build a tree automaton, a machine that reads trees, which accepts exactly the intended model.

Maire and Genet build that machine by a different route: they code the search as an answer set program and let the Clingo solver do the work. Their checker is semi-complete, in a stated sense. It finds the automaton when a regular model exists, and it finds a counterexample when the clauses cannot be satisfied. That gives a fresh tool for a task where few routes exist.
arxiv-2510-26728:
Ivo Siekmann reviews how ion channels are modelled, with an eye on what the models can and cannot pin down. Ion channels are proteins that gate ion flow across cell membranes. Aggregated Markov models describe them with several open and closed states, to capture fast and slow openings. Each state is often read as a distinct physical shape of the channel.

Siekmann shows how such models with a given number of states can be counted. He then revisits a classical result: past a stated parameter cap, models become non-identifiable, meaning different settings fit the data equally well. He gives two derivations and a close study of a three-state case. His advice is to build models on data that speaks more directly to shape changes, rather than on assumed transitions between states.
arxiv-2510-27128:
Haonan Wang, Jingyu Lu, Hongrui Li, and Xiaomeng Li present ZEBRA, a system that reconstructs what a person saw from brain scans without training on that person. Decoding images from functional MRI activity bridges neuroscience and computer vision, but most methods need subject-specific models or fine-tuning, limiting scale and real use.

ZEBRA splits brain representations into a subject-related part and a meaning-related part. Adversarial training, where a rival network tries and fails to find subject traces, isolates meaning signals that stay stable across people. The decoder then generalizes to unseen subjects with no extra scans or retraining. Experiments beat zero-shot baselines and rival fully fine-tuned models on several metrics. Code and weights are released toward universal neural decoding.
arxiv-2510-27328:
Yi-Long Lu, Jiajun Song, and Wei Wang report evidence that language models judge along one shared axis rather than separate modules. Decodable representations for distinct concepts had suggested modular design, leaving open whether judgment systems are truly independent. Across a range of models, the team finds diverse evaluative judgments computed along a dominant dimension they call the Valence-Assent Axis.

That axis jointly encodes subjective valence, what seems good, and assent to factual claims, what seems true. Direct interventions show it acts as a control signal steering generation to build rationales consistent with its evaluative state, even at the cost of factual accuracy. The authors call this the subordination of reasoning. The mechanism offers an account of response bias and hallucination rooted in coherent judgment architecture.
arxiv-2510-27628:
Sebastian Benthall and Andrew Clark argue in 2025 that agentic AI should be judged as delivered software, not as a base model. Agentic AI means programs that act on their own inside complex firms. Large language models sparked the boom, but the systems at stake are full applications, which are built products put to work for users.

Success thus rests on checks by end users and key stakeholders, not on base model scores. The tools for such checks differ sharply from model tests. With sound checks in place, the authors note, simpler and faster models can often run the core logic. Their claim is blunt: for agentic AI, validity is what you need.
arxiv-2511-00428:
Kazuya Yokota, Ryosuke Harakawa, Masaaki Baba, and Masahiro Iwahashi bring physics-informed neural networks to the study of how speech is produced. These networks train directly on the equations of vocal-fold vibration and vocal-tract acoustics, promising insight into voice behavior for linguistics and medicine. Two obstacles stand out: vocal-fold collisions break smoothness, and the vibration period is unknown ahead of time.

A differentiable approximation smooths the collision problem, letting folds be analyzed inside the framework. Treating the period as a learnable parameter yields proper periodic solutions. Coupling between airflow at the glottis and tract acoustics is enforced as a hard constraint, with no extra loss terms. Forward and inverse tests confirm the method can estimate airflow, fold state, and pressure below the glottis from speech signals alone.
arxiv-2511-00728:
Hugo Massaroli and five co-authors test whether Alzheimer's diagnosis models trained on North American scans travel to Latin America. Deep models read FDG PET brain scans with high scores on the ADNI dataset, the field's standard, but ADNI cohorts skew North American. The team benchmarks convolutional and transformer models on ADNI, then evaluates them on a new clinical cohort from the FLENI Institute in Buenos Aires.

On ADNI every model scored high. On the Argentine cohort, performance dropped substantially, exposing a clear domain shift, and the architectures performed alike, undercutting claims of transformer advantage here. Ablations finger per-image normalization and correct sampling choices as key generalization factors. Attention maps on ADNI scans focus on canonical low-activity regions for Alzheimer's cases, but blur for other classes and for FLENI scans. Population-aware validation is the clear demand.
arxiv-2511-01428:
Sebastijan Horvat, Borja Sierra Miranda, and Thomas Studer work in proof theory, the branch of logic that studies proofs as mathematical objects. Their subject is interpretability logic, a system used to reason about what one arithmetic theory can interpret inside another, and their goal is a property called uniform interpolation.

The authors build two sequent calculi for the logic, one well-founded and one that allows infinite, cyclic proof branches. The infinite version drives a cut-elimination argument covering both systems, and they show its proof theory is well behaved in the sense that cyclic proofs are enough. Those tools deliver uniform interpolation for interpretability logic, and as a corollary for the related logic ILP as well.
arxiv-2511-01528:
Rhys Ransome, Davide Proment, Ian Renfrew, and Alberto Alberello model how ocean waves lose energy as they travel into sea ice. Coupled models used in forecasting usually predict a simple exponential decay, but recent field observations show decay profiles that bend away from that shape.

Starting from a framework where wave energy is drained by drag between ice and water, the authors add a missing ingredient: the ice itself is drifting. With drift included, their analytical solutions reproduce the observed non-exponential decay and track how the effective attenuation rate changes with distance into the ice. The test case is Antarctic sea ice, where the mismatch with the older picture was documented.
arxiv-2511-01628:
Arran Carter and Torben Sell make Bayesian neural networks cheaper. These networks treat their weights as probability distributions, giving honest uncertainty estimates, but the full Bayesian treatment is often prohibitively slow and memory-hungry. Their partial trace-class designs keep only some parameters Bayesian while retaining most of the benefit.

Three architectures are proposed, all built on trace-class priors, which order a network's parameters by importance and so suggest naturally which ones deserve the full treatment. The resulting networks quantify uncertainty comparably to standard Bayesian networks while using significantly fewer Bayesian parameters, with gains in speed and memory. A simulation study verifies the claimed advantages, and a real-world dataset illustrates how the method performs in practice.
arxiv-2511-01928:
Qingyue Long, Huandong Wang, Qi Ryan Wang, and Yong Li build a single model that generates human movement patterns for any disaster in any city. Mobility forecasts drive resource allocation, emergency response, and rescue coordination. Yet movement during wildfires and hurricanes departs sharply from normal patterns. Earlier models were trained on one city or one disaster. So they fail exactly when a new crisis hits somewhere unprepared.

Their model, UniDisMob, chases two kinds of generalization. For new disaster types, physics-informed prompts and physics-guided alignment exploit the common patterns in how mobility changes after different disasters. For new cities, a meta-learning framework extracts universal patterns through shared parameters while capturing city-specific features separately. The design aims at a one-for-all generator that stays useful when the next disaster is of a kind, or in a place, the data has never seen.
arxiv-2511-02528:
Bowen Huang, Haibo Yuan, Kai Xiao, and Ruoyi Zhang recalibrate the reference stars that much of observational astronomy depends on. The Landolt standard stars anchor the classic UBVRI photometric system, but using an independent database the authors find the two main Landolt catalogues offset from each other. Each field carries its own zero-point offset of five to fourteen thousandths of a magnitude, and spatial patterns reach up to about ten thousandths within fields.

The patterns repeat across bands and fields in ways that point to averaged flat-fields from each observing run. After recalibration, the standards agree with the independent data to within a few thousandths of a magnitude in most bands for brighter stars. The team then combined atmospheric parameters from the LAMOST survey with Gaia photometry to mint 5.4 million new standard stars across the five bands, most with far more precise ultraviolet photometry than before.
arxiv-2511-02628:
Ken Ono, a number theorist, pushes a classical line of results about the shape of q-deformed counting polynomials to higher-order results. The coefficients of Gaussian q-binomials were proved unimodal by Sylvester in 1878, with a constructive proof by O'Hara in 1990 and strict unimodality for large parameters by Pak and Panova in 2013. Log-concavity and its higher-degree strengthenings, the Turán inequalities, are the natural next questions, though the coefficients do not always satisfy them.

Ono proves the inequalities do hold uniformly in the centre of the spread, within any fixed number of standard deviations of the mean. That holds for infinite families whose limiting aspect ratio stays away from zero and one. The same results extend to q-multinomial coefficients. The engine is asymptotic: after normalisation, the relevant Jensen polynomials are shadowed by Hermite polynomials, whose known behaviour delivers them in the central window.
arxiv-2511-02928:
Ilerioluwakiiye Abolade and seven colleagues built a brain tumor segmentation model tuned for hospitals in Sub-Saharan Africa. Outlining gliomas in MRI scans guides diagnosis and treatment, but scanners in the region vary widely, and that variation breaks models trained elsewhere. Their 2025 model, SegFormer3D-plus, pairs a transformer design with radiomics guidance to handle the shift between domains.

Four parts do the work: histogram matching to align brightness across scanners, radiomic sampling to pick representative training cases, a dual-path encoder with attention, and a loss that sharpens tumor borders. Pretrained on the BraTS 2023 data and fine-tuned on BraTS-Africa scans, the model drew tumor subregions and borders more accurately across varied African scans. The team highlights careful adaptation over raw scale.
arxiv-2511-03028:
Mike Krebs and Alejandro Leyva settle the coloring question for a family of network graphs built from abelian groups. Such Cayley graphs can be encoded by an integer matrix, whose column count is the rank and row count the dimension. Earlier papers gave formulas for the chromatic number, the fewest colors that keep neighbors distinct, in low cases. Their 2025 paper finishes the rank-two story.

For rank two and dimension at least five, the chromatic number is three, with three exceptions spelled out. Loops make the graph uncolorable at all. A bipartite graph needs only two colors. A zero row in the matrix can simply be deleted without changing the answer. With that, all matrices of rank at most two are covered.
arxiv-2511-03128:
Najrin Sultana, Md Rafi Ur Rashid, Kang Gu, and Shagufta Mehnaz build attack tools that use a language model's own understanding to fool language models. Sensitive uses of these models demand hard robustness checks. Their 2025 frameworks, Static Deceptor and Dynamic Deceptor, generate adversarial texts that read naturally and keep the original meaning, while steering the target model to a wrong answer.

An automated, model-driven pipeline replaces hand-built tricks, so the attacks need no external heuristics. Because the generator leans on current models, the attacks grow stronger as models advance. They also transfer to models the attacker has never seen. The authors release code and data, framing the work as a self-assessment kit for model robustness rather than a weapon.
arxiv-2511-03228:
Shantanu Agarwal, Joel Barry, Elizabeth Boschee, and Scott Miller describe SARAL, a system built for finding documents across languages. SARAL came from the Information Sciences Institute for the MATERIAL program, an IARPA effort to improve cross-language search. Rather than return only a ranked list, SARAL aims to gather a full set of documents that answer a query.

In the third phase of testing, SARAL beat the other teams in five of six test settings. Those tests covered three languages, Farsi, Kazakh, and Georgian. The report walks through how the system was built, how it adapts to new topics, and why set-based retrieval helps when a user needs broad coverage rather than a few top hits.
arxiv-2511-03328:
Jindong Hong and colleagues test whether letting vision-language models think step by step actually helps on clinical work. Newer models offer a switchable thinking mode that shows a chain of deliberation before the final answer. The team checks that mode on two leading systems across four visual medical tasks drawn from standard sets.

Gains turn out to be uneven, and reliability does not rise in step with longer thought. Careful reasoning helps some task kinds while hurting calm accuracy on others, a pattern the authors probe in detail. Their message for builders is caution: thinking mode is not a free upgrade for medicine. Clinics weighing these tools need task-level proof before trusting the slower, wordier mode.
arxiv-2511-03528:
Raymond Wiedmann and colleagues compute how quantum effects reshape the spin-wave spectrum of flat altermagnets. Magnons, the waves of tilting spins, are first treated in a minimal spin-half model on a square grid. A continuous similarity method then reshapes the system into a form that keeps magnon count fixed, easing exact calculation.

Band splitting tied to altermagnetism and the depth of a dip called the roton minimum come out quantitatively. Where the method diverges, it signals either the ordered phase breaking down or magnons decaying fast. The dynamic structure factor, what scattering experiments actually see, is also derived. Such maps help experimentalists read neutron data from candidate altermagnetic materials.
arxiv-2511-03628:
Haofei Yu, Fenghai Li, and Jiaxuan You build LiveTradeBench, a live market arena where language model agents must trade under real uncertainty. Static benchmarks test knowledge and puzzle skill, not judgment when prices move and news breaks. Live streaming of prices and news removes backtest leakage and forces choices in real time.

Agents manage whole portfolios rather than single assets, weighing risk and cross-asset links as they allocate. That design mirrors how real funds operate far better than one-stock prompts. Early runs probe whether model smarts convert into returns once fees, swings, and surprise headlines bite. A live yardstick can puncture inflated claims about model trading skill before real money follows them.
arxiv-2511-04128:
Shengyu Tang is the lead author among seven authors on DMSORT, a parallel tracking design for following many objects at sea from unmanned vessel platforms. Safe navigation and sea surveillance need robust multi-object tracking, but platform motion shakes the camera and degrades the visual scene, breaking ordinary trackers.

One branch handles spotting and re-identification, using a reversible columnar sensor and a lightweight transformer that builds appearance traits from global context. A second branch gauges camera motion, builds a projective fix, and feeds platform-motion offset into the Kalman filter. Clustering-tuned matching joins the branches. Separating vessel motion from target motion steadies true paths under rough sea conditions.
arxiv-2511-04528:
Kaveh Eskandari Miandoab leads six authors with IntelliProof, a helper for reflecting on argumentative essays. A language model first turns an essay into a graph of claims and evidence. Edges mark which claims support or attack each other.

Each link is classified and scored, with a stated reason shown to the user. Visual maps then let writers explore the strength of their argument quickly. Scores summarize coherence while a human keeps final oversight. Unlike plain essay graders, the system is built to improve thinking about an argument, not just to assign it a number.
arxiv-2511-04628:
Kylie Cancilla and three colleagues present NovisVQ for judging video quality without any reference. Streaming services need quality checks, but clean reference copies rarely exist at test time. Most label-free methods also judge single frames and miss motion over time.

NovisVQ streams through video with a temporal convolutional network. It trains on synthetic damage applied to the DAVIS dataset, learning to predict standard quality scores. At test time it needs no reference and no human opinion labels. The streaming design beats the team's own frame-based baseline and fits the scale of modern video platforms.
arxiv-2511-05028:
Dongjin Park, Hasung Yeo, and Joon-Woo Lee present OvA-LP, a light way to fine-tune base models on spread-out data whose mix differs by site. Local drift, where each site pulls the shared model its own way, is the main threat in such federated work.

OvA-LP fights drift at its source. It pairs a frozen encoder with simple probing and a one-vs-all head, in a two-stage run that keeps learned features intact. On CIFAR-100 with one hundred clients, it held most of its even-mix score, while strong rivals kept only a small share of theirs.
arxiv-2511-05128:
Andrea Ichino and co-authors ask if giving teachers test scores helps them give better track advice to students. Each year more than a million EU students pick a school track on teacher advice, with little proof that the picks are the best fit.

Using Dutch data in a near-random set-up, they build a metric based on principal stratification. They weigh short and long-term loss and check fairness across protected traits. Their findings, robust to key changes in assumptions, speak to whether score access lifts advice quality or just adds bias.
arxiv-2511-05228:
Dhrumil Bhatt and a co-author propose adaptive routing for satellite quantum networks that must keep entanglement alive as orbits and weather shift. Fixed plans built for still, ideal nets fail when links fade, move, or vary in trust.

Their routing score joins link fidelity, trust, and key rate, weighed in one metric. It also folds in orbit shape and air loss for each inter-satellite link. The aim is a path choice that updates as the fleet moves, so quantum links can hold across a real sky, not just a diagram.
arxiv-2511-05328:
Sumit Kumar Jana and co-authors show how a non-Markovian Hatano-Nelson model arises from a dissipative lattice in a near one-dimensional set-up. Most work on such non-Hermitian models treats loss as flat across frequency, but real loss can vary with frequency.

That variation makes the system keep a memory of its past, the non-Markovian trait. Using non-equilibrium Green's functions with no shortcuts, they derive the model from micro rules. The work grounds a model often just assumed, and it links memory effects in open quantum systems to a concrete lattice design.
arxiv-2511-05428:
Joy Chen and a co-author trace how energy moves across scales in turbulent flow inside a channel. The cascade comes from nonlinear terms in the Navier-Stokes equations, whose interactions must meet triadic rules that link three wave parts at once.

The authors split transfer between streamwise and spanwise scales, a split shaped by the channel's unlike directions. Each triadic act is mapped on its own, with its momentum and energy flow, then ranked. The map shows which links do the heavy lifting to keep channel turbulence alive, a detail that models of wall flow need.
arxiv-2511-05528:
Aayush Aluru and colleagues present SMAGDi, a way to shrink a team of debating AI models into one small model. Multi-agent systems often reason better than a single model, but their back-and-forth debates cost a lot of compute. SMAGDi turns those debates into a graph that a student model can learn from.

In the graph, nodes hold single reasoning steps marked right or wrong, and links show how steps connect across agents. Trained on this structure, the student kept most of the large system's accuracy on two test sets. It shrank a much larger setup into a compact model that beat older distillation methods.
arxiv-2511-05728:
Ruben Sharma and Ross King test whether the classic atom groups of chemistry earn their keep as a way to explain how molecules act. Their test comes from learning theory: a good account of data should also compress the data. So they built a self-taught search tool that hunts for parts which shorten the account of about three million life-linked molecules.

The parts it found include most groups that chemists had named by hand, plus larger patterns with more specific roles. Run on twenty-four data sets of drug-like action, the tool found set-specific groups as well. Codes built from those groups beat standard codes at guessing such action with a simple model. The authors read this as formal proof the classic groups capture real structure.
arxiv-2511-06028:
Enis Golaszewski and co-authors find a hole in a password-replacing login standard and prove it with a working attack. The FIDO Universal Authentication Framework lets devices authenticate users, and it binds the login to a communication channel for safety. The team analyzed that binding with formal methods.

The binding fails against a standard network adversary, they show. The attacker can move a server's challenge into another session and, in some settings, pose as the client to open an authenticated session. They built a proof-of-concept man-in-the-middle attack on eBay's open-source implementation. Then they proposed fixes and formally verified them. The flaw echoes a famous protocol bug found twenty-five years earlier, which the authors cite as a warning.
arxiv-2511-06228:
E. C. Tredenick and co-authors design a two-layer cathode for lithium-ion batteries using a detailed physics model. Uneven behavior inside an electrode wastes capacity and speeds up wear during charging. Stacking two different materials in layers could even out the response, and the authors optimize such a design with the multilayer Doyle-Fuller-Newman model.

Their cathode pairs a nickel manganese cobalt oxide layer with a lithium iron phosphate layer. Adjusting the carbon binder, electrolyte share, and pore structure gave the most control over charge movement. The optimized design charged from empty to ninety percent in under nineteen minutes at a fast rate, holding forty-one percent more capacity than the phosphate-only version.
arxiv-2511-06628:
Yuchen Cao and Jiongmin Yong study a class of decision problems where a controller can intervene only at chosen moments, with each intervention changing the running cost of the system. Such impulse control problems arise when actions are discrete, costly, and timed rather than continuous. The cost change makes the usual dynamic programming approach difficult to apply.

The authors derive the governing Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, which takes the form of a quasi-variational inequality containing a parameter, and show the value function is its unique viscosity solution. They then prove a maximum principle for these controls, modeled on Pontryagin's classic principle. The principle allows perturbations in the timing of the optimal impulses, giving conditions an optimal strategy must satisfy.
arxiv-2511-06728:
Vasu Dev and Yijie Shen take twistronics, the art of stacking twisted layers to create moiré patterns, off the material and into open space. Twisted bilayer materials generate striking effects, but they demand physical layers. Here the twisted lattice is a light field that fills space and carries topological textures as it propagates.

Structured light with a twist angle produced a rich zoo of new topologies: skyrmionium bags, bag superlattices, clusters, and optical quasicrystals, many never reported before, with controllable symmetry. Unlike material moiré patterns, these optical textures held their form over long travel distances, resisting spreading and shrugging off shocks and obstacles. The authors pitch them for robust information transfer and encryption.
arxiv-2511-06928:
Yushan Xie and twenty-two co-authors simulate how the Multi-Channel Imager aboard the China Survey Space Telescope will see a galaxy cluster. The imager observes together in three filters spanning the near-ultraviolet to the near-infrared, over a wide field well matched to clusters. Such simulations are needed to test data pipelines before the telescope flies.

Their system takes a strong lensing cluster from the CosmoDC2 catalog, computes its gravitational potential, and ray-traces the true positions, shapes, and light of its galaxies. Intra-cluster light and galaxy spectral energy distributions are included, enabling tests of lensing analyses such as separating diffuse cluster light from galaxy light and reconstructing mass from combined strong and weak lensing. The work benchmarks the imager's pipeline for cluster science.
arxiv-2511-07028:
Huayang Xu and five co-authors improve sequential recommendation, the task of predicting a user's next action from their history. Users' preferences mix several periodic patterns that are hard to separate in the time domain, so recent systems analyze behavior in the frequency domain. Current frequency filters are mostly static, ignoring that patterns are personal, and global Fourier analysis blurs short-term, non-stationary changes.

Their method pairs two modules. A dynamic frequency filter adjusts its filtering to each behavioral sequence, extracting personalized global structure, while a wavelet enhancement module reconstructs the sequence to restore short-term fluctuations the Fourier view smears. Together they target both comprehensive modeling and efficiency on long histories. Tests on four widely used benchmark data sets showed the combined method superior to previous methods.
arxiv-2511-07128:
Lorenzo Lazzari and nine co-authors build a hybrid photonic chip that both creates entangled photon pairs and engineers their quantum state on the same device. The source is aluminium gallium arsenide, which generates biphoton pairs in the telecom C band by spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Those pairs are transferred into a CMOS-compatible silicon-on-insulator circuit through a multimode evanescent coupling scheme.

The device yields pairs at a rate above a million per second per milliwatt, with a coincidence-to-accidental ratio up to six hundred, marking a bright source. Crucially, the coupling itself transforms the pairs' joint spectral amplitude in strong, predictable ways, so complex quantum state engineering happens entirely on chip. The compact platform is compatible with electrical pumping, a useful requirement for scalable quantum technologies.
arxiv-2511-07228:
Oleksandr Masyutka, Mikhail Moklyachuk, and Maria Sidei tackle extrapolation for multidimensional stationary sequences when some observations are missing. The goal is to estimate linear functionals that depend on unknown values of the sequence, using observations corrupted by an additive stationary noise sequence. Missing data turns a clean prediction problem into one where the estimator must be built around the gaps.

Under spectral certainty, where the spectral densities of signal and noise are known exactly, the authors derive formulas for the mean-square errors and the spectral characteristics of the optimal linear estimates. Under spectral uncertainty, with densities known only to lie in allowed sets, they apply the minimax robust method. They identify the least favorable densities and the minimax characteristics of the optimal estimates for special classes of allowed sets.
arxiv-2511-07328:
Artyom Sorokin and nine co-authors improve retrieval-augmented creation for questions that need several rounds of searching. Standard retrieval fetches context once, which fails on complex questions, and newer multi-step methods fine-tune small language models to do the searching, an expensive route that locks out larger models. Q-RAG instead fine-tunes only the embedder, the part that represents text for retrieval, using reinforcement learning with value-based training.

The embedder learns to retrieve step by step, gathering the pieces a long-context answer needs. Q-RAG proved competitive and resource-efficient for open-domain question answering and reached state-of-the-art results on the BabiLong and RULER long-context benchmarks, handling contexts up to ten million tokens. The code is publicly available, making the approach easy to adopt.
arxiv-2511-07628:
Niklas Ippisch, Markus Herklotz, and Anna-Carolina Haensch grade the graders: feedback that language models write for statistics students. Teachers value personal written feedback but cannot scale it by hand. Model feedback promises scale, yet its accuracy, depth, and teaching value are doubted.

Mock exam data from two years of an introductory course at LMU Munich supply the test bed. Generated feedback is judged against an expanded pedagogical framework. Four enhancement methods are compared for lifting quality toward what good tutors do. The study shows where model comments help, where they mislead, and what support instructors still must provide themselves.
arxiv-2511-07828:
Makoto Kawashima extends a criterion of Hermite about when special values are linearly independent. Lauricella series with rational parameters produce numbers whose independence matters. Hermite original result covered certain Abelian integrals; Kawashima version reaches a broader series family in complex and p-adic settings alike.

Padé-style fits to solutions of a reducible equation drive the proof. The hard novelty is proving the linked determinants never vanish. Direct fits extend Hermite own constructions for Abelian integrals. Independence tests support proofs that famous constants are irrational, so sharper tools travel widely across number theory.
arxiv-2511-08028:
Timo Stoll, Luis Muller, and Christopher Morris search for graph transformer design rules that hold across many domains. These models vary widely in attention style, positional information, and power, and most theory ties to one narrow design. That leaves builders without guidance that survives a change of task or scale.

The authors define a Generalized Distance Transformer using standard attention plus recent advances. They analyze how attention and positional encodings shape its representational power. Experiments span more than eight million graphs from images, molecules, code, and reasoning tasks. A few design and training choices perform well almost everywhere, including few shot transfer.
arxiv-2511-08128:
Dmitrii Tarasov, Elizaveta Goncharova, and Andrey Kuznetsov study learned tokens that compress the context a large language model must carry. Long inputs strain memory and computation, so shrinking context without losing task skill is valuable. Their sentence anchored gist approach fine tunes pretrained models to pack context into far fewer tokens.

Compression factors from two to eight times are reported without major performance loss on short and long context benchmarks. On a three billion parameter LLaMA model, the method matches rival compression techniques while reaching higher ratios. The result suggests trained models can summarize their own context internally rather than relying on outside trimming tools.
arxiv-2511-08328:
Solveig Thrun and co-authors study how matching mammograms taken over time affects deep learning breast cancer risk scoring. Screening programs repeat mammograms regularly, and risk models increasingly use earlier images to personalize intervals for high risk patients. Misalignment between visits can hide real tissue change or invent false change, degrading those models, so the match strategy itself deserves direct comparison.

Image based warping, feature level match with and without regularization, and implicit methods are tested on two large data sets. Image warping wins on accuracy, precision, recall, and warp quality, producing smooth, anatomically plausible warps. Applying image based warp fields inside feature space gives the best risk prediction of all.
arxiv-2511-08828:
Luana Passos-Reis and eleven co-authors forecast which active galactic nuclei the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory will catch shining in very-high-energy gamma rays. The coming observatory will far outstrip current instruments in sensitivity across energies from twenty giga-electronvolts to three hundred tera-electronvolts, but its target list needs care.

Working inside the observatory's science collaboration, the team uses flux variability as the selection signal, measured by normalized excess variance in Fermi-LAT satellite data. Extrapolating variability estimates from thirty-day to three-day timescales grows the usable sample from eighty-seven sources to four hundred seven. Flaring and distant nuclei that would otherwise be missed rise to the top of the list. The results now feed the observatory's extragalactic science program and a forthcoming consortium publication.
arxiv-2511-09028:
Jinkun You and three co-authors align images densely across scales without any supervision, a registration task where two views of a scene must be matched pixel by pixel. Existing unsupervised methods are either inaccurate or expensive, and the model proposed here attacks both problems at once.

Correlations between features at different scales are exploited to make the alignment easier, and the number of scales can be dialed up or down to trade accuracy against speed. A fully spatial correlation module sharpens accuracy while keeping computation low. The human visual system lends a trick: a just noticeable difference model steers effort toward regions where the eye can actually spot misalignment, erasing the errors viewers would notice. Quantitative and qualitative experiments put the method ahead of the state-of-the-art approaches compared.
arxiv-2511-09228:
Jiarui Liu, Weihao Xuan, Zhijing Jin, and Mona Diab work on stopping multimodal language models from hallucinating objects. Such models often claim objects, attributes, or relations that are not in the image. Their framework, TACO, checks a model's own answers instead of calling outside vision experts.

TACO breaks a response into atomic queries and paraphrases each one, reducing sensitivity to wording. It then estimates confidence through self-consistency or self-reported confidence, and a language model refines the answer. Across five benchmarks and two models, LLaVA-1.5-7B and CogVLM2, TACO beats direct prompting and visual contrastive decoding. It also reduces systematic biases and improves how well confidence matches correctness, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-09728:
Mohammad Mahabubur Rahman and Deepanshu Verma supply the first rigorous error bounds for physics-informed neural networks solving the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. That equation, a model of instabilities in flames and fluids, mixes nonlinearity, fourth-order dissipation, and a backward heat-like term. Its two- and 3D versions challenge both analysis and numerics.

The authors first prove global regularity criteria based on space-time integrability in Besov spaces. They then derive error bounds for the network approximation, a result no earlier study had reached for this equation. Numeric simulations confirm the theoretical bounds. The work shows classical PDE analysis and machine learning solvers can be fused with guarantees, not just heuristics.
arxiv-2511-09828:
Mingkun Yang, Ran Zhu, Qing Wang, and Jie Yang improve split federated learning, where a model is divided between clients and a central server to save client resources. The weak point is data heterogeneity: different data at each site makes gradients diverge and slows training. Their framework, SMoFi, synchronizes momentum buffers across the server-side optimizers at each step to counter that drift.

A staleness-aware alignment mechanism constrains updates of the server-side submodel throughout training. Across several real-world datasets, SMoFi raised global model accuracy by up to about seven percent and sped convergence by as much as tenfold. The gains grew with more clients and deeper models, which suits the resource-constrained settings split learning is meant for.
arxiv-2511-10428:
Ignace Bleukx and four co-authors study how to explain, step by step, why a constraint problem has no solution. Step-wise explanations show one small reasoning step at a time, each tied to the original rules, until the conflict becomes clear. Computing such sequences from scratch is expensive, which limits the size of problems they can handle.

Their idea is to reuse the proof that a certifying solver already produces while solving. They define abstract proofs, a shared format that can hold both solver proofs and explanation sequences. Conversion methods then trim and simplify the proof into a short explanation. The result is much faster generation, with explanation quality close to the best existing methods.
arxiv-2511-10728:
Aleksandra Olejak and eight co-authors revisit how the black hole binaries discovered by the Gaia mission could have formed. Standard binary evolution says these unequal-mass systems should have merged or shrunk during mass transfer, yet the observed orbits are far wider than predicted, a puzzle for conventional models.

The team runs detailed binary evolution calculations with non-conservative mass transfer. In this mode, most transferred mass leaves the system carrying the donor star's specific angular momentum, rather than being re-emitted near the accretor as usual. That geometry reproduces the orbital periods of two Gaia black hole systems remarkably well across many starting conditions. The authors speculate about eruptive mass loss before overflow, and suggest similar physics may shape neutron star and white dwarf binaries Gaia has found.
arxiv-2511-10828:
Weiheng Bai, Kefu Wu, Qiushi Wu, and Kangjie Lu speed up directed fuzzing, the security testing technique that steers a program's inputs toward a chosen target location in the code. Standard directed fuzzers guide themselves by control-flow distance to the target, but that distance ignores whether the branches along the way can actually be taken.

Their fuzzer, AFLGopher, computes a feasibility-aware distance instead. A new classification method predicts the feasibility of every branch from limited execution traces, and a runtime updating mechanism sharpens those predictions as testing proceeds. Against five state-of-the-art directed fuzzers, AFLGopher reached targets roughly two and a half to nearly four times faster, and triggered known vulnerabilities about five times faster, across the compared systems.
arxiv-2511-10928:
Kabenge Hamiss, Mohammed Alshahrani, and Mujahid Syed propose two ways to solve large sets of nonlinear equations when the answer must stay inside a convex region, a region with no dents. Both ways work without slope data, which can be costly or missing in large problems. Each method builds its search steps from known gradient-style methods, with a spectral twist in one case.

Both methods are shown to keep stepping downhill in a strong sense. One reaches the answer under weaker smoothness demands than the other. Tests with numbers show the methods work well in practice, which makes them useful for big constrained problems in science and design.
arxiv-2511-11428:
Aymeric Delteil, Stéphanie Buil, and Jean-Pierre Hermier measure the coherence and spectral wandering of light from a single B center, a blue-emitting defect in hexagonal boron nitride. Such solid-state emitters could serve quantum technologies, but fast dephasing and spectral diffusion blur their photons. Prior work on B centers leaned on resonant excitation, leaving the easier non-resonant regime largely uncharted.

Using photon correlation Fourier spectroscopy under steady illumination, they find the emission line mixes a uniform part, which widens as laser power grows, with diffusion broadening on microsecond scales. At low power and short times the line sits near twice the ideal width, while at long times it spreads past a gigahertz.
arxiv-2511-11528:
Sebastian Schneider and five co-authors test whether electron beam induced current imaging inside a transmission electron microscope can measure how charge carriers move in thin semiconductor slices. The method, called STEM EBIC, is well proven on bulk samples but had barely been tried on the thin lamellae used for microscopy.

Working with silicon photodiode slices cut by gallium and xenon ion beams, the team images p-n junctions directly and extracts diffusion lengths for electrons and holes at different thicknesses. Values come out far smaller than on bulk silicon, pointing to strong surface losses and ion beam damage. The findings set honest limits for quantitative use of the technique.
arxiv-2511-11728: Yoshiaki Goto and Genki Shibukawa study step rules whose next value is built from the last two. The rules are linear, of second order, and use fixed real weights. The paper describes when the answers rise steadily or fall steadily. Such rules show up in counting problems and in physics. As a use case, the authors give a new description of the Fibonacci numbers.
arxiv-2511-11928:
Ziyao Cui and Edric Tam question a default choice in graph learning. When node features are missing or weak, models borrow embeddings from the graph Laplacian. Its eigenvectors encode connectivity well. But other graph matrices might teach distinct, useful structure. The authors build a family that interpolates between matrices.

Interpolated Laplacian Embeddings come from that family. Spectral graph theory gives simple guarantees on what they capture. Tests ask if the richer spectral menu improves downstream learning. Feature-poor graphs are the norm in social, biological, and transaction networks. Better free representations, built from structure alone, have wide practical reach. The default deserves a challenger, and this is a principled one.
arxiv-2511-12128:
C. A. S. Vieira and four co-authors track how replacing lanthanum with barium changes a family of double perovskite oxides that contain cobalt and iridium. Iridium oxides draw interest because strong spin-orbit coupling in iridium can produce unusual physics. The team varies the barium share across four compositions and probes structure and magnetism.

X-ray diffraction and magnet tests show the crystal structure shifts as barium rises. Lower barium mixes behave as ferrimagnets, likely from opposing coupling between cobalt and iridium ions. At the highest barium level the pattern turns to a clear antiferromagnetic order for cobalt, linked to iridium losing its magnetic moment.
arxiv-2511-12228:
Ara Tonoyan and six co-authors report measurements of light emitted by sodium atoms under two-color laser excitation. They study infrared emission in a vapor cell and look at second-order correlations, which reveal whether photons tend to arrive together. Emissions in forward and backward directions are compared under varied settings.

In all cases the measured correlation at zero delay sits above one but well below the value for thermal light. Forward and backward beams at one wavelength are correlated with each other. Ripples in the correlation over time shift with laser power, which the authors link to AC Stark shifts and atomic structure in selected velocity groups. The emission appears to come from a phase-matched cooperative process.
arxiv-2511-12628:
Ke Hu, Liyao Xiang, Peng Tang and Weidong Qiu present FedTopo, a federated learning framework that uses topology to keep client representations aligned when each client's data differ. Federated models degrade under such heterogeneity because features drift apart across clients, and pixel-level objectives miss the global shape of the data that matters for visual tasks.

FedTopo first screens the network's blocks to find the one whose topological signatures best separate classes, using persistence-based summaries. That block yields a compact topological embedding for each client. A topological alignment loss then guides each client to stay consistent with the global model during training, cutting representation drift across rounds. Experiments on a fashion image benchmark are among the evaluations reported.
arxiv-2511-12728:
Lea Hergert and four co-authors test large language models on a task a child could do: saying whether an item belongs to a listed set. Models that shine on hard reasoning still stumble on prompts like asking whether apple is in a set of four fruits. The authors design their study for simplicity and scale, varying how questions are phrased, how the sets are structured, the order of elements, and which model answers, across many controlled trials.

Performance turned out brittle and unpredictable along every dimension they varied. The authors read that as evidence that the models' grasp of the set concept is fragmented rather than unified. Beyond the specific failure, they argue the method itself is the point: picking a very simple task lets researchers run experiments big enough to map failure modes completely. That makes set membership a useful probe for evaluating language models in general.
arxiv-2511-12828:
Mohammad Marufur Rahman and four co-authors examine whether Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks forget less than ordinary networks. These networks use learnable spline activations, localized by design, which led many to hope they would resist catastrophic forgetting, the tendency of models to erase old tasks while learning new ones. The authors build a theory linking forgetting to how much activation supports overlap and to the intrinsic dimension of the data. They then test the theory on synthetic and vision tasks.

The hope holds only in low-dimensional algorithmic settings. On image classification and language modeling, KANs forget much like other models. The team also introduces KAN-LoRA, an adapter for efficient continual fine-tuning of language models, and tests it on knowledge editing. Their conclusion is measured: localized activations are not a general cure. Designers get a clearer map of when this architecture helps.
arxiv-2511-13328:
Athanasia Gkogkou and 4 co-authors test ways to remove bright foregrounds from hydrogen intensity maps when the telescope beam changes with frequency. The hydrogen signal traces cosmic structure after reionization, but foregrounds outshine it by more than ten thousand times. A beam that shifts with frequency makes the cleaning far harder.

They compare fitting methods and blind separation methods, including their spherical method SDecGMCA, on simulated MeerKAT and SKA-Mid data. All methods did well under a simple blurred beam, yet SDecGMCA stayed robust under realistic distortion. It reached within about five percent accuracy at mid angular scales, though all beam inversion grew unstable at the finest scales.
arxiv-2511-13428:
Levin Maier and Francesco Ruscelli extend Mañé's critical value theory to Tonelli Lagrangians on half Lie groups. Half Lie groups include groups of smooth maps between compact spaces, so the setting is infinite-dimensional. The Lagrangians are right-invariant, live on the tangent bundle, and grow quadratically along each fiber.

They prove the Euler-Lagrange flow exists for all time and define three energy thresholds in this new setting. Above the lowest threshold, any two points can be joined by a global minimizer, which under one extra condition follows the flow itself. One payoff is global well-posedness for all Euler-Poincaré equations tied to such Lagrangians on these groups.
arxiv-2511-13528:
Emile Anand proves a link between rankwidth and balanced separation in dense graphs. Rankwidth measures how cheaply a graph can be split along cuts of low rank. The result says any graph whose rankwidth reaches a stated multiple must contain an induced subgraph where every balanced cut has high cutrank.

That induced piece acts as a well-linked core defined purely by balanced vertex cuts. As a byproduct, the theorem supports rank-expansion as the right way to measure expansion in dense graphs, where edge-based notions lose force. The work ties a global width parameter to a local separation guarantee in a new, clean form.
arxiv-2511-13728:
Maximilian Reisecker and 3 co-authors present Gaia, a system that lends graphics processors to serverless AI functions across edge, cloud, and space settings. Serverless platforms scale elastically and charge per use, but picking the right accelerator by hand fails as loads and placements shift. Static assignments miss service goals, and one-time choices waste money.

Gaia treats acceleration as a platform duty. A lightweight checker reads each function at deploy time and tags one of four execution modes, while the runtime keeps rechecking service goals and promotes or demotes jobs between processor types. Tests showed end-to-end delay cut by up to ninety-five percent, with hardware matched to each workload as conditions changed.
arxiv-2511-13828:
A. Traina and 23 co-authors measure how galaxies formed stars across most of cosmic time. Their study combines ultraviolet light, which shows young stars directly, with infrared light, which shows star birth hidden by dust. They build the first combined count of star-forming galaxies at each rate, reaching back to when the universe was young.

The team finds the two views fit together rather than overlap: ultraviolet data cover the slower star formers, while infrared data catch the fastest ones. Current computer models of galaxy growth match the counts well at early times but miss the most extreme star-forming galaxies later on. Neither view alone can give the full total rate of star birth.
arxiv-2511-14328:
Kartik Tathe and Sayan Ghosh characterize counting processes through martingales, the fair-game processes of probability theory. Their subject is non-homogeneous counting processes, where events arrive at rates that change over time, plus fractional variants built by warping the clock. They first show a weighted sum of non-homogeneous Poisson processes gives the non-homogeneous generalized counting process.

For that process they derive martingale characterizations in both compensated and exponential form and prove the two are equivalent. The analysis then extends to time-changed versions of the process and to their Skellam counterparts, which count differences between two streams, using stable and inverse stable subordinators as the random clocks.
arxiv-2511-14828:
Frances Herr turns a classic classroom craft into a research question about curves and motion. In curve stitching, straight threads strung between points on a circle trace out a smooth-looking envelope curve. Herr fixes equally spaced points on the circle, picks a multiplier, and joins each point to the point reached by multiplying its label, all modulo the count.

The stitched designs raise a sharp question: what envelope will a given multiplier produce? Herr links the discrete stitch graph to a continuous-time dynamical system and studies it with topological tools. The bridge between a hands-on activity and dynamics gives teachers and students a rare case where a craft pattern can be fully explained.
arxiv-2511-15028:
Christophe Gyurgyik, Alexander J Root, and Fredrik Kjolstad separate how bounding volume hierarchies store their data from how they are searched. These tree structures speed up graphics, simulation, and analytics by grouping nearby objects, and their speed hinges on memory layout: cache use, bandwidth, and vectorization. In most systems, layout choices are tangled into the search code, so neither side can be tuned freely.

Their language and compiler, called Scion, lets programmers state a hierarchy's layout on its own, apart from any traversal algorithm. The authors show Scion can express the broad range of layout tricks used in high-performance codes. Untangling the two choices should let one search routine run fast on many machines.
arxiv-2511-15228:
Liu Chang and Wang Ran establish a fine limit law for a noisy heat equation driven by long-memory noise. The equation spreads an initial state under a fractional Laplacian while a Gaussian noise, white in time and correlated in space like a fractional Brownian motion, keeps stirring it. Laws of the iterated logarithm describe the exact envelope within which such random solutions swing as time grows.

The authors prove Chung's version of that law for the solution at the origin, the sharpest form, which tracks the smallest excursions rather than the largest. The fractional spreading power and the noise memory must sit in stated ranges for the result to hold. Precise envelopes like this anchor the theory of stochastic partial differential equations.
arxiv-2511-16028:
Shurui Cao, Wenyue Hua, and three co-authors ask whether online talk about generative AI can forecast labor market change. Most measures of workforce AI exposure describe the present and cannot foresee disruption. Their study tests talk intensity in news media and Reddit forums as a leading signal. Thirteen job groups are covered.

Data combine a large corpus of model talk, LinkedIn job postings and millions of user profiles, and an Indeed index. Four methods link talk intensity to later job postings, net hiring, tenure patterns, jobless duration, and moves into AI roles. Talk forecast employment changes one to seven months ahead across several signs.
arxiv-2511-16128:
Zhongxian Cao proves rigidity for one remaining case of five-dimensional quasi-Einstein manifolds with constant scalar curvature. A quasi-Einstein manifold is a space whose curvature satisfies a modified Einstein equation with an extra potential function, and the manifolds here are compact, simply connected, nontrivial, and have a boundary. Earlier work by Costa, Ribeiro, and Zhou reduced the possible scalar curvature values to a list indexed by a small integer parameter.

Two of those cases were already classified. Cao settles the case indexed by three, showing it is rigid, meaning the geometry is forced into a specific form rather than allowing a family of distinct examples. The result narrows the classification program for these five-dimensional spaces with constant scalar curvature.
arxiv-2511-16528:
Özay Ezerceli and six co-authors benchmark dense and late interaction retrieval models for Turkish, a morphologically rich lower resource language. Dense encoders dominate Turkish retrieval, but late interaction models keep token level detail for finer matching. No systematic comparison existed. Their two stage pipeline adapts English and multilingual encoders on Turkish inference and similarity tasks, then converts them into late interaction retrievers.

Ten models are evaluated across five Turkish benchmark data sets spanning science, finance, and argumentation. A tiny hashed model proves hundreds of times smaller than a large dense encoder while staying competitive. Parameter efficiency is a headline finding. Results guide builders of search for languages where large models are costly to serve.
arxiv-2511-16628:
Tammam Bakeer, Max Herbers, and Steffen Marx build a Bayesian framework for structural health monitoring. It says not just what a bridge's hidden properties are, but where the sensors can actually see them. Recovering a distributed property such as flexural rigidity from sparse tilt measurements is ill-posed, and classic regularization stabilizes the math without revealing resolution limits or uncertainty.

Fisher information serves as the diagnostic tool: it measures how informative each sensor layout and load path is about each part of the parameter field. Applied to the full-scale openLAB research bridge in Dresden under controlled vehicle passages, the method estimates the rigidity profile. It attaches credible intervals that expose regions where the property simply cannot be identified. The lesson is that information content is real but unevenly spread, bounded by experiment design, which makes the framework a guide for placing sensors and trusting diagnoses.
arxiv-2511-16728:
Mario G Abadi, Gabriela Castelletti, and Namir E Kassim study the radio spectra of pulsars. Pulsars are the spinning remains of dead stars that send out radio beams. Many pulsar spectra bend down sharply at low frequencies, a shape linked to free-free absorption, where hot gas along the line of sight soaks up the radio waves.

The team gathers sixty-three pulsars with that bent shape from four earlier studies and scales each spectrum to its own peak point so the set can be compared fairly. The peak points follow a clear pattern tied to the typical slope of pulsar emission. Turnover points cluster near five hundred and fifty-eight megahertz, which points to dense gas. The patterns suggest the absorbing gas may sit close to the pulsars themselves.
arxiv-2511-17628:
Fanbo Ju, Haiyuan Shi, and Qingjian Ni address a flaw in cascaded systems for precipitation nowcasting, the task of forecasting rain minutes to hours ahead from current radar. The standard cascade first predicts an average outcome with a firm model, then adds local randomness with a second model. Trouble comes from mixing two things: a steady shift in the first model's output and the true local randomness.

That shift leaks into the second stage and warps the rain patterns and intensities it produces, above all at longer lead times. Their framework, RectiCast, splits the job in two: it first corrects the shift, then models the randomness on the cleaned result. Keeping the two apart should give forecasters rain maps that stay truer as the horizon stretches.
arxiv-2511-17828:
Guilherme Cavalcante, Jose Gabriel Moreira, Gabriel do Nascimento, and ten co-authors adapt a large foundation model to classify breast density from mammograms. Density categories guide screening decisions, and a model that works across imaging types and populations would help clinics with varied equipment.

Training a biomedical vision and language model on many tens of thousands of images gives similar accuracy for single type and multi type training, with the multi type model applying more broadly. Tests on two outside data sets confirm strong performance across groups. Heat maps show the model attends to clinically sensible regions, supporting trust in its judgments.
arxiv-2511-18128:
Dimitrios Chatzis and four co-authors present detailed calculations for holographic models of renormalization group flows. In these flows, a four dimensional quantum field theory at high energy flows to a three dimensional one at low energy. The gravity side uses smooth solutions in higher dimensional supergravity, built through twisted compactifications and flows along a Coulomb branch.

They compute a wide range of observables and analyze the dual field theories closely, including boundary terms and holographic renormalization in the simplest case. Many observables factorize into a part carrying information about the starting theory and a universal flow part. All the starting points flow to confining theories with a mass gap.
arxiv-2511-18228:
Sucai Niu and Junyi Zhu study when a wave equation with a twist has sound, lasting solutions. The equation blends the classic nonlinear Schrödinger form with extra terms named for Gerdjikov and Ivanov. To test it they use the Riemann-Hilbert method, which turns the wave task into a jump task on a line.

They build two such jump tasks and two sets of scatter data that track how waves spread. Bounds show small shifts in the start wave cause only small shifts in the scatter data, and the same holds in reverse. With no trapped modes, a global solution then exists for all time. The work firms up the base for later study of this wave type.
arxiv-2511-18328:
Akaki Mamageishvili, Christoph Schlegel, Ko Sunghun, Jinsuk Park, and Ali Taslimi test whether TimeBoost, an ahead-of-time auction for fast-lane access in blockchain trading, actually works as intended. Traders bid for a time edge, and the question is whether those bids predict the value the winner will extract. The team compares winning bids against the later markout, a measure of value gained over the auction interval, for fast-lane trades.

The link turns out weak: bids are a noisy guide to extracted value for single trades. Using the price actually paid, the second-highest bid, improves the match slightly, hinting at a common-value auction. Over long spans, though, bids and gains line up much better, so bidders read trends well even when their timing is off. Frequent bidders keep their ranking and profits throughout.
arxiv-2511-18628:
Joakim Cronvall and Aron Wennman prove that local patterns of random normal matrix eigenvalues look the same at edges, no matter the fine details. Such matrices model planar Coulomb gases, dots that repel like charges. At a soft edge the gas thins out; at a hard edge a wall cuts it. Past proofs leaned on orthogonal polynomials.

Their direct route skips that tool. Spectral embeddings of Paley-Wiener type and weighted polynomials peaked at a boundary point do the work. Results cover hard edges with no symmetry claims, soft edges for multi part droplets, and mixed edges where the two meet. One frame thus spans the edge cases. Universality of this kind anchors random matrix theory.
arxiv-2511-18828:
Edgar Dobriban documents how he solved an open problem in robust statistics with heavy help from a large language model. The problem asks for the best possible error rate when a density is estimated from data dirtied by bounded contamination, measured in Wasserstein terms. Past work by Chao and Dobriban found upper and lower bounds that did not meet, so the sharp rate stayed open.

In late 2025, with much use of GPT-5 Pro, Dobriban reports closing that gap and pinning the minimax rate. The short note walks through the collaboration and the result. It adds a dated case to the small set where a model helped prove a new math result. Human direction and machine search share the credit here.
arxiv-2511-19028:
Xilai Li, Yilin Wu, Zhengnuo Chen, Mengqi Yang, and Jie Zhang build a weakly nonlinear theory for the Rayleigh-Taylor instability on a spherical, moving interface. The instability grows when a heavy fluid pushes into a light one.
