Stacking redbacks and black widows apart showed no clear spectral split either. The null result suggests spider pulsars add little to the Galaxy's TeV glow.
arxiv-2603-28728: Mallick, Kundu, and Kompella survey the post-quantum status of nine widely used protocols. Quantum computing threatens RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, which many protocols rely on. They examine TLS, IPsec, BGP, DNSSEC, SSH, QUIC, OpenID Connect, OpenVPN, and the Signal Protocol. TLS and Signal lead, with hybrid post-quantum key exchange already deployed at scale. IPsec and SSH have standard mechanisms but little production use. DNSSEC and BGP face deep structural barriers from large signature sizes. Across protocols, key exchange migrates more easily than authentication, they find.
arxiv-2603-29028: Alves and Barata use contextuality to address the Frauchiger-Renner thought experiment. That experiment has been said to show quantum theory is not logically sound. No such clash has ever appeared in real measurements. The authors weigh the trait of contextuality, as predicted by the Kochen-Specker theorem. With that trait in place, the claimed clash cannot be reached by logic. Their argument defends the soundness of quantum theory. It adds a modal logic reading of a Wigner's friend style case.
arxiv-2603-29128: Wei and co-authors present ADUCA, a cyclic algorithm for variational inequalities. Cyclic methods are simple and fast in practice, but their theory is hard. Step sizes usually need careful tuning or line searches. ADUCA needs no Lipschitz constants and no per-epoch line search. It reuses operator information delayed by a full cycle. That delay suits parallel and distributed runs. The authors prove near-optimal oracle complexity for the method. The cost scales with the inverse of the target error.
arxiv-2603-29228: Liao and Yin present CCDNet, a network for spotting small infrared targets. Such targets have low contrast and blend into complex backgrounds. Look-alike objects also trigger false alarms. Their backbone merges multi-level features with weighted multi-branch perceptrons. A fusion neck rebuilds links between targets and backgrounds. That step highlights targets and suppresses clutter. A contrastive module then separates real targets from distractors. Experiments on infrared datasets beat leading methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-29328: Herath and co-authors present SABLE, a semantics-aware backdoor attack on federated learning. Most backdoor tests use fake corner patches that rarely occur in practice. SABLE instead builds natural, in-distribution triggers. An example is a semantic change like adding sunglasses. An aggregation-aware objective keeps attacker updates close to benign ones. Tests ran on CelebA and a traffic-sign benchmark. Only a small slice of local data was poisoned. Attack success stayed high across four aggregation rules. Benign accuracy was preserved.
arxiv-2603-29428: Wang and Wang test vision-language models on classic optical illusions. The models tend to call the illusion real, even when the image was changed to remove it. Their framework gives the model simple image tools, with no training. Tools draw lines, crop regions, compare views, and isolate channels. A routing prompt picks tools by question type. Each tool call adds a new annotated image to a shared registry. The model can then reuse any earlier view. Performance held up on unfamiliar illusion variants.
arxiv-2603-29528: Jahnke and van der Schaaf study the model theory of deeply ramified fields. They work in positive characteristic. Earlier work by Jahnke and Kartas covered the perfect case, tied to perfectoid fields. This work extends those Ax-Kochen/Ershov principles to deeply ramified fields. The fields have a fixed degree of imperfection. The results cover certain henselian valued fields of rank one. Such principles link a valued field to its residue and value data. The paper generalizes the perfect-field theory.
arxiv-2603-29928: Landsgesell, Knoll, and Wenzel build ScoringBench for judging tabular foundation models. Such models output full predictive distributions, yet benchmarks mostly grade point guesses. Their bench scores models with proper scoring rules like CRPS and interval scores. It covers 101 regression datasets from many domains. Two ranking schemes are offered, one ordinal and one magnitude-aware. Tests show rankings shift with the scoring rule chosen. Strong point scorers can slip on probabilistic measures.
arxiv-2604-00228: Tanay Gondil asks whether language models can predict their own refusals before answering, testing models forecasting refusal before responding. Across 3754 points and 300 requests, four models show introspection, with d-prime values between 2.4 and 3.5, though sensitivity falls at boundaries. Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads its family at about 96 percent against about 93 percent for Sonnet 4, while GPT-5.2 trails at about 89 percent and Llama at 80 percent with refusal bias and poor calibration. Weapons queries prove hardest, and high-confidence predictions reach about 98 percent for calibrated models, enabling confidence-based routing.
arxiv-2604-00428: Li, Zhang, and Zardini tackle multi-agent path finding in warehouses and logistics, where many robots must move without colliding. Closed-loop methods plan only the next step and replan online, which scales well but can turn shortsighted and lose global guarantees. The authors introduce certificate trajectories: conflict-free fallback plans with a fleet budget that filter each closed-loop update. A certificate keeps a safe plan in reserve, so only updates consistent with the fallback survive.
arxiv-2604-00628: Vogelgesang and colleagues present StretchBot, a neuro-symbolic coach that adapts guidance to users. Care robots could support bodily wellbeing at home and in healthcare, for instance by guiding stretching or rehabilitation sessions. Yet current systems stay largely scripted and adjust poorly to user state, settings, and live exchanges. StretchBot joins multi-sense sensing with knowledge-graph-grounded language-model logic, tuning context-aware guidance during short stretching sessions while keeping a set routine. A small pilot with three people tests scripted and flexible guidance.
arxiv-2604-00828: Lüderssen, Neumann, and Peng study four-cycle counting in arbitrary-order graph streams. They present a 3-pass algorithm that approximates the number of four-cycles within a factor of 1 plus epsilon. It uses space roughly m over the square root of T, where m counts edges and T counts four-cycles. That improves on an earlier 3-pass method and matches a known multi-pass lower bound.
arxiv-2604-01028: Wu and team develop a Non-Spherical Potential Field model for the coronal magnetic field, tackling the open-flux problem. The Potential Field Source Surface model extrapolates far less open flux than in-situ measurements imply. Their model replaces the spherical source surface with a non-spherical one, an isosurface of the total magnetic field. This surface forms concave structures beneath external current sheets, generating more open flux with a plausible open field layout. The model reproduces complex coronal topologies, interplanetary field properties, and solar wind source mappings.
arxiv-2604-01228: Dhayalkar presents a formal framework for simulating alternating finite automata with logic-gated time-shared feedforward networks. Prior neural models covered only nondeterministic machines and existential reach. Here learnable state-dependent biases act as smooth logic gates, covering both OR and AND combining in a shared linear recurrence. He proves the network class matches alternating automata in structure. A language needing 2 to the n states in a nondeterministic machine needs only n neurons. Tests show the model fully recovers topology and semantics from binary labels.
arxiv-2604-01328: Yu and colleagues offer a guide to Bayesian optimization, a chance-driven system that sets out and runs the hypothesise-experiment-refine cycle of science. Proxy models, such as Gaussian models, turn data into changing guesses. Acquisition functions guide test choice, balancing use of known ground against search of new ground. The guide frames discovery as a search problem, unpacks core parts and workflows, and shows value through case studies in catalysis, materials and molecule discovery. It also covers batched tests, context optimization and human help.
arxiv-2604-01628: Li and colleagues decompose the Milky Way stellar halo between 3 and 160 kpc into metal-rich and metal-poor components using 64,000 halo K giants from DESI Data Release 2. The two populations are nearly equal in number but chemically and kinematically distinct: metal-rich stars occupy highly radial orbits with velocity anisotropy near 0.94. Metal-poor stars exhibit a weaker radial bias turning negative beyond 80 kpc. The outer halo is simultaneously contracting and subject to reflex motions increasing with radius, reflecting perturbation from the Large Magellanic Cloud.
arxiv-2604-01728: Morlidge and colleagues present the AnIML Ontology, a vocabulary pinning down AnIML, an XML standard for storing and swapping lab data. The XML schema alone lets groups read the same files in clashing ways. So the team built an OWL 2 ontology and lined it up with the Allotrope Data Format for cross-lab sharing. Experts shaped it through LLM-aided elicitation plus ontology work. Checks turned real AnIML files into knowledge graphs, tested competency questions with SPARQL, and probed hostile negative questions enforced by SHACL rules.
arxiv-2604-01828: D'Amato and colleagues report the smallest quadruply lensed quasar, whose lensing galaxy sits at a redshift of 1.055, 5.5 billion years post-Big Bang, with a lensing mass. Gravitational lensing illuminates stars in stellar-dominated cores of elliptical galaxies, key to cosmic structure evolution. A Bayesian analysis using standard scaling relations sampled the central initial mass function with unmatched accuracy in an uncharted regime. The function matches the Milky Way's, excluding bottom-heavy functions, suggesting slow growth or early disruptive events, against the classical view of rapid, unchanged bulge formation.
arxiv-2604-03128: Yang and colleagues untangle when self-distillation helps reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a setup where a model teaches itself using privileged answers. They show signals drawn only from that privileged teacher leak information and destabilize long training. Their fix, RLSD, uses self-distillation only to size each update, while verifiable rewards set the direction, lifting the training ceiling and steadying learning.
arxiv-2604-03228: Midha and colleagues put belief propagation for quantum many-body tensor networks on firm ground. For states meeting a loop-decay rule, belief propagation plus cluster fixes predict local observables with tiny relative error, and the fixes link straight to correlation functions. Loop decay thus forces fast decay of correlations, ruling the method out at critical points, as Ising tests confirm.
arxiv-2604-03628: Caravano, Franciolini, and Renaux-Petel compute scalar-induced gravitational waves from ultra-slow-roll inflation with lattice models, growing the inflaton field in full and pulling bend ripples exactly. For mild non-Gaussianity, pen-and-paper guesses get the size roughly right but need important fixes. When non-Gaussianities run large, pen-and-paper guesses fail badly in height and spectral shape. Trusty guesses then need exact control of inflationary scalar moves.
arxiv-2604-03928: Indar Kumar and colleagues revisited Linear Discriminant Analysis on frozen image features, a classical step often skipped in transfer learning. Across six backbones and three datasets, LDA beat full features in 11 of 12 coarse-grained setups, gaining up to 4.5 percentage points while shrinking features by 48 to 87 percent. On fine-grained CUB-200, however, full features won everywhere, since LDA drops subtle cues. Plain LDA thus offers the best accuracy-cost tradeoff for coarse tasks, while fancier supervised methods rarely justify their cost.
arxiv-2604-04028: Mohsen Kazemian and Jürgen Jasperneite built a physics-aware language-model predictor for channel state information in fast-moving 6G systems. Rapidly changing channels leave very short coherence times, so pilot-based estimates go stale or cost too much overhead. Their predictor learns how OTFS channel coefficients evolve from past observations, guided by mobility clues like maximum Doppler frequency. Tests at user speeds from 100 to 500 kilometers per hour showed lower error than classical deep predictors and physics-free language-model rivals.
arxiv-2604-04128: Javier Jiménez-López and V. J. García-Garrido set out Lagrangian descriptors in the path integral frame. Taking the average of the classical marker over jitter around edge paths defines its quantum version that carries quantum effects. Fixed manifolds that sharply order old-style transport become finite-width phase space shapes under quantum jitter, and their overlap gives a shape trick for barrier crossing as jitter-driven spread of transport barriers. Tests on the Hamiltonian saddle showed spread and barrier crossing.
arxiv-2604-04428: Anand and colleagues report two forms of heterogeneous nucleation driving single-step and multi-step transitions toward synchronization in finite-size adaptive networks with delays. The team shows the transition depends on delay presence and size and on the natural frequency distribution class. Using collective coordinates, they build a mean-field description of cluster dynamics and derive an upper bound for two-cluster states, matching tests well. They extend the analysis to varied delays, giving a model for synchronization shifts in adaptive networks with delayed links.
arxiv-2604-04528: Foffano, Russo and Proutiere study trajectory optimization where system dynamics are unknown and paths cannot be run through a stand-in. The team offers Drifting MPC, an offline frame mixing drifting models and rolling-horizon planning. It learns a path distribution backed by the data, biased toward optimal plans. They show the learned distribution is the answer to an objective trading optimality against nearness to the offline prior. Tests show Drifting MPC generates near-best paths while keeping one-step inference speed, cutting generation time against diffusion-based marks.
arxiv-2604-04828: Papierz and five colleagues build a hybrid model that predicts how high-energy lasers shape metal, joining heat flow, melting, surface movement, and phase change in one three-dimensional simulation. Their design swaps some dense spectral blocks in a Fourier neural operator for a compact quantum circuit mixer shared across modes, cutting trainable parameters by 15.6 percent while lowering phase-fraction error by 26 percent and temperature error from 2.89 percent to 2.56 percent.
arxiv-2604-05028: Karwin and five co-authors map gamma-ray emission from low-brightness active galactic nuclei, most local active galaxies, yet rarely seen in gamma rays. High-energy light is forecast from both jets and disks of these galaxies, but only four had been seen by Fermi LAT. The authors study all such objects from the Palomar survey of bright northern galaxies, including faint and seen sources, using 14.4 years of LAT data. Their analysis yields a new detection of one galaxy, plus a faint-population signal through stacking, matching forecasts.
arxiv-2604-05428: Liu, Wang, and Zhu train causal convolutional networks to rebuild traits of fast-spinning neutron stars, whose full two-dimensional models run too slowly for inference work. They train on runs from the RNS code and check the nets on three sample equations of state, finding close matches to reference results. One equation of state runs in about 50 milliseconds, against roughly 30 minutes by direct computation.
arxiv-2604-05528: Antony and three colleagues study k-Inversion, where flipping arcs inside chosen vertex sets must render a directed graph acyclic. The problem is NP-complete for fixed k, yet fixed-parameter tractable on tournaments. They extend the tournament algorithm, derive one for block graphs, and give a general algorithm running in time exponential in treewidth times k plus treewidth.
arxiv-2604-06228: Magarshak introduces probabilistic language tries, a representation of the prefix structure of any generative model. Giving each edge its conditional token or action probability yields three tools. They are a lossless compressor building on arithmetic coding, a policy for games, search, and robotics, and a memoization index for repeat queries. A caching theorem shows the trie cache beats frequency-based caching below a threshold, cutting attention cost toward logarithmic when reuse is likely. A hybrid design pairs the trie-covered majority with a sparse residual store.
arxiv-2604-06528: Malik and 32 colleagues survey high-dimensional quantum photonics, where light's spatial, temporal, and spectral shapes carry multi-level quantum states. The roadmap reviews how such states are made, steered, and shared. It shows how they enable tests of quantum theory that resist noise, tough high-capacity links, and efficient data handling. Noting that work has advanced in separate strands with little cross-talk, it maps shared challenges across forms and points toward shared future quantum platforms.
arxiv-2604-06628: Ren and ten colleagues revisit the claim that supervised fine-tuning only memorizes while reinforcement learning generalizes. For reasoning fine-tuning with long chain-of-thought supervision, cross-domain transfer proves conditional, shaped jointly by training dynamics, data, and base-model strength. Short training can mislead, since performance first dips then recovers, while verified long traces help and stronger models pick up transferable habits like backtracking. The catch is asymmetry: reasoning improves while safety slips, so the question becomes under what conditions and at what cost transfer happens.
arxiv-2604-07128: Liu and nine colleagues build a privacy pipeline that lets hospitals share radiology data without leaking patient identity. Sharing scans is blocked by privacy rules, and older scrubbing asks mainly whether identity can be stripped, not whether cleaned data still trains well. Their pipeline pairs a block list of private terms with a keep list of disease terms, and swaps scans for made counterparts that keep disease signs but drop private traits. Tests on public chest X ray sets show disease accuracy holds up while identity guessing falls.
arxiv-2604-07228: Llabrés and three colleagues study how cooperation grows in public goods games played in groups, not just pairs. In their hypergraph model, each new cooperator can boost or blunt the group's gain, which shifts the point where cooperation takes off. When game sizes mix, a zone appears where coexistence and full cooperation can both hold. Uneven, scale-free group links boost cooperation more, and where cooperators start out also shapes the result.
arxiv-2604-07628: Mia and three colleagues present TrilinearCIM, a Double-Gate FeFET design for in-memory Transformer attention. Self-attention creates dynamic operands that push conventional compute-in-memory accelerators into costly memory reprogramming, hurting throughput and device life. TrilinearCIM uses back-gate modulation for a three-operand multiply-accumulate step for attention without dynamic ferroelectric reprogramming. On BERT-base over GLUE and ViT-base over ImageNet and CIFAR, it beats conventional compute-in-memory on seven of nine GLUE tasks, with up to 46.6 percent less energy and 20.4 percent lower latency.
arxiv-2604-08128: Liu, Zhu, and Gu report a crossing seam blockade in excited-state chemistry. Electronic degeneracies, including conical intersections and avoided crossings with strong vibronic couplings and nonadiabatic jumps, shape light-driven processes in chemistry, physics, and biology. Yet effects on excited-state chemical reactivity remain unclear. In this study, an open reaction channel proves completely blocked by a crossing seam in molecular shape space. Exact ab initio quantum dynamics simulations show the singlet fission channel in the hydrogen chain H4 is blocked by quantum geometry.
arxiv-2604-08228: Sun, Wu, and Wang develop fast codes that keep structure for nonlinear Maxwell-Ampere Nernst-Planck equations. In the first-order scheme, the Slotboom shift recasts the Nernst-Planck equation so positivity holds. Backward Euler plus centered finite differences solve the changed system. Two fixes are added: one enforces Gauss's law with a displacement fix, and the other keeps Faraday's law through potential rebuild. The fully discrete scheme exactly meets mass conservation, positivity, energy loss, and both laws, with known error bounds.
arxiv-2604-08428: Zeng and five colleagues argue that planet orbits around sunlike stars show a quantized pattern, like electrons confined in atoms. Trapped waves in the young planet forming disc, they propose, set standing waves tens of astronomical units wide, already hinted at by ring patterns seen with ALMA. Within one astronomical unit, such waves could carve a valley in where sub Neptune planets sit, and surveys compared in the paper support that reading.
arxiv-2604-08528: Yoo and three colleagues measure grip slip with sound instead of sight, touch films, or force sensors. Their A-SLIP system places piezoelectric microphones behind a textured silicone pad in a parallel jaw gripper and reads contact vibrations as spectrograms with a small convolutional network. The four microphone setup predicts slip presence, direction, and size with a mean direction error of 14.1 degrees, and cuts direction error by 64 percent against single microphone designs.
arxiv-2604-08828: Hsu and Balestriero propose Joint Flow Distribution Learning, a lightweight matching method bringing guidance without a classifier to ready made steady models without a spread teacher. Steady models sample in one or few steps, but current guidance needs copying from another spread teacher, capping guidance to copying methods. With the steady model as a plain changing formula solver, bell curve tests confirm the implied variance growing noise is Gaussian. The method unlocks guided making on a steady trained model while cutting FID on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64x64.
arxiv-2604-09328: Peschmann shows the perfect Euler brick problem equals an elementary question: whether two quartic expressions can both be perfect squares at once. Despite near-identical structure, differing only in the first summand, no solution has ever been found. Peschmann reduces the quartic pair to genus-3 hyperelliptic curves and develops obstructions on the elliptic quotient. There, the Kummer character is non-trivial on the 4-torsion, and 2-descent arguments exclude several square classes. Checks verify no solution exists for parameters up to 1,000, though perfect Euler bricks are not yet excluded.
arxiv-2604-09528: Lee and Millis tackle a blind spot in cold-atom imaging. Ordinary snapshots reveal only density, while the phase field stays hidden. That field exposes vortices and confirms superfluidity. The authors train a U-Net model on simulated two-dimensional condensate states to infer phase gradients from density alone. A second model locates vortex cores. Graphical post-processing then reads each vortex's quantized charge. The combination reconstructs the full phase field with high accuracy.
arxiv-2604-09828: Das and four co-authors test the Kerr hypothesis with the compact binary coalescence GW241011. A Kerr black hole's multipole moments are fixed by its mass and spin, and gravitational waves can probe moments imprinted on the inspiral phase. GW241011 lets the team test at once for spin-induced quadrupole deviations and octupole deviations in the binary parts. They find no Kerr-prediction deviations and set the first limits on spin-induced octupole moments for a compact binary. The approach complements remnant ringdown tests.
arxiv-2604-09928: Durka, Kowalski-Glikman, and Payne study kept charges in N equals 1 supergravity as a bound BF theory on the OSp algebra. Using phase-space methods, they derive bulk and boundary parts to the phase structure and build charges for Lorentz turns, SUSY, shifts, and shape changes. The boundary charge algebra matches the expected algebra, while shift charges vanish on-shell under the super-torsion constraint, leaving Lorentz and SUSY as the real sources.
arxiv-2604-10128: Xu, Pollmann, and Knap predict entanglement spectra for gapless symmetry-protected topological states in 1D. Like gapped peers, these gapless states show shared spectral degeneracies. They focus on gapless states made by applying unitary SPT entanglers to trivial critical states. A quantum channel on the trivial state's reduced density matrix yields the other state's matrix, exactly or roughly. That channel acts only near the cut, changing its boundary rule to yield the target theory. The method applies to varied central charges.
arxiv-2604-10228: Qian and eight colleagues tackle shallow reasoning in multimodal models with SVSR, a framework that builds self-checking and self-fixing into thought. Training runs in three stages: a unified preference data set refined from thought traces, forward and backward, and cold-start fine-tuning for structured multi-step thought. Semi-online preference tuning then keeps adding teacher-picked traces. The trained model improves, extends to unseen tasks and question types, and even reasons well when no traces are given.
arxiv-2604-10428: Shao tests whether average case checks can certify the HHL quantum solver. Linden and de Wolf showed good average Fourier checks serve many quantum tasks well. Inside HHL, though, phase slips between eigenspaces break that loose promise. Shao adds a tougher check that reins in the cross space coherences. Under that check, worst case HHL correctness holds in several natural settings.
arxiv-2604-10528: Baranwal, Yadav, and Rajora test whether vision language models truly see shape. Rich color and scene hints may let models fake shape sense with texture shortcuts. Their BareBones set strips scenes to bare silhouettes across six data pools. A flagship puzzle set, WTP-Bench, forces calls from edge lines alone. All 26 tested models crash under color loss, a drop the authors dub the Texture Bias Cliff.
arxiv-2604-10628: Spanio, Guler, and Rodà build a music dataset from expert transcriptions of Baroque manuscripts. The scores use LilyPond, a text-based format for writing music, little used for music study. The set holds 393 scores with 2,646 movements, marked by composer, form, instruments, and section. They also train LilyBERT, an encoder tuned to LilyPond notation. Tuning on this small hand-picked set beats broad pretraining on a far larger corpus for composer and style sorting. Mixing both reaches 84.3 percent composer accuracy.
arxiv-2604-11128: Kundu and three colleagues evaluate tech fixes for generative AI inference in constrained settings. Generative AI workloads, notably language model inference, raise memory pressure. Multimodal inputs and large-document uses incur long contexts, requiring caching of key and value states. Even low concurrent serving on mobiles adds memory pressure and care load. The authors test two emerging solutions using a roofline-based performance model. For large models, they study high bandwidth storage and its bandwidth and latency needs. For small models, they test a bonded global buffer memory chiplet.
arxiv-2604-11528: Bannikova and five colleagues simulate a self-gravitating torus around a central mass to test whether a slow lopsided mode can arise on its own. Using a high-order Hermite GPU code, they find a global m=1 mode forms from symmetric starts. Coherent apsidal alignment sustains the lopsided structure over long timescales, aided by nonlinear links of low-order modes and enough vertical thickness. The long-lived overdensity displaces the central mass from the center, offering a frame for eccentric nuclear disks like M31's and for AGN molecular tori.
arxiv-2604-11828: Mabrok argues that scientific knowledge at any moment sits at a local optimum rather than a global one. That state is shaped by historical chance, cognitive path dependence, and institutional lock-in. Likening discovery to gradient descent in machine learning, he claims science follows the steepest local gradient of tractability, accessibility, and reward, possibly bypassing better descriptions of nature. Case studies across six fields support three interlocking lock-in mechanisms, and he proposes interventions to help science escape such traps.
arxiv-2604-12128: Bae tests whether language models fail on self-reference itself or only on circular truth claims that cannot settle in finite steps. In his main test, statements refer to one another in a cycle with exactly one consistent assignment. Yet four open models still answered inconsistent far more often than on matched controls without cycles. Layer-wise truth signals recovered the answer for grounded twins but not for circular cases. This shows models read unsettled circular dependence as contradiction.
arxiv-2604-12228: Tseng and five colleagues automate turning cyber threat indicators into regular expressions for security operations, a task analysts still do by hand. Their IOCRegex-gen system groups indicator segments into capture or non-capture groups and validates candidates through iterative reasoning and multi-stage checks. On over 3,000 real threat reports and 2,400 ground-truth strings it hits 99.1 percent with only 0.8 percent false positives.
arxiv-2604-12828: Madhav Sharma and two colleagues track sodium order in a NASICON material across temperature. Synchrotron diffraction shows a shift from monoclinic order to rhombohedral disorder. The phosphate host stays intact, so sodium redistribution drives the shift. The c-axis and cell volume jump as sodium moves to Na(2) sites. Superstructure intensity strays from mean-field behavior but fits a sigmoidal model. Calorimetry finds the lower enthalpy far larger than the higher anomaly. Sodium order runs through middle states with a mixed regime.
arxiv-2604-13028: Tezcan, Viswanath, Saher, and Aliaga invert the usual urban heat workflow: instead of predicting temperatures from vegetation, they generate vegetation layouts that hit a chosen temperature goal. A forward model plus a diffusion-based generative model produce varied, physically plausible planting patterns for the same target, even combinations missing from training data. The approach gives planners controllable options for cooling cities rather than a single averaged answer.
arxiv-2604-13128: Remy, Chang, and Leung learn how people share responsibility in shared settings, how much each person shifts from their own desired behavior to make room for others. Their model captures the spread across possible allocations using a variational autoencoder plus multi-agent path forecasting, with a trainable optimization layer linking shares to observed controls. Tested on the INTERACTION driving dataset, it predicts well and yields readable patterns of multi-agent interaction.
arxiv-2604-13928: Krasnikov and colleagues test anomaly detection on real factory time series, where multi-stage processes make the data far messier than standard benchmarks. A classic Isolation Forest baseline misses the uneven, multi-scale patterns in the data. Autoencoders do consistently better across the board. Temporal convolutional autoencoders prove most robust. Recurrent and variational versions need more careful tuning to match them. In short, simple tools fail on real plant data.
arxiv-2604-14028: Ouahioune and colleagues study parity-mixing interference in helium photoionization by high-order harmonics plus a laser. Usual interference keeps parity through two-photon paths, but one- versus two-photon interference breaks it. With few-cycle harmonics and 3D electron tracking they find four parity-mixing pathways. The paths use two harmonic fields or one, and a probe photon is taken in or given out.
arxiv-2604-14128: Yao and three colleagues probe how large language models hold rhetorical questions, asked to persuade rather than to seek facts. With simple linear probes on two social media collections, they find such questions separate cleanly from genuine questions and stay visible across collections, scoring roughly 0.7 to 0.8. Yet probes trained on different collections rank examples differently, so the team argues several distinct patterns, not one shared code, carry rhetorical force.
arxiv-2604-15128: Ramhorst and colleagues build SCENIC, an open-source SmartNIC that treats its datapath as a stream computer. Commercial cards offer speed and easy software fit but little customization, while research cards often lack bandwidth, features, or true NIC behavior. SCENIC runs a 200G datapath with offloaded TCP/IP and RDMA stacks, plus a fallback path for arbitrary traffic. Shared hardware and software abstractions let infrastructure and applications be designed tightly together.
arxiv-2604-15228: Guo, Zhao, and Wang study universal quantum state purification under energy-preserving operations. Noise degrades the purity that quantum tasks rely on, and purification tries to restore it by jointly processing several noisy copies. When operations cannot exchange energy with the outside world, the team pins down exactly when no universal advantage is possible. They also give cases where an advantage open to unrestricted operations vanishes under energy conservation, and examine the cases where purification remains possible.
arxiv-2604-15428: Varas and 20 colleagues build the largest uniform catalogue of projected rotational velocities for M dwarfs from CARMENES spectra. Their oversampled convolution method with a realistic limb-darkening model, tested on synthetic spectra, yields values or upper limits for 392 M dwarfs at a median relative uncertainty of 6.8 percent, far below the 15.4 percent in past work. The list holds 36 new targets and updated values for several known ones.
arxiv-2604-15728: Wu and five colleagues route LLM asks with care for privacy, since the route step sits between users and model firms and opens new leaks. Their PPRoute speeds code that runs the chooser and the near-neighbor hunt under joint secret math, keeping route quality high. A new unsorted Top-k trick cuts link cost to order one for safe sorting in model hunt. Tests show plain-text-level route quality with about 20 times the speed of plain joint-secret-math builds.
arxiv-2604-15828: Musiat, Ebert, and Wasenmüller propose SSFT, a compact transformer that sorts hyperspectral images, which record many wavelengths per pixel, into material classes. It splits learning into spectral and spatial paths joined by cross-attention, so wavelength patterns and shapes inform each other. Tested on a mixed benchmark spanning Earth observation, fruit condition, and fine material recognition, it ranked first while using under 2 percent of the parameters of the previous leader.
arxiv-2604-16028: Yuan and Karliner point to a new source of hyperons for neutron star studies: nucleon-hyperon interactions shape neutron stars, but data are scarce for lack of sources. At a fixed-target experiment with a known-momentum proton beam and a hydrogen target, proton-proton collisions produce Lambda hyperons. Tagging the proton and kaon fixes the Lambda flux and momentum precisely, and a second target around the first turns these Lambdas into a source. The authors propose an experiment with two nested targets, adaptable to FAIR and HIAF experiments.
arxiv-2604-16228: Wang and seven colleagues introduce TRON, a trainable optical neural network that can be reshaped for different architectures. Optical processors promise vast parallelism and bandwidth with lower energy use, but scalable, reconfigurable designs have been missing. TRON uses a scattering medium and a digital mirror device as a learnable dense matrix multiplier, tunes its optics in place, and searches architectures directly on the optics.
arxiv-2604-16428: Choi, Shook and Dubrawski examine how drift shows up inside the embeddings of time-series foundation models. Borrowing the quality-control view of a process leaving a stable regime, they test mean shifts, variance changes, linear trends and long-memory persistence under controlled conditions. They find that detectability in embedding space fades smoothly as shifts weaken, rather than vanishing at a sharp threshold. Different models also fail in distinct ways, warning against treating non-stationarity as a single, model-free effect.
arxiv-2604-16828: Kim and colleagues split roles of anisotropic crack density and aimed strain energy in phase-field fracture models. Crack density anisotropy steers crack path and toughness while elastic reply stays same. Aimed strain energy bends the crack but stalls rapidly, and in open-hole tension it governs stiffness, peak force and displacement. Tested against mixed-mode experiments on a soft rubber, the mechanisms mix beyond the sum of single shares. Crack density anisotropy governs fracture resistance, while strain energy governs the driving force and elastic energy spread near concentrators.
arxiv-2604-17228: Lin revisits auxiliary losses for conditional depth routing, where some tokens take a cheap FFN and the rest the full one. Lin compares an MLP gate scoring hidden states with a JEPA-guided gate predicting full-versus-cheap outcomes. With utility and rank supervision, the JEPA-guided gate improves early optimization in 3 of 3 seeds, with lower loss and about 10.3x lower gradient norms. Removing that supervision improves loss and speed for both gates and erases its edge, because the oracle label assumes all later layers run full.
arxiv-2604-17628: Parry-Jones takes a first computational step toward testing Welsh media bias claims, examining Nation.Cymru, a Welsh political news outlet. A two-stage pipeline pairs a RoBERTa bias detector with a large language model for target-attributed sentiment scoring of flagged labels. A primary analysis of 15,583 party mentions across 2022-2026 articles finds Reform UK framed with bias at twice Plaid Cymru's rate and over three times as negative in mean sentiment. A secondary analysis across four parties finds Plaid Cymru the outlier, framed markedly more favourably than any other party.
arxiv-2604-18128: Liu studies why extreme 4-bit compression wrecks a small SwiGLU language model. Under naive rounding, validation perplexity jumps from about 24 to over 1,700. A training-time fix called Depth Registers tames the residual stream and cuts that figure to 119. Pairing it with SmoothQuant brings it under 40. A careful split of the damage shows the surviving error lives mainly in one internal matrix, w2, which rotations alone cannot bound.
arxiv-2604-18228: Tagliaferro, Guindani, Lestingi, and Rossi build an agent-based pipeline that turns plain-language safety requirements into formal properties fit for verification. Current language-model tools check syntax but miss whether formal output truly matches the plain intent. Their system pulls out needs, filters them for fit with a target formalism, and turns them into properties. Tests in three settings reach 77.8 percent accuracy for output that matches in both form and meaning.
arxiv-2604-18328: Akinfaderin and Diallo offer FregeLogic, a neuro-symbolic hybrid for judging syllogistic validity at SemEval 2026. Five language-model classifiers vote first, and a Z3 solver settles disputed cases with formal verification. The idea is that ensemble disagreement flags content-biased errors, where believability warps logical judgment. Deferring disputed cases to Z3 yields 94.3 percent accuracy in nested cross-validation on 960 cases, with content bias down 16 percent from the pure ensemble.
arxiv-2604-18528: Evans, Shen, and Omar show open, heat-law-abiding chemical networks develop oscillatory instabilities near nonequilibrium states. Nonreciprocity marks out-of-balance systems, yielding motion ruled out near equilibrium, with wobbling and spinning. Wobbles appear in linear motion, where one-way coupling appears as complex numbers from uneven matrices. Here they arise from chemostat breaking of Onsager two-way balance, while local balance keeps the energy-based structure of lossy motion. Tests confirm one-way coupling in reaction-diffusion systems yields wobbling motion that lowers free energy.
arxiv-2604-18628: Aslam and four colleagues study how a spinning black hole looks in 4D Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, lit by a sky sphere and a thin disk. They draw shadow images with a fisheye camera model and ray tracing, tracking how coupling and spin settings shape the view. The shadow shrinks while its skew grows as coupling rises. With more spin, the shadow turns ever more lopsided. They then use M87* and Sgr A* readings to bound the coupling setting, a result that backs the model's fit.
arxiv-2604-18828: Kaiser and eight colleagues present HEAT, a data set for training AI surrogate models of high explosive driven, multi material shock dynamics. No data sets existed for this domain, where shock propagation needs equations of state, plasticity, phase change, and damage. HEAT contains 2D, cylindrical simulations from a Los Alamos code, in shock cylinder and layered interface cases. Each entry lists pressure, density, temperature, position, velocity, and stress over time, showing shock motion, momentum transfer, plastic deformation, and thermal effects.
arxiv-2604-19428: Borodulin, Kostina, and Petrov study light forces on a resonant dielectric nanoparticle near a metal interface. Light there splits into free-space and surface plasmon-polariton channels. The tiny bead's strong scatter and multipolar response strongly shape the force balance. Overlap of electric and magnetic dipole moments yields highly one-way scattering, and the force tracks the angular spread of each light channel.
arxiv-2604-19628: Engel and colleagues propose adding compilation metadata to binaries to make disassembly decidable. Such files are the standard method for distributing and executing software, yet they are as opaque a representation as can be. Notes on security-relevant facts, like which data the compiler intends as instructions or how memory regions are bounded, would improve software safety and maintainability. The paper proposes a format midway between a stripped black-box binary and open source, with a tool generating notes capturing build intent.
arxiv-2604-19828: Reggiani, Alfinito, and Intini build a unified theory of generalized quantum conductance and quantum diffusion from a classical 3D gas of free quasi-particles. Their theory covers dimensionless quasi-particles and neutral massive, electric, thermal, and photon currents, starting from an analogy between the 1900 Drude model and a modified Drude model. That model adds a ballistic transport regime and does not depend on statistics, apart from excluding Bose-Einstein condensation.
arxiv-2604-20728: Scarbro and Mangal study shielding for systems with learned perception, where misclassified sensor readings can lead to unsafe decisions. A shield bars any action that might break safety. From these data they build confidence intervals for perception outcomes and model the system as a finite Interval POMDP. That enables a runtime shield with a finite-horizon guarantee. With high probability, if true rates lie within the learned intervals, then every admitted action satisfies a stated safety bound. Experiments on four case studies show improved safety over baselines.
arxiv-2604-20828: Hurvitz, Kochol, Fleurov, and Sela develop a thermodynamic view of phase transitions in monitored quantum systems driven by measurement. It rests on the arrow of time, which comes from the intrinsic irreversibility of the quantum measurements driving these transitions. They study the arrow of time, defined as the log ratio of forward and backward trajectory chances. They find that, like entanglement entropy, the arrow of time is a nonlinear function of the averaged density matrix, but unlike entanglement, it links to a local operator.
arxiv-2604-21028: Lammers and colleagues build a deep-learning surrogate for flood prediction in the Wupper catchment in North-Rhine Westphalia, Germany. Traditional flood forecasts lean on hydraulic simulations that are computationally expensive. The team tunes a U-Net design, patch generation, and data handling to predict maximum water level across a grid. Experiments show the surrogate matches traditional hydraulic simulations while running far more cheaply. The result is a rapid, reliable tool for flood hazard mapping in the catchment.
arxiv-2604-21128: Min Soe and five colleagues build a quantum-computing method for watching electromagnetic waves scatter off dielectric shapes over time. Their qubit lattice algorithm recovers Maxwell's equations to second order in grid spacing. It runs on a classical supercomputer as a stand-in for quantum hardware. A wave packet passing an elliptical dielectric traps fields that bounce repeatedly inside, a picture steady-state frequency studies miss, while a vacuum bubble shows only one strong internal reflection.
arxiv-2604-21228: Vignon Oussa delivers a Lean-certified theorem package for a four-point configuration: three lattice points plus one off-lattice point in the plane. The main theorem says the four linked vectors stay linearly independent for every nonzero square-integrable function when a symplectic area tops one and the coordinates are independent over the rationals. A second theorem covers the rational-coordinate case via Linnell's theorem. A full certification ledger is appended.
arxiv-2604-21428: Arthur Douillard and 16 colleagues break the lock-step synchronization barrier in large-scale language-model pre-training with Decoupled DiLoCo. Where single-program-multiple-data training stalls all accelerators on any slowdown or failure, their design splits compute across independent learners doing local inner steps. Learners asynchronously send parameter fragments to a central synchronizer, which skips failed or straggling learners via a minimum quorum, an adaptive grace window, and dynamic token-weighted merging. Chaos-engineering tests show strictly zero global downtime with competitive text and vision performance.
arxiv-2604-21528: Tina Šfiligoj and Oded Cats study unrealised transport networks through weighted complement graphs. A complement graph links unlinked nodes, but its edge weights cannot be fixed. Travel times as edge weights impose constraints, so the authors build complement graphs from distances between stops, combined with network velocity and waiting-time distributions. The most central nodes in the complement graph are not the least central in the original but those at the centre lacking topological links. Tests on 31 metro networks worldwide confirm this as a spatial effect.
arxiv-2604-21828: Phan and five colleagues present ProDock, an open-source Python toolkit that fixes protein-ligand docking at the workflow level rather than the scoring level. Fragmented scripts for receptor cleaning, ligand preparation, file conversion, box definition, and parsing hurt reproducibility and provenance. ProDock organises docking into four layers: preprocessing, provenance-aware execution, postprocessing of poses and interaction fingerprints, and SQLite-backed storage. Studies become explicit many-to-many campaigns across receptors, ligands, and backends, easier to compare, reuse, and audit.
arxiv-2604-21928: Bañeras-Roux and eight colleagues evaluate speech recognition with generative large language models, beyond Word Error Rate, a metric blind to meaning. They test three approaches: picking the best hypothesis of two, computing semantic distance with generative embeddings, and classifying errors by type. On the HATS dataset, the best models reach 92 to 94 percent agreement with human judges on choice, versus 63 percent for Word Error Rate. Decoder-based vectors perform as well as encoder models. The authors see promise for clear, semantic speech checks.
arxiv-2604-22028: Souza and three colleagues present FlyCatcher, an automated way to derive runtime checkers from tests. FlyCatcher generalizes checks encoded in a test case to any run. It combines LLM-based synthesis, static analysis, plus dynamic validation, inferring checkers that monitor method calls and assert properties that should hold when called. Evaluation across 400 tests spanning four widely used, complex software systems infers 334 checkers, of which 300 are correct via cross-validation. Against a leading approach, FlyCatcher infers about 3x more correct checkers, enabling detection of 5.2x more errors.
arxiv-2604-22228: For computers that link several graphics processors inside one machine, Sojoodi and four colleagues speed the chatter between chips by folding CUDA Graphs into the UCX messaging library. Sending data along several routes at once, including fast NVLink links and a path through the host machine, cuts overhead instead of relying on a single route. On a four-chip test node their method raised bandwidth by up to 2.95 times over single-path UCX at messages up to 512MB.
arxiv-2604-22528: Abi Jaber, Rey, and Sotnikov make Malliavin calculus usable with finite sums of time-based Brownian motion signatures. It handles square-integrable variables, but often lacks usable, plain forms. Signatures stay rich through broad reach, and their algebra yields rules for the Malliavin derivative of signatures of continuous Itô flows. Consequences include closed-form Clark-Ocone forms, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, and the integration-by-parts formula for such variables. These results give algebraic forms for standard operators, and the authors compute Greeks for path-dependent options.
arxiv-2604-22728: Butt, Verdoolaege, Kaye, and Kolemen revisit fusion confinement scalings with extrapolation in mind, as stronger magnets reopen the design space for compact, high-field tokamaks. They hunt for the simplest empirical scaling that best trades variance capture against robustness when stretched past the data. Low-order models near N equal to 3 or 4 win, with elongation, heating power, machine size, and plasma current leading.
arxiv-2604-22828: Cao and five colleagues present MetaEarth3D, a generative foundation model that treats spatial scale as a new axis of intelligence rather than only scaling parameters and data. It generates spatially consistent, unbounded three-dimensional scenes at planetary scale, from large terrains and cities down to street blocks. Trained on 10 million real-world images from around the globe, it shows strong visual and geospatial realism. Beyond generation, it serves as a data engine for virtual environments in Earth observation and simulation.
arxiv-2604-23328: Xia and five colleagues screen 236 semiconductors with density functional theory, seeking low mass and weak polar optical phonon scattering. They find 23 compounds with high mobility, 14 with large power factors. GaGe2Te stands out with exceptionally high cross-plane conductivity and power factor from small effective mass and small ionic dielectric constant. It also shows ultralow cross-plane thermal conductivity of 0.57 watts per meter-kelvin at 300 kelvin, from weak interlayer bonding and strong phonon anharmonicity. This demonstrates a route to decouple electron and phonon transport.
arxiv-2604-23428: Ha and Vu prove that when a certain prime ideal appears for a power of a graph's closed neighbourhood ideal, the graph cannot be very wide. Their bound ties the diameter to the power, and they show it cannot be improved, since examples reach it for every power from two upward. The result links an algebraic property of the graph to its overall shape.
arxiv-2604-23828: Pillai and Smith prove that Kac's walk on rotation matrices mixes in total variation in on the order of n squared log n steps, matching the conjectured time up to constants. The walk lacks conjugation invariance, blocking classical Fourier methods. Their proof uses a refined two-stage coupling. The second stage, a discrete analogue of Malliavin calculus for Markov chains, shows the chain's law is nearly Gaussian over the Lie algebra, its covariance well-conditioned.
arxiv-2604-24028: Chen and five colleagues propose VPFinder, a tool that spots library flaws by joining many kinds of evidence at once. Bug reports, fix notes, and code changes each describe symptoms, causes, and repairs, but earlier tools read them in isolation. A multi-head attention model pulls their shared high-level meaning together for flaw detection and type sorting. It scores 0.941 on identification, beating the best prior methods, and also leads on type classification.
arxiv-2604-24228: Piecyk and Sandeep establish a complexity dichotomy for edge subdivision to H-free graphs: whether k subdivisions can remove every induced copy of a fixed H. It is polynomial-time solvable when every component of H is a subdivided star or subdivided bistar, with at most one bistar. Otherwise it is NP-complete, and the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out subexponential-in-k algorithms in hard cases. For every fixed H, a singly exponential-in-k polynomial-time algorithm exists.
arxiv-2604-24428: Lam presents BandRouteNet, an adaptive frequency-aware neural network for EEG denoising. EEG signals suffer eye and muscle artifacts with varied, shifting spectra across frequency bands. The model denoises band by band to capture frequency-dependent artifact patterns. A routing mechanism decides where and how much to denoise in each band. A full-band conditioner processes noisy EEG for global context, setting modulation parameters and adding coarse refinement. Tests on EEGDenoiseNet beat other methods on error and signal-to-noise metrics, with only 0.2M trainable parameters.
arxiv-2604-24528: Fairbairn and Shellard map how dark matter made in a cosmic first-order phase transition differs from the usual freeze-out picture, for both scalar and vector particles. They find the shift matters most when a dark-sector transition sits near a giga-electronvolt for scalar particles. For vector ones, the key scale is near ten mega-electronvolts. In those windows the expected particle masses move away from freeze-out values, and the transitions should also leave a gravitational wave signal to hunt for.
arxiv-2604-24828: Povolotsky studies sums of binomial coefficients that represent integers, with fixed lower index k. Exact minimal bounds on summand numbers are known only in a few low cases. General existence had received less explicit treatment. He gives explicit proofs for k equals 2 and k equals 3. He compares it with classical polygonal number theory. He explains the failure of naive counting arguments for general k. Conditional and unconditional existence for general k, plus bounds and code evidence, give a unified framework.
arxiv-2604-24928: Fitzpatrick simulates the controlled ramp down of toroidal plasma current in the ITER tokamak with a simple cylindrical model. He also calculates magnetohydrodynamical stability of the plasma through the whole ramp. The only potentially unstable mode is the m=2/n=1 classical tearing mode. The envisioned 60 second ramp down is found perfectly feasible, provided the plasma is hot enough at the start. Faster ramp downs, by contrast, are predicted to trigger 2/1 tearing modes that lock onto the vacuum vessel, causing a disruption.
arxiv-2604-25028: Gupta shows Borel measurability is stronger than necessary at the symmetrization interface in VC learning. For Borel-parameterized classes on a Polish domain, the bad event of excess ghost error over training error is analytic. He constructs a concept class with a bad event that is null-measurable yet not Borel, separating it from the Borel supremum condition. He proves closure under patching, interpolation and fiber-product merging. In the realizable setting, the results weaken the hypothesis needed to reach PAC learnability from finite VC dimension.
arxiv-2604-25228: Valov improves Zakrzewski's inequality for continuous linear maps with bounded supports. Zakrzewski proved for sigma-compact spaces that a continuous linear map with dense image and supports bounded by m bounds dim Y. The bound is an expression in dim X, m and m factorial. Valov shows dim Y is at most m times dim X for Tychonoff X and Y and a continuous linear surjection with supports bounded by m. This implies: for such a surjection with Tychonoff X and Y and dim X zero, dim Y is zero.
arxiv-2604-25328: Tateishi and three colleagues build a fine-scale account of chirality-led orbital choice in helical crystals. There, chiral phonons hand spin to electron orbitals. For a threefold helical crystal with line-group symmetry, phonon-led local spins spark a spin electron-phonon link. That link drives orbital shifts under crystal spin rules. The orbital reply, at first order in perturbation theory, fades near the zone heart and the Brillouin zone edge. It peaks at mid wave vectors, a trait tied to how the phonon bands meet.
arxiv-2604-25628: Newman and Plummer study positional traits in reactive synthesis games, seeking a usable logic with assured tractable synthesis. They show every omega-regular positional trait over state- or edge-labelled game graphs is stated in linear-time temporal logic. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for such traits, and identify well-behaved subclasses. Using varieties of languages, they prove no such class can hold both a prefix-independent trait and closure under Boolean operations.
arxiv-2604-25828: Andrew and eight colleagues show fast radio burst dispersion traces matter on large scales without bias. Dispersion gauges free-electron column density, tracing diffuse ionized gas holding over 90 percent of all baryons. Baryon-mass conservation forces unit linear bias for the baryon field, and dispersion inherits it up to small stellar and neutral-gas corrections. Those corrections are bounded at the percent level using galaxy and 21 centimeter surveys, and confirmed in FLAMINGO simulations. About a hundred thousand localized bursts rival about a hundred million weak-lensing galaxy shapes.
arxiv-2604-26028: Chau and three colleagues show non-Abelian multigap topology with Euler class invariants drives magnetononlinear Hall transport. They show the effects in new kagome metal-organic frameworks that tune well. Voltage, temperature, and doping changes that preserve bulk topology and edge states control the effect. The findings reveal Euler class topology in metal-organic materials, seen in transport data.
arxiv-2604-26428: Merkt studied how heat and light drive dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene to styrene on rutile titanium dioxide surfaces. Density functional theory handled shapes, while high-level multi-reference methods captured excited states and radical intermediates. On the plain surface, both routes ran through proton-coupled electron transfer, with light color deciding whether the system escaped ground-state barriers. On oxidized surfaces, pre-adsorbed oxygen radicals enabled direct hydrogen transfer, lifting styrene yield a lot. The thesis shows why surface makeup and light color steer photocatalytic efficiency.
arxiv-2604-26528: Diplaris and four colleagues explored one impurity, a foreign atom, inside a one-dimensional quantum droplet made from a two-part Bose mix. Tuning atom-droplet links reshapes droplet density shapes and correlation patterns at will. Pulling links trap the atom inside with a density bump nearby, while pushing links split the phases apart. An extended Gross-Pitaevskii account matched densities well but overstated atom trapping. After trap release, link sign and size ruled expansion, unless strongly pulling links held the mix together.
arxiv-2604-26728: Üreyen extends Bergman spaces of H-harmonic functions over the real hyperbolic ball from powers above minus one to all real powers, using partial, normal, and side derivatives. Bergman space traits such as maps, duality, atomic splits, and subset links carry over to the wider family. The work broadens the old theory to a full real value range.
arxiv-2604-26928: Falcó and three colleagues build one working model linking cell invasion and spatial pattern formation, two faces of cell growth, repair, and disease. A multi-scale study shows the balance of cell-cell adhesion, self-diffusion, and cell division steers joint motion. Weak adhesion yields stable invading fronts, while stronger adhesion slows invasion and breaks fronts into clumps and patterns behind the edge. In two dimensions these breaks form finger-like shapes recalling cancer invasion. Adhesion control calms these breaks and restores cohesive expansion.
arxiv-2604-27228: Dietrich tests whether language models keep assigned advocate roles when analyzing political statements in multi-model chains. Systems increasingly assign distinct evaluator models adversarial roles to yield multi-perspective assessments, assuming roles hold steady. Using the TRUST pipeline and a stance sorter that reads reasoning text without surface vocabulary, he measures role loyalty across 60 statements, half English and half German, on four drift scores. Two failure types emerge in the results.
arxiv-2604-27328: Guo studies how classical-looking paths emerge from open quantum systems, where a system exchanges energy or information with its surroundings. He first derives, on his own terms, the Fokker-Planck equation governing a Gaussian mixture's mixing measure, then fits a recent generalized Ehrenfest theorem into that phase-space picture. The result separates orderly motion from irreversible effects in a frictionless harmonic setting, making the classical limit easier to follow.
arxiv-2604-27528: Angeleri Hügel, Hubery, and Krause offer a full guide to infinite-dimensional representations over tame hereditary algebras. With only basic knowledge of finite-dimensional representations, it covers all pure-injective modules in full. The torsionfree divisible modules, a key case, turn out to be precisely sums of the unique generic module. The text serves as an entry point to a topic where the infinite case adds real depth.
arxiv-2604-27828: Howell and seven colleagues study red giants in old metal-rich clusters NGC 188 and NGC 6791 via TESS photometry. Comparing Kepler and TESS for NGC 6791, similar oscillation frequencies return, with a 2.2 percent offset and 9 percent scatter in peak frequency. They blame noisier TESS data for faint stars. For brighter NGC 188, new measurements in 17 red giants give masses near one solar mass. They estimate integrated RGB mass loss near zero, supporting lower mass loss at higher metallicity. They derive an average cluster age of about 7 billion years, matching literature ages.
arxiv-2604-28028: Jivani, Maheshwari and Sarawagi improve text-to-SQL systems for questions that repeat in different forms. Their TeCoD method turns past question-and-query pairs into reusable templates, picks the right template with a fine-tuned inference model, and enforces it while generating SQL. On matched queries it raises execution accuracy by up to 36 percent over in-context learning while also cutting latency.
arxiv-2605-00028:
Jonathan Washburn, Megan Simons, and Elshad Allahyarov introduce a single landscape function meant to organize the chemical trends inside each period of the periodic table. Working on a coordinate centered at the noble gas, they define a dimensionless function built from the golden ratio. They report that it orders four basic atomic properties at once: first ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity in Mulliken's sense, and chemical hardness.

They report three bodies of evidence. The within-period ionization envelope follows the noble-gas-to-alkali descent, with its few upward deviations falling exactly at the textbook anomaly sites. Two golden-ratio identities for ionization energies are said to match national reference data within a few percent. A shared part of the function also fits electron affinity, hardness, and electronegativity across stated periods with one parameter.
arxiv-2605-00128:
Mustapha Ouchen and Alex Prygarin analyze how often collisions produce each number of charged particles, and how that pattern breaks an old scaling law. The Koba-Nielsen-Olesen scaling describes the multiplicity patterns in proton-proton collisions, and its violation is their subject. Working with ATLAS and CMS data at several collision energies, they extract the deviations from the leading exponential behavior of the scaled chance.

In those gaps they identify a reciprocal symmetry, exchanging the scaled variable with its inverse. The symmetry imposes a local constraint on the distribution at the mean multiplicity, which they verify directly in the data. That constraint lets them extract the entanglement entropy from the well-measured region near the mean, avoiding the large errors of the pattern's tail.
arxiv-2605-00728:
Fumiaki Kohsaka proves Sion's minimax theorem in Hadamard spaces, a curved setting that generalizes flat geometry while keeping key convexity properties. Minimax results balance the best outcome for one side against the worst outcome allowed by the other. Moving the theorem into this setting requires new care, because many flat-space tools no longer work in the same way.

Alongside the main result, Kohsaka studies basic properties of resolvents for saddle functions, the objects that encode such balance problems. He also applies the work to the proximal point algorithm for minimax problems in Hadamard spaces. Readers get both the core theorem and the supporting machinery needed to use it in later optimization work.
arxiv-2605-01028:
David B. Hulak, Arthur F. Ramos, and Ruy J. G. B. de Queiroz present a complete Lean 4 formalization of Stokes' theorem for smooth singular cubes in arbitrary dimension. Their version uses true differential-form pullback through the Frechet derivative, rather than a simplified substitute. The development is described as sorry-free, meaning no proof steps are left as placeholders, and it is built on the mathlib4 library.

Additional parts include a bridge to mathlib4's abstract exterior derivative. It also includes chain-level Stokes extended by linearity, a proof that applying the derivative twice gives zero for singular cubical chains, and a box version for axis-aligned cubes. Dimensional special cases are included, along with a structured comparison to Harrison's HOL Light formalization.
arxiv-2605-01228:
Abdul Hayee Shaikh and Xiaoguang Liu introduce AULAs, a family of augmented uniform linear arrays for localizing non-circular signal sources. Accurate direction-of-arrival estimation and resolving many targets are critical in modern wireless systems. Most sparse arrays optimize only the difference co-array, underusing the sum co-array that non-circular signals provide, while joint designs face a three-way performance trade-off.

AULAs combine a sparse array, two dense arrays, and two separate elements to splice holes and lags perfectly in both co-arrays, enlarging the virtual aperture and degrees of freedom. Variants shift, sparsify, or reconfigure the design to reduce redundancy or mutual coupling, all within one unified framework with closed-form placements and degrees of freedom. Simulations validate the effectiveness of the approach.
arxiv-2605-01428:
Gal Yona, Mor Geva, and Yossi Matias argue, in a position paper, that the fight against language model falsehoods has aimed at the wrong target. Most gains have come from stuffing more facts into models, not from teaching them where their knowledge ends.

Even on plain fact questions with clear answers, top models still state false things with confidence. The authors conjecture that models may never sort true from false cleanly inside, so a hard choice between errors and silence may be built in. Their way out reframes a hallucination as a confident error: a model that voices doubt in step with its real doubt can stay useful and honest at once. They call this stance faithful uncertainty, one face of metacognition. For chat it means honest hedging, and for agents it decides when to search and what to trust.
arxiv-2605-01528:
Nefriana and seven co-authors track how extremist talk on Facebook shifted across a year of the Israel-Hamas conflict, from mid-2023 to mid-2024. They sort groups into three camps, hostile to Israel, hostile to Palestine, and hostile to both, and chart engagement, tone, and topics against five major events.

The shifts line up with the events, as the team had guessed, but not uniformly. At the war's start, the both-hostile share of activity fell while the two one-sided camps grew; after Israeli troops left Khan Yunis, the pattern flipped. Negative posts surged and neutral ones shrank in all three camps. Topic drift differed by camp: one moved from faith themes toward protest and activism as the war began, while the other moved from protest toward faith themes just before it. The short study shows a conflict redrawing online hate in real time.
arxiv-2605-02028:
Tianxiang Dai and Jonathan Fan test whether language models can follow a simple rule over a long stretch without error. Agents need more than recall and reasoning over long context. They must keep an exact state while applying the same rule again and again. The authors use counting a long string of repeated characters as a clean test of that skill.

Across 126 leading model variants, every model failed to count accurately above a threshold that depends on the model and on syntax. Failures were abrupt and persisted with larger models, more compute, and external tools. Probing suggests models mimic counting with a finite set of internal states and fail when those states run out. The authors argue new architectures are needed.
arxiv-2605-02228:
Dolev Goldberger and colleagues test the validity of low-order hybridisation expansion methods for strongly correlated multi-orbital systems. Two solvers, the non-crossing and one-crossing approximations, are widely used for impurity problems, but their accuracy with several orbitals was poorly understood. The authors use a decoupled orbital limit as a controlled reference point.

They derive analytic links between multi-orbital propagators and Green's functions and their single-orbital counterparts. The diagrams behind the breakdown of low-order methods become visible in that limit. Their central finding is that accuracy is governed by the least correlated orbital, the one whose retarded Green's function decays fastest. Its traits spread to other orbitals through a spurious coupling from truncation, suppressing correlation effects.
arxiv-2605-02328:
Duy Nguyen Huu, Duy Hoang Khuong, and Ngu Huynh Cong Viet improve multi-label diagnosis of chest X-rays by adding attention modules inside a convolutional network. Chest radiography is widely used for thoracic disease, but reading films is slow and expert-dependent. Deep learning speeds feature extraction, yet class imbalance and several diseases appearing at once remain hard.

Their method inserts the Convolutional Block Attention Module into traditional CNN blocks to refine features, helping the network focus on relevant regions and channels. On the ChestXray14 data set, the model reached a mean AUC of about 0.87, beating several leading baselines in their comparison. Code for the approach is released publicly by the authors.
arxiv-2605-02628:
Eric Zipor describes a student-style project that trains a controller for parkour movement in Minecraft, the block-based video game. Parkour play means crossing terrain with maximum efficiency, using frame-precise timing of sprinting, sneaking, and mouse direction to clear hard jumps. Human players treat the game's physics as a dynamic puzzle.

The project uses a genetic algorithm, a search method that breeds and selects candidate solutions, to set the weights of a neural network. The network reads inputs about block distances, terrain, and obstacles, and judges the best pathing choices. The abstract presents the design and its goal rather than finished results. It is a compact example of evolutionary training applied to a rich, three-dimensional game world.
arxiv-2605-02728:
Guangrui Xie presents ORPilot, an open-source agent system that turns messy business problems into optimization models a solver can run. Academic tools for this task assume clean statements with data already formatted inside the prompt. Real operations work is the opposite: vague descriptions, large raw data files, and a need to switch between solver backends without rebuilding the model.

Four agents divide the labor. One interviews the user to complete the specification. One gathers data on its own. One computes model parameters from raw tables. A solver-neutral intermediate form then allows recompilation to five major solvers, with no further model calls. Retry loops read solver errors and repair the model in a targeted way. On real-world problems and standard benchmarks, the system performed promisingly.
arxiv-2605-03128:
Abhishek Chattaraj, Jeff J. Andrews, Max Briel, Tassos Fragos, Seth Gossage, Vicky Kalogera, Philipp M. Srivastava, and Elizabeth Teng study when pairs of neutron stars merge, and how metal content shifts that timing. Metal levels change star interiors and wind loss, which in turn shape the helium star stage before the second neutron star forms.

Using the POSYDON population code, they find most mergers happen no earlier than about forty million years after star birth, peaking a bit later. A minority merge fast enough to enrich short-lived systems, while many wait over a billion years. The timing shape can split into two peaks by metal content.
arxiv-2605-03228:
Yuhui Wang, Tanqiu Jiang, Jiacheng Liang, Charles Fleming, and Ting Wang present ShadowMem, a defense for language model agents against attacks that unfold over many turns. Such long-horizon threats build through extended interaction and are nearly impossible in single exchanges, yet they endanger agents in critical settings.

Borrowing the shadow stack idea from systems security, ShadowMem keeps a separate safety memory that distills key context across the whole run and checks pending actions before they execute. In tests it beat existing defenses on detection, caught most attacks early, and cost little in agent usefulness.
arxiv-2605-03828:
Hannes Jakob and Jing Zhang prove a topological rainbow Ramsey theorem in set theory, working relative to the consistency of suitable large cardinals. Ramsey theory asks what ordered structure must appear inside large colorings. Their statement concerns colorings of pairs from the second uncountable cardinal, where each color is used only countably many times.

They show it is consistent that any such countable-to-one coloring has a closed subset of order type the first uncountable cardinal. On that subset the coloring is injective, so every pair gets a distinct color. The result simultaneously strengthens theorems by Abraham, Cummings, and Smyth and by Garti and Zhang, and answers a question the latter pair raised. The proof develops new combinatorial principles involving towers of elementary submodels and games on regressive functions.
arxiv-2605-03928:
Luc Dartois, Lê Thành Dũng Nguyên, and Charles Peyrat investigate tree-to-tree Hennie machines. These tree-walking transducers generalize a classical automaton for string functions. They may rewrite node labels under a bounded visit restriction. Unlike regular tree transducers, these machines compute a larger class of functions. They have linear size-to-height increase, a growth condition linking output height to input size.

The authors prove this function class sits between linear size-to-height macro tree transducers and MSO set interpretations. It is closed under precomposition and postcomposition by suitable macro tree transducers. It contains the whole composition hierarchy of linear-height-increase transducers. That hierarchy is strict. Finally, they give an alternative characterization through a lambda-calculus with linear types. There, additive tuples encode output trees. The characterization is proved equivalent via game semantics.
arxiv-2605-04428:
Alan Kuhnle studies a preprocessing step for large subset-selection problems, such as choosing examples, features, or sensors from an enormous pool. The idea is to prune the pool to a smaller core first. The core must still contain a near-best feasible selection. That guarantee must hold for every budget up to a given size.

For monotone objectives with diminishing returns, Kuhnle proves the classic greedy factor is the best any pruning method can guarantee, even with a larger budget. For non-monotone objectives, he gives the first algorithms with a factor near one half. They work under size and knapsack limits. They even beat the known ratios for the maximisation problem itself.
arxiv-2605-05228:
Marcin Pietroń improves the accuracy of compressed neural networks by fine-tuning their quantisation choices with an evolution strategy. Quantisation shrinks models for phones and embedded devices by rounding weights to a few allowed values, usually the nearest ones. Pietroń argues that nearest rounding does not guarantee the best final accuracy for a pretrained network.

His method evolves the quantised model step by step, shifting a small percentage of weights to different allowed states in each round. With suitable operators and settings, accuracy improves quickly in his experiments. Results cover popular image architectures such as VGG and ResNet, for both classification and detection tasks, making the approach a practical post-compression polish.
arxiv-2605-05428:
Space plasmas often show velocity patterns with heavy tails, described by kappa distributions. Leonardo Herrera-Fuenzalida and Sergio Davis tackle a practical problem with those distributions: fitting their parameters is hard. The family lacks sufficient statistics, so direct fitting needs slow numerical searches with no neat update formulas.

Working inside the Beck-Cohen superstatistics picture, they treat inverse temperature as a hidden variable. That move restores the structure needed for an EM algorithm with closed-form steps. On synthetic data the algorithm climbed steadily and recovered the true parameters across the tested range, offering a clear route to fitting such systems.
arxiv-2605-05728:
Machine learning papers report warm-starting power-flow solvers cuts iterations by a third or more. Dhruv Suri, Helgi Hilmarsson, and Shourya Bose show those gains rest on the wrong baseline. Prior work compared against a flat start, but the solver's actual default start, the midpoint of the variable bounds, is already near-optimal for barrier centrality.

Against the corrected baseline, no primal-only warm start reduces iterations at all. The authors trace the failure to interior-point geometry. Their benchmark, WARP, is offered so future warm-start claims face the honest comparison from the start.
arxiv-2605-05828:
Interviewing stakeholders for software requirements is slow, and junior analysts miss the implicit questions veterans ask automatically. Dongming Jin and thirteen co-authors build OntoAgent, an interview agent guided by an experience ontology. Free-form chat with a language model omits implicit requirements and repeats questions, because it lacks that structured know-how.
