The authors present vacancy engineering as a lithography-free and gate-free route to quantum Hall physics in these films.
arxiv-2606-05428:
Ziad Ghanem presents the equivariant spectral flow in this 2026 arXiv paper, a tool for proving when symmetric systems branch as two parameters vary. Such problems ask when a family of equations gains new solutions as parameters vary. The usual route is painful to compute.

The new invariant collects the winding numbers of the linearization's values at a lone critical point into a virtual representation of the group. Ghanem proves that, for maximal twisted orbit types, the coefficient of the local quantity reduces to a closed-form dimension formula, skipping that pipeline. When the eigenvalue dependence is holomorphic, a condition from complex analysis, cancellation among the winding numbers becomes impossible, which yields unconditional local and global guarantees. Applications include Hopf branches in such systems and patterned relative equilibria of the Ginzburg-Landau equation, both read off spectral data.
arxiv-2606-05528:
Anna Mikeda asks when we should protect AI systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper proposing a precautionary framework for consciousness uncertainty. Existing schemes assess whether an AI might be conscious but say nothing about what to do with the result. When evidence is moderate, or strong on some signs and weak on others, organizations have no actionable guidance. It maps evidence onto stepped obligations.

It has three components. Five welfare-relevant dimensions, phenomenal consciousness, affective valence, metacognitive awareness, self-narrative, and agency, are grounded in the science and tied to distinct concerns. A threshold-plus-gradation hybrid sets binary triggers that switch on new kinds of duty, plus continuous scaling of protection as it grows. Two ways of combining it, one hierarchical and one architecture-agnostic, complete the framework. Case studies of a companion chatbot and an agentic system show how different profiles trigger different duties.
arxiv-2606-05828:
Zeyu Gan, Tang, and Liu teach a personal agent which skills its user silently prefers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Local agents call remote models and pick from a swelling shelf of external skills. The right pick depends on tastes the user never states. Heavy central selection systems do not fit local deployment, though. The team splits the job: statistics live on the device, while meaning stays with the remote model.

Local preference tallies nudge the remote model's choices without replacing its judgment. Wide evaluations compared the split design against memory-augmented agents. It posted the lowest cumulative regret, the running cost of wrong picks. It also posted the highest test accuracy of the group. The margin over traditional memory agents was significant, not marginal. Code is public. Preference learning, the authors argue, can ride as a light local harness beside a big remote brain.
arxiv-2606-06228:
Haowang Cui and co-authors present SAM Flow in this 2026 arXiv paper on editing images with generative models. Training free editing changes a real photo using a pretrained diffusion or flow model, with no extra training. Existing methods move the whole image representation at once, so edits leak into regions that should stay untouched. A changed object is fine, but a warped background ruins the result.

SAM Flow first builds a scout image and attention maps tied to the words of the request, which locate the regions that may change. It then applies flow updates only inside those regions. Everything else stays anchored to the source image's own trajectory. A time varying projection with soft masks and transition zones keeps the borders smooth and natural. Plugged into Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX, the method made accurate semantic edits while preserving backgrounds far better than global approaches.
arxiv-2606-06328:
Ziwen Kan, Wugeng Zheng, Tianlong Chen, and Song Wang fuse incomplete health signals in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal time series in medicine might combine heart traces, breathing channels, and movement data. Missingness comes in two shapes. One is gaps inside a channel, as when an electrode detaches. The other is a whole channel gone, as when a sensor is removed overnight. Most methods paper over both with masks and handle only one shape well.

Their framework, PAMF, estimates the missing data explicitly instead of hiding it. Prior aware flow matching fills gaps using the structure each missingness pattern carries, and weight sharing ties the imputation to the downstream prediction task. On Sleep EDF and PTB XL it was the best of the primary baselines, reaching an AUROC of zero point nine eight one on one benchmark. It ranked second on PPG DaLiA and stayed strong even with complete data.
arxiv-2606-06628:
Seokho Lee and co-authors watch a baby star breathe in and out in this 2026 arXiv paper. EC 53 is a protostar with regular burst and quiet phases, a natural experiment in accretion. The team observed it with the Webb telescope in both phases, plus ground based spectra during a burst. They targeted absorption lines of carbon monoxide and water vapor in the warm inner disk. Modeling gives temperatures near eighteen hundred kelvin for the overtone band, tracing hotter gas closer in.

Not everything varied. The water stretching mode showed no compelling change, and the overtone resisted firm conclusions. But the carbon monoxide fundamental band and the water bending mode did vary, showing deeper veiling in the burst. Burst energy spreads into cooler disk regions, and extra warm continuum dilutes those features. The hottest inner bands stay dominated by gas above eighteen hundred kelvin.
arxiv-2606-07328:
Wu, Lee, and Lee built and calibrated a simulator for a new kind of wireless channel in this 2026 arXiv paper. Integrated sensing and communication, a flagship 6G concept, lets one radio system both send data and sense its surroundings like radar. Testing such systems needs realistic simulated channels, and the standards body 3GPP recently published a reference model plus a calibration procedure. The spec is complex enough that implementations can quietly disagree.

The team built the model from the official report and compared their simulated statistics against reference results submitted by companies to 3GPP. Their distributions matched the intended behavior, confirming the build. Along the way they documented several details that shift outcomes, such as how sensing targets and background channels are generated. The simulator, datasets, and results were released openly on GitHub so other groups can reproduce and extend the work.
arxiv-2606-07628:
Da Hora reads recognition pipelines through Mary Shelley's Frankenstein to argue the technology commits an epistemic violence, in this 2026 arXiv paper for a fairness and accountability conference. Shelley supplies not a metaphor about side effects but a diagnostic method: disassembly, reconstruction, and a creature whose legitimacy comes from the procedure that made it. Da Hora coins computational epistemicide, extending a concept about destroying knowledge systems, for what embedding-based recognition does to the face. It replaces a surface with a numerical proxy treated as identity.

Each stage narrows the face to what can be pinned down as data: detection and cropping, landmarking, alignment into a frontal pose, embedding into a vector that travels across systems. Distance thresholds enforce a norm of close enough, fusing matching with one mold. The conclusion is abolitionist: reform through optimization cannot suffice, and vectorized identity should be refused as a basis for rights and access.
arxiv-2606-07728:
Gaines and Bi prove new facts about the hidden geometry of ReLU networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. A ReLU network, built from a simple kinked activation function, computes a piecewise-linear function. Its input space splits into regions, each shaped like a polyhedron, inside which the function is purely linear. How those regions connect shapes everything the network does, yet little was known beyond counts of regions.

The authors study the connectivity graph, where each region is a node and edges join regions sharing a face. They prove the average number of neighbours per region is at most twice the input dimension. Remarkably, that bound ignores the network's width and depth entirely. They also bound the graph's diameter, its longest shortest path, by a quantity that does not grow with input dimension, even though the number of regions grows exponentially. Experiments on synthetic and real trained networks support the theory.
arxiv-2606-07828:
Hickey reports building the same illustration application five times, in five programming languages, with an AI as coding partner, in this 2026 arXiv case study. One developer produced working ports in Rust, Swift, OCaml, Python, and the browser in one hundred twenty evening hours. Such scope conventionally takes multiple developer-years, so the method matters more than the app.

Two safeguards made it feasible. A precise executable YAML specification of about twenty-three thousand lines served as the source of truth for every port. The parallel implementations also tested each other, since differences between ports flagged bugs, a built-in differential-testing layer. Native code per port ranged from zero to roughly ninety-five thousand lines. Hickey frames the method as a revival of N-version programming, a 1980s reliability technique abandoned because hand-writing every version cost too much, a calculus AI changes. The study's limitations are reported honestly.
arxiv-2606-07928:
Spencer K. Clark of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence and co-authors diagnose a hidden failure of a leading AI climate emulator, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The emulator, ACE, learns to simulate the atmosphere from physics-based model output. In its training data, sea surface temperatures and carbon dioxide rose together, so the two influences are entangled. ACE fails when they vary independently.

Their remedy is new reference simulations with randomised carbon dioxide, decorrelating the drivers. A model trained on a mixture of standard, equilibrium, and random-carbon-dioxide runs, with a total-energy constraint, learned more from less. It matched earlier ACE models where they excelled, the warming and abrupt quadrupling tests, and worked where they failed. It was trained on fewer samples than either predecessor, a gain the authors attribute to removing the spurious correlation.
arxiv-2606-08028:
Wentao Zhang, Yutong Zhang, and Wentao Mo sharpen the guarantees for learning algorithms that must decide sequentially under uncertainty, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Online convex optimisation models this: each round brings a loss, the learner commits, and regret measures the gap to the best fixed decision in hindsight. High-probability regret bounds promise the gap stays small except with tiny probability, but classical bounds charge for worst-case gradient size rather than actual noise.

Three results resolve open questions. With full information, their deviation term scales with the true noise level, not the gradient bound: a multiplicative improvement when noise is small. With bandit feedback, where only the chosen action's loss is seen, the confidence cost must grow linearly in the log of the inverse failure probability, provably worse than full information. For constrained problems they give simultaneous control of regret and long-run constraint violation.
arxiv-2606-08128:
Johanna Gasse, Antonia Heinen, Hendrik Higl, and Timo Kötzing map the middle ground between black-box search and hand-tailored algorithms, using graph colouring as the testbed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gray-box optimisation gives the algorithm some problem-specific information while fitness still guides the search. The problem is vertex colouring: colour a graph's vertices so neighbours differ, using as the arena the task of reaching a proper two-colouring of a bipartite graph.

Their results draw sharp lines. Randomised local search, from a random two-colouring, finds a proper colouring in expected time on the order of n log n. The standard (1+1) evolutionary algorithm, starting from a proper n-colouring, cannot reach the two-colouring in reasonable time without extra guidance across plateaus. Gray-box operators, moves exploiting the colouring structure, improve that runtime dramatically. What information you hand the algorithm decides whether it succeeds at all.
arxiv-2606-08228:
Kamat studies how to measure what happens after a trading algorithm says no, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is algorithmic trading on decentralized exchanges, where software screens tokens and rejects most of them. Judging whether those rejections were wise requires following the rejected tokens afterward. The paper formalizes this as Post-Rejection Follow-up Sampling. Without follow-up, a strategy's record shows only accepted trades, and missed chances stay invisible.

The paper describes the sampling design, with frozen data and a reference implementation archived openly. A data-collection note in the current version corrects the record. The deposited data were in fact gathered by a production tracker that sampled every tracked token every ten minutes, not under the schedule first described. Kamat shows the coverage patterns follow fully from that tracker behavior. The work is thus both a method proposal and an audit of its own evidence.
arxiv-2606-08328:
Deo-Campo Vuong studies fair division when goods arrive one by one and cannot be split, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Equitable allocation of indivisible resources is a basic problem behind load balancing, network routing, and multi-agent systems. The setting constrains allocations to be bases of discrete polymatroids. Items arrive over time, and decisions are made without future knowledge.

The proposed algorithm, Brick-Laying, is simple and myopic. It greedily assigns each item to minimize the sum of squared loads across agents, favoring balance at every step. The paper proves this rule achieves majorization minimax-optimality. That is a universal notion of optimality based on comparing how unequal load vectors are. As a consequence, Brick-Laying guarantees minimax optimal competitive ratios and regret for all Schur-concave and Schur-convex fairness objectives, for any number of agents and resources.
arxiv-2606-08428:
Pramanik and Johora study how to harvest a renewable resource without wrecking it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sustainable resource management requires strategies that account for environmental variability: a fishery or forest grows back, but randomly. The authors model population dynamics with stochastic differential equations, where random fluctuations buffet growth. They ask for the harvesting policy that balances economic return against sustainability. Two complementary mathematical approaches are brought to bear.

The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation supplies a dynamic rule for best choices. Its solution dictates the optimal harvest at each stock level. The Feynman-Kac representation offers a probabilistic reading of expected returns, expressing the same value as an average over random population paths. A side-by-side analysis shows the two methods agree, each shedding light on the other. The pairing helps design harvest rules that pay off while keeping the stock safe in the long run.
arxiv-2606-08528:
Rosanov, Fedorov, and Arkhipov introduce a visual way to describe how quantum states move, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A wave function encodes all about a particle through its probability density and phase. Stationary states have conserved descriptors such as energy and angular momentum. But non-stationary superpositions lack equally universal descriptors of their dynamics. The authors define quantum hodographs: paths traced over time by the expectation value, the average, of vector quantities such as position.

For a free electron in a mix of three plane waves, all hodographs of the probability current lie on a universal cubic surface. Rational ratios between frequency differences produce non-contractible loops with well-defined winding numbers. In anisotropic harmonic oscillators, the paths of the average position form three-dimensional Lissajous knots. The work gives quantum motion a shape that the eye can grasp at a glance in one clear view.
arxiv-2606-09128:
Romano develops a unified theory of friction for soft contacting bodies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Friction between viscoelastic materials, rubber-like solids that both spring and flow, governs tires, seals, and robotic grippers. His model combines linear viscoelastic rheologies for bristle-like elements, tiny deflections at the interface, with nonlinear friction laws. The result is a system of semilinear partial differential equations for the frictional force, bristle bending, and internal states at the interface.

The analysis gives a welcome result: linear viscoelasticity keeps the equations hyperbolic, the wave-like structure of rolling-contact theory, so signal travel survives the added material memory. Examples cover sliding and rolling contact. Sliding and rolling, usually treated as distinct problems, exhibit closely related behavior in the framework. The theory offers a general setting for frictional systems, one language for effects from tire grip to soft robotic touch.
arxiv-2606-09328:
Pauliina Ilmonen and her co-authors tackle parameter estimation for neuron models with memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their model describes a neuron's state with a fractional differential equation, a tool that lets the present depend on the whole past rather than only the current moment. A hidden random input with mean-reverting behaviour drives the equation, producing slow, non-exponential relaxation like that seen in real neurons.

The authors propose a two-step estimation method that works from discrete observations of the neuron's state. First, they recover the parameters of the fractional dynamics from the short-time behaviour of Mittag-Leffler functions, special curves that govern the model's decay. Next, fractional differentiation reconstructs the hidden input so its parameters can also be estimated. They prove quantitative error bounds for both steps. Simulations then show how stronger memory and rougher noise each affect the accuracy of the estimates.
arxiv-2606-09428:
Giacomo Gonella, Stefano Menini, and Marco Guerini build a benchmark for testing whether vision-language models can talk people out of danger in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a crisis, an operator must guide scattered civilians through a changing physical environment, a role text-classification research does not capture. Their framework places a model in charge of simulated evacuations across nine maps of increasing structural complexity.

Narrowcast guidance, tailored continuously to each civilian, consistently produced fewer failures than one shared broadcast message at every difficulty level. Visual input drove performance, while adding an adjacency graph of the map helped some models and hurt others. Moving threats raised failure rates everywhere, since guidance had to keep adapting. With a stronger commercial model, the best narrowcast setup raised its save rate to about sixty-six percent on the hardest maps.
arxiv-2606-09628:
Nina Stilkerich and a large team squeeze a frustrated magnet to see how its order and stiffness trade places in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material is PdCrO2, where chromium spins sit on a triangular grid and cannot all settle at once. That clash is called frustration. Pull or push along one axis shifts the gaps between atoms, and the spin links react strongly.

The team joined X-ray and neutron diffraction with stress-strain tests. They found a fresh, sharp magnetic switch driven by stress alone. At the switch, the lattice shrinks by about zero point two one percent. The crystal then stiffens hard: Young's modulus jumps by near eighty gigapascals, and the Poisson ratio falls from about one to about zero point four. The new order seems to lock, no longer swayed by strain. The authors say other frustrated magnets may hide like coupling.
arxiv-2606-09728:
Arpon Basu and his co-authors show that a big quantum cost rule can be thinned to a near-linear sketch in this 2026 arXiv paper. The rule is a Quantum Cut Hamiltonian, an energy map for a system of qubits. Sparsification swaps a huge rule for a small one that keeps each state's energy near true. The team asks how thin such a swap can go.

For an n-qubit system, they reach a count near n over epsilon squared terms. Energy stays within a one plus or minus epsilon factor for every state. The proof reads as a sampling scheme on graph edges. Plain leverage-score sampling falls short here, since the matrices swell to size two to the n. The team splits the action into fixed subspaces and leans on an operator bound.
arxiv-2606-09928:
Ghader and colleagues improve a brain-inspired way of training image networks without backpropagation, the usual method that sends error signals backward through a model, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their base is the Forward-Forward algorithm, which trains each layer with local forward-only goals. Earlier versions split network channels into fixed channel-class groups, and that rigid split hurt accuracy on harder tasks.

Their fix lets the channel-class assignment be learned from data, guided by entropy and orthogonality penalties that push channels to specialize cleanly. A second idea weights each layer's vote at prediction time by how well that layer did on validation data. Built into residual convolutional networks, the method beat other forward-only approaches on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, three standard image test sets. It set new best results among Forward-Forward models and narrowed the gap with ordinary backpropagation training.
arxiv-2606-10028:
Steinwandel and his team simulate the Coma galaxy cluster many times over to interpret its observed traits, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. They build fifty high-fidelity runs of Coma-like clusters from constrained initial conditions produced by the BORG and Manticore projects, then evolve them with the IllustrisTNG galaxy formation model. The ensemble captures both cosmic variance and uncertainty in the local starting state.

The team extracts X-ray surface brightness curves from the simulated clusters and compares them with eROSITA measurements. They also compute thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich profiles, the distortion hot cluster gas imprints on cosmic background light, for comparison with Planck data. The simulations reproduce the broad shape and level of both signals, while showing the scatter expected from differing environments and assembly histories. The dataset supports tests of intracluster gas physics and calibration of cluster scaling relations.
arxiv-2606-10228:
Mani and his team make learning agents explore with more care by treating model sensitivity as an uncertainty signal, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning safety. Their approach views the actor's response to parameter shifts as a handy proxy for uncertainty, the model's own ignorance about little-visited regions. Their method, SHAPO, tests policy gradients at perturbed parameters, making updates guarded with respect to that uncertainty.

In theory, the adjustment reweighs policy gradients, boosting the weight of rare unsafe actions while tempering input from already safe ones. Learning is thereby biased toward safe-leaning conduct exactly where experience is thin. Across several continuous-control tasks, the method steadily improves both safety and task scores over existing baselines, clearly expanding their Pareto frontiers, meaning agents no longer trade as much score for caution. The authors present sharpness-aware updates as a general lever for safer search without separate uncertainty models.
arxiv-2606-10328:
Liu and Zhang design a network that separates real changes from imaging differences in satellite photo pairs, in a 2026 arXiv paper on remote sensing. Change detection finds what changed between two images of the same place, and combining spatial detail with spectral information, the color signatures of surfaces, improves it. Existing methods cannot efficiently suppress spatial and spectral differences in areas that did not actually change, producing false alarms. Their content-guided spatial-spectral integration network, CSI-Net, fuses global spatial details with spectral difference information.

Three modules divide the work. A spatial reasoning module learns spatial structure through cascaded graph convolution blocks. A spectral difference module uses feature means and variances to damp spectral variation in unchanged regions. A content-guided integration module lets high-level content steer the interaction between the two streams.
arxiv-2606-10428:
Wijewardhana and co-authors ask whether fancier versions of LoRA help when a large language model is taught to follow instructions in several languages at once, in this 2026 arXiv paper. LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, is a cheap fine-tuning method that trains small added matrices while the main model stays frozen.

The team compares basic LoRA with four newer variants on two datasets and five low-resource target languages: Urdu, Swahili, Hindi, Bengali, and Telugu. The result is negative: complex variants show no significant advantage in balancing cross-lingual transfer against forgetting older knowledge. VeRA does worse than the rest at preserving English, and embedding analysis shows every method settles into the same pattern, reasoning in English and translating only at the end.
arxiv-2606-10528:
Li, Fu, and Guo improve how language models learn from human feedback in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard methods train a reward model that scores each response with a single number. Those scores are noisy and can tie responses that differ clearly in meaning. The authors instead mine the reward model's hidden states, its internal representations, which carry richer preference information. GraphAE treats each group of sampled responses as a graph, links similar responses, and spreads reward information across the links before computing advantages.

GraphAE plugs into existing group-based algorithms such as GRPO, GSPO, and RLOO. Across three benchmarks it improves results consistently, with gains up to 6.3 points on Arena-Hard and 8.27 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 in the reported tests. The MT-Bench gain is smaller, at 0.22 points. A reward model provides far more than a scalar, and using its representations makes feedback learning more sample-efficient and robust.
arxiv-2606-10728:
Jiale Zhao and colleagues build training data for agents that write whole software repositories in this 2026 arXiv paper. Code agents are graduating from fixing single bugs to architecting projects, but verifiable training data for that long-horizon task barely exists. DeNovoSWE supplies 4,818 instances, each asking for a repository generated from documentation. A sandboxed agentic workflow constructs the data, with divide-and-conquer curation, a critic-repair loop, and difficulty-aware filtering of trajectories to balance quality against diversity.

Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B on DeNovoSWE lifts its BeyondSWE-Doc2Repo score from 5.8 percent to 47.2 percent, overtaking a larger untuned model. On a larger backbone, gains persist: 43.8 to 50.0 percent, and 23.5 to 27.1 percent on NL2RepoBench. At roughly 46 times the size of the NL2Repo collection, the data set argues long-horizon coding is limited less by models than by missing repository-scale supervision.
arxiv-2606-10828:
Eagle and a large collaboration reinterpret the gamma-ray source HESS J1857+026 in this 2026 arXiv paper. Combining Fermi-LAT, VERITAS, and HAWC data, they model the spectrum from megaelectronvolts to teraelectronvolts to decide what powers the glow. The favored source is a pulsar wind nebula, the magnetized bubble blown by the energetic pulsar PSR J1856+0245.

Evolutionary modeling dates the system to between 16 and 21 thousand years, with a magnetic field well under two microgauss. High-energy rays cluster near the pulsar, and no supernova shell or matching molecular gas supports the rival hadronic picture. A weaker low-energy part may come from a second electron population inside the same nebula.
arxiv-2606-11028:
Belgacem builds a modeling framework for gene regulatory networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. These networks, webs of genes switching each other on and off, are often written as Boolean networks. Real dynamics need continuous equations, and the usual translation uses Hill functions for each response curve.

Hill functions force production to exactly zero when an activator is absent. Real genes are never fully silent, so that choice invents a dead off-state. Belgacem uses logistic functions instead, S-shaped curves rising for activation and falling for repression. A recursive De Morgan product formula converts any Boolean rule automatically. His recovery theorem proves every Boolean steady state returns as a stable equilibrium once responses are steep enough. Thresholds stay positive and measurable, unlike rival formulations. On the eleven-gene mammalian cell-cycle network, the translation reproduces the cyclic attractor as a sustained limit cycle.
arxiv-2606-11228:
Rezaee and four co-authors introduce an open-source toolkit suite for second harmonic generation in a 2026 arXiv paper. This effect doubles light's frequency inside nonlinear crystals, a workhorse of laser physics. Realistic modeling is hard: thermal effects couple strongly to the optics in nonlinear, intertwined ways, and temperature data inside a working crystal cannot be measured.

The SHG Computational Toolkit Suite answers with a set of independent, documented toolkits, each covering one configuration or coupling mechanism, with reproducible workflows. As a case study, they add a three-dimensional space-and-time model of depleted pulsed Gaussian waves, solving three coupled equations for Type II conversion. The modular design lets researchers adapt and extend toolkits without rebuilding the infrastructure. Named future work includes other wave types and experimental validation.
arxiv-2606-11328:
Scarpe and five co-authors measure the shapes and sizes of distant quiescent galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Massive galaxies stopped forming stars surprisingly early, yet after quenching they keep growing in size. The team assembled a large multi-wavelength sample of massive quenched galaxies beyond redshift three from public JWST data: 137 candidates across the GOODS, PRIMER, and CEERS fields.

Modeling surface brightness across five bands with Sérsic profiles, they derive sizes and shapes. The size-mass relation matches previous studies: shallower at low redshift, steeper above redshift 3.5. They robustly constrain the relation's intrinsic scatter to about 0.3 dex, with no relevant dependence on redshift or filter. Sizes decrease with observed wavelength, and that gradient weakens with stellar mass, so massive ellipticals look more compact in near-infrared bands. The Sérsic index shows no significant wavelength dependence. Mass and redshift alone predict size, albeit with large scatter.
arxiv-2606-11428:
Kovalchuk, Pfeiffer, Lind, Edwards, Yakimenko, and Birkl model repeated condensate production in a 2026 arXiv paper. They study repeated Bose-Einstein condensate formation and extraction in a dimple trap inside a thermal-atom reservoir, using a kinetic model. The model includes pulsed extraction, evaporation, three-body losses, and thermal-atom input. Three protocols are compared.

Residual atoms left in the dimple after extraction seed later Bose-stimulated growth and shorten recovery time between rounds, but also raise density-dependent losses. Without replenishment, repeated cycles work for all protocols, though the number of formations is limited by depletion and heating. With continuous input, the system reaches a steady cycle after a transient, set by the imposed pulse and input rates. Partial extraction works best, especially for short periods and high input rates. Seeding by leftover atoms is the key mechanism.
arxiv-2606-11828:
Haiyun Li leads a team hiding watermarks in speech that survive tampering in this 2026 arXiv paper. Audio watermarking embeds an identifiable signal into speech without listeners noticing, for copyright and attribution. To stay inaudible, watermarks are usually kept very faint. Modern speech reconstruction tools, such as denoisers and neural codecs, rebuild clean speech from learned patterns and can strip faint marks away.

Their method, AlignMark, aligns the watermark with the speech's own feature distribution. A pre-trained speech codec generates a pseudo-speech watermark, which is fused into the spectrogram, the picture of sound frequencies, inside voiced regions, guided by voice activity and hearing-based losses. Because the mark now resembles real speech, it can carry more energy without becoming audible, and rebuilding models no longer treat it as noise to remove. Experiments show inaudibility comparable to existing methods, with much better robustness against familiar and unseen rebuilding models.
arxiv-2606-11928:
Luc Walterbos and four colleagues publish a data trove for a versatile crystal family in this 2026 arXiv paper. Halide double perovskites, crystals with a doubled unit cell, are candidates for solar cells, light-driven chemistry and radiation detectors. Their chemistry is hugely tunable, and magnetic ingredients can add spin effects.

The database covers every compound in one caesium-based family predicted stable by a modern tolerance-factor rule. Using hybrid density functional theory, the team computed spin-polarised electronic structure for over two thousand five hundred compounds. Seven hundred nineteen have band gaps in the visible range, relevant for light harvesting, and one hundred eighteen are half-metallic, conducting for one spin only. To make the collection explorable, the authors provide summary maps and an interactive app for searching composition, structure and magnetic properties together. It is the first full spin-resolved dataset for this material class.
arxiv-2606-12328:
Jiadong Zhao and co-authors halve the busywork inside speech-cleaning networks without changing their ears, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speech enhancement recovers clean voices from noise. Most systems analyze sound with the short-time Fourier transform, slicing audio into overlapping frames. Overlap keeps the analysis stable but makes neighboring frames nearly identical, so lightweight models waste computation repeating themselves. HALO is a plug-in module that halves the internal frame rate while leaving the transform itself untouched.

Learnable operators compress the frame stream before the main network and restore the full rate afterward. Both steps use lightweight dynamic convolutions. Because the module is causal and adds no algorithmic latency, real-time devices can use it. The saved budget can widen the network's channels instead. On the DNS3 benchmark, lightweight models gain consistently under matched complexity budgets. Redundancy in a standard front end is free performance waiting to be reclaimed.
arxiv-2606-12628:
Singh and Da Vitoria Lobo teach self-driving perception to use context: trains imply rails, and riders imply bicycles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard detectors judge each object alone, so small, obscured, and rare objects get missed in cluttered street scenes. Their Context-Centric Feature Fusion adds two attention modules. A local module lets candidate regions attend to each other, resolving spatial interactions among neighbors. A global module pools the top candidate features into one context token encoding which objects typically co-occur.

The fusion needs no expensive pixel-level global pooling. On Cityscapes and BDD100K, relational consistency scores reach 0.973 and 0.969 respectively, grading how sensibly detected objects hang together as a scene. Small-object detection improves substantially, and the system recovers rare classes like trains that large detectors usually lose. It runs in real time, costing only a fifth of a frame per second.
arxiv-2606-12728:
Enwerem and colleagues present EquiDexFlow, a model for dexterous robot grasps that predicts contact forces together with hand pose, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most grasp generators output a hand configuration and check forces only afterwards, so generated grasps can look right yet fail physically. EquiDexFlow instead predicts wrist pose, joint angles, fingertip contacts, surface normals, and contact forces from an object point cloud, using flow matching, a method transporting noise to data.

The architecture projects contacts onto the object surface and forces into the Coulomb friction cone by construction, so friction rules hold automatically. The model is SE(3)-equivariant: over 200 rotations, wrist residuals stayed below 0.04 degrees with zero joint deviation. Trained on 8,100 force-closure grasps across 81 objects for the 16-joint Allegro Hand, it records zero friction violations and the best quality score. Retargeted to a LEAP Hand, its grasps completed pick-and-hold trials on all 6 test objects.
arxiv-2606-13128:
Ahlvind and colleagues present a multi-epoch X-ray spectroscopic study of the superluminous supernova SN 2018bsz, the closest known stripped superluminous supernova, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It uses 4 Chandra observations and 1 XMM observation, spanning 87 to 1253 days after explosion.

The source is detected at all Chandra epochs and in the late XMM data. That makes SN 2018bsz only the second X-ray detected supernova of its class, and the third superluminous supernova detected in X-rays. Testing power sources, the authors find that a millisecond magnetar central engine underpredicts most of the observed X-ray luminosities. It also fails to reproduce the flat light curve, and accounting for ejecta absorption increases the discrepancy further. Instead, the data are better matched by early-time interaction between the ejecta and the circumstellar medium, with any magnetar emission absorbed by the ejecta.
arxiv-2606-13228:
Isabella and colleagues measure the fluid flows around bubbles during directional solidification in real time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. How bubbles behave as a freezing front advances through a bubbly liquid shapes the microstructure of materials from sea ice to cast alloys and metallic foams. Yet the fluid dynamics remain poorly understood. Several effects could move fluid near bubbles: volumetric expansion as water freezes, Marangoni flows driven by surface tension gradients, and phoretic effects driven by concentration or temperature gradients.

Using cryo-confocal microscopy with particle image velocimetry on water with surfactants and tracer particles, the authors measure the flows. Volumetric expansion rules the fluid motion, with speeds scaling in line with the solidification rate across the range of 1 to 20 micrometres per second. Marangoni flows, thought to play a key role, are negligible under their test conditions, below 5 micrometres per second. Diffusiophoresis and thermophoresis add almost nothing.
arxiv-2606-13628:
Sheshadri proves lower bounds in algebraic complexity theory in this 2026 arXiv paper. The determinantal complexity of a polynomial measures the smallest matrix of linear forms whose determinant equals it. The border version allows the polynomial to be a limit of determinants, a relaxation central to the programme. Sheshadri studies the sum of n-th powers of variables, a family. He proves its border determinantal complexity grows at least as the square, up to constants, in both the ordinary and symmetric models.

Both bounds match the matching upper bounds up to constant factors, closing the question for this family. They are the first border lower bounds of this kind for a family that grow faster than linearly in the number of variables. The proof works through conormal specialisation, a degeneration technique. Lower bounds of this kind are the field's scarcest currency: they certify that some polynomials require large determinantal forms.
arxiv-2606-13728:
Kejriwal builds an inference pipeline for the longest gravitational-wave signals in this 2026 arXiv paper. The space-based detector LISA will hear dozens of mass-ratio inspirals, small objects spiralling into massive black holes. These sources stay in band for months to years. Standard analysis tracks the signal's phase coherently over the duration, demanding waveform accuracy so high that modelling errors become built-in biases. Kejriwal's framework instead segments the data into blocks, analyses each coherently, and recombines the results incoherently.

Restricting phase tracking to short blocks prevents phase errors from accumulating. The implementation, a graphics-processor-accelerated Python package, is demonstrated on an injection in a busy environment. Fully coherent analysis of the same signal shows the biases the semi-coherent approach avoids. The trade is a loss of reach for a gain in strength, a bargain that matters when the payoff depends on trusting the recovered parameters.
arxiv-2606-13828:
Pramanick and colleagues use computer calculations to study a single atomic layer of ZrSeTe, a Janus material whose two faces differ. Selenium replaces tellurium on one side. The team asks whether the charge density wave found in the parent material survives. A charge density wave is a repeating pattern in electron density that reshapes a crystal. Their 2026 arXiv paper also tests whether the layer can superconduct, carrying current without resistance.

The calculations show a strong vibration anomaly at one point of the momentum grid, driven by electrons coupling to lattice motion. The resulting distortion opens a small indirect band gap, turning the material from semimetal toward semiconductor. The energy gained is much smaller than in the parent compound, so swapping in selenium weakens the wave. In the undistorted phase, the layer shows two-gap superconductivity. Spin-orbit coupling, a relativistic atomic effect, lowers the predicted transition temperature.
arxiv-2606-14028:
Choi turns routine model monitoring into a formal test of whether a proposed fix for shifted data is supported. Label shift means outcome frequencies change between training and deployment while the input link stays stable. Practitioners often hold a candidate correction but lack labeled outcomes. His 2026 arXiv paper reframes the task as confirmation, not estimation. Each observation's likelihood ratio acts as a conditional e-value, and their product forms a nonnegative martingale.

Ville's inequality then gives an anytime-valid rule, checkable at any sample size. The log martingale equals the cumulative gap in predictive scores between source and corrected models. For Gaussian process sources the e-values have closed forms. Simulations confirmed Type I control and an edge over re-estimation in small batches. One warning stands out: underestimating variance twofold inflated the false-alarm rate to thirty-six point four five percent, so calibration comes first.
arxiv-2606-14128:
Phosavanh and Matsypura ask which shortest route serves the most people, formalizing a tension every transit planner knows. Direct routes are cheap and fast but bypass neighborhoods; coverage-chasing routes wander. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines the k-step-central shortest path problem: among shortest paths, pick the one maximizing reachability, nodes within k hops of the path. They give an algorithm with a novel pruning rule for unweighted graphs.

Unweighted instances are solved in polynomial time, but the problem turns NP-hard once edge weights enter. The same algorithm also solves the closeness-central shortest path problem, since the centrality mimics closeness as k grows. Experiments on synthetic and real networks reached two thousand nodes. One insight stands out: reachability grows linearly with blocks riders will walk to a hub. Investing in walking paths and bike lanes can thus beat extending the route itself, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2606-14328:
Oguntola and colleagues built an open-source tool for a geothermal problem: salt in super-hot water can come out of solution and choke the rock. High-enthalpy fractured reservoirs, hotter than 200 degrees Celsius, couple multiphase flow, heat, and saltwater physics; halite scaling can severely cut flow and well output. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a model using persistent primary variables: pressure, enthalpy, and overall salt mass fraction. Phase changes are handled naturally, with no manual switching.

Fractures use a discrete fracture-matrix scheme. Saltwater properties follow Driesner correlations, evaluated by lookup instead of phase-separation runs. Kozeny-Carman-type relations let porosity and permeability shrink as halite forms. Implemented in the open-source PorePy framework, the model matched the CSMP++ simulator on a 1D salt benchmark spanning four phase regions. A 2D fractured case then predicted scaling patterns, permeability damage, and wellbore blockage risk.
arxiv-2606-14428:
Alimi and co-authors add to game theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. A potential function is one score that tracks a game. It can prove that equilibria exist. An equilibrium is a stable outcome that no one wants to leave. Nash's famous theorem promises equilibria exist. But it gives no way to build them.

The team presents entropy-based log-multinomial potential functions. They suit games where agents of different types choose acts to raise their own payoff. Payoff depends on how many agents of each type pick the same act. With these functions they give short proofs for two recent models. Those models once needed long, hard proofs. The same tools yield fast algorithms that build equilibria for much wider models. Several open problems are resolved this way.
arxiv-2606-14628:
Mikhailenko, Mikhailenko, and Lee study plasma instabilities at a tokamak's edge in a 2026 arXiv paper. A tokamak confines fusion plasma with magnetic fields. Its scrape-off layer is the thin outer region near the wall. It is inhomogeneous. The team studies electrostatic parametric instabilities there. They are driven jointly by two things. One is a high-harmonic fast wave near the thirtieth ion-cyclotron harmonic. The other is ion and electron temperature gradients.

Their numerical results show the fast wave decays parametrically. It splits into a Bernstein-type wave and a quasimode. The instability exists only within a finite wavelength band. Growth of the quasimode decay leads to parametric turbulence. It comes with anisotropic ion heating. The heating rate across the magnetic field significantly exceeds the rate along it. That matters for heating schemes and edge plasma behavior in fusion devices.
arxiv-2606-14728:
Zhang and Carlone fuse two kinds of uncertainty for vision-language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such models answer questions about images, and in settings like robotics users need to know when an answer might be wrong. Their framework, FUSE, combines aleatoric uncertainty, ambiguity inherent in the image-text input, with epistemic uncertainty, the model's own knowledge limits estimated from the diversity of its semantic responses.

A Bayesian fusion mechanism merges the two sources analytically into one scalar uncertainty score. That score reliably predicts whether the model's output is correct, which is what downstream systems actually need for deciding when to trust or escalate an answer. The authors report that FUSE beats baseline uncertainty methods and achieves state-of-the-art uncertainty calibration across their evaluations, a step toward deployable models that know what they do not know.
arxiv-2606-15028:
Trygstad and coauthors present the Swima, a subgram swimming robot with everything onboard, in a 2026 study. Most insect-scale swimmers stay tethered to outside power or depend on bulky magnetic rigs. The Swima weighs about nine hundred milligrams and carries its own battery and electronics. Two tiny actuators driven by shape-memory alloy wires supply the thrust.

A custom circuit board adds sensing and computation, including an inertial unit for heading control. One charge of the small lithium-ion cell sustains over eighteen minutes of untethered swimming. The robot reaches speeds above twenty millimeters per second and turning rates up to fourteen degrees per second. On heading-hold tests it tracks the target direction with errors of only a few degrees. The authors call it the first subgram microswimmer with onboard power, actuation, and computation. Future work targets lower current draw and a stronger propulsion system.
arxiv-2606-15228:
Dallaston analyzes how a biological invasion front smooths in a 2026 applied mathematics paper. The model couples two populations: invaders diffuse through a landscape, while residents block their spread. Invaders degrade the residents, which in turn frees their movement. Diffusion here is degenerate, meaning it switches off where the invader density vanishes. Such systems seem to form moving fronts in simulations. Dallaston studies a self-similar solution starting from a step-shaped invader profile.

He solves the problem numerically and checks the outcome with matched asymptotic analysis. As the density ahead of the step shrinks toward zero, the front speed fades. It fades only logarithmically slowly, so simulations still show an apparent front. The gradient of the solution blows up in that limit. Together these facts argue the system admits no moving interface at all. The result warns modelers that simulated fronts in such systems may be numerical artifacts.
arxiv-2606-15428:
Ioannou Sougleridis and coauthors study cylindrical sound waves in a square lattice of acoustic waveguides in a 2026 acoustics paper. A ring wave spreads outward from a source. In this network of connected air channels, the lattice's square symmetry makes dispersion, the spreading of a wave packet by frequency, depend on heading. The team derives that anisotropic dispersion relation in theory and confirms it with lab tests showing excellent agreement.

Heading changes the wave's character completely. In the gentle linear regime, some headings carry nearly clean pulses while others form Airy-like packets. At high amplitude, the same network produces sharp shock-like fronts along some headings and smooth single pulses along others. Computer runs with the Westervelt equation, a standard nonlinear acoustics model, back the analysis. Such heading-dependent shaping could be built into sound lenses, filters, and signal routers.
arxiv-2606-15628:
Kalathoor and Oefelein examine how compression and chemistry interact in 2026 inside a supersonic reacting hydrogen-air mixing layer, using a 3D numerical simulation. Whole-field averages blur the coupling, so the team instead tracks compression events, patches where dilatation passes a fixed threshold. Heat release and mixture-fraction-gradient activity are then measured against the evolving population of those events.

The record splits into startup, transition, and developed regimes, and only the developed regime carries the coupling. There, stronger heat release comes with larger maximum-event area, more events, greater overlap between compression and heat release, and shorter distance to the most exothermic regions. Timing separates the responses: scalar-gradient amplification peaks near zero lag behind area swings. The strongest response, though, precedes peak compression coverage by a lag of about 0.85 time units. Events thus organize chemistry through population, overlap, closeness, and lag, not through any dominant structure.
arxiv-2606-15728:
Komninos and colleagues argue in 2026 that digital platforms hold a distorting mirror up to their users, and that current law cannot fix it. Ambient intelligence has woven computing into daily life, and platforms treat human experience as free raw material, locking the user models they infer inside private silos. Rules like the GDPR govern inert raw data while leaving monopolies over algorithmic inference untouched.

Through four scenarios, spanning entertainment, e-commerce, fintech, and vehicle telematics, the authors trace harms they name cognitive amputation, ontological violence, and self-censorship. Their remedy is a decolonial infrastructure guaranteeing the functional transferability of algorithmic identities: users would carry portable, pre-computed profiles between services under secure disclosure. Lock-in would evaporate, and platforms would compete on service quality, price, and ethics rather than silo size. The essay reframes data rights as sovereignty over one's inferred self, not just control over raw records.
arxiv-2606-16028:
Dittrich, Potocki, and Grohs measure in 2026 how much shorter a joint description of several tasks can be than separate descriptions. Modern models often share one foundation across tasks, then fine-tune small heads per task, mirroring classical multitask learning. Sharing helps in practice, but the bit cost of describing good approximations was not rigorously pinned down under structural constraints.

The authors prove lower and upper bounds on description length for separate and joint approximation in the uniform norm. Their setting imposes orthogonality, that coordinate directions stay perpendicular, on multi-head models. An optimal joint codec, using no larger bit budget, improves over the best separate codec by an asymptotic factor tied to the task count. The gain survives orthogonality in their bounds. A constructive coding scheme based on a dyadic tree of features makes the source explicit: shared latent structure, not the heads, supplies most savings.
arxiv-2606-16228:
Yan and colleagues report in 2026 that the jet of the microquasar GRS 1915+105 swung through an unusually wide range of angles within weeks. A microquasar is a stellar-mass black hole system launching relativistic jets, a scaled-down quasar. The team observed with the East Asia VLBI Network at 6.7 gigahertz in three epochs, catching giant radio flares in 2025 flagged by RATAN-600.

The southeast-northwest jet shows the smallest position angle ever measured for this source, 118 degrees plus or minus 7 in the first epoch. Within 37 days it rises to 152 degrees plus or minus 2 in later observations. Literature values extend the range to 188 degrees since 2023, a remarkably wide swing during the source's X-ray-obscured state. X-ray spectroscopy points to a warped, precessing inner accretion disk as the likely driver. One image also shows a peculiar shape suggesting the approaching jet spreads sideways.
arxiv-2606-16828:
Bašić, Gottlieb and Krnc analyze a combinatorial game called CRIM in a 2026 mathematics paper. The game is played on an integer partition, drawn as a Young diagram of stacked boxes. A move deletes one whole row or column, and the remaining parts reattach into a single new partition. Both players share the same moves, so normal play theory decides who wins.

The authors introduce rectairs, shapes generalizing both rectangles and staircases, and settle which rectair positions are previous-player wins. A meld operation glues partitions together, and melding losing rectairs stays losing. Two parity-flavored families get special treatment: all members of one are losing positions, and the losers inside the other family are characterized. Staircases and small partitions are classified completely. Placed inside a broader classification scheme for impartial games, CRIM turns out to be neither returnable nor domestic. The authors conjecture every losing partition has even rank.
arxiv-2606-17028:
Yıldırım asks whether forecasting needs digital computation at all in a 2026 paper on optical machine learning. Simple linear models rival transformers at long-horizon forecasting, hinting the core operation is often nearly linear. If so, perhaps light itself can perform it.

HAMON is a passive diffractive optical core. Past values are encoded onto an optical aperture; future positions stay dark. Cascaded trainable phase masks then shape free-space diffraction so the forecast appears directly in the output light field. At test time, prediction is one passive pass of light, with no digital mixing layer involved. HAMON beats the digital baselines on one electricity-transformer dataset at every horizon and nearly matches on a second. It cuts squared error by up to fourteen percent in the best cases. Ablations, including phase scrambling, confirm the forecasts come from the light field itself.
arxiv-2606-17228:
Stannett presents a 2026 arXiv paper on giving meaning to computer processes that never terminate. After each step of an endless run, a residual process remains still to be executed, and its long-term shape matters. The run may settle, cycle, return often to some states, or drift away from every finite region, and a good semantics should tell these cases apart cleanly.

Stannett observes an infinite run as a stream of values in a space of observations, filtered by which sets of times count as large. Its meaning is a compact set built inside the Stone-Čech compactification of that space, namely the tail-cluster set of the stream. Basic laws cover tail invariance and behaviour under continuous observation maps. Applied to the CCS process calculus, the semantics separates stable divergence, finite recurrent divergence, mixed recurrence with escape, and escape through unbounded growth.
arxiv-2606-17628:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on OPD-Evolver, a framework for agents that genuinely improve through their own experience, not merely store it. Memory systems can keep trajectories, reflections, and skills, yet often cannot choose what matters, act on it, or keep the store healthy. The authors define an agent evolver by that fuller competence, then build one through on-policy self-distillation with a slow loop teaching a fast loop better habits over time.

At test time, the fast loop reads, uses, writes, and maintains a four-level memory hierarchy for quick adaptation. In the slow loop, outcome-scored attribution and privileged hindsight distil those four skills into the working policy. Benchmark gains over named memory systems and training-based rivals are reported across domains. A mid-size version even challenged far larger models, the authors report in their analysis.
arxiv-2606-17728:
Xu and Zhao present a 2026 arXiv paper arguing that nuclear masses can betray an exotic shape: tetrahedral symmetry in the zirconium nucleus with equal protons and neutrons. Nuclei shaped like rounded tetrahedra have been predicted for decades, yet no clear experimental sign had been pinned down. The authors study a triple difference of binding energies that isolates proton-neutron effects. They compute it with relativistic density functional theory on a three-dimensional lattice, no symmetry assumed in advance.

Measured values across the zirconium chain are matched with no adjustable parameters. A sharp peak at neutron number forty appears only when tetrahedral deformation is allowed; forcing it to zero erases the peak and breaks agreement. Energy surfaces and level patterns point to a well-localised tetrahedral minimum in that nucleus. The anomaly is thus a shape effect, not generic proton-neutron correlation as often assumed.
arxiv-2606-17828:
Guterman and Saha take up extremal questions for a graph energy based on the Seidel matrix, in a 2026 paper. A graph's Seidel matrix marks adjacent vertices with one sign and non-adjacent ones with the other, and its p-Seidel energy sums the absolute p-th powers of the matrix eigenvalues. The authors hunt for the graphs that make this quantity as small or as large as possible.

For graphs with a fixed number of vertices, they characterize the minimizer when the exponent exceeds two and the maximizer when it lies below two. They also settle both questions for certain regular graphs, including cases tied to prime power orders. Several cases remain open, and the paper closes with precise questions about them, giving spectral graph theory a clear map of what is settled and what is not.
arxiv-2606-18228:
Srivastava and colleagues read emotion from the moving jaw as well as the voice, in a 2026 paper. Speech emotion recognition usually listens only to audio, and it shines on actors performing strong feelings. Real people's expressions are subtler, and audio-only systems fade. The team's insight is that emotion also lives in articulatory motion: jaw movements, facial muscle vibration, and the tremor speech itself induces.

Their system, MAJIC, engineers features from that motion and fuses them with audio features in a multi-task learning framework. Data came from twenty non-actor participants across multiple sessions, ten languages, and both prompted and conversational speech. The combined system reached accuracy in the low nineties on their dataset, beating strong audio-only baselines. It also predicts where an utterance falls on valence and arousal scales. That points toward language-agnostic emotion tools.
arxiv-2606-18328:
Li and colleagues teach robots to learn from their mistakes twice over, gaining both a recovery skill and the concept that prevents the failure, in a 2026 robotics paper. Reinforcement learning can drill a separate recovery policy for every failure mode, but that scales badly. Their system, ReSYNC, instead discovers relational predicates, state abstractions like the concepts a planner uses, from the very episodes where recovery was needed.

Two learning loops interleave. In the skill phase the robot practices recovering from failures in training tasks. In the concept phase it proposes new predicates and refines its abstract planning model to explain those recoveries, turning local fixes into global avoidance at test time. Across four simulated domains ReSYNC improved compositional generalization and sample efficiency over baselines, and the learned skills transferred to a real robot on two long-horizon manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2606-18428:
Kelly and colleagues construct a quantum version of the Valiant-Vazirani reduction, a randomized trick in complexity theory, in a 2026 quantum computing paper. The reduction turns the satisfiability problem, which may have many solutions or none, into a version guaranteed to have at most one solution, by adding random hash constraints.

That isolation step matters because a proposed form of nonlinear quantum hardware, based on torsion effects in atomic condensates, can discriminate quantum states efficiently but seemed unable to exploit that for satisfiability. The authors build the filtered oracle for the reduction as a reversible circuit with polynomial overhead in ancilla qubits and gates. Coupled to torsion-based discrimination, the construction would solve NP problems in polynomial time in the noise-free limit, though not the counting class. The quantum reduction is no faster than the classical one; the gain comes from the nonlinear coprocessor it feeds.
arxiv-2606-18928:
Pernecker and the team design a circuit board to drive twenty-one fiber positioners at once, in a 2026 electronics paper. Surveys need high-density positioner arrays, placing fibers with five micrometer precision. But in current surveys such as SDSS-V and DESI, every positioner carries electronics. That raises wiring, cost, and power budgets.

Their board runs twenty-one theta-phi SCARA units, forty-two motors in all. It adds power supply, CAN links, and a sync line for simultaneous motion. Sensorless field-oriented control, with collision sensing and hard-stop calibration, gives positioning with no Hall sensors or encoders. Each unit keeps autonomy through its microcontroller. Validation showed datum repeatability within the fifty-micron specification. Reconfiguration took under forty seconds, using camera metrology feedback. Peak consumption was near thirty watts, against a fifty watt target. Idle power exceeds its tighter target, though, and is being addressed.
arxiv-2606-19128:
Marinho and colleagues pin down where hydrogen cyanide forms around oxygen-rich giant stars in 2026. Molecules in envelopes around asymptotic giant branch stars are usually explained by equilibrium chemistry in the atmosphere or by photochemistry in outer layers. Some molecules, though, appear in inner regions at abundances far above equilibrium forecasts. Hydrogen cyanide in oxygen-rich sources is one such case, pointing to an unknown non-equilibrium process at work near the star.

The team observed two oxygen-rich giants with ALMA at high angular resolution, targeting a hydrogen cyanide line in ground and excited vibrational states. They modeled the radial emission pattern with a radiative transfer code that allows a central hole in the abundance profile. Models with such a hole reproduce the observed emission shape well. That fit constrains the formation radius where the molecule appears. Knowing that radius narrows which routes could build the molecule.
arxiv-2606-19228:
Baburaj and colleagues present the first direct spectroscopy of the planetary-mass companion GJ 504 b in 2026, using the James Webb Space Telescope. Characterizing the coldest directly imaged companions has only recently become possible. GJ 504 b was the coldest imaged companion of the pre-Webb era, too faint for ground-based spectroscopy, so only photometric data existed. Webb's near-infrared spectrograph now opens its spectrum to direct study for the first time.

Moderate-resolution spectra were obtained with advanced post-processing and forward modeling to separate the faint companion from its bright host star. The spectrum reveals clouds in the companion's atmosphere. It also hints at possible metal enrichment relative to the host. Such enrichment would speak to how the companion formed, whether like a planet from a disk or like a low-mass star. Direct spectra of cold companions give formation tests that photometry alone cannot supply.
arxiv-2606-19428:
Schmidt and colleagues study the gravothermal evolution of dissipative self-interacting dark matter halos in 2026. Many self-interacting dark matter models include radiative processes that shed energy. How that dissipation reshapes halo evolution is unclear. The team varies dissipation and heat conduction independently in isolated halos, hunting for signatures that could constrain the models against real data.

The work presents the first extension of an N-body formalism for frequent small-angle self-interactions to include effective dissipation. All results are checked against a fluid model to test it. Dissipation changes halo evolution qualitatively, beyond merely speeding collapse. Strong central cooling can even invert the usual role of conduction, suppressing core formation so heat keeps flowing inward. Outer regions can cool rather than heat, widening the zone of mass infall. Such signatures give observers concrete density-profile shapes to test, tying dark matter microphysics to halo structure.
arxiv-2606-19728:
Rui Fukushima and Jun Tani test two-way tutoring for robot motor learning in 2026. Babies build motor skills through dense back-and-forth with caregivers. Robot learning usually treats tutoring as one-way demonstration, missing that mutual adaptation.

The pair propose that two-way tutoring lets past experience steer joint paths. Consistent behaviour patterns then form, supporting coherence and generalisation. A physical humanoid robot learns an object manipulation task in two experiments. One pairs the robot with a human tutor; the other uses an AI tutor with adaptive intervention. A free-energy-based network with generative replay learns stably from single tutored episodes. Two-way tutoring fostered consistent behaviours and stage-wise generalisation in both settings. The robot also needed steadily less guidance over time. Such tutoring thus supports step-by-step growth in machines as in small children.
arxiv-2606-20128:
Dipankar Sarkar shows that the standard way of grading LLM-written GPU kernels can certify buggy code as correct. His 2026 paper examines benchmarks such as KernelBench and TritonBench, which test a kernel on a few fixed-shape inputs and accept it when outputs nearly match a reference. He builds a corpus of twenty-four kernels: fifteen correct controls and nine variants seeded with documented transcription errors that language models actually make.

He then re-grades the corpus with op-aware seeded fuzzing, using a high-precision reference and per-op tolerances. The stricter oracle caught all nine buggy kernels and passed all fifteen controls, at no cost in precision. Repeating the test on five GPU classes, from an RTX 3060 to an H100, gave identical verdicts. Every illusion was caught, every control stayed clean, and every failure replayed from its stored seed. Fixed-shape checks manufacture false confidence in generated code.
arxiv-2606-20828:
Nikolay Marchuk, of the Steklov Mathematical Institute and the Higher School of Economics, presents gauge invariant generalizations of the Proca equation in 2026. The Proca equations from 1936 describe vector bosons, spin-one particles with nonzero mass. Unlike many field equations, they are not gauge invariant. Gauge invariance means the physics stays unchanged under certain changes of description. Stueckelberg offered one fix in 1938.

Marchuk takes a different route from Stueckelberg. An additional vector field is introduced into the Proca equation. That addition yields a gauge invariant generalization. The results are then extended to the Yang-Mills-Proca equations. The extension leads to equations with non-Abelian gauge symmetry, the richer symmetry behind strong and weak force theories. A cleaner invariant form for massive vector fields matters for field theory, where symmetry guides how new models are built and checked for consistency.
arxiv-2606-21128:
Thorsten Hertl constructs manifold bundles in a solo 2026 paper by resolving singularities of tailor-made orbifolds, with applications to G2 moduli spaces. Orbifolds allow quotient-like singular points. Resolving them through twisted families of blow-ups yields smooth bundles over the two-sphere.

The bundles are shown to determine a free subgroup in a homotopy group tied to automorphisms of the fiber. The proof generalizes a result of Sullivan. Real homotopy groups of automorphism monoids are described through derivations of a minimal model, now in a relative setting. As an application, moduli spaces of torsion-free G2 structures from Kummer-type constructions contain a free subgroup of positive rank in their second homotopy group. Such results reveal rich topology inside spaces that parametrize exceptional shapes.
arxiv-2606-21228:
Sakana AI's Fugu Team reports in 2026 on Fugu, a family of orchestrator models that direct teams of large language models rather than answering alone. Each frontier model tends to specialize, so Fugu is trained to read a query and design an agentic scaffold, a plan that assigns steps to the models best suited for them. Two versions are released: Fugu for everyday balance of speed and quality, and Fugu-Ultra for the hardest problems.

The report describes training that mixes large-scale fine-tuning, evolutionary search, and reinforcement learning, plus the infrastructure that runs the system in production. Fugu posts top results among publicly accessible models on coding, reasoning, science, and diagram benchmarks, including SWE-Bench Pro and GPQA-Diamond. The team frames query-adaptive teamwork as a route to collective intelligence beyond any single model.
arxiv-2606-21528:
Motahareh Sohrabi and four colleagues propose GOMA in 2026, a family of optimization methods for monotone variational inequalities, the problem class behind min-max training and adversarial learning. The standard extragradient method needs two gradient evaluations per step and converges slower than optimal in its last iterate. GOMA merges two-time-scale optimistic updates, which reuse past gradients, with an anchoring term borrowed from Halpern iteration to steady the iterates.

In the deterministic case, GOMA reaches the optimal accelerated last-iterate rate, order one over k squared, on the squared gradient norm. A simplified single-call version handles stochastic problems with unbounded variance at an order one over root k rate. The authors claim this is the first such guarantee for stochastic monotone Lipschitz inequalities without variance reduction or growing batches.
arxiv-2606-21728:
Matthew Marsh, Benoît Chachuat, and Antonio del Rio Chanona build neural process models that cannot break mass balances in 2026, and that admit what they do not know. Machine learning surrogates for chemical plants often ignore physical constraints and offer no principled uncertainty. Their probabilistic neural network framework guarantees linear equality constraints hold within a set tolerance, while capturing aleatoric uncertainty, the noise built into the data.

Against leading methods, it beats them on predictive accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and constraint adherence when data are scarce. On large datasets it stays competitive while training significantly faster. Two batch reactor case studies, with mass balances enforced, carry the tests. For engineers who must trust a surrogate inside optimization or control loops, guarantees plus honest error bars are the difference between a demo and a tool.
arxiv-2606-22028:
Özer and Filiz develop, in 2026, a discrete version of warped Chern-Simons gravity, a three-dimensional gravity theory whose boundary symmetries mix a Virasoro algebra with a current algebra. In the continuum theory, thermal entropy is encoded in holonomies, the gauge data accumulated around closed loops. The authors ask whether those thermodynamic structures already live at the discrete, lattice level.

Their discrete construction describes warped black hole sectors directly through boundary holonomy data, without assuming a smooth spacetime underneath. The central result is that discrete boundary monodromy data already fully encode the known entropy formula, with no need to postulate a smooth thermal cycle. Continuum warped geometries then appear only as smooth realizations recovered in the large-lattice limit. Black hole and boundary sectors get a unified treatment in one discrete framework.
arxiv-2606-22128:
Leshko develops, in 2026, a theoretical framework for how weak disorder in dot positions affects electron minibands in one-dimensional chains of spherical quantum dots. Such chains are candidate building blocks for photodetectors, solar cells, and transistors, and their states organize into minibands whose width governs transport. Real fabrication never spaces the dots perfectly, so Leshko asks what random spacing changes do to the band structure within a tight-binding, effective-medium treatment.

Averaging over a narrow Gaussian spread of spacing deviations renormalizes the hopping integral, the overlap integral, and the on-site energy shift. The resulting relation shows disorder broadens the minibands. For typical fabrication jitter of ten percent of the spacing, miniband width grows by eight to twelve percent. In this regime the Anderson localization length far exceeds the lattice constant, so states stay spread across the chain.
arxiv-2606-22228:
Karrila and colleagues determine, in 2026, the crossing probabilities for level lines of the Gaussian free field on simply connected domains with piecewise constant boundary data. Level lines are the random curves tracing a fixed height of the field, and their crossing probabilities are basic observables of two-dimensional critical phenomena. The free field is a random surface whose covariance is set by the Laplacian's Green function.

The authors show the probabilities are determined by conformal blocks of a conformal field theory with central charge one, degenerate at each insertion. Equivalently, they are ratios of explicit partition functions of fused multiple SLE curves, written with fused Specht polynomials. For the metric graph free field, crossing probabilities of level sets converge in the scaling limit to the same formulas. Not all boundary conditions fit: monotonicity constraints select which blocks appear.
arxiv-2606-22428:
Aleksandra Tepeh continues the study of k-limited domination in this 2026 paper, turning to complexity and graph products. A dominating set is k-limited when every vertex in it has at most k neighbors outside it, a capacity rule from companion work. Tepeh asks how hard the decision problem is and how the quantity behaves for combined graphs.

The first result is negative: for every fixed integer k of at least two, deciding whether a graph has a k-limited dominating set of a given size is NP-complete. No efficient general algorithm is expected, so exact study shifts to structured families. For Cartesian products, which layer two smaller graphs into a larger one, Tepeh proves general lower and upper bounds and shows both are sharp. Exact values follow for several families, including rook graphs, products of k-coronas, grid graphs, and cases involving prisms and hypercubes.
arxiv-2606-22828:
Wanfang Chen and four colleagues settle Turán-type problems for hypergraphs in this 2026 paper. A Turán number asks how many edges a hypergraph can have without containing a forbidden structure. Their forbidden objects are tight even cycles in four-uniform hypergraphs with one edge removed from the cycle.

For cycles whose length is two more than a multiple of four, and for large enough vertex counts, the authors show the extremal construction is a complete odd-bipartite four-graph. Since the shortest such cycle contains the expanded triangle, this extends earlier results by Frankl and by Keevash and Sudakov . They also show the Turán density of the full tight cycle is exactly one half for every cycle length parameter at least two. This strengthens a result of Sankar that held only for large values. A stability result rounds out the picture.
arxiv-2606-23128:
Peter Hatton speeds up defect diffusion modeling in disordered nuclear fuels in a 2026 materials paper. In mixed uranium-plutonium nitride, atoms sit in varied local chemical settings. A vacancy's jump barrier depends strongly on that setting, so the full set of barriers can never be listed. Direct simulation of long-range diffusion is therefore impractical. Hatton builds a reduced-order approach around compact stand-in functions that predict barriers from simple counts of nearby atoms.

Hatton generates migration data for several vacancy types across thousands of chemical settings using an automated workflow. The functions reproduce that data with low error. Plugged into Monte Carlo simulations, they yield long-time diffusion rates across heat levels and compositions. The results show strongly uneven behavior from two causes: species-controlled jumps on one sublattice and trapping on the other.
arxiv-2606-23228:
Mateo Cámara and colleagues train automatic detectors of acoustic landmarks in speech in a 2026 paper. Landmarks are abrupt acoustic changes tied to speech events such as closures and bursts. They offer a linguistically grounded way to represent speech for analysis. The team studies detection with Conformer models, a neural design mixing convolution and attention. Fourteen configurations vary the architecture, the training loss, the label format, the feature extractor, and the data conditions.
