Adding sperm lifts the membrane off as the fertilization membrane. An egg can even be slipped wholly out of the membrane. Such an egg still fertilizes normally and cleaves into cells with no membrane at all.
europmc-pmc2140628:
Thomas Parsons and Winifred Parsons studied carbon dioxide carriage in the blood of marine invertebrates in a 1923 paper. Carbon dioxide from the tissues must ride the blood to be shed. They measured how much of the gas the blood of crabs, lobsters, octopus, and slower forms takes up at set tensions, beside plain sea water.

The blood of active, higher forms is specially fitted for the work. At a given gas tension it takes up two to three times what sea water does. The crustaceans and cephalopods show this gain. The blood of a slow creeper, Aplysia, or of the sessile sea squirt Phallusia, shows no such gain over sea water. Yet the transport conditions in the living active animals differ in several respects from those in mammals.
europmc-pmc2140928:
Kunitz studied the hydration of gelatin in solution in a 1927 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Hydration means water bound to the gelatin itself, swelling its effective volume. The high viscosity of gelatin solutions, and the shape of their osmotic pressure curves, already suggest gelatin stays hydrated even in hot solutions. Kunitz measured the bound water by viscosity.

Correcting the concentration for that water of hydration straightened the osmotic pressure relation into a line. From it, by van't Hoff's law, the apparent molecular weight of gelatin came out as a definite large figure. The hydration itself is explained as an osmotic effect: gelatin holds insoluble particles, micellae, containing a soluble ingredient, and water gathers to them as long as they persist.
europmc-pmc2409828:
Bamford and colleagues launched COSMIC in 2004, a single home for cancer mutation data. Somatic mutations are DNA changes acquired during life that can drive cancer, and reports of them were scattered across thousands of papers. The new database aimed to collect them in one searchable place.

The team started with four genes known to mutate often in cancer: BRAF, HRAS, KRAS2, and NRAS. At launch the database held records on 66,634 samples and reported 10,647 mutations in total. Web pages let users query the data, view it as figures or tables, and export it in several formats. About 300 cancer genes were then known, so four was only a start. The authors said the catalogue would keep growing as curators added more genes and studies.
europmc-pmc2438328:
Liu, Yu, Zack, Zhu, and Qian built a database of tissue-specific gene control in 2008. Most gene databases ignore where in the body a gene acts. Their resource, TiGER, focuses on human tissues: which genes switch on where, and which control switches drive them.

TiGER holds activity profiles for 19,526 genes across human tissues. It also stores combined control patterns for 7,341 pairs of transcription factors, the proteins that bind DNA to switch genes on. A third layer lists 6,232 candidate control modules, stretches of DNA where several factors bind together, covering 2,130 well-catalogued genes. The data came from new computer methods that predict tissue-specific control from binding site patterns. The authors made the database public so others can mine how tissues keep their distinct gene programs running.
europmc-pmc2443128:
Lotrakul, Sumrithe, and Saipanish validated a Thai version of a nine-question depression screen in 2008. The PHQ-9 asks about mood symptoms over two weeks and is scored in minutes. Thai primary care lacked a short, trusted tool, since existing ones were long and impractical for routine use.

The questionnaire was translated with back-translation and cultural checks, then given to 1,000 family practice patients. A subgroup of about 300 also took two established interview and rating tools as reference standards. Internal consistency was satisfactory, at a score of 0.79 on the standard alpha measure, and scores tracked the reference severity scale moderately well. Used with a cut-off of nine or more, the screen caught 84% of true depression cases while clearing 77% of non-cases. The overall accuracy curve scored 0.89, close to the top mark of 1.
europmc-pmc2626828:
Morse surveyed in 1995 the factors that make infectious diseases emerge, infections newly appearing or rapidly expanding in range or incidence. Fresh examples then included HIV/AIDS, Lyme disease, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, and a foodborne E. coli syndrome causing kidney failure. Morse argues that in virtually every case, specific precipitating factors can be identified.

Most factors are ecological, environmental, or demographic changes that push people into contact with an unfamiliar microbe or its animal host, or that help it spread. Those pressures are growing, not shrinking. Combined with constant microbial evolution and selection for drug resistance, they imply infections will keep emerging and probably increase. Morse stresses that surveillance and control need urgent strengthening. He presents the piece as the opening of a journal series on unifying concepts for emerging infections.
europmc-pmc2631628:
Michlewski, Guil, Semple, and Cáceres explored in 2008 how a protein called hnRNP A1 helps produce one particular microRNA, and what that reveals about microRNA control generally. MicroRNAs start as longer precursors that an enzyme, Drosha, must cut. The team had found hnRNP A1 assists that cut for the precursor of miR-18a, and here they worked out how.

HnRNP A1 binds the loop at the precursor's tip and relaxes the stem below it, opening a better cleavage site for Drosha. Surveying all precursors, about 14 percent carry highly conserved loops, which the authors predict serve as landing pads for such helper factors. Blocking those loops with designer molecules, which they name LooptomiRs, abolished processing in the test tube. The results add a layer of regulation to how cells make specific microRNAs.
europmc-pmc2685828:
Judson and colleagues mapped in 2009 how much toxicity knowledge actually exists for the thousands of chemicals in daily use. Only a fraction had ever been well tested, leaving regulators to guess which of the rest deserve scarce testing first. The United States Environmental Protection Agency built a giant catalogue, ACToR, pulling data from over 200 public sources worldwide.

From that catalogue the team charted the evidence for 9,912 chemicals on a screening shortlist: industrial chemicals made in bulk, pesticide ingredients, and drinking water contaminants. For each, the catalogue holds structure, physical traits, cell-test results, animal data, and official hazard verdicts. The picture was patchy: rich files for a few famous chemicals, near silence for most. Making the gaps visible, the authors argue, is the first step to a rational testing queue.
europmc-pmc2688028:
Alstott and colleagues built a computer model in 2009 to predict what a brain injury does to the wider brain, not just the wounded spot. Damage at one site often disturbs distant, healthy areas, in ways that depend in hard-to-guess fashion on where the wound sits. Whole-brain wiring maps now let such effects be simulated before they are seen in patients.

The team placed virtual lesions in a model of resting brain activity and watched the fallout. Each site produced its own signature of changed connections between far-apart regions, often spanning both hemispheres. Wounds along the brain's midline and near the junction of the temporal and parietal lobes shook the network most. Wounds in primary seeing, hearing, or movement areas stayed local. The size of the effect could be partly read off the wiring importance of the site itself.
europmc-pmc2707628:
Shechter and co-authors tested in 2009 whether blood-borne immune cells help or harm recovery after spinal cord injury in mice. The cord sits in the central nervous system, a site long seen as shielded from immunity. Two kinds of macrophage, large cells that clear debris, gather at a lesion: resident cells and newcomers from blood.

Mice that lacked the newcomer cells recovered poorly, while adding those cells improved repair. The newcomers calmed swelling and needed interleukin 10, an anti-swelling signal, to do so. Resident cells alone did not give that benefit. The result splits a group once treated as all harmful into helpful and harmful parts.
europmc-pmc2725828:
Watson, Gayer, and Connolly reviewed in 2007 the true risk of epidemics after natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and tsunamis. A common fear links dead bodies to outbreaks, and media reports often warn of imminent epidemics. Evidence, they argue, does not support that fear in most cases.

Bodies of people killed by the disaster itself pose little outbreak risk, with narrow exceptions such as cholera deaths. Real risk comes mainly from population displacement, when crowding, unsafe water, poor sanitation, and lost health care combine with local disease patterns. Their review lists the infections most likely to matter and sets priorities for water, shelter, and care in disaster settings.
europmc-pmc2774328:
Han and Zmasek presented in 2009 phyloXML, a computer language for describing evolutionary trees together with the data attached to them. Trees sit at the center of many studies, and their nodes and branches carry labels: species names, branch lengths, support values, gene names, or events such as duplications. Older formats had no standard way to hold such varied annotations.

phyloXML supplies ready elements for the common items, from taxonomy to gene identifiers. Flexible property elements let users add new kinds of data the designers never foresaw. The language is defined by a complete formal schema, so files can be checked and exchanged reliably. The authors also built software tools to read, write, convert, and draw phyloXML data. They offer it as a shared standard for evolutionary biology and comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc2810828:
Chun and Keleş proposed a new statistics method in 2010 for studies where measured factors vastly outnumber samples, a common problem in gene research. The older method they build on, partial least squares, shrinks data into a few combined factors but keeps every variable in play, so results stay hard to read.

Their sparse version forces most variable weights to zero while it builds those combined factors, picking the useful variables and shrinking the data at the same time. They also showed the older method's reliability claims break down when variables hugely outnumber samples. Test runs against rival methods, plus a joint study of gene activity and DNA binding, showed the sparse version predicts well.
europmc-pmc2824828:
Crews and colleagues examined the cell's recycling system in 2010 in brains from patients with Lewy body disease, a group of disorders marked by clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. The recycling system, autophagy, is a main route for clearing that protein, so faults in it could let clumps build.

Compared with healthy and Alzheimer brains, patient brains showed more of a brake protein called mTor and less of a recycling gear called Atg7, while other gears stayed level. Neurons stuffed with alpha-synuclein held the most mTor and showed swollen, abnormal recycling sacs. Mice engineered to overproduce the protein showed the same pattern. In those mice, a brake-lifting drug or extra Atg7 cut the protein buildup and eased brain cell damage.
europmc-pmc2871128:
Meng and Yu reviewed in 2010 why muscle melts away with age, a condition called sarcopenia that leaves older people weak and frail. Two slow-burning processes stand behind much of the loss: oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen byproducts, and low-grade molecular inflammation inside the tissue. Both build up over years in aging muscle.

The two processes tip the balance between building muscle protein and breaking it down toward breakdown. They also harm the cell's energy factories and can push muscle cells into programmed death. The review traces the major signal pathways switched on or off along the way. Single fixes are unlikely to reverse the loss, the authors argue, so exercise, careful calorie limits, and nutrition may need to work together.
europmc-pmc2935128:
Bostock and co-authors assessed the global status of fish farming in a 2010 review, covering farmed fish, shellfish, and other aquatic animals raised for food. Farmed output already supplied a large share of aquatic food eaten by people and was still growing.

Contrary to common belief, pond fish and shellfish that feed partly on natural growth dominate the sector, though fast-growing salmon, shrimp, and catfish farms drive trade. Most farms lean on free environmental goods, so charging for them would reshape costs. Climate change, feed supply, and new breeding tools add further uncertainty about the path ahead.
europmc-pmc2943128:
Bansal and Bilaspuri reviewed how oxidative stress affects sperm and male fertility in a 2010 article. Trouble arises when reactive oxygen species, aggressive oxygen by-products, overwhelm the body's antioxidant defences.

Too much of these species drains sperm energy, damages fatty membranes, and cuts movement and survival, contributing to infertility. Yet small controlled amounts are needed for normal steps such as preparing sperm to fertilise an egg. The review covers where the species come from and how added antioxidants can protect sperm during freezing for breeding work. It also notes using oxidative stress itself as a possible contraceptive route.
europmc-pmc2978728:
McNeela and colleagues studied pneumolysin, a toxin of the pneumonia bacterium, in a 2010 immunology study. The toxin is a candidate ingredient for future subunit vaccines, and its effect on the cells that start immune responses needed clarifying.

Purified toxin matured dendritic cells without making them release signals alone, but paired with other bacterial cues it greatly boosted inflammatory messengers. Mice given toxin-primed cells mounted stronger responses to a test antigen. The toxin switched on a danger sensor complex called NLRP3, driving release of a key messenger needed for protective responses, all without the usual TLR4 route.
europmc-pmc2990028:
Crump and Sugarman, writing for a working group on ethics in global health training, set out guidelines in 2010 for students' field placements abroad. Such programmes were multiplying fast, and the trips could burden host communities even while helping trainees.

Built from published literature and members' experience, the guidelines address universities, trainees, and funders together, covering preparation, supervision, and benefit sharing. Because hard data on harms and gains were thin, the group urges building assessment into programmes from the start. The aim is training that serves hosts as fairly as it educates visitors.
europmc-pmc3042628:
Perry, Sang, Yin, Zheng, and Morel reviewed in 2011 the mouse models that stand in for human lupus, an autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own tissues. Mice that develop a lupus like illness on their own have revealed many gene regions that raise risk, and several candidate genes inside them. Other mice get the illness only after a trigger, which highlights environmental roles.

Together the models have clarified which immune cells drive the disease and how it starts and worsens. They also serve as test beds for possible lupus drugs before human trials. Because the human disease is so varied, the authors stress matching each targeted drug to what a model can actually show. Lessons from these mice keep shaping the search for safer, more precise treatments.
europmc-pmc3055228:
Wilken, Veena, Wang, and Srivatsan reviewed in 2011 the case for curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric, as an add on treatment for head and neck cancer. Curcumin has been used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine and is known to be safe, with calming and pain easing effects. Lab work shows it also slows cancer growth through many pathways at once.

It blocks a master inflammation switch inside cells and the growth, survival, and spread genes that switch controls. It also interferes with receptors and adhesion molecules that tumors use to grow new blood vessels and invade tissue. Head and neck cancers are common worldwide and their standard treatments can be disfiguring and harsh. The authors argue a safe add on could let doctors cut those burdens without losing effect. They also flag the hurdles, chiefly getting enough curcumin into the body.
europmc-pmc3155828:
Meghan Baker and colleagues pooled evidence on diabetes worsening tuberculosis outcomes in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. The two epidemics are colliding as diabetes spreads in countries where tuberculosis stays common. From three decades of literature, thirty-three studies comparing treatment results in patients with and without diabetes survived screening.

Patients with diabetes faced a clearly higher risk of treatment failure and death combined, a higher risk of death alone, and a much higher risk of relapse after apparent cure. The death risk grew even larger in the few studies that adjusted for age and other confounders. Results on early germ clearance were mixed. The authors call for diabetes testing, tighter sugar control, and closer monitoring during tuberculosis treatment.
europmc-pmc3212228:
Kan Wang and colleagues tested whether graphene oxide is safe around living tissue in this 2011 paper in Nanoscale Research Letters. Graphene oxide, a water-friendly form of the carbon sheet material, was being explored for medical uses. The team exposed human fibroblast cells and mice to a range of doses and watched for harm.

Low doses left the cultured cells unharmed, but higher doses reduced cell attachment, triggered cell death, and let particles enter internal compartments including the nucleus. In mice, low and middle injected doses caused no obvious toxicity, while the highest dose killed several animals and produced lung granulomas. Particles collected in the lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys and were barely cleared. The authors warn that dose-dependent toxicity must be weighed before body uses.
europmc-pmc3248128:
Inti Zlobec and Alessandro Lugli reviewed tumor budding in colorectal cancer in this 2010 paper in Oncotarget. At a tumor's invasive edge, pathologists often see single cells or tiny clusters that have shed their epithelial character, a change called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Those buds are not a frozen picture but a snapshot of an aggressive tumor in the act of spreading.

The authors assemble strong, consistent evidence that budding predicts spread to lymph nodes and distant sites, local recurrence, and shorter survival, independent of other factors. International cancer authorities already recognize budding as a relevant extra prognostic sign. The review argues for putting budding counts into routine diagnostic reporting and patient management, and floats the buds themselves as a possible treatment target, an oncotarget.
europmc-pmc3322928:
Lau and co-authors described a SARS patient whose illness reached her brain and spinal cord, in a 2004 case report. SARS, the severe respiratory disease that emerged in 2002, mainly attacked the lungs. The patient was a thirty two year old woman whose breathing illness followed the usual course for about three weeks.

On the twenty second day of illness she suffered a major whole body seizure. Doctors sampled the fluid around her spinal cord and tested it for the SARS coronavirus using a sensitive genetic test. The test came back positive, showing the virus was present in the fluid bathing her nervous system. The authors conclude the virus likely infected her central nervous system directly, an unusual turn that broadened the picture of what SARS could do.
europmc-pmc3409228:
Wang and co-workers compared tiny regulatory RNAs in blood serum and plasma in 2012, a practical question for disease testing. These microRNAs circulate in blood and their levels track cancers and other conditions, making them promising markers. Matched serum and plasma came from the same donors.

Serum consistently held higher microRNA concentrations than the paired plasma. Part of the gap traced to microRNAs released from platelets, suggesting the clotting that makes serum reshapes the RNA mix. Readings also varied with the measurement platform used. The authors caution that studies mixing sample types or platforms may reach false conclusions. Marker hunters, they say, must standardize before comparing numbers.
europmc-pmc3541928:
Glioblastoma vaccines made from a patient's own immune cells enter a first human test in this 2013 phase I trial report, and Surasak Phuphanich leads a fifteen-author team reporting it. Dendritic cells are grown from each patient's blood, loaded with six tumor-associated antigen fragments also found on glioma stem cells, and injected into the skin three times, two weeks apart.

Twenty-one patients enroll, most with newly diagnosed disease. The vaccine proves non-toxic. A third of newly diagnosed patients show a type I immune response. Tumors all express at least three of the six target antigens. Median progression-free survival reaches 16.9 months and overall survival 38.4 months in the newly diagnosed group, figures the authors call suggestive, not proof.
europmc-pmc3658928:
Gut germ mixes differ between heavy and lean children, Bervoets and eight colleagues report in a 2013 study in Gut Pathogens. The team enrolled 26 overweight or obese children and 27 lean children, aged 6 to 16, in a one-point-in-time study. Stool samples were grown on plates and probed by a gene-count method to size five germ groups.

Heavy children showed a higher ratio of one big germ family to another than lean children did. One species, B. vulgatus, sat lower in heavy children, while milk germs of the Lactobacillus group sat higher. Across all children, one germ group rose with energy intake. In heavy children, milk germ levels also rose with a blood marker of swelling. Shaping gut germs early might one day help manage child obesity.
europmc-pmc3694028:
Siegel and colleagues asked how donor traits shape the behaviour of human bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells, the cells widely used in regenerative and immune therapies. They isolated cells from 53 donors aged thirteen to eighty and measured surface markers, growth, colony formation, differentiation, and the ability to calm T cells.

Cells from younger donors carried more of several adhesion and signalling markers and provoked less interleukin-6 in immune co-cultures. Cells from women suppressed T cell growth more strongly. The most vigorous, fast-dividing cell preparations came disproportionately from younger female donors, and marker patterns predicted which preparations grew fastest. The authors argue that donor screening matters for consistent cell therapy.
europmc-pmc3739528:
Aron Hall and six co-authors summarized the burden of norovirus disease in the United States in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2013. Norovirus is the leading cause of epidemic gut illness across all ages, yet its everyday, non-outbreak toll was long poorly measured. Recent studies using several methods have sharpened the estimates.

Norovirus causes an average of 19 to 21 million illnesses a year in the United States. That includes about 56,000 to 71,000 hospital stays, 400,000 emergency visits, and 570 to 800 deaths. People over 65 face the greatest risk of death, while children under five have the highest rates of medical visits. Illness runs all year with a strong winter peak, and rises in years when pandemic strains appear. The authors back continued work on vaccines and other controls.
europmc-pmc3879628:
A protein methylation method paper in Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, dated 2014 in the record, comes from Ailan Guo and a large team. Methylation adds small carbon tags to proteins, tuning RNA work, gene use, and damage repair. Mapping those tags across the proteome needs tools that can fish them out.

The team built antibodies that grab five tag forms on the two main target building blocks. Pulling tagged pieces from human cells and mouse tissues, then reading them by mass spectrometry, gave over a thousand tag sites on one block type alone. That haul tops all past counts. Tag patterns differed between mouse brain and embryo, a tissue stamp. The method opens deep study of a quiet but wide control layer.
europmc-pmc3892928:
Liliana Florea, Li Song, and Steven L. Salzberg catalog gene splicing across human tissues in F1000Research in 2013. Cells can skip parts of a gene's message, called exons, to make varied proteins from one gene. The full range of that variation in healthy tissues was still unmapped.

Their software, ASprofile, mined a huge public RNA data set spanning sixteen human tissues. It found tens of thousands of likely exon skipping events that differ by tissue. Most were new to science, with new exons and new gaps. Only a small share flipped cleanly between tissue pairs, while many were absent from one or both. New events proved more tissue-specific than known ones. The catalog is a first draft of normal human splicing variety.
europmc-pmc3979728:
Rachel Poretsky and colleagues test how well a gene survey tracks lake microbes. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The survey reads one marker gene, 16S ribosomal RNA. The lake was Lake Lanier in Georgia. Four samples were taken close in time. About 40,000 marker reads came from each sample. The team set those results beside whole-community shotgun data. The shotgun data came from the same water.

Repeat samples grouped together, as they should. Bias crept in at the copying steps, though. Counts of community types agreed between the two methods. But the shotgun data found about ten times as many genera. The marker method caught broad shifts over time. Its resolution and sensitivity were blunter. Some microbe types swung sharply across the four timepoints. Real short-term change sits beneath the method's limits.
europmc-pmc4026128:
Christina R. Tyler and Andrea M. Allan review how arsenic harms the brain, in Current Environmental Health Reports in 2014. Arsenic leaks from rock into drinking water in many regions. Millions of people drink water with too much of it, and even low levels have been tied to brain harm, above all in children.

The review gathers human studies on learning, memory, and mood, then matches them with animal work on causes. In the brain, arsenic shifts gene tags, weakens the memory centre called the hippocampus, and stirs stress hormone pathways. It also upsets several signal systems that nerve cells use to talk. New nerve cell growth in adults drops, and Alzheimer-like damage rises. The authors close with early work on guards such as selenium and zinc. The piece links field findings to lab mechanisms in one account.
europmc-pmc4031128:
Soo Ching Lee and eleven co-authors link gut worms to a richer gut microbe mix in Malaysian villagers, in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. Soil worms infect more than a billion people worldwide, mostly in poorer countries. Gut microbe mixes in those countries differ from rich-country mixes, and worms were a suspect cause.

The team read microbe DNA from stool samples of fifty-one people in two villages. About seven in ten carried worms. Those with worms held more kinds of gut bacteria, with one family of bacteria notably enriched. The effect ran strongest for one worm type. A new stats approach, mixing a share-based transform with a sparse sorting method, firmed up the links between microbe kinds. The results suggest worms shape the gut community's makeup and spread. That shaping may help explain health gaps between populations with and without worms.
europmc-pmc4104028:
Hannah C. Dooley, Sharon A. Tooze, and colleagues found the link that connects a membrane lipid signal to the machinery that builds autophagosomes, the sacs cells use to eat their own worn parts. Their study appeared in Molecular Cell in 2014. Starving cells start autophagy by making a lipid called PI3P, but how that signal recruited the building complex was unknown.

A partner search among PI3P-reading proteins showed one, WIPI2b, binds directly to Atg16L1, part of the complex that attaches the marker protein LC3 to membranes. Moving WIPI2b to the cell surface dragged the complex with it. Without WIPI2b, cells could not tag LC3 or run starvation autophagy. The protein also helped clear Salmonella bacteria, gathering the complex around them.
europmc-pmc4165128:
Carolyn Anne Michael, Dale Dominey-Howes, and Maurizio Labbate set out the roots, the costs, and the care of the world crisis of drug-proof germs. Their paper came out in Frontiers in Public Health in 2014. The crisis is the rise, in all lands, of ills that no known germ drug can cure. Its cost to human life and to shared life will be grave.

Three things drive the crisis. Germs gain proof traits as an answer to wide drug use. The vast, linked mass of humans lets any germ reach all of us. And much drug use is not needed, which keeps the push on germs strong. The size of the human mass can not change fast. The two other drives can. Use far less of each drug, the team urges, and both proof traits and harm traits will grow more slowly.
europmc-pmc4202728:
Balu K. Chacko and a team of eleven co-authors proposed a single score for mitochondrial health in Clinical Science in 2014. Mitochondria make most of a cell's energy, and their failure is an early sign of trouble in many chronic diseases. New machines can profile energy function in the few cells a blood sample gives, making a clinical test practical.

By adding a series of known blockers during the test, researchers can read off spare capacity, leak, and other parts of the energy profile. The authors combine those parts into one number, the Bioenergetic Health Index, for a chosen cell type such as platelets or white blood cells. They argue the score could act like a canary in a coal mine, warning of disease risk and tracking its course, though trials must still prove its worth.
europmc-pmc4216928:
Gavin Ha and eleven co-authors presented a tumour analysis program called TITAN in Genome Research in 2014. A tumour is a mix of cell families, each carrying its own set of DNA gains and losses. Untangling that mix from one DNA sample is needed to follow how the cancer evolves.

TITAN models copy number changes and lost gene copies across the whole genome while estimating what share of cells carries each change. Tests on lab-made mixtures and on 23 breast tumour genomes showed it recovers the family structure faithfully. In an ovarian cancer sample, its predictions about rare sub-families held up under microscope checks and single-cell sequencing. The tool gives researchers a way to read a tumour's family tree from bulk DNA.
europmc-pmc4317028:
Marie Grey and six co-authors showed that exosomes, the tiny vesicles cells release, speed the clumping of alpha-synuclein. Their study appeared in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2015. The protein's clumps mark Parkinson's disease, and spread of clumping from cell to cell by way of exosomes had been proposed as how the disease advances.

Exosomes carry fatty ganglioside molecules in their membranes, and those lipids proved to be the active part: vesicles rich in gangliosides seeded clumping quickly, while other membrane mixes did not. The membrane surface acts like a catalyst where clumps first nucleate. Pinpointing that environment gives researchers a concrete target in the chain of events behind Parkinson's spread.
europmc-pmc4383928:
René Dreos, Giovanna Ambrosini, Rouayda Cavin Périer, and Philipp Bucher updated the Eukaryotic Promoter Database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Promoters are the DNA regions where gene transcription begins. The old part of the database lists promoters proven by experiment and was compiled by hand. The newer part, EPDnew, builds organism-specific promoter lists automatically from high-throughput mapping experiments that read transcription start sites directly from sequencing data.

The update reports EPDnew's growth and its extension to more model organisms. Links with the group's other servers, for signal search and chromatin data, were tightened so users can move from a promoter list to analysis in one flow. The database format had stayed stable for nearly three decades by design. Mixing hand-checked classics with genome-scale new lists gives both depth and coverage.
europmc-pmc4385028:
Sarah Heerboth and co-authors reviewed how cancer cells change state to spread, in Clinical and Translational Medicine in 2015. In the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, sheet-like epithelial cells loosen and take on a wandering, mesenchymal character; the reverse step helps them settle at new sites. Both steps are normal tools of embryo development, and tumors borrow them for metastasis. The review compares the two settings and the signals that run them.

Conserved pathways involving TGF-beta, Wnt signals, and regulators such as Snail and Twist drive the switch in embryos and tumors alike. Receptor changes in tumor and surrounding cells add further control. The authors discuss what the switch means in several tumor types. Their closing hypothesis is that reversible epigenetic changes, marks that alter gene use without altering DNA, govern both directions of the switch.
europmc-pmc4396128:
Emily Ruzich and co-authors established a reference score for autistic traits in the general public, in Molecular Autism in 2015. The Autism-Spectrum Quotient is a self-report questionnaire widely used since 2001 to measure autistic traits, in clinics and many other fields. Yet no systematic review had set what a typical adult scores. The team searched databases for studies giving the questionnaire to nonclinical adults, applying formal quality and usage criteria.

Seventy-three articles qualified, covering 6,934 people without an autism diagnosis and 1,963 matched clinical cases. The average nonclinical score was 16.94, while the average for people with an autism spectrum condition was 35.19. Scores also varied by sex within the typical sample. A firm reference norm lets future studies judge whether a group's score is truly unusual, instead of comparing against single small samples.
europmc-pmc4466628:
Brock Humphries and Chengfeng Yang reviewed the microRNA-200 family in cancer in Oncotarget in 2015. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that dial down protein production by pairing with a target message. The miR-200 family has five members, and studies increasingly tie them to cancer's start, spread, and treatment response, making them candidates for diagnosis and therapy.

In mouse models, family members helped tumor cells settle in the lungs, and many other studies found them suppressing cell change, growth, movement, invasion, and spread. The review walks through each step of the metastatic cascade, the process by which cancer colonizes new organs, and lists the targets each family member is known to control. Humphries and Yang conclude that this small family could serve as a treatment target across several cancer types. They note that its role can flip by setting. It can aid spread at one stage and block it at another.
europmc-pmc4468828:
Mohammad Hossain and eight co-authors reviewed hydrogen peroxide priming in plants in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Plants face drought, salt, heat, and other non-living stresses that cut growth and yield worldwide. Such stresses cause reactive oxygen species to surge, damaging cell parts. Yet one of those species, hydrogen peroxide, also works as a signal that switches on defenses, if its level stays controlled.

Priming means giving a plant a mild peroxide dose in advance so its defense systems stand ready. The review explains how peroxide is made, sensed, and cleaned up by detoxifying enzymes and scavengers, and how a small rise can trigger wider tolerance to later, harsher stress. Balancing production against removal is the delicate core of the system. The authors present priming as a practical route to hardier crops, grounded in the plant's own signaling chemistry.
europmc-pmc4493828:
Avram Holmes and eleven co-authors released the first data of the Brain Genomics Superstruct Project in Scientific Data in 2015. The project aims to let researchers explore links between brain function, behavior, and genes at large scale. To do that, it built a repository of brain scans tied to genetic information from healthy volunteers, screened for quality and shared openly.

The initial release covers more than fifteen hundred participants, young adults who received structural MRI scans and one or two resting-state functional scans. Subsets completed personality and cognitive testing, and most provided self-report behavioral and cognitive measures. A smaller group returned for repeat scans within six months, giving test-retest reliability data. The article documents the sample, the measures, and quality screening so other teams can use the resource with confidence.
europmc-pmc4496728:
Jianfeng Han and a large team of co-authors engineered natural killer cells against glioblastoma in Scientific Reports in 2015. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain cancer. Immune cells fitted with a chimeric antigen receptor, a synthetic targeting head, had shown promise, mostly in T cells aimed at a mutant growth receptor found in some tumors. Many more tumors carry the normal form of that receptor, EGFR.

The team built a receptor that recognizes both normal EGFR and its mutant form, and installed it in two NK cell lines and in primary human NK cells. The engineered cells killed glioblastoma cells and patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells more strongly and released more immune signal, strictly when the target carried EGFR. In two mouse models with tumors growing inside the brain, the cells were tested by direct delivery. The work extends cell therapy for this cancer beyond the mutant-only target.
europmc-pmc4628128:
José L. Balcázar, Jèssica Subirats, and Carles M. Borrego published a 2015 review of biofilms as safe houses for drug resistance in nature. Biofilms are tight groups of microbes wrapped in a slime they make themselves. Rivers and lakes are known stores of germs that resist drugs, and of the genes that grant that power.

The slime slows drug entry, and the packed cells swap genes with ease, so biofilms turn into hot spots where resistance spreads. The authors look at how drug pollution in water shifts these groups and drives new resistance through the push of daily life and of descent. What is learned here counts beyond nature, since resistance built up in rivers and pipes can move into germs that infect people.
europmc-pmc4643828:
A 2015 review from Nick M. Haddad and colleagues centres on habitat fragmentation and its lasting effects on ecosystems. Breaking habitat into small, isolated fragments is a hallmark of human land use. Ecologists agree habitat loss harms biodiversity, but they argue over the added harm of fragmentation itself. The review appeared in Science Advances and draws heavily on long-running experiments.

Across studies, fragments lose species, suffer edge effects, and change how ecosystems function, with effects that can grow for decades. Experiments that manipulate fragment size and isolation directly show fragmentation itself does damage beyond simple habitat loss. The authors argue the accumulated evidence is strong enough to act on. They call for urgent conservation and restoration work that reconnects landscapes so species can move and persist.
europmc-pmc4695828:
Ahlam Zaid Alkilani, Maelíosa T. C. McCrudden, Ryan F. Donnelly, and Diganta B. Das reviewed drug delivery through the skin in Pharmaceutics in 2015. Skin is easy to reach and painless to dose through, but its outer layer, the stratum corneum, blocks most drugs. Swallowing pills and injections each carry their own drawbacks, so crossing skin cleanly would help many patients. The review tracks the field's progress and current state.

Methods covered range from chemical helpers and electric or sound-based devices to heat and mechanical approaches. Each is weighed for strengths and limits, and products already on sale are noted. Special attention goes to microneedles, tiny projections that cross the barrier with little pain. The authors present skin delivery as a maturing field with real clinical promise. Its remaining task is matching each drug to a crossing method that stays safe and effective.
europmc-pmc4702828:
Juan Antonio Vizcaíno, Attila Csordas, Noemi del-Toro, and nine colleagues updated the PRIDE proteomics repository in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. PRIDE stores the raw mass spectrometry data behind protein studies, so others can check and reuse them. In 2014 a rebuilt system, PRIDE Archive, replaced the original database with new storage, submission, and web layers. Submissions have since surged to about 150 datasets a month through the ProteomeXchange consortium's shared standards.

The update explains the standard formats the archive accepts and the consortium rules it follows. Companion tools get status reports too: an inspector for viewing data, a converter for file formats, and the consortium submission tool. Two services in development, PRIDE Cluster and PRIDE Proteomes, will add quality-scored views across datasets. The paper shows a field's data commons being rebuilt while in heavy daily use.
europmc-pmc4755228:
Niels W. C. J. van de Donk leads eight authors in an Immunological Reviews survey from 2016 on antibody drugs aimed at CD38. CD38 is a surface protein found at low levels on many blood cells but in rich supply on plasma cells. Cancers of plasma cells, above all multiple myeloma, carry it in bulk.

The review covers three drugs in the class and how they kill. They call in immune attack, trigger cell death, and blunt the protein's enzyme work. Early patient data show strong action against myeloma with mild side effects. That mild profile lets doctors pair them with older drugs. The authors also flag trials in other blood cancers and possible uses in solid tumors and immune disease.
europmc-pmc4759128:
Bhagwan Yadav, Krister Wennerberg, Tero Aittokallio, and Jing Tang propose a new scoring model in Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal in 2015. The model judges whether two drugs help or hinder each other when given together. Such pairs matter for stubborn diseases, but older scoring rules break down on the rich dose grids that modern screens produce.

Their model, called zero interaction potency, compares how a drug's strength curve shifts when its partner joins. A single score marks the gap from the no-interaction case across the dose grid. On a large cancer drug screen, the score caught known strong pairs while keeping false alarms low. The team also maps the full grid, so users can see which dose zones help and which hurt.
europmc-pmc4780428:
Sebastien Paillusson leads seven authors in Trends in Neurosciences in 2016 on a contact zone inside cells that may tie together several brain diseases. Mitochondria, the cell's power units, touch a folded membrane system called the endoplasmic reticulum at patches named MAM. Through those patches the two trade signals that steer many jobs now known to falter in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and ALS with related dementia.

None of those diseases has a cure, and the damage in each looks scattered across cell jobs. The review gathers studies showing the contact patches themselves are disturbed in these diseases. If one shared junction underlies much of the scattered damage, it offers a single place to aim new drugs. The authors weigh the proof and mark what remains untested.
europmc-pmc4789028:
Anne Listrat leads eight authors in The Scientific World Journal in 2016 on what makes meat and fish flesh good to eat. Muscle is not one tissue but a mix: fibers that contract, connective tissue that binds, and fat marbled through. Each part leaves its mark on the plate, and the review sets out those marks for farm animals and fish alike.

Fiber type, size, and count shape color and tenderness. Connective tissue amount and makeup set chew and cooking behavior. Fat inside the muscle drives juiciness and flavor and carries much of the food value. The three parts seem to act on their own tracks, which is good news for breeders: genes and feeding can tune each one apart to raise quality without losing yield.
europmc-pmc4789228:
Paweł Grieb, writing alone in Molecular Neurobiology in 2016, questions a popular rat model of Alzheimer's disease. Injecting the compound streptozotocin into the brain's fluid spaces makes rats use less glucose in the brain and show memory and tissue changes like Alzheimer's. Many labs use the model to test drugs, assuming the compound works by dulling the brain's insulin sensors.

Grieb argues the proof for that story is thin. The compound kills cells that carry a certain glucose gate, and the brain does hold such cells, in its hormone control center and around its fluid spaces. Older work also hinted the brain may make some insulin of its own. If the injections kill glucose-sensing or insulin-making brain cells, the model means something quite different, and he calls for work to settle the mechanism.
europmc-pmc4858828:
Sofia Farkona, Eleftherios P. Diamandis, and Ivan M. Blasutig surveyed cancer immunotherapy in BMC Medicine in 2016, asking whether it marks the beginning of the end of cancer. After years of weak results, immune-based care had just won real clinical ground. Routes include cancer vaccines, viruses that attack tumors, trained immune cells given back to patients, and antibodies that free immune brakes.

Antibodies blocking two brake proteins, CTLA-4 and PD1, led the breakthrough and sped work on new targets and drug mixes. Hard problems remain, from high cost to uneven patient response. The review weighs the surge with care, mapping where immune care stands and what must improve.
europmc-pmc4896128:
Justin M. Zook and a large Genome in a Bottle team released deep sequencing data for seven human genomes in Scientific Data in 2016, to serve as benchmark reference material. Labs need truth sets to grade their sequencing and variant calls. Five of the genomes are current or candidate national reference materials, including the pilot genome NA12878, and two family trios add Ashkenazi Jewish and Chinese ancestry sets.

Data came from 12 technologies, from short reads to long-range mapping. Open release lets any lab test its pipeline against the same yardstick. Shared benchmarks raise trust in clinical genome reads, where a wrong call can steer care. The set anchors method contests and quality rules alike.
europmc-pmc4899628:
Jesse R. Zaneveld and co-authors ran a three-year field experiment in Nature Communications in 2016 on how overfishing and nutrient pollution, joined with warming, break coral reefs down to microbe scale. Reef loss worldwide demands cause maps. Plots that mimicked lost fish and added nutrients grew more turf and macroalgae, as expected.

Coral microbe communities also destabilized, with higher loads of likely pathogens. More algae, sicker microbes, and weaker coral growth and survival fed each other. Heat in warm periods sharpened the harm. Local stress cuts thus erode the reef's microbe base, lowering its odds against global warming. Reef care that only counts coral cover misses the smallest casualty layer.
europmc-pmc4911728:
Trisha Greenhalgh and co-authors studied co-creation in community health research in 2016, through a literature review and a case study. Co-creation means academics and local partners build knowledge together, a style meant to move research past the ivory tower into real services. Done well, it adapts fast to local needs and lands with impact.

Marks of success include a whole-system view, a creative focus on human experience, and careful governance of the partnership. Skip those, and joint projects stall or serve the loudest voice. The case study shows the principles at work in practice. Funders chasing real-world change gain a checklist for judging team-based bids.
europmc-pmc4931028:
Salah E. Abdel-Ghany and seven co-authors survey the sorghum transcriptome with long read sequencing. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Sorghum is a key bioenergy crop. Its genes can be cut and rejoined in alternate ways, which expands what one gene can do. Short reads struggle to rebuild those full length forms, so the team sequenced whole RNA molecules with a Pacific Biosciences machine and built a pipeline named TAPIS to sort the output.

The survey found over 11,000 splice isoforms not seen before. About 11,000 genes also used alternate ending sites, and more than 2,100 genes were new. The results sharpen sorghum's gene annotations, the reference maps other researchers build on. The authors offer TAPIS as a tool others can apply to long read data from any organism.
europmc-pmc4941128:
Simon Little leads a team testing adaptive deep brain stimulation on both sides of the brain in Parkinson's disease. Their study appeared in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry in 2016. Standard deep brain stimulation runs at a steady setting all day. Adaptive stimulation instead reads brain signals and fires only when needed. A prior trial on one side showed promise. This study applied it bilaterally in four patients with electrodes in the subthalamic nucleus.

Each side triggered on its own beta activity, a brain rhythm tied to symptoms. Blinded motor scores improved by 43 percent over no stimulation. The gain came while stimulation ran only 45 percent of the time on average. Levodopa, the main Parkinson's drug, was tolerated alongside the device. The authors conclude that two sided adaptive stimulation improves limb and body symptoms and can track changing need across drug states.
europmc-pmc4968928:
James Fujimoto and Eric Swanson recount the development and commercial spread of optical coherence tomography. Their review appeared in Investigative Ophthalmology and Visual Science in 2016. The method, known as OCT, images tissue structure in real time using light. It became standard care in eye medicine, guiding diagnosis, tracking progression, and judging treatment response. The authors write a history, not a technical survey, for a special issue of the journal.

OCT grew out of femtosecond optics and borrowed tools from optical communications. Early prototypes needed heavy engineering before clinical tests could begin. Startups and companies then carried it into hospitals worldwide, and uses spread to other specialties, research, and manufacturing. The authors credit an ecosystem of young researchers, clinician scientists, engineers, and funders. They argue steady incremental advances, well chosen and well executed, can add up to a revolution.
europmc-pmc4992028:
Britta Engelhardt and five co-authors review the gateways that connect the central nervous system to the immune system. Their review appeared in Acta Neuropathologica in 2016. The brain and spinal cord were long called immune privileged, shielded by the blood-brain barrier and lacking lymph vessels. Immune reactions plainly occur there, though, so the old picture needed revision. New high resolution imaging has sped that reassessment.

Two fluids drain the system toward nearby lymph nodes. Cerebrospinal fluid drains through lymphatic vessels and can carry antigen presenting cells with it. Interstitial fluid from brain tissue takes a narrower route, along basement membranes in vessel walls, too tight for those cells to pass. Lymphocytes enter the tissue by a two step route the review details. The authors tie the anatomy to multiple sclerosis treatment and to amyloid clearance in Alzheimer's disease.
europmc-pmc4997428:
Yue Zhou and six co-authors review natural polyphenols for cancer prevention and treatment. Their review appeared in Nutrients in 2016. Diets rich in fruits and vegetables link to lower risk of some cancers, and polyphenols, plant compounds in such foods, are credited with part of that effect. The review covers the major classes: flavonoids, phenolic acids, lignans, and stilbenes. It draws on population, cell, animal, and clinical studies from the past five years.

Population findings on intake and cancer risk were mixed, partly because intake is hard to measure. Lab studies, by contrast, broadly backed anticancer activity for compounds such as anthocyanins, EGCG, resveratrol, and curcumin. Proposed mechanisms include antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action and control of cell survival and growth pathways. The authors call for better intake measures and human trials to settle the gap between diet data and lab promise.
europmc-pmc5037628:
Chad E. Niederhuth and a large co-author group compare DNA methylation across flowering plants in Genome Biology in 2016. Methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, helps silence jumping genes and tune gene activity, and it was known to vary within a species. How widely it varies between species was open. The team read the full methylome, at single-letter detail, of 34 diverse flowering plant species and read the patterns against the family tree.

Variation proved extensive, above all outside the standard CG context. The mustard family showed low marks in one context and had lost gene-body methylation in some members. The grass family lacked the usual marks deep in silent genome regions and instead enriched marks near genes. Species spread by cloning often carried low levels of one mark type. The authors conclude that methylation patterns mirror each lineage's history and way of life.
europmc-pmc5057828:
Major F. P. Mackie recounts disease among troops in Mesopotamia in the Bristol Medico-Chirurgical Journal in 1919. Mackie served there from the end of 1915 to February 1919, first commanding the Central Laboratory at Amara and later a larger one in Baghdad, where he was consulting bacteriologist. His records stayed in Baghdad, so the address gives his experience without full statistics, as he frankly warns at the start.

He describes the laboratory system he ran, above all a mobile laboratory kept ready to rush to any outbreak. Enteric fever ran through the campaign, worst in 1916; of 660 blood cultures that year, eighty percent grew paratyphoid A and twenty percent the typhoid bacillus, with paratyphoid B rare. Later years shifted that mix, and in 1918 a strange paratyphoid strain arrived, probably from western Persia, which standard sera could not identify but which its own serum proved a distinct organism.
europmc-pmc5140128:
W. D. Sutherland discussed the Charaka Samhita, the classic Indian medical treatise, in The Indian Medical Gazette in February 1919. The hosted text carries his article on the English translation published in Calcutta by Avinash Chandra Kaviratna. Sutherland compares Charaka's revision of the older treatise of Agnivesa with the surgical work of Susruta.

The article quotes long passages on taste, the first topic of Charaka's aphorisms. Sweet taste, for example, is said to build up the body's juices, blood, flesh, and strength. It calms bile and wind, and can even mend fractures. Sour and saline tastes get their own lists of effects on appetite, digestion, and the senses. Sutherland grants the work many merits alongside defects, noting some aphorisms stay hard to grasp despite the commentators and the translator.
europmc-pmc5184128:
A long review in The British and Foreign Medico-Chirurgical Review, dated 1860 in the hosted text, takes up Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859). It also treats Alfred Russel Wallace's paper on varieties departing from the original type. Baden Powell's essays on creation come in as well. So do Joseph Dalton Hooker's works on the plants of New Zealand and Australia.

The reviewer opens by contrasting old natural history, content with dried specimens in a herbarium and stuffed birds in cases, with the deeper inquiry of the present day. Darwin's 502-page book is placed within this shift, next to Wallace's 1858 Linnean Society paper, which reached a similar view of species change independently. The bundle of works is used to weigh how naturalists should explain the distribution and kinship of living things.
europmc-pmc5187828:
Xiaojie Yu, Margarete Odenthal, and Jochen W. U. Fries reviewed exosomes as microRNA carriers in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016, with further co-authors named in the text's byline. Exosomes are among the smallest vesicles cells release, and they ferry microRNAs, gene-silencing RNAs, between cells both nearby and at a distance.

The review covers how cells build exosomes and load them with microRNAs, how receiving cells take them up, and what the transferred RNAs then do to growth and metabolism. It gives special attention to liver disease, where exosomal traffic is well studied. The authors close with the prospect of using exosomes or their cargo in personalized medicine, as markers and possibly as delivery vehicles.
europmc-pmc5297828:
Inés Mármol, Cristina Sánchez-de-Diego, Alberto Pradilla Dieste, Elena Cerrada, and María Jesús Rodriguez Yoldi surveyed colorectal cancer in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2017. It is the third most common cancer and fourth commonest cause of cancer death, with lifetime risk around 4 to 5 percent, rising in Western countries. Age, chronic disease, and lifestyle all feed the risk.

The review explains the disease's machinery. Gut microbe imbalance can drive chronic inflammation that seeds cancer, with Fusobacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, and pathogenic E. coli among the suspects. Cases split into sporadic (70 percent), familial (25 percent), and inherited (5 percent), arising through chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, or a methylator pattern. Mutations in genes such as KRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA now serve as markers guiding prognosis and drug choice. Standard care is surgery plus chemotherapy, increasingly paired with targeted antibodies; newer options include probiotics and gold-based drugs.
europmc-pmc5364328:
Ana Maria Henao-Restrepo led a huge team in the final report of an Ebola vaccine trial in the Lancet in 2017. The trial ran in Guinea during the west African outbreak. Its design was new: when a case was confirmed, a ring of the patient's contacts, and contacts of those contacts, was listed at once. Whole rings were then picked by chance for shots now or three weeks later.

The vaccine is a single shot built on a tame virus that wears an Ebola surface protein. In the chance-picked rings, more than two thousand people in the now arm took the shot. No Ebola case came up ten days or more after the pick in that arm. Sixteen cases arose in the delayed arm. The score for the shot came out at full protection. Extra rings dosed at once, children among them, backed the same result.
europmc-pmc5384228:
Maria Ouzounova and her co-authors report a 2017 Nature Communications study of immune cells that help breast and other solid tumors spread in mice. They tracked two kinds of suppressor cells from the blood-forming system. One kind gathers in the main tumor, and the other kind gathers later in the lungs, where spread tumors often grow.

The first cell kind helped tumor cells leave the main site by pushing them toward a more mobile state. The lung cell kind did the reverse, helping settled cells grow into new tumors. A gene pattern tied to these cells also matched poor survival in most human solid tumors studied. The authors say timing and place shape how these cells aid spread.
europmc-pmc5423028:
LeBlanc and co-authors review how gut bacteria help feed the body's energy system. Their review appeared in Microbial Cell Factories. Bacteria in the gut ferment fiber that human enzymes cannot break down. The process yields short-chain fatty acids. The main ones are acetate, propionate, and butyrate. The host absorbs them as fuel. Gut bacteria also make B group vitamins. Those vitamins support the chemistry that builds ATP.

The review explains how each product acts on energy metabolism. It covers resident gut bacteria first. It then covers food-grade and probiotic strains. The authors add their own lab data. They measured fatty acid and vitamin output from chosen probiotic strains. Riboflavin, folate, and thiamine were among the vitamins tracked. The team suggests such bacteria could help recover more energy from food. That could matter most where diets fall short.
europmc-pmc5516328:
Kolb and Martin present a review in BMC Medicine on lifestyle and environment in type 2 diabetes. Diabetes rates nearly doubled worldwide in a few decades. Genes alone cannot explain a surge that fast. The authors survey the suspected drivers one by one. Diet quality, inactivity, and long sitting hours lead the list.

Noise, fine dust, poor sleep, smoking, and stress also raise risk. Most factors push body weight up first. The final step is damage to insulin-making beta cells in those at genetic risk. Prevention should build a protective lifestyle, they argue. It should also harden the body against these pressures.
europmc-pmc5547528:
Barnett and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis on older adults. Their question is which features of a neighborhood support physical activity. Walking is the most common activity for this age group. The team pooled results from 100 articles.

Walkable streets showed the strongest link to more activity. Safety from crime and access to services also ranked high. Parks, shops, and recreation sites helped as well. Greenery, pleasant views, and public transport each added support. Results shifted with how activity and place were measured. Readers get a clear case for designing streets that help older people stay active.
europmc-pmc5552828:
Rena, Hardie, and Pearson present a review in Diabetologia on metformin. The drug is a main treatment for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar and cuts related complications. Yet how it works is still not fully settled, even after decades of use.

The liver was once seen as its sole main site of action. There it reduces glucose output. New evidence gives the gut a key role as well. At the cell level, the drug acts through an energy sensor called AMPK and through other routes. It can slow cell respiration, too. Dose and treatment length change the findings. Readers get a current, layered account of a widely used drug.
europmc-pmc5567328:
Troudet and co-authors analyze bias in biodiversity data in Scientific Reports. Some species draw vast public and research attention. Most others stay unknown or ignored. That skew can weaken conservation plans that need a full picture of life.

The team used 626 million records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. They covered species in 24 taxonomic classes. For each species they also counted research papers and web pages. Public preference, more than research activity, tracked the bias in records. Charismatic species are heavily over-recorded. The authors urge scientists to promote neglected species. They also back citizen science aimed at ignored groups. Readers see hard numbers behind a known fairness problem.
europmc-pmc5626828:
Dudek reviews cardiolipin in mitochondrial signaling for Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Cardiolipin is a fat found almost only in mitochondria. It supports breathing and energy conversion there. Changes in its amount or makeup damage the organelle.

The review casts cardiolipin as a signaling platform. Under stress, it surfaces on the outer membrane. Its patches then recruit key protein players. In mitophagy, it binds Beclin 1 and LC3. That call brings in the cleanup machinery. Death pathways need it as a docking site too. tBid, Bax, and caspase-8 gather on it. The inflammasome also requires cardiolipin for activation. Barth syndrome shows the stakes of getting this lipid wrong. Readers see one membrane fat wired into the cell's alarm system.
europmc-pmc5741628:
Bertrand and co-authors test whether blocking TNF helps anti-PD-1 drugs work in melanoma. Anti-PD-1 antibodies changed care for this skin cancer, yet many patients gain nothing. Others relapse after a first response. TNF, an immune signal, may play a part in that failure.

In mouse melanoma, TNF blockade paired with anti-PD-1 to strong effect. Blocking TNF kept tumor fighting T cells alive. It also held down PD-L1 and TIM-3, two further brakes on immunity. Human melanoma samples show TNF rising with both brakes. The team proposes paired anti-PD-1 and anti-TNF care for patients.
europmc-pmc5747428:
van Melick and co-authors test how best to tell which leg is dominant in healthy adults. Leg dominance matters in rehab and return to play after knee injuries. No agreed test method exists so far. The team compared what 41 adults said with what they did in set tasks.

The leg used to kick a ball matched self report in full, they find. That holds for both men and women in the study. Standing on one leg matched the kicking leg less often. Jumping matched least of all. Many people switch legs for steadying tasks, so one question cannot cover every task type.
europmc-pmc5769828:
Ostroumov and co-authors review how CD4 and CD8 T cells work together against tumors. Both cell types shape the outcome of cancer immunity. Checkpoint drugs have revived interest in how the immune system can clear even advanced tumors. Tumors grow only when these defenses are evaded or worn down.

The review covers immune control paths such as surveillance and immunoediting. It also covers senescence checks on early tumor cells. The main focus is the crosstalk between the two T cell types. Fresh clinical work on immunotherapy runs through the account. The authors weigh friend and foe effects in that interplay.
europmc-pmc5773028:
Wang and co-authors study whether brain immune cells drive stress linked depression in rats. The team exposed male rats to mild stressors for twelve weeks. They then checked the hippocampus for signs of inflammation. Brain scans, stains, and protein tests all tracked microglial activity.

Stressed rats showed depressive and anxious behavior, the authors report. Their hippocampi showed strong microglial activation and more inflammatory signals. A sensor complex tied to inflammation also switched on. Calming signals rose as well, hinting at mixed cell states. Four weeks of minocycline eased the behavior and curbed the activation.
europmc-pmc5813428:
Postler and co-authors audit why knee replacements get revised. Knee replacement eases worn joints for most patients. Some implants fail and need a second operation. Revision counts are rising in many nations.

The team tracked every revision at one specialist hospital from 2010 to 2015. They assessed 312 patients and 402 revision operations. Most patients arrived as referrals from elsewhere. Infection caused 36.1 percent of revisions, the top reason, ahead of loosening without infection at 21.9 percent and fractures near the implant at 13.7 percent. The infection share topped registry figures. Readers see why specialist centers face a harder case mix.
europmc-pmc5829628:
Schwartz and co-authors summarize Lyme disease surveillance from 2008 to 2015. Lyme is the most reported tick-borne disease in the United States. Cases cluster in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic, and upper Midwest. State health teams report each case to the CDC.

The eight years brought 275,589 reported cases. Of those, 208,834 were confirmed and 66,755 probable. Counts held steady or fell in the core high-incidence states. Neighboring states saw their counts climb instead. Cases skewed slightly male, with peaks in children and older adults. Illness can bring a rash, arthritis, facial palsy, or heart inflammation. Readers get the official shape of a focal epidemic.
europmc-pmc5859128:
Breit and co-authors review the vagus nerve and the brain-gut axis. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Psychiatry. The vagus nerve links the brain with the gut and other organs. It helps control mood, digestion, heart rate, and immune response. Signals travel both ways along this pathway. The review asks how the nerve shapes mental and gut disorders.

The authors discuss stimulation of the vagus nerve as a treatment. Early evidence supports its use for hard-to-treat depression. It may also help post-traumatic stress and bowel inflammation. Gut bacteria can affect mood in part through this nerve, they note. Breathing practice, yoga, and meditation may raise vagal tone. Such steps could build resilience against stress.
europmc-pmc5884928:
Suraweera and co-authors review combination therapy with histone deacetylase inhibitors. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. These enzymes remove acetyl groups from histones and silence genes. In many cancers, their activity goes astray. Drugs that block them have won approval as cancer agents. Alone, though, they face resistance and weak results in solid tumours. Pairing them with standard chemotherapy looks more promising.

The review sums up lab and clinical work on such pairings. Other anticancer agents are covered alongside chemo drugs. Side effects of the inhibitors get full attention. So do markers that could predict which patients respond. Choosing patients well could limit harm to healthy tissue. The aim is the full therapeutic potential of the class.
europmc-pmc5902628:
Howard and co-authors run a genome-wide study of depression traits in UK Biobank. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. They studied 322,580 participants across three depression definitions. One was broad help-seeking for nerves or low mood. Others were probable and hospital-coded major depression. Depression is highly polygenic and disabling worldwide.

They found 17 independent loci tied to depression, they report. Fourteen of those loci looked novel. Signals in a second sample pointed the same way. Linked gene sets centred on excitatory synapse pathways. Neuron spines and dendrites also stood out. Broad depression proved the most workable trait for gene hunting. Readers get new leads on depression biology.
europmc-pmc5949328:
Garcia-Mantrana and co-authors link Mediterranean diet adherence to shifts in gut microbiota. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Diet shapes gut microbes, and imbalance links to disease. Little was known about diet effects in healthy adults. The team studied 27 healthy volunteers. Diet records came from a food frequency questionnaire. Adherence was scored with the PREDIMED test.

Low adherence came with a higher Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio, they report. Heavy animal protein, saturated fat, and sugar intake cut diversity. Normal-weight volunteers held more Christensenellaceae than overweight ones. Plant-based nutrients tracked with more bifidobacteria and short-chain fatty acids. Gut profiles may mark eating habits and disease risk.
europmc-pmc5959828:
Yaniv and co-authors describe SimpleITK image-analysis notebooks as a shared space for teaching and reproducible research. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Digital Imaging. Modern science needs teams to build complex computational workflows. The notebooks rest on the Jupyter web application. They support literate programming, so steps stay documented and repeatable. SimpleITK gives a simpler face to a major image toolkit.

The setup suits scientists with varied programming skill. Online repositories make data sharing easy for users. A testing framework helps keep code sound over time. Many worked examples are free to download from GitHub. They cover segmentation, registration, and other core tasks.
europmc-pmc5995828:
Qi and co-authors use blood transcriptomic and methylation data to find gene targets for brain-related traits. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Genetic control of expression may differ between brain and blood. The team measured how top genetic effects correlate across the two. Effects at expression loci correlated strongly, at 0.70. Methylation loci correlated at 0.78. Brain and blood samples were fully independent here.

Using large blood data sets boosted discovery power, they report. Blood data found 97 genes and 295 methylation sites for four traits. Brain data found a subset of 61 genes and 167 sites. Blood can thus stand in for much brain gene hunting.
europmc-pmc6016328:
Travis, Glover, Bronstein, Scanlon, and Palgrave reassess the tolerance factor for halide perovskites and propose a revised system. Their paper appeared in Chemical Science. The tolerance factor widely predicts perovskite stability. Interest in hybrid perovskites for solar cells revived its use. The authors test it against 32 known inorganic iodide perovskites. It fails to predict their stability accurately, they report. Metal-halide bonds are more covalent than the classic radii assume.

They introduce revised cation radii that depend on the anion. A two-dimensional structural map handles halide size needs. Together these measures form a simple corrected system. It may assist the search for new perovskites.
europmc-pmc6022328:
Schorr and co-authors compare body composition in men and women with excess weight. Their study appeared in Biology of Sex Differences. The team recruited 208 adults with overweight or obesity. Imaging measured fat and muscle in fine detail. Blood tests and a glucose test tracked metabolic risk.

Women carried more total fat and less lean mass. Men held more visceral fat and more fat inside muscle and liver. Men also showed a worse risk profile at the same age and body mass index. Yet visceral fat tracked risk more strongly in women. Fat inside muscle mattered more in men. Leg fat seemed protective, mostly in women. The authors argue that imaging beats body mass index for judging risk.
europmc-pmc6041728:
Davies and co-authors explain how to read Mendelian randomisation studies. Their guide appeared in The BMJ. The method uses genetic variants as natural experiments. It tests whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. Standard observational studies often suffer from confounding.

Genes are fixed at conception, before disease develops. That timing helps avoid reverse causation problems. Findings still rest on key assumptions, though. Readers must judge whether those assumptions hold. The guide explains terms in a plain glossary. It shows what papers typically report and why. A checklist helps clinicians appraise each study. Interpretation alongside other evidence is stressed throughout. Readers get a practical route into a growing literature.
europmc-pmc6057528:
Zappia and Oshlack present clustering trees, a picture for judging cluster results. Their article appeared in GigaScience. Clustering groups similar samples inside large data sets. Analysts often must guess how many groups exist. Changing one setting can reshuffle every group.

A clustering tree shows clusters at many resolutions at once. It traces how samples move as cluster counts grow. Extra data can overlay the tree to guide choices. The authors test it on simulations and two real data sets. One is a single-cell RNA-sequencing data set. The method ships in the free clustree R package. Readers get a visual way to pick a defensible resolution.
europmc-pmc6112328:
Liao and co-authors wrote a review in Genomics, Proteomics and Bioinformatics on the YTH domain, a protein part that reads a common RNA mark. RNA molecules carry chemical marks, much like DNA and proteins do. The mark called m6A is the most abundant inside messenger RNA. It can be added and removed, so it stays dynamic.

The review explains how YTH domain proteins spot m6A and bind to it. Once bound, they steer RNA metabolism, splicing, folding, and protein production. The authors sum up recent work on each member of this reader family. Readers get a clear picture of how one small mark helps control what RNA does in the cell.
europmc-pmc6113228:
Wu and co-authors present a review in Nature Communications weighing two kinds of cancer risk factors. Intrinsic factors are random DNA copying errors, sometimes called bad luck. Non-intrinsic factors include lifestyle, exposures, and infections. Sorting out their shares matters for prevention and for public spending.

The authors review evidence that cancer has many causes acting together. They give cases where changing risk factors has prevented cancer in practice. They also urge better estimates that include how factors interact. Their position is that non-intrinsic factors drive most cancer risk. The review makes a case for putting more weight on prevention.
europmc-pmc6113628:
Nouioui and co-authors present a large study in Frontiers in Microbiology on how to classify the phylum Actinobacteria. These bacteria matter for farming, industry, clinics, and soils. Old schemes rested on shape and on one gene. That left many groups in the wrong place.

The team built family trees from draft genomes of many type strains. Most groups held up as single branches. Some did not. They propose two new orders, ten new families, and seventeen new genera. More than 100 species move to other genera. The work also adds genome size and DNA data to many species accounts.
europmc-pmc6139328:
Fabregat and Caballero-Díaz wrote a review in Frontiers in Oncology on how a growth factor reshapes liver cells. The factor is TGF-beta, part of a family that controls many cell processes. In the liver it acts at each stage of disease, from first injury to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and cancer.

The review traces how TGF-beta turns resting stellate cells into myofibroblasts, the cells that lay down scar tissue. It also covers how liver cells change identity through a shift called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. That plasticity helps tumors form and spread. Readers get a step-by-step view of one signal's role across the whole course of liver disease.
europmc-pmc6191528:
GBD 2016 Parkinson's Disease Collaborators report a systematic analysis in The Lancet Neurology on the global burden of Parkinson's disease. Neurological disorders are now the leading source of disability worldwide. Aging populations are raising the toll of brain diseases such as Parkinson's. The team measured that burden from 1990 to 2016.

Drawing on epidemiological studies, they estimated prevalence and years lived with disability for every region and country. Cases were split into mild, moderate, and severe using a standard clinical scale. A natural history model combined prevalence with excess death risk. The results show how the burden grew and where it falls heaviest. Public health and research planners can use the numbers to respond.
europmc-pmc6267528:
Van der Wel and van Steenbergen review pupil size as a sign of mental effort. Their review appeared in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review. The pupil widens when a task demands more effort. Labs have used that widening for two decades as an effort gauge. The authors focus on tasks that need cognitive control. They sort the work into updating, switching, and inhibition tasks.

Across all three areas, harder demands usually widened the pupil. Links between widening and task success were less tidy. Some studies found better work with wider pupils, and others found the reverse. An effort account can explain that split, the authors argue. Pupil change may track effort spent, not task hardness itself. The review also looks ahead to brain based theories of effort. It names what future tests should settle.
europmc-pmc6269428:
Liu and co-authors review the direct brain effects of electrical stimulation through the scalp. Their review appeared in Nature Communications.
