The method passes weak currents through the head to shift brain activity. Direct and alternating current forms are both in wide use. Clinics value its ease and its promise for long term therapy. How it changes nerve activity right away is less clear.

The review gathers lab dish, animal, and human evidence with modelling work. Models of current flow should guide study design, the authors argue. Recording errors can fake effects and must be ruled out. Skin and nerve effects outside the brain may also play a part. New devices and methods could sharpen future tests. The goal is stimulation work that others can repeat. Honest limits are named alongside the promise.
europmc-pmc6289128:
Lees and co-authors present pyseer, a software package for microbial genome-wide association studies. The tool appeared in Bioinformatics. Such studies hunt for genetic variants tied to traits like drug resistance. Microbes pose special problems for this work. Their populations are highly structured. Their genomes also vary a lot in gene content.

pyseer brings several proven methods together in one Python package. It reworks the older SEER tool and adds new models. Users gain more choice in input data formats. The package also adds ways to read and explain the results. It is free online, with a guide and a tutorial. The authors say it suits bacteria, viruses, and other structured populations.
europmc-pmc6310928:
He and co-authors sort triple-negative breast cancers by their immune profiles. Their study appeared in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. This cancer type lacks three common treatment targets. It varies a lot between patients. The team used four public data sets. They scored 29 immune signatures in each tumor. Machine learning then grouped the cancers.

Three subtypes emerged from the analysis. One group showed high immune activity and cell infiltration. Its patients had better survival outlooks. A low group showed weak immune signs and fast cell cycles. Gene networks differed sharply between the groups. The authors say this sorting could guide immunotherapy choices. It may help match patients to treatments that fit.
europmc-pmc6361828:
Chen and co-authors present a research article in Frontiers in Microbiology on how the SARS coronavirus triggers inflammation. They studied the viral 3a protein, a pore-forming viroporin. The question was whether 3a switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cell structure that releases inflammatory signals.

In primed mouse macrophages, the authors show 3a alone was enough to trigger the inflammasome. Its ion channel activity was essential for release of interleukin-1 beta. Potassium leaving the cells and reactive oxygen from mitochondria also mattered. The work highlights viroporins as drivers of virus-induced inflammation. That mechanism may help explain lung damage in SARS.
europmc-pmc6373628:
Xu and Goodacre present a comparative study in the Journal of Analysis and Testing. They test how the split of data into training and test parts changes judged model quality. Good checks matter, since scores on training data alone can hide overfitting and flatter a weak model.

They made nine simulated datasets and built two kinds of classifiers on each split. The splits used cross-validation, bootstrap forms, and fixed sampling plans such as Kennard-Stone and SPXY. On small datasets, judged quality missed true test quality by a wide gap for all methods. The gap shrank as datasets grew and models neared stable behavior. Fixed sampling plans gave the worst estimates. The split sizes also needed a fair balance to judge quality well.
europmc-pmc6377728:
Zhang and co-authors present a review in Cell and Bioscience on exosomes. These nano-sized vesicles bud inside cells and are released into body fluids. They carry proteins, lipids, and genetic material from their parent cell, and distant cells can take them up and be reprogrammed.

The review explains how exosomes form through the ESCRT machinery and multivesicular bodies. It catalogs their molecular makeup and the methods used to isolate and study them. Because cargo reflects the state of the parent cell, exosomes may serve as non-invasive diagnostic markers. The authors also assess engineered exosomes as delivery vehicles for drugs and genes.
europmc-pmc6386828:
Mariani and co-authors review biomaterials and the immune system in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Implants meant to rebuild tissue often fail because the body reacts against them. The fight starts where the material meets living tissue.

Newer designs do not just try to be inert, the authors say. They aim to guide immune cells toward healing instead. Goals include calmer neutrophils and more of the repair type of macrophage. Such tuned materials may help damaged organs regain function. The field is young, they caution, and much remains unknown.
europmc-pmc6436528:
Bowers and co-authors, with the Genome Standards Consortium, propose minimum reporting standards for genomes recovered without growing the microbe, covering single amplified genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes. Sequencing had already logged 2,866 single-cell genomes and 4,622 metagenomic genomes in the GOLD database by 2017. Without shared quality rules, such genomes are hard to compare or trust.

The standards, named MISAG and MIMAG, set completeness and contamination thresholds, quality categories, and the metadata that must travel with each genome. They extend earlier minimum-information checklists to the uncultivated majority of bacteria and archaea. Journals, databases, and sequencing teams gain a common yardstick for a fast-growing class of data.
europmc-pmc6445328:
Naas and co-authors describe the Beta-Lactamase Database, a hand-built public archive of the enzymes that destroy beta-lactam antibiotics and drive resistance. Entries sort the enzymes by class A through D, family, and subgroup, and each 3D structure held in the Protein Data Bank is shown with its entry.

Tested mutants and measured breakdown profiles round out each entry, linking shape to function. Built-in BLAST searches let users match new protein or DNA sequences against the archive, a key service for tracking resistance as it shifts. The site is free, with no sign-up. For doctors fighting drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, the archive pulls a scattered set of papers into one address.
europmc-pmc6449928:
Lopes and co-authors review DNA vaccines against cancer, covering five years of lab work and ten years of human trials. Plasmid vaccines proved safe and could raise broad, aimed immune responses, yet the braking defenses inside tumors kept the clinical gains modest. Two lines of attack organize the field's answers.

The first tunes the vaccine itself: picking better antigens, adding neoantigens unique to a tumor, and polishing the plasmid. The second pairs the shot with partners that lift the brakes in the tumor's neighborhood or grow immune cell numbers, from helper proteins to checkpoint blockade. Details matter; one popular helper also draws in braking cells. Winning approval as standard care remains the unfinished goal.
europmc-pmc6471628:
Rendon and Schäkel review psoriasis, from the immune pathways that start it to the targeted drugs those pathways produced. Plaque psoriasis accounts for about 90 percent of cases, and worldwide prevalence sits near 2 percent, rising to 11 percent in some Caucasian and Scandinavian populations. Fifteen years of pathogenesis research rewired treatment.

Initiation and maintenance run through the IL-23 and Th17 axis, with genetics, epigenetic change, and the skin microbiome feeding in. Established therapies are covered first, then the biologics aimed squarely at that axis, which deliver the high clearance earlier drugs could not. The disease now serves as a model for chronic inflammation generally.
europmc-pmc6515828:
Jajere reviews Salmonella enterica, with focus on how it causes disease. The review appeared in Veterinary World. Salmonella is a leading foodborne pathogen in humans and animals. S. enterica holds more than 2,600 known serovars. Spread runs from farm to fork, often through poultry, eggs and pork.

Some serovars infect only one host. Others range across many species. The author details virulence tools such as flagella, capsules and type 3 secretion systems. Those systems sit on pathogenicity islands SPI-1 and SPI-2. Key outbreak serovars include Typhimurium, Enteritidis, Heidelberg and Newport. The review closes on rising multidrug resistance and surveillance gaps.
europmc-pmc6523028:
Honce and Schultz-Cherry review how obesity alters influenza A virus disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic first marked obesity as a risk factor. Obese patients faced worse illness and higher death rates.

Obesity brings chronic low-grade inflammation across the body. Infected obese hosts mount delayed and blunted antiviral responses. Recovery is poor, and vaccines and antivirals work less well. Viral shedding lasts longer in these hosts. That setting may let more virulent minor variants emerge. The authors draw on human cohorts and animal models. They close with open questions on treatment for this growing group.
europmc-pmc6661828:
Isah reviews how stress and defence responses drive secondary metabolite production in plants. His article appears in Biological Research. Plants make these compounds for many cellular jobs. Output depends on species, genotype, and growth stage. Environment during growth matters just as much. Stress signals switch production up or down. Elicitors can trigger it in cell cultures too. Signalling molecules weave through the response. Salicylic acid, jasmonic acid, calcium, and nitric oxide feature.

Molecular tools are clarifying the pathways involved. They trace signals from cell level to whole plant. That knowledge feeds metabolic engineering efforts. Tuning pathways could raise yields of useful compounds. Many valuable drugs trace back to plant metabolites. Better production control widens their supply.
europmc-pmc6691128:
Johnson and co-authors test the measurement quality of the GAD-7 scale in a psychiatric sample. Their study appears in Frontiers in Psychology. The seven-item scale screens general anxiety symptoms. Its factor structure has been disputed across studies. The sample held 1,201 patients in treatment. Inpatients and outpatients both took part. Patients completed the scale before and after treatment. Depression, well-being, and other anxiety measures accompanied it. Internal consistency proved excellent overall. Convergent validity was excellent as well.

First-pass analysis indicated one clear factor. Confirmatory fitting rejected that structure at first. Correlating residuals among somatic items fixed fit. The revised model supported the one-factor solution. Variation across treatment groups was acceptable. The authors endorse the scale for mixed clinical use.
europmc-pmc6728328:
Jiang and co-authors found a cleaner way to make hydrogen peroxide with electricity. Peroxide is usually made by reducing oxygen all the way to water in fuel cells. Stopping halfway yields peroxide, a green chemical feedstock. The team placed single metal atoms on carbon nanotubes and varied their surroundings.

An iron atom setting called Fe-C-O proved best. It reached peroxide selectivity above 95% in both alkaline and neutral solutions. Its onset voltage, 0.822 volts, set a record for this current level. Swapping the metal or its neighbors could flip the reaction back toward water. The catalyst also disinfected water in a demonstration test.
europmc-pmc6736328:
Bushmanova and co-authors present rnaSPAdes, a tool that assembles transcriptomes from scratch. RNA sequencing yields huge datasets. Reference-based assemblers work only for species with finished genomes. Building transcripts without a reference stays hard because genes vary in activity and come in spliced forms. Similar genes add to the confusion.

RnaSPAdes builds on the SPAdes genome assembler. It treats transcriptome assembly as akin to single-cell genome assembly. The authors compared it with rival tools on many datasets and quality measures. No tool won on every count. Still, rnaSPAdes typically beat the others, with cleaner contigs and fewer duplicates. The report spells out each assembler's strong and weak points.
europmc-pmc6797728:
Szabo and co-authors built a single-cell map of human T cells across tissues. T cells coordinate adaptive immunity in many body compartments. Whether a T cell sits in lung, lymph node, marrow, or blood shapes its behavior, but the details were fuzzy. The team sequenced RNA from single T cells taken from all four sites, resting and after stimulation.

Over 50,000 cells were analyzed. Tissue signatures emerged for mucosal and lymphoid sites. Activation states differed by lineage, with distinct effector states for CD8 cells and an interferon-response state for CD4 cells. Tumor T cells matched mostly activated CD8 states. The map is a reference for reading T cells in disease, built entirely from healthy donors.
europmc-pmc6834528:
Zhang and co-authors review ozone pollution as a health hazard, in Frontiers in Immunology. Ground-level ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and organic vapours react in sunlight. Before clean-air rules, levels in some cities were high enough to sting eyes and trigger lung emergencies. The authors argue the danger persists at lower levels.

Day-to-day rises in ozone track with asthma cases and deaths, even below current standards. Long exposure is also linked to deaths from lung and heart disease. One study cited tied man-made ozone to an estimated 700,000 respiratory deaths in the year 2000. The review explains how ozone injures airways and why estimates differ between studies.
europmc-pmc6859528:
Srinivas and co-authors review reactive oxygen species and DNA repair in cancer, in Redox Biology. Reactive oxygen species are fleeting, aggressive molecules that can break DNA. Cancer treatment leans on that fact: chemotherapy and radiation kill partly by flooding cells with such damage. Cells answer with a repair programme, the DNA damage response.

The review explains how reactive oxygen both causes breaks and shapes the repair that follows, above all for double-strand breaks. Trials have added oxygen-modulating drugs to standard treatment, with mixed results. The same mix helps one tumour and shields another. The authors call for more lab work to learn when each effect wins.
europmc-pmc6906728:
Al-Dhabyani and co-authors describe a dataset of breast ultrasound images, in Data in Brief. Breast cancer is among the most common causes of death in women worldwide. Catching it early saves lives, and ultrasound is a front-line tool. Machine learning can sharpen ultrasound reading, but models need labelled example images to learn from. This article publishes such a collection.

The images come from Baheya Hospital, gathered with LOGIQ E9 ultrasound systems over about a year. Each image is classed as normal, benign, or malignant, with mask images marking the regions of interest. Preprocessing trimmed the original 1,100 scans to 780 images in portable network graphics format. The authors release the set for classification, detection, and segmentation research.
europmc-pmc6919428:
Jones and co-authors review survival in chronic heart failure. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in the European Journal of Heart Failure. They searched databases up to August 2018. Sixty studies gave survival data for 1.5 million people. All patients were treated in community settings.

Pooled survival was 86.5 percent at one year. It fell to 56.7 percent at five years. At ten years it was 34.9 percent. Five-year survival rose across recent decades. Older age at diagnosis cut survival time. Care in secondary settings showed the lowest mortality. Those studies also reported higher use of key drugs. The authors see wide scope for better treatment uptake.
europmc-pmc6925228:
Migliavacca and co-authors profile muscle wasting in older people across three populations. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Sarcopenia, the harmful loss of muscle mass and strength with age, limits independence and survival. Its causes in sick patients are less clear than in healthy aging.

The team compared muscle biopsies from 119 older men in Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Jamaica. Men with sarcopenia shared a clear gene activity pattern. Genes for energy production in mitochondria were turned down. Their muscle held fewer mitochondria, and levels of NAD+, a key energy molecule, ran low. Faulty NAD+ production and recycling help explain the loss, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc6943028:
Fairley and co-authors describe the International Genome Sample Resource, a home for open human genome data. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The resource grows out of the 1000 Genomes Project, which built the largest open catalogue of human variation from samples spanning five continents.

The resource keeps those data available and updates them to the current human reference genome. It adds fresh data from the same cell lines, plus samples from other open-consent studies. Its portal now shows a unified view across almost 5000 samples. Recent releases include high coverage sequence data for 2504 samples from the project's final phase. All data stay fully open and free for anyone to use.
europmc-pmc6949028:
Pique-Regi and co-authors profile single cells in the placenta during labour, at term and early. Their study appeared in eLife. More than 135 million births occur each year, yet the molecular steps of human birth stay poorly understood. The placenta mixes maternal and fetal cells, and disturbed signals between them can trigger preterm birth.

The team sequenced cells from three placental compartments in women with and without labour. Cell mix and gene activity differed by compartment and by group. Two cell types were described for the first time. Maternal macrophages in the membranes changed most with labour. Some placental signatures also showed up in mothers' blood, raising hopes for non-invasive prediction of birth timing.
europmc-pmc6959328:
Yu and co-authors show that immune cells near sensory neurons help start and sustain nerve pain. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. After peripheral nerve injury, macrophages multiply around sensory neuron cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia. Whether that expansion truly drives pain was unclear.

Removing those ganglion macrophages eased the mechanical hypersensitivity of neuropathic pain, in both male and female mice. Macrophages at the injury site itself did not have that role. Signals from injured sensory neurons coaxed the macrophages to grow. A growth factor from the neurons, CSF1, mattered mainly in males, where it also switched on spinal microglia. Even so, fewer macrophages built up in females. The findings point to drug targets on the body's periphery, rather than in the spinal cord.
europmc-pmc6996528:
Fasano argues that a leaky gut helps drive many chronic inflammatory diseases. His article appeared in F1000Research. He opens with Hippocrates and the saying that all disease begins in the gut. Modern hygiene, he notes, may have made us too clean, shifting our microbes and feeding an epidemic of inflammatory disease in rich countries.

Beyond genes and triggers, three elements stand out in his account. The gut wall can grow inappropriately permeable. The immune system can turn hyper-aggressive. And the gut microbiome shapes both, even influencing host gene activity. A protein family called zonulin controls gut permeability, and studies tie it to autoimmune, metabolic, infective, and tumour diseases. Blocking that pathway, Fasano argues, offers fresh treatment targets across many conditions.
europmc-pmc7000728:
Palmieri and co-authors show that a gas made by inflamed immune cells rewires their fuel use. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. When macrophages switch to attack mode, their inner chemistry changes in deep ways. That shift was long thought to drive their hot, harmful state.

By tracing tagged carbon and testing how cells breathe, the team pinned the change on nitric oxide the cells make themselves. The gas blocks a key enzyme, aconitase 2, and stalls the core energy cycle, so citrate piles up. It also steers fuel away from a second enzyme, so the cells lean on glutamine to top the cycle up. In time, whole parts of the cell's power chain are lost. The same pattern showed in live mice, not just in dishes. The upshot flips the old model: the shift in fuel use is a result of attack mode, not its cause.
europmc-pmc7006728:
Wainwright and co-authors issue consensus guidance for hip and knee replacement care under enhanced recovery programmes. Their statement appeared in Acta Orthopaedica. Studies of the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery approach are plentiful but uneven. A multidisciplinary panel weighed the evidence for each step of the care pathway.

Seventeen topic areas are covered. Best practice starts before the operation: prepare patients with clear education, choose anaesthesia wisely, and plan blood management to cut transfusions. Pain control should spare opioids by combining several milder drugs. Getting patients moving early is essential; some now go home the day of surgery, and most leave within two days. No single surgical technique or implant choice earned a recommendation over others. The unified protocol, the panel says, now needs testing as a whole to confirm its strength.
europmc-pmc7078228:
Liu and co-authors report a follow-up drug study in Cell Discovery. The COVID-19 outbreak demanded effective, available, and affordable medicines fast. As of 3 March 2020, China had confirmed over 80,000 cases including 2,946 deaths, with 10,566 more cases across 72 other countries. The team's earlier work had flagged remdesivir and chloroquine as in vitro inhibitors of the virus, but remdesivir was experimental and scarce.

Chloroquine looked like the practical choice for large-scale use, given its availability, safety record, and low cost. This letter tests its gentler relative, hydroxychloroquine, which doctors already prefer for long-term treatment of autoimmune disease. In infected cell cultures, hydroxychloroquine also blocked SARS-CoV-2 effectively. Experiments on virus entry showed how the drugs interfere with the endosomal route the virus takes into cells. The authors present hydroxychloroquine as the more deployable candidate of the family, pending clinical proof.
europmc-pmc7083228:
Wang and co-authors estimate the global burden of flu-linked breathing infections in children under five for 2018, in The Lancet Global Health. Their systematic review and modelling study drew on 100 published studies and 57 unpublished ones. An earlier estimate for 2008 had counted 20 million such infections in young children.

Few poor or middle-income countries routinely vaccinate young children against flu, and uptake stays low where policies exist. The team updated case, hospital admission, and death figures by region and age. Readers get a current measure of how much illness seasonal flu causes in the youngest children, and a base for vaccine policy debates.
europmc-pmc7098028:
Yi and co-authors review what had been learned about the new coronavirus disease, COVID-19, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. At the time of writing, the virus had infected over 80,000 people and killed over 3,000. The review aims to gather a fast-moving field into one account.

The authors cover the spread of the outbreak, the virus itself, diagnosis, treatment, outlook, and prevention. They compare COVID-19 with SARS and MERS throughout. COVID-19 spreads more easily than SARS, they note, but kills a smaller share of patients. Many questions stayed open, from the animal source to the best care. Readers get a broad early survey of a disease that science was still racing to understand.
europmc-pmc7140028:
Vaddepally and co-authors review every approved use of immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs against the NCCN guidelines, in Cancers. These drugs release brakes on immune cells so they can attack tumors. Since ipilimumab's approval in 2011, six more such drugs have joined it, aimed at the CTLA-4 and PD-1 pathways.

Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States, and checkpoint drugs have regressed many tumor types. For each drug, the review covers its role, the landmark trials behind approval, and the strength of evidence for each listed use. The result is a reference that maps a fast-growing treatment class onto the standard guideline recommendations.
europmc-pmc7147328:
Cuan-Baltazar and co-authors grade the quality of early online information about the Wuhan coronavirus, in JMIR Public Health and Surveillance. On 6 February 2020 they searched Google for the term then in use and took the first 110 websites. Each site was scored with three validated quality instruments and its Google ranking.

Only 2 sites (1.8%) carried the HONcode quality seal. Under the JAMA benchmark, 39.1% of sites met none of the required categories and only 10.0% met all four. The DISCERN tool rated 70.0% of sites low and none high. The authors warn that both the public and scientists must watch the quality of what they read and publish during a health crisis.
europmc-pmc7181728:
Tajik and co-authors test whether sealing a leaky gut can stop arthritis before it starts. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Gut microbe imbalance is tied to autoimmune disease, but the trigger steps are unclear. The team focused on zonulin, a protein that loosens the gut wall's tight junctions. Zonulin levels run high in autoimmune mice and humans.

High zonulin came with a leaky gut barrier and disturbed microbes. It also predicted which cases would shift into joint inflammation. Blocking the zonulin pathway in mice protected the barrier. That protection delayed or prevented arthritis onset in their tests. The authors frame the gut barrier as a checkpoint in autoimmunity. Guarding it early might keep silent autoimmunity from becoming disease.
europmc-pmc7206728:
Liang and co-authors trace how a long noncoding RNA drives breast cancer growth. Their study appeared in Molecular Cancer. Such RNAs do not build proteins, yet they steer cell behavior. BCRT1 was found at high levels in breast cancer tissue. The team confirmed this in patient samples and databases.

Raising or lowering BCRT1 changed how cancer cells grew, moved, and invaded. It also shaped how immune macrophages in the tumor behaved. BCRT1 works by soaking up a small RNA called miR-1303. That small RNA normally restrains a protein named PTBP3. Freeing PTBP3 lets the cancer progress. Patients with more miR-1303 survived better in database checks. The chain gives researchers a new target in breast cancer.
europmc-pmc7216228:
Lee and co-authors review new understanding of vascular calcification, the hardening of blood vessels by mineral deposits. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Calcification can strike the inner or middle vessel layer. The middle-layer form is common in kidney disease and diabetes. It tracks closely with cardiovascular disease overall.

Older views blamed simple chemistry: too much calcium and phosphate. Research now shows an organized biological process instead. Bone-like signaling programs switch on inside vessel walls. At the same time, the body's natural anti-calcification defenses can fail. Disturbed calcium handling inside cells is a required ingredient. The review organizes these mechanisms for researchers and clinicians. Better mechanism knowledge may yield the first real treatments.
europmc-pmc7329528:
Lebano and co-authors scope the literature on migrant and refugee health care in Europe for BMC Public Health. They reviewed 77 papers from nine European countries, covering evidence from 2011 onward. The aim was to map what is known about access to care and barriers that block it.

Despite a stated goal of equal access, the review finds lasting gaps between migrants and non-migrants. Unmet needs stood out in mental and dental care, alongside legal blocks, language problems, and discrimination. Migrants overused emergency care and underused primary care. Mental care, preventive care, and care for older migrants need more attention, the authors say. Better data on migrant health is a first step.
europmc-pmc7343828:
Richard and co-authors test how the COVID-19 virus passes between ferrets, in Nature Communications. Ferrets are a standard stand-in for human respiratory infection. Knowing whether the virus travels by touch or through air shapes control measures, so the team housed infected and healthy ferrets in contact and in air-only setups.

The virus spread efficiently both ways. Direct contact passed it within 1 to 3 days, and air-only exposure within 3 to 7 days. Recipient ferrets shed virus in the same pattern as directly infected ones, and live virus could be grown from all positive animals. The results give experimental support for airborne spread, backing distancing and other community controls.
europmc-pmc7362228:
Das and co-authors review smart polymer nanocarriers for drug delivery in Polymers. Nanocarriers are tiny polymer packages that ferry drugs, proteins, or genes through the body. A stimuli-responsive carrier holds its cargo until a trigger appears at the target site.

Triggers can come from inside the body, such as acidity, enzymes, heat, or low oxygen, or from outside, such as light, magnetism, or ultrasound. The same carriers can carry imaging agents, making combined diagnosis and treatment, called theragnosis, possible. Cancer therapy draws most of the attention in the review. Readers get a catalogue of trigger types and carrier designs, plus the hurdles before routine clinical use.
europmc-pmc7371628:
Wang and co-authors report in Nature Metabolism that killer T cells can run on an alternative fuel called inosine. Active T cells rewire their metabolism to fight infection, but tumors and inflamed tissues can starve them of glucose. The team tested whether inosine, a breakdown product of genetic material, could fill the gap.

Without glucose, T cells grew and worked using inosine, splitting it into a sugar unit that feeds energy pathways. Cancer cells, by contrast, varied widely in using inosine. Adding inosine improved checkpoint drug treatment and cell therapy in solid tumors that could not use it themselves. The trick, in effect, feeds the fighters while the tumor goes hungry. Readers get a neat metabolic lever for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc7377928:
Guo and co-authors introduce the CNGB Sequence Archive in Database, a repository for omics data held at the China National GeneBank. High-throughput sequencing now produces data faster than labs can organize it. The archive stores raw reads and analyzed results so others can reuse them.

Data are organized into six object types, from Project and Sample through Experiment and Run to Assembly and Variation. A linking model ties living samples, sample information, and analysis results together, so any piece can be traced through the whole chain. The archive follows common life-science data standards and aims at careful curation. Readers get a tour of new infrastructure behind China's genomics effort, and a case for archives as research tools.
europmc-pmc7402628:
Ali and co-authors show that COVID-19's serial interval shrank as control measures bit, in Science. The serial interval runs from symptom start in one case to symptom start in the person they infect. Textbooks treat it as a fixed trait of a disease, but transmission pair data from mainland China told another story.

In mid-January 2020 the average interval was 7.8 days; by early February it had fallen to 2.2 days. Faster finding and isolation of cases cut the chain earlier, leaving less time to pass the virus on. The shrinking interval therefore measures intervention success, and may also hint at growing population immunity. A supposedly fixed number turned out to be a policy gauge.
europmc-pmc7405628:
Banerjee and Rai reflect on loneliness under COVID-19 lockdown in the International Journal of Social Psychiatry. Their commentary opens with Pascal's line about humanity's problems stemming from the inability to sit quietly in a room alone. Billions were suddenly confined at home as nations locked down.

Isolation, the authors argue, breeds chronic loneliness and boredom, which over time damage physical and mental well-being. Uncertain timelines for the pandemic compound the strain, and mass panic and anxiety ride on top. Suspected cases face isolation inside isolation. The piece is a short, humane warning from two psychiatrists: the mental health shadow of social distancing needs planning, not just the viral curve.
europmc-pmc7410828:
The ENCODE Project Consortium reports the expanded encyclopedia of DNA elements in Nature, covering the human and mouse genomes. Genomes hold not just genes but the timing and volume controls for making RNA and proteins. Phase III of the project widened the survey across more cells and tissues.

The effort produced 5,992 new experimental datasets, spanning RNA production, chromatin shape and marks, DNA methylation, looping, and protein occupancy, including systematic maps of mouse fetal development. Integrating the data yields a registry of 926,535 candidate regulatory elements in humans and 339,815 in mice. A web server, SCREEN, gives flexible public access. Readers get the reference catalogue that much of modern genomics quietly depends on.
europmc-pmc7428328:
Wan and co-authors build a consensus atlas of gene activity in the Alzheimer's disease brain. They pooled gene expression data from 2,114 postmortem samples. From seven brain regions they found 30 modules of genes that act together.

The team compared human modules with 251 gene sets from mouse models of brain disease. Some human modules matched mouse responses to amyloid, others to tau. Age and sex shaped some signatures of disease progress. Modules rich in neuron or microglia genes matched models of several diseases and of aging. Other modules, tied to protein upkeep, did not switch on in Alzheimer's models. The atlas is a cross-species resource for testing drugs and ideas before human trials.
europmc-pmc7510528:
Kreye and co-authors isolate a protective antibody against SARS-CoV-2 and test it in hamsters. The virus spreads as a pandemic with lung and multi-organ harm. Mapping neutralizing antibodies guides vaccines and care.

From 598 human monoclonal antibodies taken from 10 patients, the team found 40 strong neutralizers. The best, CV07-209, blocked the live virus at an IC50 of 3.1 ng/mL in the lab tests. Crystal structures showed two antibodies blocking the ACE2 docking site head-on. Some near-germline antibodies also reacted with the body's own antigens. CV07-209 did not, and that matters for safety. Given before or after infection, it shielded hamsters from infection, weight loss, and lung damage. The authors back such clean neutralizers as therapy.
europmc-pmc7516028:
Abdelrahman, Li, and Wang compare SARS-CoV-2 with SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and influenza A viruses. The new virus caused a global health emergency. Open questions covered its origin, spread, severity, and risk factors.

The review sets the four respiratory viruses side by side. It weighs their origins and genomic features in turn. Transmission strength and disease-causing power get direct comparison. Receptor binding and host factors shape how sick patients get. Prevention, control, and treatment close the survey. The authors aim the work at health officials and medical experts. A clear view of kin viruses can help curb the new pandemic. Lessons from SARS, MERS, and flu frame what to expect from SARS-CoV-2.
europmc-pmc7559928:
Opatha, Titapiwatanakun and Chutoprapat review transfersomes for drug delivery through skin. Skin delivery is noninvasive and can be self-administered. The outer skin layer blocks most large or charged molecules.

Transfersomes are elastic vesicles with a bilayer structure. They can carry water-loving and fat-loving drugs alike. Their flexibility lets them squeeze through narrow skin pores. That gives higher skin passage than standard liposomes. The review covers how transfersomes are made and tested. It also covers factors that shape their properties. Recent uses in skin drug delivery are surveyed. Readers get the concept, mechanism and limits in one account.
europmc-pmc7665028:
Griffith and co-authors warn that a sampling flaw can distort COVID-19 research. Many studies draw on people in hospital, people tested, or volunteers. Such samples are not a fair cross-section of the public. The flaw is called collider bias.

When two traits each affect who gets sampled, the sample can show false links between them. Using UK Biobank data, the authors show that tested people were highly selected on many traits. These ranged from genes and behavior to heart risk and body measures. The authors urge better sampling at the design stage, not just fixes after the fact.
europmc-pmc7699628:
Skinnider and co-authors present software that predicts antibiotics hidden in microbe genomes. Most clinical antibiotics came from compounds microbes make to compete. Genome data now hint at a wealth of such compounds still unknown. The hard part is linking a gene cluster to the shape of its product.

The platform, PRISM 4, predicts chemical structures for all major classes of bacterial antibiotics in use. Machine learning then forecasts what each compound will do. Applied to more than 10,000 bacterial genomes, it charted thousands of encoded antibiotics. The tool is free online as an interactive web app.
europmc-pmc7758428:
Rutsch and co-authors review the gut-brain axis and an immune complex that links the two. Gut microbes shape brain function and inflammation through nerves, immune paths, and microbe products. This two-way network is called the gut-brain axis. When gut microbes fall out of balance, the brain's barrier can leak.

The complex in focus is the inflammasome, which fires the cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. It has been tied to multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, and mood disorders. Microbes and inflammasome activity sway each other in a loop. The authors map what is known and mark the open questions for the field.
europmc-pmc7778928:
Blum and co-authors mark 20 years of the InterPro protein database. InterPro sorts proteins into families and flags key domains and sites. Its software, InterProScan, searches a sequence against models from many member databases. InterPro merges like models and adds notes, papers, and gene terms for each entry.

Founded in 1999, it is now among the most used tools for protein annotation. This report covers version 81.0 in its 20th year. Updates span new content, a rebuilt website, and a fresh data interface. InterProScan also runs faster. The authors stress its role as genomes pour in faster than labs can test each protein.
europmc-pmc7835928:
Bajaj and co-authors review how aging changes the immune response to coronavirus infection. By early December 2020, COVID-19 had caused over 72 million cases. Deaths passed 1.6 million worldwide. Older people carried the great bulk of both. Existing illness raised their risk further.

Aging rewires the immune system over time. Worn-out immune cells pile up and work less well. At the same time, background inflammation rises. These twin traits are called immunosenescence and inflamm-aging. Both first-line and learned defenses change shape. Vaccine and drug responses shift with them. The authors argue that age must guide care for such infections.
europmc-pmc7908628:
Tudi and co-authors present a review of farming growth, pesticide use, and harm to the environment. Pesticides protect crops from weeds and insects. About one-third of farm output depends on them. Without them, fruit output would fall by 78%, the review notes. Yet the same chemicals can hurt species they were never meant to touch.

The authors trace the history of farming and of pesticide use in three periods. They sort pesticides by chemistry, function, and toxicity. Residues drift from target crops into air, water, and soil. From there they reach wildlife and people through the environment and food. Birds, fish, and helpful insects can all be harmed. Climate change adds fresh pressure on pest patterns. The review calls for care that keeps the yield gains while cutting the wider damage.
europmc-pmc8007728:
Cubuk and co-authors probe the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein, which packages the viral genome. The protein binds RNA, yet how it does so stayed unclear. The team combined single-molecule spectroscopy with all-atom simulations. Their work shows a flexible protein built for many weak contacts at once.

The authors report three dynamic disordered regions in the protein. These hold short motifs that briefly form helices and grab RNA. The two folded domains barely interact, leaving the protein loose and multivalent. Mixed with RNA, it also undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation. The authors offer a model of how one genome gets condensed alone. That model ties a nanoscale grip to a visible, test-tube effect.
europmc-pmc8063428:
Gurung and co-authors trace the full journey of an exosome, from birth inside a cell to action in the next. Exosomes are small vesicles that all cells release. They carry proteins, metabolites, and nucleic acids between cells. Trials now test them as diagnostics and as drug carriers. Sound clinical use demands a clear grip on their biology.

The review maps each step of the journey in turn. Pathways of biogenesis and secretion come first. Transport and uptake by recipient cells follow. The authors then explain the signaling the cargo triggers inside. Disputes get plain treatment as well. Even the definition and naming of exosomes remain contested. Common pitfalls that trip up new studies are flagged. The result is a field guide for careful exosome work.
europmc-pmc8145228:
Wong and Weitzer compare long COVID with myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome. Long COVID names the lasting symptoms that can follow acute COVID-19. Early reports hinted at a strong overlap between the two conditions.

The authors searched MEDLINE and PsycInfo for studies through 31 January 2021. They kept 21 studies for close comparison. Reported long COVID symptoms were set against a list of symptoms for the fatigue syndrome. The comparison aims to sharpen how both conditions are defined and managed. Readers get a side-by-side view of shared features and points of difference.
europmc-pmc8166828:
Bao and co-authors link loss of ferroportin to memory harm in Alzheimer's disease. Iron balance goes wrong in the disease, and excess iron worsens damage. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of cell death.

The team found ferroportin, the main iron exporter, reduced in mouse and human Alzheimer's brains. Deleting it in key brain neurons caused hippocampal shrinkage and memory loss in mice. The cell changes matched ferroptosis. Restoring iron export eased the harm in their tests. The work names a new target for slowing memory decline. The team checked both a mouse model and human brain samples.
europmc-pmc8213028:
Fang, Hou, and Liang review how plants respond to combined salt and alkali stress. The two stresses often strike together in nature. Together they harm growth more than either alone.

Most past work studied salt stress by itself. Mixed salt-alkali studies remain scarce, the authors note. They gather what is known about plant defence under the pair. That covers sensing, signalling, and protective chemistry. The gap matters for farming on degraded land. Clearer mechanisms could guide hardier crop breeding. The review sets an agenda for a neglected stress pairing. Sustainable farming is the practical stake behind the science.
europmc-pmc8241728:
Zhang and co-authors review how amyloid-β and tau interact in Alzheimer's disease. Plaques of amyloid-β and tangles of tau mark the disease. Each protein's harm has been studied on its own for years.

Drugs aimed at one protein alone have brought no big breakthrough. The review asks how amyloid speeds tau phosphorylation. It also traces how tau may carry amyloid's toxic effect. Joint effects on microglia and synapses come under review. The pair may damage more together than apart. Drug work on their interaction is still young, the authors note.
europmc-pmc8414028:
Weng and co-authors review vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells as a cancer treatment route. These tiny membrane packets carry proteins, lipids, RNAs, and growth signals between cells. Stem cells can help or hinder tumors, and their vesicles copy much of that action.

Because the vesicles mimic their parent cells, they may work as a cell-free treatment. They also home toward tumors on their own. The review covers their roles across cancers in plain terms. It then sums up work on engineered vesicles used as delivery trucks for anti-tumor agents. The authors close with the hurdles that still block the move from lab bench to bedside.
europmc-pmc8451728:
Barker and co-authors guide reviewers in running proportional meta-analysis. This method pools single-group data, such as rates from one arm of a study. Guidance for it is scarce next to the rich advice for two-group comparisons. Review authors need clear steps for sound use.

The guide explains when the method fits and why it matters. It walks through conduct, interpretation, and reporting in plain order. Statistical points and display choices get their own treatment. Worked cases show how past reviews used the method well. The authors wrote the piece for evidence synthesis teams. It should help single-group syntheses reach the standard set for pairwise reviews.
europmc-pmc8497028:
Evans and co-authors track body, mind, and work outcomes after hospital care for COVID-19 in the UK. How the illness shapes health and jobs months later was not well known. The PHOSP-COVID study set out to measure that impact.

Adults discharged from UK hospitals were assessed between 2 and 7 months later. The visit logged symptoms plus body and blood tests. The team modeled who felt fully recovered, with age, sex, and illness severity in view. A cluster analysis grouped outcome patterns. Breathlessness, fatigue, mental health, thinking, and fitness formed the axes. The study aims to spot who needs long-term support and why.
europmc-pmc8576828:
Pàmies and co-authors compile recent gains in palladium-catalyzed allylic substitution with handedness control. This reaction class builds chiral molecules, a core task in drug and materials work. The review traces its growth, mechanism grasp, and newest advances in one survey.

Data are sorted by the type of partner that attacks the allyl group. Stabilized carbon partners and heteroatom partners lead the field. Many chiral ligands grew up around them, so results group by ligand type. Decarboxylative and oxidative variants get their own sections. Key points on what drives high selectivity are set out in depth. Comparisons with other metals show where palladium wins and loses.
europmc-pmc8607428:
Yang and co-authors survey E3 ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that tag proteins for removal or change. These enzymes form the last step in a three-enzyme chain. They attach ubiquitin to a target protein at a lysine site. This tag system touches almost all cell work in complex life forms.

The review sorts E3 ligases by style and structure. It then traces their roles in cancer growth and spread. Faults in these enzymes can help tumors form and resist stress. That makes them a draw as drug targets. The authors also cover new drug forms that use E3 ligases to destroy target proteins. Readers get a map of a large enzyme family.
europmc-pmc8677728:
He and co-authors review the PI3K/Akt signal pathway as a target for cancer therapy. This pathway drives many cell processes and is switched on too often in tumors. That overuse helps cancers start and grow. The team examined the nodes above and below the pathway to map its full role.

Drugs that block parts of the pathway have been widely tested. Their clinical gains stay limited so far. Tumors activate the pathway by many routes, and resistance often follows. The authors favor pairing pathway blockers with standard cancer care. They also review the state of each drug class. The strategy aims to break tumor survival routes more fully.
europmc-pmc9177428:
Mitchell and co-authors map clonal dynamics of blood formation across the human lifespan. Blood-forming stem cells lose regenerative power with age, and blood cancer risk rises. Why function drops sharply after age 70 was unclear. The team sequenced 3,579 genomes from single cell-derived colonies in 10 people aged 0 to 81.

Stem cells gained a mean of 17 mutations per year after birth. Blood production stayed richly diverse in adults under 65, with vast numbers of stem cells sharing the work. After 75, diversity fell sharply, and a few dozen clones supplied much of the blood. Most of those clones began expanding before age 40. Simulations with steady driver gains explained the abrupt shift well.
europmc-pmc9338328:
Zhang and co-authors argue that pairing radiotherapy with immunotherapy opens a new era in cancer care. Radiation is given for local control, yet it can also shrink tumors far from the beam. That distant response is called the abscopal effect. Radiation seems to act like an in-place vaccine, waking body-wide immunity.

The review lays out how radiation stirs the immune system. It gathers trials to find the best dose, timing, and pairing schedules. The abscopal effect is rare, so the authors propose ways to force it. Low-dose radiation may reprogram the tumor setting, a trick they call the radscopal effect. Trials such as PACIFIC already show strong patient gains. The goal is a standard option for metastatic cancer care.
europmc-pmc9402428:
Chen and Chen report a research study on how the NLRP3 inflammasome switches on. This protein complex drives inflammation and is linked to human disease. Many unlike triggers can set it off. How they all lead to the same result was not clear.

The team found that these triggers break up the trans-Golgi network in the cell. NLRP3 is then drawn to the dispersed network. A charged lipid there, PtdIns4P, binds a basic region on NLRP3. The network acts as a scaffold where NLRP3 clumps form. Those clumps trigger the adaptor ASC and start the signal chain. Blocking the lipid bond stopped the whole response.
europmc-pmc9628128:
Zhong and co-authors review the Warburg effect in colorectal cancer, its roles in the tumor setting, and drug leads. This cancer is the third most common worldwide. It is also the second top cause of cancer death. The Warburg effect makes tumor cells burn glucose hard even with oxygen present.

That habit fuels spread and reshapes nearby tissue. It drives new vessel growth and immune suppression. It also helps form cancer linked fibroblasts and drug resistance. The review explains how glycolysis is switched on in these tumors. Gene and epigenetic controls both get coverage. Liver spread of the cancer gets its own section. Cross talk between glycolysis and each cell type follows. Drug plans that cut the glucose flow close the survey. Named targets span GLUT1, HK2, and transport blockers.
europmc-pmc9946828:
Yeh and co-authors design new luciferase enzymes from scratch with deep learning. Classic enzyme design placed active sites into natural protein scaffolds. Few good scaffolds and complex sequence rules limited that route. The team used a family-wide hallucination method instead.

The method generates many idealized protein shapes with varied pocket forms. Matching sequences are designed to encode those shapes. The team built luciferases for two synthetic luciferin fuels. Their active sites set an arginine group beside the reaction site with tight shape fit. The best enzyme was small, at 13.9 kDa. It stayed stable above 95 °C and showed high selectivity. The work shows deep learning can create working enzymes to order.
europmc-pmc9963528:
Iantomasi and co-authors detail oxidative stress and inflammation in osteoporosis, with a focus on microRNAs. Osteoporosis upsets bone balance, with resorption outpacing formation. Estrogen loss drives postmenopausal bone loss. Oxidative stress, inflammation, and faulty microRNA control all take part.

Reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signals boost bone-eating cells. They also curb bone-forming cells through MAPK routes and transcription factors. MicroRNAs tune gene activity after transcription and shift with disease state. The review shows a two-way loop among these factors. Reactive species can alter microRNA levels, and microRNAs can alter reactive species output. The authors aim to flag targets for new bone treatments. Better therapy could improve life quality for patients.
evans-wentz-milarepa-1928:
Walter Evans-Wentz, an American scholar of Celtic and Eastern religion, published Tibet's Great Yogi Milarepa in 1928. The book translates the beloved life of Milarepa, the eleventh-century Tibetan poet-saint who sang his teaching in verses. A Tibetan lama, Kazi Dawa-Samdup, did the base translation.

Milarepa's story runs from black magic and revenge in his youth to years of hard training under his teacher Marpa. His later life of caves, songs, and converts forms the heart of the book. The volume introduced Tibetan Buddhism's saints to the West in human, gripping form. Tibetan families still tell his story to children as a household tale.
fauset-plum-bun-1928:
Jessie Redmon Fauset published Plum Bun in 1928, a novel about a young Black woman in Philadelphia and New York. Angela Murray is light-skinned and wants a career as an artist. She decides to pass as white to gain freedom and a chance at success. Her sister stays in the Black community they grew up in.

Angela finds that passing brings loneliness and fear of being found out. Love and ambition pull her in opposite ways. In time she questions the price of hiding who she is. The novel is praised for its clear-eyed view of race, gender, and the cost of ambition.
ford-last-post-1928:
Last Post, published in 1928, closes Parade's End on a single long country day after the war. The armistice is past, Tietjens's brother Mark lies dying and silent, and the family's great house passes out of their hands for good.

Tietjens now lives with Valentine Wannop, selling antiques, while Sylvia's last maneuvers fail to reclaim him. Ford views the aftermath largely through other minds, letting the old order's end arrive quietly. Some readers find the volume a falling-off; others prize its elegy. Either way, it completes modernism's broadest portrait of England at war and in uneasy peace.
fortune-esoteric-orders-and-their-work-1:
How the mystery schools truly work was Dion Fortune's subject in 1928. The Esoteric Orders and Their Work surveys the Western orders from inside knowledge. Fortune wrote as one who had trained in them and led her own school.

She sets out their grades, their methods of work, and the ends they claim to serve. The book sorts true training from sham and tells the seeker what to expect at each step of the road. Few English books of its time spoke so plainly on the subject. It opened the doors of the orders to the plain reader.
freud-future-illusion-robson-scott-1928:
Sigmund Freud published The Future of an Illusion in German in 1927. The English text here is W. D. Robson-Scott's translation of 1928. Freud calls religion an illusion born of human wishes. Helpless before nature and fate, people create father-like gods for comfort and control. Civilization, he argues, rests in part on this shared wish.

He predicts that education and science will slowly loosen religion's hold. His dialogue partner raises objections, and Freud answers them in turn. The book is his clearest atheist manifesto. It angered believers and pleased free-thinkers in equal measure. Its debate on faith and reason continues today.
frus-1861-d128:
From Paris on 7 June 1861, William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 128 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Within days, France would declare its neutrality in the American war. Dayton's early June letter comes from the last stretch of doubt. It shows an envoy at work in the gap between a court's private lean and its public word. The gap between lean and word was where envoys like Dayton earned their pay. Pay of that sort was earned in the gap, and Dayton earned his in full.
frus-1861-d228:
Writing from Washington on 29 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed Mr. Fogg. The printed record keeps it as Document 228 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d28:
Henry Sanford wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 July 1861. The dispatch is document 28 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford's Brussels post made him a gatherer of news as much as a court envoy. His early July letter fed Washington a mix of fact and rumor from the heart of Europe. Such feed stock let Seward test what the great capitals told him in formal terms. Brussels news often bore on France, whose border lay a short ride from Sanford's desk. News that bore on France bore also on Spain and Italy, and Seward knew it.
frus-1862-d128:
14 August 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 128 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d228:
Document 228 is the second Seward letter to William Stuart dated 20 August 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote both letters the same day to the British legation's acting head.

Ten days after this letter, Union forces lost the second battle of Bull Run. A defeat that shook faith in the North at home and abroad. Stuart's legation reported the shock to London. Letters written just before such a blow catch the last calm of an older picture. And they help explain why foreign policy shifted so fast that fall. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d28:
Writing from Washington on 1 March 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 28 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d328:
A Dayton report dated 18 September 1862 stands as Document 328 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward the day after Antietam.

Word of the battle took more than a week to reach Paris, so this report still belongs to the pre-Antietam world in substance. Dayton wrote of the court and its plans as they appeared before the invasion failed. Read with that lag in mind, the letter shows how policy in Europe kept being made from yesterday's war. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d428:
Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington, addressed this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 May 1862. It is Document 428 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the record printed with the President's annual message.

Notes from a foreign minister in Washington carried weight that reports from abroad did not: they stated a government's formal position. Spain and the United States had live questions between them in 1862, from Cuba and the Gulf trade to the allied expedition in Mexico. Tassara's letters open the Washington side of the Spanish file. Seward's replies beside them show how the Union answered a proud power. It gave no ground and offered no insult.
frus-1862-d528:
Roest van Limburg, the Netherlands minister in Washington, replied to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 June 1862. His note is Document 528 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

The Dutch exchange of early June 1862 moved at a pace rare even in wartime Washington, with letters dated on consecutive days. Van Limburg wrote for a trading nation whose ships and colonies touched the war at many points, from Caribbean ports to the East Indies trade. His note belongs to that concentrated run of business. In it, each government stated its position in formal terms. Each then waited for the other's answer across a very short distance.
frus-1862-d628:
Edward Joy Morris sent this report from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 August 1861, the earliest paper in the volume's Turkish file. It is Document 628 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Morris wrote in the war's first summer, from a capital where American concerns were trade, travel, and the protection of citizens under treaty. His early report established the Ottoman file's character: local, practical, and remote from the rebellion except as the rebellion changed America's standing in the world. For Seward, even distant posts had to be heard from, since a global republic's business never wholly sleeps. The letter reaches back to the season when the Department was first organizing its wartime network.
frus-1863p1-d128:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 24 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 128 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, paired with the letter printed just before it.

The second sheet of a pair often held the harder point, or the one that had just ripened. Seward's mail that week pressed Britain on the ships and on fair dealing in the war. This letter is the second half of the day's work. It belongs to the close weave of orders by which Washington kept its London man in step that spring.
frus-1863p1-d228:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 July 1863, and it is document 228 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d28:
Washington's new-year line went out in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 13 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 28 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's January letters carried the government's line now that the war had a stated aim against slavery. He also had to arm Adams against the South's push in Europe, which did not slacken with the new year. This letter is one of the early-1863 sheets that set the brief. It shows Washington and London in their set rhythm: orders out by one steamer, reports back by the next.
frus-1863p1-d328:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 26 November 1862. The note is document 328 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d428:
The date 28 March 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d528:
22 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d628:
Writing on 30 September 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State addressed Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart in an official letter. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d128: Minutes of the President's meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff, held at 2 p.m. on November 15, 1943 in the President's cabin aboard the battleship Iowa, form Document 128 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. At sea on the way to Cairo, Roosevelt and his chiefs settled the American line for the coming talks. Minutes like these, taken on the spot, are the spine of the official record. The volume prints them in full.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d228:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 398 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, listing the specific operations proposed for the defeat of Germany and her satellites in 1943 and 1944. It is the American plan of work for the coming year, offered to the Combined Chiefs of Staff.

Azores facilities would support the fight against U-boats and air ferry routes. The combined bomber offensive keeps the highest priority, as a thing that must come before Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion set for 1 May 1944. Where resources run short, Overlord wins over the Mediterranean every time. The paper also covers the build-up in Britain and a standing readiness to cross the Channel early if a chance opens.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d28: Home from Quebec, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on August 26, 1943, and the message is Document 28 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Quebec talks had just set the alliance's course for the next year, and follow-up letters kept the decisions moving. The catalog record names the parties and the date, nothing more. In the published series the note belongs to the bridge between the August conference and the autumn summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d328: President Roosevelt sent Marshal Stalin a short secret telegram, marked operational priority, from Cairo on 26 November 1943. Carried by Navy channels through Harriman for delivery to Stalin, it thanks him for his message of 23 November announcing that he would reach Tehran on the 28th or 29th. Roosevelt replies that he expects to reach Tehran himself on the 27th, and closes with a single warm line: it will be good to see you.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d428:
President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Steinhardt a secret telegram from Cairo on 2 December 1943, giving the assurance Turkey's president had demanded before accepting the Cairo invitation. It answers Steinhardt's report of the same day.

Roosevelt directs Steinhardt to tell Inönü at once that he is delighted the Turkish president can come. Inönü is to be assured, in the words he had asked for, that he is being invited to a free discussion as between equals. Roosevelt adds that he is especially happy to have the occasion to talk with him. Transport planes will be waiting at Adana on the morning of 4 December, and the British are advising their ambassador in the same sense. Steinhardt is told to be sure to bring an adequate American interpreter with him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d528:
President Roosevelt sent a message to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 23, 1943, two days before Christmas and a fortnight after his return from Tehran and Cairo. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The weeks after a summit are when its promises meet the machinery of government. Roosevelt's messages to Hull in this period passed decisions and problems from the traveling President to the department that had to execute them. For readers, this cable belongs to the unglamorous but decisive phase of diplomacy: turning handshakes in Tehran into instructions, appointments, and orders in Washington.
frus-1944-quebec-d128:
From Moscow on September 10, 1944, Ambassador Harriman urgently summarized for Roosevelt and Hull the Soviet reply on Warsaw aid. The British ambassador had shown him the message Moscow sent London. Harriman called it an extremely shrewd statement for the record, one that shifted the decision, and the blame, onto the Western allies.

In paraphrase, Moscow said real aid would come from the Red Army's advance. Supply drops, it claimed, had repeatedly fallen into German hands. Still, the Soviets were prepared to join a drop operation under a prearranged plan. Harriman asked for urgent instructions on whether to open talks with the Red Army staff, and noted he lacked fresh word on how much of Warsaw the insurgents still held.
frus-1944-quebec-d228:
Hull cabled Harriman on September 12, 1944, with the president's instructions on Warsaw. Marshall was being directed to have General Deane explore the Soviet offer to cooperate in aid, working with his British colleagues. Harriman was to lend Deane every support and tell Molotov that America was prepared to do its utmost, jointly with the British and Russians, on immediate aid to the garrison.

Hull added a political warning. The Soviet decision might come too late if the garrison had shrunk too far for drops to be practical, but that question would emerge in negotiation. What mattered was that Washington show no hesitation in implementing the Soviet promise, so it could not be blamed if aid failed to arrive in time.
frus-1944-quebec-d28:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 23, 1944, the day Paris rose against its occupiers. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The last week of August 1944 carried the alliance from campaigning to conferring: France was being liberated, and the Quebec meeting was three weeks off. Roosevelt's correspondence then had to ready the big unsettled questions, above all Germany's treatment and the terms of continued aid to Britain. For readers, this message stands at the turn of the season, written while the guns were still firing in Paris.
frus-1945-50-intel-d128:
Vandenberg wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 12 September 1946. The director of central intelligence reporting to the secretary of state shows the CIG working its board members one by one. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By September, Vandenberg was looking past the summer's rulings to the group's growth: more money, more missions, and a firmer charter. A letter to Byrnes sought the support of the board's senior member. Readers can watch the director's method: win the secretaries singly, then move the board. The campaign that fills the volume's later pages, ending in the stronger agency of the 1947 law, begins in approaches like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d228:
A memorandum dated 16 October 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Acting Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The State Department prints it as document 228 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the first autumn of the new system: a fresh CIA, a fresh Council, and piles of first-year business.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d28:
Minutes of a meeting held on 16 October 1945 come next in the volume. Minutes fix who met, what was weighed, and what, if anything, was agreed. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Meeting records punctuate the letters and memoranda of this collection, marking the moments when paper gave way to talk. By mid-October 1945 the intelligence question had enough rival plans on the table to need face-to-face sorting. Readers should use the minutes as hinges. What the letters before them proposed, the meeting tested. What the meeting left open, the letters after them fought over. That rhythm, paper and meeting in turn, drives the whole five-year story.
frus-1945-50-intel-d328:
A letter dated 5 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Acting Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). Readers meet it as document 328 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d428:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 8, dated 25 May 1948, is document 428 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The spring of 1948 brought crisis in Europe, with the blockade of Berlin weeks away. At home, the Council kept adding rules for its intelligence agencies. A new directive in May shows the system still taking shape under pressure, rather than resting on the plan drawn up the year before. The Berlin crisis that summer would soon test every line of these standing orders. Orders written in calm months had to serve in wild ones, and mostly they did.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d128:
One flaw in the Germany plan bothered the President: no tough civilian voice in Berlin. Leo Pasvolsky recorded the objection on 15 November 1944, after a White House talk on the treatment of Germany. His memorandum is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Roosevelt had read the State Department's memorandum and found it satisfactory except on this point. As he saw it, Eisenhower and the British and Russian commanders would run their zones. A commission of lower-ranking soldiers would sit in Berlin. What it lacked was a strong civilian point of view. His fix: give a general's commission to some outstanding civilian and make him the American member of the Berlin commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d228:
Leave the Turkish Straits alone: that is the hope stated in a briefing paper of 21 October 1944. The “Memorandum Regarding the Question of the Turkish Straits” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It gives three reasons for wishing the subject never came up.

First, the Montreux Convention of 1936 has worked well, and Moscow itself said so, jointly with Britain, in 1941. The Straits went unused as a supply road to Russia because the Axis held the lands around them, not because of the treaty. Second, large changes would likely violate Turkish sovereignty and upset the balance in the Balkans and the Near East. Turkey, the paper adds, has been a good custodian of the Straits. Minor changes from Moscow or London would still be weighed with care.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d28: Harriman reported from Moscow on 14 December 1944, sending Roosevelt word as document 28 in this volume. The Foreign Relations editors placed his report among the leaders' letters in the Malta and Yalta record. Ambassador reports like this one grounded summit planning in what the Soviet government was actually doing, rather than what Washington hoped it might accept at the conference table.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d328:
Charles Bohlen kept the record of the first Roosevelt-Stalin talk at Yalta, held at 4 p.m. on February 4, 1945. After warm thanks for the welcome, the President said the military picture had much improved since they last met. Stalin agreed, reporting that Soviet armies were moving with success toward the line of the Oder.
