Roosevelt joked that he had bet aboard his cruiser on a race: Russians to Berlin, or Americans to Manila first. Stalin answered that Manila would likely fall first, given the hard fighting on the Oder. Bohlen's minutes catch two partners sounding each other out before the formal sessions began.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d428:
Four powers sign this early American draft of the Declaration on Liberated Europe, dated February 5, 1945. France stands among them, beside the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. The draft pledges the four governments to concert their action in helping peoples freed from Nazi rule. Former Axis satellite peoples are included too.

Their pressing political and economic problems, the draft says, are to be solved by democratic means. It speaks of the Nazi war machine in retreat and puppet regimes collapsing. Later texts at Yalta cut France from the declaration. This draft preserves the wider promise the Americans first imagined.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d128:
Ambassador Harriman confirmed his travel party to Secretary Byrnes in a telegram from Moscow on July 6, 1945. The short message is document 128 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Byrnes had invited him the day before and said the State Department party would reach Berlin on July 13.

Harriman writes that he will plan to be in Berlin when the State Department party arrives. Edward Page and his assistant, Lieutenant Meiklejohn, will travel with him. So will General Deane, Admiral Maples, and General Ritchie of the American military mission in Moscow, who had their own orders from the War and Navy Departments. The telegram completes the picture of the Moscow contingent joining the American delegation at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d228:
The State Department argued for a Council of Foreign Ministers in a briefing memorandum dated June 27, 1945. The paper is document 228 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is the full statement of the proposal the President would lay before Stalin and Churchill.

Without some machinery for peace negotiations and territorial settlements, the paper warns, confusion, political uncertainty, and economic stagnation will drag on in Europe. Versailles does not encourage faith in a full formal conference: slow, heated, and hard to ratify. The Department's formula is a council of the foreign ministers of the five permanent members of the Security Council: Britain, Russia, China, France, and the United States. Limiting the council to those five would also block bids to pack it with client states. It should meet as soon after the summit as preparations allow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d28:
Hopkins saw Stalin alone after dinner at the Kremlin on June 1, 1945. Only the interpreter Pavlov was present, and Hopkins's memorandum records the plea he made. He wanted to impress on Stalin, as earnestly as he knew how, the bad effect in America of the detaining of fourteen Poles inside Poland. He spoke specifically of those charged only with having illegal radio transmitters.

He made clear he was not talking about the others, charged with more serious crimes. If this business could be settled, he believed, the list of Polish names for consultation in Moscow would win approval without great difficulty. The memorandum shows the envoy spending his credit on prisoners.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d328:
A briefing memorandum dated June 27, 1945, makes the case for a four-power treaty to keep Germany disarmed for good. Under such a treaty, the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union would pledge their own forces to hold Germany down. The memo lists the gains early action could bring.

A firm pledge, it argues, would strengthen trust among the allies and head off other quarrels. It would also cut Soviet fears that a rebuilt Germany might one day join the West against Russia. If Germany stayed disarmed by joint promise, no grouping of European powers could threaten the Soviet Union, and Moscow could afford a softer policy elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d428:
Payment for exported German coal is Pauley's condition in his cable from Moscow of July 7, 1945. On the Potter-Hyndley report he agrees fully: action should be taken at once to export from Germany all coal above German needs, and to reach maximum production early. His telegram answers Washington's message of July 3.

But Pauley adds a warning from his reparations post. Countries that do not pay for coal they receive should be put on definite notice. Such deliveries may later count as part of reparations payments under the final plan, or stand as exports for which payment in acceptable currencies will be required. Free coal, he insists, must not slip off the books.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d528:
Ukrainian refugees in Germany are the subject of an airgram from Tittmann at Vatican City, dated July 5, 1945. He transmits a translation of a note received from the Holy See that same day. Several thousand Ukrainians are in Germany, the note says, and fear that they may be sent to Galicia, in Soviet-held territory.

On their behalf, the Holy See has been asked to use its good offices. The wish is that these poor refugees may soon be allowed to leave Germany and take refuge in France, Belgium, the Netherlands, or any other country. Anything, the note pleads, rather than being obliged to go to territories under Russian domination. A like appeal for Baltic peoples had reached the Department in May.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d628:
A top secret briefing paper on the withdrawal of Allied forces from Iran is dated June 23, 1945. It is document 628 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Iran had raised the question in formal notes to all three Allied powers on May 19.

The paper traces how foreign troops came to Iran. British and Russian forces moved in during August 1941, after the Shah failed to expel German agents. A treaty of January 1942 made their stay lawful. It set withdrawal no later than six months after all fighting with Germany and her associates had ended. That word associates matters, since Japan still fought on. The British, the paper says, intend to raise the issue at the conference themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1028: John McCloy wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 17, 1945, about a French sector for Berlin. General Clay had worked out a tentative deal with General Weeks, the British deputy governor. A French area in the city would be carved from the existing British and American areas. McCloy suggests telling Ambassador Winant that agreement looks likely. Winant should then clear the way in the European Advisory Commission to send the question to the Control Council. Clay planned to settle a firm scheme with Weeks and Koeltz that week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1128:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on 21 July 1945. With the president and the secretary of state at Potsdam, the home team kept the London embassy briefed and tasked. Winant was Washington's eyes on the British government through the summit.

A message of this kind could carry news of the talks, fresh orders, or a request for word from London. The London post was the most vital American embassy of the war years. Keeping it in step mattered even while the leaders met face to face. This cable shows the home office running that link in the middle of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1228:
Sato cabled Togo on 20 July 1945, keeping up the Moscow reports. The exchange between the two men ran almost daily through the summit. Each Sato cable tested Soviet mood; each came back with less hope than Tokyo wanted.

Japan's bid rested on a false guess: that Moscow would help end the war on mild terms. Sato, on the spot, saw the guess failing. His duty was to report what he saw without breaking Tokyo's will to hear it. This dispatch is one link in that painful chain. It shows the peace feeler dying by inches, in an envoy's careful words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1328:
Murray, the American ambassador in Iran, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. Iran sat under joint Allied occupation, with Soviet troops in the north and a vital supply route to Russia running through it. Its file was quiet at Potsdam but never cold.

An envoy's report from Tehran carried the facts of that uneasy triangle: a young shah, foreign armies, and oil beneath it all. Washington watched Iran as a test of Soviet conduct after the war. This dispatch is the Tehran post's word during the summit. It shows the coming Cold War's map being sketched in side reports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1428:
The Soviet delegation submitted a text on 29 July 1945, the first of a cluster of Soviet texts from the conference's final days. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Clusters matter: when a delegation tables paper after paper in the closing stretch, it is marking the points it refuses to leave unsettled. This text opens a run of four Soviet submissions dated within two days. Readers who line the run up against the final protocol can see the last Soviet push in full. Judge how much of it the other leaders absorbed before they signed. Few parts of the volume show bargaining pressure so plainly.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-128:
On July 28, 1945, the United States delegation added this memorandum to its Potsdam files. That was the day Attlee took his seat as prime minister and the talks resumed in full. Staff papers from the date catch the conference resetting around a changed British team. The memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Delegation memoranda were the glue of a large mission. They kept dozens of officers reading from the same page. This one preserves the team's shared picture at a turning point. For readers, it is a dated snapshot: what the Americans thought, in writing, before the closing bargains began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-28:
Thompson's minutes for the plenary session of July 19, 1945, record a frontier incident raised by Stalin. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Churchill answered a point Stalin had made at the previous meeting, about the Bulgarian-Greek frontier.

Churchill said he had made inquiries and heard of no fighting. The peoples there did not like each other much, and some sniping was likely. No Greek field division stood in northern Greece, he stressed. Greece had seven thousand guards on its Albanian and Yugoslav frontiers for internal order. Across the line stood far larger forces: thirty thousand Albanians, thirty thousand Yugoslavs, and twenty-four thousand Bulgarians. The great powers, Churchill argued, should make clear that marauding attacks would not be tolerated. Frontier questions belonged to the peace conference, and violators would prejudice their own claims.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d728:
Document 728 is a working paper of the United States delegation, dated July 20, 1945. Staff built such papers to shape options for the talks. It circulated inside the team rather than across the table. The paper was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Working papers preserve roads not taken. Options that leaders later cut still stand here in full. Readers can weigh them and guess why they fell. The document also shows drafting as teamwork: many hands, one text. In the mass of Potsdam paper, these drafts are where policy first took written shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d828:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 31, 1945, as document 828. It was offered on the conference's last full day. Late American texts aimed at the final protocol's remaining gaps. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A last-day proposal is a bid for the record as much as for the deal. Even where it failed, it marked the American position. Readers can compare it with the protocol adopted hours later. The document shows a delegation still drafting at the wire. Potsdam's paper war ended only when the conference did.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d928: The American reparations team in Moscow sent this short telegram to Edwin Pauley on July 25, 1945. It corrects two figures in their East Prussia message of the day before. Livestock and farm equipment values should read 1,250 million Reichsmarks for East Prussia as a whole, and 435 million for the northern part. Farm output should read 1,200 million, about 9 percent of the old Reich, and 425 million for the north. The team also fixes a message number in the same cable.
frus-1964-68v28:
Volume XXVIII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, is given over to Laos. The first chapter covers the spring of 1964, when the Pathet Lao attacked and a coup struck in Vientiane. It ends with U.S. photo flights and a strike in reply. Later chapters follow efforts to revive the Geneva settlement. They also trace the start of the air war against infiltration through the panhandle.

The final chapter covers 1968, the fall of Phou Pha Thi, and a fresh look at policy. Cables and memos show U.S. support for Premier Souvanna Phouma throughout. Bombing in Laos grows as the volume proceeds. The Paris peace talks form the backdrop at the close.
frus-1969-76v28:
Southern Africa fills Volume XXVIII of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. The first chapter covers regional issues as a whole. The next treats Portuguese Africa. A third follows Angola as its civil war grows in 1975. The final chapter covers the independence talks that ended Portuguese rule. Rhodesia and South Africa run through the regional chapters.

The papers show U.S. officials weighing Soviet and Cuban moves in Angola. Cables report on talks with Portugal after its 1974 coup at home. The records trace a shift from quiet ties with white regimes toward engagement with new states. The volume ends with Angola's war still open.
frus-1977-80v28:
Volume XXVIII of the 1977-1980 series turns inward, to the organization and management of foreign policy. Sections cover the National Security Council and the agency process. The longest treats intelligence policy and reform after the inquiries of the 1970s. Others treat economic reorganization, job cuts at the State Department, and the USIA overhaul. The making of IDCA and the USAID reorganization get a section. Civil service reform follows.

Late sections treat discontent in the Foreign Service and reform efforts. The last covers jobs equity and awareness at State. The volume is a record of a government reshaping its own tools. It suits readers of public administration as much as diplomacy.
galsworthy-swan-song-1928:
John Galsworthy closed the Forsyte chronicles with Swan Song, published in 1928. It ends both the second trilogy, A Modern Comedy, and Soames Forsyte's long story. Galsworthy had followed the family from Victorian wealth into the unsettled 1920s.

Fleur's unhappy love for Jon Forsyte burns on inside her marriage, while Soames grows old and oddly tender. The General Strike of 1926 shakes London in the background. A fire at Soames's house brings the saga's themes of property and love to a final test. Galsworthy gives his most possessive character a strangely moving end, and an age closes with him.
gao-gaoreports-b-296228:
Grove Resource Solutions protested a Navy award for telemedicine support in GAO decision B-296228, dated July 1, 2005. The winner was Evolvent Technologies. The work backed the Naval Medical Information Management Center in Bethesda. The firm hit the winner's place in the field and its price check.

GAO denied the protest. A flawed bid may stay in the field. The rule lets an agency keep it, though it need not. On price, the winner's rates matched like rates on federal supply lists. They looked fit to draw good staff. Both points were sound. The case shows the room an agency has on range and price calls.
gao-gaoreports-b-304228:
Two senators asked GAO for a legal opinion in B-304228. The plea hit Education Department funds for a video news release and a media study. Both acts tied to the No Child Left Behind Act. GAO issued its ruling on September 30, 2005.

The video piece broke the propaganda ban. It hid the government as its source from viewers. That flaw also broke the Antideficiency Act, since no funds could back it. The agency had to report that breach at once. The media study stood on softer ground. One party-tied point in it cost near nothing. GAO let that piece stand, with a warning. Future studies must shun such party content.
gao-gaoreports-b-308128:
Sex education grant materials face a truth rule in this GAO letter, B-308128, dated October 18, 2006. Federal grants fund abstinence education by states and groups. One clause of the Public Health Service Act is section 317P. Part of it calls for true facts on how well condoms work. The Health Department held that this rule skips grant materials.

GAO did not accept that view in full. The rule can reach materials made and used by grant takers. Reach turns on what the materials say. GAO judged no grant file for breach here. It urged the department to rethink its stand and act to ensure due care.
gao-gaoreports-b-309928:
How agencies dealt with laws the President flagged is checked in this GAO letter, B-309928, dated December 20, 2007. Two House and Senate chairmen made the request. GAO tracked ten clauses of law. The President had taken issue with each in a signing statement. Nine agencies held the duty to put the clauses to work.

GAO counted eleven cases in all, since some clauses touched two desks. In six cases the agencies acted as the law was written. Two clauses never came into play. Three had not yet been put to work, at Energy and at the emergency agency. GAO did not judge the worth of the President's qualms.
gao-gaoreports-b-310928:
Data Integrators, Inc. won its protest; the GAO decision is B-310928, dated January 31, 2008. The Government Printing Office sought print work for health sign-up packs. The packs came in English and Spanish forms. Quotes were due by 10:00 AM on a set day. Data Integrators sent its quote in time and was low. A rival quote came in that same afternoon.

GAO sustained the protest. The late quote still won the order, in breach of the call. The call took in a late-quote rule by a cross-link. That rule bars quotes sent past the due time. A due time in a call means what it says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-328:
Defense Logistics, GAO-05-328 of March 21, 2005, calls for top-tier teaming to run the Army's vast camp aid deal. The LOGCAP deal hires one firm to feed, house, wash, and power troops in war zones world wide. Its work in southwest Asia tops $15 billion in worth as of January 2005. Past GAO reports in 1997 and since urged a firmer grip on the deal.

Those probes left the wide team point aside. This one takes it up. GAO asks how far the Army has moved on past advice. It asks where the deal could serve more, if brass at the top pulled its threads as one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-528:
Fraud and abuse in federal crop insurance are targeted in GAO report GAO-05-528, released on September 30, 2005. The program gave $47 billion in coverage in 2004 at a cost of $3.6 billion. Losses from fraud and abuse were put at about $160 million. The Risk Management Agency runs the program with private insurers. A 2000 law gave it fresh tools against abuse. GAO tested how well those tools are used.

The agency claims more than $300 million saved over 4 years. Yet GAO found key tools underused. Farm offices carried out only 64 percent of the field inspections the agency requested between 2001 and 2004. Data checks on the largest farms were incomplete. About 21,000 big operations in 2003 had not named their owners, and up to $74 million in claims could be recovered. Reviews of insurers were often paper exercises. Only 114 sanctions were imposed in 4 years, though about 3,000 suspect claims arise each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-628:
A national plan for health computing is reviewed in GAO-05-628, dated May 27, 2005. The health department's new coordinator post dates to May 2004. Its July 2004 framework sets four goals and 12 strategies, from wider use of electronic patient records to records patients hold themselves. Work runs in three phases over years. Phase one is under way, but the department set no dates for finishing it, and phases two and three lack detailed plans.

The report mines lessons from the defense and veterans systems and from other nations. Those cases stress clear aims, shared standards, and steady funding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-728:
In GAO-05-728 (September 7, 2005), GAO checked how the Federal Aviation Administration trains its safety inspectors. The agency was shifting from spot checks to a risk-based way of work. That shift raised the bar for what inspectors must know about aircraft. GAO weighed how well the agency plans, builds, gives, and judges its technical courses.

GAO found the agency mostly follows sound training practice. Course planning tied training to the goal of safer flight. A set process shaped new courses. But delivery lagged the other steps. Only about half of inspectors, by GAO's survey estimate, felt they had the technical knowledge their jobs need. GAO suggested further steps to close that gap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-828:
Energy Department projects in Russia get a controls check in GAO-05-828, a report dated August 29, 2005. A 2004 law told GAO to assess threat reduction programs run by two departments. This report covers the energy side. It asks whether contract work is checked against its terms. It also asks whether payments go where they should. The work sits in a nuclear security body with three offices.

GAO found two offices documented controls for almost all contracts reviewed. Their records showed goods received, bills checked, and approvals signed. The third office documented controls for few of its contracts. For seven of nine, its papers were thin or left no trail to follow. No office reviews its controls on a set cycle, GAO added. It urged better controls where the record is weak.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-28:
A budget grading tool and its reach are assessed in GAO-06-28, a report GAO issued on October 28, 2005. The Program Assessment Rating Tool, or PART, is the budget office's way to grade federal programs. GAO asked how its advice changes agency work and results. It asked how the tool fits with the 1993 results law that it overlaps. It also asked what the budget office has done to bring Congress into the process. The study builds on GAO's January 2004 report on the tool.

PART sharpens focus on performance, GAO found. It has built an evaluation habit inside agencies. Most of its advice, though, targets better measures and data, not quick wins. By February 2005 most follow-up steps were still unfinished. Grading nearly every program spreads the effort thin. Agency staff still juggle two systems with clashing demands. Committee staff told GAO the tool would help them more if they were consulted early.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-328:
Tax agency computer defenses, improving but unfinished, are reviewed in GAO-06-328, a report dated March 23, 2006. The tax agency gathers the nation's revenue and guards its most sensitive personal data. Its systems run both money and mission work. As part of the audit of the agency's fiscal 2005 books, GAO checked old security flaws at two sites. It tested whether controls over key systems truly protect taxpayer data. The data must stay private, correct, and available.

Progress continues, GAO concluded, but more is needed. It urged the commissioner to finish building a full agency-wide security program. The commissioner agreed to all five recommendations. He said work to fix the flaws will run until every item is closed. Tax data is a prize target for thieves and fraudsters. Each weakness left open is an invitation. The report's patience has limits: it lists what remains, not just what improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1128:
A small China review panel needs tighter controls, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1128, dated September 28, 2007. Congress set up the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission in October 2000. Its 12 members judge the security weight of trade and economic ties with China, and report each year by June 1. Its budget is about $3 million.

GAO asked if the panel keeps to its charter. It checked its shape, rules, and steps for sound day-to-day running. It tested money controls for fair proof that funds are safe. The work centers on fiscal years 2005 and 2006 deals. Steps are needed, the title states, over key management work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-28:
Cities can seize private land for public projects, but nobody counts how often it happens. GAO mapped the practice in GAO-07-28, a report dated November 30, 2006. Congress ordered a nationwide study of eminent domain. GAO reviewed laws at all levels of government. It visited redevelopment sites where land was taken. It asked officials and property groups about effects. It tracked state law changes from June 2005 through July 2006.

No national or state tally of takings exists, GAO found. States keep no central records of the practice. In Virginia alone, at least 40 kinds of authorities can invoke the power. Cited uses include roads, public buildings, blight removal, and development. Officials described gains like safer roads and new housing. Property groups cited lost shops, jobs, and scattered residents. Many states rewrote their taking laws during the study window. GAO could not judge nationwide effects from the thin data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-528:
Computer security law is only partly obeyed at four big departments, and GAO-07-528, issued August 31, 2007, catalogs the shortfalls. The Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002 told each agency to build a real security program. Four years in, GAO checked the Defense, Homeland Security, Justice, and State departments. It read their rules and reports and spoke with their officials.

Common gaps recur across the four. System lists are patchy, so no one knows the full attack surface. Standard safe settings are not applied to every platform. Staff training lags. Tests of controls vary in depth, and many systems lack full sign-off to run. Weak tools and fuzzy guidance share the blame. Each department had fixes under way, State on its sign-off process and Defense on a single repair track among them. GAO urged all four to close the basics first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-828:
Reserve and Guard pay costs are examined in GAO-07-828, dated June 20, 2007. The military leans more on reserve troops for current wars. Congress has sweetened their pay and health benefits in reply. Total reserve compensation cost rose about 47 percent in six years. It went from about $13.9 billion in fiscal year 2000 to about $20.5 billion in fiscal year 2006. Those sums use constant 2006 dollars. GAO launched the study on its own authority.

Per-person cost for part-time reservists almost doubled, to about $19,100. Deferred benefits drove much of the growth. Their cost more than tripled, from $1.7 billion to $5.8 billion. Health care for future retirees leads that rise. Such costs will persist after the wars end. The Defense Department lacks a clear strategy for the pay mix, GAO found. Its cost figures also hide the full federal bill. GAO urged a strategy review and clearer cost reporting. The department partly agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-128:
Toxic release data and a rule that could shrink it are studied in GAO report GAO-08-128, dated November 30, 2007. Federal law requires plants to report yearly releases of any of 581 toxic chemicals. The data feed a public database run by the Environmental Protection Agency. In December 2006, the agency widened use of a short reporting form.

GAO found that the agency skipped key steps in its own rule-making process. The rule's costs and gains were not fully weighed. GAO also traced how widely the data are used by agencies and the public. It gave Congress a path to act if the agency did not supply the missing analysis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-28:
Wind versus water damage claims are untangled in GAO report GAO-08-28, dated December 28, 2007. After the 2005 hurricanes, owners and insurers fought over what caused each loss. Home policies shun flood damage, so many owners hold two policies. Flood cover caps building losses at $250,000 and pays no living costs. Private cover differs on both points. Splitting one storm's harm between the two is fraught.

GAO weighed how states police the adjusters who make these calls. It checked what data the flood program gathers to test their accuracy. It urged Congress to grant clear access to both wind and flood files held by program insurers.
h-e-j-1928-review-rasa-jala-nidhi-or-oce:
On page 703 of Nature for May 5, 1928, a reviewer signing E. J. H. notices two volumes of Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, or Ocean of Indian Chemistry and Alchemy. The work was compiled in Sanskrit by Bhudeb Mookerji, with his own English translation, and printed at Calcutta. The heading sits in the journal's Our Bookshelf column, among notices of other books. The reviewer tells what the author claims for his work.

Mookerji, the review says, learned from a yogi what printed books lacked, and set old Indian chemistry in order. Yet he gives no list of his authorities, and he claims the art was known millions of years ago. Recipes for mercury, and an essence of earth-worms said to cure carbuncles and leprosy, draw the reviewer's scorn. The verdict: until proof is given, the book shows only, in his words, the unscientific nature of a queer folk-pharmacology.
hall-well-of-loneliness-1928:
Radclyffe Hall published The Well of Loneliness in 1928, and it became the most famous lesbian novel of its age. Its heroine, Stephen Gordon, is born to rich English parents who wanted a son and gave her a boy's name. Stephen grows up feeling set apart, loves riding and fencing more than dances, and slowly understands that her heart turns toward women.

Hall tells Stephen's loves, losses, and exile from her family home in plain, earnest prose. She ends with a plea for the right of such people to live openly. A London court banned the book as obscene within months, and it stayed banned in Britain for decades. Courts in the United States let it be sold, and it shaped how many readers first met the subject.
hawthorne-fanshawe-1828:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Fanshawe in 1828, his first novel, issued anonymously at his own cost. He later tried to destroy every copy of the college romance he could find and burn. The book survives as the seed of the canon, essential to the origins of his art.

Fanshawe, a frail scholar at Harley College, wastes in study while a villain plots around him. Dr. Melmoth's ward Ellen is pursued by a scoundrel who lures her toward a cliff and death. Fanshawe saves her, renounces his hopeless love, and dies young of his scholar's ruined health in college. The plot is stock Gothic, but the gloom and guilt point straight to the later Hawthorne of Salem. He disowned the book so hard that his wife learned of it only late.
history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-babylonia:
Gaston Maspero gave this eighth volume to Sennacherib, king of Assyria. His reign is dated 705 to 681 before Christ in the head notes. The whole east rose in revolt at his accession, Maspero writes. Babylon, Judaea, and Egypt all tested the new king at once.

The battle of Kish in 703 and the fall of Babylon mark the wars. Merodach-baladan's league against Assyria gets full treatment. Later pages follow Arab princes and Egypt's turn to suffer. Sayce edited and McClure translated the volume. Readers get a dense, dramatic telling of Assyria at its most brutal height.
hurston-how-it-feels-to-be-colored-me-19:
How It Feels to Be Colored Me, published in 1928 in the magazine World Tomorrow, is Zora Neale Hurston's best-known essay. Hurston recalls growing up in Eatonville, Florida, where she first felt simply herself. She says she became colored when she moved to Jacksonville at age thirteen and felt set apart.

Rather than plead or boast, Hurston meets race with wit and self-assurance. She refuses pity and declares she does not feel tragically colored. Everyday images carry her points: colored bags of odds and ends, the feel of music, the shock of being watched. The essay became the most quoted personal statement of the Harlem Renaissance.
hutcheson-essay-passions-illustrations-1:
Hutcheson's Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, from 1728, is the first edition of his psychology of feeling. Its second half, the Illustrations on the Moral Sense, defends his central idea against two critics, Gilbert Burnet and John Balguy. Francis Hutcheson taught at Glasgow, where he shaped a generation of Scottish thinkers.

The essay sorts our passions and affections: calm desires, violent storms, and the steady pull of benevolence. Hutcheson asks how reason should govern feeling without killing it. The Illustrations then argue that our approval of virtue comes from a moral sense planted in our nature. The book completes the system begun in his Inquiry of 1725.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-28:
War returns in full force in Volume 28, from 1898. Thwaites covers the Hurons and Iroquois across 1646 and 1647, as peace fails. The annual report turns into a chronicle of slow disaster for Huronia.

Raids burn towns, scatter families, and close the river routes again. Priests write on, steady as ever, while their world crumbles. They bury the dead, guard the fleeing, and keep the chapels open. Each letter home carries grief, grit, and unshaken purpose at once. The volume shows a mission in its last years, still at work each day. Its writers refuse despair even as towns fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-son-of-th:
Aaron, Son of the Devil, is the name given to a portrait of an English Jew of the year 1277. It was drawn on a forest-roll of Essex, beside fines tied to a hunt near Colchester. A doe had escaped the hounds, and Jews and Christians who chased it broke the forest laws of the time.

The drawing is the earliest dated portrait of a Jew. The man wears a cowl, a mark of the professional classes, the entry says. On his clothes sits the English Jewish badge, shaped like the two tables of the Law. It was made of saffron taffeta, six fingerbreadths long and three broad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-bar-benjam:
Abba bar Benjamin bar Hiyya was a Palestinian scholar of the third and fourth centuries, a man of the same age as Abbahu. He was likely born in Babylonia and moved to Palestine, settling at Arbela. Much of the entry is spent sorting out his names, which shift across the two Talmuds.

In Palestine he is always Abba ben Benjamin, and Benjamin is sometimes given in the dialect form Minyomi. Twice he is quoted by mistake as Abaye ben Benjamin, an error of copyists, the entry argues. He must not be mixed up with Abba bar Minyomi, who is Abba ben Martha. His cited traditions most often deal with Baraitot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abeles-marcus-2:
Marcus Abeles was a physician and a lecturer at the University of Vienna, born in Bohemia in 1837. He died at Vienna on December 31, 1894. He took his medical degree there in 1863, then trained on at the General Hospital. He next settled in Cairo, where he rose fast in practice and ran the European Hospital.

His Egypt years ended at Alexandria, on the International Sanitary Commission for the Austrian state. Back in Europe from 1870, he practiced at Carlsbad in the summers and did research in Vienna. In 1884 the university called him to lecture on internal pathology, and named him privat-docent. His many papers deal chiefly with diabetes, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abishai-or-absh:
Abishai, also called Abshai, was a son of David's sister Zeruiah. He ranked as a general second only to his brother Joab. He saved David's life and killed three hundred warriors. Those feats won him a high place in the king's bodyguard.

Loyalty to David drove much of the account. Abishai wanted to kill the sleeping Saul, but David held him back. Later he joined Joab in killing Abner to avenge their brother Asahel. Rabbinic tales expand his rescue of David from Ishbi, brother of Goliath, with help from prayer and miracles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abramson-bernar: Bernard Abramson was a Russian doctor of the nineteenth century. He was a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Science. The state made him a hereditary honorary citizen for his work on public health. He drew up a study plan for the Jewish school at Uman, in Podol. In 1849 he gained the rank of collegiate councilor. He also joined the Odessa English Club that year. The entry notes that he wrote several works on medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achawa-728: Achawa is a name borne by two Jewish journals. One was a German yearbook printed at Leipsic. It ran from 1865 to 1868. A society for poor Jewish teachers and their widows and orphans put it out. It dealt most with school questions. It also ran pieces by M. Wiener on the past of the Jews in Germany. The second was a monthly at Amsterdam. A teachers' society founded it about 1888. It dealt with school work alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-nathan-82:
Nathan Adler was a German cabalist born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on December 16, 1741. He died there on September 17, 1800. As a bright child he won praise from Azulai in 1752. He studied at the school of Jacob Joshua in Frankfort. His chief teacher was David Tebele Schiff, later rabbi in London. In 1761 he opened a school of his own.

Great names learned first under him. Moses Sofer of Presburg was the most famed of his pupils. Adler gave himself to Cabala and to the prayer rite of Isaac Luria. He prayed in the Sephardic form and gave the priest blessing each day. Old school Talmud men frowned on his ways. In 1779 the town heads banned meets in his house. He paid no heed and kept his doors open day and night. In 1782 he was chosen rabbi of Boskowitz, in Moravia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agape-plural-ag:
Agape is the name for the shared meals of the first Christians. Rich and poor, master and slave, sat at one table. Rank fell away in brotherly bond. Tertullian gives a good account of the meal. It began and closed with thanks and song. In the first century it bore no set tie to the Last Supper. The poor, widows, and orphans were its chief guests.

The entry sets a like Jewish custom by its side. A rich man's table set at his door for the poor is likened to an altar. A table that holds a share for the poor is called the table before the Lord. One sage kept the door open at bread breaking and cried out for all who hungered. Johanan b. Zakkai used the altar of charity to console a pupil who mourned the Temple's fall. He cited Hosea: God wants mercy, not sacrifice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-or-ahai-928:
Aha, or Ahai, is a name shared by nearly fourscore rabbis. They appear in the Talmud and in midrashic literature. Some of them are misnamed through errors of copyists. Others appear only once or twice. Those ones cannot be identified with any real certainty.

The entry groups the most prominent teachers under this name. It singles out three sages above the rest. Those three are always quoted by the name Aha alone. They carry no patronymic and no cognomen. The rest of the entry's work is sorting the many bearers of the name by generation and deed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akhaltzyk-meani: Akhaltzyk means "New Castle" in the Georgian language. It is a fortified town of Transcaucasia, in the government of Tiflis. It stands on a stream of the Kur river, 110 miles west of Tiflis. Of its 26,000 inhabitants, about 3,000 are Jews. Some are very old settlers of the town. Others came from Abas-Tuman in the middle of the nineteenth century, fleeing Muslim persecution there. The Jews of Akhaltzyk keep a synagogue and schools. Most of them work as cotton-weavers and small traders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-al-het-1228:
'Al Het is the longer confession of sin used on the Day of Atonement. Each of its sentences opens with a set formula. "Forgive us for the sin we have committed before Thee in" it begins, and a sin follows. The sins are listed in the order of the alphabet. Sephardic use names one sin for each letter. Ashkenazic use names two for each letter.

The confession stands in every 'Amidah of the day, save the closing Ne'ilah prayer. In the north it is chanted at length in a minor key. Four breaks divide it, each marked by the plea, "For all these, O God of forgiveness, forgive us."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alt-breisach-13: Alt-Breisach is an old walled city in Baden, Germany. The entry recalls a time of horror there. In the years 1348-51 the Black Death swept the world. Jews of the city were blamed for the plague. The false charge said they had poisoned the wells. A fearful slaughter of Jews took place. The entry gives counts for the year 1900. The town held 3,000 souls in all. About 450 of them were Jews. It lists fifteen funds for good works in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-david-wer: David Werner Amram was an American lawyer in Philadelphia. He was born in that city in 1866. He took his schooling at the town schools there. He then took law and arts degrees at Penn. He held more than one post in Jewish town life. He led the Young Men's Hebrew Association of the city. He sat on the board of the Jewish Publication body. His chief book treats Jewish divorce law. It came out in Philadelphia in 1896. He wrote verse and short pieces as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angouleme-1528: Angouleme is a town in the Charente department of France. The entry records that about 1240 a dispute took place there between Nathan ben Joseph Official and the town's bishop. It also recalls harm done to the local Jews. In a letter to the bishops of Angouleme, Pope Gregory IX, who held office in 1227-41, voiced deep displeasure. His complaint was aimed at Crusader attacks on the Jews of that place. The entry is short and rests on Gross's Gallia Judaica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apamea-1628:
Apamea is a name borne by many towns, and the entry picks out those that matter for Jewish history. The first is the capital of the Syrian province of Apamene, on the Orontes south of Antioch. Like other Syrian cities, it likely held a large Jewish population, though no settlement records survive.

Josephus tells that Antipater sent his sons with soldiers to Apamea to aid Julius Caesar in a tight spot. Rabbis counted Syria, and Apamea above all, as in some degree part of Palestine. They even matched the city to Shepham, named in Numbers as a border town, on the likeness of the names. That likeness, the entry warns, bred many errors, since the word could also mean Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artaxerxes-ii-1:
Artaxerxes II, first named Arsakes and called Mnemon by the Greeks, was the eldest son of Darius II. He succeeded his father in 404 B.C. and reigned until 359, a span of 46 years. The entry grants him a noble temper and personal bravery, yet calls him weak in character. His mother Parysatis ruled him and favored her younger son Cyrus, whose revolt ended with his death at Cunaxa in 401 B.C.

Rebellion marked the reign. Egypt broke away at once and stayed free, and satraps rose across Asia Minor and Syria, while Palestine under its high priests kept clear. Greek quarrels still let him impose his will on Greece. The Peace of the King in 387 B.C. set his terms as law for the Greek states for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-jacob-abr:
Jacob Abraham ben Aryeh Loeb Kalmankes Asher was a cabalistic and rabbinical author. He was born probably at Lemberg at the start of the seventeenth century and died there on April 3, 1681. His Sefer ha-Eshel, The Book of the Grove, is a volume of sermons. Its first part, on Genesis, was printed at Lublin and also holds remarks by his grandfather, Joseph Kalmankes.

His second work opens the door to the Cabala. Ma'yan ha-Hokmah, Fountain of Wisdom, draws chiefly on the writings of Isaac Luria. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1652, at Koretz in 1684, and at Berlin in 1706 under a new title, Tob we-Yashar, Good and Right. Moses ibn Zur turned it into rhymed prose, but that version was never published.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assaban-mordeca: Mordecai Assaban was a rabbi and author, born in Morocco in 1700. He died at Aleppo about 1760. He served as chief rabbi of Leghorn, in Italy. About 1729 he emigrated to Jerusalem, where he lived for thirty years. He wrote a confession of sins, a Widdui, titled Zobeah Todah. The entry also records that he was famed as a cabalist. Its source is Azulai's Shem ha-Gedolim, and it gives no works beyond the confession.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-samuel:
Samuel b. David Tebele Auerbach was a cabalistic writer on the Bible. He worked in the seventeenth century. His father David died a martyr in the persecution of Polish Jews. Samuel himself barely escaped the same fate, at Lublin on Oct. 16, 1655, and again at Reisen, near Lissa.

His book "Ḥesed Shemo El" was published at Amsterdam in 1699. It gives midrashic and cabalistic readings of Genesis. The entry judges those readings worthless in themselves. But it prizes the book's scattered reports of the persecutions of 1648 and 1655, since Samuel saw those events with his own eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azrikam-2228: Azrikam is the name of four men in the Bible, and this entry sorts them out. One was an ancestor of a Levite living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. One was a son of Neariah, in the list of David's line. One was a son of Azel, in the family list of Benjamin, traced back to Saul. The fourth was governor of the palace under Ahaz, king of Judah. Zichri, a warrior of Ephraim, killed him in a raid, as the second book of Chronicles tells.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-asher-2328: Asher Baer was a Russian mathematician and engraver, born at Seiny in the first quarter of the nineteenth century. He died at Jerusalem in 1897. The entry credits him with key finds in mathematics and in mechanics, set out in a Königsberg paper in 1859. One was a way for one force to drive two equal cog-wheels so their motions fit each other. His engravings won a prize at Königsberg in 1858. In the later 1860s he moved to Jerusalem and wrote for Hebrew papers for many years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamberger-ludwi:
Ludwig Bamberger was a German deputy and writer on political economy, born in Mayence on July 22, 1823. He died in Berlin on March 14, 1899. He studied law at Giessen, Heidelberg, and Göttingen and practiced at Mayence. The revolution of 1848 swept him in as editor and volunteer. Condemned to death by the Bavarian authorities, he fled abroad and settled in Paris in 1853 as manager of a banking firm.

An amnesty in 1866 let Bamberger go home, and in 1871 he entered the first German Reichstag. He led among the National Liberals and shaped money laws, backing the gold standard and free trade. When Bismarck turned to protection in 1879, Bamberger broke with his party and formed a secession group in 1880. Bismarck had used his pen and his knowledge of France in 1870. The entry closes with his many books on currency and socialism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barkany-marie-2: Marie Barkany, an Austrian actress, was born at Kaschau, Hungary, on March 2, 1862. Sent to Vienna to learn bookkeeping, she studied for the stage instead. Laroche and Sonnenthal won her an engagement at Frankfort, where at fifteen she made her début as Adrienne Lecouvreur. After two years under Barnay she went to Hamburg in 1880, then to Berlin's Hoftheater. Tours took her to Moscow, Dresden, New York (1892), and St. Petersburg, where she played Sarah Bernhardt's rôles in deliberate challenge and kept her standing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basket-tax-2628:
Basket-Tax was a special tax laid on the Jews of Russia, set by an edict of Dec. 31, 1844. The entry calls it the most burdensome of those taxes. Its general part fell on kosher meat, on each head of cattle and fowl killed, and on each pound sold.

An added part came from trade licenses, inherited money, and even old style dress such as caftans and skull-caps. The tax was farmed out to high bidders, which bred abuse. Part of the income paid for Jewish schools and farm colonies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bedikah-examina:
Bedikah is a term in Talmud and ritual codes for the strict checking that settles whether a person or thing is fit under rabbinic law. The entry works through the main cases one by one, with rules drawn from codes old and new.

First comes checking the slaughter knife before and after use, then checking the cut parts of the animal. Lung flaws that bar the meat get a long list, from dry tissue to blisters and bad color. Later parts treat checks tied to leaven before Passover and to other points of ritual fitness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bells-2828:
Bells for summoning seem to have begun in the Far East and reached lands near the Mediterranean only in late Roman times. Small disks hung on pets made a sound thought to scare off evil spirits. Hebrew use of bells starts with dress, not calls.

Gold bells hung with pomegranates on the hem of the high priest's robe in Exodus, so he could be heard entering the holy place. Rabbis counted seventy-two of them. In Talmud days bells did serve to summon people. The entry also covers cattle bells, doorbells, and a hard verse in Zechariah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedict-moses-: Moses Benedict, a German banker and artist, was born in 1772 at Stuttgart and died there on July 8, 1852. He was first meant to become a sculptor. With his brother he entered the Karlsschule in Stuttgart in 1785. Later the two brothers ran the banking firm of Benedict Brothers together. Moses still showed real talent for art, and he was noted in particular for painting miniatures. He kept a long friendship and letter exchange with the painter Christian Gottlieb Schick.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berakot-blessin:
Berakot is the name of the first treatise of the first Order of the Talmud. The word names a form of prayer that opens with the words Blessed art thou, O Lord. The treatise holds Mishnah and Gemara, the latter in both Babylonian and Palestinian forms.

Its nine chapters take up the Shema, prayer, and blessings in turn. Early chapters fix the times for reading the Shema and the need for intent. Later ones cover grace at meals and disputes between the schools of Shammai and Hillel. The Gemara then widens each point with long discussion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernheim-ernst-:
Ernst Bernheim, a German historian, was born at Hamburg on Feb. 19, 1850. He studied at Berlin, Heidelberg, Strasburg, and Göttingen, taking his degree at Strasburg. His thesis on Lothar the Third and the Worms Concordat, printed in 1874, won instant respect as far more than a routine doctor's piece.

At Göttingen he wrote a second study of that concordat from fresh sources, fixing his place among German historians. He also helped edit the records of the German diets under Ruprecht. A call to Greifswald came in 1883, and his textbook on historical method appeared at Leipsic in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bethulia-b-b-b-: Bethulia was the city besieged by Holofernes. So the Book of Judith tells the story. Judith was its heroine and resident. A shorter version makes Jerusalem the besieged city. So the entry treats the name as allegorical. It may mean house of God, or Yhwh's virgin. The longer version sets the city south of Jezreel. No trace of the name survives there. Scholars have proposed several candidate sites. They include Mataliye, Sânûr, and El-Bared. None fits all the story's details.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bischoffsheim-r:
Raphael Jonathan Bischoffsheim was a Belgian financier and philanthropist. He was born at Mayence in 1808. He died at Brussels on February 6, 1883. Young, he left home for Belgium. He opened banks at Antwerp and Brussels. Both succeeded rapidly. He helped found the Union du Crédit in 1848.

He saved the National Bank from failure in 1841. The Cross of the Order of Leopold rewarded him. He sat twenty years in Belgium's Senate. He founded schools for girls and lecture courses for women. He also served the Central Consistory for years. Brussels renamed his boulevard after him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenfeld-igna: Ignatz Blumenfeld was an Austrian publisher and merchant. He was born at Brody on March 25, 1812. He died at Geneva on October 2, 1890. Wealth let him champion new Hebrew literature. In Italy he met Luzzatto and Reggio. Both became his literary correspondents. He lived in Odessa through the 1840s. Vienna held him until 1885. His "Oẓar Neḥmad" ran four volumes. It gathered literary letters on Judaism's science. Vienna published it from 1856 to 1863. Average Hebrew scholars could now read them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandeis-baruch: Baruch Judah ha-Levi Brandeis was a Bohemian rabbi and author at Prague. He lived in the second half of the eighteenth century and the start of the nineteenth. He served as assistant rabbi, or dayyan, in that city. His father Bezaleel was rabbi in Jung-Bunzlau, and Baruch printed his father's book. His own Leshon Hakamim, printed in 1815, guides the reading of the Torah, mourning, and burial. The entry calls that book incomplete and hard to read.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-broda-benjamin-: Benjamin b. Aaron Broda was a Lithuanian rabbi and Talmudist. He died on Sept. 1, 1818, at Grodno. Wealth and descent won him that city's rabbinate in 1791. The king himself signed his letters of appointment, the entry says. Many members had backed a rival, the late rabbi's son. The quarrel ran almost to the end of Broda's tenure there. At his death the community voted to leave the chief rabbinate empty for ever. That drastic step aimed to stop such fights from returning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bunzlau-bumslo-: Meir Bunzlau, son of Ephraim Fishel, was a Bohemian rabbi and Talmudist born at Bunzlau. For forty years he served at Prague as head of the rabbinical court and director of a Talmudic academy. He died there on Nov. 23, 1770. None of his works reached print. Fire destroyed all his manuscripts in 1754. His tombstone speaks of the deep love his age felt for him. He also studied Cabala and secular sciences and was famed as a preacher. One ruling by him on a first born animal survives in Ezekiel Landau's collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castellon-de-la: Castellon de la Plana is a city of Valencia, in Spain. In 1320 its Jews gained leave to lay out a cemetery. In 1432 they gained leave to build a new synagogue. In 1391, unlike most Spanish cities, Castellon's magistrates shielded Jews from violence. In 1459 thirty-one Jewish families lived there. When Jews were forced to leave in 1492, the city council demanded payment for the tax income the city would lose by their going.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ccilius-of-cala:
Cæcilius of Calacte was a rhetorician, critic, and historian of the first century B.C. Calacte was a town on the north coast of Sicily. He was the first Jew noted for literary work at Rome. Born a slave and named Archagathus, he took the name Cæcilius as a freedman. Suidas states that he was a Jew, a claim now generally accepted.

With his friend Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Cæcilius championed the Attic style of oratory against the wordy Asiatic style. Two of his works attack that rival school by name. His most telling work treats the traits of the ten Attic orators. In it he drew portraits from old documents and other sources. He fixed the dates of speeches and exposed many speeches passed off under false names. Those studies stayed a lasting source on the ten orators.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-champagne-4228:
Champagne is a former province of France, now split among several departments. Jews settled there as early as the Gallo-Roman age. They lived under the protection of the counts, and that protection cost dearly. Heavy taxes at times drove Jews to flee. Counts then made treaties with neighbors to get their Jews back.

One such treaty was made in 1198 and renewed in 1201. In 1284 Champagne passed into the kingdom of France. Philip the Fair laid a payment of 25,000 livres on its Jews as a gift for the happy event. The province won fame in the twelfth century for Talmudical schools at Troyes, Ramerupt, and Dampierre. Rashi and Jacob Tam both came from Champagne. Its religious customs are often cited in ritual law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-moritz-pse: Moritz Cohn, an Austrian writer who signed himself Conimor, was born at Kreuzburg, Silesia, on Jan. 8, 1844. Schooled at Brieg, he started as a clerk in a merchant's office. He wrote in his spare time. When some of his plays found success, he dropped trade for good. He settled at Vienna in 1875 as an author. The entry lists nine works, nearly all dramas. They run from Der Improvisator in 1874 to Der Beste Gegner in 1892. One satirical poem on Vienna and one novel also appear. He fed the press steadily as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crane-4728: Crane is a rendering in the Authorized Version of a Hebrew word that the Revised Version gives more rightly as swallow. In two other verses, though, crane is the right rendering. Isaiah pictures the bird as one that chatters. Jeremiah points out its habit of migration. The bird meant is now identified as Grus communis. It spends the summer in Palestine in large numbers and winters in northern Africa. The entry calls it the largest bird now found in Palestine, often four feet long.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cyrus-persian-k:
Cyrus was the founder of the Persian empire. Persian tradition wrapped his birth in myth, and Herodotus found four stories of his origin current. One told that he was exposed as a child and suckled by a she dog. Herodotus rejected that tale. A plainer version turned the dog into a shepherdess named Spako. The entry sorts these legends before turning to records.

The crash of Babylon came in 539, the article then shows. King Nabonid, raised to the throne in 556-55, had never held it securely. He kept away from Babylon and leaned on rural towns and their gods. Annals and inscriptions guide this part. For Jewish readers the stakes are clear: Cyrus is the king whose rise ended the Babylonian exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-abrah: David ben Abraham ha-Laban was a French religious philosopher and cabalist who lived after 1200. His grandfather Judah was rabbi of Coucy-le-Château. David wrote "Masoret ha-Berit" (The Bond of the Covenant), a work on the existence, unity, and attributes of God, and also on creation and its purpose. The entry notes that the book survives in several manuscript copies at Paris, which shows that it was much read in its time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deborah-the-son:
Song of Deborah is the triumphal ode in Judges chapter 5, verses 2 to 31, ascribed to Deborah. It celebrates the victory over Sisera in the plain of Megiddo. The entry ranks it among the early poems of the Hebrews and among the masterpieces of world poetry, though its text has corrupt spots and resists regular meter.

The poem opens with God marching from Seir. It then recalls Israel's disorder before Deborah arose. The middle part tells the march to battle and praises the tribes that came, while blaming Reuben, Dan, and Asher for staying away. The close tells of Sisera's death and of his mother waiting in vain for his return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-detmold-johann-:
Johann Hermann Detmold was a German diplomat born at Hanover on July 24, 1807. His father, the court physician there, joined the Christian Church with his whole family. Detmold studied at Göttingen and Heidelberg, then practiced law at Hanover from 1830. He entered the Hanoverian Diet in 1838 as a Conservative and was briefly jailed for attacking the government.

In 1848 Detmold sat in the German Parliament at Frankfort with the deputies of the Right. He became secretary of justice, then of the interior, in the short-lived German government. After 1849 he represented Hanover at Frankfort until 1851. His last years, spent at Hanover, went largely to the arts. He died there on March 17, 1856.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-disraeli-benjam:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, was an English statesman born at London on Dec. 21, 1804. He came from a wealthy Sephardic family of Venice. Baptized in 1817, he trained briefly in law offices and at Lincoln's Inn. He died at London on April 19, 1881.

Fame came first from novels, starting with Vivian Grey when he was twenty-two. Travel in the East, including Jerusalem, shaped his later book Tancred and his pro-Turkish policy. After failed contests he entered Parliament for Maidstone in 1837. He rebuilt the Conservative party, served as chancellor of the exchequer in 1852, and led his party until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-driver-samuel-r:
Samuel Rolles Driver was an English Christian Hebraist born at Southampton on Oct. 2, 1846. Since 1883 he had been regius professor of Hebrew at Oxford, after Pusey. He was also a canon of Christ Church. From 1876 to 1884 he sat on the Old Testament Revision Company.

With Cheyne and Robertson Smith, Driver championed biblical criticism in England. He came at it from language study. His 1874 treatise on the tenses in Hebrew stayed the fullest account of its subject. The entry stresses his conservative, moderate stance in criticism. His Introduction is called the standard English work on Old Testament literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eden-garden-of-:
The Garden of Eden is the earthly paradise where Adam and Eve lived before their fall. Genesis says God planted the garden eastward, in Eden. The word Eden may be an Assyrian loan. Its root is tied to a word for field or plain.

Where Eden stood has drawn endless guesses. Old tradition, from Josephus on, set its rivers in India and Ethiopia. A popular theory places it in Babylonia, in a lush land called the garden of Duniash. Delitzsch argued for that same region. Talmudic voices offer other doors to paradise, at Beth-Shean, in Arabia, or between the rivers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-azari:
Eleazar ben Azariah was a Mishnaic scholar of the first century C.E. His line ran back ten generations to Ezra. He was rich as well as learned, and both facts won him honor. When Gamaliel the Second was set aside as patriarch, the sages chose young Eleazar. He held the post only a short time. Gamaliel soon returned, and Eleazar stayed on as vice-president.

The entry tells of a sea trip to Rome with Gamaliel, Joshua, and Akiba. The party kept the Feast of Booths aboard ship on the way. Eleazar's wealth came from trade in wine, oil, and cattle. Under his rule the academy doors were thrown open to all. Three hundred benches, the entry says, had to be added. The entry also gives his rules of Bible reading. He set one passage beside the next to explain each.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-of-tole: Eliezer of Toledo was a rabbi at Constantinople. He lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. He was a peer of Hiyya Pontremoli in that city. His book bears the title Mishnat de-Rabbi Eliezer. It gathers his rulings on civil law in one volume. The count of those responsa is one hundred and thirty-four. They treat the laws of the Hoshen Mishpat code. Salonica printed the book in 1853. No facts of his life are given beyond his post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emden-5728:
Emden is a Prussian port town in the province of Hanover. No one knows when Jews first settled within its walls. A chronicle of 1581 names Jews there in that age. In 1590 the townsfolk lodged a formal plaint with the crown. They griped that Jews could worship in public there. They griped that Jews wore no badge to mark them out. The royal men sent to judge threw that plaint out. The Jews stayed on in town as they were before.

Later counts of the town took a warmer line. Ulrich the Second kept Jews at his own court. A rabbi once wed a Jewish pair before the whole court. That act stung a strict Lutheran priest in the town. Gluckel of Hameln names rabbis and Jews of Emden in her memoir. In 1744 the town passed to Prussia with East Friesland. The entry tracks town rule from that date on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-erach-from-the-: Erach was a tax on property levied for communal purposes. The entry sets it beside a second direct tax charged to each family. Erach fell on real estate and on movable goods. Its size rested on the owner's sworn statement of what he owned. The entry notes that the word appears in the Memorbuch of Worms. It was also in frequent use in Wurttemberg. No rates, dates, or named taxpayers are given. The entry is a short definition of a local tax term.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ewald-johann-lu:
Johann Ludwig Ewald was a German teacher, theologian, and defender of the Jews, born September 16, 1747. He died at Carlsruhe on March 19, 1822. He served as preacher and professor, ending as a government counselor in Baden. After the Congress of Vienna, Jewish affairs drew the eyes of German statesmen, and Ewald took a close interest.

Two pamphlets carry his case, printed in 1816 and 1820 against hostile writers. Jews, he argued, were no worse than others. Their faults came from persecution, and no fair judge could demand reform before granting equal rights. He pointed to Baden, where partial freedom granted in 1809 had already bettered Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finzi-moses-612: Moses Finzi was an Italian lawyer born at Florence in 1830. He studied law at Pisa and was admitted to the bar in 1856. For some years he worked with Mari. In 1900 he got the rabbinical title of maskil. He taught political economy and statistics at a technical institute in Florence. His works include a life of Adriano Mari printed in 1888. He also wrote on Jewish schools and freedom of conscience in 1898, and a short piece on a point of law in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-funes-6428: Funes, a town in Navarre in the district of Olite, got a charter in 1120 with several clauses that curbed its Jews. A Jew owed an oath on a coffin for a bill over five solidos. Notes between Jew and Christian needed a notary of the debtor side faith. Killing a Jew or a Moor cost a fine of 500 solidos. In 1171 Funes Jews gained the same rights as those of Tudela. In the attacks of 1328 many were killed and robbed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gatigno-portugu:
Gatigno is the Spanish name of a family known in the fourteenth century and still living in Turkey. The name likely comes from the old French district of Gatines. Abraham Gatigno, born in Salonica, became its chief rabbi on January 10, 1875. He founded the first modern Jewish school in Salonica. He also wrote a book printed there in 1872.

Earlier kin wrote sermons and legal replies at Salonica in the eighteenth century. Ezra ben Solomon ibn Gatigno, a pupil in Saragossa, wrote a double comment on Ibn Ezra. He split the plain sense from the mystic sense into two books. Both survive in manuscript at Oxford. A Solomon Astruc Gatigno is recalled as a martyr and Bible expositor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gersoni-henry-6:
Henry Gersoni, an American rabbi and journalist born in Wilna, Russia, in 1844, died in New York on June 17, 1897. He trained at the Wilna rabbinical seminary and at St. Petersburg. In 1868 he printed a confession of his turn to the Greek church and his return to Judaism. Senior Sachs backed the truth of his sorrow in a note to that book.

Gersoni reached the United States in 1869 and taught at Temple Emanu-El in New York. He later held pulpits at Atlanta and at Chicago. He rendered Longfellow Excelsior into Hebrew and won a kind letter from the poet. In 1878 he founded a Chicago weekly, The Advance. He also turned Russian tales by Turgenev into English.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottingen-6828:
Göttingen is a German city in Hanover, once the capital of Grubenhagen. Jews settled there by the thirteenth century. A paper of March 1, 1289, let the city take one Jew and his heirs as citizens. A ducal patent protected Göttingen's Jews on March 10, 1348. Yet the Black Death era still brought persecution. Their Jewish schoolhouse was given to the city in 1350.

Later centuries kept the pattern of small numbers and set taxes. Long and short Jews' streets appear in old records. Students of the university borrowed heavily from Jewish lenders. Rules of 1796 then cut the Jewish families allowed in town to three. The entry follows the community into the Westphalian years and beyond.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guggenheimer-ra:
Randolph Guggenheimer was an American lawyer. He was born at Lynchburg, Va., on July 20, 1846. His father grew tobacco in Virginia. In 1865 he moved to New York and studied law at New York University. He graduated in 1869 and built a practice in corporation and real estate law. In 1882 he partnered with Isaac and Samuel Untermyer. Louis Marshall joined in 1893, and the firm took the name "Guggenheimer, Untermyer & Marshall."

From 1887 he served nine years as commissioner of the common schools. He started New York's evening high-school system and its free lectures. He kept German in the school curriculum. In 1897 he was elected president of the municipal council. In that post he acted as mayor during the mayor's absence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggadah-shel-p:
The Haggadah shel Pesaḥ is the ritual book for Passover eve, built on the duty in Exodus xiii. 8 to tell a son what God did in the Exodus. The Mishnah already knows the rite. It quotes R. Gamaliel: one who has not spoken of pesaḥ, maẓẓah, and maror has not done his duty. The son asks, the father teaches, each as the child can grasp.

Oldest parts still in use include the four questions, opening "Mah Nishtannah," and the Hallel psalms. The entry follows the book's growth, its songs, and its printed forms. The first pictured edition came at Prague in 1526. Augsburg and Mantua and Venice types then set the look of Haggadot across Europe, with stock scenes of rabbis, maẓẓot making, and the Exodus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamberger-c-h-7: C. H. Hamberger was a physician in Leipsic who died on March 2, 1847, at an advanced age. He is known here for two works. He turned G. B. de Rossi's historical dictionary of Jewish authors into German, printed at Leipsic in 1839. His "Nordische Götterlehre" came out in 1826 under the pen name H. A. M. Berger. It was reissued as "Nordische Mythologie" under his own name at Zittau in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanau-11228:
Hanau is a town in the province of Hesse-Nassau, Prussia, whose Jews appear in records from the first half of the thirteenth century. Kings repeatedly assigned or pawned the Jews of Hanau and nearby towns, and the community suffered in the persecutions of 1337 and 1349 before being expelled in 1592.

Count Philipp Ludwig II. invited wealthy Jews back in 1603 and let them build a synagogue with a settled legal status. The community kept a cemetery, bakehouse, slaughter-house, hospital, and shelter for the homeless. It numbered 10 persons in 1603, 111 families in 1707, and 657 persons in 1900; in 1903 there were 670 Jews in a total population of 29,846. The town seats the provincial rabbinate of Hanau, covering 40 communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanno-raphael-7: Raphael Hanno was a German writer born in Hanau in 1791 and dead at Heidelberg in 1871. He embraced Christianity and in 1824 became professor of Oriental languages at the University of Heidelberg, a post he held until his death. His books include a Hebrew language manual for schools and academies in two parts (1825-28), a volume of poems (1825), "Das Schloss im Abendroth" (1828), and "Vorrede Meines Vetters" (1828). After his death a selection from his writings appeared at Jena in 1876 under the title "Liebe und Weisheit."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hathach-7328: Hathach was one of the eunuchs in the palace of King Ahasuerus. He waited on Queen Esther in person. When trouble rose, Esther used him to carry her messages to Mordecai. The Book of Esther names him in chapter four, verses five through ten. The entry adds only that the Greek version gives his name in a different form. It is one of the shortest notices in this stretch. No other act or fact about Hathach is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazzan-abraham-:
Abraham ben Judah Hazzan was a cantor at Kremenetz in Volhynia in the sixteenth century. In 1595 he came through a grave illness that ended in a trance. After that he set to work on a tale-based commentary on the Prophets and the Writings. He drew material from his teachers and from classic commentators.

News of a rival book from Cracow made him stop. When he saw that its plan differed from his own, he finished the work in the spring of 1597. He chose not to print it in his lifetime. It came out at Lublin in 1611 or 1612, after his death. Only a few copies are known to survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herz-markus-762:
Markus Herz, born at Berlin on June 17, 1747, was a German physician and philosophy lecturer from a very poor family. Sent toward trade, he left a clerk post at Königsberg to study. He became a pupil of Kant but left for lack of money.

Herz studied medicine at Halle and took his degree in 1774. In Berlin he served the Jewish hospital and began public lectures in 1777. Students and royal family members attended. His home with Henriette became a meeting place for leading Berlin figures. His books treated taste, dizziness, physics, and early burial. He opposed compulsory vaccination in 1801. He died at Berlin on Jan. 19, 1803.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-emil-gus:
Emil Gustav Hirsch, born in Luxemburg on May 22, 1852, was an American rabbi and professor at the University of Chicago. He came to the United States in 1866 with his father Samuel, called to a Philadelphia Reform pulpit. He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1872.

After study at Berlin and Leipsic, Hirsch led congregations at Baltimore and Louisville. From 1880 he served Sinai congregation in Chicago. He edited Jewish papers and backed Sunday as a Jewish Sabbath, though he preached Saturdays too. Since 1892 he held the Chicago chair in rabbinical literature and philosophy. He helped found a manual training school and Jewish charities groups.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-verga-judah:
Judah ibn Verga was a Spanish historian and cabalist of the fifteenth century, born at Seville. He died a martyr at Lisbon. The governor of Andalusia esteemed him. When Jews of Xerez stood accused of moving a convert's body to their cemetery, Judah used a cabalistic writing before the governor to pin the crime on priests.

He worked to keep Marranos and Jews in accord. The Inquisition wanted him to betray the Marranos. He escaped to Lisbon but was seized there and died under torture. His history of Jewish persecutions fed into the Shebet Yehudah. Writings under his name include an arithmetic manual and a tool for finding the sun's meridian, made at Lisbon about 1457.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-institut-zur-fo:
Institut zur Förderung der Israelitischen Literatur was Ludwig Philippson's society for promoting Jewish literature, publishing from Leipsic. Proposed in print on Feb. 12, 1855, it began work on May 1 with twelve hundred subscribers, rising to two thousand within the year and about three thousand at its height. Two thalers a year entitled each member to that year's books.

A committee of Philippson, Adolph Jellinek and Isaac Markus Jost chose the works and paid the authors. Austria banned joining in 1855, and Philippson was expelled from Austrian territory in 1858. In eighteen years the society issued about eighty German works of history, science, poetry, fiction and biography, including volumes of Grätz's history of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaacs-jacob-82:
Jacob Isaacs was an American inventor of the colonial and revolutionary period who died in 1798. He was living at Newport in 1755, and in 1758 he won a law case before the king in council. Ezra Stiles noted him in 1762 as the owner of a brig. His lasting project was a way to draw fresh water out of sea water.

When President Washington visited Newport in 1790, Isaacs gave him a bottle of water drawn from the ocean and freed of salt, fit for common and kitchen use. Washington said he was highly pleased with it. In 1791 Isaacs asked the House of Representatives to buy the rights to his find. The matter went to Thomas Jefferson, whose report spoke well of it. Congress, though, took no action at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-of-kefar-: Jacob of Kefar Hittaya was a Palestinian scholar of the second century, a contemporary of Judah I. The Talmud notes that he used to visit his teacher every single day. The entry is very short. Heilprin, in his chronicle, worked out that Jacob must have been a pupil of Akiba and a teacher of Judah I himself. The entry adds, plainly, that this is not certain. Nothing else about him is recorded here: no saying, no ruling, and no place beyond the village in his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jason-of-cyrene:
Jason of Cyrene was a Jewish historian who wrote a history of the Maccabean revolt in five books, now lost. The writer of Second Maccabees took his facts from Jason and says his own book is a short form of that larger work. The short version covers fifteen years, from the death of Seleucus the Fourth to the win over Nicanor.

Jason likely wrote in Greek, in a rich style still felt in the shorter book, and gathered his facts by word of mouth near the events. The entry judges his lost history one of the finest works of its kind. Even Philo knew only the short form, which soon pushed the full work out of use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-david-88: Joseph David was rabbi of Salonica in the first half of the eighteenth century, a fellow worker of Solomon Amarillo and Joseph Covo I. Azulai calls him Joseph David the Saint and says he was chief rabbi of Salonica. If so, his term fell between those of Amarillo and Covo. He wrote Bet Dawid, legal notes on the four Turim, printed at Salonica in 1740-46. His other books are sermons, a preaching commentary on the Pentateuch with rules for preachers, and notes on Abot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kahn-lehman-912:
Lehman Kahn, a Belgian teacher and writer, was born on Sept. 9, 1827, at Breisach, in Baden, Germany. He trained at schools in Breisach and Carlsruhe and taught in his home country and at the Jewish school of Hegenheim, in Alsace. In 1855 he was called to Brussels as head of the Jewish school there.

In October 1863 Kahn founded L'Institut International Kahn, a school of commerce and modern languages that was still running when the entry was written. His own books deal with mixed marriage, a fight over the closing of Jewish cemeteries in Brussels, and the ties between Romans and Jews up to the fall of Jerusalem. His study of Rome and the Jews won a prize from the Academy of Sciences of Brussels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-karpeles-elieze: Eliezer Karpeles, usually called R. Lazar Karpeles, was an Austrian rabbi. He was born at Prague about 1754. He died on April 27, 1832, at Lieben, near Prague. For nearly forty years he served as district rabbi of Kaurzim. His home was at Lieben all that time. He wrote two books of Talmud notes. The first, printed at Prague in 1801, treats Horayot and parts of Maimonides. The second, from 1815, treats 'Arakin and Ḥullin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kingdom-of-god-:
Kingdom of God means the reign or sovereignty of God. It stands against the kingdoms of the worldly powers. Prophecy and psalms voice the hope that God will be King over all the earth.
