Losing FABP5 shifted key identity genes, weakening the master eye gene PAX6 and one keratin while raising another, and inflammation changed the picture further. The results position FABP5 as one link between the known genetic cause and the failing cornea, a possible handle for future treatment.
plos-pone-0347328:
Alice Plebe asks a simple question with wide consequences: do large language models have a built-in tendency to trust others? Her 2026 paper tested nineteen models in two ways. One used a questionnaire borrowed from human psychology. The other placed models in simulated situations where they had to decide whether to hand a task to someone else.

Every model claimed high trust on the questionnaire, which Plebe links to training that rewards agreeable answers. The simulations told a different story. Stronger models adjusted their choices when given clues about whether a partner was competent, while weaker ones handed over tasks almost blindly. Questionnaires alone, she argues, cannot reveal how these systems will actually behave.
plos-pone-0347428:
Zhiyi Zhang surveyed five hundred fashion design students at eighteen Chinese universities about learning with generative artificial intelligence. The 2026 study asks how different kinds of teacher support shape students' use of these tools, and whether that use builds creative skill and better coursework. Zhang tested the links with a statistical technique that maps chains of cause and effect.

Practical help, both technical and teaching-focused, predicted how much students used the tools, while emotional encouragement showed no direct link. Tool use in turn strengthened creative design ability, which then lifted learning outcomes. Most of the benefit of technical support travelled through this chain. Zhang advises schools to invest in hands-on guidance rather than cheerleading alone.
plos-pone-0347528:
Azrin Shah Abu Bakar and two co-workers asked two hundred state staff in Malaysia what helps them live well with long-term ills. The staff work in the town of Putrajaya. Book facts alone do not change how folk act. So the team weighed facts known, stance, and help from the crowd and the state.

Stance was the key link. It shaped good care on its own. It also passed on the force of facts known, which did not move acts by itself. Help from the crowd and the state lent its own push. The team says plans should work on stance and on crowd help, not just hand out facts.
plos-pone-0347828:
Rebecca H Correia, Andrew P Costa, and co-authors asked whether Ontario family doctors with extra training or a focused practice in elder care actually practice differently from their peers. Older adults depend heavily on family physicians, yet the payoff of added geriatric credentials was unproven. Their 2026 study matched two hundred thirty-two such physicians to more than nine hundred similar doctors and compared eleven accepted quality measures using health system data.

Most measures showed no meaningful difference. The specially trained group did more testing aligned with the national dementia consensus, but also prescribed more potentially inappropriate medicines and antipsychotics to older patients. The authors offer three readings: the training may change little, everyday practice constraints may swamp it, or the measures themselves may be too blunt to catch real differences.
plos-pone-0348028:
Guanxi Chen and Jiajun Chen study how city tourists come to feel like partners in creating their own trip's value, in this 2026 PLOS ONE tourism paper. They distinguish contact with government services from contact with local residents, and ask whether artificial intelligence tools, such as smart guides, change these relationships.

Survey analysis combined with a case-based method showed both kinds of interaction raised tourists' sense of empowerment, and empowerment, in turn, raised their wish to co-create experiences; neither interaction worked directly. AI tools strengthened the government path but not the resident path. Cities chasing engaged visitors, the study suggests, should empower tourists through services while keeping human contact human.
plos-pone-0348128:
Bora Lee, Soojin Im, and Sungho Won questioned whether the usual yardsticks for body weight, smoking, and blood fats sort people by death risk as well as sharper ones could. Loose definitions can mislead studies, so they tested refined measures in two large Korean health cohorts linked to death records, covering hundreds of thousands of people.

Their refinements split obesity by belly fat as well as body mass, scaled smoking exposure against age, and combined several fat ratios instead of single values. In the main analyses, underweight people carried higher death risk across all age groups. The authors argue that tidier definitions change who counts as high risk, which matters for both doctors counseling patients and researchers pooling health data.
plos-pone-0348228:
Important notice first: an earlier version of this study by Md Saiful Islam and three colleagues was retracted by PLOS One. The authors had found an error in their p-value math. Editors concluded that one conclusion, drawn from a large validation dataset, was incorrect. The journal invited this corrected and republished version, which is what this entry holds. The core method was judged sound.

The work itself tackles uncertainty in matching-based policy evaluation. When several matched pairs look equally good, different algorithms can yield different verdicts. The authors propose faster algorithms that test whether a causal conclusion survives all reasonable assignments. They validate the approach on California hospital data. Applied there, the Medicare readmission penalty programme showed no causal link to rises in readmissions at other hospitals. The scalable test lets analysts check big observational studies without prohibitive computing cost.
plos-pone-0348628:
Seokmin Kim and Christopher Searcy led a test of sea travel by plant seeds. Many island plants bear fleshy fruit. Can their seeds float on currents and stay alive? The team picked fourteen such species from Caribbean shores. They timed how long each fruit floats in salt water. They also traced more than a thousand drift buoys to map links between forty-four islands.

Float times ran from zero days to more than ninety. Species that floated longer did live on more islands. The best floater could cross the widest gap in the sea. Yet maps of currents failed to explain which islands hold which plants. Human use of the plants did a better job. The team calls for gene studies next.
plos-pone-0349028:
Corinna Leppin and colleagues fine-tuned the algorithms behind a phone-based quit-smoking coach that is meant to intervene at the exact moment a craving threatens. Thirty-seven quitters answered sixteen short check-ins a day for ten days, reporting mood, setting, cravings, and slips. The team then varied how many check-ins, how many predictors, and whose past data the prediction forests learned from.

Average accuracy was modest and swung wildly between people, with many setups falling below accepted minimums. Predicting actual slips worked better than predicting cravings. Fewer check-ins oddly improved slip prediction on one score while hurting craving prediction across the board, and trimming predictors cost almost nothing for slips. The authors say designers must balance nagging users against accuracy outcome by outcome, not chase a single setting.
plos-pone-0349128:
Riya Mukherjee and Chung-Ming Chang lined up a quarter century of osteoarthritis burden against the research world's response, asking whether science and translation keep pace with need. Osteoarthritis is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Their 2026 analysis merged global burden estimates from 1999 to 2023 with yearly counts of publications, experimental models, clinical trials, and funding drawn from major databases.

Disability from the disease roughly doubled while publication volume more than quadrupled, growing faster than burden. Trial starts, though, peaked in the late two thousands and have since declined, remaining a small slice of all papers. Human-relevant experimental work held a modest, steady share. The authors conclude the field publishes abundantly but translates thinly, and they frame the mismatch as a planning problem for funders.
plos-pone-0349328: Deuber and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for the REVELIO pilot trial, run on a test track. Healthy adults who use cannabis for leisure will drive on a closed track in a planned trial. Sensors in the car will try to detect cannabis-impaired driving in real time. The single-centre trial uses random assignment and a control group. Roadside tools of this kind are a live policy question where cannabis is legal.
plos-pone-0349828:
Tran Le Hong Ngoc and colleagues tested a metal printing method that lays wire along part edges to focus heat where it helps most. Edge guided paths narrow heat damage and ease leftover stress versus standard wire arc printing. Printed steel samples were bent under standard tests, and a neural network learned to predict stress curves from process settings.

Best printed samples more than doubled the bend strength of plain base steel and beat typical standard prints, with far better strength per weight. Layer thickness mattered most among settings. The method even formed inner spiral channels while keeping heat controlled. Strong, light printed parts suit repair and custom metal work.
plos-pone-0350128:
Rana Muhammad Zahid Mushtaq and co-authors surveyed pharmacists across Pakistan about what keeps them well at work. Pharmacists carry heavy responsibility in stressful settings, and their well-being guards patient safety. Their 2026 study questioned five hundred sixty-four licensed pharmacists about job demands and control, how strongly they identified with their work, how they reshaped their own jobs, and their overall psychological well-being.

Job content itself showed no direct tie to well-being. Instead, two middle steps carried the effect: pharmacists who identified with their work, and those who actively crafted their jobs, reported better well-being. A chained path ran from job content through identity and crafting to well-being. The authors advise caution given some model limits, but suggest building professional identity and room to reshape tasks as practical levers.
plos-pone-0350328:
Yange Chen and co-authors adapted a light object detection model for finding key traffic elements in messy road scenes in 2026. Self driving and traffic systems miss small or partly hidden signs and vehicles, and heavy detectors are too slow for the roadside.

Their version of a compact detection family adds flexible convolution for odd shapes, a slimmer feature merging neck, and an attention step that mutes background clutter. On a road data set it missed far fewer objects and scored higher overall, while staying small and fast. Fewer missed road elements is a direct safety gain, not just a benchmark gain.
plos-pone-0350628:
Nosayba Al-Damook and colleagues mapped how lung and breast cancers rewire their fuel use in 2026. Tumors feed growth by changing metabolism, but each cancer type does so differently, and treatments rarely exploit those quirks.

Combining several public databases, the team compared three lung and breast cancer groups and a set of spread breast tumors. One lung type leaned on sugar burning, another mixed two routes, breast tumors favored building fats, and spread tumors stressed defense and recycling. Known drugs already touch some of the genes involved. The map points drug hunters toward weak spots specific to each cancer.
plos-pone-0350728:
Elisa Liberati and a team including senior psychiatrists describe a protocol for studying how MDMA works in therapy by giving it, carefully, to psychotherapists themselves. MDMA-assisted therapy shows strong trial results for post-traumatic stress, but its psychological mechanism is untheorized: trials measure brains and symptoms, not the felt, relational process. About twenty-five experienced psychoanalytic therapists will take two supervised doses and be interviewed before, during, and long after.

The interviews follow a phenomenological method, pressing on the texture of the experience and on how trained clinicians afterward understand what the drug does in a therapeutic relationship. As a protocol it reports no findings. The bet is that expert witnesses, people who both undergo the state and hold a theory of mind, can name mechanisms that symptom scales walk past.
plos-pone-0350828:
María Heredia-Torrejón and colleagues present a laboratory protocol for growing fibroblast cells from a skin sample the size of a pinhead, designed for children. Skin cells power research into genetic disease, but standard biopsies need stitches, anesthesia by injection, and wound care, a heavy ask of a child. Their method shrinks the punch to one millimeter across and simplifies every step around ordinary cell culture equipment.

Even from that speck of tissue, the team reports, primary fibroblast cultures establish reliably, and no complications have been reported so far. A smaller wound means less fear, no sutures, and samples that clinics can take during ordinary visits. For pediatric biobanks and rare-disease studies, where every donor family weighs burden against benefit, a near-painless protocol can be the difference between a sample and a refusal.
plos-pone-0350928:
Yang Yang, Bochun Lu, and Shimeng Wang surveyed more than a thousand Chinese college students in 2026 on exercise and coping with crisis. They asked whether moving more links to steadier coping, and whether looping negative thoughts and emotion habits carry that link.

Students reported activity, crisis coping styles, rumination, and two ways of handling feelings: reshaping thoughts and bottling expression. Activity tied to both healthy and unhealthy coping. Paths through rumination and emotion habits, including a chain of the two, helped explain the pattern. Campus programs, the authors suggest, should pair exercise with skills for handling thoughts and feelings, not treat sweat alone as the cure.
plos-pone-0351128:
Carlos Rivera and colleagues linked lab style sprint tests with match tracking in fourteen elite female field hockey players. Players ran six thirty metre sprints with short rests, while satellite trackers logged four top level matches within three weeks. Sprint speed, step rate, and step length were set beside match sprinting and high speed running loads.

Sprint speed in tests tracked match sprint distance, sprint pace, high speed running, and hard accelerations very strongly. Step rate also tracked those match loads, including top acceleration. Step length tracked nothing clearly. Coaches can read match readiness from simple repeated sprint speed and step rate tests, without waiting for match data.
plos-pone-0351328:
Bradley A Sheffield and co-authors mine a huge United States health record network for patients with progressive lung scarring who never receive the diagnosis code. The condition worsens steadily and anti-scarring drugs can slow it, yet coded prevalence looked far below earlier estimates. The team built three proxy definitions of increasing strictness from related lung diagnoses plus signs of progression, then compared coded and proxy patients on treatment and outcomes.

Coded cases were rare, while even the strictest proxy found many times more likely patients. Anti-scarring drug use was low everywhere, but far lower in proxy groups than in coded patients, who still went untreated most of the time. Sheffield and colleagues argue many Americans with this disease sit unrecognized and untreated inside ordinary records.
plos-pone-0351428:
Jianguang Song and five colleagues build a hybrid forecasting system for electricity demand in this 2026 study. Accurate load forecasts keep power grids stable and cheap to run. Demand curves are knotted and nonlinear, and standard optimisers get stuck in local traps. The team combined three deep learning networks that read time patterns differently. Their outputs were merged by weight. An improved parrot-inspired optimisation algorithm then tuned the system, with an error-correction step on top.

The combined model converged far faster than gradient descent training. It reached strong accuracy in about two hundred rounds, where the standard route needed well over three hundred. Final accuracy was higher too. On a British distribution network dataset, its long-term forecast errors were the lowest among rival methods. Extra machinery guarded against drifting weights and short-term bias. Grid operators gain a forecaster that learns quickly and stays honest over long horizons.
plos-pone-0351628:
Emmanuel Ahene and a large Ghanaian team built a solar-powered, camera-watching fish farm system meant to free small producers from grid power and constant manual checking. Fish farming in controlled ponds promises protein with less waste, but labor, electricity costs, and missed water problems kill margins and fish. Their system watches behavior and water, manages feeding and waste, and runs on sunlight, with learning software reading the camera feed.

Development ran from architecture to a complete working build, trained on custom video and sensor datasets from real ponds. Computer vision flags abnormal behavior and water trouble in real time, the events a farmer otherwise discovers too late. For regions where the grid is dear or unreliable, an autonomous, solar fish attendant is not a gadget but a route to making green aquaculture pay.
plos-pone-0352028:
Eugene Lee and Youngjoo Chae measured a gap that quietly drives returns in online clothing sales. A fabric feels one way in the hand. It looks another way on a screen. The team made plain and twill weaves at varied densities, weights, and thicknesses. True roughness came from atomic-level surface scans. Screen roughness came from the product images shoppers actually see.

Weave build decided the size of the gap. In plain weaves, a looser weft with a tighter warp photographed most honestly. In twills, heavier cloth with a looser weft did best. These are knobs a mill or a photo studio can turn. Teaching a flat image to tell the truth about touch has real value. It cuts returns, waste, and let-down at the door.
plos-pone-0352328:
Olivier Toubia and Jonah Berger argue that creative thinking depends not just on which ideas a person finds, but on the order in which the ideas arrive. Wandering far through memory wastes effort; moving in a tidy sequence may not. They built a short test that asks people to link concepts and scores how direct their path is, a quality they call circuitousness when it goes wrong.

Across five validation studies, people's path scores predicted creative performance better than older measures alone, and added information those measures missed. A straighter sequence through related ideas went with stronger creative work. If the test holds up, teachers and employers could spot creative thinkers with a quick exercise. The authors also note where the scoring tools still need sharpening before wide use.
plos-pone-0352428:
Arturo Octavio Gonzales-Rodriguez and co-authors examined whether the bacteria in a mother's breastmilk relate to her baby's anemia. Anemia is a widespread problem in rural Peru. Their 2026 study recruited forty-six mother and child pairs in the coastal town of Talara. It sequenced the bacterial DNA in milk samples. The children were grouped as healthy, iron-deficient anemic, or anemic for other reasons.

Two bacterial genera dominated nearly all samples. Milk from mothers of children with non-iron anemia carried a richer mix of bacteria. Milk tied to iron-deficiency anemia held more of a few genera, including Corynebacterium and Acinetobacter. It held somewhat fewer Streptococcus. The authors treat these patterns as early clues, not proof. They call for larger studies of how milk microbes and infant iron interact.
plos-pone-0353128:
Erika Yawata and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One hospital study of accidental hypothermia. In such patients, blood tests and scans often look like pancreas inflammation. The team reviewed nearly one hundred seventy cases at a Japanese critical care center. The cases spanned more than a decade. They asked when such findings truly matter. They also asked what blood level should prompt a detailed scan.

About one in five patients had raised pancreatic enzyme levels. Almost all patients with pancreas-like scan findings were in that group. The authors name an enzyme level above which scanning is worth weighing. A raised level alone, though, predicted scan findings poorly. Happily, no patient developed severe pancreas damage. None needed invasive care. Most recovered well with fluids and feeding support.
plos-pone-0353228:
Sen Yang and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study comparing muscle strength in young men with and without obesity. Seventy-five university students, split between normal weight and obese groups, completed grip tests, maximal lifts, and machine-based strength tests at four joints. All measures were scaled to body weight, the fairest way to ask how much strength each person carries per unit of load.

By that measure the obese group was weaker on every single test, a pattern the authors call a strength-to-load imbalance. A variable-selection technique picked five predictors of grip strength, including several elbow and shoulder measures, and group membership itself remained a predictor even after joint strength was counted. The authors suggest grip strength could serve as a quick screen of overall muscle function in this population, pending larger studies.
plos-pone-0353528:
Yilmazer and colleagues tested vineyard fungicides on cabbage white butterflies in a 2026 study. Fungicides are sprayed often and assumed gentle on insects, yet proof is thin. Caterpillars met three common sprays either by eating treated leaves or by direct contact, and survival plus development were tracked.

Eating treated leaves did not raise deaths, though sulphur sprays lengthened the pupal stage and another spray shortened early growth. Direct contact caused clearer harm. Risk thus depends on how the insect meets the spray, not only on the chemical. Timing sprays to avoid direct hits on caterpillars could cut the hidden cost to helpful and harmless insects.
plos-pone-0353728:
Yinjie Huang and three colleagues published this 2026 machine learning paper on data that arrives as an endless stream. Such streams shift over time, and rare classes get swamped by common ones, so a fixed model quickly goes stale. Their design adds a reshaping layer to an online learning machine, plus a forgetting factor that lets old patterns fade.

A drift alarm based on balanced accuracy watches for change, and several of these learners vote together as an ensemble. Across nine artificial streams and two real ones, the system handled imbalance and shifting patterns better than rivals. Banks, sensors, and hospitals all depend on stream models that stay honest.
plos-pone-0354028:
Madelestin Melhan and colleagues modelled how heavy rain destabilises tropical hillsides in Pagar Alam, South Sumatra. Intense rain soaks near-surface soil, weakening the suction that helps hold slopes together. Their 2026 study used lab-measured soil properties and terrain-based slope shapes, testing both uniform and layered ground under simulated rainfall.

Safety margins fell fast once rain infiltrated. Steeper slopes lost more of their margin than gentler ones. Layered ground generally ended less stable than uniform ground, even though failure shapes looked similar. Melhan and colleagues say slope angle and hidden layering should both feature in local hazard maps, since either one can tip a hillside toward failure during long storms.
plos-pone-0354128:
Joao Manoel Rossi Neto and colleagues studied a tense drug question. It faces people waiting for a heart transplant. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Many such patients survive on a drip of dobutamine. That drug helps the heart pump. Clinicians disagree about also giving beta-blocker pills. The two drugs pull in opposite directions.

The team looked back at fifty-three patients. All had tolerated both drugs for at least a month. Those who stayed on beta-blockers reached transplant far more often. They also died before surgery far less. The sample is small, and the authors urge caution. Still, the results argue for prospective trials.
plos-pone-0354728:
Arafat and colleagues, in a 2026 review, weigh whether blood tests can catch breast cancer early. Finding cancer sooner improves outcomes, but mammograms can miss tumors in dense breasts and can also raise false alarms. Two blood-based signals are candidates: tiny gene regulators called microRNAs, and patterns in blood fats and related chemicals.

The team gathered thirty-two studies with nearly seven thousand people, about half of them cancer cases, and pooled their accuracy figures. On average, the blood tests found most cancers while keeping false alarms moderate, and their combined scores looked strong. Results varied a fair amount between studies, which the authors probed with standard checks for bias and unevenness. They present these blood markers as a promising companion to imaging, not a replacement, and their pooled numbers give future test designers a benchmark to beat.
plos-pone-0354928: Grund, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on an age quirk in pro soccer. In youth sport, children born just after an age cutoff often gain an edge over younger teammates. Grund asks how strong that pattern is in pro football, how it differs from one country to the next, and how it has shifted over time. The work speaks to scouts and coaches who weigh birth dates when judging young talent.
plos-pone-0355228:
Alejandro Vázquez and co-authors test in 2026 whether a scale of psychological adjustment to a new culture works fairly for Latino caregivers in the United States. Caregivers of young people with emotional or behaviour problems answered in English or Spanish. The scale measures belonging and emotional attachment to each culture, and the team checked its structure and consistency.

Scores held together very well and pointed mainly to one overall dimension, though a two part split also appeared with heavy overlap. Crucially, the English and Spanish forms did not line up in the same structure, so comparing scores across languages needs care. The authors support cautious use as a short proxy measure.
plos-pone-0355628:
Kadek Surya Atmaja and co-authors pooled studies on blood sugar control and lung function in type 2 diabetes. The lung is not usually counted among diabetes target organs, yet tissue changes may quietly reduce breathing capacity. Their 2026 meta-analysis compared adults whose long-term sugar marker showed good versus poor control.

People with poor control blew out smaller air volumes on standard breathing tests. Both a one-second measure and a total capacity measure were clearly lower. The ratio between them, though, was slightly higher, which points to smaller lungs rather than blocked airways. Results were consistent across studies. The authors argue breathing checks deserve a place in diabetes care when control stays poor.
plos-pone-0355728:
Cole Baird Brookson and Ariel Greiner ask a blunt money question about coral reef rescue: when does planting new coral actually hold? Planting is popular, but reefs also face local harms such as overfishing and nutrient runoff on top of warming seas. The authors combine a math model of reef growth with records from real planting projects to find when planted coral can sustain thick cover on its own.

Healthy starting reefs with low seaweed and strong baby coral supply needed only modest planting to stay thick. As fishing and nutrient pressure rose, the planting needed grew steeply, past the point of practical use. Brookson and Greiner advise funders to cut local pressure first and plant second, or risk pouring coral into conditions where it cannot last.
plos-pone-0355828:
Qing Huang and colleagues compare in 2026 four Malaysian plant extracts for their power to guard cells against damage from oxidation. After standard lab tests picked the strongest extract, they studied it in nerve like cells and in formed muscle cells. They checked cell survival, damage to DNA, and markers tied to a cleanup process inside cells.

The winning extract came from a plant long used in folk practice, and it cut DNA damage without plainly harming the cells. Markers suggested the cleanup process became more active as dose rose. The authors present it as a candidate for more study, not as a proven treatment.
plos-pone-0356528:
Md Nahidul Alam led a team of five authors building a smart monitoring system for poultry farms, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Small farms in developing countries lose birds to heat stress and disease they cannot see coming. The team's internet-of-things system watches farm conditions in real time and flags trouble early.

Alam's sensors track the environment inside poultry sheds, sending alerts before flocks sicken. Early warning is the difference between treating a shed and losing it. Low cost is central to the design, since small farmers cannot buy pricey gear. The work shows how cheap connected sensors, well aimed, can protect both livelihoods and food supply in places where a lost flock means a lost income.
plos-pone-0356728:
Marianna Graziosi and colleagues report repeated attempts to reproduce three famous findings about awe, the feeling stirred by vast or beautiful scenes. Earlier studies had claimed that awe makes people see hidden purpose, act more generously, and feel better overall. The new team tried video, writing, and virtual reality inductions in online and lab settings, then ran three larger direct repeats of the original tasks.

The claimed effects generally failed to appear, in both the looser attempts and the larger, closer repeats. Graziosi and colleagues discuss whether online tools can stir real awe at all, and they offer guidance for future emotion research. Their report adds to a growing record that some celebrated emotion effects are weaker or less reliable than first claimed.
plos-pone-0357028:
Chenliang Zhao, Jianrong Xiong, and Yongxiang Li measured vitamin D in the blood of 131 hospitalized adults. They compared the readings with each patient's score on a standard fall risk scale. Their 2026 cross-sectional study sorted patients into low, moderate, and high fall risk. It asked which personal factors traveled with the highest-risk category. Most patients fell into that category.

Vitamin D ran lowest in the high-risk group. Each small rise in blood vitamin D came with lower odds of being classed high risk. That held even after accounting for other factors. Older age pushed risk the other way. Sex made no independent difference. Because the study captures one moment, it cannot show deficiency causes falls. The authors call for follow-up studies on whether correcting it helps.
plos-pone-0357628: Liu and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on where drones and air taxis might fly in cities. They used fluid-flow simulation, a method borrowed from wind engineering, to find low-altitude traffic corridors. Air at low height twists around buildings, so safe lanes must respect that flow. Early corridor maps could help cities plan drone routes before the skies get busy.
plos-pone-0357828:
Kyle A. Emery and coauthors published a 2026 ecology study in PLOS ONE on California's Northern Channel Islands, where waves wash seaweed and kelp onto sandy beaches. This washed-up material, called wrack, feeds crowds of small beach invertebrates, whose activity releases carbon dioxide as it rots. The team compared fourteen beaches that differed hugely in wrack cover, measuring the animals present and the gas escaping from the sand at the high-tide line.

Beaches with more wrack held richer, larger invertebrate communities, and carbon dioxide output rose strongly with wrack cover. The animals themselves accounted for about a tenth of beach emissions on average, though their share varied widely from beach to beach, and total consumer respiration differed fifty-fold between sites. Material drifting in from the sea, they conclude, powers this shoreline food web and its carbon processing, a link sea-level rise and coastal building threaten.
plos-pone-0358128:
Yoshiyuki Nishimiya studied gene signals on a plant virus, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Tobacco mosaic virus is a classic lab virus with a well-known RNA genome. Nishimiya used cDNA analysis to detect bacterial gene expression elements carried on that viral RNA.

The work probes how gene-expression signals behave when placed on a viral RNA scaffold. Such basic questions matter for synthetic biology, where viruses are often used as delivery tools or production platforms. Knowing which bacterial signals still function in that setting helps engineers design more reliable systems. The study is small in scope but precise: one virus, one method, and a clear test of whether foreign signals are read as expected.
plos-pone-0358228:
Gang Ren leads a team of six asking why students keep using, or abandon, artificial intelligence learning devices, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gadgets, tablets and robots carrying large language models, win easy first trials. Staying power is the real question. Surveying seven hundred twenty-six first year high school students with device experience, the team modeled how product features feed basic psychological needs, enjoyment, and the intention to continue.

Feeling related, connected through the device, drove enjoyment more strongly than any other link in the model. Warm friendliness in the device's manner showed the largest pull among the product features. Two expected links failed: feeling the device was personalized did not raise students' sense of autonomy, and fast responses did not build relatedness. Altogether the model explained about half of both enjoyment and the wish to continue. Designers are advised to engineer companionship, not just speed and tailoring.
plos-pone-0358428:
Jing Liu and Chaoqun Niu worked in 2026 on the printable silver paste used to draw fine conducting lines on a type of solar cell called TOPCon. The front side lines must be tall and narrow, a high aspect ratio, so they carry current well while shading as little of the cell as possible. The paste's organic vehicle, the liquid mixture that carries the silver particles through printing, largely decides whether those fine lines hold their shape.

The authors engineer that vehicle and study how its properties affect the printed lines. Small printing gains matter at factory scale, where a fraction more sunlight converted means large amounts of extra power across millions of panels. The study sits in the practical engineering that keeps solar costs falling.
plos-pone-0359528: Umar and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a gene family in bread wheat. The genes, called ITPK, help make a signaling compound inside cells. The team searched the whole wheat genome to find every member of the family and then analyzed them. A full census of these genes gives breeders and biologists a map for work on growth and stress tolerance.
plos-pone-0359628:
Muhammad Bilal Riaz, A Zahra, and S A Mardan published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines PSR J0952–0607, a massive pulsar, a spinning neutron star heavier than most of its kind. The authors test the star's physical viability within a polytropic framework, a mathematical model of how pressure and density relate inside it.

Neutron stars pack more than the Sun's mass into a city-sized ball, and models must show such an object can exist without collapsing. Checking a record-heavy pulsar against a framework helps physicists judge which equations of matter are believable. Astrophysicists studying dense matter are the readers for this test.
plos-pone-0359728: Chang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on teamwork inside a semi-closed chat network. In urgent moments, knowledge sits with scattered experts who must be reached fast. The study examines how that know-how gets coordinated so it can be used in time. The lessons apply to crisis teams, hospitals, and firms where the right expert is online but hard to mobilize.
pmc-10652528:
Xue Jia and co-authors published this medical education study in 2023. Chinese medical schools grant two kinds of postgraduate degrees: professional degrees aimed at clinical practice and academic degrees aimed at research. The team surveyed students at one major medical school in 2020 with a 29-item questionnaire about the curriculum, its content, and how classes are run. Of 908 students, 645 responded.

The two groups wanted different things. Professional-degree students prized specialized knowledge and clinical skills, and they complained about too many required courses and too few electives. They also felt the curriculum clashed with clinical work and questioned class attendance rules. Academic-degree students instead flagged thin interdisciplinary content and repeated material, and they rated the curriculum's importance higher. The authors offer the results as a baseline for reforming postgraduate medical courses in China.
pmc-10653428:
Xijuan Niu and co-authors propose a robust way to estimate averages for small areas when some data points are outliers, in a statistics paper from 2023. Small area methods borrow strength across regions to estimate local means from survey data. The standard Bayesian method works best under tidy assumptions and breaks down when odd values appear.

Their method rests on a divergence measure that downweights outliers. They give the estimation equations, the large-sample behavior of the estimates, and a rule for picking the tuning value. Predictors for unit and area means follow, with error measured by resampling. Simulations and real data showed the robust method handled outlier cases better than the standard one. The work guards small area studies against a few bad points.
pmc-10656528:
Yardfon Tanongkankit and co-authors study freeze-dried coconut water in a 2023 food science paper. Drying coconut water into powder makes it easy to store and ship. Coating agents can protect its scent and quality during that drying. The team tried three agents at several strengths. Two kinds of freezer prepared the samples before drying. They then measured scent compounds, moisture, and other traits of the powders.

Freezing time did not change the moisture or water activity of the final powder. The choice of coating agent was the main factor shaping scent. A sugar-like agent at the highest strength gave the best result. The dried product kept a mix of esters and other scent notes. The authors say the right coating improves the aroma of dried coconut water. Their recipe offers a base for a shelf-stable coconut drink powder.
pmc-10657428:
Zhong and a large team of colleagues train a deep net to flag hid lung node spread from scans in this twenty twenty-three study. Hid spread to chest nodes shapes the whole cure plan for lung cancer. Scans that claim a clean chest can still miss small spread in some cases.

Inside, near two thousand cases built the net's grade mark from paired scan types. Fresh sets from a second ward and a planned ward run then graded it in full. The paired-scan net beat lone-scan nets, a trait-based grade, and ward eyes by clear gaps. Its marks held firm for both near and far node spread calls. The team says the net could guide cure picks when scans look clean.
pmc-10667628:
Lawrence P Wackett compiles an annotated guide to websites about plasmids in environmental microbes. The 2023 guide serves readers of an environmental microbiology venue who want curated entry points rather than raw search results. Plasmids, small DNA circles that move between bacteria, shape traits from resistance to pollutant breakdown.

Each entry pairs a link with a short note on what the resource offers. One highlighted study surveys plasmids broadly across environments, noting that famous traits like antibiotic resistance cover only a small share of plasmid genes. Others cover how communities affect plasmid transfer, a vendor catalog of plasmids for one bacterial genus, and an opinion piece on how plasmids may steer their hosts. A blog entry explains selection methods used in cloning. The guide is a starting shelf, not a research report.
pmc-10687028:
Kazuki Aoyama and co-authors set out the protocol for a trial of telemedicine in pregnancy diabetes, in work published in 2023. Diabetes that appears in pregnancy needs strict sugar control to protect mother and baby. Many patients need insulin, and frequent hospital visits to adjust the dose are a burden.

The trial will run at one university hospital in Japan. Eligible patients are those diagnosed by a glucose test before thirty weeks who already monitor their own sugar and inject insulin. One group will use a telemedicine system for care, while the other attends face-to-face visits every two to three weeks. The main measures are patient satisfaction and health costs. Sugar control and birth outcomes are secondary measures. The design tests whether remote care can match clinic care.
pmc-10689928:
Vinicius Calado Nogueira de Moura and four co-authors build a drug response chart for slow-growing mycobacteria in the United States. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. These kin of the TB germ are hard to treat, and lab response tests take weeks. A pooled chart can guide first drug picks.

They pool over ten thousand samples sent to one lab across five years. Most are of the avium complex, from spit, and from Florida. Two drugs, clarithromycin and amikacin, work on most kinds. Gene reads for two marks call response or resistance with high truth. The chart is set out for clinicians who face these slow germs.
pmc-10692128:
Ruan and coauthors review iron-driven cell death as a target in ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer of the surface type kills at a high rate. The death path, called ferroptosis, needs iron and is set off by fat peroxides. Fresh work hints tumors are prone to that path.

The review first lays out how ferroptosis works in cells. It then maps its role in tumor start and growth. Forcing that death may undo drug resistance in tumors. The team sums up drugs and scores built on that path. Open questions on resistance close the review.
pmc-10693128:
Juan Joseph Young and a large team of co-authors published this study in 2023. It examines a group of immune cells in the blood whose gene activity changes with age. The authors ask whether those age-linked changes also show up in people with Alzheimer's disease, and whether they track thinking ability.

The team first searched public data sets and found twenty-nine genes that might differ in Alzheimer's. Nine of them belonged to the aging pattern of these immune cells. Blood tests on 121 adults then confirmed that eight genes differed between patients and healthy peers. Five of those eight came from the aging pattern and had not been tied to the disease before. Patients also fell into three gene-based groups with clearly different test scores for memory and thinking.
pmc-10693228:
Lisa James and Apostolos Georgopoulos examined in 2023 whether multiple sclerosis and brain cancer share part of their genetic risk. Earlier work had found higher brain cancer risk in people with multiple sclerosis. Separately, a family of immune genes called HLA had been linked to protection or risk for both conditions, raising the question of a shared immune pattern.

The authors built an immune-gene profile for each condition from allele frequencies and disease rates across fourteen western European countries. The two profiles matched closely overall and across all six HLA genes studied, most strongly for one gene in particular. Readers get evidence for overlapping immune influence, discussed alongside how these genes respond to viruses.
pmc-10696828:
Bruno Stein Barbosa Menechino and co-authors present a 2023 journal article on how dengue and Zika viruses grip a human cell receptor. Both viruses ride the same mosquitoes and court the same sugar-reading receptor, DC-SIGN, on dendritic cells, so they may compete for it in the field. The team docked each virus's envelope protein onto the receptor in simulation, then ran motion studies and energy accounting.

One receptor residue did most of the gripping for both. Zika bound with lower energy and recruited extra, unexpected contact residues. Exposure maps showed the two envelopes presenting slightly different faces. The authors conclude Zika likely outcompetes dengue at this doorway.
pmc-10699628:
Rachel Forse and a team of co-authors ask whether cash help and health insurance are acceptable to families hit by tuberculosis in Vietnam, in two thousand twenty-three. Most Vietnamese hold social health insurance, yet well over half of tuberculosis households still face ruinous costs. The team interviewed patients and held group talks in Ho Chi Minh City.

Both tied and untied cash payments, paired with insurance, were judged acceptable on all measures used. Cash eased out-of-pocket costs, helped patients stick to treatment, and lifted mood. The amount, though, was too small to lift the full burden. Conditions on cash added work for the tuberculosis program, which raised doubts about scale-up.
pmc-10700628:
Estelle Clerc and co-authors report marine research from two thousand twenty-three on how ocean bacteria swim toward large sugar molecules. Bacteria steer by chemical gradients, which shapes who meets whom and how fast nutrients cycle. Most past work used small molecules as the lure, yet ocean organic matter is mostly large polymers.

Using tests in the sea and the lab, the team showed bacteria are strongly drawn to two common algal polysaccharides. The pull was stronger than that of their small building blocks. A second algal compound, called DMSP, boosted the attraction further by donating methyl groups that sharpen gradient sensing. The authors say such navigation may speed polymer turnover in the ocean and affect carbon cycling.
pmc-10701928:
Avalon Sundqvist and co-authors describe a 2023 study of follow-up after a cervix procedure in Sweden. The procedure, called conization, cuts out abnormal tissue found by screening. Good follow-up care after it is key to stop later cancer, and visit rates must stay high.

The team tracked thousands of women treated in one region over six years, with years of follow-up time. Nine in ten women gave a cell sample within a year of the procedure. Shares with a clean test of cure rose at each check point out to two years. The virus that drives the disease cleared in most women by eight months. Among women with a clean early test, no cancer appeared in follow-up. The authors call the later risk very low.
pmc-10704628:
Lu, Xiong, Wen, Yang, and Liu study a blood marker in newborns with a fast heart rhythm disorder in twenty twenty-three. The disorder, supraventricular tachycardia, is a common serious arrhythmia in neonates. It can lead to acute heart failure. The team sought early factors that predict that complication.

They analysed forty-three newborns treated for the disorder over six years. Slow control of the fast rhythm, high potassium, and anaemia raised the risk of heart failure. A peptide called BNP, released by the stressed heart, also predicted it. A cutoff value gave fair sensitivity and high specificity for the prediction. Babies above that cutoff more often needed second line drugs to stop the rhythm. The authors propose BNP to guide early treatment choices.
pmc-10706628:
Caroline Steigenberger and co-authors present a 2023 study on why rapid tests for chest infections are so seldom used in European clinics. Quick tests done at the point of care can cut needless antibiotic use, a driver of drug resistance. The team looked at how pricing and funding rules in five countries help or block their use.

Experts from public bodies in Austria, Estonia, France, Poland, and Sweden were interviewed. Barriers included weak evidence and assessment methods built for drugs rather than tests. None of the countries set test prices directly, and buying through local bodies weakened purchasing power. Coverage of test costs and fair pay for doctors using the tests were seen as helpful steps.
pmc-10707228:
Ivan Jurak and co-authors review team-based rehab for chronic low back pain in this 2023 systematic review. The condition affected about six hundred million people in 2020 and is set to grow with aging. Their method compared many treatments at once through a network meta-analysis. Six databases were searched under standard review rules. Programs mixed behavioral, teaching, and work-conditioning parts. Exercise therapy, minimal care, and usual care served as comparisons.

The focus was short-term change in pain and disability. Team programs of this kind treat pain as body, mind, and social life together. That breadth sets them apart from exercise-only plans. The network approach lets programs be ranked even without direct head-to-head trials. The authors aimed to show which mix helps most, soonest. Clinics planning back pain services are the main audience.
pmc-10708728:
Williams Adeyemi and colleagues tested self-sensing composite joints in two thousand twenty-three. The joints use carbon and epoxy stitched with memory alloy wires. Such stitching already strengthens joints against splitting. The team asked whether it could also sense impacts. Large deformations change the wires' electrical resistance sharply. A small controller read those changes in real time.

Impact tests struck joints at two energy levels. The system captured each impact's timing accurately. It also located where splitting began inside the joint. One material thus provides strength and sensing together. Aircraft and bridge builders value such dual use. Hidden damage becomes visible without extra sensors.
pmc-10713628:
Han Yu and co-authors present UniKP, a framework that predicts enzyme speed parameters from sequence and substrate in a 2023 paper. Enzyme engineers need numbers like turnover rate and binding strength, but measuring them is slow. Existing predictors performed unevenly across tasks.

UniKP builds on pretrained language models for proteins and small molecules. It predicts three core kinetic parameters in one system. An extended version adds pH and temperature effects for robustness. Re-weighting tricks cut errors on the hardest high-value cases. The team demonstrated the tool in enzyme discovery and directed evolution, finding new enzymes and mutants with higher activity than their starting points.
pmc-10714528:
Habib Alagbo and a large team examine who writes health papers about the Russia-Ukraine war in this two thousand twenty-three review. The war disrupted Ukrainian research through death, displacement, and destroyed labs. Yet Ukrainian scholars have kept publishing on the war's health toll. The team searched two databases for health-related papers on the war. They then charted publication trends and the share of Ukrainian authors.

Such counts reveal whose voices shape the record of a crisis. Gaps between local and outside authorship raise fairness questions for journals. The review gives editors and funders a baseline to act on. It also honors the persistence of researchers working under fire. Global health and publishing ethics readers are the audience.
pmc-10714628:
Innocent Ngaruye and nine colleagues estimated child stunting rates for every sector of Rwanda, the country's smallest administrative level. Globally, over 148 million young children were stunted in twenty twenty-two. Rwanda's national rate stood at about thirty-four percent, but national averages cannot guide local interventions. Survey data are too sparse to measure each of 416 sectors directly. Small area estimation borrows strength from related data through a statistical model.

The model combined survey results with significant covariates to produce sector estimates with error bounds. Only forty sectors had met the national target of nineteen percent or less. Nearly half, 194 sectors, remained far from it. The twenty twenty-three map tells planners exactly where nutrition programs are failing, sector by sector, instead of hiding pockets of crisis inside a national mean.
pmc-10715128:
Melinek and four co-authors draft a grade-first plan for cell-free protein brew in this twenty twenty-three review. The brew makes proteins in cell soup with no live cells in the tank. Firms eye it for fast small runs of heal drugs and test kits.

Inside, soup traits like protein and fuel loads swing from batch to batch. That swing makes end grade hard to prove for firm-scale runs. The team names scant lore share as a top block to firm growth. Small test tools and set log rules form their first fix list. Grade-by-build steps, long used in drug plants, frame the whole plan.
pmc-10716728:
An EFSA panel weighs a volcanic rock dust proposed as a feed additive for all farm animals in a 2023 opinion. The product is ground Neapolitan Yellow Tufa, a stone from the Campi Flegrei volcanic area of Italy, holding at least half zeolites, a family of porous minerals. It would serve as an anticaking agent, keeping feed flowing. The European Commission asked for a safety and efficacy ruling.

The panel worked through the standard risk assessment: identity, safety for the animals, for consumers of animal products, for workers, and for the environment, plus whether it works. On parts of the dossier the data ran thin, and the opinion records where conclusions could and could not be reached. Opinions of this kind gate what may be sold into Europe's feed chain.
pmc-10719328:
Xinyuan Tang and colleagues tested the upper lip bite test in 2023. Clinicians use the test to predict hard airway cases. Patients bite their upper lip with lower teeth. Data on predicting hard tube placement were lacking. The study checked adults having planned surgery. It was an observational case-cohort design.

Patients needed a breathing tube under general anaesthesia. Higher bite grades showed only modest accuracy. Mouth opening predicted difficulty better than the bite test. Curve scores favoured mouth opening clearly. Grade patterns were reported step by step. The authors report exact sensitivity and specificity values. Readers can judge the test limits directly.
pmc-10722528:
Wade, Lewis, and Kang add, in a 2023 comment, a missing number to another group's study of two heat-loving enzymes. The original paper measured how the enzymes TrSOX and BSOX unfold with heat, reporting the energy absorbed and the melting temperature. What it left out was entropy, the disorder term that, with energy, decides stability. The commenters compute the entropy changes from the published data.

With entropy restored, a pattern appears: the two proteins show enthalpy-entropy compensation, the two terms trading off so that melting temperatures barely move. That trade-off, the authors argue, sharpens the reading of the original results and of protein heat stability generally, a property that matters wherever enzymes work in hot industrial, farm, or food processes. The comment is short and pointed. It does not dispute the measurements; it completes them, and in completing them changes what they mean.
pmc-10729028:
Ross Goldstone and co-authors survey global health activity among health students and NHS staff in England in this 2023 paper. Global health work includes events, placements, and projects beyond local care. An online survey ran from July to November 2021. It reached hospitals and universities across England.

The survey drew 3,955 replies, most from NHS staff. Four in five respondents had never taken part in a global health activity. Only a small share were taking part at the time. Attending events was the most common past activity. The top reason for not taking part was not knowing about chances to do so. Many respondents said they wanted to take part in future.
pmc-10732428:
Zuriah Meacham and colleagues borrow a virus weapon to make the gene-editing enzyme Cas9 destroy itself in human cells, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Bacteria use CRISPR-Cas as immunity; the phages that hunt them answer with anti-CRISPR proteins. One of them, AcrIIA1, latches onto Cas9's cutting domain.

The surprise was what happened next in human cell culture: Cas9 vanished. The anti-CRISPR did not merely block the enzyme, it triggered its degradation, for both the common Streptococcus and Staphylococcus versions. Mutations that broke the physical grip between the two proteins abolished the effect, proving contact is required. A built-in self-destruct could one day limit how long Cas9 lingers in a patient, trimming off-target risk. The authors also sketch using the small, specific protein as the targeting half of designer protein-degradation drugs.
pmc-10736128:
Melissa Macri, Jihan Abbas, and six colleagues review screening and intervention tools for older women facing intimate partner and family violence, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Such violence hits women of all ages. Yet research has largely skipped older populations, and older women face extra barriers to reporting abuse.

The scoping review searched six major databases plus grey literature sources. It had two aims. The first was to judge how useful and suitable existing tools are for women aged fifty-five and over. The second was to map the gaps in policy, practice, and research. Scoping reviews chart a field rather than test one treatment. By gathering what exists, the authors show where tools designed for younger women may misfit older lives. The review is meant to guide better screening and support for a group whose abuse often stays hidden.
pmc-10736328:
Freya Diederich studied how migration history shapes care in old age in a 2023 paper. Policy is often weighed by its laws alone, yet how a host land frames and views a migrant group can mark people for life. The Mariel boatlift of 1980, when many Cubans reached the United States, gives a sharp case.

Federal framing set these arrivals apart from other Cuban cohorts of the era. Diederich asks whether that early framing tracks with how the group arranges care decades later, as formal services or family help. The study shows why the welcome a cohort gets belongs in any account of later needs.
pmc-10736428:
Doris Yu and co-authors test a game-like training program for mild cognitive impairment in a 2023 paper. Such impairment is common in older adults and raises dementia risk, yet professional training is time-limited. Their program turns Sudoku solving into structured brain training.

A trial randomized 288 older adults to the 24-week program or usual care. Training ran twelve weeks, then twelve weeks of home practice followed. The trained group gained more in global cognition, memory, and language right after training. Gains held to the end of the study. Interviews probed why participants felt the program helped.
pmc-10737028:
Lindsay Wilkinson and three co-authors study how the COVID pandemic shook older adult volunteers and their sense of purpose, in a 2023 survey study. The sample held sixty-five adults, aged fifty-seven to eighty-nine, who served in grandparent and companion programs in one Nebraska city. Lockdowns and distancing cut many of them off from the people they served. The team asked how hard the pandemic felt and whether purpose had slipped.

One in four said their sense of purpose had fallen during the pandemic. Those who felt the pandemic as hard or a hardship also found it harder to visit clients. New hurdles in the role, in turn, tracked with a lost sense of purpose. The authors read the chain as a path from pandemic strain to weaker purpose. They urge support for older volunteers in future crises.
pmc-10737328:
Chang and five co-authors study how caregiver neglect of people with dementia changes under different definitions. Neglect is among the most common forms of elder mistreatment, yet its thresholds vary. The team drew on 244 caregiver and care-recipient pairs from diverse backgrounds.

With the loosest definition, one-week neglect prevalence reached 43 percent. The strictest definition, requiring no other help at all, gave 11 percent. Male caregivers and African American caregivers showed higher risk only under the loose definition. More social support for the caregiver lowered risk under the stricter definitions. The authors say clear definitions matter for designing help. Support for caregivers may itself prevent neglect.
pmc-10738028:
Dennis Lox, in a 2023 review, surveys how exercise and drugs that mimic it may slow parts of the aging process. The focus is a cell pathway that senses energy and helps keep cells working well. When that pathway fades, cells drift into states that drive swelling, wear, and further decline in a self-feeding loop.

Exercise switches the pathway on, and trained muscle releases helpful signals while low body fat adds more. Compounds such as metformin and a small peptide from cell power plants can also switch it on. Some may help people who cannot exercise, and some seem to add to the gains from training. Lox frames the goal as keeping the cell setting that supports healthy aging.
pmc-10738228:
Misa Nakamura and seven co-authors published a 2023 study of a blood protein, transthyretin, as a possible early marker of fading memory and thinking. The protein had been linked to mild impairment and dementia in earlier work. The team tested 211 community-dwelling older adults, sorted by a standard cognitive exam into normal, mildly impaired, and dementia groups, then followed a smaller group for 32 months.

In the normal group, protein levels tracked exam scores, with links to memory and language in particular. No such link appeared in the impaired or dementia groups. In the follow-up, women who later slipped into mild impairment had started with higher protein levels than women who stayed normal. The authors suggest the protein may flag risk before symptoms show, at least in women.
pmc-10738528:
Jeanne Koller and Paul Urbanski report in 2023 on the lived experience of aging as a transgender or gender nonconforming adult. Older adults in this group face higher rates of poverty, homelessness, isolation, and depression than their peers. The study set out to hear their own accounts of later life.

The team interviewed twenty people aged fifty and older. Many spoke of fearing or losing ties with family after coming out. Health care raised hard questions, most of all the thought of needing long-term care. Others spoke of the relief of living as their true self, and of strength drawn from community and partners. Age at transition shaped many stories.
pmc-10739528:
Hannah Hausman, Linda Azizi, and Frank Pajonk test whether tiny cell parcels can slow the return of an aggressive brain cancer after radiation, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Glioblastoma often returns because radiation pushes some tumor cells into a stem-like state that regrows the mass. Parcels from cancer stem cells, called exosomes, were added to radiated cells in dishes.

As parcel dose rose, a marker for the stem-like state fell. Fewer radiated cells switched into the fast-growing stem-like form after parcel contact. The authors suggest the parcels signal that stem cells are already present, so fewer new ones form. More work is needed, but readers see a possible way to blunt recurrence.
pmc-10740828:
Omar Shareef and co-authors review a severe eye infection in a 2023 paper. Acanthamoeba keratitis is caused by a protozoan and can lead to lasting vision loss. It is hard to diagnose because its symptoms overlap with other corneal infections, and treatment is tricky.

The team searched recent English-language studies, covering 2018 to 2023, and kept 87 of 265 papers found. Lab tests based on PCR may soon reach clinics, while antibody and machine-learning tools hold promise for later. A single-drug eye therapy may improve access and results. An oral drug offers an option for stubborn cases that resist standard care.
pmc-10745128:
Goohyeon Hong and Patrick Geraghty present a case report from twenty twenty-three on a rare crisis sparked by a lung cancer drug. Tumor lysis syndrome hits when cancer cells die fast and flood the blood with their innards. It is a known threat in blood cancers, rare in solid tumors. The patient was a man in his late fifties with lung adenocarcinoma that had spread wide.

He took afatinib, a drug aimed at a growth switch found in his tumor. Four days in, his kidneys failed and his breath worsened. Labs fit tumor lysis from the drug. The team calls it the first such case for this drug in this cancer, with a tour of past reports.
pmc-10746028:
Selenium particles at nanoscale size kill microbes, but they clump unless held apart. Anastasiya Blinova and co-authors keep them apart with cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, a common surfactant, making the particles by chemical reduction in water. They map how the amounts used and the way they are made set particle size and micelle formation, and image the results with electron microscopy.

Tests showed the sol's fate depends on acidity and on the ions around it; added positive ions swelled the positive sol's particles more than the negative sol's. Against the bacteria Escherichia coli and Micrococcus luteus and the fungus Mucor, some mixes clearly killed bacteria and fungi at set doses. The authors conclude this pairing merits more study for use in veterinary drugs, medicines, and cosmetics.
pmc-10753428:
Kulkarni and eight co-authors review treatments that improve sleep for people with skin disease. Severe skin conditions often wreck sleep, yet few studies measure that side of care. The team searched five databases and kept 25 treatment studies covering more than 11,000 patients, grading each for strength.

One drug, dupilumab, had the best support for better sleep in eczema, though side effects were common. Creams and ointments mostly failed to help sleep, while procedural treatments showed some promise. Work on other skin diseases was thin. The authors urge future skin trials to measure sleep as a standard outcome. They frame sleep as part of treatment success, not an afterthought.
pmc-10761028:
Wenwen Zhao and co-authors track how the flavor and nutrient makeup of pepino fruit changes as it grows, in a 2023 study. Pepino, a sweet melon-like fruit, has spread across China's highlands in the past twenty years and is prized for its taste and nutrition. The team studied one cultivar grown on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, sampling fruit at three growth stages.

Chemical profiling found 187 compounds in the fruit, spanning amino acids, organic acids, sugars, and phenols. Ninety-four of these shifted clearly between stages. The stretch from growth to ripening proved to be the key window when nutrients and flavor build up. Gene activity data pointed to four genes tied to both an amino acid and a phenolic acid, suggesting shared control of nutrition and taste chemistry. The authors offer the map as breeding guidance.
pmc-10767828:
Varadi, Bertoni, Magana, and co-authors report the 2024 state of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The free database holds predicted shapes for proteins, the folded chains that do most work inside cells. By 2024 it covered well over two hundred million protein sequences.

The resource began in 2021 with a far smaller first release of predicted shapes. Its growth since then has reshaped how biologists plan experiments, since a good shape hints at what a protein does. The update explains the scale of coverage and why open access to these shapes speeds basic research worldwide.
pmc-10784828:
Chen-Ying Ma and co-authors published a 2023 study on nutrition problems in cervical cancer patients treated with radiation. Radiation to the belly and pelvis often inflames the gut. That damage hampers eating, digestion, and the use of nutrients. Poor nutrition can then blunt how well the treatment works and raise the chance of side effects.

The team followed fifty patients through their radiation course. Fifteen also received an internal form of radiation afterward. Weight, body makeup, a standard nutrition risk score, and blood tests were tracked over time. Muscle loss was a special focus, since it weakens patients quietly. A chemical profiling method searched the blood for fat-related patterns tied to the gut injury. The study also screened for clinical factors linked to changes in one key fat. The authors map how nutrition, muscle, and fat chemistry shift together during treatment.
pmc-10805828:
Pancreatic cancer is the deadliest common solid tumor, and most cases carry a fault in the KRAS gene. Fan Yang and co-authors built a model to predict outcomes for patients with that fault. They drew on one hundred eighty-four patients from one genome atlas and four hundred twelve from an international set. Gene activity and survival patterns yielded a seven-gene score. The study was published in twenty twenty-three.

The score separated patients into low and high risk with good accuracy. Pathway analysis then compared the two groups. A cell-death route called ferroptosis stood out among the differences. Such a score could guide care choices and point drug work toward the pathways that split the groups.
pmc-10833228:
Wang Rui and co-authors analyze factors in long-term survival after surgery for esophageal cancer, in a research paper from 2023. The cancer of the food pipe has poor outcomes, and blood indices may carry prognostic value next to tumor traits. A clear split of risk factors can guide follow-up care after radical surgery.

The study covers two hundred six patients who had full tumor removal. Blood tests, tumor traits, surgery data, and survival were compared between groups. Deeper invasion, later stage, vessel and nerve invasion, and lymph spread all raised risk. Heart disease, low differentiation, mid-chest tumor place, and nerve invasion stood as independent risks. The paper ranks what shortens survival most.
pmc-10836428:
Chunyan Liu, Tianqiang Wu, and Na Ren review gut-hormone drugs as a candidate therapy for diabetic nerve damage, in an overview from two thousand twenty-three. The condition, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, brings pain and numbness and can end in amputation. Current pain care leans on antidepressants, and nothing yet slows the damage itself.

The drugs, GLP-1 receptor agonists, control blood sugar in diabetes care. Animal and early human evidence hints they also guard nerves by calming inflammation and oxidative stress. Clinical proof for nerve outcomes stays thin and mixed, the authors stress. The review gathers both sides of the case.
pmc-11001328:
Le Gong and seven co-authors review natural compounds that protect the kidney's filter cells in diabetic kidney disease, in a paper from 2023. Damage to those cells, called podocytes, lets protein leak into urine, a key sign of the disease. The review sorts the disease's five stages and the jobs of thirteen podocyte proteins, then sums up fifteen natural compounds.

Lab and animal work shows the compounds ease inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death through several known pathways. Two filter proteins, nephrin and podocin, were the most studied targets. The authors map which compound acts through which pathway to guide later drug work.
pmc-11128728:
Zohreh Karimiankakolaki and colleagues published a 2023 study teaching smoking husbands about secondhand smoke risks. Their wives were pregnant at the time. Smoke exposure harms unborn babies. Pregnancy can motivate men to change. The study ran in health centers in Isfahan, Iran.

One hundred forty men joined the trial. Half received targeted training sessions. Half formed the control group. A custom questionnaire measured confidence to avoid exposing others. Scores were taken before and after. The tool itself was validated carefully. Whether confidence becomes lasting behavior change is the open question. Training partners may protect pregnancies more cheaply than treating harm later.
pmc-11532428:
Agustí, Martínez-Fuentes, Mesejo, Marzal, and Reig trace, published in 2024, the gene chain by which a sprayed plant hormone thins citrus fruit. The synthetic auxin 3,5,6-TPA is sprayed as young fruit naturally begin to drop. Treated trees drop more fruitlets and carry fewer, larger fruit to harvest. The team tracked sugar genes in leaf and fruit to find the mechanism. The spray acts through the leaves first.

Leaf genes for carbon capture and sugar making switched down. Sugar mover genes fell too, so less sugar reached the fruit. In the fruit, sugar-splitting and cell-division genes were repressed as well, along with auxin-handling genes. Starved of sugar and division signals, the fruit raised ethylene, the gas that triggers drop. The authors map a full leaf-to-fruit chain for a tool growers already use, opening ways to tune dose and timing.
pmc-11534228:
Kolkman, Lee, and Van Witteloostuijn argued in twenty twenty-four that machine learning can build theory, not just guess outcomes. Stock talk ties such tools to scores at the cost of sense. They set a five-step loop that joins three thought moves in one cycle.

Steps run from part picks and scans to claim builds, claim tests, and theory. A firm growth case with real data walks the loop in full. The cycle, named co-duction, gives learned reads a place in proof work. Guess strength and sense can rise as one, they show.
pmc-11535028:
Jakub Korkus and five co-authors published a microbiology study in twenty twenty-four on a respiration gene that Campylobacter jejuni needs to build strong biofilms. The bacterium is a leading cause of food-borne illness, and biofilms help it survive hostile conditions. Which genes control its biofilms was largely unknown.

The team scrambled the genome with random insertions in a laboratory strain and screened thirteen hundred fifty mutants. Twenty-four built weaker biofilms, most carrying insertions in uncharacterized genes. One hit, cydB, handles cellular respiration and had never been tied to biofilms. Deleting it produced a thin, loosely organized film; restoring it restored the film. A new link between breathing and community building in this pathogen.
pmc-11536528:
Sandra Blomqvist, Hugo Westerlund, and Linda Magnusson Hanson study whether job troubles during the COVID-19 pandemic raised suicidal thoughts among Swedish workers, in a 2024 study. Their data came from a long-running work and health survey, with extra waves in early 2021 and 2022. The analysis covered 1,558 people who had worked before the pandemic. Exposures included job loss, furlough, downsizing, and rising insecurity.

Job loss, downsizing, and insecurity each came with clearly higher odds of thoughts of suicide or self-harm. The links held after accounting for age, income standing, and earlier mental health. Furlough was the exception, with no clear link. Adding personality measures softened some links but did not erase them. The authors frame job protection as part of suicide prevention during crises.
pmc-11548128:
Karen Koelzer and colleagues published a field study in 2024 on what honeybees actually feed on inside a large city. Working in Vienna, Austria, the team examined honey from apiaries spread across urban and suburban areas. Their goal was to learn which plants supply urban bees and what that pollen mix says about city green space.

Under the microscope, the researchers counted pollen grains in fifty honey samples and identified more than two hundred plant types. Trees made up only about a quarter of those types, yet tree pollen appeared in surprisingly large amounts. Planted and managed green spaces, the authors conclude, can give city pollinators a steady food supply.
pmc-11549328:
Xia Wang, Yu Song, Yicong Ji, Anming Chen, and Shancheng Si report a two thousand twenty-four study of a severe eye infection caused by Klebsiella bacteria spreading from inside the body. Unlike post-surgery eye infections, this kind arrives through the bloodstream. Its warning pattern in China needed mapping.

Affected eyes were compared with surgery-related infection cases. Every body-spread patient had fever, and nearly all had liver abscesses. Half also had lung involvement. Blood protein levels ran low. Statistical checks singled out fever and low protein as independent markers. Doctors seeing such a pattern should suspect this dangerous route early.
pmc-11573128:
Jan Endrikat and five co-authors ask whether allergic reactions to a scan dye differ by sex, race, or country, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. The dye, iopromide, is injected for X-ray and vessel scans. Reactions are uncommon but can be serious, so fair risk data matter.

One analysis pooled four studies with over one hundred fifty thousand patients in thirty-seven countries. A second mined the maker's global safety database, covering tens of millions of doses. Women reacted more often than men in the pooled studies, though the gap shrank after adjustment. The safety database backed the pattern. Race and region results are laid out for comparison. The authors give doctors a firmer base for consent talks.
pmc-11575028:
Chee Cheen Yeong and co-authors published this study in 2024. It offers a hand-measured stand-in for a heart strain score that normally needs special software. The score, global longitudinal strain, flags weak heart muscle early. Speckle tracking software computes it from ultrasound images, but many sites lack the tool. The team measured the same strain manually, from mid-wall lengths, in 154 Australian hospital patients.

Hand measures tracked the software values almost perfectly. They also matched ejection fraction, the standard pump measure, whether or not parts of the wall moved oddly. Cutoff checks agreed in over ninety-five percent of cases at both the healthy and sick ends. No case landed on opposite sides of the line by the two methods. The authors back hand measurement as a reliable fallback for clinics and studies.
pmc-11577028:
Rok Janža and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on how background vibration noise scrambles the courtship signals of a stink bug that talks through plant stems. Sound research links masking to frequency overlap, but vibration sense works differently. The team played noise of varied spectra while males courted and while recording from sensory nerves.

Noise hurt courtship whether or not its frequencies overlapped the signal. Males struggled to recognize and locate the female's call. Overlapping noise dulled the nerves' sensitivity, while all noise warped the signal's timing code, which the legs use to triangulate the source. The authors warn that human-made vibration may trouble insect communication more than expected.
pmc-11577628:
Fereshteh Abbasvandi and a large team of co-authors test a cancer probe that checks breast surgery cavity edges for missed cancer during the operation itself. Clear edges matter, since leftover cancer can force a second surgery. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The probe had already raised found rates for bad edges over the quick frozen test. Here the team shows it can find bad cavity side edges that the final lab check of the tumor side missed.
