Of the edges the probe flagged, a set held invasive cancer or early duct forms that the lab report had not called bad. The authors say the live probe keeps a role even beside the final lab check.
pmc-11577828:
Francesco Palumbo and co-authors test whether more plant fiber in a sow's diet changes gut microbes in sows and piglets. The fiber class in focus is hemicelluloses, a part of plant cell walls. Sows ate varied fiber levels while nursing their litters. The team tracked nutrient uptake, stool acids, and stool microbes in sows and their young.

Higher fiber raised uptake of fiber and energy but cut protein uptake. Stool acid mixes shifted on set days of the trial. Microbe mixes in sows changed under the diets, with smaller shifts in piglets. Fast and slow growing piglets kept their own microbe traits in any case. Growth and stool acids in piglets showed no diet effect.
pmc-11579728:
Yachen Liu leads a team on cross run features for proteomics data. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. Single run methods often lack depth and consistency.

A new tool pools hybrid features across runs. It aims to raise reliable peptide finds. Benchmarks ran on several public data sets. One set was a three species test mixture. The tool found more precursors, peptides, and proteins. False find rates stayed under control in the tests. Reproducibility across runs also improved with it.  The tool is public on a code host.
pmc-11585228:
Shaun R Seaman and Ruth H Keogh present a two thousand twenty-four methods paper on simulating survival data for causal models. Marginal structural models estimate treatment effects when confounders change over time. Testing methods for them needs realistic fake data.

Earlier simulation approaches forced awkward limits on how data could be generated. The new algorithm removes those limits for several model types. It handles treatments that are categories or continuous values. The authors show the method with a short simulation study. Statisticians get a freer tool for checking whether their survival methods behave before trusting them on real patients.
pmc-11585628:
Lu and co-authors report a new drug candidate against the virus that causes COVID-19. Drug hunters target several viral enzymes, among them the papain-like protease, which the virus needs to copy itself and to blunt host defenses. Blocking that enzyme could slow infection at its source.

The team found an inhibitor of this protease that can be taken by mouth. Oral dosing matters because early COVID care happens at home, not in hospitals. The compound was built for strong uptake after swallowing. The work presents the discovery as a possible treatment path for COVID-19 care.
pmc-11585928:
Gia-Bao Nguyen and nine co-authors report a methods study from 2024 on screening drugs against malaria parasites. New drugs need to kill the parasite in the liver, before it causes symptoms, as well as in the blood. Liver tests are costly, so the team adapted a cheap light-based test that uses common lab supplies.

They tuned the test with mouse liver cells and a mouse parasite that glows, then checked it against known drugs. The test gave stable signals and clear dose results with few parasites per well. They then used it to screen a shared drug box and checked the hits for harm to liver cells.  A low-cost test of this kind could widen screening work in labs with tight budgets.
pmc-11589828:
Pablo Pedrosa, Zhenguang Zhang, Victor Nuñez-Quintela, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests a bold idea: briefly switching on the genes that can reset a cell to a stem-like state may slow lung tumors instead of feeding them.

Four genes, known by the initials OSKM, can reprogram adult cells when left on, which risks new tumors. The team instead pulsed them briefly in lung cancer cells. Growth stalled, as many cells died or slipped into a dormant state. Two of the genes did most of this work, acting through a cell-cycle brake called p21. In several mouse tests, including tumors grown from a cancer-driving gene, the brief pulses shrank tumor burden. The authors say the tactic could open a new line of cancer treatment.
pmc-11592828:
Yudaeva, Kostyusheva, Kachanov, and a team of co-authors review the state of gene therapy that uses viruses to carry new genes. Their review is from two thousand twenty-four. Some such therapies have already been cleared for use in care. Most now use adeno-associated viruses or the herpes virus as the carrier.

Viral carriers can bring genes into target cells well and keep them active. Yet they have tight size limits and can stir up immune or swelling responses. They also carry a risk of harm where the gene lands. The review sorts DNA and RNA virus carriers by type and use. It then looks at ways to make them safer and more strong, from design tweaks to drug and nano tools.
pmc-11593528:
Antonio Mazzotti and nine co-authors tell of a young man whose growth-plate ill showed most as joint loose-part harm in many joints. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The ill bends growth plates, brings joint pain in youth, and can shorten height. Its most known form stems from flaws in the COMP gene and oft hits hips most.

The man, aged twenty-four, had loose-part harm all over, a sign seen in kin gene forms but not this one. Gene proof found a fresh flaw in the COMP gene, and kin bore the ill too. The team say this sign must join the known list for COMP flaws.
pmc-11594228:
Peirong Yu and his team study shifts in grade of old tangerine peel in store and how brews of it act in lab models of gut work. Their 2024 study looks at a peel used in a wide way as food, and in old Chinese herb care.

Gas watch in fake store states tracked how the peel breathes. Air with the gas O2 and the gas CO2 were put forth as safe marks. Five flavonoid goods were grade marks. Their grades shifted a lot with how long the peel was kept and how old it was. Heat and wet air swayed scent goods sent out in a strong way. Eighteen goods were put forth as marks of the age span. Eight more were put forth as marks of rot grade. The study tested gut work of peel brews in male and female model states on their own.
pmc-11594928:
Alanis-Gómez and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on magnesium-doped bone mineral nanofibers. The fibers mimic bone mineral while adding magnesium's benefits. A microwave-assisted water method makes them in the lab. Checks confirm pure, hexagonal fibers with magnesium built in. The crystal lattice shrinks slightly from the doping. Skin-type cells grow better on the doped fibers than controls. Plain commercial mineral shows no germ fighting at all.

The doped fibers strongly kill both bacterial classes tested. Fungal killing is moderate in their assays. No cell toxicity appears at helpful doses. Implant infection prevention is the target use.
pmc-11596928:
Aisha Farhana and a team of co-authors study iron-carrying transporters in the TB germ, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. These ABC transporters move iron bound to siderophores, small helper molecules the germ uses to grab iron. The team described the build and behavior of the exporter IrtA and the importer pair IrtB with Rv2895c.

One binding part worked alone, while its partner shifted between single and paired forms. Adding ATP pushed the motor parts of both transporters to pair up. Heat and acidity shifts changed how firmly the parts held their cargo. The work maps shape changes that drive iron uptake, a possible drug target.
pmc-11597128:
Liaqat Ali and a large team of co-authors locked silver specks in moringa gum to fight drug proof germs. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with a world threat: germs that shrug off antibiotics, fed by drug misuse. The team made silver nanoparticles from moringa leaves. Light, heat, and X-ray reads set their size and build. The specks were then set in the plant's own guard gum at set mixes.

That lock holds the specks in place for use. Germ kill tests ran on proof strains from human infections. Readers in green nano work get a plant made germ shield that needs no new antibiotic to work.
pmc-11599528:
Dejaco and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-four on target-controlled dialysis for antibiotics. Dialysis shifts drug levels in intensive care patients in hard-to-predict ways. Too little drug risks failed treatment and resistance; too much risks harm. Their idea spikes drug into the dialysis fluid itself. Transport physics then pulls blood levels toward the fluid's target level. Five common antibiotics are tested in a lab model. A protein solution stands in for patient blood. Three clinical scenarios are mimicked in the setup.

Levels move toward the target from both low and high starts. Targets can be set and held regardless of starting point. Drugs stay stable in dialysis fluids over half a day. The authors call careful patient trials the next step.
pmc-11600628:
Aya Saitoh and Yugo Shobugawa survey Japanese parents on vaccine hesitancy in this 2024 study. Over three thousand parents of children up to age eleven answered a standard attitudes questionnaire in early 2023. Hesitancy ran at about half for routine infant shots and nearly three quarters for COVID-19 vaccines. Parents trusted pediatric doctors less and followed schedules less for the newer vaccine.

Safety worries topped fifty percent for both kinds. Inner conflict about the decision predicted hesitancy for both, and fear of COVID itself predicted routine-shot hesitancy. The authors urge stronger trust between doctors and parents, clearer information, and tools that help parents decide. They frame the results as groundwork for the next pandemic's vaccine rollout.
pmc-11602028:
Moore and a large team ran a trial in twenty twenty-four on how young adults look at packs of small flavored cigars. Taste draws young folks to start and keep use, and pack art may add to that pull. They used eye-track gear to time where the gaze rests on each pack part.

Folks aged in their teens and twenties saw twelve packs, with or without taste names. The health warn took the most gaze in both groups. The taste group gazed at taste names far more and recalled them best after. The team says cuts to taste words and art on packs may curb their pull.
pmc-11603028:
Johan Busselez and colleagues describe how a giant molecular motor strips helper proteins off immature ribosomes so the finished parts can leave the cell nucleus. The motor, called Rea one, is built from a ring of energy-using domains plus a very long linker arm ending in a gripping tip. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team shows that the linker is not a passive tail. It rotates and swings toward the ring through a sequence of steps, some needing fuel from ATP breakdown and some proceeding without it.

Fuel use lets the linker engage the ring and dock its gripping tip in place. That contact sends force directly to the bound helper proteins, pulling them off the growing ribosome part. The detailed picture explains how one of the largest enzymes in the cell does its mechanical work, a basic step in how all cells build their protein factories.
pmc-11603628:
Baleng Wutor and co-authors survey, in a 2024 study, why doctors in Ghana plan to leave for practice abroad. Health worker outflow strains care in poorer countries, and Ghana is a known source. An online survey in March 2024 drew over six hundred doctors working in the country.

Nearly three quarters said they intend to emigrate. The United States led the wish list, then the United Kingdom and Canada. Younger doctors, men, lower-ranked doctors, and those in diagnostics showed the strongest intent after adjustments. Pay, training chances, and working conditions drove the pull. The authors urge retention steps aimed at the groups most set on leaving.
pmc-11603728:
Alison Chisholm and others studied home blood pressure monitoring in pregnancy in 2024. Remote care for mothers grew during the pandemic. Self-checks became one remote part. Trial women shared their experiences after. Women told of gains and burdens frankly. Equity of access was a concern.

Experiences varied across the trial groups. Self-checks changed how visits worked, in part. Findings clarify where monitoring fits best. Face-to-face care still matters greatly. Remote care must balance against it. Services now weigh post-pandemic pathways with care. Best ways need this evidence base. Fair access must guide rollout choices. Women's voices anchor the review.
pmc-11605928:
Yusuf Ersali wrote a solo study in two thousand twenty-four on a growth disorder in lab-grown pistachio shoots. The disorder, called hyperhydricity, makes shoots waterlogged and glassy, and it is the most common problem in plant tissue culture. It can deform shoots and badly damage a propagation program.

Ersali varied the recipe of a standard growth medium for a wild pistachio species used as rootstock. He tested two salts and two growth hormones at several doses. One recipe cut the disorder to about a third of shoots, while another pushed it near seventy percent. The best recipe also gave strong shoot numbers and length.
pmc-11607028:
Haixia Liu and ten co-authors test whether a marked subset of stem cells treats multiple sclerosis better in mice, in a 2024 study. Mesenchymal stem cells from umbilical cords are being explored as a therapy that calms the immune attack on nerves. Cells carrying the surface marker VCAM-1 were compared with cells lacking it. The test bed was a mouse model that mimics the disease, called EAE.

Both cell types were infused into sick mice, and the team checked symptoms, myelin loss, glial activity, and inflammation in brain and spinal cord. Gene activity scans added a molecular view. The VCAM-1 positive cells showed the stronger protective effect, as the title reports. Sorting cells by this marker before infusion could sharpen a therapy that today varies from batch to batch.
pmc-11607128:
Andrea Schneider and colleagues published a 2024 study of home intravenous feeding for cancer patients in Germany. Advanced cancer can block normal eating. Feeding by vein continues at home after discharge. Patients' own views on this life were rarely recorded. Ten hospitals enrolled patients for the study.

Quality of life stayed broadly stable over weeks. A standard cancer questionnaire tracked it. Catheter problems caused few readmissions. Patients weighed benefits and burdens in their answers. Home feeding freed them from hospital stays. Burdens included time and dependence on equipment. The results support home feeding as a humane palliative option.
pmc-11608228:
Georgia Lazoglou and six colleagues map the parts of the Mediterranean most at risk from climate change, in a twenty twenty-four study. The whole region is a known hotspot, but risk is uneven inside it. Past work leaned on average weather, while extremes hit people and nature hardest. The team built a new index centered on heat, rain, and drought extremes and paired it with an older index of mean change.

Both indices flagged the southeast Mediterranean as high risk. Southern Italy ranked high on mean change, the north on extremes. The Iberian Peninsula and Greece also stood out as needing extra care. Twenty subregions were sorted into risk groups to guide local planning.
pmc-11610228:
Zoë van der Heijden and seven co-authors map digital diet programs for youth in a scoping review from two thousand twenty-four. Childhood overweight has risen fast, and many app or web programs now target eating habits. No coherent overview of their design and results existed.

Three databases yielded fifty-one studies covering forty-one distinct programs. Apps were the commonest format, then websites and computer tools. Most programs involved stakeholders in design, though few used true co-design. Programs used about six behavior change techniques each, most often feedback and rewards. Among trials, results were mostly mixed, with few programs favorable on all outcomes. The authors say varied methods make firm verdicts on what works hard to reach.
pmc-11612228:
Dongwang Tao and co-authors predict how far buildings drift in earthquakes using real monitoring records, in a 2024 study. The peak drift ratio is a key clue to damage, yet most prediction models train on simulations or lab models, not real buildings. The team used the largest public set of true building responses, with 41 features per record. They trained a support vector regression model on all features, then a leaner one on the ten most useful.

Both models beat standard regression approaches and other machine learning rivals. The building's natural frequency proved an especially strong input. The lean model kept most of the accuracy while asking only for features that are easy to obtain. The authors say it could feed near-real-time damage checks after a quake, when response teams need fast answers.
pmc-11612428:
Daniel Assumpcao and co-authors present a 2024 thin-film lithium niobate photonics platform for quantum networks. Future quantum nodes will juggle many qubits and memories at once. Their control circuits must work at visible and near-infrared wavelengths with minimal loss.

The chip packs in low-loss couplers, strong switches, and very fast electro-optic modulators. It shifted light frequency well and controlled laser amplitude and frequency at one time. A plan for multiplexing quantum memories is outlined, promising roughly a hundredfold gain in entanglement rates over single-memory nodes. Scalable quantum networking hardware takes a concrete step.
pmc-11612528:
Carlos Marras and nine co-authors describe a game-based training tool that helps health staff talk patients into switching to biosimilar drugs, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Biosimilars are near-copies of costly biologic drugs, and switching is safe and saves money. Yet patients may feel worse on the copy just because they expect to, a nocebo effect shaped by how the switch is explained. The team built the tool from interviews and group talks with staff and patients.

Clinicians and nurses listed the claims they use and the pushback they hear. Patients with and without switch experience added their side. Those talks shaped trust-building lines and a talk guide inside the game. The authors present the Rapid Switch Trainer as a way to make switch talks smoother across clinics.
pmc-11614028:
Aniruddha Jog and three colleagues present a young stroke patient with two competing explanations, in a case report published in two thousand twenty-four. A quarter of ischemic strokes have no determined source. Two rare candidates appeared in this one patient simultaneously.

A free-floating thrombus in the carotid artery can shed emboli directly. A large patent foramen ovale, a heart flap persisting from birth, can let venous clots cross into arterial circulation. Young patients with significant ovales usually lack carotid disease, making the pairing unusual. No guidelines govern floating thrombus management. The authors pose the culprit question openly rather than pretending certainty. Such cases expose how stroke medicine reasons when two plausible mechanisms demand different treatments.
pmc-11615028:
Francesca Huwyler and co-authors studied whether response to a first round of chemotherapy predicts survival in advanced head and neck cancer, in a 2024 study. This opening chemotherapy, given before radiation with drugs or surgery, remains an option for locally advanced cases. Their single-center study looked back at patients treated at a major cancer center.

Of 48 patients who got the opening therapy, 33 could be judged for response on scans. Most got one of two drug pairs or triplets. About 70 percent shrank their tumors by at least 30 percent, and nearly all had disease control. Two-year survival figures are reported for the group, and nonresponders with throat tumors fared notably worse.
pmc-11615128:
Ten authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four introducing a way to map bacteria across a wound. Damage to the skin lets harmful microbes settle, feeding wound infections and chronic wounds. Standard swabs and biopsies say little about where in the wound the bacteria actually sit.

Their method, called Bactogram, grows the bacteria in place and yields a picture of their spread across the wound and nearby skin. In a trial, they applied it to forty-eight blister wounds in twenty-four healthy volunteers. Bacteria grew in all wounds, mostly under the dressing and near wound edges. Two scoring methods agreed closely with each other.
pmc-11617328:
Bold coloring in animals is often reported with bold behavior. One old idea blames shared chemistry: the pathways building dark pigments also shape aggression. Sarah Ruckman and co-authors test the color-and-behavior link across the animal kingdom with a formal meta-analysis of experiments. They gathered seventy-four studies, seventy on vertebrates and four on invertebrates, measuring color and aggression. Their analysis corrected for species relatedness and publication bias.

A positive link survived both corrections: more colorful animals tended to act more aggressive, with a modest average effect. The link was not limited to dark pigment coloring, which weakens the shared-chemistry idea. It also did not depend on body condition, social rank, or age. The authors favor the badge-of-status idea, where arbitrary traits evolve as honest signals of fighting ability. They suggest the genetic tie between color and aggression helps such badges evolve.
pmc-11619628:
Fabiola Bof de Andrade and co-authors follow Brazilian older adults to test whether oral health tracks physical performance over time, in work from twenty twenty-four. Teeth and gums support eating and general health. Whether they shape strength and mobility in old age was less clear.

Data came from three waves of a Sao Paulo aging cohort spanning twenty oh six to twenty fifteen. Each extra tooth raised the chance of a better score on a standard performance battery. Denture wearers also scored higher than non wearers. Gum pocket presence showed no link in the dentate group. Tooth count helped there too. The authors read oral health as part of healthy aging, not a side issue.
pmc-11623028:
Ericles Bellei and co-authors present a 2024 review of certified health management software on the Brazilian market. Clinics and hospitals run on such suites for bookings, billing, and care records. The review maps which features the certified tools carry. Most suites blend running, money, and clinical needs in one frame. Standout shared traits span record sharing across systems, rule compliance aids, and data-led choice support.

Gaps remain in fresh ideas and in how deeply the parts fuse. Buyers can read which suites cover the core trio well. Makers see where the next gains sit: tighter joins and smarter aids. Brazil's size makes it a telling test bed for health software in growth markets.
pmc-11625128:
Hongmin Ye and eight colleagues map symptom clusters in COVID-era coronavirus infections, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Clusters and networks could sharpen symptom management. Four hundred eighteen patients at a Chongqing hospital answered a forty-symptom questionnaire. Statistical factoring grouped their experiences.

Eight clusters emerged: nasopharyngeal, circulatory, neural, physical, digestive, respiratory, fever, and sensory. Network analysis ranked which symptoms sit most centrally. Chest tightness topped all three centrality measures. Regression then probed which patient factors drive each cluster's severity. The approach turns a long symptom list into manageable groups. It also flags the symptoms whose relief may ease many others. Such maps could guide targeted care for infected patients.
pmc-11627428:
Alanzi and co-authors run a fully computational hunt for new cancer drug candidates in this 2024 study. Their target is EGFR, a growth signal receptor that goes wrong in many cancers. Blocking it is a proven drug strategy.

Starting from the receptor's known bound drug, they built a shape-based search model. Screening nine commercial databases produced 1,271 candidate hits. Docking those into the receptor's crystal structure ranked the top ten by binding strength. Three finalists showed the best predicted absorption traits. Molecular dynamics simulations then checked whether their grip on the receptor stays stable over time. The pipeline narrows a huge library to a few testable leads without any wet-lab work.
pmc-11628428:
Chalirmporn Atasilp and co-authors study whether variants in a gene change how Thai patients with colon cancer react to a common drug, in a paper from 2024. The drug, called 5-fluorouracil, can cause strong side effects in the blood. The gene, called DPYD, helps the body break the drug down.

Seventy-five patients were tested for five gene variants, and their blood side effects were tracked over the first two treatment rounds. One variant stood out. Patients with two copies of that variant form all showed low white cell counts in the first round, some of them severe. The same variant linked to low platelet counts as well. A second variant linked to fewer effects in the second round. The results support gene checks before treatment.
pmc-11629228:
Badr El-Haitout and co-authors test corrosion shields for steel in strong acid in a 2024 paper. Oil and chemical plants wash steel with fifteen percent hydrochloric acid, which eats the metal fast. Two related compounds, one plain and one carrying zinc, were tried as inhibitors. Lab electrochemistry, microscope surface checks, and quantum chemical modeling all weighed in.

The zinc compound protected best, with overall blocking up to about ninety-five percent. Both compounds acted on both poles of the corrosion cell. Surface photos showed a smooth film where the inhibitors sat, against pitted bare steel. The molecules lie flat on the surface in a classic single-layer pattern. Cheap organic shields like these can stretch the life of plant steel.
pmc-11630028:
Small-cell lung cancer often spreads to the brain, so doctors long gave preventive radiation to the head after treatment. Kei Ito and co-authors ask whether that step is still needed now that MRI scans catch early spread. They study patients whose cancer fully responded to combined chemo and radiation at two centers, and match 50 patients without the preventive treatment against 25 with it.

After about 29 months of follow-up, brain spread was somewhat more common without preventive radiation, 26 versus 17 percent at one year, but the gap was not firm. Cases of many brain spots were equally rare in both groups. Deaths from nerve causes and overall survival at two years were similar. The authors suggest the preventive step may be safely skipped when MRI guides staging and follow-up.
pmc-11632428:
Dongming Zhang and co-authors compare lung germ mixes in lung cancer patients who did or did not develop lung swelling on immune therapy, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Lung wash samples from fifty-two patients were gene-sequenced. Thirty-three patients had the swelling side effect and nineteen did not.

Overall germ variety looked much the same in both groups. Two large germ groups ran higher in the swelling group, with clear statistical weight. The same three groups led both lists, so the shift is one of share, not of cast. The work is an early probe, not a test for clinic use. Readers get a candidate lung signal for a hard side effect.
pmc-11632528:
Philip Mannion reviewed dinosaur diversity through time and space in 2024. Fossil sampling is very uneven globally. Gaps distort our view of diversity. Radiation timing becomes hard to pin down. Latitude patterns also blur under bias. Famous extinction boundaries suffer similar problems.

Sampling windows differ across regions and eras. Some apparent turnovers may be artefacts. Richness may have changed little, he argues. Stability could follow the first radiation. That stability might last until the end. Better sampling knowledge is essential first. Holistic reconstruction offers a way forward. Hypotheses need testing against bias directly.
pmc-11636028:
Evers, Stolz, and Klein test brain-sport drills for poise in stroke rehab hosts. Brain-sport drills came from pro sport and spread to care work. Proof of their worth had stayed poor in past print runs. Sense drills for sight and feel may lift poise in stroke hosts. The trial set daily brain drills next to stock move care. Both arms ran for four weeks of ward rehab in the trial. In sum, 19 hosts with clot or bleed strokes took part.

Poise came from the Berg scale, the gold mark for such checks. Both arms gained poise past the four weeks in the trial. The drill arm hit a high score past the stock arm. Its lead ran half the spread size of the scale marks. The team reads this as a hint, not a firm vow.
pmc-11639828:
Costanza Maria Cristiani and co-authors test blood forms of the tau protein as a marker for a rare brain disease. Their 2024 pilot study covers progressive supranuclear palsy, a disease whose signs overlap a lot with Parkinson disease. A blood test that split the two would aid early care.

The team measured six tau forms in small groups of patients with each disease and in healthy controls. Only one form, a tagged variant, could be found in blood at all. Its levels were higher in both patient groups than in controls, but the two diseases overlapped too much to split them. Levels did track how severe the palsy was, though. The authors see staging value in the marker, even if diagnosis needs other tools.
pmc-11639928:
Mao and seven colleagues review enzyme engineering for the food industry in twenty twenty-four. Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. Better enzymes can improve food quality, flavour, and safety. The review covers design methods, new enzyme sources, and uses in food work.

Methods such as directed evolution raise enzyme stability and efficiency. Immobilization makes enzymes reusable and more fit for industry. Enzymes from extreme environments work well under harsh conditions. In food processing, enzymes improve quality and flavour. Paired with sensors, they detect allergens, pollutants, and pesticide residues fast. They also extend shelf life and curb microbial growth. The authors expect computer design and AI to drive smarter, multi use enzymes.
pmc-11640428:
Pablo Nova-Baeza and co-authors pool studies on variants of the internal jugular vein in a review from two thousand twenty-four. The vein drains blood from the head and neck and sits near key nerves and glands. Its exact position guides neck surgery.

The team searched six databases through August two thousand twenty-four and kept ten studies that met their rules. Pooled results put variant frequency near three point four percent, though studies varied a lot. No subgroup contrast reached significance. The authors stress that knowing where this vein can sit aids early diagnosis and safer neck work, such as thyroid surgery and tracheostomy. They urge care with its position in planning.
pmc-11640528:
Liu, Kovacs, and Hou review dormant cancer cells and how to treat them in twenty twenty-four. Cancer cells can enter a latent state with paused, reversible growth. Dormancy contributes to drug resistance, recurrence, and spread of cancer. It is thus a critical phase in cancer development.

Treatment ideas split into two opposite camps. One camp aims to lock dormant cells in sleep forever. The other aims to wake them so they can be killed, or to kill them as they sleep. The review covers current progress for both approaches. It also discusses future strategies that target this small cell population. The authors present dormancy as a promising avenue for new cancer treatments. Breakthroughs may come from resolving the wake or sleep dilemma.
pmc-11640828:
Federico Greco and co-authors linked CT scan values to a fat-related gene in kidney cancer in two thousand twenty-four. Clear cell renal cancer rewires its metabolism and stores lipids, driven partly by a protein called ADFP. Radiogenomics seeks scan traits that reveal such molecular states without a biopsy.

They analyzed scans from one hundred eighty-five patients and compared density values in liver and tumor across gene expression groups. Low-grade tumors expressing the gene showed lower minimum density in both tissues, a sign of more lipid. Expression also tied to body fat stores in a mixed pattern. The authors say scan density could flag tumor lipid state, pending larger validation studies.
pmc-11641328:
Maxine Fleckner and co-authors bathe human skin cells in carbon dioxide fluid to see if scar-type change can be curbed, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. A growth signal that pushes cells toward scar form drove the test. Life, growth, and drift of the cells were all checked.

An hour of the gas left cells alive and moving as before. Yet the scar marker protein fell sharply, more with longer and stronger doses. Cell energy making dropped in step, by a route not shared with a nitrogen control. The team reads the gas as a brake on scar change via energy. Readers get a fresh lead against thick scars and keloids.
pmc-11641728:
Bożena Bukowska and João Pedro Silva review plant compounds from Cannabis sativa for use in disease care, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The plant holds many active parts, among them two well-known ones found in approved drugs. One pure drug treats some forms of epilepsy, and a spray form helps stiff muscles in one nerve disease.

Lab and animal work points to roles in some cancers and in viral illness, though human proof is still thin. The review also covers early work on lupus, diabetes, and brain diseases. It aims to show what is known now and where tests should go next.
pmc-11643628:
Yogesh Sharma and co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-four on a humble question in pneumonia care: do patients who take daily multivitamins fare better in hospital? The team read records for over eight thousand cases of lung infection caught outside hospital, at two big Australian centers.

About seven in a hundred patients were on multivitamins when they came in. They were younger on the whole but carried more other illness. The team matched like with like on twenty-two traits to fair the odds, then weighed stay length, intensive care use, death in hospital, and return within a month. Illness scores, frailty, and food intake were all logged. The study tests whether a cheap daily habit leaves a mark on hard outcomes once sickness is in the chart.
pmc-11643828:
Mahsa Mortaja and co-authors study how a potent cancer drug reshapes the immune scene inside tumors over time, in a research paper from 2024. The drug, a cell-killing payload used in targeted medicines, is ferried by peptides that wake up only inside tumors. Tumors raise levels of cutting enzymes, and the peptides use those enzymes as the key.

In mouse cancer models, the team tracked how the payload changed immune cell behavior across days. The peptide carriers proved flexible for delivering the drug to tumors. The time pattern matters: the same drug can stir or settle immune activity depending on when one looks. The work guides pairing such payloads with immune therapy.
pmc-11644528:
Liliya Dimeyeva and co-authors study a rare relic plant clinging to low mountains in Kazakhstan, in this 2024 paper. Incarvillea semiretschenskia grows only in the Shu-Ile range and sits in the national Red Data Book. Its home ground, company, and family tree were partly unmapped.

The team found it on rocky slopes and valley floors in thin chestnut soils, among one hundred sixty-four plant species, five of them fellow endemics. Grazing, fires, and limestone mining threaten its stands. DNA work adds new detail on how the genus branched and when. The study arms conservation with facts.
pmc-11644628:
Fogarty, Condell, and Leavey build LOTUS, a tool to process wearable sensor data. The EmbracePlus wristband tracks pulse, skin response, heat, and motion. Raw data rest in short time chunks in avro files. That layout saves memory but needs coding skill to merge. No easy tool existed to rebuild full time series.

LOTUS gives a point-and-click screen for that rebuild job. Users pick time spans and export Excel or Matlab files. The open-source code sits on GitHub for free use. Standard signal tools can then read the merged data. The authors plan more analysis features in later versions.
pmc-11645028:
Jian Chen and co-authors (2024) propose a systematic model for designing the service touchpoints of smart products. A touchpoint is every moment where a user meets the product, from first intention to final judgment. Older design methods lean on user research alone and can miss what users truly need. The result is extra mental load and poorer experience. The authors' BEDFITA model starts from user behavior and walks through seven stages, ending with failure risk analysis.

Two established tools plug into the pipeline. The Kano model sorts user needs during the requirement stage, sharpening the design targets. Failure modes and effects analysis then grades the risks of the finished design. A smart desk case study tests the whole flow. The authors report that the model produced a design matching user needs with checked reliability. They present BEDFITA as a fuller route from behavior to robust service design.
pmc-11647328:
Qiaoling Wei, Qian Chen, Chen Zhao, and Rui Jiang test whether a no-code machine learning tool can spot eye disease in ultrasound scans. Doctors built three models on a cloud platform using close to four thousand scans of the back of the eye. One model split scans into normal and abnormal. A second named single diseases, and a third could tag more than one disease per scan.

The simple model scored best, on par with custom-built models from past work. The model that named diseases also scored well. The paper shows that clinic staff can build sound scan tools without deep coding skill.
pmc-11647828:
Shayan Khan Kakar, Jing Wang, Noman Arshed, Tran Thi Le Hien, and Nazir Muhammad Abdullahi test if tech innovation and financial technology can help conserve biodiversity across developing countries. Human growth and new tech threaten species worldwide. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Panel data over two decades from dozens of countries fed a lag model built for linked cross country data. A fresh FinTech index was built for the test. Growth showed an inverted U link to biodiversity. Growth, clean energy, and FinTech all aided conservation in the results. The authors argue green finance can steer funds away from nature harming projects toward friendly ones.
pmc-11648628:
Xueqing Zhang, Zhe Li, Wei Sun, Yuhua Zhang, Jinlin Li, and Li Wang wrapped an iron catalyst in a skin of graphene, in a study published in 2024. Their goal was to clean up a classic fuel-making process. The process turns gas into liquid fuels. But iron catalysts waste much carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, keeping efficiency under half.

The graphene skin steadied the active iron carbide phase. Crucially, it also suppressed the side reaction behind the waste gases. With the best recipe, carbon dioxide fell to under five percent of output. Methane fell to under six percent. About ninety percent of the carbon ended in valued products. The catalyst also survived air exposure without needing reactivation. The design points toward far less wasteful fuel synthesis.
pmc-11649128:
Taryn Kong, Bruce Taylor, and Victoria Graham study why groups from unlike sectors would team up to restore coral reefs at large scale. Their paper was published in twenty twenty-four. Reefs feed and shield millions of people, yet current repair work falls far short of what is needed to protect them worldwide.

The team used Australia's Reef Restoration and Adaptation Program on the Great Barrier Reef as a case. They found would-be partners across ten sectors, bringing different mixes of gear, people, and organizing skill. Partners named nine roles they could play, many tied to growing the effort. Gains that drew them fell into seven classes, from helping nature to business openings and public standing. The paper maps what each side gives and gets, as a guide for building reef partnerships.
pmc-11650328:
Chaima Jemai and co-authors report lipodystrophy with an uncommon presentation in a patient with insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, in a case report from 2024. A woman aged sixty-seven had severe, repeat low blood sugar episodes that came at odd times. Her diabetes was long-standing and had been well controlled until five months before.

Exam found a firm, painless swelling at her favored insulin injection site on the abdomen. Needle reuse for up to a week and poor site rotation explained the fat growth, called lipohypertrophy. Insulin absorbed from such tissue in an erratic way, which drove the swings. The case warns on injection habits in insulin care.
pmc-11650628:
Xintong Xu and eight co-authors published a neuro-ophthalmology trial report in twenty twenty-four on an immune drug for a relapsing eye disease that had exhausted other options. Ten patients with MOG antibody-related optic neuritis, resistant to prior immunotherapies, received tocilizumab, which blocks an interleukin receptor, alone or added to existing treatment.

Seven of the ten stayed relapse-free over at least a year of follow-up. The median yearly relapse rate fell sharply from before treatment. Vision outcomes and side effects were tracked alongside. The trial was small, open-label, and uncontrolled, limits the authors state in the design itself. Still, for patients cycling through failed therapies, a seventy percent relapse-free rate makes the drug a serious candidate for controlled testing.
pmc-11653028:
The European Food Safety Authority issues a scientific opinion setting safe residue definitions and intake limits for ethiprole, a pesticide active substance not approved in Europe. The opinion came out in 2024. A company had applied for an import tolerance for ethiprole in rice, but the process was redirected to defining residues and safety values only.

From the toxicology data, the authority derived a daily intake limit and an acute reference dose for consumers. For enforcement, residues are defined simply as ethiprole itself, with validated methods able to detect it at very low levels in dry goods. For risk assessment, the definition also covers two breakdown products. The definitions apply to treated crops generally, and to processed foods as well.
pmc-11653828:
Victor Nguyen and colleagues link radiation dose to heart parts with later heart events in oesophageal cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-four reviews patients treated with definitive radiotherapy. Radiation cures can strain the heart over time. Which heart substructures matter most was unclear for this cancer.

Just over one hundred twenty patients had heart structures mapped automatically. Dose records were extracted for atria, ventricles, and heart muscle. Most patients already carried high cardiovascular risk at baseline. Serious heart events appeared in a notable share during follow-up. The team tested which dose measures tracked those events. Findings could help planners shield the most sensitive heart regions.
pmc-11653928:
Nobuyuki Nosaka, Ayako Noguchi, Takashi Takeuchi, and Kenji Wakabayashi published a 2024 follow-up study of PTSD symptoms in families of severe COVID-19 patients. A loved one's intensive care stay can scar relatives long after discharge, a burden the pandemic deepened. At a Tokyo hospital, 97 family members enrolled and 68 took part, answering surveys at 6, 12, and 18 months after discharge.

At least one PTSD-related symptom appeared in 26 percent of participants across the period, and the share did not fade: 16, 23, then 25 percent at the three checks. Fifteen percent showed delayed onset, with symptoms arriving late. Those with symptoms reported worse quality of life, above all in mental and social parts. The authors urge long-term support for ICU families.
pmc-11654128:
William Hoyos, Kenia Hoyos, Rander Ruiz, and Jose Aguilar build an explainable analysis of diabetes that blends statistics with artificial intelligence. Their 2024 study works with a small data set of social and clinical profiles from people with and without the disease. The aim is early detection plus a clear account of which factors drive the risk.

Classical tests first explored how variables associate with diabetes status. Four learning models then classified cases. One gradient boosting model scored perfectly on accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in their tests. A fuzzy cognitive map model stood out differently: it let the team trace how variables feed the prediction through scenarios. Pairing a strong classifier with a readable model serves both screening and clinical trust.
pmc-11654328:
Rong-xuan Hu and co-authors report a Chinese child carrying two autoimmune diseases at once, lupus and a spinal cord and optic nerve disorder, in a case report from two thousand twenty-four. Such pairing is known in adults but very rare in children. The girl, aged fourteen, arrived with fever, low blood counts, and kidney leakage.

The paper reviews her course and lab picture in detail. It then compares her case with earlier child reports in the literature. Both diseases attack through misdirected antibodies, though at different targets. The authors call for more study of how the two overlap in the young. Early spotting matters for both, they note.
pmc-11654428:
Ana Fandino and co-authors show how oregano oil vapor primes grapevines to resist downy mildew, in this 2024 paper. Growers want natural priming agents to cut synthetic and copper sprays. Earlier work found the vapor switches on defense genes; this study adds the chemistry side of the story.

Treated vines shifted their metabolite mix in telling ways. A pathway that builds defensive plant compounds was strongly modulated. Stress-response genes rose while a key antioxidant fell, matching an oxidative burst pattern. Terpenes and other likely antifungal compounds piled up. The combined picture explains how a scent can ready the vine's immune system before attack.
pmc-11655128:
Karina Tozatto-Maio and co-authors review inflammation pathways and anti inflammatory therapies in sickle cell disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. The disease stems from a single gene change, yet its course varies widely. Inflammation sits at its center and drives much of the harm.

Sickled hemoglobin breaks open red cells and frees heme, which sparks many inflammatory paths. Those paths feed a cycle of vessel blockage, cell rupture, and more swelling. The review maps the immune cells and signals at work. It asks whether swelling level predicts complications, a link still unproven. Many therapies cut inflammation, though patient outcomes vary a lot. Few markers now predict who will fare worst.
pmc-11655928:
Zhimin Wu and six co-authors build a survival predictor for throat cancer from seven long non-coding RNAs tied to mitochondria and drug resistance. The prognosis of laryngeal cancer worsens sharply when chemotherapy fails. The team combined cancer atlas and expression database data with a mitochondrial gene catalog, and screened for resistance-linked RNAs.

A stats screen narrowed the field to seven RNAs that form a risk model. It gave survival odds on its own, apart from other factors. Its scores at one, three, and five years beat some models that exist. High- and low-risk patients differed in immune activity, pathway enrichment, and drug sensitivity, in ways the team connect to treatment choice. A nomogram wraps the score for clinical use. The work puts mitochondrial non-coding RNAs forth as biomarkers of use.
pmc-11657128:
Li and Ye reviewed genetic testing for thalassemia in this paper from twenty twenty-four. The disease is an inherited blood disorder common in tropical and southern China. Its severe forms can kill infants or demand lifelong, costly care. Finding carriers before birth sharply cuts the number of severe cases.

Standard tests catch almost all carriers but miss rare gene variants. Third-generation sequencing reads long DNA stretches in one pass, which fills those gaps. The review walks through the alpha and beta forms of the disease and their risks. It compares the standard tools with the newer sequencing approach. The authors say the new method strengthens counseling and prenatal diagnosis in high-risk regions.
pmc-11657428:
Yulei Song and co-authors present a 2024 study on predicting nursing workload in digestive disease wards. Workload drives staffing choices and performance reviews, and it links closely to patient safety. Most past studies took a single snapshot, so they missed how needs shift day by day during a stay.

The team ran a forward-looking study in two general hospitals in China from March 2019 to August 2021. They tracked 133 patients over 1,339 hospital days and timed the direct care each one received. Regression picked out patient traits that drove nursing time. Machine learning models then learned to predict each patient's daily need. Daily workload varied widely across stays, which supports dynamic staffing plans.
pmc-11662928:
Ben Cashen and seven co-authors study a protein from LINE-1, a jumping gene that has copied itself across much of the human genome. The protein, ORF1p, coats the gene's RNA copy and helps it paste into new spots. It can also help other jumping elements move. The team used optical tweezers, which pull on single molecules with light, to watch how the protein coats a single strand of DNA.

How the coating acts depends on how much protein is present. At just enough protein to coat the strand, the bundle is tight and stable. Extra protein loosens the bundle and lets it grab a second strand at once. The authors suggest this loosening may free coated RNA during copying. Freed bundles could then be stolen by other elements, which would explain how they spread.
pmc-11666528:
Lin Yao led a team reviewing acupuncture for primary insomnia in a 2024 paper. Long-term sleeplessness harms health, work, and quality of life. Standard drugs bring side effects and dependence risk. Clinical work suggests needle therapy is safe and improves sleep in this condition, and pairing it with drugs can raise benefit while lowering drug dose.

The review gathers clinical and lab evidence on how the therapy acts in the brain. It reports shifts in brain regions tied to thinking and emotion, plus changes in body chemicals, clock genes, inflammation, and energy use. Even one session shifted brain activity like repeated sessions. The authors call for larger, high-quality trials with brain imaging.
pmc-11667128:
Orthelo Léonel Gbètoho Atigossou and co-authors set out, in a 2024 protocol, a study of how assistive devices affect people with disabilities in Benin. Many people in low-resource countries need at least one such device for daily function, yet proof of how well the devices serve them is scarce. The study will survey device users across the country.

Standard tools will score mental state, device satisfaction, felt function gains, well-being, and life quality. A rapid survey from the World Health Organization adds background on use and access. Recruitment began in late 2024, with a year of data gathering planned. Results will be sorted by a known outcome frame covering effect, social weight, and personal well-being.
pmc-11667628:
Greta Lisa Carlin and four co-authors report a layered repair for pelvic organ prolapse after radical bladder removal. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-four. The earlier surgery weakens pelvic support, and this patient's prolapse had already resisted two repairs.

The seventy-year-old woman's second repair had also torn at the vaginal cuff. Surgeons checked the belly for scar tissue and tumor return. Dead tissue at the vaginal top was removed. A thigh muscle flap was laid in a Z pattern over the pelvic opening. The entry was then partly closed by an older technique. A year later, anatomy held and the patient was highly satisfied. The team credits close work across three specialties.
pmc-11672128:
Munekazu Motoyama and a team of co-authors watch lithium form at a battery interface, live under a microscope, in two thousand twenty-four. Controlling how lithium starts and grows is key to metal batteries that can be recharged many times. Gold alloy layers lower the push needed for lithium to start, but the alloying step itself was unclear.

Using a microscope that can tell apart heavy and light elements and surface shape, they saw uneven processes at the interface. Some lithium dissolved again even as more was being laid down. Lithium seemed to start as an unstable phase inside the alloy film. That spread the growth sites out, which could help even wear.
pmc-11672628:
Yaks raised indoors for meat grow better on rich feed, but heavy grain diets can disturb the stomach microbes that keep them healthy. Ben Zhang and co-authors feed sixteen young yaks two diets in this 2024 study, one with forty percent concentrate and one with sixty, then track growth, blood, and rumen bacteria.

The richer diet raised daily intake and weight gain, plus a blood protein marker. Gut microbe mixes shifted clearly, with one major group gaining share and another losing it. Predicted microbe functions changed too, toward pathways tied to tissue interaction. The authors conclude rich feed fattens yaks while reshaping their inner ecosystem.
pmc-11672928:
Kang Liu and co-authors test two cheap markers for bacterial infection in a child's swollen testicle cord in a 2024 study. The condition, acute epididymitis, is often not bacterial in children, yet most patients still receive antibiotics. A sharper test could spare needless drugs.

Records from a Taiwan hospital covered 289 boys treated over a decade. Urine cultures split cases into bacterial and non-bacterial groups. About a third of tested cases grew bacteria, while three quarters of all patients got antibiotics anyway. The team compared a blood inflammation marker against urine dipstick results for accuracy. Both are routine and fast, so the winner could guide everyday decisions. The study quantifies how much overtreatment current habits produce.
pmc-11673228:
Mario Peñacoba and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on planning routes for disinfection robots. The head byline lists four authors while the catalog names seven, so the work is described with team framing. These robots roam rooms shining ultraviolet light that kills germs on surfaces. A poor route wastes time, leaves spots untouched, or overexposes some areas.

The team tuned routes with four algorithms copied from nature: gazelle escapes, whale hunting spirals, bat echo hunting, and flocking swarms. Each adjusts the robot's path and its pauses at key points. Tests showed the methods adapted routes well to varied room layouts. Hospitals and hotels could use such planning to clean faster and more evenly.
pmc-11674028:
Selma Tvrtković-Hasandić and Pınar Ünal-Aydın test a virtual reality mindfulness program for gaming disorder in a 2024 paper. Problem gamers often quit talk therapy because sessions feel long and dull. Headset scenes, by contrast, pull the same gadget-loving attention toward calm focus. The program ran four weekly sessions of twenty minutes each.

Nine patients with the disorder took the program, beside ten casual gamers and eight non-gamers as comparisons. Symptoms and weekend gaming time fell clearly in the patient group after treatment. The sample is tiny, and the authors treat the result as a first signal. A short, attractive format could keep patients in care long enough for mindfulness to work.
pmc-11674128:
Sonia Choudhary and co-authors study a tiny freshwater alga that can clean metal pollution while making useful products, in a 2024 paper. The alga, Chlorella minutissima, faces trivalent chromium, a toxic metal that builds up in water and harms health. Microalgae are attractive because they can absorb such pollutants and also yield oils for biofuel and other valuable compounds. The study probes how the alga defends itself against the metal.

The team combined chromium removal with boosting the alga's lipid stores and its outer sugar layers, called EPS. The goal is a single process that treats waste water and produces feedstocks at once, a biorefinery idea. Results help judge whether this alga could serve farms, fuel makers, and cleanup crews at the same time.
pmc-11675128:
Lin and co-authors test two part adds on froze egg rolls for hot pot fare. Egg rolls are a core part of old Chinese hot pot meals. They ship most by cold chains, which sets their store needs. Freeze and thaw can weep the gel and bend its feel. Adds in view are whey part and soy part at three loads. A bent root starch joins the adds at three loads too.

Weep fell from 9 point 01 percent to 1 point 16 percent in top mix runs. That mix held 3 percent starch and 2 percent whey part. Soy at 1 point 0 percent cut weep to 2 point 01 percent. Whey at 1 point 0 percent cut it to 3 point 05 percent. The top mix also held feel best past 15 days froze. That held with 20 percent more wet in the rolls.
pmc-11675328:
Daniel Waweru and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on stirring the pulp of an African fruit into cow's milk yogurt. The fruit, from the kei apple tree, is rich in vitamin C and plant compounds but little used in dairy goods. The team made yogurts with up to fifteen percent pulp and watched them weekly through three weeks of cold storage. They tracked chemistry, microbes, texture, and taste scores.

More pulp meant more vitamin C, polyphenols, fiber, acidity, and yellow color. It also meant less fat, protein, thickness, and lower taste scores from the panel. Moisture, ash, and water-holding did not move with pulp level. Over storage, acidity rose and pH fell while thickness held. No coliforms, yeasts, or molds appeared in any batch. The team calls the fruit a strong candidate for nutritious fruit yogurts, with taste tuning still to do.
pmc-11675928:
Isabella Delgado and co-authors study falls in older adults who feel their memory is slipping, in a paper from 2024. Falls can cost older people their health, freedom, and money. Memory complaints rise with age, but how they link to falls is less clear.

The team ran a case-control study in adults over fifty years old. Each person took memory and thinking tests and a timed walk test. People who fell were older and more often had high blood pressure. They also had more past stumbles, slower walk times, and uneven arm swing. Weak word fluency and weak copying of a complex shape were also more common. The strongest risks were being female, older age, high blood pressure, and past stumbles. The authors urge wider checks in fall risk reviews.
pmc-11676128:
Milenkovic and co-authors measure a protein called renalase in people with chronic myeloid leukemia. The cancer's inflamed setting may be one reason standard drugs fail to control it fully. Renalase calms inflammation and protects cells from death. It appears in many tissues, including tumors. The team compared blood levels in new patients, patients in remission on therapy, and healthy people.

New, untreated patients had far lower renalase than every other group. Levels in treated patients sat closer to normal. The drugs in use were imatinib and nilotinib, both standard for this leukemia. The shift hints that therapy partly restores the protein's balance. The authors see renalase as a marker worth tracking.
pmc-11676228:
Hee Jin Cho and co-authors look at data on gene activity, to show roles, split by cell type, for odorant receptors in glioblastoma. Their 2024 transcriptomic study deals with receptors best known for smell, but found more and more in other parts of the body.

The team joined large atlas data with single-cell sequencing from patients. They mapped patterns for the receptors across cell types in the tumour. One receptor, at high levels in cells that back blood vessels, was linked to remodelling of vessels and to angiogenesis. A second was tied to tumour macrophages that back suppression of the immune response. A third was tied to synaptic activity in tumours that came back. That may show neurons that adapt as care is given. Glioblastoma is highly aggressive, with a short median survival. The team puts these receptors forth as targets that may be of use for therapy.
pmc-11676428:
Eltahir and a large team tested frankincense resin against kidney damage in rats in twenty twenty-four. The resin comes from Boswellia serrata trees. Kidneys filter blood and face many toxic threats; a chemical called CCl4 is a standard way to injure them in the lab through oxidative stress and inflammation.

Rats got CCl4 twice weekly for six weeks, then two weeks of resin extract or a standard protective drug, silymarin. The resin improved kidney function markers and antioxidant status. It sharply cut inflammatory signals, including TNF-alpha and several interleukins, plus a scarring factor. Tissue under the microscope also looked healthier. The authors credit the resin's antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions and see therapeutic potential worth further study.
pmc-11676928:
Cristina Hernandez leads a team on how sitagliptin eye drops spread. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses male rabbits for early stage tests. Early diabetic eye disease lacks good cures at this time.

The drops aim to guard nerves and small vessels in the eye. They do so sans any gain in blood sugar control. Rabbits got drops at two strengths for this work. Blood and eye parts were sampled at set times after dosing. A lab method measured drug levels in each sample. Drug curves in eye and blood were then worked out.
pmc-11677128:
Pengyu Guo and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on a tomato gene that sits where three hormone signals meet. The transcription factor SlUPA-like was already known to shift jasmonate responses and gibberellin levels when overproduced. Deeper tests showed it also moves brassinolide amounts, and gene-wide scans found hormone pathway genes widely retuned.

Protein interaction tests tied the factor to three partners from the three pathways. It also switches on a gibberellin-related gene directly, by gripping a short motif in that gene's promoter. The authors frame the factor as a crosstalk node coordinating growth signals, and a base for further work on tomato development.
pmc-11678728:
Jia-Lu Li and seven co-authors test how wide flower strips beside maize fields should be to shelter pest-eating spiders and beetles, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Three strip widths were compared with plain maize controls over two years.

Flower strips clearly beat controls for both predator groups, and the four- and six-meter strips held the most biodiversity. Communities grouped tightly by strip type in the first year and blended more in the second. Spider activity peaked at the edges of four-meter strips and was lowest in two-meter strips. Beetles also favored wider strips' edges. Neither predator wandered far into the crop. The authors recommend strips of at least four meters to lift natural pest control.
pmc-11678828:
Dali Ge and co-authors build a light powered slider in this 2024 paper. The slider moves itself across a surface with uneven friction. Its motor is a string made of liquid crystal elastomer, a material that contracts when heated by light. The system holds a hollow slide, two such fibers, and a mass ball.

As the ball moves, the fibers pass in and out of light and contract in turn. That steady cycle feeds energy back into the motion. Uneven friction turns the back and forth motion into steady forward travel. The team derived the governing equations and simulated two modes. They also map the conditions needed to start moving and the traits that set speed.
pmc-11678928:
Luca Tonietti and a large team review a bacterium that leaches metals from ores. Their review from twenty twenty-four covers Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans. The bacterium thrives in extreme acid conditions that kill most life. It frees a wide range of valuable and toxic elements.

Its chemistry produces iron ions that attack metal sulfides. That attack releases elements from lithium to uranium. The review explains mechanisms behind each mobilisation route. Biomining with this organism cuts energy use versus smelting. Recovery of industrial metals from low-grade ores improves as well. The authors map where this microbe already serves mining. Greener extraction methods gain a versatile biological worker.
pmc-11680128:
Peter Bennett and co-authors map the demographics of lymphoma in Australian cats across more than seventeen hundred cases. Their 2024 study compares those cases with a reference population of tens of thousands of clinic cats. Lymphoma is the most common blood cancer of cats, yet large local studies of breed and sex risk were missing.

Eight breeds showed higher potential risk and three showed lower. Male cats carried modestly higher odds than females. Cases were older and lighter than controls on average. Some breeds also differed in where in the body the cancer appeared. Australia's isolation and quarantine rules make its cat gene pool distinctive, so local numbers guide local screening and breeding advice.
pmc-11683728:
Lundström and four co-authors used a Swedish-wide list in twenty twenty-four to test if the count of loose tumor bits in bowel cancer sets outlook. Such bits are known to worsen outlook when no nodes are hit, but stage rules skip them when nodes are hit. They tracked folks who had curative cuts in a four-year span.

More than fourteen thousand folks were in the check, and one in eight had such bits. Life at five years fell step by step as bit count rose. Spread to far sites rose with count in the same way. Count held as a lone bad sign past nodes and prior care.
pmc-11686228:
Kazim Panjwani and co-authors profile single immune cells in a 2024 study to trace where a special kind of natural killer cell comes from. Natural killer cells are part of the fast, innate arm of immunity. Yet people who have had a common virus, cytomegalovirus, often carry a distinct group of these cells that acts like memory, a trait of the slower adaptive arm.

The team measured the traits, gene activity, and function of killer cell subsets one cell at a time. They found immature precursors of the adaptive cells in people with and without the virus alike. The adaptive cells showed a gene program apart from most mature killer cells, one shared with a bright immature subset. The work draws a family line from a naive-like start to the virus-shaped memory state.
pmc-11689528:
Qi Li and four co-authors map patterns of sitting time in Chinese care homes, in twenty twenty-four. Their study covers two hundred eighty-three adults in eleven homes. Each person had lived in the home at least three months and was aged sixty-five or older. They reported daily time spent on eight seated acts, such as watching TV, chatting, and doing nothing, over the past week.

Mean seated time was close to twelve hours a day. Four patterns emerged, from a high-sitting group to a balanced group. Two patterns, high sitting and high passive sitting, linked to higher low mood scores than the balanced group. A small group sat much but kept their minds active.
pmc-11690328:
Charles Hoy-Ellis and Karen Fredriksen-Goldsen published this 2024 symposium overview on fortitude among sexual and gender minority older adults, drawn from the Aging with Pride national study. This population ages under stacked adversities, and the studies in the symposium, cross-sectional and longitudinal, hunt for their strengths as much as their wounds.

One presentation maps the heavy burden of violence and abuse on older transgender adults, tying partner violence and stigma to mental health. A second tackles the digital divide in health technology use. A third asks what predicts generativity, the drive to give to younger generations, and how social resources blunt stigma. Together the talks argue that health and identity navigation, handled well, become sources of resilience services should build on.
pmc-11691628:
Amarjot Gill and Suzanne Sullivan published a review in 2024 on older adults' experiences of loneliness inside residential care facilities. Moving into a care home detaches residents from their meaningful social relationships. That loneliness can harm health and disrupt well-being and quality of life.

The pair searched four databases for studies in English from 2018 to 2023. Of more than seven thousand articles found, only ten fit. Three core themes emerged from those studies. One was about how loneliness is experienced differently by each person and relationship. One was about perception and emotional distress. The last was about how the setting and a person's own thoughts shape the experience. The review builds a model of the underlying process. It points to the perceived loss of control over one's life as a key trigger of loneliness in such homes.
pmc-11691728:
Leah Hanson and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on the role of gait speed, sense of smell, and psychological factors in cognitive function among older adults. Slower walking, loss of smell, and increased depression, anxiety, and stress have all been linked to lower scores.

The study sits within a Minnesota project following adults aged fifty-five and older. Each year, participants complete a cognitive assessment, a smell test, and a gait speed test, plus questionnaires on mood, stress, and social support. Smell and gait scores were both linked to those scores. Both were worse in impaired participants than in intact ones. More reported complaints came with lower scores. Participants with greater resilience and social support reported fewer complaints, while those with more stress and depression reported more. Smell and gait pointed to who would decline over the next five years.
pmc-11691828:
Karen Tracy and co-authors survey clinicians on blood tests for Alzheimer's disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. Blood based markers of amyloid and tau could make diagnosis faster and cheaper than brain scans or spinal fluid tests. A global initiative is preparing clinics for wide use of such tests.

Family doctor and aging society members answered surveys in spring twenty twenty-four. They shared current awareness of the tests, views on their value, and how they might use them in practice. They also named what they need to trust the tests: more knowledge and clearer guidance. Early detection matters since timely diagnosis still lags in clinics. The results guide training for the roll out.
pmc-11691928:
Brandy Weathers and co-authors study why worms with a stress-defense switch stuck in the on position stop avoiding a dangerous bacterium, in a 2024 paper. The switch, a protein called SKN-1, is the worm version of a human defense regulator. Normal worms learn to crawl away from the pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The switched-on worms stay and keep feeding on it.

The team traced the apathy to the switch acting in neurons and gut tissue at once, which scrambled serotonin signaling in both places. Serotonin levels dropped sharply in the mutant worms. Adding serotonin from outside largely restored normal avoidance. The authors argue the case shows how a defense program, when left running, can blunt the chemical signals an animal needs to steer away from harm. The work was done in a standard lab roundworm.
pmc-11694028:
Wanqing Wang and co-authors review FBXW7, a tumor-suppressor gene that tags growth-promoting proteins for destruction. The protein acts as the recognition part of a cellular shredding machine. In gut cancers especially, the gene is often mutated or deleted, letting its targets pile up and drive growth, spread, and drug resistance. The review lays out how the protein works, which cancer-driving substrates it controls, and what its loss does to tumors of the stomach, bowel, and liver.

The authors discuss the gene's promise as a marker for prognosis and for choosing treatment. They also sketch strategies that aim at the pathways unleashed when the gene fails, since the missing shredder itself is hard to replace with a drug. The review is aimed at researchers planning precision treatments for gastrointestinal cancers. It argues that a patient's FBXW7 status should inform trial design and therapy choice.
pmc-11710328:
Jack C Taylor tested whether fine details from a short phone task can track the severity of frontotemporal dementia, in a study published in 2025. The task, part of a mobile app built for this disease group, asks users to respond to arrows on a screen. It takes about two minutes and one hundred trials.

Taylor pulled hundreds of timing measures from the task scores of people with early or clear symptoms and from healthy controls. Simple models sorted controls from people with symptoms well, and the new measures helped most at the clearer stage. A basic total score did just as well for the earliest group. The work shows phone tasks could give clinics a quick, low-cost way to follow change over time.
pmc-11710828:
Chelsea N Johnson and co-authors study diet, sex, and gene effects on muscle energy in a 2025 mouse report. The APOE4 gene variant is the strongest common genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease, and its carriers show altered body metabolism. Muscle burns much of the body's fuel, yet how the variant affects muscle was little known.

The team fed mice with the human APOE3 or APOE4 gene a high-fat or low-fat diet for four months. In females with APOE4, the low-fat diet already shifted energy proteins. The high-fat diet changed hundreds of muscle proteins in that group alone, and raised their fuel burning. Other groups changed far less. The authors say muscle may help explain how this gene shapes whole-body metabolism.
pmc-11711128:
Hee Jin Park and colleagues test a live gut bacterium against systemic sclerosis in mice, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The disease, in which immunity attacks the self, stiffens skin and organs, with no treatments that work well. Gut microbes are suspected in how it starts. Patient blood showed low antibodies against one gut species.

That species, a Bifidobacterium strain called RAPO, was fed to sclerosis-model mice. Skin and lung fibrosis eased after treatment. Inflammatory monocytes and macrophages moved in less, and pro-inflammatory signals fell. Gut diversity came back, and short-chain fatty acid producers grew in number. Fecal butyrate rose, and its receptor was upregulated in lymph nodes. In culture, the bacterium and its fluid calmed macrophage genes for inflammation. It also blocked fibroblasts from turning into scar-forming myofibroblasts. The findings support live-bacterium treatment as a fibrosis strategy.
pmc-11712328:
Naaheed Mukadam and a large group of co-authors report how dementia experts weigh risk factors in a 2025 commission update. An earlier Lancet report listed twelve changeable risks, from hearing loss to smoking, that might prevent up to forty percent of dementia cases. The group met again to check the old list and judge new candidate risks.

The experts used a life-course view, since risks act at different ages. They weighed review papers and fresh analyses, and debated how strong each claim was. They also asked whether risks hit some ethnic or income groups harder. Two new risks had strong enough support to join the model. The report also names risks that fell short, to guide future research.
pmc-11712628:
Noelle Callizot and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how lecanemab, an approved drug for Alzheimer's disease, changes the brain's immune and support cells. The drug binds early clumps of amyloid, a protein that builds up in the illness. What it does to the cells that react to those clumps was still vague.

The team grew rat brain cells in dishes, harmed them with amyloid, and added the drug an hour before. They also gave the drug to aged mice with amyloid placed in the brain. Amyloid alone raised the share of attack-ready immune cells. The paper tracks how the drug shifts those cell states in both setups, which may help explain how it works.
pmc-11712728:
Lukas Heinrich and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a tiny brain stem hub that may help some older adults keep their thinking despite Alzheimer's changes. The hub is among the first places tau lands. People with rich schooling and work history also tend to hold up better, a shield known as cognitive reserve.

The team scanned 154 adults from a Harvard aging study and grouped them by reserve and disease load. In the high-load, high-reserve group, a sounder hub went with slower loss of thinking over time. The result ties the hub to the reserve effect in living people. It hints that guarding this small hub could matter a lot.
pmc-11713128:
Melita H Terry and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on keeping community partnerships alive after a research study finishes recruiting. Efforts to include more diverse groups in dementia research have poured money into recruitment. The authors argue that trust with communities of color starts long before recruitment and should not end when it closes.

Drawing on their work at a federally funded Alzheimer's research center, they separate trust-building from the narrower task of signing people up. Real cases from their program show the steps that keep partners engaged over years. Lasting ties, they argue, help future studies and honor what communities give to research.
pmc-11713228:
Joyce Chan and Kelvin Tsoi pooled the trial evidence in 2025 on virtual reality as treatment for mild mental impairment, the borderland state between normal aging and dementia. Mental training and actual exercise each help such patients, and virtual reality can deliver both at once, wrapping memory tasks in engaging modeled worlds or guiding motion games. Whether the mix truly boosts cognition, beyond novelty and focus, was unproven at the level of joined evidence.

The reviewers searched the major medical and psychology data stores for randomized controlled trials of VR-based mental training, exercise. Or both in people with mild mental impairment, pooling global mental function and memory measured by standard tests as standardized mean gaps. Sixteen trials with just under nine hundred people. Whose average ages spanned the late sixties to late eighties, met the rules, and subgroup studies separated the effects by the kind of virtual reality intervention used.
pmc-11713328:
Yi Lu and co-authors study how a drug called bexarotene changes gene activity in mouse brains, in this 2025 paper. The mice carry genes that mimic Alzheimer's disease. Earlier work found that the drug helped the mice clear amyloid and think better.

The team treated the mice with the drug or a plain control, then read gene activity cell by cell. They also mapped how open or closed each cell's DNA was, using two single-cell methods. Joining the two maps shows which cell types respond to the drug and which gene networks switch on. The results may help explain how the drug protects the brain.
pmc-11713528:
Ruiz-Castillo and co-authors link bone fracture risk to thinking scores in older adults in Mexico, in this 2025 paper. Weak bones and dementia often appear together, yet proof from lower-income countries is thin. A standard tool scores fracture risk from health facts even without a bone scan.
