The study enrolled five hundred adults aged sixty and older at a dementia clinic. Each person got a fracture risk score, a brief thinking test, a brain scan, and a broad health review. Higher fracture risk went with worse thinking scores, the title reports. The authors weigh what shared causes, such as frailty or poor blood flow, might explain the link.
pmc-11713828:
Byron Jaeger and co-authors revisit long-term deaths in the SPRINT blood pressure trial in this 2025 report. The trial tested a tight systolic target below 120 against standard care. It enrolled adults aged fifty and over with high blood pressure and raised heart risk. People with diabetes or a past stroke were not included. Tight control cut heart events and deaths during the trial itself.

After the trial ended in 2015, blood pressure levels drifted up in both groups. An earlier check with about four years of added data saw the benefit fade. This report uses a newer data set with about eight years of follow-up. Deaths were tracked through a national death index. The authors re-test whether the early gain in survival held over the longer span. The answer matters for how hard clinics should push blood pressure down.
pmc-11714328:
Xiaoyan Leng and eight co-authors ask whether a wide mix of daily activities goes with sharper thinking in older adults, in a 2025 conference paper. Variety counts both how many kinds of activity a person does and how evenly time is spread. Past work links high variety to better scores, apart from how often a person is active.

The data come from the U.S. POINTER study, with 1,688 adults at the start point. The group had a mean age near 68, and two thirds were women. The team scored variety across 41 mental, physical, and social activities. They then matched variety to scores for memory, speed, and planning. Models also weighed age, schooling, health, and area need. The study helps set the base for a lifestyle trial now under way.
pmc-11714528:
Julien Lagarde and co-authors study patients who look like early onset Alzheimer's cases but whose amyloid scans come back clear, in a 2025 conference paper. In one large study, about a quarter of such patients test negative for amyloid. Their true illness is thus in doubt.

The team gave 74 of these patients a second scan that maps brain fuel use. A data driven method, checked twelve ways, split patients into normal and low fuel groups. The team then compared the groups on clinic facts, brain shape scans, and fluid tests. A grouping method searched for shared low fuel patterns among the low group. The aim is to sort out which other illnesses hide behind the early onset label.
pmc-11715128:
Melanie Campbell and co-authors used light tricks to tell two kinds of protein clumps apart in the eye. The retina at the back of the eye is part of the brain's own tissue. Clumps of amyloid mark Alzheimer's disease, while clumps of alpha synuclein mark two other brain diseases. If the eye shows which clump is which, a quick scan could sort patients early.

Donated eyes and brains came from twelve people with known brain states. The team lit the flat-mounted retinas with polarized light and read how each clump bent it. Hundreds of clumps were read across the three disease groups. On their own, most light measures blurred the two clump kinds. Mixed as a set, though, they let two smart programs sort the kinds well. The work backs the eye as a cheap window on brain disease.
pmc-11715328:
Tsz Wing Fan and co-authors published this methods paper in two thousand twenty-five on a new test for faint brain markers in blood. Markers like neurofilament light chain can warn of nerve harm, but they occur in tiny amounts that most tests miss or measure only with costly gear.

The team's method, called SPEAR, uses a two-key check that wipes out background noise. It needs no washing steps, runs on common lab gear, and reads results on standard PCR machines. With a single microliter of diluted blood plasma, it matched the reach of leading tests. Checks for accuracy, repeat runs, and mix-ups with like proteins all came out well. The authors say the method could make frequent, large-scale blood screening for brain disease far cheaper and easier.
pmc-11715428:
Guglielmo Di Molfetta and co-authors tried a new blood panel that reads more than a hundred brain-linked proteins at once. Most blood tests for Alzheimer's disease read one sign at a time. A wide panel could find extra signs with added worth. The team ran the panel on folk with mild thought loss whose amyloid state was known.

Two cohorts took part, one small and one larger, with one hundred thirty-one samples in all. In the small group, one tau sign stood alone past a strict bar. In the larger group, three tau signs and a support-cell sign all held past that bar. The top tau sign led in both groups by a wide gap. The panel thus backs the known lead sign and gives a way to hunt for more in one run.
pmc-11721228:
Biyang Zhou and ten co-authors study how dormant viruses inside a staph bacterium change its defenses in a 2024 paper. Many clinical staph strains carry integrated phages that switch off a bacterial enzyme. That enzyme breaks down fats from blood, and its activity affects which fats end up in the bacterial membrane.

The team shows a toxic fat from blood harms the bacterium when it builds up in the membrane. A second fat, released by the enzyme, competes with the toxic one for uptake. When the enzyme is off, toxic fat rises and the bacterium adapts more slowly to a certain antibiotic. Blocking both fat synthesis and the enzyme may form a useful combined treatment strategy.
pmc-11722128:
Laurenz Ursch and a large team of co-authors study the genomic safety of CRISPR-edited T cells in two thousand twenty-four. Such edited cells lead new cancer treatments, but CRISPR can cause large deletions and chromosome errors. Past safety work focused on the editing tools, less on the T cells themselves.

The team found that strong T cell stimulation and fast growth correlate with larger deletions. Editing quiet, non-activated cells cut that risk but lowered knockout rates. Adding a small molecule, pifithrin-alpha, also limited deletions, translocations, and chromosome count errors. It did so without hurting the cells' function, including in CAR T cells. Both strategies are easy to adopt, the authors say.
pmc-11725428:
Leanne Lee Leung and three co-authors review tiny sacs shed by cells as a test source for mouth cancer in this 2024 survey. Such sacs ride in spit, blood, and node fluid and carry scraps of the cells that shed them. A fluid test based on them could spot cancer with no cut. It might also track how well a cure works.

The survey spans twenty years of work in English. Seventeen case sets met the field's own guide lines: ten from spit, six from blood, and one from node fluid. The gaps are plain. Few teams run wide multi-part reads of sac cargo. Marks of drug strength in sacs are barely probed. And the chip tools that could take sac tests to the clinic sit near unused. The field, the four say, has hope but much ground to win.
pmc-11726728:
Seba Shbailat and Ibtisam Aslan track digestion genes in duck embryos in a 2024 paper. How the yolk sac and gut split the work of digesting yolk protein was unexplored in ducks. They measured several enzyme and transporter genes in the yolk sac across incubation, plus a stomach enzyme in the gut's first chamber and transporters in the small intestine. Each gene followed its own timetable.

Yolk sac activity peaked late, then fell, matching roles in breaking down and absorbing yolk peptides and fats. The stomach chamber's enzyme peaked mid-incubation. Transporters were strongest in the mid and end gut at hatch, marking them as the main uptake sites.
pmc-11728128:
Kryg and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on nanocellulose films for protecting wooden artefacts. Cracked historic wood needs patches that shield without harming looks. Plain cellulose nanopapers prove brittle, stiff, and wavy. Chemical treatment with silanes packs their structure tighter. Treated papers hold far less moisture and resist mould slightly better. Glycerol softening makes the papers flexible, flatter, and smoother. Softened papers do take up more moisture and mould more easily, though.

All versions glue onto wood and take color from common finishes. The team judge silane-treated, glycerol-softened papers most promising. They could slow further decay of cracked surfaces. The study weighs each tweak's trade-offs in detail.
pmc-11728728:
Thin films of aluminum mixed with molybdenum can be far harder than plain aluminum. The authors made such films with molybdenum content up to about ten percent, using a sputtering method that deposits both metals at once. They studied the films with X-ray and microscope tools and tested hardness by pressing a tiny tip into the surface. Some molybdenum atoms dissolved inside the aluminum crystals. The rest gathered at the borders between crystals, more strongly as the content rose.

No new compounds formed in any film. As molybdenum increased, the crystals grew smaller and the hardness climbed from 2.2 to 4.9 gigapascals. The team split the gain into parts: finer grains gave the largest share, over sixty percent. Dissolved atoms gave about thirty percent, and a pinning effect of atoms in tiny crystals gave the rest. The study explains why these alloy films strengthen as they do.
pmc-11757928:
Jean-Baptiste Koehl and five colleagues published a geology study in two thousand twenty-four on ancient magmatism beneath Svalbard. The islands' younger volcanic history is well studied, but Paleozoic events hid under sediment with few outcrops. Seismic surveys offered a way to see them.

Reflection data revealed west-dipping sills in eastern Spitsbergen dating to the Devonian and Mississippian. They cut an older thrust system and lie beneath much younger, undisturbed rocks. Mineral clues link them to diamond-bearing kimberlites of northwestern Russia. The authors read the sills as products of crustal stretching after mountain building. They may belong to a vast igneous province spanning the northern hemisphere.
pmc-11782128:
Liam Forbes and four co-authors test light switches for gene use in a photosynthetic germ. Their study head is dated twenty twenty-four. Such germs can turn waste gas into goods as green cell shops, but fine gene dials are few. Two light switch kits from kin germs were put in one strain and read by glow and gene tests.

One kit, of non-germ birth, ran weak with a small span past tries to lift it. The kin-born kit sang: green light hiked glow six-fold in half an hour. Gene reads taped on-off speed, and a tweak to its out switch hiked force more. Cross-kind ports are hard, the team stress.
pmc-11794528:
Paul Leon-Gomez and Vanessa Romero review how vaginal microbes may shape cervical cancer in a paper published in 2024. Lasting infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus is the main driver of this cancer. Yet only a small share of infected women develop cancer, so other factors must matter. The review asks what role the vaginal microbiome plays.

The authors searched three databases for studies that join microbe data, virus status, and cancer stage. Healthy women tended to host a narrow mix rich in Lactobacillus. Infected women showed a wider mix, with more of several other genera linked to imbalance. Two genera stood out as possible markers of infection and progression. Gene activity in patients also shifted with the microbe mix. The authors say the links look real but need firmer proof.
pmc-11804128:
Dag Ottesen and three colleagues published a geology study in two thousand twenty-four on the glacial past of the North Sea. How often ice sheets covered the central basin has long been disputed. Old readings claimed several early advances.

Detailed 3D seismic images showed landforms and sediments under the seabed at fine scale. A single ground-ice advance from Norway during the Early Pleistocene appears in the record, probably about one point one million years ago. It left till up to one hundred twenty metres thick across over ten thousand square kilometres. The rest of the period shows seabed pockmarks and current-carved grooves, not ice. The findings reconcile sea and land evidence for northwest Europe.
pmc-11842328:
Longfei Duan and co-authors assemble the genome of a konjac plant and probe how it resists a blight, in this study published in 2024. The plant, Amorphophallus albus, is a cash crop prized for a thickening gum in its corms and for standing up to disease better than its kin. Southern blight is the threat they focus on.

The genome came out at about 5.9 billion letters, arranged at chromosome scale with nearly twenty thousand gene families. Its size hints at a recent doubling of the whole genome. The team then tracked gene activity and small molecules across three stages of infection. Defense chemistry lit up along a few shared routes, including the making of protective plant compounds and hormone signals that raise the alarm. The authors say the genome and the defense map give breeders a base for stronger konjac lines.
pmc-11863728:
Kristie Hing Chi Leung and co-authors check whether eye blood vessels mirror Alzheimer's disease in a 2024 pilot study. The retina at the back of the eye shares tiny vessels with the brain. Eye photos are cheap and painless, unlike brain scans. Past work tied eye vessels to cases judged by symptoms alone, which can be wrong.

Here, each case was confirmed by brain scans showing the disease proteins. A wide-field eye camera captured much more of the retina than older photos did. Software measured vessel width and branching in fine detail. Vessel traits differed between confirmed patients and healthy adults. Eye screening will not replace brain scans, but it may help flag who needs one.
pmc-11887828:
Dibakar Borthakur and four co-authors report an unusual nerve pattern in a 2024 case. During routine teaching dissection of a sixty-seven-year-old man's arm, one nerve was missing on the left side. That nerve normally supplies three upper-arm muscles and forearm skin. Here a small branch from a nearby cord fed one muscle directly. The neighboring median nerve supplied the other two muscles and continued as the skin nerve of the forearm.

Such takeovers can confuse clinical and electrical tests for nerve injury, the authors warn. They propose adding a new subcategory for this pattern to the existing classification of variations for this nerve.
pmc-11939128:
Madison Wesenberg and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of how students judge a campus sexual violence scenario. Known risk factors for perpetration include heavy drinking, rape-supportive attitudes, and bad peer influence. Whether students weigh those factors was untested.

Nearly three hundred students read a vignette with or without the three risk factors present. Their risk perceptions of the person causing harm were then measured. The factors did not significantly move student judgments. Students seemed to rely on intuition over evidence-based cues. The authors discuss what that means for campus safety education and prevention programs.
pmc-11972428:
Pearl Amber Väth and four co-authors tested whether adding brain talk to an explanation makes people rate it as better than it is, in this 2024 study. The effect, called the seductive allure of neuroscience explanations, has been reported before: empty brain details can flatter weak explanations. The team ran a classroom experiment and then a larger online replication.

In the classroom, students actually rated good explanations without the extra brain detail highest. In the online study with 430 people, good explanations beat bad ones at every expertise level, with or without the added detail. Even so, the added brain talk lifted ratings among less expert readers. The authors argue for teaching that trains people to tell real explanations from dressed-up ones.
pmc-11975528:
Xu Liu and co-authors published this study in 2024. It asks whether an ultrasound stiffness scan can reveal the biology of invasive breast cancer without extra tissue tests. The scan, shear wave elastography, measures how stiff a tumor is, and stiffness often mirrors how aggressive a cancer is.

The team scanned 258 confirmed malignant lumps and compared five stiffness readings against pathology reports. Several readings tracked tumor size, type, and grade, and two tracked spread to armpit lymph nodes and vessel invasion. A new measure introduced here, the characteristic frequency of the mass, tracked the hormone receptors that guide drug choice. Readings also differed across molecular subtypes, and sideways scans proved slightly more informative than lengthwise ones. The authors suggest the scan can add useful prognostic hints before surgery.
pmc-12308628:
Raquel Lopez-Gonzalez and colleagues published a registry report in 2024. They counted child and teen cancers in Madrid. Cases covered four years in the twenty tens. Cancer is a leading cause of death in Spanish children. A regional registry tracks cases and survival there. The report gives rates by sex and age group. It also breaks cases down by tumor type. Stage at diagnosis is reported where available.

Registry staff gathered cases from many sources. Hospital, primary care, and death records were cross-checked. Every possible case was validated against medical charts. New diagnoses under age twenty were included. The report offers a population-level picture, not a sample. Planners can see which cancers appear most often. Stage data show how early cancers are found. Such baselines guide services and later comparisons.
pmc-12660828:
A large team of co-authors reports a new tool in a paper from two thousand twenty-five for watching immune cells as they grow. Cell therapies, such as T cell treatments, need close checks during culture. Sampling the cells can break sterility and adds cost, and weak checks lead to uneven batches.

The team built a small, low-cost imaging platform that reads cells without dyes or labels. The method, called quantitative phase imaging, works inside the growth vessel while culture runs. Image-based tests built by the team measured how many cells were alive and how active they were. The tests held up across cells from more than fifty donors.
pmc-12663228:
Habib and co-authors measure iron-rich food intake among toddlers across South Asia in this 2025 survey analysis. Iron matters for brain development in children aged 6 to 23 months. The team pooled the latest national health surveys from six countries, covering 84,234 children living with their mothers.

Overall only 21.5 percent of children ate iron-rich foods. The Maldives led at 71.9 percent and Bangladesh followed at 69.6, while India sat lowest at 17.4 percent. Boys, breastfed children, and rural children had lower odds of eating such foods. Children of less-educated mothers also fared worse. Mother's schooling and good prenatal care stood out as strong levers for improvement.
pmc-12687528:
Hannah Preßler and co-authors published this study in 2025 on Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, a disorder where the immune system weakens the signal from nerve to muscle. When a tumor triggers it, the syndrome is called paraneoplastic. That link is famous for small-cell lung cancer but murky for other cancers. The team compared registry patients across three forms: tumor-linked small-cell, tumor-linked other cancers, and autoimmune.

Balance problems in walking were more common in both tumor-linked groups than in the autoimmune group. Weakness scores tracked the cancer's course, easing as tumors were treated and worsening when cancer returned. The team gathered 115 published cases of the non-small-cell form; the commonest tumors were non-small cell lung cancer, Merkel cell carcinoma, and blood cancers. Most patients with outcome data improved after tumor treatment. The authors argue for tumor screening beyond the classic suspect.
pmc-12692628:
Robyn Lindley presents a 2025 review of a new class of drugs that tune enzymes called deaminases. These enzymes edit chemical letters in DNA, RNA, and other cell parts. Some of them drive mutation and sit inside pathways tied to inflammation. When they misfire, disease can follow. Drugs that raise or lower their action could treat that disease at its source.

Few such drugs have won approval so far, but many more are in trials. The review walks through cases that show what tuning these enzymes can do. It also names the hard parts: hitting one enzyme and not its kin, and judging long-term safety. The field is young, yet the targets sit close to core cell work. Lindley frames the area as a fresh front for drug design.
pmc-12694828:
Freihat, Sipos, Aamir, and Kovacs chart in twenty twenty-five the global burden of non-communicable diseases and project it to twenty fifty. Heart disease, cancers, lung diseases, and diabetes already cause most deaths worldwide and threaten a global goal to cut early deaths by a third. Using the standard global burden dataset, they tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years across two decades, split by region, wealth, and sex.

Diabetes cases climbed fastest, while heart deaths edged up. Richer regions led diabetes rates and Europe led heart deaths, with men hit harder. Projections see deaths and lost years swelling by mid-century, driven mostly by heart disease. Risk from metabolism, above all blood pressure, dominated. The authors demand equity-focused prevention.
pmc-12696128:
Guillaume Grosbois and three co-authors published a 2025 study of kettle lakes that sit on eskers in eastern Canada. These small lakes formed as glaciers retreated and often have no stream links to other waters. The team asked how the presence of fish shapes waterbirds and small water animals in the lakes, and compared them with the region's more common clay-belt lakes.

Water chemistry differed sharply between the two lake types, but not between esker lakes with and without fish. Several bird species fared worse where fish were present, and the small animal communities also shifted with fish. Fish numbers grew where human disturbance near shore was higher. The authors argue that fishless esker lakes hold rare value and need protection.
pmc-12700428:
Dongliang Liu and three co-authors trace how an aging switch in vessel cells worsens spinal cord injury. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. After injury, the cord's tiny blood vessels must regrow, and cell aging can stall that repair.

A protein called UTX and a classic aging marker both rose in vessel lining cells over two weeks after injury. Mice bred to lack UTX only in those cells showed less aging and more growth, in animals and in dishes. Gene scans found UTX directly controls a second protein, Top2β, holding it down. Removing that second protein erased the benefit. The authors name the pair a drug target for helping vessels rebuild after cord injury.
pmc-12701828:
Huan-Wei Chen proposes, in a 2025 technical report, that gentle lengthwise pulling of the spine might stir the fluid flows that clear waste from the brain. Poor clearance is blamed in part for Alzheimer's and kindred diseases. The method fixes the pelvis and stretches the spine briefly along its axis, which could set up pressure shifts in the spinal fluid.

The author has used the method in practice for over eight years with no lasting harms seen, though no formal safety trial exists. Better sleep was the most common patient report, notable because deep sleep drives brain clearance. The report gives force settings and a full procedure so others can test the idea.
pmc-12704428:
Yi-Tien Li and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study of brain connectivity as an early warning in preterm babies without severe brain injury. Even without major injury, many preterm children face developmental problems. Resting brain scans at term age might forecast who needs help.

Babies born very early had functional scans when they reached their due-date age. Development was scored at two years with standard scales. Connectivity patterns were related to thinking, language, and movement outcomes. Learning models combined scan features with early-life exposures. The aim is earlier, targeted support for babies whose brains quietly mature off track.
pmc-12705428:
Herzog, Thunström, and Eriksson published a 2025 paper on a faster way to solve a classic physics model of materials with strongly interacting electrons. The model treats one special atom embedded in a host material, and solving it is a heavy step inside a common theory of such materials. Their solver uses a method called configuration interaction and runs well even on a laptop, where older solvers often need large machines.

The team tested the solver on the metal cerium in three of its phases. As the metal was squeezed, its key electrons shifted from staying put on their atoms to roaming through the material. One middle phase stood apart, with electrons locked into a paired state. The paper also offers the solver as open-source software for other researchers.
pmc-12706528:
Jiayi Shi and co-authors report a field study from two thousand twenty-five on how cities help the American bullfrog invade China's Yangtze Basin. Bullfrogs are a global invader that harms native frogs. The COVID lockdowns cut human movement sharply, creating a natural experiment on how people spread the invader.

Paired surveys crossed city-versus-country and invaded-versus-clean sites during quiet and busy periods. Bullfrog densities averaged about one point seven times higher in urban than rural habitats, a gap not explained by habitat traits. Four native frog species declined where bullfrogs settled, with harsher losses in cities, while one toad species oddly increased. When activity resumed, rural bullfrog numbers jumped more than urban ones, suggesting rural spread rides on human transport.
pmc-12709828:
Zahra Cheraghi, Bita Azmi-Naei, Parvin Cheraghi, and Amin Doosti-Irani pool world data on uncontrolled blood pressure in a paper from 2025. Two hundred studies survived screening from thirty-five hundred candidates. Across them, about fifty-five percent of treated hypertensive patients still ran high. Regional rates varied from the mid-forties to sixty percent. The Eastern Mediterranean ranked highest, South-East Asia lowest.

Variation between studies was enormous, which the authors report honestly. The picture is of a global treatment gap despite cheap, effective drugs. Screening followed standard review guidelines with bias checks. The authors call uncontrolled hypertension a persistent worldwide burden. Better follow-through on known therapy is the implied remedy.
pmc-12713228:
Yan Ju and co-authors built a gene-based score that predicts whether a tumor carries loose rings of DNA and how it will answer immune therapy. These rings, called extrachromosomal DNA, help cancers grow and evade the immune system, but detecting them directly is costly and technically hard. Combining three machine learning selection methods on tumor gene activity data, the team distilled a signature of twelve genes.

The score identified ring-carrying tumors reliably in two patient groups and was confirmed against microscope-based DNA tests in cells and tissue samples. High scores marked worse survival across several immunotherapy cohorts, alongside faster cell division and a suppressed immune environment with fewer infiltrating lymphocytes. The authors propose the score as a cheap stand-in test for treatment planning.
pmc-12714728:
Rameshwar U. Kadam and colleagues published a drug design study in 2025 aimed at influenza A viruses. Flu enters cells when a surface protein changes shape and fuses membranes. Blocking that shape change can stop infection. The team copied a key binding loop from a llama antibody.

Antibody loops from llamas are long yet efficient binders. The researchers turned that loop into a ring-shaped synthetic peptide. The peptide bound the flu protein at very low concentrations. It neutralized varied flu A strains in lab tests. X-ray images showed the peptide mimicking the parent antibody closely. One candidate looks promising for protection against a major flu group. The approach may generalize to other targets.
pmc-12715228:
Shahbazi, Saeidi, Rouleau, and Chesnaux give a practical method for rock block geometry, in work from twenty twenty-five. Fractured rock masses split into blocks where joint sets cross. Block volume and surface area control stability, water flow, and excavation behavior in mines and tunnels.

Their method handles blocks formed by three persistent joint sets. Formulas link volume and surface to true joint spacing and to angles between block edges and joint normals. Stereographic projections make those angles easy to determine from field data. A practical calculation lets engineers estimate block sizes without heavy three dimensional modeling.
pmc-12716128:
A claim that a lead rock laced with copper conducts with no loss at room heat set off a rush of checks in 2023. Most tests blamed dirt in the samples and found no sign of true lossless flow. Guoliang Liu and four co-authors ran deep math models in 2025 on the rock's electron layout, going past the one-copper swaps tried before. They tried pairs of copper atoms and chains of them along one axis.

Some one-copper forms looked like metals, but all forms shared one flaw: the bands near the key level were too thin and none rose steeply. A known model of lossless flow needs both flat and steep bands side by side. With that pair missing, the team judge the rock and its kin are not true lossless conductors.
pmc-12716728:
Thatcha Yimthin and co-authors study the sugar capsule of a pathogenic mycoplasma of goats, in a research paper from 2025. These bacteria lack cell walls and cause serious farm animal disease. The strain studied can switch its capsule on or off, which creates diversity in the population and may change how the host immune system reacts.

Blood cells from goats and cattle were exposed to the normal strain and to a capsule-free mutant. The normal strain barely stirred the cells and survived inside macrophages, a furtive style that aids spread. The mutant exposed surface proteins, killed more cells, and triggered strong inflammatory signals. Capsule state thus steers the immune response in a dramatic way.
pmc-12717728:
Dongze Ye, Haipeng Luo, Carolee Winstein, and Nicolas Schweighofer propose an artificial intelligence system to tailor stroke rehabilitation, in two thousand twenty-five. Stroke leaves varied damage, and patients recover along unlike paths. The right therapy dose at the right time for the right person is the stated goal.

Their system learns a model of each patient and adjusts timing, dose, and intensity step by step. It works alongside clinicians and patients, honoring their judgment and limits. In simulations with one hundred fifty made-up patients, its advice grew better over time. Its plans beat fixed dosing schedules that give everyone the same pattern, whether rising, falling, or flat.
pmc-12722428:
Máté Pápista and colleagues published a 2025 study of switching bowel disease patients to a cheaper drug copy. The original antibody drug is costly. A biosimilar copy promises the same effect. Patients switched for financial, not medical, reasons. The team followed them for a year.

Over one hundred forty patients took part. Checks tracked symptoms, labs, and drug levels. Time points spread across the full year. Survival-style analysis watched for treatment failure. Costs were analyzed alongside clinical results. Real-world switches often worry patients and doctors. Evidence like this shows whether savings come at a clinical price.
pmc-12723828:
Fatemeh Haririzadeh Jouriani and co-authors test whether friendly gut germs can protect lungs from nickel harm, in a study from 2025. Nickel in air and at work can stress lung tissue and spark swelling. The team asked if native probiotic strains, given after exposure, could calm that harm in mice.

Male mice were exposed to nickel for sixty days and then given the probiotics. The team read gene activity in lung tissue to track stress and swelling signals. Nickel lowered the activity of genes that guard cells from stress. The probiotic treatment raised that activity back up. The results suggest these strains may help guard lungs, though the work was done only in mice.
pmc-12729128:
Stacey Peart and colleagues published a 2025 protocol describing a planned trial in Australian maternity hospitals about oxygen for newborn babies. Babies born several weeks early often need help breathing in the delivery room, and staff must choose how much extra oxygen to start with. For moderately preterm babies, hard evidence for that choice is thin, and practice varies.

Hospitals in the trial will alternate between starting with plain air and starting with a moderately enriched oxygen mix. The main question is whether babies still need breathing support when they leave the delivery room. The protocol lays out the design so results can be judged fairly when they arrive.
pmc-12729328:
Jiang and co-authors report a rare fungal infection in a captive bottlenose dolphin in Quanzhou, China. The male dolphin, kept at a public aquarium, vomited over a long period in 2024. Antibiotics given for an extended time did not help, and his condition kept worsening until death.

Blood tests during life and checks after death pointed to Cladosporium, a mold rarely blamed for dolphin illness. The case shows how a fungal cause can hide behind signs that look bacterial. The authors urge vets to test for fungi when aquarium animals fail standard treatment.
pmc-12730128:
Morgan Potier and four co-authors test a hybrid hearing aid strategy for lopsided hearing loss in a 2025 study. When one ear hears far worse than the other, plain amplification on both sides can backfire. Routing sound from the bad side to the good ear helps only for sounds arriving on the bad side.

Eighteen participants wore the aids at home for a month in three switchable modes. One mode merges cross-routing with two-ear amplification. Device logs showed people chose the hybrid mode about three quarters of the time. Speech-in-noise tests favored the hybrid when voices and noise came from opposite sides. Quality of life questionnaires completed the picture. The hybrid offers a practical middle path for a stubborn fitting problem.
pmc-12731028:
Rayane El-Khoury and six co-authors study body weight and survival in heart failure patients who also have diabetes, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Extra weight is usually seen as a risk, yet in heart failure heavier patients sometimes fare better, a puzzle called the obesity paradox.

The team used a national hospital database spanning several years and kept patients with weight data, more than twenty-six thousand in all. Patients were sorted from underweight to the highest obesity classes. Underweight patients had the highest death risk in hospital, while obese classes showed lower odds of death and return visits. The pattern sharpens debate on weight goals in heart care.
pmc-12733728:
Giovanni Ottonelli and five co-authors ask whether a chatbot can pick lens powers for cataract surgery. Their 2025 proof-of-concept study tests DeepSeek, an open generative AI. Surgeons must choose an implant lens that lands the eye on target focus. Standard formulas, not chatbots, hold that job today.

Fifty eyes from fifty patients at a Milan hospital formed the test set. All had smooth surgery with one lens model. A month later, measured focus was compared with each method's forecast. DeepSeek's errors were set against the Barrett Universal II formula. Accuracy statistics and error spreads were tallied for both. The study probes whether a cheap, open tool can approach clinical grade. Lens choice is unforgiving, so the bar is high.
pmc-12733928:
Jorg Wipplinger and a team of co-authors review all human evidence on trifluoroacetic acid, a persistent chemical known as TFA. Their twenty twenty-five rapid review notes that standard toxicity assessments often skip human data. TFA forms as many products break down, and people meet it after anesthesia, in the environment, and in chemical accidents.

The team searched two large databases in April twenty twenty-five and found seventeen studies: case reports, case series, observational work, and drug-tracking studies. All showed clear exposure and at least one measured outcome. Some acute exposures passed proposed threshold values. Yet no study showed a clinically relevant effect from TFA itself. As a strong acid, it burns on contact, but no wider organ harm was seen.
pmc-12734128:
Daniel Ahlert and co-authors study blood pressure on the way to hospital after brain injury. Their 2025 study reviews six hundred eighty patients treated in Zurich. Keeping systolic pressure in a target band may limit second injury to the brain. Guidelines now aim for one hundred ten to one hundred forty-nine.

Three quarters of the patients had moderate to severe injury, and one hundred seventeen died. About half started in the target band, and half stayed there for most of the trip. Pressure level and swings predicted survival on their own. In the full model, though, those links faded. Other factors may carry the real weight. The profile still maps how often targets are missed in practice.
pmc-12735228:
Rocchina Vilella and co-authors review, in a 2025 study, outcomes and side effects of a shortened radiation course given after prostate removal. Sixty-seven patients were treated with a focused arc method, as added insurance or as salvage when signs returned. Doses were packed into a median of twenty-five sessions, and three in five also had the wider pelvis treated.

At a median of four years, freedom from chemical relapse stood at about eighty percent at three years and sixty-nine at five. No severe early side effects occurred. Later bowel and urinary effects were mostly mild, though a few severe cases appeared. Adding pelvic treatment raised late side effect risk, the key caution from the data.
pmc-12736328:
Lidia Kozak and colleagues warn about pitfalls in multi-technique analysis of archaeological pottery. Their 2025 article uses ceramics from archaeological sites to show how results can be misread.

The first stage analysed complete museum vessels for elemental composition using X-ray fluorescence. The second stage split a single vessel fragment into thirty samples and analysed them separately. Results scattered because the ceramic material itself is heterogeneous. Grinding those samples allowed further tests of mineral composition and iron forms, revealing raw materials and firing methods. The authors caution that relying only on popular non-destructive methods can lead to misinterpretation of archaeological materials.
pmc-12737128:
Federico Zoila and co-authors wrote a review from 2025 on yoga as a therapy for diseases that slowly destroy brain cells. Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease keep spreading worldwide and have no cure. Drugs slow them at best, so gentle add-on options draw interest. The review gathers clinical results, mechanism studies, and marker data on yoga for both diseases.

Across studies, regular yoga practice improved movement and thinking scores, mood, and quality of life in patients. At the molecular level, yoga raised a growth factor that nourishes brain cells. It also lowered swelling signals and oxidative stress, and may help preserve gray matter in key regions. The pattern suggests yoga nudges the brain toward repair-friendly change. The authors warn that studies vary widely in design, length, and size. Few used brain scans or marker panels, so firmer trials are needed to pin down how yoga helps.
pmc-12738628:
Hernandez-Lopez, Milne, and Wang built a math model in twenty twenty-five of how cancer cells, killer T cells, and a blood cell kind act in a tumor's zone. The blood cells can wake killer cells by wear-ing tumor marks on their skin. The model tracks growth, waning, and that wake act in linked rules.

They find the steady states, test which hold, and map where the system flips form. The wake rate from blood cells is the key knob in that map. High wake can tip the zone to clear the tumor, while low wake lets it grow. Maps of flip zones may guide paired drug care.
pmc-12738728:
Plants grown in space flower on a different schedule, and a gene called FT seems to carry part of the space signal into the flowering pathway. Junyan Xie and eight co-authors grew normal and altered thale cress plants on the Chinese space station and compared their gene activity with matching plants on the ground, in a 2025 study. Some plants lacked or overproduced parts of a known three-part flowering module.

All plants shared a core response to weightlessness, yet each altered line also answered in its own way. Certain families of gene switches stood out in those private responses. The authors propose these switches as the modules that merge space signals with flowering.
pmc-12744228:
Jia Liu, Fangfei Li, Xiaolong Liang, and Jiahui Niu compare two filling pastes for single-visit root canal treatment, in a 2025 study. The patients suffered acute irreversible pulpitis, a hot, throbbing tooth inflammation. After cleaning the canal, the filling choice may decide how fast pain settles.

Records covered 112 patients treated at one center between 2022 and 2024, split evenly by filling used. One group received an iodoform and calcium hydroxide paste known for germ killing and tissue friendliness. The other got the standard combination of rubber points with a zinc-based sealer, packed by a classic technique. The team timed pain relief and swelling resolution, among other outcomes. Head-to-head data on this paste in one-visit care had been scarce.
pmc-12746628:
Naglaa Zaki and six co-authors test a nanoparticle treatment for drug-induced liver damage in rats, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The antibiotic levofloxacin can injure the liver. Zinc oxide particles carrying resveratrol, a plant compound, might protect it.

Fifty rats were split into five groups and treated every other day for two months. The nanoparticle group showed lower liver enzymes and kidney markers than the drug-only group. Oxidative stress markers fell, and protective enzymes rose back toward normal. Genes steering cells toward death or survival shifted in a protective direction. Tissue damage under the microscope eased as well. The authors credit the particles with blunting inflammation and oxidative stress.
pmc-12748428:
Yubin Huang and co-authors report stray cancer cells in the blood of three patients whose lung tumors were rated the earliest, non-invasive stage, in this 2025 paper. Textbook teaching says such in-situ tumors cannot breach the membrane that would let cells into circulation. Finding cells and cell clusters there challenges that picture.

A dedicated capture device found mixed populations of circulating tumor cells and microemboli in all three patients. The authors argue the cells may carry a dormant risk of spread. They propose blood checks for these cells as a pre-surgery input when judging outlook and planning care for lung cancer patients.
pmc-12753728:
Eleven researchers report a study from two thousand twenty-five on devices that make power from falling water drops. Such droplet-based generators give sharp spikes of power that fade fast. For real energy harvesting, what matters is a steadier average output, so those short spikes are a problem to solve.

The team added a thin water layer inside the device, caught from the working drops themselves. The layer has a strong ability to store charge. It raised both how much charge moved and how long each transfer lasted. With peaks held about equal, the steadier flow lifted the average output, which the authors show is the gain that counts.
pmc-12756128:
Jiahuan Gong and co-authors review the mechanisms of diabetic kidney disease and the new multi-target treatments for it, in a review paper from 2025. The disease is now the leading cause of end-stage kidney failure worldwide. Its drivers mix sugar damage, oxidation, inflammation, and scarring pathways.

Standard care slows the disease with blood pressure drugs that block the renin-angiotensin system, but it cannot undo scarring. Newer options include SGLT2 inhibitors, which ease pressure inside the kidney filter, and anti-inflammatory drugs that block scarring signals. The review also covers herbal multi-target formulas, nano-scale drug delivery, stem cells, and gene editing. The authors urge better early markers and multi-omics work to sort patient subtypes.
pmc-12766028:
Yangyao Peng, Yuting Zhan, and Qing Zhang searched brain scans for early signs of depression in a 2025 paper. Depression affects hundreds of millions of people, yet doctors lack solid biological markers to spot risk early. The team asked whether the way brain networks flex during emotional tasks can predict who becomes depressed.

They analyzed brain data from 14,376 adults in seven large international databases. Machine learning sorted people into four network patterns. One rigid pattern, held by about nineteen percent, came with over four times the depression rate of the most flexible pattern during follow-up. The authors suggest such patterns could one day guide personal prevention plans, though the work is an early step.
pmc-12766128:
Xi Li, Xinru Zhang, Yu Guo, and Weiqing Ruan follow family caregivers of adults with stomach feeding tubes across five care stages in China, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Twelve caregivers at a Guangzhou hospital were interviewed at each stage, from diagnosis to settled care. A timing frame sorted needs by stage.

Early stages brought worry, low know-how, and passive roles in choices. Mid stages shifted to comfort care, skill training, and access worries. Late stages raised daily care strain, role rebuild, and hope versus fact clashes. The authors call for stage-matched, culture-aware support. Readers see caregiver need as a moving target, not a fixed list.
pmc-12766328:
Rohlin and five co-authors run a trial of fluoridated milk in teens, in work from twenty twenty-five. Tooth decay in enamel can be prevented with fluoride, usually from toothpaste and water. Milk could deliver a small daily dose in a routine teens already follow.

Teenagers with a mean age of thirteen at three Swedish dental clinics were randomized. The intervention group drank milk with a low fluoride supplement daily, on top of normal fluoridated toothpaste use. Exams at baseline and after two years tracked decay in enamel and dentine. The authors report the fluoridated milk was effective in preventing enamel caries.
pmc-12766828:
Christina Kotoula and co-authors set out a trial protocol in a 2025 paper. The trial asks a plain question: does paracetamol add anything for chronic pain patients already on strong opioids? World Health Organization guidance pairs the two at its top step, yet proof for the pairing is thin. Paracetamol is safe at normal doses but can harm the liver in excess.

One hundred forty patients at two Swiss hospitals will join. All already take strong opioids plus at least a set daily dose of paracetamol. Half will keep their exact dose in look-alike capsules; half will get dummy capsules instead. After one week all blinded dosing stops, with follow-up to day fourteen. Pain diaries, pill counts, and blood levels track adherence. The main test is the average pain score on day seven, with a small gap set as clinically irrelevant.
pmc-12767428:
Olsson and co-authors ask Swedish diabetes nurses what helps and blocks their support for young adults who move from child to adult care, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The move is a risky time for young people with type 1 diabetes. Ten specialist nurses from six hospitals were interviewed in depth about their daily work.

Nurses said they aim for support shaped to each person but feel tied by system barriers. Strong bonds and long-term self-care goals sit at the heart of their work. Access to care after the move was a sore point, and handover practice varied by site with no shared national rule. Readers see a call for training that covers life change, not just blood sugar.
pmc-12768628:
Victor Flores, Paulina Quirola, Fernanda Parreño, and Elizabeth Guambo report work from twenty twenty-five on drug lists in Ecuador. They deal with which cancer drugs should join the national list of essential medicines. That choice is complex, since it weighs need, cost, and social factors. In Ecuador, choices have rested on proof of safety and effect from past studies alone.

The team put forward a model that uses many tests at once. A key part is the smallest change in health that patients would count as real. They also drew on a European scale for the size of cancer drug benefit. Readers see a way to judge real impact, not just proof on paper.
pmc-12768928:
Hong-Wu Yao and co-authors map infections caught in hospitals across China from 2015 to 2019, in work published in 2025. They use national data from 6,867 sampled hospitals. Such infections, made worse by drug resistance, threaten every health system. The study counts about 4,959,230 cases over the five years. Rates stand near one point one per hundred inpatients, with prevalence near two point three per hundred, and both trend down over time.

Among resistant organisms, a carbapenem-resistant strain of Acinetobacter baumannii shows the highest detection rate, at fifty-one point one percent. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus follows, at thirty-one percent. Detection falls for several resistant types, though one resistant Klebsiella type rises. Hospitals in urban areas carry higher infection risk, and rates differ by region. The authors present the map as a base for targeting infection control where it is needed most.
pmc-12771228:
Niancheng Yu and co-authors build an AI tool for children's allergy care in this 2025 study. Allergic rhinitis is a common nose allergy in children. Traditional Chinese medicine sorts it into cold and heat patterns, but that call rests on a doctor's judgment. The team wanted a more objective way to make the call.

They gathered records and tongue photos from 391 children. One network read the tongue images, while a second model merged image features with symptoms and history. The combined model sorted cold from heat cases with strong accuracy on held-out data. It beat single-source models on every score they tracked. Such a tool could help doctors sort patterns faster and more evenly.
pmc-12776028:
Yong Zhou and Bin Chen reviewed the Asian species of a little-known beetle subgenus in twenty twenty-five. The group, Lagria (Lagriella), stands out for strong gaps between the sexes, with females that cannot fly. Three Asian species were already known. The paper adds a fourth, found across parts of southern China.

The new species, named cordata, is the first record of the subgenus in China. The authors set name-bearing type specimens for two of the known species to fix their names. The paper gives photos of the new species and of the types of the known ones, notes on where it lives, and the traits that mark it out. A key lets readers tell all four Asian species apart. The work firms up a group that had been barely studied.
pmc-12776228:
Fangfang Du, Yang Guo, Xiangyu Shi, and Xiaomin Liu build a four-gene risk score from fat metabolism for lower-grade gliomas. These brain tumors vary so much that outlook and treatment choices stay cloudy. Fat metabolism shifts are tied to tumor start, growth, and spread. Tumor genome data yielded a score built from four fat-linked genes.

High-risk patients died at markedly higher rates than low-risk ones. Their tumors also showed more immune checkpoint gene activity. That pattern hints at a better shot from immune therapy. Drug screens suggest stronger chemo response in the high-risk group as well. Protein checks backed three genes as high in tumors, with the fourth low or absent.
pmc-12776628:
Mi Zhou, Biying Wang, and Rumeng Zhang present a two thousand twenty-five survey study of green talent management among Chinese civil servants. Green human resource practices are common in business but little studied in government. The study asks whether they lift job satisfaction in public service.

Over three hundred civil servants answered a structured survey. Both hard and soft green practices raised satisfaction. A shared green identity inside the organisation carried much of the effect. Artificial intelligence tools changed how hard practices shaped that identity. Public managers get evidence that sustainability-minded staffing can also serve staff wellbeing.
pmc-12779428:
Lim and co-authors report one center's experience using scope surgery to clear stones from transplanted kidneys, plus a world review. Stones in a donor kidney are rare but can be serious. Scope treatment was long seen as a backup option. The team reviewed cases at Singapore General Hospital from 2015 to 2023. Records covered patient traits, stone size and site, and surgery details. Stone-free rates and complications were the main outcomes.

A parallel search of five databases gathered studies through August 2023. All English study types were allowed, with bias checks on each. The combined view weighs whether scope surgery should move earlier in care. Transplant kidneys leave less room for error than native ones.
pmc-12781228:
Chad Beyer, Chanel Robinson, and Dan J Stein present a 2025 journal article grading the most cited papers in evolutionary psychiatry. The field explains mental illness through evolution, a lens prone to errors like calling a disease an adaptation. Building on a leading scholar's criteria, the team scored the twenty most cited articles for quality and error count.

The classics averaged good quality yet carried important errors. Neither quality nor errors predicted citation counts at all, so fame in this field tracks something else. The authors ask the field to agree on shared quality standards and a common list of mistakes to avoid.
pmc-12781528:
Atalay Eshetie Demilie and co-authors gauge how often cancer drug treatment causes harmful side effects in hospitals in the Amhara region of Ethiopia, in work from 2025. Such side effects limit care and worsen results, yet local rates were not well mapped. The study followed patients forward in time across centers.

In all, 572 patients took part, and about seventy-eight percent had at least one side effect. Events were graded on a standard cancer scale. One drug, cisplatin, stood out for the share of events tied to it. The team weighed which traits raised the odds of harm. They argue that knowing local rates and risk traits can guide safer dosing and closer watch of high-risk patients.
pmc-12782128:
Kajal Shah and co-authors published this 2025 case report on a cardiac arrest the patient heard happening. Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with obesity, sleep apnea, and repeated fainting, admitted with chest pain and breathlessness. In hospital, a nitroglycerin dose dropped her heart rate, atropine followed, and she slid into ventricular tachycardia, shocked back to rhythm twice.

Through the resuscitation she lay unresponsive yet aware, hearing the team and feeling the shocks, a rare and unnerving state tied to carbon dioxide buildup in obesity hypoventilation. A full cardiac workup found no blocked arteries or acute heart damage. She received an implanted defibrillator and went home, then fainted again days later, this time with no awareness at all. The authors use the case to untangle breathing, brain, and rhythm.
pmc-12785828:
Marialuisa Zedde, Fabrizio Piazza, and Rosario Pascarella wrote a review from 2025 on an overlooked corner of a brain vessel disease. The disease lays a protein called amyloid into the walls of small brain vessels, mostly in older people. It is known for causing bleeding in the brain's outer lobes and for driving decline in thinking. The review turns to the dura, the tough sac around the brain, and its lymph vessels.

Those lymph vessels may drain amyloid out of the brain with the fluid that bathes it. If that drainage falters, amyloid could pile up faster and worsen the disease. The review also weighs the disease's link with bleeding under the dura. Such bleeds may signal a higher risk of further bleeding events. Fragile vessel walls and chronic swelling are offered as the ties. The authors frame the dura as a possible route for future treatments.
pmc-12787328:
Miguel Cruz and a large team test in twenty twenty-five a home kit of smart devices that scores frailty in older adults without clinic visits. Frailty checks guide care for independent living, but standard tests need trained staff. Their kit pairs precise indoor positioning with a smart scale, a grip meter, and a speakerphone, together covering the five classic frailty signs.

Volunteers across a wide age span took both the sensor tests and the standard clinical ones in a mock home. Sensor scores lined up very strongly with the classic phenotype scale, and well with two other frailty scales. The authors say cheap off-the-shelf gear can give objective, repeatable frailty tracking at home, aiding early action.
pmc-12787528:
Ivan Fetisov, Olga Eizikovich, Dominique Charles Diouf, Elena Romanova, and Parfait Kezimana review how molecular breeding changes soybean crops. New gains have sped up work on better farm and food traits. The review sums up four approaches: marker-assisted selection, genomic selection, CRISPR gene editing, and RNA interference.

Marker-assisted selection uses simple sequence repeats and single-nucleotide polymorphisms. It finds and adds traits such as disease resistance, stress tolerance, and seed quality with speed. Genomic selection pairs genome-wide markers with field data. That lifts how well complex traits like yield can be predicted. CRISPR editing has made soybeans with better oil mix and more isoflavone, and beans that resist biotic stress. RNA interference tunes gene expression, which helps set food traits and stress responses. They also hold out climate-resilient, high-yield varieties.
pmc-12794428:
Seven researchers led by Sudha Bala screened working women in Hyderabad, India, for hidden heart rhythm faults using a portable wireless heart monitor. They compared one hundred nine women in information technology jobs with the same number in other work. A survey also rated each woman's stress level.

Rhythm faults showed in about five of each hundred tech workers, and fewer in the other group. Cases in younger tech workers included fast rhythms and pauses. Heart rate range and recovery measures ran higher in the tech group, hinting at stress effects. The authors call for simple screening tools and habits that protect heart health at work.
pmc-12798828:
Alaa Fadl, Aya Fadl, and Rashid Nadeem wrote a 2025 case report on a heart that would not keep its rhythm. A healthy forty-year-old woman had surgery to remove a womb growth. During the operation her heart fell into a chaotic rhythm and she went into shock. Standard resuscitation took forty-five minutes to restart circulation.

Scans showed her heart pumping at only about ten percent of normal strength. A machine that oxygenates blood outside the body was started fifteen hours after the first event and ran for six days. That support bought time for heart checks and rhythm monitoring while the heart recovered. The case shows how such a machine can carry a young patient through a rhythm crisis that drugs cannot stop.
pmc-12801028:
Wolf Petersen, Yizhou Ge, Amelie Klaumünzer, and Martin Häner describe a surgical technique note for straightening a bowed knee in a 2025 paper. Some knees carry a double deformity: the shin bone angles inward and its top surface also slopes too steeply backward. The modified operation corrects both in one opening-wedge cut high in the tibia.

Three tweaks do the work: the hinge sits forward and above the fibula, a small front wedge is removed, and pins guide the slope correction. A locking plate fixes the result. Recovery means six weeks of partial weight-bearing with free knee motion. The note gives exact angle thresholds for when this variant applies.
pmc-12805728:
Alba Méndez-Brito and colleagues published a 2025 survey mapping the world's public health intelligence teams, the groups that scan for emerging health threats. Fast detection depends on these teams cooperating across borders, yet nobody had catalogued who they are or what they do. The survey reached teams through regional disease control centers and global health networks.

The researchers identified more than one hundred thirty teams in eighty-seven countries, mostly inside public health institutes and health ministries. They recorded each team's methods, staffing, training, and challenges. A shared map of this landscape helps teams find partners, compare standards, and close gaps before the next health emergency.
pmc-12808628:
Swetha Pinjerla and co-authors design a multi-stage filter for lowering sample rates in internet-of-things gateways, in this 2025 paper. Wireless systems often must thin a fast signal stream without letting echoes fold back. Cascaded integrator-comb filters do that job with no multipliers, so they run fast and cheap. Their weak spot is a droop across the passband, which the team fixes with a compensation stage.

The design splits the filtering across stages using a polyphase layout, then builds it on a programmable chip. Pipelining keeps latency low and throughput high. Against earlier designs, the build used far fewer hardware blocks, with savings up to ninety-four percent in one block type. The authors pitch it for software-defined radio gateways that need real-time filtering on a tight budget.
pmc-12821828:
Nirmalya Syam and Muhammad Zaheer Abbas revisit, in a 2025 paper, the World Trade Organization fight over patent rights during the COVID-19 pandemic. India and South Africa had proposed a broad waiver of trade-related patent duties so vaccines could be made more widely. After twenty months of talks, ministers adopted a far narrower decision in June 2022.

Members then deadlocked on whether to extend the decision to COVID tests and treatments, though the decision set a six-month deadline for that call. Syam and Abbas argue the extension was both fitting and needed. They also propose ways for poorer countries to use patent flexibilities without waiting on waiver talks, and reforms that would let waiver decisions be made fast in future emergencies.
pmc-12822228:
Badreddine Belayachi and six colleagues published a 2025 study on surgery for dangerous heart rhythm storms. An electrical storm means the heart keeps falling into fast, harmful rhythms. In some patients, drugs, ablation, and implanted devices all fail to stop the attacks.

The team reviewed 11 patients treated at a hospital in Grenoble, France, between 2019 and 2024. Each had keyhole surgery on both sides of the chest to cut nerves that feed the heart's stress response. The cuts targeted the stellate ganglion and nearby nerve chains. Records show how often storms came back, what problems arose, and how patients fared. Surgery of this kind is a last option for a very sick group.
pmc-12824028:
Abirami Vetriselvan and five co-authors ran a computer simulation study, published in 2025, on straightening lower front teeth. Teeth that erupt too far are often pulled back with mini-screws anchored in the jaw. The angle at which a screw is placed may change how stress spreads through the ligament that holds each tooth.

The team built six finite element models covering four or six front teeth, with screws set at 30, 60, or 90 degrees. Stress was highest at the 30-degree angle and lowest at 90 degrees in both setups. The models also tracked how teeth shifted toward the tongue and along their roots. Results like these can guide orthodontists on screw placement.
pmc-12827128:
Víctor Juan Vera-Ponce and co-authors analyze, in twenty twenty-five, gaps in medical check-ups for people with diabetes and hypertension in Peru. Regular eye, blood pressure, and glucose checks are essential for both diseases, yet performance varies. The team used Peru's national demographic and family health survey, from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-two. Check-up rates in the past year were fairly high. Blood pressure checks topped eighty percent for hypertension patients. Glucose checks topped eighty percent for diabetes patients. Eye exams were lower.

Trends were flat from twenty fourteen to twenty nineteen. They dipped notably in twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one, above all for eye exams, then recovered in twenty twenty-two. The study identifies the most consistent factors behind who gets checked.
pmc-12830928:
Rui Hu and Wenyuan Wang build a structural model of perceived physical literacy among sports college students, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Their instrument asks students how physically literate they feel. Eighteen candidate items were content-checked by experts. Factor analyses then shaped the final model.

The validated model kept sixteen items across three factors. Item loadings were strong in both exploratory and confirmatory rounds. Reliability scores sat comfortably in the acceptable range. Students showed a fairly comprehensive range of perceived literacy. The authors caution that a rich sports environment alone does not guarantee that perception. It may not even be necessary for it. The instrument, they conclude, is valid for this population.
pmc-12837528: Azzahra Muhamad Asri and three colleagues report a rare eye case pairing two serious conditions, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. A sixty-one-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes and hypertension lost vision in his right eye to internal infection. Cultures confirmed Staphylococcus aureus, and the eye was removed despite injected antibiotics. A week into admission, his left eye developed worsening cotton-wool spots without infection signs. The team read them as Purtscher-like retinopathy. They urge suspicion of this pattern even without trauma history.
pmc-12839628:
Kinga Wnorowska and co-authors examine false teeth and quality of life in older adults in a 2025 study from Poland. Tooth loss marks aging and can hurt eating, mood, and health. The team used records from a large population study of adults aged fifty and older. They sorted people by missing teeth and by whether they wore removable false teeth.

Close to one thousand people were included in the analysis. Life satisfaction scores were much the same across all groups. Scores for oral health and daily comfort did differ, though. People with no missing teeth scored best, while false teeth users often disliked how the teeth looked and felt when eating. The study questions how much such teeth help daily life.
pmc-12840628:
András Szabó and six colleagues published a population genetics study in two thousand twenty-five on the Seklers of Transylvania. The Seklers are Hungarian-speaking communities in Romania with a long, debated history. Genome-wide data on them were scarce.

Seventeen Sekler groups were genotyped across the genome and compared with regional populations. Overall patterns placed all groups in one cluster shared with Hungarians, with no major internal splits. Finer haplotype methods mostly agreed. Two villages stood slightly apart, showing more internal relatedness, a sign of stronger local drift and smaller effective size. The authors describe a cohesive, regionally distinct population shaped mainly by shared history.
pmc-12841828:
Wenting Peng and colleagues review efferocytosis, the process by which dying cells are quickly eaten and cleared by other cells before they burst. Clearing matters because a burst cell spills harmful and inflammatory contents into nearby tissue. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors explain the steps and signals of the process, then trace what happens when clearance fails. Failed clearance feeds chronic inflammation, which in turn worsens several heart and blood vessel diseases.

The review links weak clearance to plaque buildup in arteries, heart attacks, heart failure after heart attacks, and inflammation of the heart muscle. Molecular pathways are mapped for each condition so that drug targets can be spotted. Readers get a compact account of a quiet housekeeping process and a case for treating it as a lever in cardiovascular care.
pmc-12842828:
Deepak Sharma and four co-authors add bone sap vents to a lone-row scope fix for full shoulder cord tears. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Lone-row fixes are plain and cheap but weak in build, and vents may free growth parts to heal the cord. Twenty-two folks with scan-set full tears had the fix, with holes poked by the joint spot.

Twenty-one folks were read at six months with fresh scans. Use scores rose a lot for all. Scans showed heal in all but one case. No folk or life mark swayed the end. One stiff joint case cleared with drugs and drills.
pmc-12844728:
Firdevs Demirel leads a team on plane tree extract in liposomes for wounds. Their work from twenty twenty-five deals with Platanus orientalis extract. Wound healing turns on swelling, stress, and cell regrowth.

Four extracts were made with distinct solvents and methods. Chem profiles were mapped with a high grade lab tool. One compound showed in all and was picked as reference. Fat bubbles were then loaded with the extract blend. Size, charge, and load rates were checked for the bubbles. Cell tests and release tests followed in vitro.  Wound tests in cells followed the bubble checks.
pmc-12846628:
Yuanyuan Zhu and eleven co-authors check the safety of a new chickenpox vaccine given to school children, in a 2025 study. The vaccine is grown in a human cell line called SV-1, the first vaccine made on that base. The study used health records from Jiangsu Province in China. It covered children aged seven to twelve who received the vaccine between July 2024 and March 2025.

Reports of side effects after vaccination were drawn from the national reporting system. The team counted how often such events were reported and described their types and patterns across age and sex groups. Large real-world checks like this matter because rare problems may not appear in smaller pre-release trials. The findings inform parents, schools, and health officials running the program.
pmc-12847728:
Twelve researchers design a carrier screening panel for Asian populations in Singapore in a paper from 2025. Carrier screening checks would-be parents for hidden recessive disease genes. Older panels were built on other populations and miss conditions common in Asia. The team mined genomic data from more than nine thousand local participants. They focused on severe childhood-onset conditions in Chinese, Indian, and Malay groups.

Their process produced a panel of about one hundred five genes. It is predicted to flag a small but meaningful share of at-risk couples. A narrower panel raised the predicted yield slightly but complicated counselling. The authors argue local data improve fairness in screening programs. National sequencing efforts can extend the approach.
pmc-12847928:
Ibai Diez and seven colleagues test whether the brain's wiring honors its embryonic construction order, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Their hypothesis: circuits born early in development become the connectome's strongest hubs. The brain's architecture would then carry a fossil record of its own assembly.

Brain regions were segmented by embryogenic age. Early-born nodes indeed showed greater structural centrality. Functional connectivity showed the opposite trend. Age gaps between regions predicted whether links existed and how strong they were. Gene expression data tied age and centrality to development and synapse genes. Developmental timing thus leaves measurable fingerprints on adult networks, with implications for why some hubs fail first in disease.
pmc-12853828:
Johannes Lemcke and co-authors describe how a large health panel was recruited in Germany, in a research report from 2025. The panel, Health in Germany, will follow a broad sample of the public for health research over time. It was built by the Robert Koch Institute with a random sample drawn from town registers.

Recruitment used both web and paper forms, with the order set by age group. The report gives response rates by group and checks who took part. It also looks for tilt in the sample. Such checks matter, since a panel that skews from the public can bend later findings. The paper is a guide for like panels.
pmc-12860128:
Qingqing Liu leads a large team studying air and lung health in one district of Shanghai in this twenty twenty-five paper. Dirty air is known to harm the lungs, but the authors also wanted to know what local people grasp about that risk. They used a survey in Minhang District.

Residents gave details on their health, their daily habits, and things around them that shape air exposure. The team then checked which survey factors lined up with long-term lung disease, with a close look at one common chronic lung condition. The study also scored how well the survey flagged sick residents, giving local health staff a base for clean-air work.
pmc-13086428:
Elcid Pangilinan and co-authors build a fast classifier for malaria parasite genes in a 2026 paper. The parasite's var genes code for a surface protein that drives disease severity and immune escape. Sorting these genes into upstream groups guides research, but partial sequences make the call hard. Their tool, upsML, learned from over twenty-five hundred curated genes.

Seven methods were compared, from support vector machines to profile models. The best reached eighty-three percent accuracy on short tag sequences and ninety-two percent on full proteins. That clearly beat existing tools. A side model tells internal genes from end-of-chromosome ones. Run on global parasite genomes, it found more internal genes in Asia. The tool sorts twenty genomes in under a second. The authors offer it openly for large-scale var gene studies.
pmc-13124628:
Imanishi and a large team study how radiation reshapes blood immune cells and how a gout drug can blunt that change, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Radiation can injure blood vessels and stir inflammation long after exposure. The team treated human blood cells from one healthy donor with the drug, then gave a dose of radiation.

Radiation did not change total immune cell counts after one day. But it switched on a growth signal in one patrolling cell type and grew that group. Two proteins tied to age-related blood changes fell at the same time. The drug blocked the growth of that cell group. It did not restore the two proteins. The team sees a new way the drug may calm radiation-driven swelling.
pmc-13125128:
Oleksandra Romaniuk, Jörg Mühlhans, and Ulrich Ansorge present a 2026 eye-tracking study of women viewing romantic scenes. People may not recall well what truly drew their gaze. The team set measured gaze against what women later said had stood out. Sixty-eight women viewed ten scenes of couples while a tracker logged where their eyes went.

Five zones were scored: each partner's face and body, plus the backdrop. Women dwelled most on the woman in each scene. Faces drew early looks and long holds, while men's bodies drew the least gaze. Self-reports matched hold length best and counts of looks not at all. At the level of single cues, smiles and other traits drew mixed recall. The study shows that memory of attraction rests on some gaze habits more than others.
pmc-13128428:
Eliza Russu and co-authors study how nutrition before surgery links to bad outcomes after repair of a swollen aorta in the abdomen, in work published in 2026. The swelling can burst, which is often fatal. The team reviewed 125 patients who had open repair surgery at one hospital.

Patients averaged about 73 years of age, and most were men. Over half arrived with a burst swelling, and nearly half died within thirty days. Patients with poor outcomes had lower blood protein levels and worse nutrition scores before surgery. Those measures predicted both rupture on arrival and early death with strong accuracy. After accounting for other factors, low protein and poor scores still stood out. The authors argue nutrition checks should guide risk talks before this surgery.
pmc-13132228:
Hanyu Cao and co-authors compare the muscle proteins of a prized Chinese pig breed against a Western Yorkshire, hunting the chemistry of better pork. Their study appeared in 2026. The Huoshou black pig is famous for meat quality. Deep protein scans of the loin muscle found 262 proteins differing between the breeds, split nearly evenly between higher and lower in the Chinese pig. The differing proteins clustered in small-molecule metabolism, energy handling, and three major growth pathways.

Cross-checking with gene activity narrowed the field to five candidate genes, and targeted tests confirmed each differs at both message and protein level. The authors say these five are leads for breeding programs that want Yorkshire efficiency with Huoshou flavor.
pmc-13138628:
Ke Wang and co-authors rebuild how sand and mud flowed from land to lake in a rift basin of northeast China over two eras, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Seismic, drilling, and log data frame six stacked units. Fault pace and routes steered where fans and deltas grew.

Early rifting laid steep fans near slopes, while peak rifting mixed fan types by zone. Late stages turned to broad, gentle river deltas as the basin merged into one lake. Fan size tracked valley width, depth, and cross area in the peak phase. The maps aim to guide oil hunts in like basins. Readers get a full life story of a rift lake's plumbing.
pmc-13141328:
Sushumna Satyanarayana and seven colleagues show that diabetes remodels the heart's right ventricle earlier than the left, by a different fuel route. Diabetic heart disease is usually defined by left ventricular failure. Both ventricles, though, gorge on fatty acids until the surplus turns toxic. The team tracked remodeling timing in two mouse models of type 2 diabetes and studied mechanisms in a pig model of type 1.

Right ventricular changes began early, before any left-sided structural or functional shift. The right side also raised fatty acid uptake through a pathway distinct from the left's. Chamber-specific metabolism explains why right-sided failure can surprise clinicians watching only the left. The twenty twenty-six findings argue for scanning both ventricles in diabetic hearts and for therapies aimed at each chamber's own fuel handling.
pmc-13141528:
Louise Koller-Smith and colleagues examine whether childbearing history, body mass index, and smoking affect rheumatoid arthritis risk in Australian women. Their 2026 study uses a long-running national women's health dataset.

Among over forty thousand women, three hundred thirty-two developed rheumatoid arthritis, identified through medication dispensing records. Lower parity associated with higher arthritis odds after adjustment for other factors. Ever smoking also associated with higher risk in adjusted models. Each unit increase in body mass index raised odds significantly in some models. Earlier studies in European, American, and Asian populations suggested these links, but none had tested them in Australia before.
pmc-13147728:
