Ramy Saad and co-authors link a cocoa compound to slower aging marks in a 2025 study. The compound is theobromine, the mild stimulant in cocoa and chocolate. It has been tied to longer life in simple organisms and to health gains in people. The team asked whether blood levels of it track with epigenetic aging, the chemical marks on DNA that gauge how fast a body ages.

In a British twin cohort of about five hundred people, higher theobromine went with slower aging on two DNA measures. The same links appeared in a German cohort of over a thousand people. Checks against other cocoa and coffee compounds suggested the effect belongs to theobromine itself. The authors say diet may reach down to the molecular marks of aging. They call the finding a lead for deeper study, not yet a prescription.
pmc-13152228:
Miki and co-authors review whether phone-based health programs help workers move more and sit less, and whether work gains follow. Mobile health tools are popular, but their effect on work outcomes was unclear. Outcomes of interest include absence, working while sick, and work ability.

The team searched major databases for all work up to September 12, 2025, with no language limits. Only full studies of workers in trials or other intervention designs counted. Papers had to link the programs to work-related results. The review sums up what that body of work shows for employers and health planners.
pmc-13152928:
Temilade Aderounmu, Babatunde Adeyemi, and Aisha Bolarinwa review kidney injury in newborns after oxygen shortage at birth, in this 2026 paper. Birth asphyxia harms many organs, and the kidneys are often hit. Yet how common the injury is, and how it ends, varies across reports. The team mapped thirty studies from 1995 to 2025 across regions and designs.

Reported rates ranged from twenty percent to over sixty percent of asphyxiated newborns. The spread reflects varied definitions and illness severity. Injury tracked with severe asphyxia, multi-organ failure, longer intensive care, and death. Interest grew after standard newborn definitions spread. The authors flag gaps in early detection, long-term kidney data, and evidence from poorer countries, and urge standard monitoring and marker checks.
pmc-13162028:
Sumit Kaushik and five co-authors present a 2026 study on how to judge real improvement in patients with a painful shoulder joint condition. The joint in question links the collarbone to the shoulder blade. Doctors use several score forms to track pain and function, but no one had set the smallest change that patients can actually feel for this condition.

The team followed 170 patients for twelve months, split between surgery and non-surgical care. All score forms proved steady and tracked patient-rated change well. The authors set thresholds for a felt improvement, a large benefit, and a state patients find acceptable, worked out apart for each care path. About nine in ten patients who felt a real gain also reached the acceptable state. These cutoffs help doctors read trial and clinic results with more confidence.
pmc-13163828:
Shih-Lung Cheng argues that interleukin-5, long cast as a one-job cytokine, actually works as a network regulator across airway diseases, in this review from twenty twenty-six. IL-5's textbook role is raising eosinophils, the white cells behind allergic inflammation. Cheng assembles the evidence that this undersells it.

IL-5 receptors turn up on many other cells: airway lining, mast cells, antibody factories, fibroblasts. Through them the cytokine touches barrier integrity, tissue remodeling, and mucus. That breadth explains the uneven record of IL-5-blocking drugs: superb in severe asthma, patchier in sinus disease and COPD, where local tissue context rules. The author calls for treatment aimed at networks and contexts, not single pathways.
pmc-13172628:
Tong Yang and co-authors test a traditional Chinese herbal formula in a 2026 lab study of lung disease. COPD leaves airways inflamed and airflow limited for good. The formula, Bu-Fei, eases symptoms in clinic use, but the molecular route of its help was a knowledge gap. The team traces that route to the cell's power plants and a known inflammation switch.

They built a COPD-like model in rats with cigarette smoke and a bacterial trigger, and a cell model with smoke extract. The formula was given for eight weeks at rising doses. Stains and electron images checked lung harm, scarring, and the shape of immune cells. Measures of the switch, called the NLRP3 inflammasome, and its products showed the formula calms hyperactive mitochondria, which in turn holds the switch down.
pmc-13173428:
Diego Gomez and co-authors reviewed 104 horse cases of a deadly brain disease in a 2026 study. Eastern equine encephalitis is passed by mosquitoes and kills most horses it strikes. Despite its toll, firm data on its signs, spread, and survival factors were thin.

The team pulled records for horses treated at a teaching hospital from 1979 to 2017. All had shown signs of broad brain disease. They charted each horse's signs, lab results, and outcome, then used a stats model to find traits tied to survival. The long case run gives vets a sharper picture of which horses might pull through and which need the most support.
pmc-13175228:
Mary Elaine Graham and four co-authors review women health issues after kidney transplant in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Transplant has greatly raised survival for women with end stage kidney disease. Long term care must now cover routine women health needs as well.

The authors cover heavy or odd bleeding, early menopause, fibroids, pelvic pain, and prolapse in this group. Hormone faults, life long immune suppressing drugs, and past surgery make each issue harder to treat. Cancer screening, birth control, hormone therapy, and bone health all need special care. Proof is thin in many areas, the authors note. They call for close teamwork among transplant, women health, and primary care staff.
pmc-13179428:
When diabetes rots the bone in a foot, doctors biopsy the bone to name the germ, and many first ask whether antibiotics given early spoil that test. They searched three databases for studies comparing culture results in patients who did or did not get antibiotics before the biopsy.

Four studies qualified. Pooled, the odds of a positive culture were nearly the same in both groups, with a ratio of zero point seven eight and a wide margin that crossed no effect. The result was far from significant. The team concludes that holding antibiotics before biopsy does not seem to change what the culture finds, so treatment need not wait on the test.
pmc-13186028:
Anqi Chen, Yinuo Huang, Han Li, Lin Shi, and Shu Zhang publish a data set profiling a widely used heart cell line in a 2026 paper. HL-1 cells, from mouse heart tissue, are a standard model in cardiac research. Yet a combined reference of their gene activity and genome marks was missing from public databases.

Together they show which genes are on and what controls them in these cells. Other researchers can mine the resource to model gene networks in heart cells and heart disease without repeating costly experiments.
pmc-13191628:
Kazuhisa Yamamoto and co-authors trace what happens to transplanted cell sheets inside the middle ear in a 2026 study. After ear surgery, the middle ear lining must regrow fast to keep the space aired and protect hearing. Sheets of a patient's own nasal lining cells have already shown clinical benefit when laid over the bare bone. What the grafted cells do over time, and how they help, was not clear.

In immune-deficient rats, the team removed the middle ear lining and laid on sheets of nasal cells tagged with a glowing marker. Over weeks they followed the glow, sectioned tissue for stains, and scanned the ear with micro-CT. The tracking shows whether the sheets take hold, persist, and turn into true ear lining. That fate map is the missing logic behind a therapy already in use.
pmc-13195228:
Kazim Sahin and Gozde Erek review chronic variable stress and a proposed supplement pairing in a 2026 article. Chronic variable stress, a lab model applying varied mild stressors unpredictably, mimics long-term human stress load. It overactivates stress hormones and drives oxidative damage, harming not just the brain but the gut-liver-brain axis, the network linking gut, liver, and brain.

The review gathers evidence that stress breaks gut barrier integrity, fattens the liver, disturbs iron handling, and fuels inflammation. A complex pairing magnesium with L-theanine, an amino acid from green tea, protected barriers and liver in animal studies, partly through metabolic regulators. Human data on the separate ingredients suggest calming and sleep benefits, supporting further study.
pmc-13195628:
Hamid Tahernia is first author on a 2026 case report described as the first known coexistence of plasma cell gingivitis and multiple sclerosis in one patient. Plasma cell gingivitis is a rare, benign gum inflammation packed with plasma cells, of uncertain cause. Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease damaging nerve insulation in the brain and spinal cord.

The patient was a twenty-six year old woman with nine years of stable, well-controlled multiple sclerosis, presenting with gum pain and spontaneous bleeding. Examination showed widespread red, swollen gums, and a biopsy confirmed dense plasma cell infiltration. Steroid mouthwash brought symptomatic improvement, and her multiple sclerosis stayed stable over six months of follow-up. Whether the pairing is shared immune pathways or coincidence remains open.
pmc-13196128:
Abdulkhalek Dakhel and colleagues report a 2026 study of a changed form of vimentin in the sick brain. Vimentin is a support protein inside cells. The team studied brains affected by Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease, two illnesses where clumped proteins harm brain cells.

Using a special antibody called 84-1, they found a distinct vimentin pool that common tests miss. It formed deposits in harmed brain areas, often beside clumped proteins. The pool was mostly cut protein pieces in tough clumps. Levels were also high in spinal fluid from patients. Levels rose in human astrocytes, a type of brain support cell, exposed to harmful protein clumps. The form may serve as a marker or future drug target.
pmc-13196228:
Lin Tang and four co-authors dissect a Chinese herbal formula for psoriasis in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease driven by the immune system, and current therapies have limits. The formula, used on the skin, works in the clinic, but its active parts and mechanism were unclear.

The team identified forty-two active components by mass spectrometry. In psoriatic mice, the formula eased redness and lesion thickness and lowered inflammatory signals. In skin cells, it curbed overgrowth and stress in a dose-dependent way. Network and gene analyses pointed to one target, IL-17A, and two signaling pathways it feeds. Docking tests showed six ingredients bind key proteins well.
pmc-13196928:
Qiaoling Pan leads a large team in mining a drug harm report base for risks after lung surgery. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Breath shortness, cough, heart flutter, and chest pain dog many patients after such surgery and slow their heal. Which drugs feed those ills was murky.

They use ratio tests to rank the drugs most tied to each of the four signs. A small set earns a high signal mark, and a mid set joins it. Three of the high set are drugs for lung artery hypertension. A deeper read pins the link on the drug class trait itself. The list can guide drug picks after lung surgery.
pmc-13197028:
Tadayuki Hashimoto and colleagues wrote a 2026 tutorial on hidden harms in medical teaching. Drug trials watch closely for side effects, yet teaching programs rarely get the same check. The authors argue that lessons and training can harm learners in ways that stay unseen.

They list twelve such harms with a tip to curb each. Examples include rising confidence without real skill, rewards that sap inner drive, and heavy content that overloads memory. Others cover safety that exists on paper only and overuse of AI tools that dulls thinking. The harms fall into three groups: in the learner, in the setting, and in study methods. Each tip aims to spot harm early.
pmc-13197628:
Shida Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on stomach and bowel upset from metformin, a first-line diabetes drug. Nausea, diarrhea, belly pain, and bloating are common and often lead patients to quit a drug that works well. The review sorts causes into two groups to guide care.

First come fixable exposure factors: dose size, how fast the dose rises, pill type, taking it with food, kidney function, and other drugs. If symptoms persist, host factors come next, such as gut sensitivity, gut microbes, and bile handling. Fixing fixable factors first can spare needless drug stops. The authors offer a stepwise plan for clinic use.
pmc-13201528:
Many machines need three-phase power where only a single-phase supply exists, and a 2026 engineering article headed by Heba Abdellatif Nagi proposes a converter with fewer parts. The research article presents a single-phase to three-phase boost converter that drives motors while using only six controlled semiconductor switches.

The design pairs its switching layout with a simple sinusoidal pulse width modulation strategy instead of more complex space vector control. Fewer switches and passive parts should cut losses and improve current quality, the authors argue. They tested the circuit in MATLAB and Simulink simulations and then confirmed the results with a laboratory prototype run through a real-time controller.
pmc-13202028:
China bought insulin in bulk to cut diabetes costs, and a 2026 quasi-experimental study authored by Hongbin Yi evaluates what that policy did to prices, use, and spending. The research article analyzes the national volume-based procurement policy for insulin, introduced in May 2022, using quarterly hospital procurement data.

Data covered fifteen insulins from 761 public hospitals across thirty provinces, spanning late 2020 through 2023. After the policy began, winning-bid insulin prices fell by roughly half while procured volumes rose and total expenditure dropped substantially. Every insulin group showed significant price reductions, and the authors conclude centralized procurement improved affordability and use of insulin in China.
pmc-13202128:
Training may cut cancer recurrence risk, but delivering programs remotely raises practical questions, and a 2026 plan led by Gillian Jackson plans to study the delivery itself. The plan presents a mixed-methods process review embedded in CANFit, a feasibility trial of personalized remote physical activity support in England.

The trial serves people at high risk of breast, lung, or bowel cancer returning, using a basket design across the three cancers. The review will gather surveys, interviews, adherence logs, trainer diaries, and observations from participants and staff. Guided by an implementation guide, the team will judge acceptability, fidelity, reach, and sustainability, then refine how the program is meant to work.
pmc-13204328:
Xinzhe Lu and co-authors build and test a tree-climbing robot modeled on a gibbon, in a paper from 2026. Robots that climb trees can prune and pick crops high above the ground. Most have stiff joints that limit how they handle messy, real trunks. The team's robot has three arms with claws, echoing how a gibbon swings and grips.

The prototype has fourteen moving joints and weighs about two and a half kilos. Models of its arm motion were checked in simulations before field tests. The claws gripped wet bark, worked wood, and smooth steel plates. The robot climbed trunks tilted from steep to straight up, carrying a load of nearly two kilos. One full climbing cycle took about four minutes. The tests show the ape-inspired design works in real forest settings.
pmc-13207928:
Desaree Tan and six co-authors reviewed the early cell death paths that scar the heart after a heart attack, in a paper published in 2026. Fast restoration of blood flow is the standard treatment, but it cannot stop the death chains in stressed heart cells at the edge of the injury. Drugs against scarring are still few. The team maps the death signals and the drug leads that chase them.

The scar paths are tightly braided, so blocking one alone often fails. Drugs against inflammation, stress, and load shone in laboratory tests but have often failed in clinics. The time window to act is narrow, the authors stress. New leads use RNA drugs, cell reprogramming, and targeted delivery to reach the right cells fast. The team supports a shift to early, cell-targeted care to keep weak heart tissue alive and head off heart failure.
pmc-13209028:
Hu and six co-authors make layered model rocks by three dimensional printing, in work from twenty twenty-six. Layered rocks break in ways that depend on layer angle, a risk for tunnels and slopes. Real samples with set angles are hard to obtain.

Cement based printing can build rock like blocks layer by layer, partly from recycled waste. That printing itself creates direction dependent traits that were not well measured. The team tested strength, wave speed, and scan density of printed rocks at varied angles. They compared failure styles with natural layered sandstone. Calibrated printed rocks could stand in for scarce natural samples in lab tests.
pmc-13211228:
Meitong Lin and colleagues review how engineers are rebuilding the artificial lens itself to prevent cataract surgery's two great complications, in this paper from twenty twenty-six. Implanted lenses can cloud over years later as cells creep across the capsule, and infection inside the eye, though rare, can blind. A smarter lens could fight both from inside.

The review sorts the field into three families. Surface engineering changes the lens skin so cells cannot grip or grow. Drug-delivery lenses carry antibiotics or anti-growth agents and release them slowly. Photo-responsive lenses wake up under light to kill cells or microbes on demand. Newer work combines all three into multifunctional systems. The authors weigh each approach's mechanism, strengths, and limits, and close with strategies to move these lenses from bench novelty to operating room standard.
pmc-13211328:
Salam and coauthors outline next-step vaccines for lung and gut germs. Standard vaccines rest on antibodies and often fade with time. They may also fail to guard the wet surfaces germs first strike. New designs aim for longer and broader guard at those surfaces.

One route builds antigens that call up T cells in tissue. A next route boosts local antibody in nose and gut lining. A third route trains first-line immune cells for faster response. New carriers and boosters make those routes more exact. The team sees the mix as a path to stronger, cross-strain guard.
pmc-13214428:
P. Harish and colleagues present in 2026 a twelve-year-old girl whose heart murmur led doctors to a hidden birth defect. The wall between the coronary sinus and the left atrium was missing, so blood shunted the wrong way. Her right heart chambers were enlarged despite an intact main atrial wall.

A saline bubble test through a left arm vein gave the clue, as bubbles appeared in chambers on both sides in a telling pattern that skipped the left atrium. Closer ultrasound views showed the defect directly, and CT scanning confirmed the type. Surgeons closed the defect. The case shows how a simple contrast study can expose a rare shunt that ordinary views miss.
pmc-13215628:
Kosuke Hayashi and colleagues report a 2026 randomized crossover trial comparing fixed and lottery payments for using a walking app. The app rewards brisk walking bouts, and the team wanted to know which reward style keeps people engaged.

Twenty volunteers used each version for four weeks, with a washout period between. Both versions paid the same expected value per completed challenge, either a small fixed sum or a one-in-five chance at five times as much. Weekly challenge completions, daily steps, and distance did not differ significantly between the two styles. The authors lean toward fixed payments simply because they are easier to run, and they frame the trial as an early-phase test.
pmc-13216128:
Agata Krawczyk and co-authors present a 2026 cell study on whether a static magnetic field changes the antioxidant power of two pomegranate compounds used in skin care. Little is known about steady magnetic fields in cosmetics, despite their wider use in medicine.

Human skin cells were stressed with hydrogen peroxide, then treated with ellagic acid or punicic acid, with or without the magnetic field. The stressor alone suppressed antioxidant genes. The pomegranate compounds restored and raised their expression, and the magnetic field strengthened that response, with enzyme activity matching the gene results. The authors interpret this as a magnetically boosted cell defence against reactive oxygen species.
pmc-13216528:
Xiangyu Jin and co-authors present a 2026 photonics study of flat optical surfaces that sculpt light with carefully patterned polarization, called vectorial optical fields. Making such fields on a chip has been hampered because earlier surfaces steered only the phase of light, not its amplitude.

The team's metasurfaces are driven by surface waves running along the chip and control amplitude, phase, and polarization of the scattered light independently. Built and tested at terahertz frequencies, the devices produced paired beams with chosen polarizations and intensities, two focal spots of unequal brightness, and holographic images. The images, both plain and polarization-patterned, looked cleaner than phase-only versions. The authors pitch the platform for compact holography and augmented reality hardware.
pmc-13218128:
Muhammed İnan and Cenk Aypak argue in a 2026 perspective piece that family medicine needs to move from linear guidelines toward complexity science. Evidence-based medicine standardized care, yet its step-by-step models treat the body like a machine with predictable inputs and outputs. That assumption breaks down for primary care patients who live with several chronic conditions at once.

Through clinical vignettes, the authors show how stacking single-disease guidelines can create treatment burdens no patient can sustain. They also point to non-linear analyses of physiological signals that may flag frailty years before a clinical diagnosis. Their proposal is to build tools from soft computing, including fuzzy logic, fractal analysis, and causal inference, into everyday general practice. Rather than treating family medicine as an exception to evidence-based practice, they frame it as the setting where evidence that respects complexity is needed most urgently.
pmc-13220328:
Mapelli and seven co-authors report heart findings in a young athlete with a sunken chest, in work from twenty twenty-six. Pectus excavatum is the most common chest wall deformity from birth. It can shift the heart and mildly impair function, and may mask or mimic heart muscle disease.

Their patient was an asymptomatic male athlete aged twenty-four with severe deformity. He had frequent early heartbeats of a single shape. The case traces a diagnostic loop: were the heart changes due to chest shape pressure, or to true cardiomyopathy? Careful distinction matters before clearing an athlete for sport.
pmc-13220528:
Ángeles Hueso-Gil, Jesús Miró-Bueno, and Ángel Goñi-Moreno present a study dated 2026 on using growth control to tune how cells host engineered genes. A genetic circuit behaves differently depending on its host cell's state, and that context is hard to steer. The team took direct control of growth in a soil bacterium.

They replaced the natural controls on two parts of the cell's gene-reading machine with a switch driven by a chemical signal. Adding the signal set growth into distinct stable states. Reporter genes and NOT gates behaved differently in each state, in ways specific to each part. A model sorted the effects into three classes. Growth even served as one input of a NAND logic gate, pointing toward computing with cell bodies.
pmc-13222628:
Yulin Wu and co-authors search for early signs that predict death in patients with the most severe immune side effects of cancer immunotherapy, in a 2026 triangulation study. Only twenty-six intensive care patients with grade 4 events were available, so the team cross-checked traditional statistics against several machine learning methods, keeping only features both routes flagged.

Eight features survived the cross-check. Needing vasopressors or oxygen, pneumonia, high lactate, and a high neutrophil share tracked with higher mortality. Higher body mass index and receiving a VEGF-blocking drug tracked the other way. Shock, breathing failure, and inflammation dominate the picture. The authors stress the exploratory scale while offering the list for early vigilance.
pmc-13223028:
Hadeel Alsolai and her team plan a clear-to-grasp kit that tells how cure work will end for sick folk with poor move skill and harm to nerves. Their 2026 model, Rehab-DRLX, joins deep learn by prize with net kits that track time.

The kit works on care files, sense data on moves, and brain pics as one. It joins them with cure paths that rest on time. A learn-by-prize part codes move traits through space and time. It learns cure rules led by prizes. A guess part with heed steps makes calls clear to see and to grasp. The build tells ends such as the odds that a sick man or woman can act on his or her own. Tests showed marked gains past plain black-box guess tools. The team sets those gains out in the work.
pmc-13224128:
Ying Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 rapid test kit for three pig viruses that cause severe diarrhoea and often infect herds together. Farm-side diagnosis usually needs laboratory equipment, which slows response. Their portable platform combines a fast copying method with CRISPR-based detection and gives a result that can be read by eye.

The test picked out each target virus without reacting to other swine pathogens, and it detected only a few copies of viral material per microlitre. Repeat runs agreed closely. On twenty clinical swab samples, results matched standard laboratory methods in almost every case. The whole process, from sample to answer, finished within fifty-five minutes.
pmc-13224628:
Lina Zhao and colleagues compare a 2026 update of the SOFA score, the standard tool for grading organ failure in sepsis, against its original version. The update revises thresholds and reflects modern organ-support practice, but nobody knew whether it would change who counts as septic. The team studied 11,669 intensive-care admissions at three Chinese hospitals, then checked findings in a large American database.

The updated score labelled a moderately larger share of patients as septic, while agreeing strongly with the original overall. It also assigned higher scores in the middle-to-serious range and captured more organ dysfunction. Prediction of intensive-care death improved slightly in both datasets, and the authors suggest the existing diagnostic threshold can stay unchanged.
pmc-13224928:
Nona Ehyaei and co-authors examine a 2026 crystallography study of an artificial protein built to mimic rhodopsin, the light-sensing pigment used in vision. Real rhodopsins flip a retinal molecule between shapes when light strikes, starting signals in the eye and in microbes. A fully tunable mimic lets researchers watch that flip inside single crystals at atomic detail.

The second, nicknamed photodehydration, had never been documented before in such a system. Capturing both pathways in the same designed protein gives chemists a controlled test bed for how protein surroundings steer light-driven chemistry.
pmc-13226828:
Marla Almeida-Silva and eight co-authors build draft genome maps and marker sets for two wild Latin American trees. Their data paper appeared in twenty twenty-six. Both trees have long folk use for ills like malaria, gut pain, and diabetes. Few gene tools existed for them, which blocked study of wild stands.

Reads ran into the tens of millions for each tree, and draft maps held tens of thousands of parts. More than eleven thousand repeat spots were found in each map as mark seeds. Prime kits were then cut to small sets and grouped for cheap joint tests. The kits let labs read kin and change in wild stands at low cost.
pmc-13232828:
Giang Do Hoang and colleagues test in 2026 whether plastic caught in smoking fuel leaves dangerous pollutants in chicken meat in Vietnam. Backyard smoking sometimes burns packaging or coated scrap wood alongside clean fuel. The team smoked chicken over plain wood and over wood mixed with three common plastics, then measured pollutant levels.

Plain wood left only low contamination, while each plastic raised the load in its own pattern. One plastic added lighter compounds, another added mid-weight ones, and the chlorine-bearing plastic caused the worst contamination, with many dioxins and cancer-linked compounds. The ranking ran wood, then the two safer plastics, then the chlorinated one far ahead. Keeping plastic out of smoking fires is a plain food-safety rule the data support.
pmc-13233028:
Georgios Balatsos and colleagues published a 2026 field study testing mosquito traps in Cyprus. The team compared traps baited with a scent lure, carbon dioxide, both together, or nothing, rotating setups between sites in Larnaca and Nicosia.

The authors warn that standard baiting recipes cannot be trusted everywhere and need local testing before surveillance programs rely on them.
pmc-13233728:
Suman Karki, Shanker Raj Barsila, Naba Raj Devkota, and Masaaki Toyomizu fed young Sakini chickens diets with different protein levels in two thousand twenty-six. Sakini is a local breed in Nepal, often said to do well on low protein. The trial ran through the starter phase of growth.

Three hundred chicks ate diets with eighteen to twenty-two percent crude protein from day eight to day sixty-three. Birds on twenty percent or more grew heavier and used feed better. Gut measures in one gut part improved, and stress signs fell at the top level. Only birds on twenty-one or twenty-two percent reached safe antibody levels after vaccination against Newcastle disease.
pmc-13233828:
Granit Thaqi and colleagues published a 2026 data study cataloguing the proteins of the bovine corpus luteum. Proteins were then measured with high-grade mass spectrometry.

Roughly 3,783 individual proteins were identified. Their levels shifted across stages in patterns that mirror the gland's life story, especially near the transition toward regression, when the gland either survives to sustain pregnancy or breaks down. Because well-characterized tissue is scarce in many species, the authors offer the catalogue as a reference for reproductive biology beyond cattle.
pmc-13233928:
Johannes Vogeler and colleagues published a 2026 trial on keeping intravenous catheters attached to sweaty skin in emergency care. Clingfilm resisted the strongest pull, with cohesive bandage a close second. The Velcro device held well against gentle tugs but gave way sharply at higher force, while elastic gauze was weakest throughout. Clingfilm was also by far the cheapest option. The authors recommend clingfilm or cohesive dressings wherever catheter loss is likely.
pmc-13234228:
Mingjun Liang and colleagues published a 2026 cattle genetics study connecting a gene switch to beef quality. The authors nominate ZBTB18 as a target for precision breeding programs that want better beef without sacrificing yield.
pmc-13234528:
Chengsong Yuan and colleagues used in 2026 combined genetic and protein data to search for new drug targets in bipolar disorder. Eight genes passed the first screen, and a gene called DOC2A stood out as the leading candidate. Several checks supported a causal link, with lower DOC2A activity seen in bipolar brain tissue and lab-grown neurons. Network analysis placed the gene near processes for releasing chemical messengers between brain cells. Computer docking suggested existing neuroactive compounds can bind the protein with favourable energy. The authors nominate DOC2A as a target for future drug development.
pmc-13235328:
Louise Pierneef and co-authors surveyed in 2026 schoolchildren in Indonesia for antibodies signalling recent leprosy transmission in their communities. About twelve percent of children tested positive overall in the survey. Rural sites showed far higher rates than urban sites, with one rural district near one third positive. Children at schools serving poorer families were positive much more often than peers at wealthier schools. Worm infections also tracked with higher antibody levels and positivity in the data. The authors call for combined control of leprosy and worm infections in rural, disadvantaged areas.
pmc-13235528:
Zeina Merabi and Arij Daou modelled in 2026 how brain cells can respond selectively to pairs of sounds separated by long delays. Their computer model used realistic cell and connection properties drawn from experiments. An inhibitory circuit upstream was built to hold information about the first sound briefly.

The output cell need not keep firing during the gap for the mechanism to work. Delay length tunes which stimulus spacing the cell prefers in the simulated circuit. The authors offer the scheme as a general bridge between instant coincidence detection and longer-term timing in sensory systems.
pmc-13236028:

For each drug they compiled measures such as half-life, the time the body takes to clear half the dose. A single graded resource helps labs judge test results with care. That can turn a blame talk into a support plan for patients.
pmc-13236928:
Darellynn Oo and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the role of tumor-draining lymph nodes, the first nodes that fluid from a tumor reaches, in cancer immunity. pmc-13237428:
Delaney and nine co-authors counted immune cells in fat tissue for this study from twenty twenty-six. Fat immune cells are suspected drivers of type 2 diabetes. In thigh fat, the diabetes group held more T cells than lean women. In belly fat, several T cell types and one macrophage type rose step by step from lean to obese to diabetic. pmc-13238128:
Chenyi Di, Yun Long, and Huaiwu He wrote a 2026 letter on a study of electrical impedance tomography, a bedside imaging method, for detecting pulmonary embolism. The study had combined animal vessel blockage, advanced CT comparisons, and patient validation. Di and co-authors praise the regional model while disputing how its headline index should be read.

Their point is that the wasted-ventilation index tracks a ventilation-weighted pattern of air reaching under-perfused lung regions, not the total burden of blocked vessels. Equating the score with anatomical clot burden, they warn, overstates what the test shows. The distinction matters for how clinicians phrase diagnoses and judge severity. They frame the index as a physiological phenotype score within a growing bedside monitoring approach.
pmc-13239128:
Sai Jiang and eight co-authors read Nansi Lake health through its water bird packs in China. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Bird packs sort by trade, not kind, and may tell marsh health in a plain way. A few math ways were run side by side: pack counts gainst world grades, tree learn runs, and shrink fits.

Bird packs tied most to the top two world grades, one a plankton swap and one high air with low waste load. Fish eat birds rose with the clean grade. Waste and mud marks bore down on pack marks, while fish kinds and shore growth bore up. Ways agreed, which firms trust.
pmc-13239328:
Yvette von Aarburg and co-authors present a 2026 case report about acute myeloid leukemia returning in an unusual place long after treatment. A man first treated in 2007 received a donor stem cell transplant and stayed in remission for many years.

Thirteen years later he developed a testicular mass that proved to be a myeloid sarcoma, a solid form of the leukemia growing outside the marrow. Sequencing compared his original tumour with the new growth and found only one shared change, in a gene called HNRNPK. Tests also showed the relapse came from his own cells rather than the donor's. The case supports lifelong watchfulness after transplant.
pmc-13239728:
Pingping Qi and colleagues investigate a long non-coding RNA as both a warning signal and a possible treatment lever in sepsis during 2026. Sepsis, the body's damaging response to infection, often injures the heart, and the molecule called MIR503HG drops sharply in patients who develop that complication.

The team studied 102 patients, comparing those with and without sepsis-related heart dysfunction, alongside a rat model of the condition. Lower MIR503HG levels tracked higher heart injury markers, stronger inflammation, and worse severity scores. Raising the molecule in animals eased heart strain and calmed inflammation, partly by soaking up a smaller RNA that otherwise suppresses a protective brain factor.
pmc-13240028:
Hiroyuki Miura and colleagues report a frightening relapse of muscle paralysis after lung surgery in a 2026 case paper. An 82-year-old man had part of his left lung removed for squamous cell cancer, and the team reversed his muscle relaxant drug with sugammadex before he returned to the ward apparently recovered.

Thirty-five minutes later he suddenly stopped breathing. Scans of chest and head showed nothing wrong, pointing to the relaxant's effect returning, a rare event called recurarization. A fresh dose of sugammadex restored him promptly. The authors note this is the first such report after lung cancer surgery and urge keeping the reversal drug within reach.
pmc-13240328:
Yuto Matsuo and co-authors test daily plan tweaks in proton therapy for pancreas cancer using each day's scans, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Ten past patients got fresh proton plans checked against five daily scans each. Tweaks fired only when dose rules failed.

Across fifty sittings, about two fifths needed a new plan, near two per patient. Daily tweaks raised target dose and cut gut dose on the day checks. Pooled dose kept the target gain with no extra risk-organ cost. Tumor control odds rose while harm odds held flat. The authors back need-based tweaks, not blind daily ones. Readers get a smart pace for adaptive care.
pmc-13240728:
Mario Augusto Ferrari de Castro and colleagues offer a 2026 review of artificial intelligence support for throat cancer care. The cancer in question starts in the oropharynx, the middle part of the throat. Established national guidelines serve as the yardstick for judging the tools.

Large language models were tested on how well their management advice matched guideline-based care. Most outputs aligned with the recommended approach. Mismatches clustered in areas where automated support remains weak. The authors stress that these systems should assist doctors rather than replace them. Readers get a measured view of where AI can help treatment planning today and where human judgment stays in charge.
pmc-13240828:
Daniel Enériz and colleagues describe a 2026 open hardware system for testing brain-computer interface devices. Their board, called DEEGMUX, replays recorded brain signals as physical outputs. This lets embedded systems face realistic electroencephalography data before use with people.

The write-up lists the hardware under neuroscience, with open licenses for both the board designs and the software. Total build cost is stated in the specifications, and design files sit in a public repository. The authors note that models trained in simulation can fail on real signals full of noise and drift. A replay device closes that gap by supporting hardware-in-the-loop checks. No commercial equivalent is listed, which underlines the niche this low-cost board fills.
pmc-13240928:
Hong Ngoc and colleagues in Ho Chi Minh City developed an edge-focused variant of wire arc additive manufacturing for steel parts. Guiding the arc along edges concentrates heat and narrows the damaged zone. Builds used CT38 steel with a standard filler wire. Three-point bending tests compared the new route against plain substrate and conventional printing.

Best builds more than doubled the substrate's flexural strength, beating typical conventional prints as well. Strength per unit mass rose about forty percent over the substrate. A neural network rebuilt full stress-strain curves from process settings with high fidelity. Layer thickness emerged as the single most influential parameter.
pmc-13241428:
Krause's team at Erlangen surveyed German-speaking transplant centers on readying leukemia and MDS patients for donor stem cells. Twenty-two centers replied across five typical clinical scenarios. Options ranged from transplanting immediately to bridging with chemotherapy first. Practice proved strikingly inconsistent between centers. The scenarios spanned newly found disease and disease that came back.

Two-thirds favored upfront transplantation for intermediate-risk MDS cases. For AML already in remission, most favored chemotherapy as the bridge. AML that came back split the field, with gentler agents and induction both defended. The authors call for prospective trials to settle the pathways.
pmc-13241528:
Khoshnoud's team in Tübingen asked which Parkinson's patients gain the most quality of life from deep brain stimulation. Outcomes after the procedure vary widely between patients. The team studied 130 surgical patients with a machine learning model that shows its reasoning. Inputs ranged from mood and motor scores to the exact lead position on imaging.

Three factors foretold real gains: younger age, heavier mood burden from the disease before surgery, and a specific lead spot. Leads sitting at the motor-associative border of the right subthalamic nucleus fared best. The model sorted patients fairly well on held-out data. The authors offer the cut-offs as aids for planning care patient by patient.
pmc-13241628:
Remark Jie Peng and co-authors report a 2026 cell study of a small RNA called mascRNA in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma. This throat cancer makes up most laryngeal malignancies, and survival for advanced disease has barely improved. The small RNA is cut from a longer transcript known to matter in several cancers.

Cancer samples showed higher mascRNA levels than expected. In laboratory experiments, the RNA raised the growth capacity of the cancer cells. It also increased their ability to move and invade surrounding material. These behaviors are the steps that let a tumor spread. The authors position mascRNA as a driver worth targeting in future treatment research for this cancer type.
pmc-13241928:
Matheus Santos Moitinho and co-authors report a 2026 study on building infographics that teach patient blood management along the surgical pathway. Blood management bundles several practices that conserve blood and use transfusions wisely. Getting busy surgical teams to absorb those principles is a communication challenge.

A mixed team of clinicians, a graphic designer, and blood management specialists worked through five design stages. They built narrative first, then sketches, digital artwork, expert review, and a real-world applicability check. The finished pieces use icons, color gradients, pathway symbols, and QR codes linking to extra material. Reviewers judged them accurate, engaging, and easy to use. The authors say visual tools can shift habits toward more rational blood use.
pmc-13242028:
Ghaith B Heilat and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of liver and kidney blood tests in breast cancer patients in Jordan. Chemotherapy saves lives but can strain both organs. Records covered patients treated at one university hospital over more than a decade.

Standard enzyme levels barely moved after four chemotherapy cycles. Combined ratio measures told a different story, rising significantly after treatment. Patients whose post-treatment ratios stayed low lived notably longer than those with high ratios. The authors argue that composite markers capture treatment stress that single tests miss. Adding these ratios to routine monitoring could sharpen survival prediction for breast cancer care.
pmc-13242328:
Vieira and Vieira in Porto propose a mentoring cascade for radiology training. Senior trainees mentor junior trainees; juniors then guide students. The model maps onto the European training curriculum for radiology. Defined roles run from senior faculty down to first-year students.

Case talks, bedside teaching, research projects, and structured feedback fill each tier of it. Each level both learns and teaches. Teaching deepens the teacher's own skill while spreading the faculty load. Early student contact doubles as a draw into a specialty short on staff. The authors argue steady oversight, feedback, and review make the cascade last.
pmc-13242628:
Chan Cheah and co-authors ran an early-phase trial of a chemotherapy-free triplet for newly diagnosed, advanced follicular lymphoma. Their study appeared in HemaSphere in 2026. Fifty patients with high tumor burden received obinutuzumab, lenalidomide, and venetoclax in six induction cycles, with venetoclax dose levels tested along the way. Responders then moved to two years of maintenance antibody, and blood-based tumor DNA was tracked for residual disease.

Complete responses came in at eighty-six percent, and nearly all patients responded at least partly. Two years out, almost all patients were alive and free of progression in this follow-up window. Low white cell counts, diarrhea, and chest infections were the most common side effects. Clearing tumor DNA after just one cycle predicted a very high chance of staying negative. The authors present the regimen as a strong chemotherapy-free candidate now ready for larger comparison trials.
pmc-13242828:
Xuepeng Chi and co-authors present a 2026 mouse study of vesicles derived from royal jelly, the food of queen bees, against liver cancer. Royal jelly has broad reported health effects, yet its active components are unsettled. The team isolated its tiny extracellular vesicles and fed them to tumor-bearing mice.

The vesicles accumulated in the liver and showed moderate tumor-fighting activity. Immune and antioxidant responses improved. Gut microbe composition shifted, with one helpful family increasing, and short-chain fatty acid handling improved. Inside tumor cells, the vesicles adjusted protein-building networks and a growth pathway in ways that promoted tumor cell death. The authors identify the vesicles as key carriers of royal jelly activity.
pmc-13243028:
Jinping Hu and co-authors publish a 2026 network meta-analysis of exercise for depression in children and adolescents, including dose. Twenty-six randomized trials covering several thousand young people were pooled. The analysis compared exercise types directly and indirectly, then modeled how benefit changes with weekly dose.

Group training showed the largest symptom reduction, and aerobic exercise also helped significantly. Mixed training and mind-body exercise did not show clear effects. Benefit followed a curved dose pattern rather than rising forever. A minimum weekly dose marked the first significant effect, with peak benefit at a moderate level and uncertainty beyond a high level. The authors propose starting low and staying moderate. They caution that trial quality varied.
pmc-13244128:
Mohammed Al-Rumaih and co-authors offer a 2026 review of orthobiologics in trauma care, from platelet concentrates to stem cells and growth proteins. Broken bones that stall, and soft-tissue injuries that linger, push surgeons toward biological boosters. Evidence quality varies sharply by product.

Bone morphogenetic proteins show solid results in open fractures. Platelet and marrow products help healing in stubborn non-unions and cut revision surgeries. Mixed trial results and differences in how products are made limit firm conclusions. The review looks ahead to biomarker-guided precision use and cell-free exosome therapies, while calling for strict trials and standard protocols.
pmc-13245028:
Keith Fraser and colleagues modeled where yellow fever could ignite if an infected traveler carried it into three at-risk countries. Their study appeared in BMC Global and Public Health in 2026. Djibouti, Somalia, and Yemen are classed as potential or moderate risk, ringed by endemic regions. The team coupled a movement model, estimating imported cases, with a transmission model for what happens next, and multiplied the risks.

Three zones stand out: Yemen's western coast, Somali regions bordering Ethiopia and Kenya, and Djibouti City. In such places, a single imported infectious case carries better than even odds of sparking an outbreak, thanks to suitable climate and mosquito conditions. Elsewhere the combined risk runs lower but not zero. The authors urge surveillance systems to treat travel-linked fever as a possible introduction. The exercise is preparedness mathematics: knowing where sparks catch before one lands.
pmc-13246728:
Luisa Fernanda Duque Monsalve and co-authors study social ties and disaster recovery in Colombia in a 2026 multiple case study. Social capital, the web of trust and ties in a community, is widely praised in disaster work. Which forms help at which stage was less clear.

The team compared three towns exposed to flood and landslide risk. Two had suffered the country's deadliest flash floods of the decade, and one had not yet faced a major event. Close ties, wider ties, and ties to power each helped at distinct stages of the risk cycle. Shared memory and learning carried much of the effect. Ties alone were not enough without other resources and sound governance.
pmc-13247828:
Gezgin, Kabatas, and Kılıç used computer simulation to squeeze more power from paper-thin solar cells, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their device stacks an ultrathin copper indium gallium selenide absorber, barely four hundred nanometers thick, with standard partner layers. In the SCAPS-1D simulator they swept doping, defect densities, and band alignment to find what helps and what kills performance in such a thin cell.

Heavier acceptor doping strengthened the internal field and lifted efficiency, while interface and bulk defects caused severe recombination losses. The best band alignment sat at a slightly negative offset. Among candidate back-surface field layers, copper oxide won on its wide band gap and strong rear field, producing a simulated efficiency near forty percent in the model. The authors offer the design map to experimentalists building ultrathin cells.
pmc-13249428:
Christine Li, Michael Guo, and Ahmer Karimuddin swap sterile water for tap water in endoscopy and count the savings, in a 2026 study. Sterile irrigation was habit, not evidence; the literature already deemed tap water safe for most procedures. The unit compared one month on each, with advanced cases staying sterile throughout. Procedure counts held steady across the two months.

Sterile bottle use fell from 336 to 192 a month. Water cost per procedure dropped 41 percent, and 144 fewer bottles meant about seventeen kilograms less monthly waste. Production alone of the saved bottles carried a fifty-four kilogram carbon footprint. The authors call the switch a simple, safe step toward greener endoscopy.
pmc-13249528:
Zhang and co-authors ran a sixty-day transplant experiment on freshwater bacteria, reported in 2026. The question was what steers a microbial community's makeup over time: its own history, the chemistry around it, or new arrivals washing in. The team crossed three factors, swapping source communities between media and adding either normal or boosted immigration.

Early on, the arrival rate mattered most, with extra immigration enriching diversity. By day sixty, history dominated: communities from the same source stayed on distinct paths no matter where they lived or who arrived. The authors call this a priority effect, where early settlers lock in the future, and they argue it makes freshwater communities partly predictable from their past.
pmc-13249728:
Keno and co-authors warn that corn plants steal from their neighbors in breeding trials, in a 2026 Theoretical and Applied Genetics paper. Cash-strapped African breeding programs plant early hybrid trials in single rows, where each plot competes with the next for light, water, and nitrogen. Analyzing four hundred seventy-eight Ethiopian hybrids across six trials, the team modeled each genotype's direct worth and its effect on neighbors separately.

Both effects varied by site, and rankings shifted when competition was counted. Between a fifth and seventy percent of the top selections changed; under low nitrogen, the mismatch reached ninety percent. Ignoring competition, the authors argue, quietly slows genetic progress exactly where harvests need it most.
pmc-13249828:
Vogel and co-authors froze two insulin-blocking molecules in the act, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Congenital hyperinsulinism makes the body release too much insulin, and one treatment idea is a molecule that jams the insulin receptor. The candidates each carry two arms, gripping the receptor's two insulin binding sites at once, and a sibling molecule with the arms swapped paradoxically activates the receptor instead.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team showed both blockers holding the receptor in its inactive shape, explaining why they block rather than trigger it. Subtle differences in how each touches the receptor also appeared. The authors say the pictures should guide safer next-generation blockers.
pmc-13249928:
Vraggalas and a European team found a splicing factor that shapes tomato fruit before it blooms, in a 2026 Plant Molecular Biology study. Splicing factors edit gene messages, and one called RS2Z36 is active in ovaries and very young fruit. Plants lacking it grew ovaries with altered patterning and produced smaller, elongated tomatoes.

Gene and protein readings in the mutant ovaries showed hundreds of messages spliced differently or switched in amount, including cell wall proteins that steer expansion. Mutant skins also deposited more of certain wall sugars. Because the cell shape changes were set before flowering, the authors place this splicing control at the very start of fruit formation.
pmc-13250028:
Zhou and co-authors demonstrated holograms that control light's polarization as well as its brightness, in a 2026 Discover Nano study. Ordinary holograms shape only intensity, wasting half the information light carries. Their surface stacks metal and insulator layers in tiny patterned cells, a standard structure that usually fails at visible wavelengths because the metal absorbs too much light.

An improved design algorithm, splitting the light field into parts, produced cells that steer both properties at once. In full-wave simulations under circularly polarized red light, the surface generated the intended vectorial holographic images. The authors present the work as a step toward compact displays and optical devices that use polarization as a working channel.
pmc-13250628:
Mark Kern and colleagues examine how ageing changes swallowing in this 2026 study. Swallowing links the throat and the upper food pipe in a timed sequence, but how that teamwork shifts in healthy older people had not been mapped in detail.

Thirty-three healthy volunteers were studied with pressure sensors, split into elderly and younger groups. The team found the food pipe's swallowing motion runs in four periods, from rising empty, to receiving the food, to pushing it down. The early periods differed clearly in older subjects, and a link between flow and squeeze strength seen in the young faded with age. Weak throat muscles may explain the change.
pmc-13250828:
Tsubasa Mikie and co-authors report a design shortcut for plastic electronics in this 2026 chemistry paper. Polymers that carry electric charge well usually need fused rings locked into the backbone, but this team reached high performance without any fused rings.

They tuned a feature called quinoid character, which controls how bond lengths alternate along the chain, by varying one building block's length. Stronger quinoid character evened out the bonds and let charge flow more freely along each chain. Test transistors carried both charge types at high speeds despite modest crystal order. The authors propose bond pattern tuning as a fresh design lever for organic electronics.
pmc-13251028:
Capucci and colleagues clarify a confusing blood marker in rabbits vaccinated or infected with hemorrhagic disease virus. Their 2026 Veterinary Research study combines two vaccination experiments with a three-month farm watch during an unexpected outbreak. Antibody readings in rabbits are widely used, but the IgA class was hard to interpret.

Vaccination alone produced only traces of IgA for a few weeks in about half the rabbits. A real oral challenge, by contrast, triggered a marked and rapid IgA rise in the animals. On the farm, steady IgA marked the oldest does, survivors of an earlier epidemic, and new positives appeared with the outbreak. The authors conclude that IgA works as a sign of reinfection rather than of vaccination.
pmc-13251328:
Lonergan and co-authors show that nitric oxide, a short-lived gas signal, rewrites the makeup of microbe weapons called phenazines. Their 2026 study uses a Pseudomonas microbe that gives off these germ-killing pigments to shape the area around it. Whether released compounds react with nitric oxide, and what follows, had been little studied.

Nitric oxide reacted with certain phenazines to form stable, distinct products with much weaker germ-killing action. A rival germ, Staphylococcus aureus, shrugged off the altered compounds in tests. Pseudomonas itself, though, died quickly when its own phenazines met nitric oxide, even with the rival present. The authors say this tuning of what microbes give off could steer which germs win inside the body.
pmc-13253128:
SunMin Kim and colleagues use machine learning to place bird flu surveillance where risk actually runs highest in South Korea, reporting in 2026. Wild birds carry highly pathogenic avian influenza, and testing their droppings serves as an early warning system for poultry farms. Sampling sites, however, were chosen without a quantitative measure of risk.

The team divided 110 surveillance areas into one-kilometer hexagonal cells and assembled fecal testing results from the winters of 2021 to 2024 alongside climate, landscape, and population data. Four algorithms estimated each cell's chance of a positive detection, and an ensemble combining them performed best. Climate factors, sampling effort, human population, and elevation proved the strongest predictors. The risk map did not match where sampling currently happens, leaving some high-risk cells unwatched. The authors propose shifting effort toward the flagged cells to sharpen early warning and better shield poultry.
pmc-13253328:
Alexandra Schmuck and colleagues weigh the trade-offs of post-sorting plastic packaging waste in a 2026 analysis. Households inevitably mis-throw some packaging into residual waste, and recovering it later at sorting plants could raise recycling rates. Critics worry that material fished from mixed waste is too contaminated to recycle well.

At a single material recovery facility, the team compared bales from household source separation with bales recovered by post-sorting. Purity, the share of target polymer, came out similar across the two routes. Post-sorted bales, though, carried more contamination overall, including heavy metals such as cadmium and lead picked up from non-packaging items. They also held more moisture and dirt, which would demand extra washing and complicates both mechanical and chemical recycling. The authors conclude post-sorting is a useful supplement that grows feedstock supply.
pmc-13254428:
Sreeja Gandamsetty and co-authors test a heart tracing marker for early rhythm problems in a 2026 cohort study. They enrolled 196 patients with a first acute myocardial infarction, or heart attack, and tracked rhythm events within 48 hours. The marker is the Tp-e interval, the span from T wave peak to end on an ECG.

Rhythm problems occurred in 65.3 percent of patients, most often ventricular tachycardia. A longer Tp-e interval and higher Killip class, a severity grade, independently predicted these events. A cutoff of 98 milliseconds gave 77.3 percent sensitivity and 69 percent overall accuracy.
pmc-13254628:
Ignacio Ruiz del Olmo-Izuzquiza and colleagues follow heart and fitness changes in short children treated with growth hormone in a 2026 prospective study. Thirty prepubertal children, eighteen with growth hormone deficiency and twelve with other causes of short stature, received the hormone for twelve months. The team measured aerobic capacity on a treadmill protocol and used advanced ultrasound strain imaging to catch subtle changes in heart muscle.

Treatment raised growth factor levels and increased left ventricular mass, a favorable remodeling of the heart. Aerobic capacity, however, did not improve overall, and in the hormone-deficient group it actually fell, most noticeably in girls, despite electronically verified high adherence. A strain rate measure of heart muscle contraction improved by six months in the deficient group, while overall strain stayed flat. The authors say strain imaging is a useful early window on cardiac adaptation.
pmc-13255628:
Yi Yang and co-authors report a 2026 study of triptolide, a compound from a traditional medicinal plant, in Alzheimer's disease models. High cholesterol is a known risk factor for the disease, and brain immune cells called microglia drive much of its inflammation. The team traced how triptolide connects cholesterol control to calmer brain immunity.

In the liver, triptolide restrained a cholesterol-making pathway, which lowered expression of CD33, an immune brake found on microglia. With CD33 reduced, a signaling route recovered and microglia shifted from an inflammatory state to a protective one. In a tau-based mouse model of the disease, inflammation eased and thinking decline slowed. The authors present cholesterol metabolism as the lever behind the compound's benefit, while noting it remains a research-stage finding.
pmc-13256028:
Julian Bauer and colleagues present a 2026 case of heart failure after childbirth that turned out to have a genetic cause. Their patient, a 31-year-old woman, arrived ten weeks after delivery with advanced heart failure, and scans showed severely weakened pumping. She was first diagnosed with peripartum cardiomyopathy and started standard therapy plus bromocriptine.

A heart biopsy found lingering parvovirus B19 but no active inflammation. Genetic testing then revealed the surprise: a deletion across exons 44 to 50 of the dystrophin gene on her X chromosome, a change usually linked to muscle disease in boys. She had no muscle symptoms; pregnancy stress apparently unmasked the heart condition. The authors stress that finding a genetic cause changes management and enables screening of relatives who may silently carry the same risk.
pmc-13256628:
Yang Yi and colleagues present a 2026 review of store-operated calcium entry, the pathway by which cells refill internal calcium stores through STIM sensor proteins and Orai membrane channels. Their focus is how this entry route goes wrong in fibrosis, the scarring process that stiffens organs such as the lung, liver, and kidney.

The review first lays out how STIM proteins detect emptied stores and open Orai channels to sustain calcium signals. It then gathers evidence that faulty entry drives fibrotic progression across major organ systems. The final sections survey drugs and strategies aimed at this pathway. Framing calcium entry as a shared driver of scarring gives researchers a common target for antifibrotic therapy.
pmc-13257428:
Tingxuan Tang and co-authors review single-cell evidence on bone-eating cells in osteoarthritis in a 2026 article. Osteoarthritis is now seen as whole-joint failure, with bone under the cartilage remodeling early and driving pain. Osteoclast trials have disappointed, perhaps because these cells are not one uniform type.

Single-cell and spatial methods reveal osteoclast lineages differing by origin, state, output, and local niche. Disease stage and joint microenvironment organize that diversity better than a fixed subtype list. Distinct programs feed bone loss, vessel coupling, interface instability, and pain pathways. Rheumatology readers get a state-spectrum framework to replace the old uniform picture. Matching drugs to the active program in each patient is the proposed route forward, with stratification tools still to be built.
pmc-13257628:
Francisca Sempere-Ferre and colleagues compare pure eugenol with whole clove oil against three crop fungi in a 2026 study. Clove oil is rich in eugenol, and growers need to know whether the pure compound or the full oil works better as a natural fungicide. Growth tests ran on agar at a single matched dose.

Eugenol beat the oil against every fungus tested, and it stopped one wilt pathogen completely. The oil, despite holding over eighty-seven percent eugenol, protected less well. Minor oil components appear to dilute or blunt the main compound's action rather than help it. Crop protection researchers get a clear formulation lesson: simpler can be stronger. Pure eugenol offers a sharper biofungicide candidate, though field trials on real plants must still prove dose, safety, and staying power.
pmc-13257928:
Shawn A Thomas and co-authors wrote a 2026 United States public health report on drinking alcohol during pregnancy. Alcohol in pregnancy can harm birth outcomes and cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, and no amount is known to be safe. The team analyzed survey data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System for 2021 to 2024. It covered pregnant women aged eighteen to forty-nine across the United States.

In the past thirty days, 15.2 percent of pregnant women reported current drinking, 4.9 percent reported binge drinking, and 2.2 percent reported heavy drinking. Rates were higher among women who were not married and women with frequent mental distress. The authors suggest routine screening in clinics, plus community steps such as warning signs at sale points and alcohol taxes, to cut drinking in pregnancy.
pmc-13258128:
Sen Yang, Yi Liu, and Liping Xu wrote a 2026 tourism study of how food experiences shape what tourists do next. Their case was food tourism in Zibo, Shandong, China, a city whose food scene drove a strong post-epidemic tourism recovery. An online survey gathered 447 valid responses from tourists who had taken part. The authors used mental imagery theory, which holds that people rebuild sensory experiences in the mind, to model engagement behavior.

Food sensory experience, covering sight, smell, taste, and touch, had a significant positive effect on engagement. Its strongest effects were on feedback intention and revisit intention. Two factors carried the effect in parallel: food memory, the stored sensory record, and mental imagery, the active rebuilding of the experience. Imagery mattered more for recommending the place, while memory mattered more for wanting to return.
pmc-13258428:
Jakub Magdziarz Ibrahim-El-Nur leads a 2026 study asking whether language changes a language model's medical reasoning. Thirty real patient vignettes were given to six models in English and in Polish, with careful back-translation to keep cases equal. Two physicians scored hundreds of responses on a structured rubric, with a third settling disputes.

Four models scored significantly better in English, one showing a wide gap, while two models showed no detectable language difference. Gaps concentrated in building the differential list, justifying reasoning, and planning examinations, more than in the final diagnosis itself. Broader workups in the weaker language also raised implied testing costs. Health systems outside English gain a predeployment warning: validate models in the local language, because reasoning quality, not only accuracy, can slip quietly.
pmc-13258528:
Rafał Studnicki leads a 2026 sham controlled trial of a fast elbow manipulation in karting drivers. Fifteen drivers each had one arm treated and the other given a gentle sham procedure. Muscle signals from four forearm muscles were recorded during standard grip tests around two short simulated races.

The treated extensor muscle showed a different signal pattern across test points than the sham side. Other forearm muscles served as checks for whether effects stayed local. Testing happened in a laboratory grip task, not during real driving. Results speak to short term muscle recovery after steering load. Clinicians treating forearm fatigue in drivers get careful, narrow evidence rather than broad claims.
pmc-13259228:
Yinbo Zhang and colleagues recover depth images through smoke with single photon lidar in a 2026 paper. Smoke backscatter normally buries the target signal in this sensitive imaging method. Their approach checks echo shape correlation to flag smoke presence without fitting a detailed echo model.

Smoke detection reached perfect accuracy across two hundred fifty frames in heavy test conditions. Target recovery beat the conventional method by a wide margin even when smoke blocked nearly all the view. Fast denoising then rebuilds a usable depth image from the same capture. Fireground and battlefield imaging gain a rapid method that works in severe obscuration.
pmc-13259628:
Daphne Menssen and colleagues sketch a factory future for lab-grown cartilage. Damaged joint cartilage burdens millions, yet regenerative repairs stay costly, fiddly, and rarely reimbursed. Their 2026 review backs a modular fix: grow tiny cartilage balls, then assemble them into full implants.

Every production step, from freeing cells to forming and harvesting microtissues, has an automated version somewhere in the literature. Nobody has yet chained them into one cheap, compliant production line. The authors map the design choices that matter early, including automatic quality checks and cleaning. Building for scale from day one, they argue, decides whether patients ever benefit.
pmc-13259928:
Hannah Ochner and co-authors presented in 2026 a way to map chemicals inside single cells while also picturing their structure. Electron cryomicroscopy gives sharp images of frozen cells but cannot say which molecules fill each shape it shows. The team paired that imaging with mass spectrometry imaging, which identifies chemicals spot by spot.

Their combined workflow located molecules inside bacterial cells and worked on thin slices of larger cells too. As a test, they tracked bisphenol-AF, a common pollutant chemical, taken up by environmental bacteria. The chemical gathered in droplet-like stores inside the cell that the cell's own pumps could not clear, even though those pumps switched on strongly. The method could help researchers see where drugs or pollutants end up inside cells.
pmc-13260428:
Daniel Aristizábal Torres and colleagues mapped in 2026 the research field behind routing refrigerated delivery vehicles. The problem blends route planning with cold chain care for perishable goods. Their team ran a co-citation analysis on 469 articles from a major citation index, building a network of over three thousand linked works.

Four research perspectives stood out in the map. One centers on algorithms and mathematical modeling, and another on perishable logistics and cold chain operations. A third joins inventory choices with routing, while a fourth covers dynamic, smart, multi-goal systems. Across all four, most models wrongly assume cargo temperature stays constant along a route. The authors urge future work to couple routing with changing heat, spoilage, and energy use for more realistic planning.
pmc-13261328:
Zhifu Kou and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study of residential green space, genes, and irritable bowel syndrome. IBS is a chronic bowel disorder with recurring pain and changed bowel habits. Whether nearby greenery interacts with genetic risk was unexplored.

Within a 1000 m buffer, each interquartile-range rise in greenness meant a 5% lower IBS risk. Greater distance to water was also linked to lower risk. pmc-13261428:
Margery Ryan and co-authors reassessed in 2026 how much platinum group metal recycling really happens, using the market models of Johnson Matthey. Published recycling figures rest on open-market data, which miss metal that loops straight back inside a company. Their estimate counts that closed loop for the first time in print.

Between half and three fifths of the metal going into new products now comes from recycling, on global average. Because recycled metal carries a far smaller climate footprint than mined metal, the correction matters for sustainability models. Their scenarios show the warming impact of these metals dropping by about tenfold when a closed loop operates. The authors urge routine recovery that keeps metal in use.
pmc-13262228:
Jinjin Ni and co-authors described in 2026 a man whose only clue to a heart tumor was a slow pulse found by chance. The fifty-two-year-old felt no dizziness or blackouts, yet his resting rate sat in the low forties. Electrical tracings showed the heart running on a backup rhythm from the junction tissue.

The authors advise considering a cardiac tumor when slow rhythm has no plain cause.
pmc-13262428:
Stephania T Miller and colleagues describe patient partnership in a diabetes trial in a 2026 journal article. The SISTER study tested self-care support for African American women with type 2 diabetes. A Patient Advisory Group of women with the condition joined the work from the start, in 2020, rather than only taking part as subjects.

pmc-13262528:
Tanusya M Murali and colleagues adapted in 2026 peptide-exchange technology to study how killer-cell receptors read the peptides shown by HLA molecules. pmc-13262928:
Lena Jaki and co-authors show drug resistance hiding inside herpes viruses before any drug arrives. Aciclovir failures in immunocompromised patients emerge during long treatment, puzzling clinicians. pmc-13263228:
Seven researchers led by Magida Tabbara tested adding a factory-made bacterial mass to feed for Pacific white shrimp. Shrimp farmers care most about survival, growth, and health, and active feed extras are often used to help. The team mixed the bacterial mass into feed at six levels, from none to a fifth of the diet, and tracked feeding by sound sensors.

Young shrimp ate and grew for six weeks on each diet. The mix with a tenth bacterial mass gave the best weight gain at the standard ration. A slightly larger ration of the same feed did even better. Blood and body tests showed no harm to health at that level.
pmc-13263328:
Corinna Patzina-Mehling and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on West Nile virus in mosquitoes across a small part of Berlin, Germany. West Nile virus spreads between birds and mosquitoes and can infect people. The team sampled mosquitoes at five sites within one square kilometer over the 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Infection rates reached nearly five percent in some samples, and risk varied sharply over short distances. Homes and cemeteries showed the highest monthly infection rates, while restored nature areas and a sponge city site, built to soak up rainwater, showed much lower ones. Mosquito numbers and species did not explain the pattern. The shape of each habitat and its bird community mattered more.
pmc-13263528:
Lennart Essmann and colleagues read a decade of Swiss hospital records for infections in and around the brain. Over twenty-three thousand cases of meningitis or encephalitis span twenty twelve to twenty twenty-one in their 2026 study of the whole country. Pathogens and outcomes split sharply by age.

Case counts climbed year by year until twenty nineteen, then dropped hard during the pandemic years. Meningitis from pneumococcus and enterovirus fell furthest, hinting that the same curbs blocked them too. Young children carried enterovirus and streptococcus, while patients over fifty hosted pneumococcus, listeria, and tick-borne viruses. Bacterial cases landed in the ICU and died far more often than viral ones.
pmc-13263928:
Chunmei Sun and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on growing a medicinal orchid, Dendrobium devonianum, on China fir trees in Yunnan, China. The orchid grows on other plants without harming them, and its stems are valued in herbal medicine. The team compared plants grown on dead tree frames with plants on living standing trees.

Living trees hosted richer root microbe communities, including groups linked to lower disease, and the orchids built up more flavonoids and polysaccharides, prized medicinal compounds. The authors conclude living-tree cultivation gives the better balance of disease resistance and medicinal quality.
pmc-13264028:
Jordan J. Minnell, Jochem N. A. Vink and Rebecca E. McKenzie comment in 2026 on a new approach to keeping messenger RNA vaccines working under cell stress. Standard vaccines rely on cap-dependent translation, the usual route cells use to make proteins from RNA. Stress at a vaccination site, such as low oxygen or inflammation, can weaken that route and lower antigen production.
