pmc-13280328:
Ut Phuong Dang and colleagues published a 2026 dataset paper sharing survey responses on scientific literacy among trainee teachers in Vietnam. The dataset holds 807 complete, anonymized responses gathered in May 2025 through an online Vietnamese-language form. Its 42 rating-scale items span five areas: self-rated skill, how respondents apply it, how important they judge it, measures for strengthening it, and factors shaping it. It is treated here as part of global citizenship training for future teachers.

Six background items record gender, study year, grades, teaching practice, felt need, and readiness to use it. The bundle includes the raw data, a codebook, the original form, an English version, and a guide file. The authors intend the material for basic analysis, subgroup contrasts, reliability checks, and scale reuse in other contexts. Because responses are self-reported, the dataset measures felt rather than demonstrated literacy, a distinction reusers should keep.
pmc-13280628:
Marriam Ahmed and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on exosomes in cancer. Exosomes are tiny sacs that cells release into blood and other fluids. They carry proteins and bits of gene code from the cell that made them. That cargo can show what is going on inside a tumor.

The review explains how these sacs form and how labs find and measure their proteins. It describes how the sacs can help tumors grow and can change how the immune system reacts. It also looks at ways to block or use those proteins as drug targets. The authors argue that exosome tests could one day make cancer care more exact and more personal.
pmc-13281328:
Candice Peart and colleagues described a youth project on loneliness in a 2026 paper from Australia. Loneliness is rising among young adults and can shadow health for years. The project, called a/part of the crowd, built a web response with young people, not just for them. It drew on one hundred twenty-eight short works sent in by people aged eighteen to twenty-five. The works spanned stories, poems, art, and music.

A twelve-member advisory group of young adults with lived experience guided the design. Five of them also served as paid co-researchers on the team. Their notes shaped the web space, outreach, and user tests. The group found that a steady coordinator kept the team linked and heard. Shared meetings, where all read the data together, built trust. The authors say deep roles, not token seats, made the work stronger.
pmc-13281928:
Hazal Ünlügenç and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a guidewire lost during central line placement that hid inside a patient for almost nine years before nearly killing him. Losing a guidewire is a never event, a mishap that should not happen, yet wires can slip away unnoticed and migrate. Their patient, a 61-year-old man, presented with chest and abdominal pain that mimicked a heart attack. His first scans, heart tracing, and blood tests stayed inconclusive.

Fever and abdominal tenderness prompted a CT scan, which revealed a line running from the femoral vein through the right atrium and aorta, with blood leaking into the sac around the heart. Surgery removed the wire. Reviewing imaging showed it had sat undetected for nine years. The authors review how distraction and poor supervision cause such losses, and stress that a retained wire can stay silent for years.
pmc-13282028:
Jesús Martínez-Ortega and Sri Naidnur report a blood blister that mimicked skin cancer, in a case report dated twenty twenty-six. A fifty-four-year-old man had a dark spot on the finger's palm side. To the eye it looked reddish-brown, raising fear of melanoma.

A skin scope showed a plain red pattern with no cancer-type marks. The team named it a subcorneal hematoma, blood trapped under the skin's top layer, and chose watchful care. Digital color checks backed the call: red tones dominated both views. The case shows how scope optics sharpen color contrast already in the spot.
pmc-13282128:
Evonne Zoe Younan and co-authors describe a 2026 case of advanced bile duct cancer treated with a complex liver operation. Bile duct cancer, called cholangiocarcinoma, is often deemed inoperable when it grows into nearby blood vessels. The patient was a seventy-one-year-old woman whose tumour had invaded the vessels at the liver gateway. The team removed the extended left side of her liver.

Rather than cutting all vessels at once, the surgeons rebuilt them one by one. They reconstructed the liver artery, the portal vein, and the large vein to the heart before removing the specimen in one piece. Keeping blood flowing lowered the risk of starving the liver of oxygen. She left hospital on day fourteen after a smooth recovery. Forty-four months later she remained well, with no sign of return on scans.
pmc-13282428:
Norio Tomita and co-authors present a 2026 exploratory trial on how hands-on therapies change a deep back tissue layer in people with chronic low back pain. The layer, the thoracolumbar fascia, may contribute to pain without a clear cause. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to acupuncture, chiropractic care, or a three-week waitlist. After waiting, the control group received massage, allowing a within-person second phase.

Quantitative ultrasound measured how the fascia slides and strains. Chiropractic care reduced the cumulative strain measure, while controls grew worse and acupuncture showed no clear change. Massage after the waitlist cut both strain measures strongly. Only chiropractic care improved a disability score, and strain changes did not track disability changes. A tissue structure measure detected no changes at all. The authors say ultrasound strain can capture short-term mechanical responses to some therapies, offering a biomarker for how such treatments work.
pmc-13283328:
A freshwater sponge from Brazil's Cerrado hosts microbes quite unlike the water around it, Carla Patricia Pereira Alves's group found in 2026. Sponges are among the oldest animals and host rich microbe partners. Freshwater sponge microbes are far less studied than marine sponge microbes.

Samples of Metania sponge and nearby water came from the Brazilian Cerrado. Gene tests found 17 phyla across bacteria and archaea in the samples. The sponge host held a distinct microbe mix from the water around it. Only about a quarter of taxa were shared between the two sets. Sponge microbes were rich in defense systems that block virus attack. Water microbes leaned toward traits for life in open conditions.
pmc-13283428:
Sean P Woytowitz and Charles Manchee present a 2026 case of repeated confusion in a man treated for blood cancer and mental illness. Altered mental state in cancer care often has many drivers at once. Sorting the main cause is vital to cut harm and recurrence.

The man was in his 60s with relapsed plasma cell cancer after stem cell transplant. Episodes arose during chemo combined with many psychiatric drugs at once. Brain scans ruled out structural or vessel causes for his episodes. Kidney function dipped mildly at times without a full metabolic crisis. Care improved after his drug list was simplified by the team. Team-based review is urged for such complex cases.
pmc-13283728:
Peeling cartilage inside the hip socket can worsen if left alone, and Leandro Calil De Lazari with colleagues evaluated a drilling method meant to heal it from behind in 2026. Their reverse approach drills from above the socket rim so the joint surface stays intact.

Forty patients had keyhole hip surgery with impingement repair plus the drilling step. Scores for hip function rose sharply and pain scores fell sharply by final checks. Bone angles improved after surgery in line with the impingement repair work. MRI follow-up ran for at least two years in every patient. Results support the method as a low-cost, cartilage-sparing option worth wider testing.
pmc-13284028:
A cilia gene runs higher in tissue from boys with undescended testis in a 2026 study by Sinan Kilic and colleagues. Testis descent failure has known hormone and mechanical angles, but genetic angles are thin. Hair-like cell structures guide many development steps in embryos.

Tissue came from 24 young patients and 24 matched controls during surgery. Five dynein heavy chain genes were measured against a standard reference gene. Only DNAH9 stood out, at over twice the level in patient tissue. Other genes shifted little and without statistical firmness in tests. Mean ages matched closely between groups, near two years old. Ciliary paths merit study.
pmc-13284428:
Marc Shi and colleagues ran a community-engaged qualitative study in 2026 on immigration-related stress among immigrants living with HIV or at risk of it. Immigrants in the United States face higher HIV burden and worse outcomes than US-born peers, and migration stress touches housing, work, and income. The study set out to trace how those stressors shape access to care and health, working with the community it studied.

The authors name a pattern they call migratory grief, a sense of loss tied to exile and forced departure. Their headline findings stress that structural barriers, not individual choices, drove much of the stress reported. Services designed for people living with HIV helped participants clear those barriers, and accompaniment by community supporters stood out as a key model of help.
pmc-13285428:
Cristina Ioan Alexe and five co-authors review the evidence on new running shoe technologies, above all carbon-fiber plates paired with highly springy foams. Their systematic review came out in 2026. Such shoes promise better running economy, meaning less energy spent at a given speed.

Fourteen experimental studies met their standards. Plate-and-foam shoes improved economy by roughly three to four percent, and cut heart rate and blood lactate during runs. They also reduced joint work and changed stride mechanics. Maximalist cushioning, by contrast, raised impact loading, and carbon insoles alone gave no benefit. The authors caution that effects depend on the runner and the setting. They call for research on long-term adaptation, injury risk, and shoes fitted to the individual.
pmc-13285528:
Do trusted evidence reviews rest in part on work by repeat fraudsters? Theint Moh Moh Zaw, James Heathers, and Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz check Cochrane reviews in a 2026 study. Cochrane sets high bars for rigor, yet its reviews may still hold studies from authors with long retraction lists. The team flagged authors with at least twenty-four retractions and traced their papers.

Of 9,323 reviews, eighty-one held or cited at least one suspect study, and thirty-two folded such work into pooled results. When reviews shut such studies out, stated grounds seldom named trust worries. Only a small share of the affected reviews ran checks on whether dropping bad work moved the verdict. The authors urge closer screening.
pmc-13285628:
Severe leaking eye vessels struck a 10-year-old boy with a rare body syndrome, Eiji Kishi and co-authors report in a 2026 case. Bardet-Biedl syndrome had already left him with fading retinas, weak kidneys, weight gain, and learning delay, and gene tests pinned paired faults in the BBS2 gene. He arrived with sight down to bare light sensing in both eyes.

Scans showed heavy fluid leakage, retinal lifting, and a bleed in the left eye, plus pressure climbing there from new vessel growth. Laser treatment, surgery on both eyes, and an injected growth blocker followed. A month on, sight stayed at light level, yet pressure sat controlled with drops. The authors tie the vessel harm to blocked retinal flow.
pmc-13285928:
Xiaping Yao and colleagues build a gel eye drop for dry eye disease in a 2026 formulation study. Quercetin, a plant compound, calms inflammation and fights oxidative stress, but it barely dissolves in water and washes off the eye fast. The team packed it into coated fat bubbles, then set those bubbles in a gum that turns to gel on the eye.

The finished gel held tiny, even particles and trapped most of the quercetin loaded into it. It clung to the eye surface far longer than the bubbles alone and raised drug levels in tears and eye tissues. In mice with induced dry eye, the gel restored tear flow, healed surface damage, and cut two key inflammation signals. Results matched a standard prescription drop, with no irritation seen, which marks the gel as a strong candidate.
pmc-13286328:
Kimbra Edwards and co-authors survey how patients feel about AI writing research documents in a 2026 questionnaire study. Drug firms increasingly draft plain-language trial summaries with generative tools, stirring questions about accuracy and trust. An online panel of 1,010 patients across the United States and Europe reported their familiarity with AI and how much human hand they want in such documents.

Nearly two thirds had used AI before, and three quarters called themselves somewhat or very familiar with it. Over half believed AI drafting would cut grammar and data errors. Yet trust cratered when documents came from AI alone and peaked for human-only writing, and 95% rated human review as important. Most also demanded open disclosure when AI helps write public documents, a transparency call the authors say firms cannot skip.
pmc-13286528:
Sergio M-Cam and colleagues compare game-based and plain versions of ear training for young adults in a 2026 cross-sectional comparison. Tone discrimination drills support hearing rehabilitation, but months of repetition bore younger users into quitting. Both systems delivered identical pure-tone tasks and scoring; only one wrapped them in dual-task game play. Eleven volunteers aged 18 to 30 tried each build and rated experience, usability, and engagement.

The game version won six of eleven questionnaire dimensions, sweeping focused attention, looks, reward, and novelty. Raw performance, though, refused to budge: response speed, accuracy, and combined scores matched between systems. Plain software held a slight usability edge, suggesting simpler screens still navigate easier. Gamified drills thus look safe for keeping users hooked without dulling the training itself, pending longer trials.
pmc-13287028: A short 2026 retraction notice from the editors and publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy withdraws a 2019 study of a long noncoding RNA in hemangioma cells. A third party raised concerns in 2024, and the journal's check found image panels from different treatment conditions looking unusually alike, plus blots overlapping with an unrelated group's earlier article. The authors did not answer the queries. The original article stays online, watermarked as retracted, to preserve the scholarly record.
pmc-13287328:
Emmanuel N Nkuruemma and co-authors reviewed 81 studies in 2026 on making levan, a fructose-based chain sugar with food, medical, and industrial uses. Output figures vary wildly between labs, partly because microbe choice, growing conditions, and reporting styles all differ.

The enzyme that builds levan, and where it sits in the cell, shapes both yield and chain size. Oxygen supply and sugar strength emerged as major but under-studied controls. Recovery steps use much energy and solvent and can damage product quality. The authors propose a shared engineering framework so future plants can scale up with standard measures and cleaner processing.
pmc-13289328:
Yilin Liu and colleagues describe a 2026 effort to make nattokinase in engineered bacteria and test its promise for obesity care. Nattokinase is an enzyme that breaks down blood clots and may help heart and metabolic health. Normal production gives low yields, which blocks wider medical and factory use of the enzyme.

The team rebuilt Bacillus subtilis with a strong always-on promoter and a glowing fusion tag to watch output live. Flask cultures reached activity far above older methods, and a fed-batch run in a 5-liter bioreactor pushed output higher still. Animal work then probed effects on fat metabolism and heart complications linked to obesity. Higher, cheaper supply could make trials and products far more practical.
pmc-13289428:
Benoit de Witte and co-authors published a study in 2026 on DNA damage and cancer. Stress from oxygen-based chemicals can wound DNA. If the wounds are not fixed, they can build up as changes in the code and may help start cancer.

The team measured how prone each short DNA motif is to this kind of damage. Motifs that are easy to oxidize showed the highest damage levels in genome-wide data. The same pattern held for the mutation marks seen in cancers, most of all in lung cancer. The link showed up in both coding and non-coding parts of the genome. It also held for changes found in normal tissue. The authors say the work helps pinpoint genome regions most at risk.
pmc-13289528:
Lena Schemet and Sarah Friedrich-Welz present a 2026 simulation study on statistics after variable selection in Cox survival models. Cox models estimate how factors affect time to an event, but standard math assumes factors were fixed in advance. When data-driven selection picks factors first, naive follow-up results can mislead badly, and censoring adds more uncertainty.

The study tests several fixes after Lasso selection, including sample splitting, selection-aware methods, and a debiased approach. Each method targets a different question, so coverage, interval width, power, and error rates must be read with that target in mind. Simulations used realistic biomedical data patterns, plus a public survival dataset example. Findings guide analysts toward honest uncertainty after selection.
pmc-13290728:
AI has moved into the clinical skills classroom mostly as a virtual patient, Birpartap Thind and colleagues map in a 2026 scoping review. They collected implemented uses of AI in undergraduate medical clinical skills teaching from January 2022 through January 2026.

From 1,130 records, 39 studies qualified, and their uses sorted into eight themes. Large language model virtual patients and simulations dominated with 19 studies, followed by AI-augmented exam and simulation assessment at six. Robots, procedural trainers, documentation tools, and tutoring systems filled the rest, with publication activity bunching in 2024 and 2025. Nearly everywhere, AI played a supporting, formative role rather than replacing teachers. Thind and colleagues note that hard evidence on long-term learning impact is still thin and call for longitudinal evaluation to keep pace with adoption.
pmc-13290828:
Patients fresh from hernia repair preferred the stiffer belly support, Kryspin Mitura and colleagues report in a randomized cross-over study from 2026. Abdominal binders are routine after ventral hernia repair despite thin evidence, and clinicians worry semi-rigid corsets will be tolerated badly in the first days.

Twenty-three patients after open sublay repair of large hernias each wore an elastic binder and a semi-rigid corset for about three hours on day two or three. Self-rated health on a visual scale matched between devices, and no quality-of-life domain scored worse with the corset; usual activities and anxiety ratings even improved. About 70% preferred the corset, and nearly all would recommend it, against two-thirds for the binder. Mitura and colleagues say rigidity is no early barrier, though long-term adherence went untested.
pmc-13290928:
Gene-guided prescribing gets a cautious welcome inside early psychosis services, A. Jameson and colleagues report in a qualitative study from 2026. Pharmacogenomic testing could sharpen antipsychotic choice, but how it would land in Early Intervention in Psychosis teams, with patients and carers, was largely unexplored.

The team interviewed 12 service users and ran focus groups with 18 staff and 3 carers across three NHS sites. Stakeholders saw early psychosis care as a complex ecosystem and knew uneven amounts about genetic testing. Overall the test felt acceptable, much like routine medicines-safety checks. Support came with conditions: offer timing matters, communication must be clear, expectations must stay realistic, and the service must be funded well enough not to crowd out other therapy. The authors frame testing as a supportive extra, never the decider.
pmc-13291028:
What daily life feels like for people who cannot stop turning the same thoughts over is the subject of a 2026 qualitative study led by Aleš Oblak. Rumination is tied to distress, self-criticism, and the course of many mental disorders, yet accounts of the lived experience itself have stayed thin.

Fifty-one people from general and clinical groups gave 107 interviews covering 79 episodes, studied through close phenomenological methods that track body, space, time, feeling, and relationships. Rumination emerged as an effort to settle doubt and make meaning after everyday understanding breaks down. Episodes carried feelings of paralysis and emptiness, and a drift away from bodily, gut-level response toward pure thought, offering clinicians a richer picture to work from.
pmc-13291128:
A farm chemical caused rare brain poisoning in a 2026 case by Luye Wang and colleagues. The chemical is chloropicrin, a soil fumigant. It is known for harming eyes, lungs, and skin. Brain effects are almost never reported.

Their patient was a 53-year-old man. He lost clear awareness after exposure. Stroke, infection, and immune causes were ruled out. Brain scans looked largely normal. Brain wave tests backed the toxic brain diagnosis. Mild lung signs could not explain his state. Support care and high-pressure oxygen helped him gain ground. He went home after three weeks of care.
pmc-13291328:
Two toothpastes for sensitive teeth are compared in a 2026 trial led by Kohei Ishii. Sharp tooth pain starts in exposed dentin tubules. One paste held potassium nitrate alone. The other added aluminum lactate to the same base.

The trial held 127 people in three blinded groups. Pain scores were taken by touch and air blasts. Both real pastes beat the dummy paste from week two. Gains showed right after first brushing too. The combined paste edged ahead at set later checks. At eight weeks it won on both test types. Adding the second agent thus helps some users more.
pmc-13291528:
Nan Xu writes a 2026 letter questioning a claimed carbon sink in the Taklamakan Desert. A recent study praised tree planting at the desert edge. Green cover and plant activity rose there. Xu urges care before crediting a human-made sink.

The carbon trend carries an error bar as large as itself. Such a signal may not differ from zero at all. Other causes of greening were not ruled out. Watering, groundwater shifts, and carbon dioxide gains could all play a part. No untreated desert comparison was made. Bare sand also trades carbon gas without life. Heat and salt chemistry drive that dead exchange. Stronger proof is needed, Xu argues.
pmc-13291728:
Muhammad Salameh and colleagues build a national consensus on root canal skills for Syrian dental students in 2026. Syria's dental schools lack a formal competency list for endodontics, the root canal field. Care by general dentists is often judged substandard there. The study used a modified Delphi method, where experts rate and re-rate items until they converge. Five consultants drafted the starting list at Syrian Virtual University.

Fifty-three experts scored the draft in round one, and thirty-eight returned for round two. Items averaging above a set threshold counted as essential. The final set held thirty-one competencies, split into nine knowledge, thirteen skill, and nine attitude items. Agreement statistics were strong, with reliability scores above 0.9 in both rounds. The authors intend the list to anchor a standardized national curriculum. It may also guide schools in similar low-resource settings.
pmc-13292328:
Jared Omundo, with co-authors, reviews a 2026 youth mental health idea: Discovery Colleges, recovery-oriented learning spaces adapted from adult Recovery Colleges for young people. Youth services face soaring demand, staff shortages, and broken referral paths. The narrative review pulled together journal articles, program descriptions, and implementation reports on these colleges and kin initiatives.

Four strands define the model: recovery-focused learning fitted to development, ways of drawing young people into participation, effects on organizations and professions, and a seat spanning education, community, and clinical sectors. Framing help as shared learning rather than treatment alone is the core shift. The authors also name friction points around safeguarding, staying true to the model, funding, and joining up sectors. They call the concept promising but still lightly evidenced.
pmc-13293128:
Khalid Abu-Zeinah leads a 2026 chart review of Lyme arthritis, the joint swelling that can follow Lyme disease spread in the body. Most patients clear with antibiotics, yet some keep inflamed joints after the germ is gone.

Records covered 77 patients with lab-confirmed joint infection treated from 2004 to 2025, including 13 children. One swollen knee was the usual picture, while children had fever more often and higher white cell counts in joint fluid. Among adults, 41 recovered fully with antibiotics, while 19 kept inflamed joints afterward. Longer antibiotic courses in that group showed no clear benefit, urging care in drug use.
pmc-13293428:
Lauren Wakefield and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a simulation tool to judge deer farm screening for chronic wasting disease. Farmed deer live close together and move often between sites, so this fatal brain disease can spread fast once it takes hold.

Testing only a few deer early on can easily miss infection, and a clean small sample does not prove a herd is free. The tool blends herd age data, movement records, and past test results to estimate the chance that screening would catch disease at each farm. Data from 23 Texas facilities show how agencies could aim checks where risk runs highest.
pmc-13293928:
Yonghao Li and coauthors lay out a 2026 trial protocol testing Guipi Mixture, a Chinese patent medicine, for early extra heartbeats called premature ventricular contractions. The trial targets heart-spleen deficiency syndrome and pairs the mixture with metoprolol, a standard drug whose single target and long-term risks limit it. Eighteen centers will enroll 200 people in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design.

Half get the mixture plus metoprolol and half get a dummy mixture plus metoprolol over 12 weeks. The main measure is change in 24-hour extra beat counts by week 8 on ambulatory monitoring. Quality of life, sleep, syndrome scores, and safety events are also tracked.
pmc-13294328:
Mohammed Naveez Valathoor and Anand Prem Rajan review a food germ's attack tools and drug shield through a One Health lens in 2026. Salmonella Typhimurium spreads among people, farm stock, food, and the wild. It causes gut illness and deep infection across the globe. Entry genes, needle pumps, sticky hairs, and slime mats power host entry and life inside cells.

Drug shield spreads by gene swaps and gene change, across key drug groups. Multi-drug strains now blunt first cures. The review weighs toll data, trends in India and beyond, current drugs, and vaccine hopes. Shared weak spots where attack and shield meet are the prize.
pmc-13294428:
Julien Dejean-Servieres and a large team re-read wrist scans for missed ligament anchor tears in a 2026 study. Foveal tears of the triangular fibrocartilage can drive ulnar wrist pain and joint looseness, yet first reports often skip them. Two blinded specialists reviewed 149 arthro-CT scans and compared fresh reads with first reports, clinic notes, and surgery.

Fresh review found cartilage complex tears in 59% of patients. Forty-five tears had been underreported, 89% of them ulnar and most at the foveal bundle in the reported shares. Complete ulnar tears tied strongly to pain and looseness. Twelve patients had surgery, and review agreed with operative findings even where first reports were negative.
pmc-13294928:
El Mahdi Choukri and colleagues present a frightening bleeding case in a 2026 report from the emergency ward. A thirty-five-year-old mother of five arrived ten days after an abortion and uterine scraping procedure with renewed heavy bleeding, shock, and severe anemia that required transfusion. The danger in such cases is mistaking a high-flow tangle of blood vessels in the womb wall for ordinary retained tissue, because another blind scraping could make the bleeding far worse.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed leftover pregnancy tissue in the upper womb, sitting next to a zone of abnormal, worm-like vessels within the muscle wall. Contrast images lit those vessels up early, raising concern for an acquired arteriovenous malformation or simply markedly increased blood flow tied to the retained tissue. Blocking the uterine artery was proposed as a womb-sparing option. The authors stress careful naming when no confirming angiogram exists.
pmc-13295028:
Fei Yuan and colleagues model how a resting iron mass shapes blast furnace hearth safety in a 2026 study. The hearth holds molten iron under harsh heat, and lining erosion there can end a furnace's life. A partly floating coke mass, called the deadman, influences heat, flow, and wear inside.

A three-dimensional model linked heat flow, liquid movement, carbon transport, iron freezing, and material stress for a locally eroded hearth. Raising the deadman float height and keeping its base size and slope low encouraged a protective frozen iron layer and eased stress. A rounded base beat a flat base on layer thickness, stress, and carbon loss.
pmc-13295728:
Na Ri Seo and colleagues compare two dental implants in fake bone models in a 2026 study. How tightly an implant screws in matters most where bone is weak or support is missing. The KS 3 design was set against the established TSIII design in three standardised setups.

Models mimicked weak bone, a fresh tooth socket with reduced support, and the hollow upper jaw sinus area. The newer implant reached higher peak and final screwing forces in the weak and socket models. Sinus results shifted with leftover bone height and drilling style. The authors stress the findings show bench behaviour only, not proof of better patient outcomes.
pmc-13295828:
Betül Dikkanoğlu Demirok and colleagues group lupus patients by symptom pattern in a 2026 study. Lupus varies hugely between people, making outlook hard to judge at diagnosis. Records of 199 patients at one Turkish university clinic were clustered at diagnosis and again at the last visit.

Three groups appeared at diagnosis: joint-led, kidney and blood-led, and skin-led patterns. At the last visit, after a median 168 months of follow-up, a fourth mixed group carried the heaviest organ damage scores. Skin-led patients faced about double the odds of drifting into that poor-outlook group. Death rates did not differ between groups, so the clusters mainly warn about damage ahead.
pmc-13297228:
Marya K. Kolokolova and colleagues develop, in 2026, a quick fluorescence test for 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid, a growth regulator and herbicide ingredient needing environmental monitoring. Their antibody-based assay runs in fifteen minutes and detects the chemical at very low levels across a wide range.

Open water samples spiked with known amounts returned near-complete recoveries. The hard part is a close chemical cousin that fools the antibody, so two fixes are offered. One runs paired tests and solves both levels with maths. The other strips the cousin out first on a capture column. Both routes worked in the study.
pmc-13297328:
Cesare Mancuso and Rosaria Santangelo review carbon monoxide, a gas the body makes in small amounts, as a regulator of the stress system in a 2026 article. The gas forms when an enzyme family breaks down heme, the iron-bearing part of blood pigment. One family member switches on under strain, while another works steadily at all times.

Inside cells the gas acts on iron-bearing proteins and steers growth of energy factories, ion channels, and gene switches. In the brain's stress centre, it holds back the release of hormones that drive the stress response during inflammation, lowering output down the chain to cortisol. Its effects shift with context, the authors stress, which makes it a subtle lever rather than a simple brake.
pmc-13297428:
Manuel E. Soto-Martinez, Wojciech Feleszko, and Alexander Moeller review bacteria-based products that train the immune system to ward off chest infections in children, in a 2026 article. Such infections strike most young children again and again, and early episodes raise later asthma risk. Four products were weighed, all built from bacterial parts or strains.

All four strengthen the airway barrier and tune immune responses in like ways. One, OM-85, holds by far the strongest trial record, cutting infections by roughly a quarter to a third across studies. The others act through gut-lung links or trained immunity, with thinner proof. Open gaps include treatment length and which children gain most, so direct comparison trials come first.
pmc-13298528:
Morgan Bou Zerdan and others report pregnancy outcomes after exposure to immune checkpoint inhibitors, in a 2026 study pairing two new cases with a review of earlier reports. Immunotherapy has improved cancer care for younger patients, yet safety during pregnancy remains unclear. The authors describe what happened when exposure occurred before results were known.

Most pregnancies in the collected reports ended in healthy live births. Still, miscarriage, preterm delivery, and poor fetal growth appeared at notable rates, and rare effects in newborns were documented. The team stresses avoiding pregnancy during treatment, plus careful counselling and monitoring after exposure, while more research gathers firmer numbers.
pmc-13298928:
Putting a primary care doctor inside the sickle cell clinic sharply raised preventive care, report Sherraine Della-Moretta and colleagues in a 2026 cohort study. At one tertiary center, 174 of 388 adults with sickle cell disease saw an internist embedded full-time in the hematology team between 2020 and 2025.

Those patients were far more likely to receive cervical cancer screening, depression screening, and tetanus vaccination, with odds ratios up to 7.97, and also scored better on sickle-specific care such as eye exams and urine protein checks. Outpatient visits rose from 2.7 to 4.2 per year while admissions drifted down without reaching significance. The authors credit coordinated, outpatient-focused management.
pmc-13299128:
Michelle G. Santoyo-Suárez leads a team charting how Krüppel-like factors, a family of gene regulators, switch on and off after heart injury, in a 2026 rat study. Drug-induced injury produced progressive enlargement, structural disorder, and lasting scarring over three weeks of tissue sampling. Human cardiac datasets supplied a translational comparison, alongside interaction network building.

Family members acted in coordinated phases: early members tied to inflammation, middle members tied to growth signalling, and late members tied to cell death and scar formation. Patterns paralleled changes in inflammatory, electrical, and calcium-handling genes. The authors position this family as regulatory nodes and possible treatment targets in heart remodelling.
pmc-13299828:
A A Askarinejad and others link a combined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic staging system to outcomes in atrial fibrillation, using two prospective registries from Europe and East Asia, reported in 2026. More than five thousand patients with staging data were grouped into low, middling, and high joint-risk categories. Most patients landed in the high group.

High combined risk carried roughly double the hazard for death and for major cardiovascular events compared with the low group, after adjustment. Clot and bleeding outcomes were also examined in the regression models. The authors recommend holistic, integrated care for these patients rather than rhythm-focused management alone, given how strongly the combined burden predicted harm.
pmc-13300128:
Y Zhao, F J Ha, A J Brown, and A Nerlekar pool randomised trials of lifestyle and risk factor clinics for atrial fibrillation care, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Eleven trials covering more than three thousand patients compared dedicated clinics with usual care, half of them around catheter ablation treatment.

Clinics cut rhythm recurrence after ablation by a large margin and reduced total plus rhythm-related hospitalisations. Quality-of-life scores improved clearly as well. No significant difference appeared for cardiovascular deaths, stroke, or heart failure admissions. The authors support a multidisciplinary lifestyle model as part of fibrillation management, noting follow-up across trials ranged from a few months to two years.
pmc-13300428:
Kayla R. Whitebrook and colleagues examine who leaves a transitional care program housed, in a 2026 study of Durham Homeless Care Transitions. The program serves people who are homeless, often after illness or injury. The authors mined its records for traits tied to being housed again at discharge. Traits covered background basics, self-efficacy, mental health care status, and unmet needs for identity papers and contact, such as lacking ID documents or technology access.

In both simple and adjusted analyses, non-White participants were less likely to be rehoused than White participants. More unmet needs of that kind also predicted lower chances of housing, a factor the authors say has not been studied before. They frame that second finding as one programs can act on: help with papers and contact access could start earlier. The racial gap, they argue, calls for more targeted and fair rehousing efforts.
pmc-13300528:
Rachel S. Carling and co-authors report England's switch to one commercial reagent kit across its national newborn screening program, in a 2026 evaluation. Thirteen laboratories had relied mostly on home-developed tests, making results hard to harmonize, and adding screening for hereditary tyrosinemia forced changes anyway. The study checked whether the shared kit improved analytical performance and agreement between laboratories.

Verification across all thirteen sites did show reduced variation between laboratories for every analyte, a harmonization gain. That gain, however, depended on significant instrument-specific correction factors, which the authors read as a lack of true standardization. One new analyte also suffered instrument-dependent background interference from a labeled internal standard. They conclude that evidence-based cut-off values matter more than published thresholds, and they press for traceable reference materials to anchor quality across the program.
pmc-13300628:
Dariya V. Karaseva and co-authors build a computational map of microRNA control over IRF1, a transcription factor tied to immunotherapy response in lung cancer, in a 2026 study. PD-L1 testing predicts checkpoint inhibitor benefit imperfectly, and IRF1 directly drives PD-L1 production, so its regulators could serve as better markers. Using Cancer Genome Atlas data for lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, the team searched for microRNAs whose levels move opposite to IRF1.

Twenty microRNAs qualified in both cancer types. Only one, miR-301b, carries conserved binding sites in IRF1 itself, pointing to direct repression. Two others appear to work indirectly through partner transcription factors, NFKB1 and STAT4, which themselves track with better survival in treated patients. Because no treated cohort with microRNA data was publicly available, the authors stress that the biomarker idea stays hypothetical until laboratory and clinical validation arrive.
pmc-13300728:
J Reventos-Presmanes and co-authors present the NIAVAS-2 study on finding dangerous ventricular tissue without invasive mapping, published in 2026. In non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, the scar that breeds ventricular tachycardia is often patchy. It also sits away from the slow conduction zones that matter, so imaging alone misleads. The team tested a dispersion measure from non-invasive electrocardiographic imaging in forty-seven patients. Twenty-seven were sent for ablation after known tachycardia, and twenty were at the prevention stage.

Regions later proven to hold deceleration zones on invasive mapping showed much higher dispersion, in both natural rhythm and paced rhythm. That link held no matter whether magnetic resonance imaging showed scar in the region. Prevention stage patients showed no such contrast between scarred and unscarred regions, a sign of electrically quiet tissue. The authors propose the measure to tell active arrhythmia substrate apart from harmless scar and refine defibrillator choices.
pmc-13301028:
Long cast as a bone vitamin, vitamin D also steers the immune system, Sandesh Shende and Jaishriram Rathored argue in a 2026 narrative review. Searching five databases, they gather mechanistic, population, and clinical work on vitamin D as an immuno-endocrine modulator in autoimmune and infectious disease.

Through its receptor, the vitamin switches on antimicrobial peptides, steadies macrophages and natural killer cells, and favors tolerogenic dendritic cells that calm adaptive responses. Trial results, however, swing widely with starting vitamin D levels, dose schedules, genes, and the disease in question. The authors call for sharper randomized trials to find who truly benefits and at what dose.
pmc-13301128:
Katharina Tscheu and co-authors compare how healthy and osteoporotic human bone cells respond to vitamins K2 and D3 on a roughened titanium surface, in a 2026 laboratory study. The question matters for anchoring joint replacements in fragile bone. Primary bone forming cells from healthy and osteoporotic donors grew on plastic and on implant-like titanium, with each vitamin alone, both together, or neither. The team tracked shape, mineral deposits, and a differentiation enzyme.

Osteoporotic cells behaved distinctly on titanium, forming noticeably more cell to cell contacts under vitamin K2. The rough surface itself boosted their mineralization, and that effect grew stronger with K2 added. Vitamin D3 acted mainly in the early phase of differentiation. Overall, K2 influenced the osteoporotic cells' mineral building far more than expected. The authors suggest K2 deserves a larger place in thinking about bone metabolism around implants.
pmc-13301228:
Réka Niklai and co-authors expose four orthodontic wire alloys to acidic drinks in a 2026 laboratory study. The wires were nickel titanium, its copper bearing cousin, a titanium molybdenum alloy, and stainless steel. Samples were soaked in two commercial acidic beverages at different pH levels. They were then examined by atomic force and electron microscopy plus elemental analysis, to see how they held up.

The alloys split clearly. Stainless steel and the titanium molybdenum alloy grew rougher clearly and showed obvious surface alteration. Both nickel titanium based wires kept comparatively stable surfaces. Elemental readings shifted in specific ways, suggesting selective surface chemistry rather than uniform corrosion. The authors tie the split to each alloy's composition, microstructure, and the toughness of its passive oxide skin. For orthodontics, rougher wire means more friction against brackets, so drink contact joins the list of practical counseling points.
pmc-13301428:
T Inoue and co-authors ask whether a rhythm provoked in the lab deserves the same treatment as one that appears on its own in a 2026 study. Among 864 ablations for rhythm problems across nine Japanese institutions, 311 patients had an atrial tachycardia ablated during the redo procedure. Of these, 154 had it induced by burst pacing and 157 had it running or appearing spontaneously.

Over a follow-up of 666 days, the induced group fared worse, with three year recurrence of fibrillation or tachycardia at about fifty-four percent against thirty-two percent. The excess was tachycardia, forty-one versus twenty percent, while fibrillation recurrence matched. Induced cases skewed toward right atrial circuits and focal sources rather than the flutter circuit. Adjusted analysis kept induction status a predictor of relapse. The authors advise restraint: burning a rhythm the lab manufactured may treat an artifact of provocation, so its indication needs careful thought.
pmc-13301928:
Two pills may beat three for clearing stomach bacteria, Nikolay Georgiev and colleagues find in a 2026 meta-analysis of Helicobacter pylori treatment. Five randomized trials with 1,363 adults compared vonoprazan plus amoxicillin against the classic clarithromycin-based triple therapy. Resistance has been eroding the older regimen for years, setting up the contest.

Dual therapy cleared the infection more often, with a risk ratio of 1.17 in favor of the two-drug arm and low disagreement between trials. Stronger, steadier acid control from vonoprazan likely props up amoxicillin's killing power. The authors still want larger, well-built trials before dual therapy takes the first-line crown, and safety data remain thinner than efficacy data.
pmc-13303428:
Joseline Jiménez-Venegas leads a 2026 systematic review of bacteria that tolerate or clean up toxic metals in mining settings. Industrial activity releases metals such as cadmium, chromium, copper, iron, lead, and zinc into soil and water.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched Web of Science and Scopus for work from 2000 to 2025. Some bacterial families tolerated high metal levels in alkaline sites, while genera such as Acidithiobacillus worked actively in acid sites through leaching, settling, or uptake. Bacillus subtilis and Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans both tolerated metals and removed them well. Mixed methods across studies mean standard lab tests are needed before wide field use.
pmc-13303828:
Raluca Rilla heads a 2026 commentary warning that online behavior studies are being distorted by participants who quietly use large language models. Paid survey platforms promise genuine human answers, yet audits now find frequent model use by respondents.

Three forms of contamination are set out: partial help from a model, full hand-off of the task, and spillover effects beyond single answers. Together they skew samples, bias conclusions, and spark a costly methods arms race. Countermeasures are proposed at three levels, covering researcher habits, platform responsibility, and shared community adjustment to protect study quality.
pmc-13304128:
Yufeng Liu and co-authors hunt brewing microbes that make a smoky aroma compound in a 2026 screening study. The compound, 4-ethylguaiacol, gives fermented foods and Baijiu liquor prized woody and spicy notes.

Isolates from Baijiu pit mud yielded a Bacillus coagulans strain, JN11, that produced the aroma in sorghum juice. Its key enzyme gene was copied and grown in lab bacteria for testing. The enzyme worked best at mild acidity and moderate heat, liked one starting acid far above others, and gained activity with iron while zinc blocked it. Shape modeling hints why the favored acid fits so well.
pmc-13305428:
Kabir Brar leads a 2026 scoping synthesis of ticks and their germs in Australian wildlife. Ticks bite wildlife, farm animals, and people, yet records for unique Australian fauna remain scattered across a century of reports.

Studies from 1940 to March 2024 yielded 133 usable records across three major databases. Fifty tick species were found on 160 wildlife hosts, mostly marsupials such as bandicoots, wallabies, and possums. Germ records stayed thin and mostly showed mere presence rather than proven spread. Sampling favored the east, and deeper germ screening plus unified health surveillance are called for in future work.
pmc-13305728:
Keyan Gao mapped eight years of publishing on fatty liver disease and muscle loss in a 2026 bibliometric study covering 2012 to 2025. English articles and reviews were drawn from two large databases, giving 701 distinct papers for analysis.

Output grew fast, averaging 36.6% per year in the authors' count, with China, South Korea and the United States as the main network. Topics moved from basic mechanisms toward risk prediction, lifestyle steps and combined metabolic care. Topic modelling found three rising themes, while cohort evidence linked low muscle mass or weak function to higher risk of liver disease starting or worsening.
pmc-13306028:
Leyla Kaya built a new family of carbazole ester compounds as possible diabetes drugs in a 2026 chemistry study. Starting alcohols were reacted with varied acid chlorides to give ten single esters and ten double esters for testing.

Most compounds blocked alpha-amylase only weakly but hit alpha-glucosidase more strongly and selectively in lab assays. The strongest compound reached an IC50 of 22.79 µM in the reported figure, beating the standard drug acarbose on that measure. Computer docking explored how the molecules fit the target enzyme, supporting further work on this selective group.
pmc-13306528:
Abigail Chari mapped uneven child undernutrition across Ethiopia in a 2026 spatial study. Survey data from the 2019 national demographic and health round were joined to local boundaries and analysed at village cluster level.

Children in northern and north-eastern clusters faced higher undernutrition than elsewhere on the thematic maps. Dryness, rainfall, skilled health worker supply, location and mothers' schooling each shaped rates in the reported model. Neighbouring clusters also influenced each other, with clear spillover for stunting, wasting and overall undernutrition, so the authors urge targeted resources for underserved areas. The team calls for joint action on food, care and school for young girls and boys.
pmc-13307028:
Yuwei Bao and colleagues compare oily sludge from three Chinese oilfields in 2026, asking why cleanup difficulty varies by source. Samples from Panjin, Daqing, and Xinjiang were analysed for elements, oil chemistry, minerals, and oil-solid bonding. A room-temperature high-speed stirring wash tested removal under gentle conditions.

Panjin sludge was most oxidised, rich in heavy resins and asphaltenes, and formed tight film-like structures with the least mobile oil. Daqing sludge held lighter compounds and the weakest bonding, while Xinjiang sat between the two. Washing removed roughly eighty-one to ninety percent of oil depending on origin, with Panjin hardest to clean. Higher oxidation and polar content strengthened adhesion and slowed release. The authors argue treatment settings should be tuned to sludge character, and they present stirring as an energy-saving option.
pmc-13307728:
Vitelbina Núñez Rangel and co-authors turn coral snake venom in 2026 into a crop protection tool against plant bacteria and fungi. Venoms from three Micrurus species were tested on Xanthomonas and Fusarium strains that cut fruit and vegetable yields. Activity tracking and mass analysis identified one enzyme family as the main weapon.

The enzyme, an L-amino acid oxidase, was purified and set into gelatin films, alone and within whole venom. Films kept strong antimicrobial action in laboratory tests and on strawberries in place. Treated fruit lost less weight and kept its appearance longer, extending shelf life without changing the fruit's measured properties. The authors propose venom-based films as active packaging and biocontrol alternatives. Synthetic farm chemicals carry health and environmental costs, which motivates their search.
pmc-13308428:
Liying Sun and co-authors review antigen delivery tools in 2026, the rides that decide how well a vaccine teaches the immune system. Plain subunit shots are safe but weak because antigens degrade or miss the display cells. Delivery design aims to fix aiming, lymph node arrival, and the cross-display needed for killer T cells.

Tuned nanoparticles are set by size, charge, and surface ligand density to steer their cell journey. Biomimetic options include cell-derived sacs, virus-like particles, and membrane-coated particles that borrow natural aiming tricks. Skin routes such as microneedle patches and electroporation place antigen straight where display cells gather. Tailored cancer vaccines and paired immune treatments are the showcase uses. The authors combine matter science, immunology, and building into one map for vaccination.
pmc-13308728:
Rano K Sinuraya and co-authors review in 2026 fair access blocks for vaccines and screening in low and middle income lands, where gains in cover have not reached all groups alike. Their search drew on PubMed and Scopus, with screening proof drawn mostly from cervical and HPV linked programmes.

Blocks stacked at home, town, clinic, and state levels, from poverty and travel cost to stigma and thin staffing in clinics. Vaccine work faced cold chain faults and drive based delivery, while screening faced repeat trips and weak follow up chains. Rural folk, poor homes, women, migrants, and disabled people bore the brunt. Strong front line care and fair data use anchor the fix list.
pmc-13308828:
Héléna Vassilieff and co-authors mine in 2026 plant genomes for fossil virus bits that trace the deep past of the Caulimoviridae, the sole double strand DNA virus family of plants. They scanned 93 genomes across all main land plant groups and found 47,135 such bits in 75 of the genomes.

The bits fell into 71 groups, and 35 of those groups had never been named before this scan. One old branch sat only in a Gondwanan conifer family, which hints at very deep roots for the clan. Family trees of virus and host lined up well, which backs shared splitting as the main driver of spread over vast time.
pmc-13309828:
Xunqi Huang and colleagues combine two blood markers in 2026 to sharpen prediction of kidney injury after non-cardiac surgery. A Korean database supplied 269 injury cases matched with about a thousand controls on age, sex, body mass, and baseline kidney function. The markers were a stress sugar ratio and a sensitive inflammation protein.

The sugar ratio showed a U-shaped risk pattern: both low and high values raised injury odds compared with the middle range. Raised inflammation protein lifted risk further within every sugar band. Adding both markers to standard models improved classification and reclassification measures measurably. Postoperative kidney injury strikes a large share of surgical patients worldwide, so better flags matter. The authors propose paired metabolic and inflammatory checks before surgery. Patients flagged high, they argue, deserve intensified monitoring and kidney-protective management around the operation.
pmc-13310628:
Qian Feng and co-authors trace in 2026 how shrimp turn sugar metabolism into stronger antibacterial defence. Infection switched on a glucose side pathway in blood cells of the whiteleg shrimp, raising output of a sugar tag that enzymes attach to proteins. The main target proved to be hemocyanin, the blood protein best known for carrying oxygen.

Tagging hemocyanin at one specific site stiffened its shape and improved its grip on bacterial surface molecules. Tagged hemocyanin bound, clumped, and killed bacteria more effectively. Blocking the sugar pathway or the tagging enzyme weakened bacterial clearance, while blocking tag removal strengthened defence. Shrimp farming loses heavily to bacterial disease, so an internal metabolic lever is valuable. The study links metabolism and immunity in an invertebrate through a single modified protein. Findings may guide feed or breeding strategies for disease control in aquaculture.
pmc-13310828:
Isabella Monteiro Carvalho led a 2026 study comparing a urine infecting germ found in patients and in a polluted bay in Brazil. Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes many urine infections, yet its life outside clinics is little known. The team asked if bay strains carry the same risky traits as clinic strains.

Forty strains were tested, split evenly between clinic and bay sources. Gene patterns and harm traits looked alike across sources. Bay strains resisted many drugs, formed biofilms, and harmed test larvae much like clinic strains. A virus that attacks germs killed many strains and broke biofilms. Watch of dirty coastal water is warranted.
pmc-13310928:
Janka Pecuchová and colleagues release a dataset of student software models with smart feedback in a 2026 paper. Students in a software course built UML diagrams, and a large language model gave written feedback in Slovak. The set lets scholars test automated grading in a non English, technical class.

Files hold 112 student records, 448 feedback notes, and 700 raw XML reports from a design tool. Each record links the model, feedback, scores, grades, student ratings of helpfulness, and human ratings. Prompt drafts and scoring rules are shared for repeat tests. Work in the 2024 to 2025 school year at a university in Nitra grounds the set.
pmc-13311028:
Xing Lin and co-authors build a physics simulation for magnetic touch sensors in a 2026 study. Touch feedback guides fine robot assembly when sight is blocked, and magnetic sensors are fast and compact. A lack of true to life simulation blocks training of robot policies, so a joint frame was built.

Soft material bending is modeled with a particle method at fine scale on modest hardware. A masked learning model compresses touch point clouds by over 88 percent of size while keeping shape error tiny. A mapping model then projects real signals into the simulated space. Mapped forms kept contact shape and aligned domains well for later real use.
pmc-13311128:
Alysson Fellipe Costa Telles led a 2026 gene study on long COVID in Brazilian health workers. Long COVID has many causes, and gene variants in a virus entry helper gene may shape risk. Two variants were tested against illness reports in a self report survey with mouth cell gene checks.

Workers totaled 363 in number from mixed clinic roles. For long COVID overall, only clinical traits such as symptom load and severity mattered. For brain fog, the top named symptom, women and young adults were most at risk, and one variant showed a link in select models. The other variant showed no link. Case control work must clarify the fog link.
pmc-13311328:
Simon Østergaard and colleagues, in 2026, share a case where an invasive Ureaplasma infection copied the look of returning lymphoma. The germ usually lives quietly in the urinary tract but can turn invasive when immunity is weak.

The patient had finished chemoimmunotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and stayed in remission. A growing, tissue-eating sore on the scrotum and belly wall looked like cancer spread, yet standard cultures found nothing. Gene-based microbe scanning named Ureaplasma urealyticum as the cause. Two antibiotics given over a long course cleared the infection fully. Early gene testing could spare such patients needless cancer workups.
pmc-13311628:
Anhong Li and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol to find the right dose of oliceridine, a newer opioid, for keeping patients still and cough-free during bronchoscopy under remimazolam sedation.

The single-center trial will enroll adults aged 18 to 65 having painless flexible bronchoscopy. Each patient gets oliceridine first, then a set dose of remimazolam. The starting oliceridine dose is 40 micrograms per kilogram, moved up or down in steps based on the prior patient's response, with men and women tracked apart. Middle and high effective doses will be estimated for each sex, alongside safety events.
pmc-13311828:
Lindsey M. Philpot and co-authors share a 2026 practice-based case series on building virtual care partnerships at Mayo Clinic. Millions of Americans face gaps in primary and specialty care because of distance, provider shortages, and inequity. The paper describes how an academic medical center folded outside virtual providers into its own services, using both collaborative arrangements, where virtual clinicians work alongside in-house teams, and referral arrangements.

Six design principles anchor the account: acute access, continuity, convenience, cost, reach, and smooth transitions between virtual and in-person care. The authors stress that partnerships hold up only when they fit the host organization's culture, rest on secure data sharing, and sit on reimbursement structures that pay for the work. For other health systems weighing similar partnerships, the case series offers a tested template and a warning that technology alone does not integrate care.
pmc-13311928:
Jie Qiao, Qing Kou, and Ji Qiu present a 2026 study pairing engineered macrophages with a CD47-blocking antibody against ovarian cancer. The macrophages carry a receptor that homes to HER2 on tumor cells.

Cell tests showed the engineered macrophages found and killed HER2-positive ovarian cancer cells. Adding the CD47 antibody boosted their eating of tumor cells, pushed them toward an inflammatory mode, and raised their signal output. In mice bearing human tumors, the pair shrank tumor burden more than single treatments. Blocking the don't-eat-me signal, it seems, frees the engineered cells to work harder.
pmc-13312028:
Yi Tang Chen and Sebastian Kurtek propose, in a 2026 statistics paper, an elastic functional Cox regression model for survival data. Their target problem is phase variability. When a predictor is a whole curve, such as a growth trajectory, its peaks and dips land at different times for different people. That timing jitter blurs the shape features that matter. Ordinary models can lose predictive power by ignoring it.

Their model aligns curves before estimating how shape relates to a time-to-event outcome. The alignment itself is guided by the survival response. Fitting alternates between removing phase variation and estimating the coefficient function, with small gradient updates at each pass. Simulations and two real data sets show estimation and prediction matching or beating rival methods. The method also held up when the approximating basis was misspecified. The paper lets analysts make curve shape, not timing accidents, drive survival predictions.
pmc-13312528:
Jessica T. Jacobs and Jacob C. Nordman present a 2026 hypothesis-driven review linking early life stress to lifelong aggression through changes in synapse structure. Stress early in life is a major risk factor for reactive aggression that can outlast the original hardship by decades. The machinery that locks the change into the brain was poorly defined.

The authors gather clinical, postmortem, imaging, and animal evidence around NMDA receptor-dependent structural plasticity in aggression circuits, centered on the pathway from the medial amygdala to the ventromedial hypothalamus. Animal work suggests stress adds dendritic spines and excitatory synapses there, placed where they drive firing hardest, which would raise circuit excitability and lower the bar for aggressive outbursts. The review closes by weighing two approved NMDA blockers, ketamine and memantine, as candidate tools against this rewiring.
pmc-13312828:
Hao Liu and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, the first complete mitochondrial genome of the fly Helina trivittata. Its genus is one of the largest in the house fly family, with 683 known species. Yet mitochondrial sequences existed for only two of them, leaving the group's family tree resting on thin genetic evidence.

The genome runs 18,959 base pairs and holds the standard set of 37 mitochondrial genes, with adenine and thymine making up 82.01 percent of its letters. Family tree analysis supported the subfamily Phaoniinae as a single natural group. It placed Helina as the closest relative of the genus Phaonia, a relationship once blurred when Helina was treated as a mere synonym of Phaonia. Specimens came from Inner Mongolia, China. The authors offer the sequence as a reference for future evolutionary and classification work on the family.
pmc-13312928:
Shamsun Nahar and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study showing how two common genetic changes team up to make endometrial cancer aggressive. Endometrioid endometrial cancer is usually caught early with a good outlook, but late-stage disease kills most patients. Tumors carrying both PTEN loss and CTNNB1 mutation are known to fare worst without anyone knowing exactly why.

The team engineered mice whose uteruses lacked Pten, carried a stabilized Ctnnb1, or both. Double-mutant mice died sooner than single mutants and developed invasive, metastatic cancer, with muscle-wall invasion already present at four weeks of age. Gene profiling showed WNT, PI3K/AKT, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programs switched on together, and tissue staining confirmed the transition's hallmarks. The authors present the pair as a synergistic engine of early invasion and spread.
pmc-13313828:
Amal Aboelmaaty and co-authors tracked how season changes the ovaries and blood chemistry of native mares across their heat cycles. Using Doppler ultrasound and blood samples over three cycles in cold months and three in hot months, they measured follicle growth, blood flow, hormone levels, and several enzymes. Hot months brought fewer follicles overall, and season interacted with cycle day on many measures. Follicle size and flow patterns shifted, as did hormone and enzyme levels.

The basic rhythm of follicle growth and recruitment survived the heat. What broke down were blood-flow mediators, enzymes, and biochemicals that may disturb the fluid around the egg and lower egg quality. The authors recommend breeding mares in the cold months, when conditions and green feed are better. The study separates the visible cycle, which looks robust, from hidden chemistry that heat quietly perturbs.
pmc-13314328:
Zahraa Fadhil Abbas, Osama Hadi Al-Obaidy, and Monyer Abdulameir Abd Alfatlawi follow, in a 2026 rat study, what giardia infection does to iron handling and body chemistry in the young. The parasite causes malabsorption, of iron, but its systemic fingerprints were murky. Thirty-six weaned male rats were split into uninfected controls, an acutely infected group sampled at day seven, and a post-infection group sampled at day twenty-one. A panel of metabolite measurements was taken.

Infected rats showed lower blood iron, transferrin saturation, albumin, and citrulline, an amino acid marking gut function. Iron storage and its regulator hepcidin fell after infection even as inflammation markers rose, and the red cell indices drifted toward anemia. Gut-derived metabolites told a story, with short-chain fatty acids down and stress compounds up. The authors argue giardiasis leaves a disturbance that outlasts the parasite's stay in the intestine.
pmc-13314928:
Rashad A. Bishara and colleagues report results, in a 2026 follow-up study, of foam sclerotherapy injected around venous leg ulcers to shut down the vein network beneath them. The randomized trial had shown the added treatment speeds healing. The question was whether healed ulcers stay healed. Sixty-five trial patients were tracked for twelve months after healing, with fifty-eight completing follow-up averaging 2.2 years. Recurrence, severity scores, quality of life, and ultrasound findings were recorded.

The treated group relapsed far less: recurrence hit 12 percent of the foam group against 45 percent of controls, and the adjusted hazard of recurrence was one-fifth as large. Treated patients enjoyed longer ulcer-free time, averaging 1,059 days against 736 days in the comparison, and finished with better severity scores. Ultrasound proof that the veins stayed closed predicted the longest freedom from recurrence. The authors recommend the treatment as recurrence insurance, not a healing accelerator.
pmc-13315528:
NGA Mulyantini S․S․ and colleagues fed broiler chickens in 2026 with diets where soybean meal was partly swapped for cricket nymph meal and moringa leaf meal. Two hundred forty day-old broilers were split into four diets, with the swap replacing 10, 20, or 30 percent of the soybean share using a three-to-one blend.

Birds on the 10 and 20 percent swaps gained more weight than controls, while the 30 percent group grew less despite eating more. Carcass weight and thigh yield also rose at the two lower swaps. Protein and organic matter digestibility fell at higher swap levels, marking a practical limit for the blend.
pmc-13316228:
Auguste Vadisiute and colleagues deleted the release gene Snap25 in 2026 in selected mouse brain cells to study how long synaptic silence reshapes glial support cells in aging. Blocking transmitter release in layer 5 cortex cells and dentate granule cells let them watch glial change across connected regions and the spinal cord.

Silenced cortex zones showed strong astrocyte reactivity and more microglia, while downstream targets such as the superior colliculus and CA3 showed marked microglial remodeling and synaptic change, and CA1 changed mildly. In the spinal cord microglia fell while astrocytes rose. Aging amplified the glial responses.
pmc-13316528:
Haowen Hu, Jason Oliver, Puchun Niu, April Leytem, and Kristan Reed test how consistent manure nutrient results are across six commercial labs. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Manure analyses guide farm nutrient plans and greenhouse gas counts, yet the size of lab error was little studied.

Fresh slurry from a dairy barn was split into portions. Some got plain water, some a glucose spike, and some an ammonium salt spike at two levels. Each lab measured volatile solids and two nitrogen forms. The team computed repeat spread within labs and agreement across labs, plus how much of each spike was recovered. The design shows which nutrients labs measure tightly and which wander. That tells farmers and regulators how much trust to place in a single report.
pmc-13316628:
Ana Costa-Ribeiro and colleagues compared, in a 2026 food safety study, fast ways to find Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a germ that causes illness from raw or undercooked seafood, in mussels. Since shellfish spoil fast, same-day answers carry real value for sellers and inspectors.

Three digital PCR machines were set against standard gene tests and a rapid loop method, all after the enrichment steps of the official standard. After the first enrichment, gene testing could find about 15 germ units per 25 grams, while digital systems read negative despite faint signals; a second enrichment improved all methods. Among growth plates, one brand proved most specific. Sample preparation, the authors stress, decides success more than machine sensitivity alone.
pmc-13317828:
Tingting Hu and colleagues follow, in a 2026 community cohort study, whether thyroid hormone levels predict early muscle-loss obesity in people whose thyroid tests sit in the normal range. The condition pairs shrinking muscle with deep belly fat, a risky blend in aging adults.

A total of 1,280 residents over forty were recruited in 2013 to 2014 and rechecked about two years later, with MRI belly fat and body composition measures. Those starting in the highest third of free T3 hormone levels faced notably higher risk of the combined condition, with a risk ratio of 1.82 against the lowest third in the adjusted model. Rising hormone levels over time also tracked with new cases. Normal range, they note, does not mean no effect.
pmc-13318928:
Shujing Hu and co-authors report a 2026 study of two blood indices in older adults with depression, with or without obstructive sleep apnoea. One index blends inflammation, triglycerides, and glucose. The other counts immune cells from routine blood tests. Both are cheap and quick to calculate.

The sample held 52 patients with both conditions and 108 with depression alone. The combined group had higher body mass and more men. Their glucose, triglycerides, and inflammation markers all ran higher. Immune cell ratios and the inflammation index were also raised. Modelling linked male sex and higher values on both indices to having sleep apnoea. The authors propose the pair as helpful flags in depressed older patients.
pmc-13319028:
Shijiao Cao presents a 2026 study of how a university's spread of disciplines relates to PhD student research output. The sample covers 1,418 accounting dissertations sent to Chinese universities between 1999 and 2022. Cao builds a new measure of university-level disciplinary diversity. Poisson models control for student, supervisor, and institution factors.

A simple model showed a negative overall link between diversity and productivity. Closer analysis showed an upside-down U shape instead. Moderate diversity helped output, and richer universities gained from more of it. Harm clustered where fields were lopsided or sprawled into unrelated areas. Students at diverse universities did more cross-discipline work with greater impact. The author argues for keeping healthy diversity without chasing breadth for its own sake.
pmc-13320028:
Dunja Scheepmaker and co-authors compare ways to prepare cartilage for joint repair in a 2026 lab study. Chopped own cartilage offers a cheap one step fix for worn joint patches, but chopping may kill cells and cut new tissue growth. Hand chopping, scope guided chopping, freed cell clusters, and freed lone cells were grown side by side for four weeks.

At day 28 lone cells and cell clusters stayed alive at rates above nine in ten in the counts reported, while scope chopped bits lived least well of all. Freed cells also laid down more of the springy filler that gives cartilage its bounce, while chopped bits lost ground. Loose bits from real surgery varied wildly in weight and cell content, which flags quality risks.
pmc-13320228:
Pritpal Singh and co-authors present a hands on workflow for mapping proteins in tissue in a 2026 methods article. Protein maps that keep place intact show where each protein sits in cells and tissue, which can reveal new disease signs. Full start to finish workflows that stay open, repeatable, and easy to steer have been scarce, so a boxed step pipeline was built.

Steps cover cell outlining, grouping of like cells with optional batch fixes, checks of groups on the image, and clear displays of cell types. A form based screen lets users run or tune each step with a click. Trials on healthy tonsil and bowel cancer tissue, stained for dozens of proteins at once, showed the flow in action.
pmc-13320328:
Kyle Mueller, Aleodor A. Andea and Drew Kuraitis report, in 2026, a widespread rash resembling lichen nitidus that appeared soon after a single dose of dupilumab. Lichen nitidus is an uncommon condition of tiny grouped skin-coloured bumps, usually localised in young people. Generalised forms in adults are rarer still, and dupilumab is not a recognised trigger.

Their patient was a 71-year-old man treated for moderate to severe eczema with a standard loading dose. Two weeks later, flat-topped pale papules covered his trunk and limbs while sparing the face, palms and soles. Tissue examination showed circumscribed inflammation hugging the upper skin layer in the classic pattern for the condition, with granuloma-like features. The timing, with no other changes, led the authors to suspect the drug.
pmc-13321028:
R Ibusuki and colleagues examine gene faults that blunt a lung cancer drug in a 2026 study. Patients had advanced lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR faults and received first line osimertinib. Faults in TP53 often go with worse outcomes, but the effect of one class, gain-of-function faults, on drug resistance was unknown.

Gene activity scans pointed to raised ephrin signalling in that group.
pmc-13322728:
Pawel Jankowski and his ten co-authors, publishing in 2026, study a failure mode of neck deformity surgery: the spine kinking just below the lowest fused vertebra. Surgeons lack a clear rule for where the fusion should end. Borrowing a concept from scoliosis care, the team defined a stable end vertebra using three checks: tilt, position relative to a known landmark, and bone density on scans.

Among the 21 patients whose fusion ended at a stable vertebra, the rate was under 10 percent, against 30 percent for the rest. The authors say the rule should guide planning for these operations, while noting the data come from a single center.
pmc-13322928:
Jie Yang and co-authors review how liver immune cells talk to each other in autoimmune hepatitis, in a 2026 article on disease origins and drug discovery. This chronic liver disease is rising in frequency, and its tangled causes make treatment hard.

Focus falls on faulty activation in dendritic cells, macrophages and T and B cells, plus signal exchange among liver cells, bile duct cells and immune cells. Viewing the disease as a regulatory network, rather than a single faulty molecule, opens new drug targets. The authors survey drugs now in use, compounds in development and candidate agents, weigh the limits of current care, and judge how far network-based targets might carry future treatment.
pmc-13323028:
Hanan M Al Kadri leads a review of inducing labour when a baby is suspected to be very large, published in 2026. Macrosomia, set at a birth weight of 4,000 grams or more, raises risks such as caesarean birth, shoulder dystocia and nerve injury, and guidance on timing remains unsettled.

Induction did not change caesarean rates against waiting, in a pooled estimate centred near no difference. Further outcomes covered shoulder dystocia, low Apgar scores and brachial plexus palsy, split by study design. The authors call for clearer shared decision-making until stronger guidance exists.
pmc-13323428:
Myriam Catalano and co-authors published a 2026 study of how astrocytes, the star-shaped cells of the brain, restrain glioma tumor cells through a tiny RNA strand they pass on, miR-124. Astrocytes help set the volume of such tumor cells. Volume determines how well the cells can invade. The strand travels in small packages that the astrocytes shed, called vesicles.
