Activation of the channel, driven by calcium from the store, fell sharply in the presence of the strand. Tumor cells in three dimensions moved less.
pmc-13323528:
Ximing Liao, Qiang Li, and Ko-pen Wang trace how doctors learned to reach small lung nodules through the airways, long likened to shooting at a moving target blind. Their 2026 review follows the shift from hand-guided bronchoscopes and X-ray guidance to robotic scopes and combined navigation tools. Small peripheral nodules matter because finding lung cancer early, while it can still be treated, often starts with such a spot on a scan.

Each new generation of tools fixed one old weakness and exposed the next, the authors argue, moving the problem from finding the nodule to reaching it and then proving the diagnosis. They describe cryobiopsy, which freezes a tissue sample, as a partner method that pairs with other tools through tunneling. The review closes on the gap that remains: flawless navigation still does not guarantee a firm diagnosis, and closing that gap is the next frontier.
pmc-13325628:
Can Zhang and colleagues feed yeast nucleotides to weaned kittens to test growth and immune effects in a 2026 animal study. Young cats face stress at weaning, and nucleotides support gut and immune tissue.

Sixteen four-month-old kittens were split into plain feed and feed with 0.03 percent yeast nucleotides for 42 days. The supplemented group showed higher blood protein, albumin, and creatinine readings. Digestion of dry matter, organic matter, and protein all improved over controls. Growth hormone, IGF-1, and antibody levels for IgG, IgA, and IgM rose sharply. Gut microbe balance shifted too, with Sellimonas and Acutalibacter gaining ground. The additive looks useful for kitten diets.
pmc-13326028:
Yu Luo and colleagues use vesicles from dental pulp stem cells against oral cancer in a 2026 study. Oral squamous cell carcinoma kills about half of patients within five years and often returns after treatment.

Vesicles harvested from inside the stem cells slowed tumor growth in dishes and in animals. Treated cancer cells divided less, invaded less, and died more. The vesicles carried the tumor suppressor PTEN into cancer cells, damping the PI3K, AKT, and mTOR growth pathway. Pairing them with the autophagy blocker 3-methyladenine deepened the effect and stressed mitochondria. The authors pitch the vesicles as a safe, scalable option worth clinical study.
pmc-13326128:
Lisa-Maria Rosenthal and colleagues analyze the heart transplant waitlist for children in Germany in a 2026 registry study. Most waitlist data come from North America, leaving European outcomes less clear.

The registry held 780 candidates listed between 2006 and 2020. Transplants reached 56.5 percent of children, while 17.9 percent died waiting and 7.8 percent recovered enough to leave the list. Mean waiting time was 197 days, longest for ages 1 to 10. Death risk ran highest in children under 2 with diagnoses other than dilated cardiomyopathy. Recovery clustered in infants under 1 year. Wider use of ABO-mismatched grafts is proposed.
pmc-13326328:
Chirwa and co-authors set out a trial plan to test a mental health literacy course for Malawi university students. Mental health knowledge in Malawi is low, the protocol notes. Illness is often blamed on substance use or spirit possession, which fuels stigma and poor treatment of those affected.

The online course, called MHLeC, would run across universities in a cluster randomised feasibility trial. Short staffing and thin services limit care access in Malawi, so a low-cost course could widen reach. The trial first checks if the course can be delivered well and accepted by students before any larger study.
pmc-13326528:
Johnathan A. Napier reviews the long road to making fish oils in plants. His 2026 short review traces transgenic omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid production from proof of principle to regulated and approved crops. The journey took more than 25 years and involved public and private teams. Assembling these fatty acids in a plant host ranks among the most complex heterologous pathway builds attempted, and several sophisticated aspects remain unresolved.

The review walks through the analogue-age origins, foundational studies, the gold rush of pathway extension to DHA, and the epigenetic heart of the problem. It aims to prompt renewed consideration of silencing and related risks. The stakes are a fully sustainable bioeconomy that no longer depends on marine fish for omega-3 supply.
pmc-13327428:
Gal Levi and co-authors test a quick tissue check used during surgery on the voice box, in a 2026 study. When a growth on the vocal folds might be an early cancer, surgeons can take a frozen section sample and read it while the patient is still in surgery. The result guides whether to remove part of the fold at once.

The team reviewed cases from two large hospitals between 2017 and 2024, covering 91 lesions in 70 patients. They compared each frozen result with the final lab report. The quick check matched the final verdict in about 94.5 percent of cases, for both cancer spread and the need for surgery. There were no false alarms for invasive cancer, which supports using the check to guide treatment.
pmc-13328328:
Mengdie Hu and co-authors define a gut frailty pattern in chronic heart failure in a 2026 study. Among 270 patients, gut frailty meant a symptom rating score of at least 3, and the team hunted clinical drivers plus microbe signatures in a balanced subgroup of sixty. Diet stood out sharply in the modeling.

A meat-rich diet independently raised gut frailty odds, with an odds ratio of 3.995 in the adjusted model, while vegetarian adherence lowered them, at 0.148 in the same model. Frail guts held far fewer microbe types, lost short-chain fatty acid producers such as Faecalibacterium, and gained potential troublemakers, with microbe chemistry shifting toward stress handling. Food and microbe care may ease this hidden burden.
pmc-13329128:
Richard W. Willy and co-authors validate a running watch with an accelerometer as a tool for estimating the impact forces runners absorb, without a laboratory treadmill. Their 2026 cross-sectional study first tests eighteen trained runners on an instrumented treadmill across a range of speeds, comparing watch estimates against the treadmill's force measurements.

The published estimation equation systematically underestimated peak vertical ground reaction force by about a tenth. A corrected equation derived from that data was then tested in ten fresh runners. The corrected version showed excellent agreement with the treadmill, with trivial bias and errors of only a few percent. Estimates of cumulative weighted damage per kilometre, a measure relevant to bone stress injury, were likewise accurate. The authors provide an online calculator and suggest the methods could monitor training load in runners at risk of bone stress injuries.
pmc-13329328:
Mokunfayo O Fajemisin and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of a video aid for end-of-life talks after injury. Each year many older adults enter hospital after trauma, yet talks about life-sustaining care and code status often fall short. The single-centre randomised trial, called ADVISE, will test a video conversation aid against usual care.

Eligible patients are trauma patients aged 65 or older admitted after injury, with some groups excluded, such as people already under do-not-resuscitate orders. The main outcome is change in code status. Other outcomes cover views of resuscitation, knowledge, conflict over choices, and days free of hospital or intensive care. The pilot aims to estimate benefit and guide wider use.
pmc-13329728:
P. Sreejindeth and T. Padmavathy propose Eco-FinOps, a system for cutting cloud cost and energy waste, in a 2026 article. Dashboards need constant watching, while deep learning tools need costly graphics chips and hide their logic. The proposed system runs on standard processors and aims to act on its own with clear reasons.

It links live usage data, cause-mapping methods, and effect checks to split real demand swings from waste. A prime target is idle servers that use little processor power yet hold much memory. Language tools then draft fix scripts that people can audit. On five fault tests from Alibaba cluster data, scores for precision and recall were high in the reported results. Cause checks cut false alarms sharply.
pmc-13330328:
Sikiru Baruwa and team tested whether malaria training lifts guideline compliance among community health workers in Nigeria. Their 2026 evaluation, using propensity score matching and average treatment effect estimation, studied the IntegratE Project 2.0 malaria training module for community pharmacists and patent medicine vendors across eleven Nigerian states. These workers are often the first contact for fever care, yet they now diagnose based on symptoms alone, and their practice needs to match World Health Organization malaria treatment guidelines.

Training raised knowledge of malaria diagnosis and treatment and take-up of the test, treat, and refer rules among trained workers. However, training had no effect on compliance with treatment rules or spotting quality drugs. The team concludes that malaria training slightly raises knowledge and take-up among private workers. It urges scale-up of training for these workers, and calls for further research on the harder problem of rule compliance.
pmc-13330528:
Yuan Xu and colleagues compare how surgical teachers and trainees rate core skills in China in a 2026 study. Surveys ran in March 2025 across three training bases in Guizhou, covering 100 skill items in five fields. In total, 42 faculty and 68 residents gave valid replies, rating how vital each item seemed.

Agreement ran high for general surgery and neurosurgery items in the reported results. Half of the orthopaedic items split the groups, with trainees rating them higher. On life monitoring and resuscitation items, faculty gave top scores while trainees scored lower. Overall agreement was weak. Both groups backed stronger training in records and patient talk. Skill lists need joint review, the authors argue.
pmc-13331428:
Amir Molaie and Jeffrey L. Saver write a 2026 commentary on biomarker use in stroke clot removal choices. They aim to fix a growing mix-up between two biomarker kinds in patients with large vessel block and large damaged cores. One kind forecasts outcome whatever the treatment. The other kind changes how much a treatment helps.

Core volume acts as the first kind: bigger cores mean worse outlook in all groups, the authors argue. Penumbra measures and mismatch ratios act as the second kind, marking who gains from removal. Graphs in the piece show the split in plain form. Treating a forecast marker as a selection marker can mislead trial reading and bedside calls, they warn.
pmc-13332228:
Wu-Lung Chuang and four co-authors ask if a common diabetes drug class raises the risk of liver abscess. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses health records for all of Taiwan. The drugs, called SGLT2 inhibitors, help control blood sugar. A pus-filled liver abscess is a grave infection that is rising in East Asia, above all in people with diabetes.

The team matched more than half a million users and non-users in pairs. Abscess rates came out a bit lower in drug users. Many extra checks, such as one using bone breaks as a dummy outcome, supported the main result. The drug class does not seem to add this risk.
pmc-13333028:
Fredrik Sandesjö and colleagues compare 2026 treatment persistence in childhood-onset multiple sclerosis using Swedish national registry data. Comparative studies in paediatric-onset disease that include highly effective monoclonal antibody therapies are rare. The team treated persistence on a drug as a proxy for effectiveness and tolerability across disease-modifying therapies. The nationwide cohort drew on the Swedish MS Registry for people with onset before age eighteen from 2000 through 2024, analyzed with survival and Cox models.

A total of 383 people were included, about sixty-nine percent female, with median onset near sixteen and first treatment near seventeen. Follow-up ran a median of about ten years, yielding 934 treatment episodes across rituximab, injectables, natalizumab, fingolimod, and dimethyl fumarate. pmc-13333328:
Alexander R. Zhu and colleagues study 2026 how pre-surgery dementia or thinking problems affects outcomes after planned first-time total shoulder replacement. Cognitive impairment or dementia has been linked to worse outcomes in bone surgery, yet studies of its impact after shoulder replacement have been limited. The team looked back to identify patients undergoing planned first-time shoulder replacement over 2021 through 2023 in a US surgical quality database. Patients with and without dementia were matched on demographics and other illnesses.

A total of 6,120 patients were identified, and after five-to-one matching, 219 with pre-surgery dementia and 1,095 without were included. Thirty-day outcomes such as length of stay and problems were compared with simple tests. The dementia cohort, on average, experienced a longer stay and more complications. The study helps surgeons counsel patients with thinking problems and plan perioperative support for shoulder replacement.
pmc-13333528:

It treats nuclear transcripts as the fresh, unspliced pool and cytoplasmic ones as the mature pool, then feeds the pair into the scVelo dynamical model. Applied to melanoma tissue maps, it reconstructed tumor cell progression paths and the differentiation routes of T cells, and it flagged cluster-specific dynamic genes. Those genes tied to patient prognosis and networked into protein clusters rich in immune pathways. The authors offer the method as a bridge between spatial biology and transcriptional dynamics, usable on the spatial datasets laboratories already hold.
pmc-13333628:
A French version of the Sport Psychological Safety Inventory gets its validation in a 2026 study by Véronique Boudreault and co-authors. Psychological safety affects athlete wellbeing and lasting performance, but measurement tools have mostly existed in English.

The team surveyed 210 French-speaking elite youth athletes aged 14 to 25 across many sports in 2024. Scores lined up with wellbeing and coach relationship quality in expected directions, and ran opposite to reports of interpersonal violence in sport. pmc-13334228:

pmc-13334428:

Positive cognitive outcomes showed in 40.4 percent of studies, and 23.6 percent found mixed or conditional effects. ChatGPT dominated the work looked at, and over half the studies used no defined teaching strategy. Over-reliance was the leading risk, named in 33.7 percent of studies, ahead of lost analysis autonomy and cognitive offloading. pmc-13335828:

The team used copper ions to switch the enzyme on while also turning a green tea compound into the drug form the enzyme needs. In mice, tumours shrank by eighty-five percent with good safety. The authors call it a new treatment pattern.
pmc-13335928:

pmc-13336028:
Jiancheng He and colleagues study 2026 beta-elemene rescuing radiation gut injury by running a host-microbe circuit that fuels gene-tagging DNA repair. At the same time, beta-elemene boosts Lactobacillus gasseri, raising gut lactate output. The meeting of host priming and high lactate availability triggers a metabo-gene-tagging cascade. pmc-13336128:
Ying-Xin Qiao and co-authors engineer a plastic that splits water with sunlight far better than its siblings. The one-nitrogen version won by a wide margin, delivering a photocurrent three to over two hundred times higher than the others at the standard test voltage. Ultrafast light measurements showed why: charges separated in under a picosecond and piled up efficiently, ready to drive chemistry. Theory confirmed that linker polarity strengthens the built-in field that pulls charges apart. The authors frame the work as a design rule linking molecular structure to the speed of charge motion in organic solar fuel devices.
pmc-13336228:

The work ran from May to July 2021: the team surveyed how care was then delivered, discussed what telenursing could add, built tools, and tested the technology. Sixteen nurses joined. They saw telenursing's potential while flagging scarce time, staff, and infrastructure as limits. Jointly they produced a patient suitability and risk form, a visit script, and a care plan. The report concludes workshops work as training, and that ongoing training underpins practice changes of this kind.
pmc-13336428:
Tianyu Qin and colleagues study 2026 targeting Dnmt3a/m5C/RelA axis attenuating brain immune inflammatory response and improving after-surgery recovery in chronic squeezing neck spinal cord injury. Chronic squeezing neck spinal cord injury (cCSCI) is a major cause of adult spinal cord trouble. Using a mouse cCSCI model, the authors performed single-nucleus RNA reading to map brain immune states, calculated an m5C control score, and checked m5C changes via dot blot. Single-nucleus RNA reading showed a main pro-swelling brain immune subgroup (C1) after pressure relief, rich in NF-κB signals. The C1 subgroup showed a high m5C score and higher Dnmt3a levels.
pmc-13336828:

Quercetin naturally sticks to the outer membrane of those power units, a trait the team used as a homing device.

In a rodent stroke model the particles crossed the damaged blood-brain barrier and reached neuron power units. They steadied the units, stopped DNA leakage, calmed immune activation, and improved recovery. Natural products may hide targeting skills worth building into medicines.
pmc-13337028:

The work points to proline-directed phosphorylation as a master switch in stroke damage.
pmc-13337428:
Thales M. H. Dourado and co-authors test whether a hormone receptor starts alcohol's early damage to heart and kidney in a 2026 rat study. It also prevented a hydrogen peroxide rise seen only in kidney tissue and erased ethanol-driven increases in thromboxane and prostaglandin signals. The findings place this receptor at the opening steps of alcohol-related cardiorenal injury, nominating it as an early intervention point.
pmc-13337628:

pmc-13339028:
Carsten Strobel and a large team improve graphene hot-electron transistors for fast electronics in a 2026 study. An atom-thin graphene base promises very fast switching, but weak injection limited earlier devices. Tuning the emitter and base stack was the lever used here.

A molybdenum disulfide and graphene stack pushed output near 2000 A per square centimeter as reported, also a record. Cutoff speeds approached 1 GHz even before full tuning. Results narrow the terahertz gap from the electronics side, pointing toward faster nano devices.
pmc-13339228:
Baraa J. Abdelghne and an undergraduate team test plant extracts on worm movement in a 2026 study. Cannabis, ginger, pepper tree, saffron, and tobacco extracts faced Caenorhabditis elegans worms.

Worms placed at plate centers chose between extract and solvent zones. Only tobacco strongly repelled the worms in the reported tests, while the other extracts showed no clear effect. The work came from a teaching laboratory course, giving students research training. Results single out tobacco chemistry for deeper study of nerve and behavior effects.
pmc-13339528:
Zakir Khan and Frank Moriarty argued in 2026 that drug safety reporting must better capture withdrawal reactions when a drug is stopped. Current forms and guidance do not fully accommodate that subset.

The authors discuss revisions to adverse reaction forms that would record stopping, timing, and withdrawal features more clearly. Better capture would sharpen safety signals and help clinicians distinguish relapse from withdrawal. The proposal aims at a practical form change with wide safety benefits.
pmc-13339828:
Mizuhiro Kominato and colleagues catch a fleeting water dimer ion form in gas in a 2026 spectroscopy study. The hemibonded form of two water molecules sharing charge had been seen only inside helium droplets before. Ultraviolet and visible spectra of small water cluster ions were recorded.

A charge resonance band matching the hemibonded form appeared for the two-water ion as reported. Three-water clusters were measured alongside for contrast. Electronic spectra thus become a sensitive test for this elusive structure. Confirming it in plain gas sharpens models of radiation damage in water, where such ions appear first.
pmc-13340028:
Giovanni Milani and colleagues test two adhesion genes in a toxin-producing E. coli strain from raw milk cheese in a 2026 study. Some dangerous strains lack the classic attachment locus yet still infect people. Their alternative island, LAA, carries hes and sisA genes.

Mutants missing toxin genes, the hes-sisA pair, or both were built by recombineering. Wax moth larvae measured virulence, while cell and film tests measured sticking and biofilm. Deleting hes-sisA lowered larval death, biofilm, and attachment to intestinal cells clearly as reported. The pair likely helps colonization and persistence, marking a target for control.
pmc-13341328:
Yu Chang and colleagues compared psychiatric outcomes in 2026 after starting GLP-1 drugs versus SGLT2 drugs in patients with type 2 diabetes and treated depression. Using TriNetX health records, the team ran a retrospective new user cohort study with active comparators. Patients had depression and antidepressant treatment within six months before starting either drug class.

After one to one propensity matching, 34,761 patients sat in each group, and Cox models compared suicidality and antipsychotic use over one year, with all cause death as a secondary outcome. pmc-13341428:
Other illnesses weigh heavily on life quality in Ménière's disease, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Zhongbao Zhang and colleagues. The single-center analysis covered 473 patients, collecting their conditions alongside anxiety, depression, and disease-specific quality of life scores.

Hypertension appeared in 49.0% of patients, sleep disorders in 36.6%, and diabetes in 28.8%, while clear anxiety and depression symptoms showed in over half. Average quality of life score was 43.62 on the disease questionnaire. Hypertension correlated most strongly with worse quality of life at r = −0.521. Treating the ear condition alone, the authors imply, misses much of the burden.
pmc-13341528:
Food knowledge and eating confidence cluster together in liver cancer patients, in a 2026 survey by Ziang Liu and colleagues. The cross-sectional study recruited 456 patients from three tertiary hospitals between April and October 2025, using questionnaires on nutrition literacy, diet self-efficacy, fatigue, and social support.

Latent profile analysis found two groups: a low literacy, low confidence profile covering 47.37% of patients, and a high-high profile covering 52.63%. Attempts to split profiles by gender failed because the subgroups grew too small for stable solutions. Nearly half of patients thus face treatment with weak nutrition skills, a clear target for dietitian support.
pmc-13341828:
Davide Mohammad Reza Beigi and colleagues tested lung scans in 2026 for lung scarring in systemic sclerosis at two referral centres with one shared protocol. Two scan scores were tested: at least ten B lines and pleural line faults by Fairchild rules, alone and joined, against high resolution CT. The study used same day scans and CT with a fourteen zone protocol.

Lung scarring meant at least ten percent lung harm on CT. Scan scores were judged by either-or and both-criteria rules. Scans could offer a radiation free, bedside screen for lung disease in scleroderma care if accuracy holds. The shared protocol tests whether scores travel between centres.
pmc-13341928:
Knee loads while walking shift with age, sex, and activity, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Hanna Zadoń and colleagues. Motion and force data fed a musculoskeletal model that computed internal knee reaction forces across the gait cycle, compared across age bands and activity levels.

Inactive people showed higher forces mid-stance, significantly in young women and in both sexes aged 46 to 65. Men exceeded women only in some age groups and early stance. Older walkers shifted peak loading earlier in foot contact, suggesting compensatory strategy changes. Joint loading analyses that ignore who is walking, the authors argue, miss where the stress actually lands.
pmc-13342628:
Mark H. Nelson questioned the labels doctors use in 2026 for eyes that keep leaking fluid despite retinal treatment. Words like poor response, persistent fluid, treatment resistance, and tachyphylaxis get applied to eyes that do not fully dry out, relapse early, or resist longer gaps between shots. Agreeing on words is useful, yet shared words do not explain why treatment fails.

Nelson asks whether ongoing leakage means the drug has not fully blocked a key pathway, or whether the drug simply does not match the biology that keeps fluid coming during therapy. Eyes that look alike when they fail may differ deeply in choroidal vessel biology. The essay urges doctors to think in mechanisms, not labels, for eyes that keep leaking.
pmc-13343128:
Madhuri Tribhuvan and Shashikant N Phatke write a 2026 letter commenting on a broiler chicken study that compared several zinc sources for uptake and growth. The original work used a depletion-repletion model plus a floor-pen trial, and the letter writers praise that design while raising points that could sharpen its reading.

Bone zinc, they note, shows exposure but not whether bones actually grow stronger, since no strength or structure tests were done. Mixed diets also strayed from target zinc levels, which could skew uptake rankings, and added phytase in all feeds may have freed extra zinc on its own. Broader farm validation, they argue, would firm up claims for organic zinc products.
pmc-13343228:
Chris Packer and co-authors profile the hydrosol of Utah juniper in a 2026 lab study, testing its chemistry and biological effects. The scented water left from juniper processing had barely been characterized, so the team measured its phenolic makeup and ran antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays in vitro.

Chromatography found naringenin as the only measurable flavonoid, a sparse profile typical of hydrosols. The liquid showed antioxidant activity and mildly slowed both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, with stronger effects at higher doses, yet produced no antibacterial zones under the method used. The authors call for cell and safety models to judge whether the hydrosol holds real bioactive promise.
pmc-13343428:
Yumin Wang and colleagues reported a fusion milestone in 2026, high confinement mode discharges for the first time in proton boron plasmas on the EXL-50U spherical torus. A working gas mix of 30 percent diborane and 70 percent hydrogen was used, with boron powder injection for real time boronisation, giving an estimated plasma boron concentration near 10 percent.

High confinement mode was obtained with neutral beam injection at 0.5 to 2.5 megawatts on axis magnetic field conditions described in the letter. Proton boron fusion avoids neutron heavy reactions, making it attractive if confinement can be sustained. The first H mode in this fuel mix marks a step toward cleaner fusion approaches.
pmc-13343628:
Vincent A. Ricigliano and colleagues studied amitraz resistance in 2026 in Varroa mites, the gravest threat to kept honeybees. Mite control relies on few chemical miticides, and amitraz is widely used for strong mite kill and fairly low bee toxicity. Rising resistance threatens its long term value. Gene changes in the mite beta2 octopamine receptor strongly track resistance, yet uptake and efflux routes may also add to it.

ATP binding cassette transporters, with ABCB1 P-glycoproteins, are known mediators of toxin transport and were probed as resistance drivers. Grasping efflux based resistance helps beekeepers rotate treatments and preserve amitraz. The work backs joined mite care as resistance spreads.
pmc-13343728:
Steve Kevin Njouonkep Sime and co-authors examine whether metabolic syndrome changes how older adults move between frailty states, in both directions. Frailty is dynamic, yet most research treats metabolic risk as a one-way driver. Their 2026 study uses the Whitehall II cohort of British civil servants, with 4,750 participants followed for just under seven years on average.

At baseline most participants were robust, about a third pre-frail, and 36.9 percent had metabolic syndrome. Recovery transitions were commoner than deteriorations at every stage. Overall, metabolic syndrome was not significantly associated with moving between states. One component stood out: abdominal obesity raised the hazard of slipping from robust to early pre-frailty by twenty-seven percent. The authors conclude the syndrome as a whole matters less than specific components, and that frailty trajectories can improve as well as worsen.
pmc-13343928:
Luisa Nardini and co-authors show that gut bacteria can blunt insecticide power in malaria mosquitoes, in a 2026 study. Antibiotic feeding stripped the gut flora of susceptible Anopheles strains, yet the treated mosquitoes oddly survived the insecticide deltamethrin far better, with tolerance rising over 50 percent.

Blocking the mosquitoes' P450 detox enzymes erased the effect, tying tolerance to that system. Antibiotics cleared most gut tenants but let one Aeromonas type bloom, and seeding that microbe alone into untreated mosquitoes copied the tolerance. In Africa, where self-medication with antibiotics is common, the authors warn, gut disruption could quietly erode bed net and spraying programs built on insecticides.
pmc-13346428:
Almusharraf, Rhouati, Cialla-May, Popp, and Zourob develop in twenty twenty-six a fast sensor test for checking diphtheria vaccine quality. Vaccine batches need strict quality checks at every stage, yet standard tests are slow mixes of lab assays. Their test uses aptamers, short strands selected to bind the vaccine's weakened toxin tightly, mounted on gold electrodes.

After many selection rounds, one aptamer bound the toxin extremely tightly. The sensor read toxin levels across a wide range with a very low detection floor, without labels. It barely reacted to the tetanus and pertussis partners usually mixed with the vaccine. Tests on real vaccine samples worked well. The authors pitch it as a fast, cheap, accurate quality tool.
pmc-13346828:
Qizhi Duan, Minghan Yang, Shuai Chen, Huijuan Li, and Hongyun Xie propose steering reactor power shape by coolant flow in a paper from 2026. Pressurized water reactors usually shape axial power with boron and control rods. Boron shifts create liquid waste, and rods complicate core design. The new method adjusts flow rate instead. Because the core is a distributed system, the team derives a matching stability condition. A state observer estimates quantities no sensor can read directly.

Simulations show the method flattens power peaks and removes hot spots. The authors argue flow control could slim future core designs. Less boron handling also means less waste to treat. Stability is proven within their framework.
pmc-13347328:
Gökhan Akarca and co-authors test magnetic fields on bread yeast, in a food study from 2026. Cultures of Saccharomyces cerevisiae were exposed at 180, 240. 300 microtesla strengths, then used for dough and bread that were checked for acidity, water activity, texture, rising, pore size, and acid content.

The middle strength stood out, with treated yeast giving bread at a pH value of 4.35 and the highest levels of several organic acids in the reported measures. Doughs from treated cultures felt softer while finished breads rose more and held larger pores, and sourdough cultures shifted more than commercial ones. The authors propose field treatment as a cheap way to lift bread quality.
pmc-13348528:
Chunyan Lu and a team of co-authors mapped how peer rejection links to teen depression at fine grain. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, notes that most past work treats both as single blocks. Both are in fact mixed, with distinct types and signs. The team used network analysis to join types of rejection to single depressive signs. Their main set held close to twenty-four thousand teens from the broad public.

They built the network in that set, then checked how it shifts by age and sex. A clinical sample let them set public and patient webs side by side. Readers who work on teen mental health see which links are the strong bridges. Those bridges may be the best points to step in.
pmc-13349928:
Zhen Zhang and colleagues reported a fatal case in 2026 of severe skin destruction, toxic epidermal necrolysis, after treatment with a new PD-1 blocking drug, pucotenlimab. Their patient, a man aged 67 with stage IIIB lung adenocarcinoma, had finished chest radiotherapy before immunotherapy.

Seven days after a single dose, scattered red spots spread fast until about 80 percent of his skin surface detached. Scores used at readmission predicted a death risk above 90 percent, and immune testing showed sharply lowered PD-1 on T cells with raised interleukin-6. Steroids, immunoglobulin, and intensive support did not save him. The case alerts clinicians to a rare but deadly reaction.
pmc-13351128:
Yestle Kim and colleagues traced how fatty liver disease progresses to end-stage liver disease in United States adults in a 2026 records and claims study. Among 49,983 patients with the inflamed form of the disease, a third already had advanced liver damage at first record.

Of those without it, 15.9 percent progressed, with a median of just 10.6 months to the first severe event, most often decompensated cirrhosis. Use of non-invasive tests around diagnosis, predictors of decline, hospital use, and costs were all mapped. Such speed of progression argues for finding and treating these patients far earlier than current practice manages.
pmc-13352428:
Yang Liu headed a 2026 network meta-study comparing first-line drug care for advanced urothelial cancer, a cancer of the urinary tract lining. Doctors can choose among several body-wide regimens, yet head-to-head trials rarely test every option against every other. The study was built to rank the regimens on benefit and harm using all the trial evidence jointly.

The team searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library through November 2025 and joined random trials in a Bayesian random-effects model. Living and worsening results were expressed as hazard ratios, while side effects were treated as binary results. Readers receive a comparative picture of which first-line regimens look strongest, which carry heavier risks, and where the results remain thin.
pmc-13352628:
S. Zappalà and colleagues study mixing at the molybdenum and silica interface during graphene growth in 2026. Pairing graphene with metal layers suits electronics and optics, but heat during growth can blur the boundary. Graphene was grown by vapour deposition on a flat 35 nm molybdenum film and on tiny molybdenum patterns, both over a 1.6 micrometre silica layer.

On flat film, growth formed molybdenum-silicon and molybdenum-carbon phases and about 15 graphene layers. Patterned metal balled up instead, yielding only about 5 layers. Mixing ran one way on flat film but many ways in small patterns, losing carbon and gaining silicon. Below a critical size, evenness collapses, so layout size must enter device design.
pmc-13353928:
Jefferson David Melo de Matos and others tried to improve alginate impression stuff by adding condensation silicone, in 2026. Alginate is cheap and widely used for dental impressions, but it loses sized truth over time, which matters when pouring a model is delayed. A more stable mix could preserve truth without abandoning a familiar stuff.

Three groups of ten specimens were matched: usual alginate, an long-pour alginate, and alginate changed with condensation silicone, all made with standard ways. Sized change over time showed whether the silicone addition helped. Dentists gain a useful option for impressions that must wait before pouring.
pmc-13354028:
Ayubu E Mashambo leads a 2026 case report on severe malnutrition in a young adult with tangled causes. A 24-year-old woman had failed to gain weight for over 10 years despite adequate intake, with worsening leg weakness, body-wide swelling, delayed puberty, and no periods. Repeated hospital stays and feeding plans failed to reverse her decline.

Deep checks found Helicobacter pylori gastritis with micronutrient gaps, plus a hidden psoas abscess driving strong inflammation. Eradication therapy, surgical drainage, antibiotics, and structured feeding followed. She then gained weight steadily, swelling cleared, mobility returned, and periods began. The case shows hidden infection can quietly anchor severe malnutrition.
pmc-13354128:
Abdurrahim Rahimian and others built a set bank of heart flow SPECT images to support heart artery disease research, in 2026. Heart disease remains the leading global cause of heart death, and flow imaging is widely used, yet AI tools have been held back by a shortage of modern, always tagged banks.

The team in hindsight built 144 rest-stress MIBI SPECT studies acquired under standard plans, reconstructed them with filtered back projection, and had them interpreted independently. The resulting bank offers teams a uniform resource for training and testing diagnostic rules. It should speed the growth of tools that read flow scans more well.
pmc-13355528:
Simonetta Genovesi and co-authors stage a 2026 pro-and-con debate on stroke prevention for dialysis patients with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises stroke risk. These patients were left out of the big drug trials, so whether blood thinners help or harm them is unclear. One side favors thinners or a heart closure procedure for carefully chosen patients.

The other side notes that many studies show no clear stroke gain from thinners but clearly more major bleeding, plus possible harm to blood vessels. Both sides agree that choices must be personal, made with the patient, and that large, well-powered trials comparing thinners, closure, and no treatment are badly needed.
pmc-13356728:
Akin A Adio and co-authors studied in 2026 how post-traumatic stress disorder shapes recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. PTSD can alter pain sensing and raise substance risks, yet its effect after this common shoulder surgery was unclear. Using a large health network, they matched 2,262 patients with PTSD to the same number without it on health and demographic traits.

At ninety days, medical complications and opioid prescription counts did not differ. But patients with PTSD visited emergency departments more, at about 17 versus 11 percent, and had more sleep disorders. By two years, cannabis use disorder was nearly three times as common. The authors stress tending to mental health factors in recovery.
pmc-13356928:
Sweta Shrivastava and co-authors present a 2026 case series of six women treated for ectopic pregnancy at a hospital in western India. An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the womb and can burst, causing life-threatening bleeding. The series spanned three burst tube pregnancies, one intact tube pregnancy, one pregnancy in a horn of the womb, and one early tube miscarriage.

One unstable patient needed open surgery, while the other five had keyhole surgery guided by symptoms, blood tests, and ultrasound. Five recovered smoothly; one developed kidney injury after surgery but recovered with intensive team care. The authors stress early diagnosis, tailored surgery, and close watch after the operation.
pmc-13358428:
Isobel set out a perspective in 2026 on what trauma and violence informed research should mean for mental health nursing studies and service evaluations. Guides for trauma informed research are growing, and they stress safety, trust, choice, teamwork, and empowerment when working with people likely to have lived through trauma. Isobel argues the lens must widen to violence in its structural form, the slow harm done by systems that disadvantage people.

Being trauma and violence informed, in this account, means applying care principles in every contact with participants and data. Also weighing how a study's design, measures, and findings can compound harm. Research holds power over whose knowledge counts, and evaluations can repeat the very inequities they study. The piece calls for steady reflection at each decision point, informed by how trauma and violence cause and sustain distress, so nursing research supports recovery rather than adding to the burden.
pmc-13358528:
Wenli Zhong and others found medical factors linked to long care in breast illness unrelated to childbirth, ran the look-back cohort study in 2026. This benign swelling breast disease runs a long course and much impairs quality of life, yet factors forecasting long care were unclear. Personal care needs those signs.

Women aged eighteen to sixty with clinically and histopathologically diagnosed disease were studied through digital records. They had reached cure at China-Japan Friendship Hospital between January 2017 and September 2022, leaving out pregnancy, lactation, and malignancy. Care duration was related to medical traits. Doctors gain signs that help set expectations and tailor follow-up for this frustrating illness.
pmc-13358828:
Kerui Cen and co-authors apply a math tool to COVID-19 case curves in a 2026 study. Epidemic waves rise and fall at several speeds at once, and standard methods can blur the timing of policy effects. The team used adaptive Fourier decomposition, a method that splits a wavy signal into clean layers, on daily case data from Washington, D.C.

They checked the city's case series against official records, then matched the layers' turning points with the dates of public health measures. A second test on London data checked whether the method holds elsewhere. Sharper timing pictures could help officials judge which measures truly bent the curve in past outbreaks.
pmc-13359528:
Ki Ju Cho and co-authors review a family of proteins as drug targets in thyroid cancer in a 2026 paper. Thyroid cancer is the most common hormone gland cancer and is rising fast. Most cases are curable, but some stop responding to standard care or turn highly aggressive. The seven sirtuin proteins help control cell stress and energy, and each can either feed or fight tumors.

The review maps what each sirtuin does in this cancer and gathers new links to immune control and to ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. The authors propose pairing sirtuin drugs with existing treatments and flag which ideas are ready for early patient testing.
pmc-13359628:
Camilo Jubino Londoño and Binhai Zheng review the scar that forms after spinal cord injury in a 2026 paper. At the injury site, a fibrotic scar grows at the core, ringed by a second scar from support cells. The fibrotic part was long overlooked. It seals the wound and limits further damage, yet its persistence can block nerve fibers from regrowing.

The review traces how this scar builds over weeks, which cells and signals drive it, and how it interacts with its neighbors. New treatments aim to soften the scar without losing its protection. The authors close with the open questions that must be answered before such treatments reach patients.
pmc-13359928:
Josphat Martin Muchangi and seventeen co-authors published this survey in 2026. It lays the groundwork for folding deworming campaigns into everyday primary care in western Kenya. Mass drug drives have long fought schistosomiasis and worm infections, yet the diseases persist, and donors want a lasting local model.

The baseline covered 1,229 households and twenty-four health facilities, half set to switch models and half not. Trust in facility-led treatment was high, thanks to staff credibility, and clinics scored well on drug stocks and reporting. Still, nearly everyone got treatment from household campaign visits, showing how deep the old habit runs. Stock-outs occurred, and worker training varied widely. Community health promoters remained the key information channel for low-literacy families. The authors say the ground is ready, given standard procedures, stronger supply chains, and more promoter outreach.
pmc-13360128:
Tzu-Chin Yang and co-authors present a 2026 computer system that spots tuberculosis on chest X-rays. Reading these X-rays is hard, and expert marking of each sore spot is slow and costly. Their system, called CPM-XNet, learns from whole images without needing those detailed marks. A special mask in the system guides it to weigh the lung area while still seeing the full picture.

The team tested the system on hospital images and on public data sets. It beat similar models trained on plain, unmarked images, and one main setup gave steadier, stronger scores across repeat runs. Tests that removed one part at a time showed the mask did most of the work. The authors say the system is a promising first step, but it needs checks across more hospitals before clinic use.
pmc-13360228:
Jacopo Lanari and co-authors report 14 years of experience using heat to destroy liver tumors that spread from other cancers. The cancers were not colorectal; they included breast cancer, gut stromal tumors, and pancreatic cancer, eight types in all. The team treated 138 patients with microwave ablation, which cooks tumor tissue with heat. The heat probe went in through a small cut or through the skin.

The treatment proved safe, with few major problems and short hospital stays. Survival differed a lot by which cancer the tumors came from. Patients treated through the small-cut route lived longer than those treated through the skin. The results help doctors judge when this gentle option suits patients who cannot have surgery.
pmc-13360328:
Rohmah and colleagues rank forms of talk therapy for poor sleep in teens. The therapy, called CBT-I, can come in more than one form. It may be face to face, in a group, by phone app, or on the web. The team pooled twenty-two trials. They used a method that ranks all forms at once. Web-based therapy came out on top for most gains.

Teens on web therapy slept about half an hour more each night. They fell asleep faster and slept more soundly. Their sleep problem scores fell too. Time awake in the night did not change much. The team backs web therapy as a first choice in school and clinic care.
pmc-13360728:
Regina Mikheeva and co-authors mapped big genome changes in a famous cancer cell line in a 2026 study. HCT116, a colon cancer line, is a workhorse for drug testing and cell studies. Its small gene typos are well known, but its large DNA rearrangements and copy changes are not. The team read several samples of the line with long-read Nanopore sequencing, including samples from a public database.

They found over 22,000 large rearrangements shared across the samples. Most of the big duplicated and deleted stretches were confirmed on a second check. The team also sorted which changes were common and which were unique to one sample. The map warns lab workers that this standard line varies more than many assume, which matters when results must repeat.
pmc-13360928:
Jorge F Beltrán and co-authors tracked protein changes in salmon cells fighting a kidney disease germ in a 2026 study. The germ, Renibacterium salmoninarum, lives inside fish immune cells and is hard to study at the protein level. The team infected a salmon macrophage-like cell line and sampled it across 48 hours. A scanning method counted thousands of proteins without labels.

Of about 6,800 proteins tracked, more than 2,200 shifted in amount after infection at some point. The changes showed how the host cell reshapes itself early in the fight. The team also tested whether classic cell-death paths switch on broadly. Maps like this can reveal weak points of the germ and guide vaccines or treatments for a disease that costs salmon farms dearly.
pmc-13361528:
Dilinare Abdurehman and co-authors used artificial intelligence to test a food plant against diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 study. This kidney damage is a heavy burden of diabetes, driven by inflammation and scarring. The plant, Coreopsis tinctoria, is edible and rich in polyphenols, but how it might help was unclear. The team combined network pharmacology with machine learning to rank its active compounds.

A learning model trained on millions of compound and target pairs predicted how 36 plant polyphenols interact with disease genes. The top 100 targets were grouped into pathways. Promising paths were then checked in rats made diabetic by a high-fat diet and a drug. Blending computation with animal proof can speed the search for food-based aids against this disease.
pmc-13361828:
Peipei Zhang and co-authors studied a hormone's effect on sheep egg maturation in a 2026 paper. Growing eggs well in the lab is a gateway to making embryos outside the body. Anti-Müllerian hormone, made by cells around the egg, normally reins in early follicle growth. The team added the hormone to lab cultures of sheep eggs and watched many quality traits.

They tracked cell activity, the movement of granules that prepare the egg, its inner skeleton, and its power plants. Single-cell gene reading added a deep view of egg development. A mid dose improved the share of eggs that matured and kept key structures in their normal pattern. Knowing the right dose helps farms and labs raise embryo production in sheep breeding programs.
pmc-13362328:
Lianlen Joy Go Distor and co-authors review a calcium channel that links cancer and heart rhythm trouble in a 2026 paper. Heart disease and cancer are the world's top killers, and many cancer drugs raise the risk of heart damage and arrhythmias. The channel, CaV1.3, lets calcium into heart cells and helps set the heartbeat's pace in its natural pacemaker. In several cancers, the same channel helps tumors grow, move, and resist therapy.

Cancer treatment stresses, such as oxidative damage, inflammation, and low oxygen, can reshape how much of this channel is made and how it behaves. Those shifts disturb the heart's resting rhythm and favor arrhythmias. The authors map this two-way link so oncologists and cardiologists can anticipate rhythm trouble in survivors.
pmc-13363928:
Alessandra Iannuzzi and a large team present a 2026 field study on whether water stress shortens telomeres in grapevines, the protective caps on chromosomes that also serve as aging markers in animals. Aglianico vines grew under rainfed or carefully limited irrigation in a real vineyard. The team joined leaf water measures, drone vegetation reads, and berry chemistry with a DNA test for telomere length across the season.

Rainfed vines were thirstier and loaded more stress compounds in their berries. Telomeres shrank over the season in both groups, but ended shorter in the rainfed vines, with paired checks backing the gap. The authors call the proof early, yet they propose telomere length as a fresh lens on how field stress ages vines.
pmc-13364228:
Larissa Carvalho Ferreira and Katia Viana Xavier present a 2026 study hunting Florida farm fungi that can fight celery early blight, a leaf spot disease that makes celery unsellable. They collected 48 fungi from leaves and soils near celery fields and screened each against the blight fungus in dishes, then moved the best performer into greenhouse plants.

Twelve isolates cut the pathogen's growth by more than half, spanning five fungal groups, and leaf-born isolates proved strongest over time. Two Mucor isolates led the screen, and one of them, Mucor nidicola KX3187, also suppressed the disease on living plants. The authors call the work a first step toward a biological spray for celery growers.
pmc-13366928:
Alina Zorn and others showed that KTX207-run PDE4D breakdown disrupts tumour moving, spread, and vessel-growing power, in 2026. PDE 4 enzymes control cyclic AMP and influence cancer-key steps, while spread and vessel growth depend on cell-frame shifts and integrin signals. KTX207, a cereblon-based PROTAC, had before been shown to degrade PDE4D short forms and suppress proliferation.

Further testing tested KTX207 effects on cancer cell moving, spread, and vessel growth-related conduct. Degrading PDE4D disrupted the coordinated steps that let tumour cells move, invade tissue, and recruit blood vessels. Cancer teams gain a aimed breakdown plan that attacks metastatic power, not only tumour growth.
pmc-13369628: Temiz and Kargin published a correction in 2026 to their study of how copper and zinc oxide nanoparticles affect antioxidant defenses in the brains of male Swiss albino mice. The first author's name was misspelled in the article and its running headers, and the corrected spelling now stands in the record. Figures one and two are also replaced with full versions, covering brain antioxidant enzyme activity and damage markers in mice dosed orally for fourteen days at several nanoparticle levels. The journal record has been updated.
pmc-13371028:
Santosh Mahalik and co-workers test in 2026 how well a scan sign and a liver bit check call bile duct lack in sick new borns. The ill scars the bile tubes shut and needs fast knife care for best odds. The team reads 34 young babes with yellow skin at one big site.

All babes get a sound scan with flow read, a glow scan, and a liver bit read by a set score. A dye test in the op room is the gold call. Marks for each test come from that match. The pilot sets the base for a wide test of cheap calls.
pmc-13374128:
Nida Nur Adiyan and others survey university students on AI views, body regard, and online diet reading skill in a 2026 study. The team questioned 440 undergraduates aged 18 to 30 at Gaziantep University with scales for AI views, body regard, and e-healthy diet reading skill. Scores averaged in the mid range on each scale.

Positive AI views rose alongside body regard and diet reading skill. Male students scored higher on AI views, while female students scored higher on body regard, with no sex gap in diet reading skill. In regression models, higher body regard predicted more positive AI views. The study suggests that digital health education should link AI reading skill with body image and nutrition skills, rather than teaching AI tools in isolation.
pmc-13374228:
Antonina Maria Lin and colleagues review stewardship interventions to cut unnecessary urinary antibiotics in aged care in a 2026 paper. Much urinary prescribing in aged care does not match guidelines, yet it was unclear which interventions actually reduce it. The review followed PRISMA rules, searching six databases to June 2024 and excluding hospital and non-interventional studies.

Twenty studies were included, with four randomised trials pooled in meta-analysis. Education paired with routine audits emerged as effective for reducing urinary prescribing, while hospitalisation effects were also pooled. Risk of bias was judged with the ROBINS-I tool. The synthesis gives aged care homes a practical recipe: teach, audit, and feedback, rather than relying on guidelines alone.
pmc-13374628:
Bernier and colleagues test whether HIV-related stigma pushes people with HIV toward heavier drinking, and whether depression carries that effect, in 2026 behavioral health research. The cross-sectional study drew 331 participants with unhealthy alcohol use from two intervention trials, one for chronic pain and one for physical inactivity, both burdens in HIV care. Participants averaged 47.9 years of age; 51.4 percent were African American and 16.6 percent were women in the combined sample analyzed.

Stigma was associated with alcohol-related consequences across the combined sample, with significant indirect effects running through depressive symptoms. The fuller pattern, stigma tied to drinking severity and daily drinks via depression, appeared only among participants in the chronic pain trial. No trial-specific effects emerged in the inactivity trial sample. Bernier argues depression is a pathway worth treating in its own right, and that chronic pain may amplify how stigma translates into alcohol involvement for people with HIV.
pmc-13375528:
Pratley and colleagues test whether an antibody that blocks myostatin can preserve muscle during weight loss driven by tirzepatide, in the 2026 phase 2 EMBRAZE trial. Incretin drugs such as tirzepatide cut weight powerfully, but a share of the loss is lean mass, which can harm strength and function. Apitegromab inhibits activation of myostatin, a protein that restrains muscle growth. The double-blind trial randomized 102 adults with overweight or obesity, half to tirzepatide plus apitegromab and half to tirzepatide plus placebo.

At week 24, the apitegromab group had lost 1.9 kilograms less lean mass than the placebo group, a significant difference, despite similar weight loss between groups. That spared amount represented 54.9 percent retention of lean mass relative to placebo. Adverse events were similar: 76 percent of apitegromab participants and 71 percent of placebo participants reported one, with one serious event in each arm. Pratley calls the result proof of concept for pairing the drug classes.
pmc-13375928:
Yoonah Jang and four co-authors screen Chinese cabbage seedlings for heat response with 3D multispectral imaging and time based checks. Chinese cabbage is a cool season crop sold widely in Asian markets, and heat above its comfort range harms growth. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team grew seedlings from a set of types under heat or normal air for two weeks. A scanner tracked shape and spectral traits without harming the plants. Main pattern checks captured most of the spread in the data, and a distance measure scored how stable each type stayed. The clearest split between heat and control plants came three days in, which shows how fast this crop feels heat.
pmc-13376628:
Xuan Zhao and Rui Lu schedule linear megaprojects with an eye on future inventions in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Roads and pipelines stretch in lines, and new technology may arrive mid-build, welcome but unpredictable. Their model folds expected innovation time into the plan as scattered buffers.

Time, cost, and robustness are optimized together under a linear scheduling method suited to such projects. A tuned genetic algorithm searches for the best trade-offs. When expected innovation time stays under one-eighth of the deadline, plans can balance all three goals well. Past half the deadline, delays balloon while costs barely move. Case studies show the model works in practice. The thresholds give managers a rule of thumb.
pmc-13376728:
Jianliang Xu and Jin Qian build a self-drive cart brain in a 2026 paper. Yard carts that drive on their own must hold a path true in spite of wind, load shifts, and wear. Fixed math of the cart is hard to get, so the team skips it.

Their way learns the cart's acts from in and out data alone. A web-based watch then spots and feeds back shake and push from the road. A slide rule with a shift rate does the wheel calls, fast when far off and soft when near. The mix aims for true paths with less shake of the wheel.
pmc-13377028:
Peter Ducos and four co-authors picture the full machine that restarts stalled DNA copying in a bacterium, in a 2026 structure study. When a copying fork stalls and is left behind, the cell must rebuild it or die. Three proteins, PriA, PriB, and DnaT, join on the stalled fork to start that rebuild. The team froze the group at two stages and read its shape at fine detail.

One shape shows an early stage, with a single tail piece of DnaT bound to the other two proteins and the DNA. The mature shape shows many such pieces lined up in a thread. The thread hands the loose DNA strand from PriB to DnaT, which sets up the restart. A head piece of DnaT forms its own cluster apart. The authors note a likeness to the protein that starts fresh copying.
pmc-13377728:
Gülsen Kiraz and co-authors scored root-heal work in young dead teeth in a 2026 study. The heal path uses the body's own fix craft to seal the root and let it grow on. Teeth cared for from 2018 to 2024 were read, with at least one year of watch.

Film reads logged root length, tip width, and root wall zone. Heal was classed as healed, in heal, or still sick. Tingle tests checked if the tooth could feel once more. Which facts at the start flagged a good end was the team's hunt. Such flags can help dentists pick this path or a plain fill with more care.
pmc-13377828:
Yuhe Liu and co-authors ask why rural old folk in China shun web care in a 2026 study. Web elder care is pushed to meet age growth, yet take-up stays low in the country, even when gear and cost are fixed. Views on right and wrong care may be the true block.

A survey of 400 folk aged 60 and up in one Chongqing zone fed set math. Deep talks with 15 odd-case folk then dug into their rules on care, shame, and kin duty. If a web aid feels fair to take, that feel drove use most. Tech skill did not. Care that jars with kin duty will stall, gear or no gear.
pmc-13378228:
Uma Maheswara Rao Munipalli and Visalakshi Annepu present a 2026 computer model for detecting Alzheimer's disease from brain scans at an early stage. Alzheimer's develops slowly, and telling apart normal ageing, mild memory problems, and dementia is hard. Their model sorts scans into those three groups.

The model combines three methods: one that extracts detailed image features, one that focuses attention on key areas, and one that reads patterns in sequence. It was trained on scans from 2,100 people and then tested on 900 people from a separate source. Accuracy was high on both sets, and better than simpler models. Tests removing each part confirmed that each one helped.
pmc-13380228:
Shuhan Pan and colleagues tested whether dietary taurine eases transport stress in broiler chicks, in a 2026 feeding study. Post-hatch transport depresses growth, antioxidant defenses, and gut barrier strength in young birds. The team split 180 one-day-old yellow-feathered chicks into five groups: control, transport stress, and stress plus taurine at 0.25, 0.50, or 0.75 percent, for two weeks.

Transport cut final weight, daily gain, catalase activity, and gut villus height at day 7, while raising liver stress enzymes, cortisol, and heat shock gene expression. Taurine lifted weight, gain, glucose at day 14, catalase, and duodenal villus height, while lowering liver enzyme activity and crypt depth. The amino acid looks like a practical feed aid for shipped chicks.
pmc-13381028:
Dheenadhayalan MJ, Roshini N, and Kalpana Ramachandran report a 2026 anatomical case found during routine dissection of a donated body. In the right arm of an adult woman, the main arm artery split into its two end branches unusually high, in the upper third of the arm rather than at the elbow. Branching differences like this matter during surgery and grafting.

The split sat a few centimetres below the point where a chest muscle attaches, and the main arm nerve ran between the two branches. One branch ran down the thumb side of the arm and the other down the little-finger side. The left arm, by contrast, showed the usual pattern. Surgeons who know such variants can avoid mishaps.
pmc-13382028:
Bolin Liu and a large team published a 2026 study of how microbes in estuary water capture carbon in the dark, powered by ammonia. This dark carbon fixation adds to plant-based production in the oceans. Ammonia oxidation provides much of its energy, but the two processes had not been studied together systematically in estuaries.

Working in the Yangtze Estuary in China, the team measured both rates in water samples using isotope tracers. Rates varied widely between samples, and higher ammonia levels went with faster rates of both processes. Gene surveys identified which microbe groups were doing the fixing, split between two chemical pathways. The results help place estuaries in the global carbon picture.
pmc-13383528:
Li Wang's team investigates how yeast culture shapes fiber-digesting gut microbes in the rumen, in a 2026 study. Yeast culture is widely fed to ease rumen acidity and fiber digestion problems under starch-rich diets, but the microbe mechanism was a key gap. The study asks how yeast culture steers fiber-breaking communities and affects energy hydrogen flow in the rumen.

The work centers on yeast culture's steering of fiber-breaking bacterial groups and energy H2 flow, with butyrate-making fiber digesters proposed as an inside-cells hydrogen sink. The question matters because H2 routing decides how well grazing animals digest fiber and how much methane they emit.
pmc-13385728:
Liyuan Yu and colleagues pinpoint an epigenetic brake on bone growth in human fat-derived stem cells in 2026 work. Large skull and jaw defects heal poorly on their own, so new repair routes are prized. The enzyme HDAC4 was found to repress bone formation by limiting a key signal gene, SMAD4.

Blocking HDAC4, by gene cuts or by the drug tasquinimod, raised gene-opening marks and freed SMAD4 expression. A slow-release gel carrying the drug then boosted bone regrowth in mouse skull and jaw defects of critical size. The authors propose local epigenetic therapy as a practical path for craniofacial repair.
pmc-13385928:
Hao Zhang's team resolved excited-state motion in a single-molecule device, in a 2026 study. Charge transport through single molecules reveals linked quantum states for tiny devices, but sorting out excited-state motion needed both high time and energy detail at once. The team used fast conductance tests on a single-molecule radical junction.

Singlet and triplet states, bridged by doublet states, joined transport within about 150 ns, mapped in both time and energy domains. Transient peak spots shifted by up to about 440 milli-electron volts over hundreds of ns, matching a dynamic shift at the molecule-contact junction. The work clarifies many-body effects in molecular circuits.
pmc-13386828:
Julia Gata-de-Benito and colleagues delete a single gene from African swine fever virus and watch disease soften in 2026 work. The gene, MGF110-2L, was cut from a virulent strain that normally drives severe illness in pigs. In cell tests, the altered virus let interferon responses rise higher than the parent strain did.

In animals, the picture flipped: the parent virus triggered excessive interferon and inflammation, while the deleted version kept responses controlled. Pigs given the altered virus showed markedly milder disease and full protection against later challenge with the virulent strain. The authors name the gene a virulence factor and a vaccine design lead.
pmc-13388028:
Amina Bibi and co-authors systematically study how molecular attachments called auxochromes change the way fluorescent molecules glow under different conditions. Two quenching processes, photo-induced electron transfer together with twisted intramolecular charge transfer, dim fluorescence, but their response to the environment had never been mapped together. Their 2026 study builds a matrix of twenty-four compounds.

Eight amine auxochromes were combined with three light-emitting cores, and fluorescence was measured while varying temperature, acidity, and viscosity. Both quenching processes grew stronger at higher temperatures. Low acidity blocked the electron transfer pathway but left the twisting pathway largely unaffected. Increasing viscosity disrupted both pathways. The authors say the map will help chemists design fluorescent molecules deliberately sensitive to temperature, pH, or thickness of their surroundings, for uses such as sensing and imaging.
pmc-13388428:
Lars Olaf Cardell and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on immune switches found on T cells in the first lymph nodes that drain mouth cancers. Tumors coat themselves in sugars that press these switches and dull the immune attack. The first draining nodes can be groomed by a tumor into safe havens for spread.

The team took such nodes from patients during standard biopsy care, plus healthy nodes from people having benign surgery. They counted the switches on two T cell classes. One switch ran lower on T cells in nodes where cancer had already landed. Another ran lower in nodes of patients with larger main tumors. The pattern may mark how tumors soften their first landing sites.
pmc-13388528:
Javier Jiménez-Garrido's team prove sharper versions of the Borel-Ritt theorem, which asks whether any formal power series can appear as the asymptotic expansion of a genuine function. They work with functions that expand uniformly on an unbounded sector of the logarithmic Riemann surface. In that setting, classical results demanded a strong closure condition on the weight sequence.

For Roumieu classes, a much weaker rule now suffices, and for Beurling classes they improve a classical result of Schmets and Valdivia and give a new proof of a result by Debrouwere. Their rule also yields surjectivity in suitably small sectors, adapting a procedure rooted in the work of Thilliez, Chaumat, and Chollet.
pmc-13389728:
Hilma Clemen, Sangeetha Ramu, and Lena Uller propose, in 2026, a triple-hit account of lung harm from combined exposures. In daily life, people rarely meet e-cigarette vapour, fine dust particles, or respiratory viruses one at a time, yet most research tests them alone.

The authors review how vaping creates fat-filled lung defence cells and harms airway lining and tiny beating hairs, while fine particles push defence cells first toward inflammation and later toward tissue remodelling. Both exposures weaken defence against viruses such as flu and the coronavirus that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome. Together the three hits may reinforce each other. Lung researchers gain a testable framework for studying combined exposures rather than single risks in isolation.
pmc-13390328:
Malgorzata Dec-Cwiek and co-authors published a study in 2026 on mood after stroke. Low mood and anxiety are common after a stroke that blocks a brain artery. The team asked how often each appears three months later, alone or together, and what foretells them.

They followed 579 patients who filled mood surveys at discharge and again at three months. About half had no mood problem at three months. The joint form, both low mood and anxiety, was the largest single group. Anxiety at discharge more than doubled the odds of later anxiety. Low mood at discharge nearly quadrupled the odds of later low mood. Older age added a small push to low mood risk. The authors urge routine mood checks at discharge to catch high-risk patients early.
pmc-13391228:
Shinju Matsuoka leads a 2026 single-centre Japanese review of stent-assisted coiling for burst wide-neck brain aneurysms treated in the first hours after bleeding. Adding a stent widens endovascular options, but using one during acute subarachnoid haemorrhage is controversial because blood thinners raise bleeding risk while the stent itself can provoke clots.

The series covers patients treated within forty-eight hours of rupture and judges whether the approach proved feasible and safe in that window. Neurosurgeons and interventional radiologists gain centre-level outcome data for a timing dilemma. One path secures a difficult aneurysm early with stent support. The other avoids stent-related drug burdens during the most fragile phase.
pmc-13392028:
Kim Chi Vo's team found two sleeper-made RNA-binding proteins that firmly suppress liver-stage copying in repeat malaria. Plasmodium vivax forms dormant liver sleepers that later awaken to cause blood-stage relapses, and the team guessed that sleep requires firm suppression of splitting.

Expressing each protein alone in rodent malaria liver stages, which never form sleepers, blocked splitting, leaving parasites small and single-nucleus. The proteins bound distinct, highly exact RNA motifs, hinting they stall copying by trapping motif-carrying RNAs, and the team named them IESI-1 and IESI-2.
pmc-13392628:
Rajab Msemo and a large clinical team describe a seven-month-old girl born with a lump at the base of her spine that could have signalled far graver problems. Two look-alike conditions dominate worry in such cases: a spinal sac defect and a germ-cell tumour of the tailbone area. Getting the distinction right decides whether a baby needs major spinal surgery or a simple removal.

Magnetic resonance imaging ruled out both feared diagnoses, pointing instead to a fatty lump sitting under the skin. Surgeons removed it cleanly, and laboratory study of the tissue confirmed a lipoma in an unusual spot for infancy. The authors stress the value of good imaging before operating, since a benign lump can closely mimic lesions with very different risks and operations.
pmc-13393828:
James Downs argues that eating disorders are misframed when treatment casts recovery as a solo test of motivation and willpower. Agency matters, the paper grants, but the lens is too narrow. Downs draws on ecological systems theory, ecosocial health thinking, evolutionary psychiatry, and lived experience. He builds the case that eating disorders grow inside interacting systems. Bodily weak spots, close ties, cultural pressures, institutions, and political economy all play a part at once.

Individualistic models, the argument runs, breed shame and stigma, silence patient knowledge, and pile excess blame on the ill person, most where care is patchy, delayed, or unequal. A systems reading treats them as bodily, socially patterned suffering that behaviour change alone cannot fix. If the causes sit in whole systems, the paper concludes, the work of prevention, treatment, and recovery must be shared and structural too.
pmc-13393928:
Tim Van Den Bossche leads a twenty-nine-author community statement arguing that metaproteomics cannot mature without standardised reporting and better shared data habits. The field studies all proteins in microbial communities. Workflows differ wildly between labs at both bench and computer stages, so results resist comparison and cannot merge cleanly with other omics layers. The paper presents a reporting checklist built by the community for the field's specific needs.

Alongside the checklist, the authors outline efforts to capture experiment metadata in structured, shareable forms, borrowing standards from proteomics and microbiome research wherever they fit. Transparent reporting aligned with the FAIR principles, covering findable, open, shareable, and reusable data, is the goal. The recommendations aim to make studies repeatable and cumulative rather than one-off.
pmc-13394628:
Atsunari Kawashima and colleagues review, in 2026, how microbes may drive cancers of the bladder, kidney, and urinary tract. Gut microbes can change how the body handles cancer-causing chemicals and can prime swelling. Mouse work shows diet and microbes together can shift tumour growth. The review also weighs a newer signal: germ DNA carried in tiny parcels in the blood.

Those blood signals track with immune features of tumours and with replies to checkpoint drugs. Blood holds very little germ matter, so dirt in samples is a real risk. The authors urge careful checks and outside proof. They frame the signals as a hopeful biopsy tool, not a settled one.
pmc-13395328:
Peris Mutena writes, in 2026, an essay on healing for university students through nature and peer-led action, with Kenya in mind. Students face money strain, heavy study loads, family pressure, and hard settling-in. Many report stress and anxiety well above general rates. The essay frames the pain as a crisis of disconnection from self, community, and the natural world.

Short-term fixes often leave root causes untouched, Mutena argues. Eco-therapy, care rooted in time and movement in nature, offers a deeper path. Peer-led programs could rebuild power and belonging on campus. The piece blends world data with Kenyan campus life. It calls for care that restores ties, not just calms symptoms.
pmc-13395428:
Tia R. Tropea and co-authors test, in 2026, a fast way to build text reminders that help people take antidepressants. Forgetting and slow benefit are common reasons doses get missed. The team drafted 83 reminder texts from known barriers, half by hand and half by AI. An online panel of 181 adults on such drugs rated subsets of the texts.

Panel members gave more than seven thousand ratings in short order. AI texts scored higher than human ones on felt helpfulness. Texts that spoke to slow benefit beat other barrier themes. Self-tracking and habit-building tricks also scored top marks. The authors back online panels as a quick test bed before costly trials.
pmc-13396028:
August Romeo and co-authors studied the tiny eye drifts that occur while people hold their gaze still, and how those drifts shape what they see, in a 2026 report. The eyes never rest fully; small movements keep shifting the image on the retina, and each eye partly moves on its own.

Volunteers stared at a central point while viewing textures of short line segments and judged whether a figure was hidden in the middle. The team recorded drift and tiny rapid movements from both eyes at once. Two distinct modes of drift appeared during the figure-ground task, which argues against the old view that such movement is pure noise and supports a working role in vision.
pmc-13396328:
Mickael Vourc'h and colleagues studied lung injury after heart surgery in patients who received blood transfusions, focusing on cases with no antibody cause. Their 2026 study, set at Nantes University Hospital, looks at a signal pair, SDF-1α and its receptor CXCR4, that guides immune cells.

Adults having planned heart surgery between September 2016 and March 2021 who received one to five red cell units during the operation were included. Lung injury was defined by a low ratio of blood oxygen to breathed oxygen within three days. The team examined what each transfused unit contained, aiming to link unit composition to injury and to explain transfusion-related lung harm that antibody tests miss.
pmc-13396428:
Fadi Abualhommos and co-authors followed a girl with Ohtahara syndrome from birth to age seven, charting the breathing problems that came to dominate her care, in a 2026 case report. The syndrome is a severe epilepsy of newborns, marked by tonic spasms and a distinctive burst pattern on brain recordings.

Four seizure drugs together could not fully control her attacks, and her development stayed severely impaired. Between ages one and seven she was admitted at least 15 times with chest infections, often short of oxygen and sometimes with choking episodes pointing to swallowing trouble. Supportive breathing care and antibiotics kept her alive to school age in a setting with limited resources.
pmc-13397028:
Upama Aich and co-authors exposed eastern mosquitofish to a hormone-mimicking farm pollutant to test the hidden costs for immunity and breeding. Their 2026 study uses 17β-trenbolone, an androgen-like compound from livestock waste that reaches waterways at real-world levels.

Male hormones run both defense and reproduction, so a pollutant that imitates them could force trade-offs between the two. Adult fish were dosed at concentrations found in the environment, then checked for immune strength and how much they invested in reproduction. Small fish like mosquitofish are sentinels for waterways, and results here warn how farm runoff may quietly weaken wild populations.
pmc-13397328:
