Isam Ahmed Abdeljaleel Taha and co-authors review outcomes of near-total pancreas removal in Sudanese infants whose pancreas releases insulin without pause, driving blood sugar dangerously low. Their 2026 study comes from Al Ribat University Hospital and covers operations from January 2019 to December 2024.

Congenital hyperinsulinism is the leading cause of lasting low blood sugar in babies. Rich hospitals separate focal from diffuse disease with genetic tests and advanced scans, then tailor treatment. In Sudan those tools and the needed medicines are scarce, so surgery comes early. The authors chart the children's features, operations, and results, giving low-resource teams a record to plan against.
pmc-13397528:
W Nicholas Jungbauer and co-authors examine whether the pain drug ketorolac, given around facelift surgery, cuts how much opioid pain relief patients need afterward. Their 2026 study looks back at cases from one practice. Good pain control also guards against spikes in blood pressure and heart rate, which can trigger bleeding under the skin.

Charts compared facelift patients who got intravenous ketorolac with those who did not, tallying narcotic use after surgery. Older pain drugs in this drug family had been studied in facial surgery, but hard data on ketorolac by vein were thin. Weighing pain relief against bleeding risk helps surgeons decide whether the drug belongs in standard facelift care.
pmc-13397628:
Javiera Jara-Jara and fellow authors built knowledge tests on teen depression and anxiety for adults who work in Chilean schools. Their 2026 study responds to a shortage of tools that measure what teachers know about these disorders. Staff who spot warning signs early can steer students toward help sooner.

Ten expert judges checked the content, 16 teachers took part in thinking-aloud interviews, and 304 school professionals sat the tests. Items drew on published literature plus the DSM-5 diagnostic manual, with agreement scored by Aiken's V method. Using classical test theory, the team checked how hard each item was and how well it separated strong from weak knowledge.
pmc-13397828:
Junaid Ihsan and colleagues made atom-thin sheets mixing four metals (ruthenium, molybdenum, vanadium and niobium) with selenium, hunting for better hydrogen-making catalysts. Their 2026 paper builds the quaternary alloy by colloidal chemistry, varying the ruthenium share from none to full. Splitting water for hydrogen fuel needs catalysts that work well in any water chemistry, and layering extra metals can tune a sheet's electronic character.

Adding ruthenium kept the sheets flat and layered while nudging their crystal form from the 2H toward the 1T pattern, and theory backed even mixing of the atoms. The four-metal sheets beat the three-metal version at driving hydrogen release in alkaline, acidic and neutral fluids alike. Calculations credit ruthenium atoms with gripping hydrogen just tightly enough to speed the reaction.
pmc-13398128:
Ying Ying Ch'ng and co-authors coat copper catalysts with a chlorine-bearing silane to turn carbon dioxide into richer fuels and feedstocks. Their 2026 study attacks three stubborn blocks: slow CO2 activation, a high energy wall for joining carbon pairs and hydrogen gas stealing the current. Chlorine helps wake CO2 up, while silane layers steer charge, but using each alone splits their benefits apart.

One molecule, CPTMS, carries both tricks and was laid onto copper in a single plating step. The treated catalyst reached a faradaic efficiency of about 75 percent for multi-carbon products, five times the roughly 15 percent of unmodified copper oxide in their tests. Performance held at a set voltage with strong current toward the prized products.
pmc-13398928:
Russell and co-authors explore, in 2026, how science students experience support for teaching and learning at a UK post-92 university, using surveys and focus groups with 15 students. The sample reflected widening access intakes: 33 percent were first in their family to attend university and 20 percent came from abroad. Thematic analysis sorted their accounts into three themes: motivations, barriers, and belonging.

Students were driven by interest in science and bioscience career goals, with some describing foundation years as blessings that opened the door. Progress was hampered by money strain, pandemic-era loss of lab access, and feelings of cultural exclusion. Belonging came through peer networks students built themselves, while formal support was patchy and curriculum gaps limited hands-on lab skill growth. The authors recommend teaching that blends active hands-on learning, codesigned courses, and built-in support to improve retention and equity in bioscience education.
pmc-13399328:
Sadat Ibrahim and colleagues ran a case-control study in Hohoe Municipality, Ghana, to find what raised or lowered a person's chance of catching SARS-CoV-2, reporting in 2026. The team matched each confirmed case with two people who tested negative. They compared social habits, health conditions, and activity levels through structured interviews.

The study enrolled 234 participants: 78 cases confirmed by PCR or rapid antigen testing and 156 controls, matched by age and sex. Moderate or high social interaction tripled the odds of infection, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.00 in the final model. Having no underlying health condition cut the odds to 0.25 in the same analysis. Regular physical activity was also protective, at an adjusted ratio of 0.18 as reported. The authors recommend campaigns stressing close-contact risks and promoting active, healthy lifestyles for pandemic readiness.
pmc-13399628:
Jiao Wang and team tested whether urea treatment can cut false alarms in syphilis ELISA testing. Their 2026 work takes on a day-to-day lab snag: weak, non-specific antibody binding can make a screen read positive when follow-up tests say otherwise. A simple break-up step could spare patients needless worry and repeat testing.

The team treated 11 false-positive samples, plus positive and negative controls, with urea at varied strengths and times, then weighed signal ratios before and after. Longer or stronger urea exposure pushed most false-positive signals below the positive cutoff, while true positives stayed positive and negatives stayed negative. Signal gaps before and after treatment were clear-cut. The work backs urea break-up as a cheap triage aid, pending larger checks.
pmc-13400228:
Christina Signoretti and colleagues showed that an enzyme variant can reshape chromosome folding in blood vessels and protect against vascular disease. Their 2026 study uses CRISPR-engineered rats modeling two human glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase variants: a deficient S188F form and a non-deficient N126D form. How three-dimensional genome structure controls vessel gene activity had been poorly mapped.

Only the deficient variant altered aortic genome folding, raising TET enzymes and anti-growth genes while suppressing inflammatory, clotting, and scarring genes. That pattern reduced angiotensin-induced aortic stiffness and high blood pressure. The deficient enzyme interacted with the scaffold protein MATRIN-3 and enriched a histone mark linked to genome structure. The paper links metabolism, genome folding, and vessel health, with human relevance still to confirm.
pmc-13400628:
Yupiao Zheng and colleagues identify, in 2026, the enzyme that erases a key chemical mark during cell division. As chromosomes condense and separate, a mark on histone H3 at one position helps guide the process, then must be balanced. The kinase adding the mark was known; the eraser was not.

Screening phosphatase genes from across the human genome, the team found a nuclear enzyme called SCP4 that removes that mark. It also shapes where a chromosome-guiding complex gathers during division. Too much or too little SCP4 caused chromosomes to separate badly and end up in wrong numbers. Mouse eggs lacking the enzyme stumbled at their very first division, underlining its basic role in faithful reproduction.
pmc-13400828:
Takashi Ikeda and colleagues pool, in 2026, trials asking whether eating more protein at breakfast builds muscle in older adults. Preventing age-related muscle loss is a major goal, and shifting protein toward the morning has been proposed while keeping daily intake steady. Timing evidence, however, was unsettled.

Seven randomized trials with 305 participants aged sixty and over met the criteria. Breakfast protein showed no clear benefit for lean mass, grip strength, leg strength or physical performance, with pooled effects hovering near zero. It slightly reduced total daily food intake, significantly so in trials without exercise. The authors conclude morning loading alone may not help muscle, though certainty is limited by few, small trials.
pmc-13400928:
Alejandra Machado and colleagues check, in 2026, whether real-world pregnancy care for women with multiple sclerosis in Sweden matches national guidelines. Managing the disease around pregnancy means balancing disease control against drug safety for mother and fetus. Clinicians often adapt standard advice to each case.

The study linked survey responses from 130 women, covering 153 pregnancies, to the national MS register. Before conception, most cases involved drugs for which guidelines advise stopping before pregnancy. One drug, rituximab, accounted for nearly half of all cases. Many women continued treatment, or had recent treatment, around conception. After birth, over half resumed therapy. Many others delayed, likely for breastfeeding. Practice broadly aligned with national guidance, the authors conclude.
pmc-13401428:
Mason Arbabi and co-authors describe a 2026 case report suggesting a probable link between hidradenitis suppurativa, a chronic skin disease of painful nodules and tunnels in skin folds, and inflammatory bowel disease. Both conditions involve misdirected immune responses, and their overlap is increasingly noticed.

Their patient was a 64-year-old man with longstanding hidradenitis, a chronic colostomy, and several other health problems who arrived with bright red blood passed from the rectum. Workup found multiple open fistulous tracts around the anus with scarring, large external hemorrhoids, active chronic proctitis with focal crypt abscesses and erosion, and diverticulitis, while infection testing came back negative. His skin disease stayed active throughout the hospital stay. The authors review the shared roots of the two diseases, from follicle blockage and microbes to genes and environment.
pmc-13401528:
Seiji Mabuchi, Ai Kusakabe, and Tomoyuki Sasano wrote a 2026 review of mirvetuximab soravtansine, a targeted drug for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, a setting with few options and poor outcomes. Standard treatments give only modest benefit, and immune checkpoint drugs help little in unselected patients.

The drug is an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at folate receptor alpha, a protein found at high levels in many epithelial ovarian cancers. The antibody delivers a cell-killing payload called DM4 inside tumour cells, with a bystander effect on neighbours and a manageable safety profile. In the SORAYA and MIRASOL trials it improved response rates and both progression-free and overall survival in patients whose tumours scored high for the receptor. The review also covers combination plans, earlier use, maintenance strategies, resistance, and biomarker testing questions.
pmc-13402228:
Tan writes, in a 2026 letter to the editor, about what the Philippines can borrow from Brazil's healthy lifestyle promotion model. He responds to an article by Ferrari on implementing such policy. Both countries carry a dual disease burden, with noncommunicable diseases like hypertension and diabetes climbing alongside persistent infections, and both struggle with sustained implementation, multi-sector coordination, and cultural fit of imported programs.

The letter grounds the comparison in Filipino daily life: fiesta culture, communal eating known as salu-salo, and body image norms shape diet and activity in ways policy must respect. A cited study by Pengpid and colleagues found seven in ten Filipino adolescents had skipped one or more meals within a month. Meal skipping was tied to poorer dietary and mental health outcomes. Filipino adults show high obesity and hypertension rates linked to salty, refined-carbohydrate diets. The author urges socioculturally aligned policy design.
pmc-13402828:
Huang and co-authors design, in 2026, a superhydrophobic coating that can be peeled off on command without damaging the metal beneath. It solves the disposal problem of durable protective coatings, inspired by how snakes shed skin. Their coating stacks an electro-responsive epoxy ionic adhesive under a carbon nanotube water-repelling layer, sprayed in sequence onto the substrate.

Applying 90 volts of direct current for just 3 minutes flips the adhesive's free ions from disordered to ordered arrangements, collapsing its grip: adhesion energy to stainless steel plunged from 2.46 to 0.01 kilojoules per square meter, a removal efficiency of about 99.6 percent in their measurements. The coating stripped cleanly even after 10 recoating cycles on the same sheets. The authors propose the switch-off strategy as a general, sustainable route for protecting large metal equipment while allowing substrate recycling, balancing in-service durability with end-of-life removability.
pmc-13403428:
Qian Jiang and colleagues synthesized risk factors for major adverse events after stenting in women with acute coronary syndrome. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pools 22 cohort studies with 16,500 women, addressing inconsistent single-study results due to size and region. Stenting is the mainstay for acute coronary syndrome, yet adverse events after the procedure remain a major challenge.

Eight factors significantly raised event risk, including older age, reduced pumping function, diabetes, and other clinical markers detailed in the analysis. All studies reported adjusted odds ratios, and quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The paper gives clinicians a higher-level risk profile for women after stenting, while noting that pooled observational data cannot prove cause for any single factor.
pmc-13403528:
Maria das Graças Lins Brandão described in 2026 a database that gathers old records of folk plant use in Brazil. Unlike China or India, Brazil lacks one neat written line for such knowledge, and sources lie scattered. The database pulls its entries from 114 books printed up to 1950.

It now covers 3,464 plant species with their original names kept. Entries sort plants into 170 healing uses, with the largest group aimed at infectious and parasite diseases. Uses that lasted for centuries mark plants as resilient, the author argues. The resource can guide new plant-based products and spread pride in Brazil's plant wealth.
pmc-13403728:
Zhuohao Liu, Gang Li, and Kaiying Wang argued in a 2026 review that tiny power stores must be judged as parts of whole systems. Micro-supercapacitors can give quick bursts of power in chips, wearables, and implants. Most studies still grade them alone, by lab numbers that ignore real use.

The review sets out design logic that starts from what a system needs: space, build steps, and loss between parts. It compares building the store into the chip against adding it as a partner piece. Each route trades output, ease of making, and room to grow. The roadmap aims at stores that ship inside real products.
pmc-13404428:
Chia-You Chou and colleagues synthesized randomized trials of wide-awake, tourniquet-free anesthesia for carpal tunnel release. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis addresses WALANT, local anesthesia without a tourniquet, which avoids tourniquet discomfort and allows active testing during surgery. Earlier reviews mixed nonrandomized designs and varied hand procedures, leaving pain and recovery effects unclear.

Pooling eight randomized trials, operative time did not differ overall, though WALANT took longer in open procedures. WALANT consistently lowered intraoperative pain, while early postoperative pain varied across studies, with smaller gaps in endoscopic cases. Patient satisfaction ran higher with WALANT, while adverse events were uncommon and comparable, and function scores favored WALANT in pooled analysis. The paper supports WALANT as a patient-friendly option.
pmc-13404528:
Joel Victoria-Martínez and José Martín-Nieto review, in 2026, what the eye can reveal about Alzheimer disease. The retina belongs to the central nervous system and shares many features with the brain. Changes there might flag the disease early and track its course without invasive testing.

Their survey covers molecular, structural and functional changes found in the retina and in other eye parts such as the cornea, lens and tear fluid. Detection relies on methods like electroretinography, optical coherence tomography and scanning laser ophthalmoscopy, all painless and fairly cheap. The authors weigh how far eye findings can support diagnosis now. They also consider whether eye measures might predict how the brain disease will progress.
pmc-13404628:
Lena Elise Wessing and a large team set out, in 2026, to measure how common multiple long-term conditions are during pregnancy worldwide. Having two or more physical or mental conditions raises the risk of complications and specialist care in pregnancy. How studies define that state also varies, which muddies comparisons.

Four databases were searched for observational studies published between January 2015 and September 2025, with no limits on language or country. Eligible studies needed at least 200 pregnant women and reported prevalence figures. Two reviewers screened, extracted and graded studies on their own, following PRISMA 2020 and Joanna Briggs guidance. Regional and global pooled rates, plus the range of definitions used, form the core output.
pmc-13408128:
Monireh Panah and co-authors uncover, in 2026, a single control point governing the maturation of most RNA in human cells. Repeated genome-wide screens hunted factors controlling the famous cancer-linked long RNA MALAT1. Its survival depends on unusual tail processing. The screens landed on two proteins, TRNAU1AP and PRPF39, which together form a previously unrecognised control pathway.

That pathway also governs processing of other abundant non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA spacers, and transfer RNA leaders, the raw materials of protein production. Everything funnels through one exon in a shared component of two ancient RNA-cutting machines, RNase MRP and RNase P: include the exon and both machines work. Upstream, a four-pronged feedback circuit stabilises the whole system, which touches over ninety percent of the cell's RNA content.
pmc-13408428:
Katreddi Rohith and team propose a blockchain-backed zero-trust frame to guard 6G health care networks full of linked medical devices. Their 2026 work takes on wider attack fronts, device variety, and real-time security needs that perimeter defenses cannot handle. Web-linked medical devices in hospitals need firm, low-lag protection.

Guided by the MITRE D3FEND defense ontology, the frame joins zero-trust micro-segmentation, a random forest intrusion spotter, and a light proof-of-authority blockchain for policy enforcement. Simulations across 30 trials in a 62-device hospital setting reported a 99.10 percent threat neutralization rate, mean enforcement lag of 76.68 milliseconds, and a composite security score of 91.8 against five rival frames. The authors stress that physical testbed checks and hostile testing stay priority next steps.
pmc-13408628:
Jiechang Wang, Linfeng Lan, and Hongyu Zhang study in 2026 organic crystals that bend in the cold and change their glow colour while doing it. Such crystals could serve adaptive photonics and low-temperature sensing, yet nobody knew why cooling pushes their light toward blue in some cases and red in others. Their material was a flexible crystal built on a naphthalene-based Schiff base.

The crystals stayed elastic and orderly from room temperature down to near liquid-nitrogen cold. X-ray snapshots during cooling showed the lattice contracting reversibly with no disorder creeping in. Where neighbouring flat molecules overlapped more as they cooled, their coupling strengthened and the glow shifted red, in one case dramatically; where overlap stayed absent, the emission stayed blue and molecule-like. That overlap rule gives designers a geometric handle for predicting and programming cold-responsive optical materials.
pmc-13409028:
Eric Nyarko and colleagues ask frontline health workers in two rural Ghanaian districts in 2026 which of the World Health Organization's twenty-four snakebite activities deserve priority. The agency aims to halve snakebite death and disability by 2030, and local ranking can guide where scarce money goes first. Workers weighed the activities against each other in a choice experiment, analysed with a classical scaling method and five machine-learning models.

One priority towered over the rest: getting safe, effective antivenoms to everyone, at a price all can afford. First aid and ambulance transport came second, then coordinated data management, then advocacy and communication. The agreement between classic and machine-learning analyses strengthens confidence in the ranking. The authors recommend that Ghana's health system build its snakebite plan outward from the antivenom supply chain.
pmc-13410528:
Shu-Qin He, Peng Ye, and Ting Zheng reply in 2026 to readers who questioned their trial of two nerve blocks for pain after kidney surgery. The trial compared a block near the lower back muscles with one beside the spine. Readers had asked why skin sensation area served as the main sign of block success.

The authors explain that the nerves in question lie too deep to monitor directly at the bedside. Mapping where skin feeling fades gives a quick, repeatable picture of where the block reached. Since surgical cuts map to known skin zones, that picture can predict whether pain cover matches the operation site. Unusual spread of numbness can also give early warning of stray anesthetic reaching risky spaces.
pmc-13410828:
Liang Sun and colleagues engineer in 2026 a battery that breathes carbon dioxide and stores energy at unusually high voltage. Lithium-carbon dioxide batteries promise to use a waste gas while powering devices, yet their standard reaction runs slowly and wastes voltage. A smarter catalyst can steer the reaction down a better path.

Their catalyst pairs a ruthenium-copper alloy with a nitrogen-doped support that grips it tightly. That grip reshaped the alloy's electron layout, verified by spectra and computer models. The new path forms a less stubborn product and cuts the key energy barrier sharply. Cells reached high discharge voltage with low waste, plus very large capacity in tests, which marks a design route for durable versions.
pmc-13411128:
Elena Fortin and co-authors check in 2026 whether a diabetes drug changes levels of copeptin, a stand-in marker for the water-balance hormone vasopressin, after a heart attack. The drug class protects hearts, possibly by shifting body fluids, yet long-term hormone effects were unknown. Data came from a blinded trial in patients with fresh blood sugar problems.

Forty-two patients took empagliflozin or a placebo for seven months, then stopped for three. Blood concentration, a fluid shift sign, differed between groups at seven months, while copeptin did not. Both measures drifted back after stopping, with no clear overall treatment pattern. Copeptin also showed no link to the drug's sugar-lowering effect, which weakens the hormone theory of its benefit.
pmc-13411328:
Anecita Fadol and colleagues describe a 2026 global training program for nurses who care for cancer patients with heart disease. As more people survive cancer, heart problems from the disease and its treatments have grown, yet nurses lacked a shared standard course for spotting and managing those risks.

The Cardio-Oncology Nursing Education program offers 27 online modules worth 18.25 contact hours, covering risk checks, drug side effects, survivorship, and team coordination. Nursing leaders can adopt it to give cancer nurses a common skill base, with hybrid and simulation training planned next for nurses worldwide.
pmc-13413828:
Marcello Marchetta and co-authors argue in 2026 that congestion in heart failure should be read as venous pressure hurting organs, not simply as extra fluid. Bedside exams and single scans often miss how pressure transmits into the liver, gut, and kidneys. Their review centres on VExUS, an ultrasound score combining the vena cava with Doppler traces from hepatic, portal, and kidney veins.

Observational studies tie abnormal VExUS patterns to invasive pressure readings and to kidney injury, poor diuretic response, readmission, and death in the literature surveyed. Repeated scoring may also track whether treatment is working over time. No randomized trial has yet tested care guided by the score, so the authors keep it as one voice inside a multimodal assessment that includes lung ultrasound, biomarkers, and clinical response.
pmc-13415428:
Sajawal Abbas Baloch and Aysha Zafar derive exact wave solutions for a nonlinear equation modeling blood vessel behavior, in 2026. The Murray equation here allows vessel wall properties to vary along the vessel. Using transformations and a bilinear approach, they generate many solution families.

Solutions include lump waves, lumps riding with one or two kinks, breathers, periodic waves, and rogue waves. Each pattern maps to a vessel story: lumps mimic local pressure pulses, while rogue waves mimic sudden extreme pressure spikes. Graphs in two and three dimensions show how parameters change wave height and travel. The authors claim this solution range is new for the equation.
pmc-13415528:
Wenqin Huang and co-authors introduce a chip based hollow waveguide whose walls are mostly open air, in 2026. Hollow cores let light interact strongly with gases and liquids, yet sealed walls block molecules from drifting in. Their scaffold design reaches eighty percent openness in the cladding while keeping light losses near those of closed guides.

Guidance mixes anti-resonant confinement with Bloch modes in a segmented membrane, printed in 3D at nanoscale precision. Tests confirmed the principle and loss behavior against a resonator based model. Open walls sped molecular diffusion into the core for sensing. Single photons also passed efficiently, suiting quantum photonics and fluid analysis on one chip.
pmc-13415628:
Toby Falodun, John Masterson, and Nazir I. Lone track how often critical care survivors move between hospital wards, in a 2026 Scottish cohort study. Records covered 12,836 patients admitted through emergency departments at three hospitals between 2017 and 2022, each with a critical care stay before discharge.

Age, illness burden, smoking, deprivation, and organ support level each tracked with how often patients moved. More moves meant higher odds of returning to the emergency department within seven days and a longer hospital stay. Readmission within thirty days and death within thirty days showed no such link. Frequent moves may flag complex patients who need closer early follow-up.
pmc-13416028:
P. Florio and colleagues map which city districts worldwide hold buildings least ready for their climate, in a 2026 global assessment. Building age and compactness stand in for energy efficiency, since old, poorly shaped buildings waste heating or cooling. Stock data and satellite observations were merged across the planet.

About 43 percent of buildings predate 1980, when efficiency rules barely existed, concentrated in temperate and cold cities of rich countries. Vulnerable zones currently house forty-eight million people. Under likely futures that population could grow ten to thirty percent by 2100, shifting toward the Sahel, Gulf states, and Pakistan. Light recent building in poorer countries raises their heat risk.
pmc-13416228:
Rúnarsdóttir and colleagues run a double blind trial in Iceland. It asks what a shellfish derived supplement, chitosan, adds to a lifestyle program for women with obesity. Chitosan is sold as a fat binder, but proof is thin. Their 2026 study randomizes thirty three women to three grams a day of chitosan or placebo for twelve weeks, inside a rehabilitation program. It tracks body makeup by DXA, strength, blood pressure, and gut microbes from stool.

The lifestyle program did the heavy lifting: grip strength, endurance, lean mass, and self rated health all rose, while body fat and blood pressure fell, in both arms. Chitosan's fingerprint was microbial, lowering the ratio between two bacteria groups without singling out any one species. Women with the highest body mass index lost microbe diversity regardless of arm. With thirty three participants, the authors frame the microbe shifts as leads for trials, not verdicts.
pmc-13417728:
The EFSA GMO Panel assesses a stacked modified soybean in a 2026 opinion for the European Food Safety Authority. The soybean joins two past events so plants can survive four herbicide types. Each event had passed past panel reviews with no safety concerns. New data on the single events raised no fresh issues.

Checks of the plant's make up, field traits, and food value found no new concerns from the stack. Tests for harm, allergy, and nutrition were also clear. The panel judges the soybean as safe as standard types for food and feed. No post market food checks are needed, and spilled seed raises no green concerns.
pmc-13418128:
Dukhyun Back, Kihye Han, and Hyang Baek sort South Korean hospital nurses into climate behaviour profiles, in a 2026 survey study. Nurses are the largest health workforce, and hospitals emit heavily, so their habits matter. Survey data from 861 nurses fed a latent profile analysis based on eight behaviour items covering daily mitigation actions.

Three profiles emerged: low engagement at about 9 percent, moderate at 45 percent, and high at 46 percent. Driving less separated low from moderate groups most. High engagers reported more extreme weather experience and stronger confidence, individually and collectively. Oddly, more climate information exposure linked to lower engagement, while short staffing blocked greener habits.
pmc-13418728:
Sarra K Mohamed Ahmed and colleagues describe an 87-year-old woman whose thyroid failure reached a life-threatening stage even though her blood tests looked only mildly off. She carried long-term hypothyroidism, adrenal failure, pituitary disease, and heart disease into the hospital with a urinary infection. Her body temperature, pulse, and blood pressure all fell, her awareness faded, and her gut slowed despite standard antibiotic care.

Her thyroid tests showed a mildly raised stimulating hormone with a near-normal thyroxine level, which could have misled the team. Slow-relaxing ankle reflexes on a repeat exam pointed the other way, and a standard scoring system gave strong support for the severe diagnosis. Care shifted to steroid and thyroid hormone drips, active warming, and close support, and she recovered well. The case warns clinicians to trust the full clinical picture over mild lab values.
pmc-13419128:
Min Joo Yoon and six colleagues compared two acid-suppressing drug classes for preventing stomach bleeding in patients on blood thinners. Potassium-competitive acid blockers are newer than proton pump inhibitors. Trials hinted they prevent ulcer recurrence better in aspirin users. Real-world evidence across varied antithrombotic regimens was thin. The twenty twenty-six retrospective cohort study used hospital Common Data Model records from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-four.

The cohort held 2,255 patients with arterial thrombotic disease on antithrombotic therapy. Fifty-three upper gastrointestinal bleeding events occurred during follow-up. Drug exposure was modeled as time-varying to avoid immortal-time bias. P-CAB use was associated with lower bleeding risk in the adjusted analysis. The study informs which protective drug to pair with long-term blood-thinning treatment.
pmc-13419228:
Elizabeth A. McHuron and colleagues build formulas for the daily energy cost of milk production in marine mammals, where direct measures are rare or missing. Energy budgets help scientists judge how disturbance, like noise or lost feeding time, may hit seal and whale populations. Milk feeding is one of the largest costs a mother pays, so getting it right matters for the whole budget.

The team derived links from the species where milk intake and energy density have been measured. Fully water-living whales may break the pattern set by seals, a caveat the authors flag for care. Checks against fresh estimates supported the formulas for seals, sea lions, and marine mustelids, with stated limits. Wildlife managers can now fill a key gap for species that have never been measured directly.
pmc-13420128:
Lloyd-Bradley and Hattersley reviewed records for 18 cats fitted with a subcutaneous ureteral bypass device, an implanted tube system that reroutes urine around a blocked ureter, between 2016 and 2022. Their referral-center study asked how often blood appears in the urine after this surgery, a finding whose importance for the cats was unclear.

All 18 cats developed microscopic blood in the urine after surgery, first detected at a median of one month and usually on the very first urine check. Fourteen cats, or 78 percent, had persistent findings, and severe blood levels appeared in 13 cats at some point. Visible bloody urine was rare, reported in only 2 of the 18 cats overall. In 11 cats the blood appeared without any positive urine culture, and the authors call for work on its cause and significance.
pmc-13420328:
Marion Caumeil and co-authors present a case showing how blood-based monitoring can expose drug resistance in lung cancer before scans do. Their 2026 report follows a woman aged 66 whose lung cancer carried the KRAS G12C mutation treated with adagrasib, a drug targeting that mutation, after chemotherapy and immunotherapy failed.

Tumour DNA in her blood fell sharply after seven weeks, showing an initial response, then rose at months four and six. Sequencing revealed three new KRAS mutations alongside the original one, a pattern called polyclonal resistance, where several resistant cell groups grow at once. Her scans stayed stable by standard criteria throughout this period. Significant clinical decline followed about eight weeks after the first DNA rise, and she died two months after the resistance mutations were found. The authors argue serial liquid biopsies can flag resistance early.
pmc-13421428:
Ulziijargal Bayarsaikhan and five colleagues record, in a 2026 paper, the moth tribe Artonini in Korea for the first time in organised form. These small day-flying moths belong to the burnet moth family, and the Korean fauna of this tribe had not been reviewed as a group.

Five species in two genera are documented. One, Amuria baei, is described as new to science. The paper illustrates adults and their genitalia — the structures taxonomists rely on to separate close species — for every recorded member of the tribe. It closes with a checklist of all zygaenid moths known from Korea, arranged under a 2024 classification. The work gives Korean entomology a reference point for this group.
pmc-13421528:
Michael Wendel and co-authors compared blood marks in diabetic and plain pregnancies in a 2026 study. A mother's diabetes brings swelling across the body and links to slow growth of the child's brain and skills. Marks in her blood and in the cord blood at birth may carry that story.

The team enrolled 98 pregnant women, some with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and some with none. In the last third of pregnancy they read two swelling marks and a brain growth factor in both mother and cord blood. Gaps between the groups may flag which babies need early developmental watch.
pmc-13422828:
Kwesiga and co-authors compare two ways of reaching depressed young people in Kampala, Uganda, in this 2026 qualitative study. One is tele-support psychotherapy delivered by phone with lay counselors. The other is standard in-person mental health services. Interviews and focus groups with youth aged 15 to 30 and with counselors were analyzed against an implementation science framework.

The backdrop is stark engagement data from the parent trial, where 61.69 percent of youth assigned to phone therapy actually engaged, against just 10.27 percent for in-person services in the figures reported. Phone delivery won on cost, travel, and flexible scheduling, and counselors' rapport skills helped, but unreliable mobile connectivity undermined it. In-person care suffered from high costs and low public awareness. Social support and higher income eased participation in both arms, and the authors call for fixing connectivity and literacy gaps.
pmc-13422928:
Cascio and a large team collect stories rather than scores in this 2026 Italian narrative medicine project, named DIAMOND, spanning 19 centers. Patients with chronic pain, epilepsy, serious Gram-positive infections, or depression wrote illness stories. So did the people who cared for them. Treating doctors kept matching charts, recording the same visits from their side.

The project took in stories from 64 patients and 56 family carers, plus 40 charts from 20 doctors. Pain came up in the stories as an embodied weight. It was shown through metaphors of darkness and distortion. Fear and shock at diagnosis sometimes grew into acceptance. Family carers spoke of heavy burdens and frequent helplessness. Doctors' charts ran more technical and forward-looking, showing a perceptual gap about what illness means. Most people found the writing itself helpful. The authors argue such story methods surface unmet needs that checklists miss.
pmc-13423828:
Sarah Brunner heads a 36-author mouse study showing that gut microbes actively limit how much dietary fat the intestine absorbs. Using isotope-labelled fats in germ-free and colonised mice, the team modelled whole-body lipid handling. Colonised animals kept far more fat in the gut. Their intestinal contents held up to twelve times more lipid than those of germ-free mice.

Protein and lipid profiling traced the chain: microbes trigger a host signalling pathway that lifts production of the bile salt taurocholate. That salt switches on a fat-splitting enzyme in bile, which destroys phosphatidylcholine, a molecule needed to package fat for uptake. Richer microbial communities meant less of that packaging lipid, and so less absorption.
pmc-13424028:
Tkachenko and colleagues mapped in 2026 how the sheep lung develops, cell by cell, in health and in cystic fibrosis. Sheep lungs resemble human lungs, and sheep let researchers study late pregnancy stages that cannot be studied in people. The team read gene activity in single cells from upper and lower lung at three points from mid pregnancy to birth. They studied normal sheep and sheep engineered to lack a working CFTR gene.

Tkachenko traced changes in cell identity and counts that show how support, vessel, and lining cells mature over time. Sheep without CFTR, the gene whose loss causes cystic fibrosis, already showed distinct cell signatures in the lung before birth. Those early signatures may help explain features of the disease seen soon after birth in babies. The atlas gives a baseline for judging lung development and early disease shifts.
pmc-13424128:
Weijia Fu and six colleagues use genetics to find genes whose activity in the prostate predicts how long men survive prostate cancer. Linking inherited predictors of gene expression with survival data from a Swedish cohort, then checking a large American trial cohort, they scanned across tissues: healthy prostate, primary tumours, and metastatic tumours.

Seven genes at one spot on chromosome 1 passed both discovery and validation. Higher activity of RCC1 tracked with faster return of a blood marker signalling relapse, while higher PHACTR4 appeared in tumours of worse grade. The authors note the work covers European ancestry only and shows association, not cause, so wider populations and lab tests must follow.
pmc-13424428:
Reid Weisberg and seven colleagues teach a large language model to pull a standard arthritis activity score out of free-text clinic notes, where such scores usually hide. The Clinical Disease Activity Index guides rheumatoid arthritis care, and the team worked in a warehouse holding records for over 4.5 million patients at a New York academic centre.

Among 2,756 patients with arthritis notes, the index or its parts could be extracted for a minority, 15.4% of the antibody-positive group showing documented remission or low activity among them. Documentation ran richer for patients with many notes and for faculty authors. Against expert chart review the automated extraction scored 0.97 on precision, recall, and combined measure, a first for this zero-shot approach.
pmc-13424728:
Aisling McCarthy leads an eleven-author analysis of gender differences in low blood sugar among people with type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, from the ten-week Hypo-METRICS study. Nearly six hundred participants took part: 321 with type 2 diabetes and 274 with type 1. All wore blinded glucose sensors and logged symptoms in real time through a dedicated phone app.

Time spent in low glucose did not differ between women and men in either group. Experience told another story: women reported more symptomatic episodes per week than men, even though the sensors saw equal exposure. Autonomic symptoms such as hunger and shaking and brain-fog symptoms such as confusion were catalogued separately. The authors stress that counting sensor lows alone understates the lived burden for women.
pmc-13425528:
Shanshan Liu, Lu Liu, and Jian Dong evaluated blood biomarkers for early heart injury in severe community-acquired pneumonia in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Heart injury in such patients is often missed, and troponin readings can be muddied by kidney problems and critical illness. The team tested admission interleukin-8 and soluble ST2, alone and combined, in 146 patients.

Injury was defined by high-sensitivity troponin I above the assay cutoff, and receiver operating curve analysis with cross-validation judged how well each marker flagged cases. Kidney-function-stratified troponin thresholds were also explored, offering readers candidate tools for earlier risk sorting in severe pneumonia.
pmc-13425828: Shaosen Zhang and coauthors issued a correction concerning their protocol for growing organoids from normal and cancer-prone human esophageal tissue. During manuscript preparation, a duplicated portion of the high-grade lesion image was mistakenly placed over the low-grade image in the floating organoids row of Figure 1D. The notice supplies the corrected panel and states that the error does not change the conclusions of the figure or the protocol, with an apology for any inconvenience. The notice is a correction only and carries no new experimental content.
pmc-13426028:
Katherine Brittain and colleagues used DNA evidence to test whether the tiny freshwater crocodiles of rocky uplands in northern Australia form a separate species. These pygmy crocodiles mature earlier and reach only about half the adult size of downstream crocodiles.

The team read two stretches of DNA passed down from mothers, plus thousands of markers from across the genome. Pygmy and normal crocodiles shared the same DNA types, and grouping followed place more than body size. No clear genetic line split the pygmy form off as its own species, though each upland group still differed somewhat. Brittain argues the pygmy crocodiles still merit strong protection as distinct, isolated populations facing invaders and climate change.
pmc-13426228:
Tom N. Durrant and coauthors define a feedback loop between Rac and PI3K-beta in platelet activation in a 2026 study. The collagen receptor GPVI triggers platelet responses partly through PI3K-beta, an enzyme unusual among its class because small GTPases such as Rac can switch it on. Knockin mice carrying two mutations in the Rho-binding domain of the enzyme's catalytic subunit showed impaired GPVI signaling, function, and spreading on fibrinogen.

A selective PI3K-beta inhibitor reproduced most defects, and blocking Rac or Cdc42 in normal platelets copied the knockin pattern. The loop helps explain how platelets build stable clots under high shear flow.
pmc-13426428:
Ward Vleeshouwers and colleagues show that the time of day when the immune system first meets a germ shapes the memory cells it keeps. Memory CD8 T cells are the long-lived defenders that respond fast when a virus returns.

Vaccination during the active phase of the day produced more early-stage memory cells and stronger protection against later virus challenge. The effect ran through dendritic cells, the messenger cells that present germs to T cells and steer their fate. Those cells carry their own body clocks, which timed how much of a helper signal called CD70 they showed. Vleeshouwers suggests timing vaccines to the body clock could sharpen lasting immunity.
pmc-13427428:
Jacob B. O'Brien and colleagues measured return to sport after reverse shoulder replacement in an active Australian cohort in a 2026 retrospective single-surgeon study. Reverse arthroplasty is increasingly offered to younger, active patients with shoulder arthritis or rotator cuff arthropathy, yet sport outcomes were rarely reported. The series covered 152 physically active patients operated between January 2020 and January 2024 with one implant system.

Twelve-month outcomes captured return rate, timing, performance level, pain, and satisfaction with function, with regression hunting predictors of success. Patients weighing this operation gain realistic timelines for resuming sport. One skilled pair of hands did each case, which keeps skill gaps from cloud the tale, though it may not match less deft hands in small towns.
pmc-13427628:
Bingya Zhang and Yihang Gao review, in 2026, cancer drug carriers modeled on exosomes, the tiny parcels cells naturally use to pass material between them. Standard cancer drugs spread through the whole body, causing harm while often reaching tumors poorly. Exosomes slip past many body barriers and are well tolerated, which makes them attractive delivery vehicles. The review covers natural exosomes, altered ones, hybrids, and lab-made mimics.

These carriers can haul chemotherapy drugs, gene material, and immune treatments, and some combine therapy with imaging. Production remains the hard part: yields are low, loads vary, and quality is hard to standardize. Safety testing and approval rules also lag behind the science. Readers weighing this field get both the promise and the manufacturing reality in one place.
pmc-13427928:
Tibben and colleagues published a 2026 report setting standard labels for a drug-processing gene. The gene, NAT2, helps the body break down certain drugs and chemicals. Gene variants make people fast or slow processors, with real dosing effects. An expert panel from a global pharmacogenetics group reviewed the evidence allele by allele.

The panel assigned plain clinical labels to 59 known variants of the gene. Two variants earned the increased-function label, the fast-processing kind. Forty variants were classed as decreased function, the slow-processing kind. Ten stayed uncertain and seven unknown for lack of solid evidence. Shared labels should help labs and doctors read test results the same way. The labels feed genotype-to-phenotype tables that clinics use every day.
pmc-13428428:
Zhang and colleagues asked whether body composition predicts sleep disturbance in American adults, using the ratio of skeletal muscle mass to visceral fat as a combined marker of sarcopenic obesity. Their analysis drew on 1,564 participants from the national NHANES survey with complete body composition, sleep, and covariate data.

Sleep disturbance was reported by 15.22 percent of participants in the weighted national sample analyzed. After full adjustment, each unit increase in the muscle-to-fat ratio came with 91.1 percent lower odds of sleep disturbance in the model. The highest ratio quartile showed 57.4 percent lower risk than the lowest, with a clear linear dose-response pattern across quartiles. Inflammation and accelerated biological aging partly explained the link, mediating 10.64 percent through one composite index, 36.43 percent through another, and 15.99 percent through phenotypic age acceleration.
pmc-13428728:
Oliver M. Schleicher and co-authors study how often high-grade cervical cell changes disappear without treatment in young women. Their 2026 retrospective study follows women aged 30 or younger who were managed by observation at a certified dysplasia unit in Erlangen between 2014 and 2025.

The cohort held 45 patients with the more severe CIN3 changes and 38 with CIN2 changes. Regression occurred in 46.7 percent of the CIN3 group and 63.2 percent of the CIN2 group, most of it within the first year of follow-up. Regression was linked to clearance of human papillomavirus in both groups, and no patient progressed to invasive cancer. The authors suggest virus clearance, HPV16 status, and vaccination history could help select patients for watchful management.
pmc-13429128:
Alicia C. Espinosa-Moreno and co-authors check, in a 2026 Mexican study, whether deliberately flipping the correction axis of a toric lens harms vision quality. Toric lenses implanted at cataract surgery cancel astigmatism, and surgeons sometimes aim for slight overcorrection that flips the remaining error to the opposite axis. Eighty eyes were sorted into flipped and non-flipped groups after uneventful surgery. Wavefront analysis measured fine distortions of incoming light, beyond the basic prescription.

Vision and refraction matched between groups on every standard measure. Most fine distortions also matched, with one exception: a distortion pattern called trefoil measured higher in the flipped group. Adjusted analysis confirmed the flip itself tracked with that single distortion. No other outcome moved with it. Patients can be told that a planned flip costs nothing in ordinary vision terms, based on these results.
pmc-13429228:
Daniel A. DeUgarte and colleagues drop the hospital opioid sliding scale, where pain scores of 4 to 6 earned a low dose and scores of 7 to 10 earned a higher one. They hypothesised that a single threshold plus electronic record nudges would lift best practice and stewardship.

Focus groups with stakeholders shaped an order set favouring non-opioids, with opioids only from a pain score of 5 to 10. Records for inpatients staying up to 30 days were compared before and after, with a closer look at people who had an operation. Average morphine-equivalent doses were the headline measure, giving hospitals a tested redesign for safer pain orders.
pmc-13430528:
Gerardo Arreola Jardón and colleagues made thin films of zinc telluride mixed with copper and oxygen, aiming at better parts for solar cells. They used a spraying method called radio-frequency sputtering, firing material from a single mixed target onto heated surfaces.

Copper and oxygen levels ran from 3 to 13 percent of atoms, and films grew at two heat settings. Tests showed all films held two crystal forms of zinc telluride, and richer mixes grew a second, copper-rich phase. That phase cut infrared light passing through the films and made them conduct far better, with resistance dropping by about ten thousand times. Arreola Jardón links these traits to back-contact layers, the metal-facing parts of cadmium telluride solar cells.
pmc-13430828:
Carlo Fiore and colleagues tracked the nerve fiber layer at the back of the eye after four types of glaucoma surgery. Glaucoma means a group of eye diseases that slowly kill the nerve cells carrying vision to the brain.

The team reviewed 462 eyes treated with four different operations or drainage devices, following scans for two years. Eye pressure and the number of pressure-lowering drugs fell in every group, and eyesight stayed stable. Yet the nerve fiber layer kept thinning during the first year after surgery in all four groups. No clear further thinning showed in the second year, so Fiore advises watching this layer closely after any glaucoma operation.
pmc-13431028:
Disantis and colleagues set the score changes that count as success for young people with acetabular dysplasia, a shallow hip socket, who choose physiotherapy over surgery. Scores alone mean little without a bar for what patients feel. Their 2026 study follows 45 patients aged 10 to 35 at two centers through eight to ten weeks of therapy. It uses a twelve item hip questionnaire plus anchor questions on satisfaction and function.

Just over half the patients landed in the improved group. The smallest change patients can feel, the minimal clinically important difference, came out at eight and a half points. A change of about fifteen points marked the state patients call acceptable, and a score of 62 separated satisfied from unsatisfied patients with good accuracy. A maximal outcome improvement bar, near a quarter above baseline, was also set. Clinicians can now judge therapy against what patients themselves call enough.
pmc-13431228:
Finna E Indriany and a large team piloted a phone-based home watch system for heart failure patients in Indonesia in 2026, mixing build work with a small trial of effects. Home self-checks aim to cut fresh hospital stays and lift daily life for such patients. Sixty patients joined, split evenly between the new system and standard care.

Fresh stays struck a fifth of the watch group and well over two fifths of the standard group, a gap the small trial could not confirm with firm proof. Scores on a heart health survey rose more in the watch group across most areas, from body limits to daily quality. Deaths ran lower in the watch group as well. The authors call the setup workable and ask for larger trials to settle its worth.
pmc-13431428:
Zijin Zhou, Yanxin Li, and Jun Lu published a 2026 letter that picks apart a trial of a pain drug placed beside a thigh nerve for relief after knee replacement surgery. The trial pitted a standard numbing drug alone against the same drug plus the added agent in sixty patients. It found one lower pain score and less rescue pain drug use in the first day for the added-agent group.

That gap matters, since the lone time point with a group gap is the one in doubt. The letter also faults loose repeat testing with no set main time point. A fuller model of pain over time would give a sounder read, the writers argue.
pmc-13433128:
Kowal and colleagues check for chemical tags on mitochondrial DNA in dog mammary tumors in this preliminary 2026 study. Mammary tumors are among the most common cancers in female dogs, and epigenetic change has been studied mainly in the cell nucleus. The team measured methylation in the mitochondrial control region. Methylation is a gene-regulating tag, and the region governs DNA copying. Tumor and normal tissue came from six German Shepherd dogs.

Two of the three sequence contexts examined, called CpG and CHH, varied more between tumor and normal tissue than the third, CHG, which stayed comparatively stable throughout. Differences in the two variable contexts moved together with a strong correlation in this small sample, suggesting coordinated change in tumors. The authors stress the group of six dogs is too small for conclusions and frame the work as a first indication worth testing at scale.
pmc-13433428:
Rafael A Guillén-Marmolejos and co-authors piloted a heart tracing upgrade in 2026 that blends vector reads with AI, set against scans as the gold test for clogged heart arteries. Plain resting tracings miss most hidden flow cuts, a sore gap where scan access runs thin. The blind pilot enrolled 104 adults with suspected disease at one center.

Scans found plaque in twenty-nine patients across three grades. The new tracing caught all but one case, a catch rate near total, while the plain tracing caught two. Grade by grade, the new tool hit full marks at the low and high ends. The authors pitch it as a sorting gate before scans or specialist trips, with larger multi-center trials still owed.
pmc-13434128:
Jessica J King and coauthors present a 2026 method for mapping where cells sit inside lab grown balls of cells and how those cells respond to drugs. DNA tags mark each cell by its place in the ball. The team builds the balls layer by layer and then reads gene activity cell by cell.

Tests with HeLa cell balls show that cells in one place do not all react to a drug in the same way. The authors link the uneven response to how far a drug can spread, plus gaps in food, energy use, and cell stress. Readers gain a clear route to richer drug screens that keep place and gene activity together.
pmc-13434228:
Ortega-Ramos and co-authors published a study in 2026 on a restless volcano in southern Italy. The Campi Flegrei caldera is one of the world's most dangerous volcanic systems. Where its magma sits, and how deep, shapes the risk to nearby cities.

The team used quake waves that bounce off inner layers to build the first full three-dimensional image down to fifty kilometers. Two slow zones stood out as likely magma stores. A shallow one, ten kilometers down, looks like a local transfer pocket. A deeper, thicker one runs from sixteen to thirty-three kilometers and may hold up to thirty percent melt. The picture matches rock studies and sharpens hazard models for the caldera.
pmc-13434928:
Critén and colleagues followed Swedish older adults for twenty-three years in 2026 to test whether serious gum disease at the start predicted death from any cause. Gum disease has been tied to heart disease and diabetes, but long-run evidence on death risk is thinner. The study drew on a national aging project in Karlskrona. Dental and X-ray exams covered 340 people who entered in their early sixties, back in 2001 to 2003, and were followed from there.

About one in six participants had moderate-to-severe gum disease at baseline, and just over half of that group died during follow-up. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, and other factors, the gum disease group carried about a one-and-a-half-fold higher risk of death. The authors note the link sits at the edge of statistical certainty.
pmc-13435428:
Sungmin Woo's team, writing for the ACR VI-RADS steering committee in 2026, set out what comes next for bladder MRI reporting. VI-RADS scores MRI for muscle invasion in bladder cancer, and many studies back its accuracy, yet gaps remain in performance and daily use. The paper lists seven open areas rather than new trial data, giving radiologists a shared agenda for the system.

Topics run from contrast versus no-contrast scans and numeric measures of invasion, through tricky anatomy and image quality, to response scoring after chemotherapy, wider training, and artificial intelligence. Readers get a concise update on where bladder MRI standards are headed and what proof is still needed. It suits radiologists and urologists who use the score in care.
pmc-13436428:
Rafael M Batista and coauthors test whether telling people the cost of holding savings beside card debt changes behavior in 2026. Banking records over thirty eight months show co holding in twenty three percent of card users. A field trial then messaged 125,328 customers through their bank app.

Messages spelled out the waste and offered one tap transfers to pay debt. Repayment amounts did not move in any real way. Customers did repay more often and paid above minimums more. Habit and mental buckets, not ignorance, seem to hold the pattern. Banks may need stronger tools than clear information.
pmc-13437428:
Ke Ren and co-authors used computer modeling to ask whether half a dose of a leading heart failure drug does nearly as much good as the full dose for Chinese patients. Guidelines push sacubitril/valsartan to a top dose, yet many patients stall lower over side effects. Their 2026 study built a body-based simulator of how the drug moves and acts, checked it against real patient data, and extended it to kidney and heart failure groups.

The simulator matched real drug levels closely, with nearly nine in ten predictions landing near measured values. When the team linked those levels to a heart strain marker, raising the dose from half to full added little extra benefit. The same step deepened blood pressure drops and the tolerance worries that come with them. They offer the model as early support for holding at the lower dose.
pmc-13437528:
Katarzyna Lisowicz and colleagues measured work stress among nurses and hunted for the factors that push it up. Nursing joins heavy responsibility with close contact with suffering, and long strain harms both staff health and patient care. Their 2026 survey covered 588 nurses in three hospitals, using a standard work appraisal questionnaire plus the team's own questions.

Stress ran high across the group. It peaked in nurses working overtime and in those caring for many patients at once. Intensive care units recorded the highest levels, while primary care posts recorded the lowest. In the combined model, older age and being female raised stress, while longer service lowered it; education, shift system, and overtime each played a part. The authors read stress as a many-sided problem in which workplace design weighs at least as much as personal traits. Cutting ratios and overtime, they argue, is the most direct lever.
pmc-13438128:
Mahalingam and colleagues study how alcohol distorts the hunger hormone ghrelin in this 2026 cell study. Ghrelin, made in the stomach, normally rises during fasting, but chronic drinking raises it further, fueling craving and worsening liver disease. The cellular mechanism was unknown, so the team exposed ghrelin-producing stomach and pancreatic cell lines to alcohol for 48 hours and measured hormone production and energy metabolism.

Alcohol increased ghrelin secretion and switched on the genes for ghrelin and for the enzyme that activates it. Normally, high glucose suppresses ghrelin release, but alcohol pretreatment blunted that brake, so cells behaved as if starving amid plenty. Alcohol also raised glucose uptake while cutting the cells' sugar-burning capacity. It profoundly reduced three rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes. The authors propose that combination as a therapeutic target.
pmc-13439028:
Alfina Nur Isyrofi and colleagues offer a 2026 review that compares three food fibres and their effects on metabolism. The fibres are oat beta-glucan, rice bran, and flour made from unripe bananas. Each works in a distinct way, through thickness in the gut, plant compounds that affect fats, or starch that feeds gut microbes. Past trials mostly tested one fibre at a time, often with few people and short follow-up.

Following the PRISMA 2020 rules for reviews, the authors gather human studies on blood sugar, blood fats, and blood pressure. They weigh dose, food form, and how each fibre acts in the body. Readers get a side-by-side account meant to guide food choices for people at risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of weight, sugar, and pressure problems.
pmc-13439128:
Douglas A Corley and colleagues study a large integrated care model in the United States and its links to death rates and lifespan, in work published in 2026. The model joins many proven population health steps across diseases in one system. Few data showed what happens when such steps run together at scale. The team compared members with several other groups, including national figures and people with like insurance and health profiles.

Nearly four million people were followed in the analysis. Adjusted death rates ran lower for nine of ten leading causes, counting cancer, heart disease, stroke, injury, and lung disease. Members lived notably longer than the national average in 2023, with the largest gains in the 50 to 72 age range. Gaps between demographic groups also ran smaller than in the comparison groups.
pmc-13439228:
Yingxiu Wang, Sizhe Xu, Jingzhu Guo, and Timothy Noel Stephens survey sleep among hospital staff in Haikou, China, just after the COVID pandemic, in a 2026 study. Poor sleep harms health workers and patient safety alike, yet post-pandemic drivers were unclear. In April 2023 the team invited clinical staff at one large hospital to answer a 33-item survey. Replies came from 525 staff and covered sleep quality, anxiety, and low mood with standard short scales.

Over half the staff scored in the poor sleep range. Nurses slept worse than doctors and other clinical staff, while staff with more schooling slept better. Night shifts, anxiety, and low mood each linked to worse sleep on their own. The authors urge hospitals to spot staff at risk early and to test ways of guarding sleep in shift-based care.
pmc-13439528:
David M Whalley and co-authors unveil a fast, single route to glutarimide building blocks prized in protein-degrader drugs, reporting in 2026. Glutarimides anchor medicines that hijack cereblon, a cell protein that tags other proteins for disposal. Drugs from thalidomide kin to newer degraders rely on the motif, yet older syntheses took many steps and slowed testing of new variants. Their platform starts from common nitrogen ring compounds and runs three steps in sequence.

A phosphine-catalysed bond formation, a metal-free radical addition, and an acid-driven ring closing deliver varied glutarimides with high selectivity. The route tolerates many chemical groups and scales from grams to rapid parallel batches. With it, the team built cereblon binder libraries, control analogues, and late-stage tweaks of active molecules. The authors pitch the platform as a way to speed degrader discovery.
pmc-13439928: Bouillon and colleagues published a correction in 2026. It amends their paper on genes and fruit traits in cider apples, in the journal G3. The note is a correction, and it fixes two short parts of the methods. One part now states the cut-off used to call a gene link real. The other part now gives the right first line on how mean fruit traits were worked out by year.
pmc-13441228:
Yang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of acute aortic dissection that unfolded without the sudden severe pain the condition is famous for. The condition is a tear in the wall of the body's main artery. The patient was a 55-year-old woman brought in with weakness, agitation, and breathlessness. A painless start is uncommon and dangerous, because teams may look elsewhere while the tear spreads.

A first bedside ultrasound looked reassuring, but the woman stayed agitated and developed belly tenderness. A repeat ultrasound then showed signs of dissection, and a CT scan confirmed a tear in the rising aorta, the most lethal type. Despite intense resuscitation, her condition collapsed quickly and she could not be saved. The authors urge repeat scanning whenever symptoms shift in ways that do not fit the first picture.
pmc-13441328:
Lucas Cruz and colleagues survey how music is chosen and used inside psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy trials, publishing a 2026 systematic review. Music shapes psychedelic sessions in clinic and recreational settings alike, and may sway outcomes. Searches across five databases under standard review rules found thirty-six articles, of which twenty-five described music use. Most work targeted depression and post-traumatic stress, using psilocybin or MDMA as the drug partner.

Playlist building varied widely between studies, from fixed canonical lists to personalised sets, with little shared protocol. Differences in disorder and substance explained part of the spread, though reporting habits explained plenty more. Few papers described who chose tracks, when music changed across a session, or how volume and genre were set. pmc-13442528:
Addison Kitrel and colleagues probe how loneliness ties to low mood in older adults with cancer in a 2026 study. The group held 258 people aged 70 years or more who had joined a talk-therapy trial for distress. Each person rated social isolation, mood, worry, views on aging, and a sense of lost meaning at the trial start.

Isolation scores rose hand in hand with low mood scores on two mood scales, with strong links in the raw checks. Full models that weighed age, sex, and other traits still tied isolation to low mood on its own. Worry and lost meaning also held solo links to low mood. The authors argue that loneliness is not just a shadow of other woes in this group. Clinics that screen for isolation may catch a treatable driver of distress in older cancer care.
pmc-13442928:
Snake venom reshapes the blood protein profile of mice within hours, and antivenom only partly steers it back, in a 2026 study by Bianca de Barros and co-authors. The team used mass spectrometry to track proteins and protein fragments in mouse plasma. Samples came at three, six, and twenty four hours after venom, with and without treatment.

Clotting and defense proteins fell while damage markers rose. At first the response looked the same with or without antivenom. By one day the treated mice had shifted toward recovery while the untreated stayed inflamed. Thousands of protein fragments pointed to wide breakdown of key blood proteins.
pmc-13443628:
Neerajan Nepal and colleagues present a 2026 simulation study of detection limits for gold nanoparticles inside small-animal-sized objects imaged by benchtop X-ray fluorescence tomography. The Monte Carlo model mirrors the team's cone-beam system, upgraded with a larger pixelated detector covering a 3 centimeter phantom holding three test wells.

pmc-13444128:
Leon French and colleagues test whether two giant mouse brain atlases name the same cell crowds in a 2026 study. Each atlas sorted more than 4 million cells into more than 5,000 clusters, one from whole cells and one from nuclei. Neighbor votes across full gene profiles checked which clusters match both ways.

A total of 2,009 cluster pairs matched in return, with shared map spots and gene tunes, also seen in other species' sets. Cerebellum clusters matched best, since that zone holds less cell variety. pmc-13445828:
Izzeddin Swidan and colleagues survey a 2026 study of parental knowledge about congenital heart disease across the West Bank, where timely recognition of warning signs can save infants. Warning-sign knowledge scored a median 6 out of 10 and risk-factor knowledge 6 out of 9, with most parents intending appropriate emergency action for blue skin. Gaps persisted, notably the false belief that heart murmurs always signal disease. Better warning-sign knowledge tracked correct emergency responses, pointing to targeted parent education.
pmc-13447428:

Two patients were treated with the gentler approach.

pmc-13447628:

pmc-13448028:
Sulagna Mukherjee and four co-authors show how a ginseng compound wakes bone-building cells through a growth path in the cell. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, tests it in thin-bone disease.

The team also tried it in mice whose thin bones came from loss of the egg glands.
pmc-13448428:
Starzer and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract CLTR-08, early results from a prospective observational registry of metastatic breast cancer patients with leptomeningeal disease. Half the cohort was treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan, a modern antibody-drug conjugate, including nine patients whose tumors counted as HER2-low. Median time on that drug was six months; eight patients had stopped for progression and two for toxicity, while four remained on treatment. Spinal fluid sampling proved workable: of seven patients successfully tested, six carried targetable genomic alterations.
pmc-13448928:

They conclude that carving substeps into the flat face offers a practical route to better films for advanced devices.
pmc-13449928:

pmc-13450028:

pmc-13450228:

For each platform it summarizes structure, delivery mechanism, uses, and barriers to clinical translation. A unified structure-function-application frame helps readers compare options. The piece serves as a map for choosing and improving carriers that must reach the right cells without viral risks.
pmc-13450528:
Pham Quang Trung and colleagues tested a blood mutation as a prognosis marker for hepatitis B-related liver cancer in 2026. pmc-13451428: The journal Bioscience Reports issued an Expression of Concern in 2026 about a paper by Liang and colleagues. That paper claimed a small RNA protects the lungs in acute respiratory distress syndrome. It was said to act by targeting p65. The journal cites peer-review concerns and duplicated images. Panels closely matched images in a 2020 paper by Wei. The authors supplied raw data, but the originally submitted images were absent. Western blot scans carried a labelling discrepancy. The article stays published, with this permanent notice attached.
pmc-13452128:

Yet the same snip can act in opposed ways, lab reads vary, and no trial has yet tested them in care. The authors call for shared lab rules and hard proof before clinics adopt the snips.
pmc-13452228:

pmc-13453028:

pmc-13453528:
Lucas S Santana and fourteen co-authors search for inherited gene changes in people whose high blood pressure stems from both adrenal glands making too much aldosterone. Carriers needed more pressure drugs and showed more gland changes on scans, yet had low potassium less often. All the changes remain of uncertain weight, the authors note, so more proof is needed.
pmc-13454228:

pmc-13454328:

The authors say support programs should target family habits, not just the patient.
pmc-13454828:

A chart combining the three beat each factor alone at sorting risk in the training group. The check group supported the chart's value. The authors offer the tool for earlier, sharper treatment planning, while noting the small single-hospital sample behind it.
pmc-13455128:
Yinfeng Hu and others built a wound-care grade score set in 2026, on Donabedian's structure-process-outcome frame. The set joins many traits across structure, process, and outcome, to back standard, proof-based nurse care. Hospitals gain a clinic-ready frame to watch and lift wound-care grade.
pmc-13455628:
Zhang and colleagues improve an imaging method for monitoring a cancer therapy called electroporation in this 2026 study. Electroporation uses electric pulses to open cell membranes, and electroacoustic tomography images the treated zone from sound waves the pulses generate. In clinics only a single viewing angle is practical, which badly distorts the reconstructed image. The team built a two-stage deep learning model, EXPP-Net, to repair it.

The first stage predicts the missing views from one measured view, and the second polishes the rough reconstruction into a full-view-quality image. Trained on water-tank experiments with rotating electrodes, the model rebuilt images that closely matched full-view scans, reaching structural similarity scores of about 0.997 with the linear probe setup tested. Tests with a second probe type and in a living mouse also showed strong distortion correction.
pmc-13457328:
Alessio Giordano and colleagues compare stents with emergency surgery for blocked left colon cancer in a 2026 Italian cohort study. A blocked left colon often forces emergency surgery with high stoma rates, while a metal stent can reopen the bowel and turn the operation into a planned one. The CROSCO-1 study followed 216 adults with obstructive, non-metastatic left colon cancer from June 2023 to October 2024. A total of 144 received emergency surgery, and 72 received a stent as a bridge to surgery.

Stent failure hit 8.3 percent, and major harm and death at 30 and 90 days were similar, yet the one-year stoma rate fell from 73.4 percent after emergency surgery to 44.4 percent after stenting. Stented patients also had fewer 30-day readmissions and started chemotherapy sooner, with comparable cancer outcomes at one year and better quality of life. Experienced centres gain support for a tailored stent-first path in selected patients.
pmc-13457728:
Anna Sikora and Anna Detman-Ignatowska weigh an unequal contest inside anaerobic digestion, the process that turns organic waste into gas. Methane forms at the chain's end and already powers a mature biogas industry. Hydrogen appears earlier, during acid formation, and capturing it in a two-stage system promises more total energy from the same feedstock, at least on paper.

Their 2026 review explains why practice lags theory. Dark fermentation is boxed in by the microbes' own metabolism: rival pathways divert intermediates, yields stay low no matter the tuning, and acetogenic routes reliably hand substrates onward to methane makers. Work on simple sugars such as glucose clarifies the competing reactions, though real waste streams behave messier. The authors map the biological ceilings on hydrogen output, the engineering constraints keeping it at research stage, and where recovery might fit inside integrated systems producing several products from one digestion line.
pmc-13457928:
Christopher Nichols and Daniel Albershardt describe a gentler machine for moving fat around the body. Vacuum suction, the usual harvest method, swings in pressure and batters fragile fat cells, which can kill the cells a graft depends on. Their 2026 report lays out a closed-circuit system driven by a reversible peristaltic pump, refined over five years and more than 160 aesthetic and reconstructive procedures.

Because the pump rolls fluid through tubing in either direction, the same loop aspirates fat and reinjects it without the tissue ever being handled or meeting air. The surgeons report continuous flow, minimal air entrainment, and rare clogging across face, breast, and body cases, with volumes tuned to each site. Precise pressure control should mean more consistent graft quality, less tissue trauma, and less surgeon fatigue. The authors are clear this is a feasibility description: controlled comparisons of cell survival and outcomes still need doing.
pmc-13458528:
Jeremy Cheng and Jeremy Grummet comment on the PRESERVE trial of focal therapy for prostate cancer, published in the January 2026 issue of European Urology. The approach zaps the main tumor with irreversible electroporation (the NanoKnife system), watching the rest of the gland. The trial treated 121 men with intermediate-risk grade group 2 or 3 cancer across 17 centers, biopsying them at twelve months.

The endpoint, a cancer-free biopsy inside the treated field, was met by 71 percent, rising to 84 percent under a looser definition forgiving low-grade finds. Cheng and Grummet spotlight what the trial underplayed. Significant cancer anywhere in the gland appeared in 26 percent of men at one year. They judge that failure rate too high for focal therapy to win acceptance, especially since it can only grow with time. Re-treatment was rare. They close by weighing selection and imaging factors that might push early failure to an acceptable level.
pmc-13458828:
Sanjay Konakondla and colleagues give thoracic endoscopic spine surgery its missing anatomical map. Lumbar endoscopy navigates by Kambin's triangle, a safe posterolateral window, but the thoracic spine breaks its assumptions: narrower openings, the cord in harm's way, angled pedicles, and ribs crowding the corridor.
