Their 2026 framework paper defines the Konakondla-Telfeian-Shen (KTS) Thoracic Pyramid, a six-faced corridor for reaching disease at the canal's front.

Each face of the pyramid is a named structure: the exiting nerve root, the lower pedicle, the facet's articular process, the disc complex, the cord, and the rib head joint. The corridor shrinks from T12 to T1 while the rib head climbs toward the disc plane and pedicle angles steepen, so the limiting face changes by level. The authors layer in variations from degeneration, prior fusion, and vascular anatomy, aiming to standardize planning language, shorten the learning curve, and enable comparative studies.
pmc-13458928:
Juri Iwata, Masanori Yamamoto, and a large OCEAN-TAVI investigator group examined in 2026 how patients on hemodialysis fare after transcatheter aortic valve replacement with current devices. Dialysis patients are known to do poorly after this valve procedure, yet results with the newest devices have been unclear. The registry supplied 760 dialysis patients and 3,928 patients not on dialysis.

Before matching, one-year death rates were far higher in the dialysis group. Once 490 pairs were matched on baseline traits, mortality was nearly identical between groups, and stroke and heart failure readmission also matched. Dialysis itself still predicted death in the unmatched analysis, pointing to the heavy burden of other illnesses these patients carry.
pmc-13459328:
Laetitia Lengelé and co-authors explore links between ultra-processed food and drink intake, gut microbes, and inflammation, in a study from 2026. Such foods have been tied to body-wide inflammation and metabolic problems. The team followed 20 adult volunteers over three visits.

At each visit, the volunteers recalled a full day of eating on three days, gave stool samples, and had breath and saliva tests. High intake did not change the overall diversity of gut microbes, but some groups rose and others fell. Sweet drinks linked to lower breath hydrogen and higher levels of one inflammation signal in saliva. Total intake linked to higher levels of another signal. The authors stress that these are associations from a small exploratory study.
pmc-13460228:
Fanghao Liu and colleagues tested in 2026 a simple trick to prevent collapsed lung during needle localization of lung nodules before surgery. Injecting numbing fluid just outside the chest lining and inserting the needle on the gravity-dependent side, where lung tissue rests against the chest wall, formed the combined strategy. Their Kunming study covered 166 patients localized and operated on between June and November 2024, split into four groups by which elements they received.

Collapsed lung struck half the patients receiving neither element, yet only one of thirty-three patients receiving both. Each element independently cut the odds sharply in adjusted models. Patients given the fluid also reported far less pain, with over half feeling none at all. The authors recommend the paired technique for routine localization work.
pmc-13461428:
Ebru Güzel Kuyucu and Nurettin Göksu Çini surveyed in 2026 four hundred four football fans in three Turkish cities. They asked about collective narcissism among supporters, the inflated belief that one's own fan group is superior, and its link to dysfunctional behavior. Face-to-face surveys during the 2025-2026 season also measured how fans rated the stadium atmosphere. They captured schadenfreude, the pleasure taken in a rival's misfortune, with local versus distant fans accounted for.

Collective narcissism predicted worse behavior directly. A richer perceived stadium atmosphere weakened that link, acting as a brake, while that pleasure strengthened it, acting as an accelerant. Distant fans behaved better than locals overall. The model explained a little over a third of the spread, and the authors suggest clubs work on atmosphere quality and rivalry culture rather than only policing individuals.
pmc-13461728:
Lim and colleagues measured a 2026 study of quality of life in Russian children with inflammatory bowel disease at a Moscow university clinic. The disease, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, burdens daily life beyond gut symptoms alone. Biologic drugs have improved control, but their link to children's lived experience was poorly defined.

One hundred and five children aged eight to seventeen took part, fifty-nine with Crohn's disease and forty-six with ulcerative colitis. Lim used three questionnaires covering disease specific quality of life, general quality of life, and family functioning. No significant differences appeared between biologic treated and conventionally treated children on any total score. Scores also matched between the two disease types, though emotional functioning scored lowest and social functioning highest across groups.
pmc-13461928:
Camilla Heldbjerg Drabe and co-authors describe a Danish family in which a brand new variant of the immune gene STAT3 causes hyper-IgE syndrome. The disorder brings recurrent staph abscesses and eczema, with strikingly different severity across five generations. The variant swaps one amino acid at position 417 and appears in no population database. In their 2026 study, lab tests on patient cells resolved conflicting computer predictions. The altered protein still bound DNA normally, but its response to the IL-6 signal was reduced, a partial rather than total loss of function.

Patient immune cells also failed to suppress an inflammatory molecule properly under IL-10, matching the partial defect. Clinically, relatives carrying the variant shared the syndrome's skin infections, eczema, and facial features, yet extra features like retained baby teeth varied markedly between them. Subtle partial defects, invisible to simple dominance tests, can still cause the full syndrome, the authors show.
pmc-13462328:
Zhi-Hui Zha and colleagues solved near-atomic structures in 2026 for a plant transporter that moves fats and hormones into small cell compartments called peroxisomes. The transporter, named CTS, comes from thale cress, a small lab plant, and faults in it stunt growth. Its cargo list spans fatty fuel molecules, a plant hormone, and a weedkiller-like compound.

Lab tests showed CTS carries a broad mix of fatty cargoes plus the hormone precursor IBA and the weedkiller 2,4-DB. Five frozen-electron-microscope structures caught the transporter empty, fuelled with energy, and bound to three cargoes, each folded in a U shape. Mutating key grip points broke transport, which maps how fat burning, hormone control, and weedkiller action link, with hints for crop and herbicide work.
pmc-13462428:
Tian Lin and colleagues build and test, in a 2026 lab study, a two-target antibody for neuroblastoma, the most common solid tumor outside the skull in children. Standard antibody treatment aims at a surface marker, GD2, yet some tumors escape by losing that marker or resisting treatment. Their antibody, G/R-001, grabs GD2 and a second marker, ROR1. Cells carrying either marker could be attacked, widening the net.

The antibody was produced in human cells and checked for structure. Binding tests showed strong attachment to both targets on real cancer cells. In killing tests it destroyed target cells more effectively than either single-target antibody. Cells carrying both markers died most, with killing above eighty percent at the top dose. The authors suggest the dual design may also rally natural killer immune cells. All results come from lab dishes, a first step before animal and patient studies.
pmc-13462728:
Abir Aldhalimi and co-authors argue, in a 2026 viewpoint article, that United States rules for artificial intelligence in mental health care are splintering by state and need a federal floor. Mental health needs keep rising, among young people, while provider shortages leave many without care. Chatbots and AI tools rushed into that gap after 2022. With no federal framework, states have begun writing their own laws. The team read the texts of four states: Illinois, Utah, New York, and Nevada.

 One regulates how AI is used in clinical settings, while the other regulates the technology itself, and some states blend both. Each leaves holes: protections vary by state, and developers, clinicians, and sellers face uncertain duties. Since mental health AI spans clinic and consumer use, neither approach alone covers the risks. The authors call for a federal baseline, sorted by risk, that keeps protections even nationwide.
pmc-13462928:
Anne-Sophie M C Marques leads a 2026 chemical biology study building tools to destroy a protein called NUDT5 inside cells. The tools help reveal how it shapes response to the leukemia drug 6-thioguanine. The drug needs activation inside the cell, and a sister protein trimming its active forms was known. Genome-wide knockout screens flagged NUDT5 as a key mediator of the drug's toxicity. The team built degrader molecules that drag NUDT5 to the cell's disposal system.

The degraders were checked for binding, three-part complex formation, speed of protein loss, and effects across the protein set. Removing the NUDT5 protein changed drug response in a way blocking its enzyme action would not predict, pointing to a scaffolding role beyond chemistry. The authors say the split between enzyme action and protein presence matters for combining this drug class in patients.
pmc-13463628:
Oisakede and colleagues mapped in 2026 what helps and what blocks near-infrared photoimmunotherapy. The treatment pairs an antibody carrying a light-sensitive dye with laser-like light. It kills tumor cells precisely where the light falls. Their scoping review followed standard mapping guidelines across five databases. It focused on the only version in clinical use, an epidermal growth factor receptor targeted drug approved first in Japan.

The 28 eligible studies showed the treatment kills cancer cells only where light reaches. Success concentrated in recurrent head and neck cancers. Doctors can reach those tumors with endoscopes and imaging guidance. Repeat sessions caused no accumulating harm. The main barriers were physical, since light penetrates tissue poorly. Deep or widespread tumors therefore stay out of reach. The method also needs specialized equipment and trained teams. Most side effects stayed local and manageable, though rare serious complications appeared in case reports.
pmc-13463928:
Lomangino and colleagues tested in 2026 whether image features from PET/CT scans can predict hidden lymph node spread in early-stage lung cancer. Patients staged as node-negative sometimes prove to have cancer in nodes after surgery, a surprise called nodal upstaging that changes treatment. All patients were scanned and treated at one institution with identical protocols.

The team extracted first- and second-level texture features from the scans and trained a machine learning model to flag patients with occult node disease. Using one center kept scan settings uniform, removing a common source of noise in such studies. The authors argue that a homogeneous, if small, dataset is the right way to find a reliable signal. Once refined, such a model could personalize the diagnostic path and the surgical plan for each patient.
pmc-13464328:
Alper Özkök and four colleagues published this 2026 postmortem case-control study of men who died of ischemic heart disease. They asked what the hearts look like when sildenafil, the erectile dysfunction drug, is found in the body. Erectile dysfunction and cardiovascular disease share roots, but the cardiac profile of users was unknown. Among 154 men, 77 sildenafil-positive cases faced age-matched controls on autopsy and toxicology findings.

Acute findings did not differ: neither coronary clots nor heart-muscle ischemia were more common in the positive group. Chronic damage was heavier: coronary disease, heart failure, bypass surgery, heavier hearts and coronary calcification all ran higher among sildenafil-positive men. After adjusting for other cardiovascular factors, only coronary calcification stayed linked, with about 2.6-fold odds. The authors read calcification as a marker of the vascular disease behind erectile dysfunction and heart disease, and counsel cardiovascular risk checks for users.
pmc-13465128:
Mu and colleagues tested in 2026 whether tannin from Caragana korshinskii, a shrub used as forage in northern China, protects sheep stomach lining cells from bacterial toxin injury. The rumen lining absorbs nutrients and shields the body, but a toxin called lipopolysaccharide can inflame and damage it in intensively fed animals.

Cells pretreated with the tannin before toxin exposure showed less injury across several measures. Inflammatory responses were weaker, oxidative damage was lower, and fewer cells died by apoptosis, a controlled cell death process. The protection tracked with reduced activity of a signaling chain that starts at the TLR4 receptor and drives inflammation. The authors conclude the tannin eased toxin injury under their lab conditions, a result that could inform feed additive research for sheep.
pmc-13466228:
Nava and colleagues reviewed in 2026 which implant choice works better after skin-reducing mastectomy, a surgery for women with large or sagging breasts that allows single-stage implant reconstruction. Placing the implant in front of the chest muscle avoids muscle dissection but needs healthy skin flaps. Placing it behind the muscle gives reliable coverage at the cost of pain and animation deformity, where the breast moves with the muscle.

Under PRISMA guidelines, they pooled twenty-six studies with 863 patients and 1,106 reconstructions, 432 prepectoral and 674 retropectoral. The pooled complication rate was similar, at twenty percent for prepectoral and twenty-five percent for retropectoral placement, and no single complication, from implant loss to skin necrosis, differed significantly. Patient-reported BREAST-Q scores favored prepectoral placement across satisfaction and wellbeing domains, though not by a clear margin. The authors suggest prepectoral placement may be preferred when flaps allow.
pmc-13466528:
Kuroda and co-authors asked in 2026 whether Japanese towns keeping senior prevention programs running through COVID-19 saw slower growth in care needs. Japan's long-term care insurance certifies need through a standard national process, and towns run local programs in five areas, from exercise to nutrition. The study linked a 2021 town survey to certification rates from 2018 to 2023. Of 1,741 towns invited, 1,114 entered the main analysis.

Full delivery was rare. Only about 16 percent of towns fully ran their exercise programs as planned for 2020, and about 14 percent did so for brain training. Towns fully delivering exercise programs saw certification rates rise more slowly during the pandemic years. The gap was about a tenth of a percentage point against towns that fell short. Brain training showed a similar protective gap. Other areas showed no clear pattern. The authors read this as evidence that keeping community prevention alive in a crisis pays off.
pmc-13466628:
Alessandro Conforti and colleagues follow knee arthritis patients starting the weight-loss drug semaglutide, tracking far more than body weight, in a 2026 real-world study. Ninety-three adults in routine rheumatology care began the drug, and eighty-eight finished six months of follow-up. Pain, daily function scores, body measures, inflammation markers, blood sugar, and fats were all recorded.

Each patient served as their own comparison, with no untreated group alongside. The authors therefore call every link they find non-causal, a caution stated up front. Modeling weighed weight lost against the highest dose reached, and a clustering step grouped patients into response patterns that paired joint relief with metabolic change in different mixes.
pmc-13466728:
Jia-Feng Duan, Tian Li, Qiu-Juan Zhang, and Jia-Hui Lu report a woman treated at once for an aggressive breast cancer and a hormone-secreting pituitary tumor, in a 2026 case report. The fifty-six-year-old had lived with a prolactinoma for five years, its hormone output held normal by medicine, when a painless breast lump present for two years proved to be invasive HER2-positive cancer.

Imaging had flagged only a tiny spiked nodule, and biopsy confirmed cancer that had already reached an armpit node. Given the node's involvement, the tumor's closeness to the nipple, and her refusal of breast-conserving surgery, she chose full mastectomy. No guideline covers pairing dual HER2 therapy with ongoing pituitary treatment, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13466928:
Bin Zhang, Zhen Yang, and Xiquan Zhang report pulling two long-abandoned vein filters out through blood vessels even though parts of them pierced into the duodenum, in a 2026 case report. Filters in the inferior vena cava stop clots traveling to the lungs, but devices left past their removal window cause rising harm. These two had sat for nine and eight years.

Both patients came with upper belly pain, and a scope showed filter parts poking into the bowel. Open surgery has been the usual answer given bleeding and bowel injury risks. The team's new vessel-based technique succeeded in both extreme cases, and they detail the steps and cautions for others facing the same trap.
pmc-13467128:
Pavelescu, Curici, and Călin critically review methods for detecting two reactive oxygen molecules in living mammalian systems in this 2026 paper. Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide act as useful signals at low levels but damage tissue when they build up. A widely used dye, DCFH-DA, has long been the default probe, yet it reacts with many substances and can mislead.

Covering work from 2015 to 2026, the authors compare five measurement platforms, from spin-trapping spectroscopy and fluorescent probes to genetically encoded sensors inside cells. Boronate-based probes have largely replaced the old dye for hydrogen peroxide imaging, the review finds. No single method wins on every measure. Selectivity, sensitivity, and resolution all matter. So the authors insist claims should rest on at least two complementary approaches, rather than one probe alone.
pmc-13467428:
Ruiying Wang and co-authors review in 2026 how China handles aluminum dross, the hazardous residue left when aluminum is melted and refined. Dross holds harmful substances such as aluminum nitride, fluorides, and chlorides, yet it also contains recoverable metal and alumina. The review pulls together the sources, makeup, and risks of the waste, then compares treatment options.

Cleanup methods aim to strip out nitrogen, fluorine, and chlorine compounds, using either water-based or heat-based routes. First-round dross can give back metallic aluminum, while the leaner second-round residue can feed refractory bricks, building materials, water-treatment agents, or alumina recovery. The authors weigh the strengths and limits of each route, framing dross as both an environmental liability and a resource stream worth mining.
pmc-13467628:
Haonan Qiu and co-authors develop in 2026 a lipid nanoparticle that carries imperatorin, a plant coumarin with antioxidant and anti-aging promise that dissolves poorly in water and is badly absorbed when swallowed. The carriers were built from grape seed oil and a food-grade fat, then squeezed through a high-pressure homogenizer. The finished particles were uniform spheres about 187 nanometers wide.

The carriers held nearly all of their cargo, with encapsulation efficiency of 99.54 percent in the reported tests. They stayed stable in simulated stomach fluid and released about 90.56 percent of the drug over 48 hours in simulated intestinal fluid. The team also built a two-cell gut model with a mucus layer to watch the particles cross, and checked safety and blood levels in animals. Their results indicate the carrier markedly improves how much imperatorin gets through.
pmc-13467928:
Shi and colleagues test how the dose of a single cycling session affects thinking skills in children with autism spectrum disorder, in 2026 exercise science research. Executive function covers mental control skills such as stopping impulses and holding information in mind. Thirty children completed a sedentary control session plus four cycling sessions: low or moderate intensity, lasting 20 or 40 minutes, with intensity tracked by heart rate. Computer tasks then measured impulse control and working memory.

Exercise condition changed reaction times and accuracy on the go/no-go impulse task, with the joint inhibitory-control score showing the strongest effect. Moderate-intensity sessions produced the clearest benefits, beating the sedentary condition in head-to-head comparisons. Working memory results were less consistent across the doses tested. Shi argues that brief moderate cycling could serve as a handy pre-activity primer for autistic children, while noting the dose details need work.
pmc-13468328:
Nurlan Almas and co-authors review in 2026 cadmium sulfide materials that kill bacteria with light, an approach gaining urgency as antibiotic resistance spreads through water and food chains. Cadmium sulfide absorbs visible light and generates reactive oxygen species that attack microbes; it can also release cadmium ions and physically disrupt membranes. The review maps how crystal form, particle shape from quantum dots to branched structures, and synthesis route set those behaviors.

A detailed tabulated analysis spans three material classes: plain cadmium sulfide, two-component composites, and three-part Z-scheme heterostructures that separate charges more cleverly. Computer calculations and molecular docking add mechanistic support. The authors also face the obvious challenges, including the toxicity of cadmium itself, and chart what must be solved before light-activated antibacterial coatings can be trusted in real water and food settings.
pmc-13468428:
Yaru Sun and co-authors test in 2026 a blast-resistant sandwich panel built around a self-adhesive stiffened polyimide foam between steel faces. Sandwich panels protect vehicles and structures from explosions, but their commonest failure is the face sheets peeling off the core. The self-adhesive foam was designed to grip the steel and resist that debonding. Blast experiments were paired with computer simulations of the dynamic response.

The foam itself proved thermally tough, keeping more than 36.2 percent of its mass at 800 degrees Celsius. Under blasts at the closer test distance, the new panel center displaced only 8.5 millimeters against 15.0 millimeters for a panel with plain polyimide foam, a 43.3 percent improvement. At the farther distance, displacement was 6.7 millimeters. The authors present the adhesive stiffened core as a practical upgrade for protective structures that cannot afford face-core separation.
pmc-13468928:
Andrea Hållstam, Charlotte Angelhoff, and Linda Gellerstedt report a qualitative study, published in 2026. It explores how people with chronic pain experience pain and sleep together. The authors interviewed patients in groups and individually. All had completed a pain rehabilitation programme in Sweden. It was an interdisciplinary programme. The accounts were analysed thematically.

Patients described a vicious circle. Pain and poor sleep fed each other. The two were hard to pull apart. Consequences were practical, emotional, and social. Daily life suffered in all three ways. Rehabilitation should pay more direct attention to sleep, the authors conclude. Sleep hygiene deserves focus. So does sleep ergonomics, the physical set-up for sleeping. This sits within a holistic approach to chronic pain.
pmc-13469228:
Roisin O’Donovan and a large Irish team umbrella-review in 2026 the research on human milk banking services, the systems that collect donated breast milk for infants whose mothers cannot supply it. An umbrella review synthesizes existing systematic reviews rather than single studies. Following recognized evidence synthesis guidance, the team searched seven databases plus grey literature for work published between 2000 and June 2025, screening with two independent reviewers.

Thirteen reviews were identified, covering milk banks in middle- and high-income countries and the donors, recipient families, and staff who keep them running. The authors note how little standardized information exists on governance, quality, and sustainability criteria, the very things a bank needs to supply milk consistently and equitably. Their synthesis will feed a co-designed evidence framework for setting up and scaling milk bank services, a resource new banks currently reinvent country by country.
pmc-13469428:
Hu and colleagues measured brain activity in this 2026 study to test whether natural sounds improve the emotional state of psychiatric healthcare workers, a group under heavy daily stress. Forty participants listened to birdsong, insect sounds, and rain sounds while electroencephalography, a scalp recording of brain waves, tracked emotional indicators before and after each exposure.

Birdsong lowered stress readings and raised relaxation scores among the workers. Insect sounds reduced directed attention, while rain sounds reduced engagement with the task at hand. At the same time, insect and rain sounds produced significantly higher scores on the study's engagement and interest indices than birdsong did. The authors conclude that short exposure to natural sounds can shift measured emotional states in a positive direction for this stressed workforce.
pmc-13469728:
Korkmaz examines how the chemotherapy drug methotrexate stresses ovarian cancer cells in this 2026 laboratory study. The drug mainly blocks the folate pathway, but it also creates oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen molecules, which pushes cells toward self-destruction. Working with OVCAR-3 cells, a standard ovarian cancer cell line, the author tested whether four antioxidant compounds could soften these effects.

After 24 hours, methotrexate lowered the cells' antioxidant capacity while raising oxidant levels and a marker of fat damage. Two protective proteins, Nrf2 and HO-1, also fell. Meanwhile, signals for the cell's built-in death program rose. Those included a higher Bax to Bcl-2 ratio and active caspase enzymes. Adding antioxidants partly restored balance and calmed the death signals, with resveratrol showing the strongest effect among the doses tested.
pmc-13469828:
Charlotte Spurway and colleagues report in 2026 a qualitative study of how brace and wheelchair users in Cambodia reach rehabilitation services. Access to such care is a recognized human right, yet shortages of staff and fragmented services limit it in many poorer countries. Seventeen current or former patients of a Phnom Penh rehabilitation center, aged eighteen to sixty five, described their experiences in translated interviews.

Three themes organize the accounts: early illness and care seeking, the routes taken to obtain a brace or wheelchair, and the effect of finally receiving one. Participants described long delays and uneven experiences with medical care and physiotherapy along the way. Even so, the devices proved central to daily life and independence. The authors use the accounts to show where service pathways break down.
pmc-13470328:
Matevž Rumpret and co-authors report in 2026 a strep protein that hides during lab growth yet becomes a target of protection during real infection. Vaccine hunters usually study surface proteins that bacteria show in culture flasks. The protein Slr sits in every strain of Streptococcus pyogenes, the cause of strep throat and invasive disease, but it does not appear on cells grown in broth.

Experiments showed a zinc sensing regulator keeps Slr switched off until zinc runs low, as happens inside a host. Antibodies against Slr protected mice in both passive transfer and vaccination tests against invasive infection. Human and mouse antibody responses to Slr matched those against the classic M protein. Oddly, the response focused on one repeated motif region, which the authors read as a possible escape trick.
pmc-13470728:
Yu Qiao and eight colleagues published this 2026 study of gas held in deep coal on the eastern edge of China's Ordos Basin. Deep coalbed methane is a cleaner fuel trapped in coal seams more than 2,000 metres down. The team studied how the gas sits in the coal, and how its carbon isotopes, slightly different forms of carbon, shift as gas escapes. They used both field desorption tests and computer models of coal molecules.

In the field tests, the ratio of free gas to adsorbed gas, gas stuck to coal surfaces, ranged from 0.94 to 2.22 during release. The methane isotope values were generally heavy and grew heavier across temperature stages. The simulations showed free gas sitting in large pores and cracks, while small pores held both free and adsorbed gas. They also showed the isotope forms moving at different speeds, which explains the shift seen in the field.
pmc-13471328:
Pipatkullachart and colleagues at a Thai medical center tested whether a home-grown hospital guideline could cut needless follow-up visits for newborns with jaundice, a yellowing of the skin caused by bilirubin buildup. Their 2026 before-and-after study compared care in the six months before the guideline with the six months after it. The study covered 274 babies born at 35 weeks or later who went home without light therapy.

Follow-up visits dropped sharply once the guideline took effect: 34.3% of babies in the later group needed a return visit, compared with 49.6% in the earlier group. Readmissions barely moved, affecting 3.6% of babies after the change versus 2.9% before it, a gap the authors judged not meaningful. The team concludes that adapting global guidance to local needs can trim wasted visits without early signs of harm.
pmc-13472928:
Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence for spotting osteoporosis in scans taken for other reasons. Bone thinning often goes undetected until a fracture, and the standard bone density test is hard to access. Opportunistic screening lets AI read routine images for bone health at no extra scan cost. The team followed standard review methods across three databases to February 2026.

Fifty-seven studies were included, most of them retrospective and from single centers. CT scans were the most used image source, with models judged mainly by discrimination scores for osteoporosis, low bone mass, and fracture risk. The review also mapped why results vary so much between studies. The pattern is promising but immature: before hospitals trust AI bone checks on every scan, the field needs shared standards and prospective, multi-center proof.
pmc-13473028:
Sutaşır and co-authors review what emergency physicians need to know when nuclear medicine scans and treatments go wrong, from tracer leaking out of the vein to allergic reactions. Their 2026 narrative review searched four databases for studies from 2020 to 2024 on acute events after radiopharmaceutical administration.

Leakage is commoner than charts suggest: systematic checks found partial or complete tracer extravasation in about 15% of PET/CT examinations, with center rates from 2.9% to over 20% depending on technique. One multicenter quality program cut detected extravasation from 13.3% to 2.9% over 25 weeks of process work. In a 1,002-patient cohort, 18.7% reported at least one adverse event, though only 43% of those were judged possibly drug-related.
pmc-13473228:
Anh Tran, Tytus Mak, and Meghan Burke Harris check how exact ion mobility readings are in 2026 protein work. Ion mobility adds a size-and-shape measure that helps name proteins in complex mixes. Small errors in that measure can weaken searches against stored reference data. The team studied how tuning choices and scan timing near a peak top shift the values.

A tuning mix made from lab-built peptides improved how steady the readings were. Readings tied to full scans and to fragment scans did not always agree, and the gap is spelled out in detail. Careful timing and shared tuning steps narrowed the spread. Protein labs gain clear steps for building cleaner reference sets that other groups can trust and reuse.
pmc-13473328:
Yuyang Wang and fellow authors trace how brain harm unfolds after a burst brain aneurysm in a 2026 review. Bleeding around the brain kills many people early and leaves others with lasting damage. Days later, a second wave of harm can strike when blood flow to brain areas falls. Past work blamed vessel spasm alone, but the full picture is wider.

The review links early events, such as pressure spikes and tiny clots, to later swelling, inflammation, and barrier leaks. Small vessels narrow, fine channels clog, and blood supply fails to meet demand across wide areas. That chain ends in delayed flow failure and tissue death. By joining the phases into one story, the review points to new spots where care might break the chain.
pmc-13473528:
Janine M. Schwarz and four colleagues tested in 2026 whether a common insecticide harms solitary bees at doses they might meet in fields. Bees face many pesticides at once, but sub-lethal effects on eating, foraging, and learning remain poorly understood. Sulfoxaflor is marketed as an alternative to neonicotinoids, yet its impact alone or with azoxystrobin on solitary bees was unknown. The team exposed red mason bees, Osmia bicornis, to field-realistic doses in the laboratory and on artificial flowers.

Sulfoxaflor cut sugar solution intake by an average of 23.8 percent and interacted antagonistically with azoxystrobin, meaning the pair did less than the sum of separate effects might suggest. Exposed bees also learned to tell rewarding from unrewarding flower colours less efficiently, while other foraging measures were unharmed. The authors read the eating and learning losses as pathways by which everyday exposure could lower bee fitness and harm solitary bee populations.
pmc-13473628:
Komal Attri and four colleagues developed in 2026 curcumin-stabilised silver nanoparticles aimed at Helicobacter pylori and stomach cancer cells. Chronic H. pylori infection drives lasting stomach inflammation and tumour growth by reshaping the local environment, yet treatments that hit both bacterial virulence and cancer cell survival at once are scarce. The particles, chemically made at 15 nanometres across, combine silver, valued for killing microbes, with curcumin, a plant compound that calms inflammation and fights tumours.

Against H. pylori the particles showed potent killing, at a half-maximal concentration of 3.86 micrograms per millilitre, and blocked urease, an enzyme the bacterium needs to settle in the stomach, by 80.46 percent at the highest tested dose. They also cut viability of human gastric cancer cells by 73.99 percent and showed broad effects against other strains. The authors present the formulation as a promising microbiome-directed treatment, while noting that laboratory results still need further animal testing.
pmc-13474828:
Peng and colleagues report clinical results in 2026 for a workflow that tests IVF embryos for single-gene diseases before transfer. The workflow rests on the Asian Screening Array, a chip reading hundreds of thousands of DNA markers. The goal is to stop parents who carry a harmful variant from passing it to a child. Their method combines family linkage analysis, which tracks which chromosome copy an embryo inherited, with direct checks of the exact mutation.

The team reviewed 377 families in preclinical work-up and 367 treatment cycles covering 1,677 embryos tested with the array-based workflow at their center. Marker density near target genes proved sufficient for linkage in most cases, and custom direct tests confirmed the array calls where they were used. After linkage and chromosome screening, 636 embryos were cleared as suitable for transfer, and long-read sequencing beat single-sperm typing for families lacking relatives' samples.
pmc-13475228:
Huthsteiner and colleagues tracked in 2026 how long hair samples can be stored before hormone measurements drift. Hair analysis reads stress hormones such as cortisol from a strand's length. The team collected hair from eighty-one healthy people and stored portions for up to twenty-four months, measuring hormones and related compounds at set points.

Hair cortisol and cortisone fell roughly linearly across the two years. Between twelve and twenty-four months they dropped by about six and nine percent respectively, though the cortisol drop was not significant. Cortisol's relative stability also weakened with longer storage, as stored values matched fresh ones less closely. The authors warn that storage duration is a methodological factor labs must report and control. Their two-year follow-up gives concrete decay figures for planning hair endocrine studies.
pmc-13477128:
Garry W Hamilton and co-authors test in 2026 whether using both radial arteries as grafts lengthens life after bypass surgery. A two-nation database held 59,608 patients from 2001 to 2020 who got at least two grafts. Groups split into no radial use, one radial graft, and two radial grafts. Weighting balanced starting traits, and deaths from any cause formed the outcome.

Both radial groups outlived the no-radial group over a median five years of follow-up. Two radial grafts beat one, with a further clear survival edge. Full arterial grafting rates rose steeply across the three groups. Skilled centers may offer both-arm grafting to suitable patients.
pmc-13477328:
Stephan Nienaber and colleagues published a 2026 report on medium-term results after catheter-based aortic valve replacement in patients born with a two-leaflet valve. The patients all had severe narrowing of that valve and were treated at University Hospital Cologne between 2018 and 2023. The study compares balloon-expandable valves with self-expanding valves placed through a catheter.

Ninety-two patients were followed for an average of about three years. Death from any cause reached about 26 percent, and stroke about 14 percent, with no clear difference between valve types. Technical success was high at about 97 percent, and serious leakage around the new valve was uncommon. Self-expanding valves left lower pressure gradients across the valve. The authors say overall event rates remain high enough to justify randomized trials.
pmc-13478328:
Cui and co-authors surveyed female students at Guangdong Medical University in mid-2024 about the HPV vaccine, which prevents cervical cancer, focusing on the gap between intending to vaccinate and actually doing it. Among 2,884 students who said they intended to get the vaccine, the team measured online health literacy and health beliefs, then checked who had received at least one dose. The survey ran from June 16 to July 16, 2024.

Only 41.3 percent of intenders had turned intention into a first dose, leaving a wide intention-behavior gap in this student group. Urban background, higher spending power, family income, and parental education each raised the odds of following through, with adjusted odds ratios between 1.10 and 1.24 in the model. Trust in formal information helped, at an adjusted ratio of 1.10, while perceived barriers cut conversion sharply, at 0.72, so the authors target costs and doubts.
pmc-13478528:
Ayan Mandal and coauthors published a 2026 study asking why the liver enzyme GGT rises in fatty liver disease combined with type 2 diabetes. The two conditions often coexist through insulin resistance, yet GGT gets less attention than other liver enzymes. The team combined a hospital cohort of 498 patients with validation in a United States survey dataset of 2,586 people.

Patients with both conditions had the highest GGT and insulin resistance scores. Genetic analyses using Mendelian randomization pointed to a causal push from genetically higher fasting insulin toward higher GGT, separate from other metabolic traits. Functional mapping of GGT-linked gene variants added biological context. The authors conclude that insulin resistance itself drives much of the enzyme elevation, which may sharpen how clinicians read this routine test.
pmc-13479928:
Xiaodong Chen and coauthors published a 2026 retrospective study of a CT imaging marker that may predict irregular heartbeat after bypass surgery. Postoperative atrial fibrillation is common after heart surgery and is tied to inflammation in the fat hugging the coronary arteries. The fat attenuation index measures that inflammation from scans patients already receive before surgery.

Patients who had off-pump bypass surgery with a recent coronary CT scan were included. Heart rhythm monitoring during the first week after surgery identified who developed the rhythm problem. Statistical models combined the fat marker with clinical factors significant in early screening. A reliable preoperative warning would let teams start preventive treatment only for patients who need it, rather than exposing everyone to extra drugs.
pmc-13480228:
Maryam Taheri and co-authors present a 2026 report on artery flaws in the chest wall vessel most surgeons favour for heart bypass grafts. Spontaneous tears in heart arteries often pair with body-wide artery weakness, yet the internal mammary artery is seldom checked. Two women with repeated heart artery tears showed flaws in that vessel.

One woman with a gene-based artery condition had neck pain and showed a tear in a neck artery plus a bulge with a suspected tear in the chest vessel. The second woman had widespread fibromuscular dysplasia, a beading artery condition, with beaded unevenness in the same chest vessel. Both were managed without surgery. The cases argue for scanning the graft vessel before bypass surgery in such patients, since a flawed conduit could fail or tear.
pmc-13480328:
Agarwal and co-authors re-analyzed the CONFIDENCE trial in 2026 to ask whether pairing two kidney drugs lowers blood pressure more than either alone in chronic kidney disease with type 2 diabetes. The 800 participants took finerenone, empagliflozin, or both, and the team split them by starting systolic pressure, the top blood pressure number. Two thirds, 532 people, began at or above 130 millimeters of mercury.

In that higher-pressure group the combination clearly beat each single drug, while below 130 it added nothing measurable to pressure control in this analysis. The odds of a strong pressure response were 83 percent higher on the pair than on finerenone alone, and starting pressure itself was the strongest predictor of response. Early pressure drops explained less than 10 percent of the pair's kidney benefit, measured by urine protein, and kidney injury and high potassium rates stayed similar across groups.
pmc-13483128:
Miyakoshi, Toyoda, Katayama, and Hayashi checked in twenty twenty-six if the growth rate of an eye web wing can tell how well sight heals after its cut-out. The wing is a film that grows over the clear front of the eye and warps its shape. Late surgery may leave that warp only part-fixed.

They tracked one hundred thirty-four eyes and read warp and fine flaws before and a month after surgery. Faster wing growth matched worse warp before surgery. Set rate cuts split eyes that healed to normal from those that did not. The team says the rate can help time surgery while full heal is still in reach.
pmc-13483528:
Xiaofeng Tan and co-authors use single-cell gene reads to trace scarring inside the testes of men with unexplained sperm absence, in a 2026 study. This condition, idiopathic non-obstructive azoospermia, is the harshest form of male infertility and mostly lacks a known cause. The team profiled testis tissue cell by cell against healthy controls, then confirmed patterns with tissue stains.

One cell type stood out: the muscle-like cells wrapping the sperm tubules were laying down the scar tissue. Signals from immune macrophages, built around a growth factor called PDGF, pushed those cells toward fibrosis. Scarred tissue also stirred nearby immune cells into an inflamed state. Computer drug matching flagged regorafenib, an existing cancer drug, as a candidate to block the scarring circuit. The work names both a mechanism and a possible treatment lead.
pmc-13483628:
Vidal-Folch and team used a large genetic screening dataset to clarify the hidden forms of a gene linked to spinal muscular atrophy, a severe muscle-wasting disease. Most carrier tests count copies of one gene section, but some carriers hold hybrid genes stitched from two similar genes, which simple counts misread. Their 2026 study analyzed screening results from 18,015 people and rechecked selected cases with a precise counting method.

The screen found 457 carriers, about 2.5 percent of everyone tested in the cohort. Roughly half the carriers had lost one gene section only, and the rechecks showed most of those actually held hybrid genes. The other half had lost both sections in one continuous deletion. Vidal-Folch concludes hybrids are more common than older studies suggested, which matters for interpreting carrier results.
pmc-13486628:
Gallo and a large Italian study group set out in 2026 to agree on one clear rule for reading nerve tests in two treatable nerve diseases. The diseases, known by the short names CIDP and MMN, weaken limbs when the immune system harms nerve insulation. A key test sign is conduction block, a sharp drop in signal strength along a nerve. Labs have long split on which drop counts.

The group re-read test waves from 106 patients with the first disease, 87 with the second, and 234 healthy controls. A drop of at least three tenths in signal height matched fancier area based rules and beat stricter cut points. For a second sign, spread of the signal in time, the length of the whole wave added real value next to the main peak gauge. The authors back one shared block rule for both diseases.
pmc-13487928:
Beate Oerbeck and colleagues report a 2026 national study of CLN3 Batten disease, a childhood brain disorder that causes vision loss and decline in thinking and movement. They assessed behavior, emotions, and quality of life in twenty affected people aged seven to twenty-nine, comparing them with their siblings and surveying parents.

Affected individuals scored in a borderline clinical range for behavior problems, while siblings scored in the normal range. Quality of life was sharply reduced for patients and parents, yet siblings remained in the normal range. Families also described strengths, such as determination and humor in affected children. The authors press for support aimed at the whole family.
pmc-13488228:
Pei Zhang and co-authors build a prediction chart for death within thirty days in drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection in a 2026 retrospective study. The bacterium resists carbapenems, a last-line antibiotic family, which makes its infections hard to treat. Records covered 290 patients at a public health center in Shandong between 2022 and 2025. Patients were split by survival at thirty days. Statistical models hunted for independent predictors to place on a nomogram, a visual scoring tool.

About twenty-one percent of patients died within the month. Septic shock raised risk sharply, while timely suitable antibiotics and healthier platelet counts protected in the reported models. A score for other illnesses added smaller risk. The chart separated outcomes well and matched observed results closely in internal checks.
pmc-13489728:
Toshiaki Inomo and Masahiro Aoyama report removing a slipped disc high in the neck through the vertebra itself, guided by live navigation. C2–C3 herniations are extremely rare, under 1 percent of neck disc cases, and standard routes there are risky or invasive.

The patient was an 80-year-old woman with worsening numbness and pain in her left arm plus unsteady walking. Scans showed the disc pressing on her spinal cord, and standard care had barely helped, so surgery followed. Through a 4-centimetre neck cut and a 6-millimetre bone window, the team removed the fragment with no complications. Her symptoms eased at once, Inomo reports, and she went home one week later.
pmc-13490028:
Rahim Mehdioghli, Alireza Chavshin, Fatemeh Bakhshipour, and Haleh Hanifian review parasites as a possible cancer treatment base in a 2026 mini-review of preclinical evidence. Parasites reshape host immunity in powerful ways, sometimes helping tumors and sometimes attacking them. The review covers malaria-type protozoa, Toxoplasma, Leishmania, and selected worms, plus products parasites release, tested mostly in mouse cancer models.

Reported antitumor actions include waking killer immune cells, rebalancing immune signals, blocking new blood vessels, and pushing cancer cells toward death. Other parasites instead drive cancer through long inflammation and tissue damage, which underlines the double edge. Safety worries, complex life cycles, and missing delivery standards block clinical use for now, the authors stress.
pmc-13491328:
Apoorva Sharma, Khansa Ahmad, and Shea E. Hogan discuss sex-based results for a dissolving leg scaffold in a 2026 commentary on the LIFE-BTK trial. The disease in focus is chronic limb-threatening ischemia, the severest stage of leg artery disease, where below-knee arteries are small, chalky, and prone to failure after balloon treatment. A drug-eluting resorbable scaffold props the vessel open briefly, delivers a growth-slowing drug, then dissolves, avoiding a permanent metal cage.

Earlier trial data at one and two years showed better vessel openness and less renarrowing than balloon treatment alone, with similar safety in the results the authors recap. Fair device evaluation demands checking groups who may respond differently, and sex is the lens applied here. The piece frames why parity in outcomes matters.
pmc-13492028:
Kubilay Çanga and co-authors measure fetal brain growth in diabetic pregnancies in this 2026 study. Gestational diabetes raises blood sugar during pregnancy. Whether it shapes the unborn baby's frontal lobe was unknown. The team scanned seventy-three diabetic and seventy-three healthy pregnancies at similar stages. They measured frontal width, head width, and a ventricle ratio.

Babies in the diabetic group were heavier, and frontal proportions ran slightly higher. The ventricle ratio, a check on fluid spaces, stayed the same. After adjusting for size and mother factors, only the proportion shifts held. Diet versus insulin care made no difference to the measures. The meaning for later development remains open.
pmc-13492428:
Ellie K Bruce, Alexander J Hutchinson, and Charles C Anderson follow in 2026 an adolescent boy whose two faulty copies of the TECRL gene produced a rare and dangerous rhythm disorder. The condition blends features of two known syndromes, stress-triggered ventricular rhythm chaos and prolonged electrical recovery, and often announces itself through sudden cardiac arrest. The boy's family history already included sudden death.

His tracing showed borderline QT prolongation, and he suffered ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest despite standard beta-blocker treatment. He also developed atrial fibrillation, unusual at his age. Adding the drug propafenone to the beta-blocker brought both his atrial and ventricular rhythm problems under control in long-term follow-up. The authors suggest the combination deserves consideration for other patients with TECRL-related disease, whose options are few.
pmc-13493828:
Coşkun Rodoplu leads a nine-author team testing in 2026 whether foam rolling beats simply resting after an explosive jump workout. Twenty-one active young men completed both recovery styles in a randomized crossover, so each man served as his own comparison. The workout was five sets of loaded and bodyweight squat jumps, with balance, jumping, and muscle electrical activity measured before, right after, and after recovery.

Foam rolling protected balance better than rest, both standing still and moving, and it preserved horizontal jump distance more effectively. Vertical jump height gained nothing extra from rolling. Muscle excitation mostly just recovered with time in both conditions, with rolling helping only a few muscles. The authors suggest rolling as a practical between-session tool while asking for studies in wider populations.
pmc-13493928:
Lamaakal and colleagues built a wearable activity recogniser that knows when it is unsure, designed to run on the tiny microcontrollers inside cheap fitness bands. Existing systems either trust a single confidence score that breaks when a sensor shifts position, or use heavy mathematics small chips cannot afford. Their 2026 framework encodes each burst of motion data as a very long binary pattern and reads three uncertainty signals from comparing it with stored prototypes.

A statistical layer turns those signals into a small set of possible activities with a coverage promise, plus a plain-language code explaining why doubt rose. Across four public datasets, including tests with rotated or missing sensor axes, the sets stayed tight on clean data, averaging barely above one activity. Detection of out-of-place data scored strongly. The system answered within a few milliseconds using only a few kilobytes of memory.
pmc-13494028:
Jin and colleagues combine several kinds of molecular data to understand laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, a throat cancer with stubbornly poor outcomes. Their 2026 analysis links two themes: m6A, a chemical tag placed on RNA that tunes how genes are used, and senescence, the state where cells stop dividing. Searching bulk and single-cell gene data, mutation records, and protein measures, the team found 93 genes tying the two themes together that also carried information about survival.

Those genes split patients into subtypes with different immune surroundings, survival prospects, and mutation loads. One candidate stood out: HMGA2, a protein that helps organise DNA, was produced at higher levels in tumour tissue, and patients with more of it fared worse. When the team dialled HMGA2 down in cancer cell lines, the cells grew, invaded, and migrated less. The authors nominate it as a drug target.
pmc-13494128:
Alba X Realpe leads a 2026 qualitative study on whether taking part in a large drug trial felt acceptable to autistic adults. The STRATA trial tests sertraline, a common antidepressant, for anxiety in autistic adults, a group often left out of such research. The team interviewed 64 autistic adults at varied stages of the trial and sorted their views using a standard framework for judging acceptability.

Most participants found the blinded trial low in burden, fair in design, and clear in purpose. Views shifted between what people expected before joining and what they felt once inside the trial, so acceptability proved fluid rather than fixed. People weighed gains, effort, and their own confidence in unlike ways. The authors say acceptability grows when autistic people help shape a trial from the start, when study materials stay easy to use, and when staff keep in close touch.
pmc-13494628:
MacKenzie R Peltier and co-authors respond, in a 2026 personal view, to new United States alcohol guidance issued in January 2026. For decades the dietary guidelines gave clear per-day caps, two drinks for men and one for women. The new guidance drops those caps and tells Americans only to consume less for better health, advice the authors call vague.

They stress that drinking stays a top cause of preventable disease and death, linked to about three million deaths a year worldwide. Women's drinking has risen of late, and women face sharper health risks from alcohol, so dropping sex-specific caps hits them hardest. The article sorts out conflicting reports on alcohol and health, sums up what is firmly known, and treats women as a group needing direct attention. It closes with steps to protect public health, restoring the clarity the new wording lost.
pmc-13495428:
Huan Liu and others present Coformer, a deep-learning model for guessing cotton traits across settings and years. In 2026, the hybrid Transformer-code net squeezes gene markers into a compact code, catching long-range links among variants without direct setting terms. Older gene models often overfit such data.

Tested on a merged multi-setting, multi-year data set, Coformer stayed robust across varying data sizes and found key gene loci behind target traits. A browser-based guessing system bundles data prep, training, and reading into one visual screen with batch runs and charts. Breeders, including non-experts, gain a handy bridge from gene work to picking.
pmc-13498928:
Helena Dujic and five colleagues published a scoping review in two thousand twenty-six on tooth decay in older adults. More people now keep their own teeth into old age, which means more surfaces at risk. Age brings dry mouth from medicines, weaker cleaning skills, and fading memory, all raising risk.

The reviewers mapped five hundred thirty-three studies from the past twenty-five years. Most counted decay or hunted its causes; the standard index dominated. Reported decay shares swung wildly between studies. Seventy-five risk variables appeared, led by age, sex, and schooling. Few studies used formal risk tools. Treatments were rarely covered with practical detail. Quality of life was measured in ninety-eight studies.
pmc-13499528:
Caroline Kikawa leads a large team reporting in 2026 a near real-time snapshot of human antibody defences against seasonal flu, gathered to guide vaccine strain selection. Flu viruses evolve constantly, and twice a year experts decide which strains the next vaccine should match. Using a library of flu surface proteins reflecting viruses circulating in late 2025 and early 2026, the team ran high-throughput neutralisation tests with 302 human blood samples collected in late 2025.

The dataset holds more than twenty-seven thousand individual measurements across both major flu A subtypes. Many samples neutralised two recently dominant virus subgroups poorly, one within each subtype, and certain added mutations in key surface regions weakened antibody action further. All data and visualisations were released publicly so vaccine committees and other researchers can use the measurements directly in strain decisions.
pmc-13499828:
Federico Rojo and colleagues report in 2026 a European verification study for blood tests that detect ESR1 gene mutations in metastatic breast cancer that feeds on hormones yet lacks the HER2 target. Such mutations drive resistance to hormone-blocking drugs, and guidelines favour liquid biopsy, meaning a blood draw searched for tumour DNA, when disease progresses. Six referral institutions checked two testing platforms against shared reference materials carrying clinically relevant mutations.

Both digital PCR, a method that counts single DNA molecules, and sequencing-based assays detected mutations at very low fractions of total DNA in the reported ranges, with blank limits low across laboratories. Sensitivity and specificity work centred on the two most tested mutation sites. Total DNA input needs differed by platform, and the authors present the shared benchmarks as support for validated in-house testing under European rules.
pmc-13500728:
锦强 李 and others review bladder instillation therapy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, which accounts for about three quarters of new bladder cancer cases. In 2026, the Chinese-language review covers treatment after transurethral resection, where recurrence remains high and post-operative drug therapy is crucial. Options now span immune therapy, aimed therapy, antibody-drug conjugates, and novel giving systems.

Checkpoint blockers help high-risk patients who do not respond to BCG, while the conjugate RC-48 shows action in selected groups and erdafitinib targets FGFR-mutated tumours. New giving systems include a mitomycin hydrogel approved in the United States and sustained-release gemcitabine and erdafitinib devices. The review aims to guide evidence-based, personalized choices and combination plans.
pmc-13501628:
Liang Kong leads a three-author team with a 2026 scoping review of oral health damage linked to olanzapine, a widely used antipsychotic drug. Following JBI scoping methods, the team searched four major databases from their start to the end of 2025 and kept 18 studies on olanzapine and mouth outcomes. Reported problems were frequent: dry mouth affected 30 to 60 percent of patients across studies, and moderate-to-severe gum disease affected 35.9 to 60 percent of those examined in the included reports.

Decay indices were high, with DMFT scores from 13.5 to 28.6, and tongue movement problems carried an odds ratio of 6.7. The authors propose a four-pathway model joining anticholinergic drying, metabolic disturbance, microbial imbalance, and brain-behaviour effects. Management today rests mostly on oral health education, and 70.6 percent of outcome measures were not standardized. A stepwise framework covering assessment, prevention, intervention, and teamwork is offered as a hypothesis for testing.
pmc-13501728:
Moski Morisho Nasibu leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of malaria parasite genetics in sick and healthy children in Kindu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The study enrolled 522 children aged six months to twelve years from health centres and schools. Dried blood spots supplied DNA for nested PCR typing of the parasite's msp2 gene, which reveals strain families and how many strains infect one child. Quantitative PCR estimated gene copy number.

Symptomatic children were younger, averaging 5.77 years against 7.25 years, and more often male. Parasite prevalence reached 69.8 percent in the symptomatic group. The FC27 strain family carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.50 for symptoms, and infections with multiple strains an even larger ratio of 24.58 on that measure. Copy number ran higher in sick children but dropped out as an independent predictor after adjustment. The authors conclude that strain diversity, not parasite amount, tracks illness.
pmc-13505028:
Yanhua Chen leads a team reviewing sarcopenic obesity in liver cirrhosis, a pairing of muscle loss with excess fat, in a 2026 paper. The pairing hides in plain sight, since fat can mask shrinking muscle on the scale. How it should be diagnosed and what it forecasts were unsettled.

The review sorts recent studies by how each defined muscle loss and obesity, then weighs outlook across seven outcome areas. The pairing clearly tracks with higher death rates and worse results after liver transplant. Links to classic cirrhosis complications look likely but rest on thin data. Heart events, quality of life, and adding the pairing to standard risk scores are barely studied. The authors frame it as a key, changeable risk that early lifestyle care may soften.
pmc-13505128:
Tetsuya Yumoto and a large team of Japanese researchers, working as the J-RESPECT study group, published this 2026 analysis of when families of brain-dead patients first hear about organ donation. Japanese guidance says the option should be raised after doctors judge a state matching brain death. The authors checked whether real practice at hospitals followed that order, and how much timing varied between sites.

The team reviewed 190 adult brain-dead donors at 16 institutions between 2010 and 2023. In 40 percent of cases the donation talk came after the brain-death judgement, and in 60 percent it came before. Age was the only factor linked to the order, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.03 for each added year of age. Median time from admission to the talk was five days in one group and two days in the other group. Hospital policy itself showed no link to the order used.
pmc-13505928:
Madalitso Chelenga and five co-authors set out a plan for a review of a parasite in animals in a 2026 protocol paper. The parasite harms breeding in cattle and causes lasting diarrhea in cats, while pigs often carry it without illness. Reports of new strains and drug resistance make its true spread unclear.

The planned review will search five major databases with no limits on language or country. Studies that report infection rates in cattle, cats, or pigs will be included. Two reviewers will screen papers, extract data, and judge bias risk on their own. A combined analysis will then estimate how common the parasite is in each host around the world.
pmc-13506128:
Ovais Mehboob and co-authors tracked thirty-two patients whose shinbone fractures near the knee were fixed with locking plates fitted to each fracture pattern. Enrolled over eight months in 2023, patients were scored five times, from before surgery to six months. Radiological scores judged how well the joint surface was restored, while clinical scores covered pain, walking, and stability.

By six months every patient had reached a good or excellent radiological grade, and imaging scores had climbed steeply. Functional recovery told a slower story: about forty-four percent reached a good or excellent clinical grade, and none of the thirteen with excellent X-rays earned an excellent functional grade. These score types showed no correlation at six months. The authors caution that function after such fractures often keeps improving for one to two years, so the gap should narrow, and larger multi-centre studies must confirm it.
pmc-13506328:
Timothy Johnston and a large team of co-authors dissect the fresh antibodies people make against new coronavirus variants, apart from the recalled ones. Their study appeared in 2026. Immune memory usually answers a drifted variant with antibodies aimed at the first strain met, a bias called imprinting. The team isolated hundreds of antibodies after staged variant exposures in people imprinted by the ancestral strain. The fresh, variant-specific antibodies used different gene pieces, sat closer to their germline form, and hit different spots on the spike.

Those fresh antibodies neutralized later variants strongly. Yet responses to the updated 2024-2025 booster were still dominated by the old cross-reactive set. The authors say vaccine design must find ways to grow the fresh response, which aims better at the future.
pmc-13507228:
Xiao-Chen Xie leads a 2026 team that traces autoimmune thyroiditis in mice to leaked mitochondrial DNA igniting an innate alarm pathway called cGAS-STING. Damaged mitochondria spill their DNA into the cell fluid, where sensors read it as danger. A cleanup process, mitophagy, removes failing mitochondria before leaks grow large.

The team found that mitochondrial stress activates a damage response chain ending in a tag on the adapter TAX1BP1, which recruits worn mitochondria into disposal sacs. When that chain breaks, DNA leaks and inflammation follows through the alarm pathway. A drug blocking STING slowed disease in mice. Shielding mitochondria or silencing the alarm offers two candidate treatment routes.
pmc-13507328:
Jun Zhao leads a 2026 team that boosts triboelectric nanogenerator output fourfold simply by running the device in with a solvent wash. These generators harvest motion energy from contact and separation of surfaces, but early wear debris chokes charge buildup. During break-in sliding with dimethyl sulfoxide present, debris and transferred material clear away instead of lingering.

Surface analysis and simulations show friction also snaps bonds in the polyimide film, freeing amide groups that migrate to the surface as molecular brushes. Their exposed oxygen-rich ends grab electrons eagerly from the partner layer. Charge density reached 2.5 millicoulombs per square meter without changing materials. Break-in protocol becomes a design lever for self-powered sensors.
pmc-13508128:
Anthony Vincent Razzano, a solo author, published a review in 2026 on health data tools in the United States. Low-income patients face more hardship with money, housing, and food. Health systems now try to spot those social risks with smart software.

The review covered studies from 2010 to early 2026 found in four databases. Of 209 papers screened, seventeen met the rules for the review. Most used patient records to build risk models or to mine notes for social facts. Only one study tested a real aid program, one that helped cancer patients with money strain. Few models were checked outside their home system. Some worked worse for poor or minority groups. Razzano calls for more checks on fairness and on real aid steps.
pmc-13508228:
Kalee Jack and five co-authors set out a protocol for studying how measurement-based care lasts in child and youth mental health clinics, in 2026 work. In this approach, clinicians routinely use patient-reported outcome forms to guide treatment choices. Starting the practice is hard enough, and keeping it going after outside help ends is poorly understood. The project covers eight public community clinics in one urban area. Clients are aged 11 to 17, and staff will also take part.

Surveys and health record data will first measure how well the practice held up at each site. Interviews will then probe what events, routines, and local conditions helped it survive. Two established frameworks will shape the reading of both data sets. The authors expect the case lessons to help other clinics plan for staying power from the start, rather than treating it as an afterthought.
pmc-13509328:
Qin Zhang and Firdaus Abdullah set out a 2026 model for how humanlike chatbots shape consumer choices. Their dual-pathway account holds that humanlike cues can pull people toward quick, feeling-based trust, or push them toward careful checking when cues clash with each other. Three experiments with 832 people in total tested the model by varying how humanlike the chatbot seemed and whether its cues stayed consistent.

Humanlike design raised trust through a sense of social closeness, while clashing cues triggered slower, more careful thought. People who judged their own thinking well used the chatbot help more wisely, and decision quality followed a curved pattern, rising then falling as the chatbot grew more humanlike. Personal goals also shifted which path dominated, which gives designers a clearer guide for balancing warmth and caution.
pmc-13510228:
Hamad Almutlaq reviews real-world use of upadacitinib for stubborn eczema at one Saudi hospital. The oral drug blocks a Janus kinase tied to immune overdrive. Middle East clinic data on it remain scarce. Records covered thirty patients treated between 2023 and 2025.

Twenty-eight had follow-up clear enough to judge response. Doctors logged improvement in twenty-seven of those patients. Most responses showed within four weeks of starting. Itch and sleep scores each fell from a median of eight to two. Five patients stopped the drug, two of them over safety or lab worries. Careful picking and close lab watch are the author's advice.
pmc-13511528:
Milda Butkienė and twelve co-authors compare two strength training styles for brain structure in older men, in a 2026 trial. Sixty-three men were assigned to blood-flow restriction training, heavy resistance training, or a control group for twelve weeks, and 48 finished brain and thigh imaging before and after. One style uses light loads with a cuff that limits blood flow, while the other uses heavy loads in the standard way.

Only the heavy training group showed a clear gain in cortical thickness, in a left parietal zone covering movement and body-sense areas. Further checks found changes scattered across other left-side regions in that group. The cuff group instead showed change in a white matter wiring measure within the parietal zone. Thigh muscle size was tracked alongside brain outcomes. The authors frame the work as exploratory, with each training style touching the aging brain in a different way.
pmc-13513028:
Recep Karasu, Mustafa Dinç, and Gökay Eken set patient-centered thresholds for judging success after trigger finger release. Their 2026 study covers a small procedure that frees a snapping finger tendon, with or without a steroid shot. Surgeons lacked agreed cut-offs for how much change patients actually feel.

The team studied two equal groups of patients, one with the shot and one without. They derived three kinds of thresholds for pain and two hand function scores: the smallest change that matters, a large benefit level, and a state patients find acceptable. One hand questionnaire showed the strongest tie to patient judgment. The thresholds let future trials report responder rates that mean something to patients, not just average score shifts.
pmc-13515028:
Meryem Altay, Hakan Aydın, and Adem Karşı investigate, in a 2026 engineering study, how powder choice and energy settings shape multi-layer laser cladding on ductile cast iron. Laser cladding rebuilds worn moulds by melting metal powder into the surface layer by layer,. The team deposited three commercial powders onto a cast iron grade used for moulds, comparing steady energy input against strategies that varied energy from layer to layer.

Powder composition proved decisive. Ferro 55 gave the lowest porosity, the most favourable hardness spread, and low residual stress, while Metco 41C produced heavy porosity, low hardness, severe crosswise cracking, and high tensile stress. Castolin 16604 landed in between, with deeper hard penetration and compressive stress. Tailoring energy by layer improved porosity and hardness for the two stronger powders, although starving the process of energy limited hardness depth.
pmc-13516328:
Rong-Jun Gong leads an eleven-author team reporting the first whole-genome look at a drug-resistant Providencia stuartii strain from cattle in China, in a 2026 study. The germ usually troubles hospitals, and its life in farm animals was poorly mapped. The strain came from a rectal swab of a diarrhoeic beef animal on a commercial farm in Anhui Province. Full sequencing read its genome, and lab tests profiled drug resistance and disease-causing potential.

The genome ran to about four point two million letters. The strain resisted eight antimicrobial agents and carried many resistance and virulence genes, plus mobile DNA islands and dormant viruses. In mice, heavy doses injected into the belly killed in a dose-dependent way and left lesions in organs. The authors are careful: that test does not prove the germ invaded cattle tissue or caused the diarrhoea.
pmc-13516728:
Rafael Toledo and six colleagues survey community pharmacists in Spain's Murcia region about medication mistakes made by family caregivers, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Older patients often rely on relatives to handle complex drug routines, and errors creep in. One hundred forty-eight pharmacy staff, mostly pharmacists, answered an online questionnaire about the errors they spot, their causes, and their prevention habits, split by urban, town, and rural workplaces.

Wrong timing of doses topped the list, reported by about sixty-two percent, followed by missed doses and wrong amounts. Complex regimens and many-drug prescriptions were blamed most. Prevention habits barely differed across settings. Rural staff reported somewhat fewer errors, though their subgroup was tiny. Toledo's team concludes that pharmacy teams play a steady, proactive guard role everywhere, and that standard prevention packages could roll out broadly with extra support tailored to rural posts.
pmc-13517628:
Thomas Lang and five colleagues review hemodiafiltration, an upgraded form of dialysis, in a 2026 article. The method adds convection to the usual diffusion, flushing a large volume of fluid through the filter to drag out mid-sized toxins. Europe and parts of Asia adopted it widely; rules, payment, and infrastructure slowed it elsewhere. Fresh trials revived interest, above all in high-volume treatment pushing at least twenty-three litres per session.

That high-volume version clears middle molecules consistently better than standard dialysis and may calm low-grade inflammation. Protein-bound toxins remain its weak spot, since albumin holds them back from any filter. Safety looks good where pure fluids, modern machines, trained staff, and sound access are in place, with fewer blood-pressure crashes during sessions. Lang's team supports wider use under those conditions while pushing for new tricks against the bound toxins.
pmc-13517928:
Gizem Karadag and seven colleagues genotype a cattle virus in Türkiye's Thrace region in a 2026 study. Bovine viral diarrhea virus drains herds through lung and gut disease and lost calves, and Thrace borders the European Union, making its strains a regional concern. The team swabbed five hundred thirty-three animals on twenty-six sick farms and sequenced the positives.

Virus turned up on nine farms, about eighteen percent of samples. Positivity tracked both the sampling year and the animals' ages. Most strains were subgenotype 1a, forming their own cluster apart from older Turkish isolates, with one 1f strain beside them. One sample held Pestivirus brazilense, never before reported in Thrace, which stretches that species' known map. Karadag's team feeds the family tree into control-programme design and vaccine planning, arguing that border regions need strain-level watching, not just case counts.
pmc-13518328:
Alexandre Vigier and four colleagues examine the insulation of inhibitory neurons in epileptic mouse brains in a 2026 study. Temporal lobe epilepsy rewires the hippocampus, and its parvalbumin interneurons, normally resistant to cell death, carry partial myelin coats whose fate was unknown. The team tracked these cells, their coating patterns, the brain's immune cells, and the coat-making lineage across disease build-up and the chronic phase.

The interneurons held their numbers throughout, yet their myelin patterning broke down markedly. The damage peaked while seizures were developing, alongside a surge of activated microglia and churn in the coating-cell family. A drug blocking microglial growth, given for eight days around the triggering seizure event, prevented both the myelin changes and the lineage churn. Vigier's team draws a direct line from immune-cell flare to interneuron insulation loss, echoing mechanisms in multiple sclerosis and hinting at shared drug targets.
pmc-13518428:
Phuong Thanh Nguyen and others evaluate donor-derived cell-free DNA for kidney transplant tracking in a forward-looking single-center study. In 2026, the long-term study collects 322 blood samples from thirty-nine kidney recipients, most in the first year and up to five years post-transplant. It quantifies donor DNA with a modified aimed reading protocol using a 1,000-SNP panel tailored to East Asian backgrounds. Non-invasive rejection markers are urgently needed, since biopsy is invasive.

Raised donor-derived cell-free DNA consistently linked to acute rejection and graft injuries, clearly distinguishing rejection from non-rejection episodes and aligning moderately with serum markers and biopsies. Surges appeared in antibody-mediated rejection and various injuries. Unlike standard markers, donor DNA inversely correlated with immune-quieting trough levels, suggesting superior tracking of immune-quieting response.
pmc-13518828:
Jiaxin Han leads an eight-author team proposing a 2026 anomaly detector for multivariate industrial sensor streams. Factories need early warnings from many linked sensors, yet real data shift constantly, true system wiring is unknown, and labeled failures are scarce. Older detectors lean on rigid assumptions and fixed network maps.
