Their method pre-trains in hyperbolic space, a curved geometry that fits layered data, to capture cross-variable links. A graph module then learns the connection structure itself and prunes it over time, pinpointing where and when anomalies arise. Attention layers plus a small-sample threshold rule steady the output. Benchmarks showed gains of 10 to 30 percent, with detection, diagnosis, and explanation unified in one framework.
pmc-13518928:
Gong-jie Ye, Yi-ru Weng, Shi Zheng, and Zhou-zhou Dong test bedside blood-gas shortcuts in 2026 for judging circulation in septic shock. Directly measuring cardiac output and oxygen balance is invasive, so intensive care teams want stand-ins drawn from venous and arterial blood. Their records review covered 597 patients treated between 2018 and 2024.

The carbon dioxide gap between venous and arterial blood tracked cardiac output with a correlation of minus 0.63 in the full group. A ratio combining that gap with the oxygen content difference tracked the oxygen delivery-to-use balance even more closely. Links were strongest in the 127 patients whose hearts were weakened by sepsis. Both measures, the authors conclude, can serve as practical surrogates.
pmc-13521928:
Chun-Liang Wu and colleagues quantify in 2026 injury risk tied to diabetes and substance use, separately and combined, in nationwide Taiwan insurance data. Two matched cohorts were followed, one for diabetes covering 2000 to 2013 and one for substance use covering 2013 to 2022.

Diabetes alone carried about 1.7 times the injury risk of matched controls, while substance use carried about 1.44 times the risk. Among substance users, suicide risk stood out at roughly ten times the comparison level, with intentional injury and falls also raised. Female sex, low income and major illness amplified risk further. Joint effects for people with both conditions follow.
pmc-13522128:
Saeed Khodayari and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. High-grade breast tumors gain stem-like traits as they worsen. Complex gene networks drive that slide inside the tumor's surroundings. The team hunts for a microRNA cluster behind the stemness shift. Their guide is mammary gland development, where similar switches shape normal tissue. Reanalysis of array data finds genes and microRNAs that differ by tumor grade. Larger public data sets strengthen the search.

Spatial links between messages and microRNAs are mapped within each grade. Lab tests then check a growth receptor and the cell shape-change program it drives. The named cluster is 7, 17, and 155. Cancer biologists get a candidate driver set for the high-grade turn. A cluster acting together is a richer drug target than a lone gene. Grade-linked maps also help explain why some tumors resist treatment once they change state.
pmc-13522328:
Piotr Rutkowski and colleagues test in 2026 under-skin delivery of cetrelimab, a PD-1 blocking antibody, for advanced solid tumours in a phase I study. Participants had exhausted or lacked standard options and had never received checkpoint blockade before.

Thirty patients joined two parts testing a dilute then a concentrated formula, with a loading dose added in the second part. Median treatment lasted about two months in a heavily pretreated group. Drug-linked side effects affected 70 percent, with no drug-linked serious events or systemic infusion reactions. Two durable responses appeared, while loading dosing reached target exposure faster, supporting under-skin delivery for later trials.
pmc-13523228:
Di Yang and co-authors build a prediction model for short-term outcomes after bowel cancer surgery in older patients in a 2026 prospective study. Patients aged sixty or older undergoing planned keyhole removal of colorectal cancer completed a comprehensive geriatric assessment covering function, nutrition, and muscle mass. Major adverse events within ninety days of surgery were the outcome of interest.

About one patient in four experienced a major adverse event in both the development and validation groups. Six preoperative factors independently predicted events: weight loss, daily activity score, a kidney blood marker, muscle mass index, low albumin, and tumor stage. The model discriminated well and calibrated excellently in both groups. The authors offer the tool for personal risk estimates and for targeting extra support to high-risk older patients before surgery.
pmc-13523328:
Daniel Mulat Eshetu and colleagues identify drivers of HIV treatment failure in northwest Ethiopia in a 2026 case-control study. Three hundred sixty-nine adults on first-line antiretroviral therapy were compared: one hundred twenty-three whose virus remained uncontrolled on repeated tests and two hundred forty-six whose virus stayed suppressed. Records and interviews supplied clinical and behavioral information for regression analysis.

Six factors independently raised the odds of failure. They were not disclosing HIV status, a high viral load soon after starting treatment, poor adherence, treatment interruption, being single, and a very low immune cell count. Interruption and poor adherence carried the largest effects. The authors recommend stronger support for staying on treatment, keeping patients in care, and counseling around disclosure, to reduce failure in the region's health facilities.
pmc-13523428:
Kevin Fitzmartin, Zakir Khan, Christopher James, and Adeel A Faruki describe building a new electroconvulsive therapy service at a major medical center in a 2026 article. Expansion of inpatient psychiatry at their Colorado campus in 2023 created the opening. A team spanning psychiatry, anesthesia, nursing, pharmacy, and technology planned staffing, medication handling, emergency protocols, and record workflows, informed by visits to peer centers.

The service launched with success and ran for two years with a core anesthesia and nursing group. Early challenges included uneven patient volume that strained staffing, hard consent questions of an ethical and legal nature, and patients with serious other conditions such as pregnancy and heart disease. Revised staffing, a serial anesthesia consent process, and stronger team communication improved efficiency and safety. The authors offer the account as hands-on guidance for other centers.
pmc-13523528:
Yuchen Wu and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 prospective quasi-experimental study, a nurse-led program that brings trained family members into intensive care to support patients. Delirium is a common, serious complication in critical illness, and family-centered care is a promising non-drug strategy. Structured programs led by nurses had limited evidence.

Patients from three tertiary hospitals in Gansu Province received either the family program or usual care without family participation, and matching produced 365 patients per group. Delirium occurred in 26.85 percent of the program group against 34.25 percent of controls. Hospital and intensive care stays were shorter, ventilation time was lower, and costs were slightly less. Mortality at six months and one year, weakness, infection, and adverse events did not differ significantly.
pmc-13525028:
Mustafa Hariri and seven co-authors compare two knee replacement styles by what patients themselves report, in a study dated 2026. When only the outer side of the knee is worn, surgeons can replace just that part or the whole joint. Evidence on how patients feel afterward has been thin for the partial option on the lateral side.

The team matched thirty-one pairs of patients on age, body weight, sex, and starting knee function. Both groups answered standard scores on pain, function, activity, and how natural the joint feels. After surgery the main knee score did not differ significantly between the groups. The study also tracked who reached improvements patients would notice and who reached a state they find acceptable. Matched designs like this help surgeons counsel patients facing the choice.
pmc-13525728:
Kallimanis and Prodromidis review twelve years of a plant-based cream for facial seborrheic dermatitis. Their 2026 retrospective study covers just ten patients, eight men and two women aged 40 to 78, with disease from mild to very severe. All applied a cream containing Greek sage leaf extract, naturally rich in carnosic acid and carnosol, once nightly as their only treatment.

Every patient cleared completely, reaching a severity score of zero within an average of about eight days, with redness and scaling falling and itch easing quickly. Remissions lasted from twenty days to ten months. Later flares cleared faster on retreatment, averaging under five days, and no relapses occurred during long-term nightly or alternate-night maintenance. No local or systemic safety problems were recorded over follow-up stretching to five years. The authors call the results promising but demand randomised trials.
pmc-13525928:
Keily Portillo Avila and co-authors present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 29-year-old woman. Her lower front gums receded at several teeth. This happened after orthodontic treatment. Thin gum tissue left roots exposed. Bone support was also limited. Teeth 22 through 27 were affected. Appearance and root sensitivity were the concerns.

The team used cone beam imaging to plan surgery. They covered the roots with a connective tissue graft. The graft came from the palate. A flap was pulled upward over it. Healing was uneventful. At one month the patient had thicker gums. Root coverage was substantial and appearance improved. The gains held at the six-month follow-up visit.
pmc-13526028:
Navid Farassat and co-authors present a study dated 2026 giving reference measures of the human eye socket. Doctors need normal ranges for the orbit's size and parts, but measuring MRI scans by hand is slow. The team built a deep learning system that outlines fifteen structures in the socket on its own.

They ran it on brain scans from 30,868 people in a German national health cohort. After quality checks, 28,779 people remained, with a mean age of about forty-eight. The model matched expert hand drawings closely. Average eye length was 23.5 millimeters, and total socket content volume was about 34.4 cubic centimeters. Men had larger measures across the board, and the lens kept growing with age.
pmc-13526128:
Yéléna Le Prieult, Marie-Luise Otte, Mike Schmitgen, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It scans the hearing cortex of women with borderline personality disorder who hear voices, and finds the brain's folding pattern altered exactly where sound is first processed.

Hearing voices is not unique to schizophrenia; it also strikes people with borderline personality disorder, where its brain basis is barely studied. The team compared twenty patients with a history of voices, twenty-seven without, and thirty healthy women on detailed brain scans. Measures covered the folding, thickness, and volume of frontotemporal speech regions. Only one difference stood out: the voice-hearing group showed reduced folding in the right transverse temporal gyrus, home of the early auditory cortex. The authors read this as a structural vulnerability that may bias the brain toward generating voices.
pmc-13527128:
Sang Won Cheon and colleagues report, in a 2026 structural study, how the atypical kinase HASPIN selectively recognizes two inhibitors that mimic ATP, the cell's energy currency. Kinase drug design struggles for selectivity because the ATP pocket looks similar across hundreds of kinases. HASPIN, a kinase active in germ cells, offered a test case for ATP-like scaffolds.

Crystal structures of the enzyme bound to each inhibitor, solved at high resolution, showed ATP-like poses inside the catalytic pocket. The protein's internal spines were preorganized by dense hydrophobic packing, holding a key helix in place without any nucleotide present. Despite similar poses, one compound bound about ten times more tightly and showed roughly tenfold stronger enzyme inhibition and hundredfold stronger cell-killing selectivity. The pocket's distinctive architecture explains the discrimination.
pmc-13528028:
Khyobeni Mozhui and eight colleagues study epigenetic entropy in a 2026 paper drawn from the Women's Health Initiative. Entropy here means rising randomness in DNA methylation marks as people age. The main group held 2,192 women. Two more groups, near two thousand and nine hundred women, were used to check the findings. The team compared entropy with income, schooling, health, and death risk.

Lower income and less schooling were tied to higher entropy. The tie was strongest in DNA regions guarded by polycomb proteins, which manage cell memory. Higher income linked with lower entropy in White women, but the pattern was weaker in Black and Hispanic women. A pace-of-aging score predicted death risk. Keeping marks at enhancer regions linked with better survival. The authors see social conditions written into the aging epigenome.
pmc-13530228:
Afsana Akter Rupa and co-authors test in 2026 whether a leftover signal from a common TB test can flag other mycobacterial infections. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria mimic tuberculosis yet need different care. Occasionally the rapid test shows a gene signal while ruling out true TB, and that hint usually goes unused.

Fifty such specimens from Bangladesh screening centers went through culture, targeted gene tests, and sequencing. Most grew atypical mycobacteria, and sequencing named species in the majority. A signal timing cutoff separated true positives with fair accuracy at no extra cost, giving clinics a free clue from tests already run.
pmc-13531828:
Mara Warnhoff and colleagues validate in 2026 a 3D planning program for judging bone loss before redo shoulder replacement surgery. Forty-seven patients revising the same shoulder implant design had defect shape judged from ordinary scans, 3D reconstructions, and direct surgical findings. Loosening caused most revisions, about seven years after first surgery.

Surgeons found about 68 percent of defects contained. The 3D planning view matched that call in about 81 percent of cases, beating the roughly 66 percent match for flat scans. Agreement statistics favored 3D as well. Better containment calls help surgeons plan grafts and implants.
pmc-13531928:
Shuhui Deng and co-authors test in 2026 a light-controlled fusion protein that copies a brain histamine receptor long-term behavior. The tool joins a light sensor to the receptor signaling tail, letting laser pulses switch it on inside neurons and lab cells. Earlier work covered only its quick effects.

Sustained light steadily raised the number of protein clusters inside cells, and most sat in early recycling compartments, the signature of receptor internalization. A drug blocking the arrestin pathway blunted that rise, matching natural receptor behavior under histamine. The tool can now probe both fast signaling and slow shutdown of this receptor.
pmc-13532228:
Valentina Dimartino and co-authors build in 2026 a rapid gene test for hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae, a strain type increasingly merging with drug resistance. Current checks rely on a crude stickiness test or full genome reading, both flawed for routine surveillance. Their multiplex test targets the main virulence gene sets at once.

Testing covered 110 clinical isolates and nine blood cultures against genome and stickiness references. The panel caught every top-scoring virulence profile and most middle ones, with fair agreement against genomes and stronger agreement against the stickiness test. Direct blood testing worked in principle, needing wider validation.
pmc-13532628:
Jodi Gedallovich and colleagues report in 2026 a benign kidney growth that was first read as cancer. The growth, a fibromyxoid form of nephrogenic adenoma, is harmless yet can mimic renal cell carcinoma in scans, cells, and stains. A 72-year-old man with kidney stones had a right kidney mass sampled by needle.

Stains were positive for several marks also seen in cancer, which led to a cancer call before surgery. Removal showed a cyst with trapped spindle cells in stringy tissue and focal benign traits. Readers learn why small needle samples of this rare lesion need extra caution.
pmc-13532928:
Fougerousse reports a case of stubborn itchy skin nodules that eased sharply after a diabetes drug was started. The condition, prurigo nodularis, brings hard, intensely itchy bumps on the trunk and limbs. Newer drugs help many patients, but some stay uncontrolled. The patient was a 64-year-old man whose disease had resisted four years of treatment. Failed options included strong steroid creams, dupilumab, and methotrexate. Semaglutide was begun for obesity, with his skin regimen unchanged.

His skin then improved in a marked, steady way. The author notes this as the first such report for this drug class in this disease. The case hints at anti-inflammatory effects worth formal study.
pmc-13533028:
Priyanka Kumari and a team of co-authors build a drug-loaded nanofiber mat to treat hidden womb infection in cattle. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The infection quietly cuts fertility and milk yield, while standard antibiotic routes leave weak drug levels and residue risks.

The mat is spun from two friendly polymers and carries the antibiotic ofloxacin. Fine tuning gave uniform fibers about two hundred nanometers wide with nearly all the drug trapped inside. The drug seeped out steadily for nine days. Tests showed strong sticking to womb lining, no cell harm, and good germ killing. Cow trials supported local placement in the womb. The authors pitch it as a cleaner option for repeat breeders.
pmc-13534628:
Vedat Tumen and colleagues adapt in 2026 an enzyme-inspired optimiser for the travelling salesman problem, with a tourism case in Bitlis, Turkiye. Finding the shortest route through scattered sights is a classic hard planning task. Their discrete version uses random-key coding, varied neighbourhood moves, and a selective local polish step.

On standard test problems the method matched or beat three recent rival methods on best, average, and spread measures, with statistical tests backing most gains. Applied to 46 tourist points in Bitlis, it produced shorter and steadier routes with clear geographic logic for planners.
pmc-13536628:
Ayu Hutami Syarif and colleagues map in 2026 how immune and tissue cells interact across lung compartments in advanced COPD using spatial gene mapping. Such compartment detail was missing for this chronic lung disease. Lung tissue zones were profiled and checked with cell sorting, staining, and cell culture tests.

Distinct niches appeared: macrophage-rich and stress zones in the lung body, plus airway zones shifting toward mucus and adaptive immune patterns. Killer T cells sat beside key lining and mucus cells, with signals hinting they drive tissue damage. The T-cell axis emerges as a treatment target worth testing.
pmc-13536728:
Revati Amin leads a 2026 interview study of parents in coastal Karnataka, India, on teen diet and activity habits tied to long-term disease risk. Sixteen parents of adolescents aged 11 to 17 years took part in recorded talks chosen to span school types and income levels. Answers were grouped into themes using behavior models that weigh ability, chance, and drive to act.

Parents knew what healthy habits looked like yet struggled to sustain them at home. Talks described home life as negotiation rather than control, with unhealthy foods and missed activity treated as normal breaks. Heavy school demands, growing teen independence, and gender and cultural norms further limited change. The authors recommend joint family, school, and community steps that fit local pressures.
pmc-13537728:
Gennaro Liccardi and six colleagues write about a hidden route of cat allergen exposure: passive transport. Cat allergen rides on clothes and hair into places cats never enter. Schools, offices, hotels, and buses can all carry it. There it can sensitize people and trigger symptoms without any cat in sight.

The writers respond to a review of new ways to cut cat allergen at its source. Those methods help owners in their own homes, they grant. They do nothing for other people's cats or public spaces. Steps against carried allergen, by contrast, protect everyone everywhere. The letter faults the field for saying little about such prevention. It urges guidance that treats cat allergen as a public presence, not just a pet problem.
pmc-13538028:
Chen-Syuan Huang and others watched brain calcium during ultrasound seizure treatment in 2026. Whole-body seizures often resist drug treatment. Focused ultrasound can suppress seizure action. How calcium plays its part stayed poorly known. Glowing calcium signals were caught live. Fibre photometry tracked networks during seizures.

Ultrasound shifted the balance of firing and calming in a clear way. Calcium signals showed the anti-seizure effect. Live readouts matched the electrical traces well. It acted as a stand-in for the mechanism. Treatment effect could be judged live. Closed-loop pulsing may follow this work. Ultrasound dose could adapt to signals. Epilepsy care gains a tracking tool.
pmc-13539928:
Swetang J Shah and five colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a 12-year-old girl whose raised prolactin levels looked like a pituitary gland problem yet traced back to her behaviour medicine. She lives with Landau-Kleffner syndrome, autism, and intellectual disability, and had taken risperidone for a long time.

Milk discharge, failing vision, and falls prompted tests that found high prolactin with a normal scan of the pituitary. Stopping risperidone worsened behaviour, so clinicians switched her to olanzapine. Within three months the discharge stopped, vision improved, and prolactin normalised. The authors urge regular prolactin checks for children on such medicines, especially those who cannot describe discomfort.
pmc-13540328:
Aline Marzano-Miranda and six colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, why malaria from Plasmodium vivax makes people anaemic even though the parasite infects few red blood cells. Attention turns to antibodies the body aims at its own red cell surface protein Band 3.

Blood came from 79 anaemic and 95 non-anaemic infected patients, plus healthy donors, and a smaller group was followed for a month after treatment. Computer prediction picked six exposed loops of the protein for testing. Anaemic patients reacted strongly to loops four and six, mainly with an inflammatory antibody subclass that lingered after the parasites cleared. The authors propose these self-antibodies help destroy uninfected red cells.
pmc-13540828:
Shiyun Qian and colleagues devise a new sorting system in a 2026 study. The system uses three-dimensional CT scans of hip fractures. It aims to predict a key surgical question in advance. Which breaks will resist being nudged back into place? Surgeons now learn that only during the operation.

Records and scans covered 609 patients at the start. The analysis kept 318 fractures of the intertrochanteric type. Viewed from the side, each break looked flexed, neutral, or extended. Just over half reduced well in theatre. Hard cases in the flexed group split into three subtypes. The extended group split the same way. Scan features defined each subtype.
pmc-13543028:
Junhao Xie, Aoife Gowen, and Jun-Li Xu linked a vision model to a microscope to hunt microplastics automatically, in a paper published in 2026. Tiny plastic particles are a worldwide pollutant, and counts by hand are slow. Their workflow has the model spot particles in microscope photos, then turns the spots into microscope moves for shape readings and light scans. The model trained on more than 600 photos with 7,000 labeled particles.

On clean test sets it beat a plain threshold rule by a wide gap and edged a rival network as well. Scores fell when the background grew dirty, as with salt samples. The team solved the joining steps: focus for each field, true microscope positions from model output, and scripted microscope control. Code and data are free for others to build on.
pmc-13545028:
Waalewijn and co-authors published a 2026 modelling study for children living with HIV, the virus that attacks the immune system. About 1.4 million children have the virus, yet few drug forms suit small bodies. The team used computer simulation to design one fixed dose tablet combining dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide.

Using published models of how children's bodies handle each drug, Waalewijn simulated doses across weight bands from three to twenty kilograms. The chosen ratio put dolutegravir above its lowest target in over ninety-eight percent of simulated children. Tenofovir alafenamide cleared its target in more than ninety percent, while its breakdown product stayed below harmful levels everywhere. For heavier children the adult tablet is proposed instead.
pmc-13545128:
Masatoshi Yamashita and colleagues, writing in 2026, grouped children with ADHD, autism, or both by chemistry rather than by diagnosis alone. Their team measured monoamine breakdown products in urine from 83 affected children and compared the results with 83 typically developing controls. Machine learning sorted the affected children into two clusters that cut across the usual diagnostic labels.

One cluster of 18 children showed high levels of three metabolites, while a larger cluster of 65 showed low levels. The low group scored worse on cognitive control, flexibility, and inhibition, and brain scans showed distinct patterns of gray matter change in each cluster. Readers gain a possible biological basis for splitting these conditions into subtypes.
pmc-13545328:
Mandeep Gill Sagoo and co-authors described in 2026 a university module that mixes art, design, and biomedical engineering into anatomy teaching. Over ten weeks, student groups invent and 3D-print anatomical structures that break clinical and evolutionary rules, such as bionic arms, human wings, and hybrid hearts. Visiting artists and engineering doctoral students run supporting workshops, and each group presents its models at an unmanned display.

Feedback gathered over three years from 89 students and six tutors pointed to creative exploration, hands-on learning, and teamwork across disciplines as the main gains. One former student's prosthetic chest-wall design for cancer patients later reached publication and television coverage. The module keeps evolving through student feedback and reflection.
pmc-13546728:
Fritz Trillo-Zárate and colleagues fed Creole goats flour made from sweet potato vines in 2026, testing a cheap local feed for small farmers in Peru whose pastures often fall short nutritionally. Twelve milking goats received diets with no vine flour or with three rising shares, up to 7.5 percent, over eight weeks. Milk volume, body weight, and milk composition were tracked.

The highest flour share gave the most milk, about 411 milliliters a day, clearly above the control group. A small inclusion already lifted milk protein and lactose. Higher shares changed milk composition in less favorable ways past the middle dose. The authors also note that flour can be made from discarded sweet potato tubers, turning waste into feed.
pmc-13546828:
Fatemeh Zabihollahy and co-authors introduced in 2026 a software method, CurvReg, for lining up microscope images of the same liver biopsy stained in different ways. Pathologists increasingly compare several stains of one sample, yet curved biopsy shapes, warping, and color differences make alignment hard. Their approach cuts each biopsy into anatomical segments, aligns the pieces, then refines the warp using tissue masks rather than stain colors.

Across three liver datasets, alignment error fell by more than half, often by over 70 percent, and overlap scores rose to near-perfect levels. A public kidney dataset showed the method also transfers to other tissue. The team shows stain-derived vessel maps can then be carried onto the main diagnostic stain reliably.
pmc-13547228:
Mohammed H. Al-Qahtani and colleagues screened a library of natural compounds wholly by computer in 2026, hunting for a breast cancer candidate that grips five cancer-driving proteins at once. Resistance often defeats single-target drugs, so one molecule gripping five targets could hold the line better. One compound, named 2-Aoeobenoxmide in the study, rose to the top across docking runs against the estrogen receptor and four growth-related enzymes.

Its predicted binding beat the approved drug tucatinib on every target, and long simulations suggested steadier, calmer complexes than the comparison drug formed. Checks of drug-like behavior and water effects also favored it. The authors stress that all of this is hypothesis until laboratory tests check the compound.
pmc-13547628:
Sae Hwi Ki, Gun Hee Lee, and Do Hyuk Chung reported in 2026 a rare skin cancer, atypical fibroxanthoma, on the cheek of a 90-year-old woman. A first biopsy could not name the tumor. Such cancers arise on sun-exposed skin in older people and mimic several other spindle-cell tumors under the microscope. Her nodule grew fast and ulcerated, and an initial sample showed only spindle cell growth without a verdict.

A second, deeper punch biopsy confirmed the diagnosis, and scans found no spread. Surgeons removed the tumor with a one-centimeter margin and covered the area with a full-thickness skin graft. One year on, there was no return or spread, and the cosmetic result pleased the team. The authors stress careful pathology and long follow-up for this uncommon cancer.
pmc-13549428:
Lifeng Zhang and co-authors test a new PET tracer for staging neuroblastoma in children at first diagnosis. Their study appeared in 2026. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer of nerve tissue. The tracer homes in on a transporter that these tumor cells carry. It had already beaten the standard scan in children whose cancer returned. The team enrolled newly diagnosed children and gave each the new scan plus full body imaging.

Each scan was read on its own, and stages were recorded by an international system. A subgroup also had a second PET scan for comparison. The study asks whether the new tracer adds staging detail beyond CT, MRI, and ultrasound, and whether it agrees with the older scan. A sharper baseline map could steer first treatment more precisely.
pmc-13550628:
Ammar Armghan, with six colleagues, published a 2026 computer study of laser links between satellites. Such links can carry data at 160 gigabits per second. They serve global coverage and deep space work. Yet long range, pointing errors, and small dishes weaken the signal. The design mixed several ways to pack and send data, plus signal cleanup steps.

The team judged the link by error rate and signal clarity. They varied range, laser power, and dish size in the tests. The link held full speed over 7,000 kilometers in the model. The received signal stayed clear at the reported error levels. The results show how dish size and power trade off on long space links.
pmc-13550828:
Huaxiucairang Yang leads a team that reviews low oxygen, gut change, and insomnia. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with high altitude low oxygen. Thin air often breaks sleep and harms how folks adapt.

Proof points to the gut and brain axis in this ill. Low oxygen can harm the gut wall and let germ parts leak. Gut germ mix shifts cut good acids and reroute food paths. Swell signals then reach the brain through a few routes. Stress hormones may add to the link with poor sleep. Germ based fixes are weighed.
pmc-13550928:
Nitika Sharma, leading co-authors including Sridhar Manohar and A B Satish Rao, published a 2026 study of cryptocurrency market structure that listens to expert talk instead of price charts. Quantitative work dominates this field, leaving qualitative views underexplored. The team treated twelve domain podcasts as primary data and processed their transcripts with lexicometric software, which groups vocabulary into clusters.

Five clusters emerged, covering institutional infrastructure, market foundations, efficiency and resilience, forecasting, and market structure. A further analysis distilled three main forces behind the talk: how markets are built, how forecasts are made, and how markets absorb shocks. The authors claim podcasts are a novel source for qualitative finance, giving practitioners and scholars a view shaped by both technology and regulation.
pmc-13551528:
Titus A Chan's team reviewed how health care groups build patient input into their planning and care, in a 2026 scoping review. Patient input is widely praised as a pillar of good care, yet little synthesis existed of the models groups actually use to put it into practice. They searched four databases for work from 2014 to 2024 and used a standard five-stage review method plus community input.

From 7,870 records, only 13 studies met the bar, giving 11 models of varied shape and depth. No single model emerged, though many placed input on a sliding scale from light consultation to full co-design, and most models came from hospitals. The review urges future models to fit their local setting, rest on clearer theory, and track equity and impact. Leaders could then scale input across a whole group rather than at the bedside alone.
pmc-13551928:
Yaxun Jia, Zhu Yuan, Yunchao Gong, Haixiang Yang, and Zuo-lin Xiang published a 2026 study of software that finds drug interactions in medical texts. Such interactions matter for drug safety watch. Neural networks often miss key clues in a sentence. The team built a model with two channels. One channel reads the word sequence with a biomedical language model. The other maps word links as a graph.

A cross-attention step merges proof from both channels. The merged view then decides the interaction type. On a benchmark set, the method beat top prior systems. The team credits the dual view for the gain. Sequence plus graph keeps fine clues that one view alone would drop. They offer the model for mining safety facts from the growing medical literature.
pmc-13552028:
Ezgi Arslan Yuksel and her four co-authors, publishing in 2026, study how diet and iron interact in pregnancy-related anxiety. Good diet quality is thought to support mental health through nutrients the brain uses. Iron needs rise sharply in pregnancy. The team surveyed 293 pregnant women in Istanbul, scoring their diets, their iron intake against recommended levels, and their anxiety with standard scales.

Neither diet quality nor iron intake alone predicted anxiety. Their combination did. Better diets went with lower anxiety only in women whose iron intake was relatively high. Age, income, and whether the pregnancy was planned also tracked with anxiety. The authors are careful about the limits: iron was the only nutrient tested as a moderator, and blood iron was not measured. They call for longer studies with blood-based measures of several nutrients.
pmc-13552228:
Tom Andre Pedersen's team ran a pragmatic trial to test whether AI polyp-spotting help in colonoscopy builds skill or erodes it, in a 2026 report. Computer-aided detection is meant to raise polyp finds, yet recent real-world reports have raised doubts, including a worry that doctors lean on the tool and lose sharpness. The trial tracked 13 endoscopists, seven less skilled and six skilled, across three phases.

Each doctor scoped first without the AI aid, then with it, then after it was removed, covering 5,013 colonoscopies in total. The aid lifted detection of polyps at least 5 millimetres for less skilled doctors while it was on, but that gain faded once it was taken away. Skilled doctors showed no clear change. The lesson is reassuring and modest: the tool helps novices in the moment without measurably training or dulling them afterwards.
pmc-13552828:
Elaine Lin and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on making cleft care results readable for families. Children born with a cleft lip or palate answer standard surveys about how they look, feel, and function. Those results usually stay with clinicians. Sharing them back could help families join decisions, but raw scores are hard to read.

The team designed a graphic report card following shared guidelines for patient-facing tools. Patients and families then judged draft formats in rounds, doing reading tasks and rating clarity. Feedback on layout, color, and labels steered the design. The paper shows how to turn a clinical score into a page a family can use at the kitchen table.
pmc-13554028:
Lu and a large team test dark field CT for tracking lung disease in mice over time in twenty twenty-six. Early changes in lung microstructure drive diseases such as COPD and acute lung injury. Standard CT, based on attenuation, cannot see those changes. Dark field CT senses small angle scattering from intact air sac structures.

Prior animal studies were one time snapshots, not true follow ups. The team built a lab system for repeated imaging over twelve weeks. It includes dose optimized scanning and deep learning lung segmentation. A dark field measure changed earlier and more clearly than attenuation. Its paths differed by disease model and even between like treated animals. Results matched final tissue histology. The authors propose it as an early damage biomarker.
pmc-13555928:
Nathália Petraconi leads a seven-author team reviewing whether sitting too much harms children's thinking in a 2026 analysis. Only observational studies of typical children aged six to twelve qualified, comparing inactive children with active peers. Five databases were searched from their start to February 2026. Bias was graded with a standard tool for exposure studies.

From more than five thousand papers, just two studies directly compared the groups, and they disagreed. One linked sustained moderate-to-vigorous activity paths to better school results over time. The other found mixed ties, with some activity measures linking to weaker verbal skills. Both studies carried high bias risk and weak control of other factors. The authors urge caution and better-designed work before firm claims.
pmc-13556228:
Viron and colleagues published a 2026 study on racing, stretching nuclei in a model fungus. During mating in Podospora anserina, male nuclei travel through a thin female tube. Female nuclei sit still and round, while male nuclei move and deform wildly. The team filmed the trip with glowing markers under the microscope.

Male nuclei hit the fastest speeds and wildest stretches ever recorded for moving nuclei. They squeezed through narrow gates between tube sections without tearing apart. Breaking down actin, one cell skeleton system, did not slow the trip. Wrecking microtubules, the other system, halted movement and stretching completely. The tube's microtubule network runs in one clear direction, guiding travel. Live-cell filming captured the motion in real time for close measurement.
pmc-13556728:
Ukai and a large team tested whether the drug lurasidone can ease social problems in a rat model of schizophrenia. People with schizophrenia often struggle at work and with others. Stress before birth and stress in youth can harm brain growth and raise that risk. The team built those two stress hits into their model.

Rats got a viral mimic before birth and were then raised alone after birth. The team watched how the rats acted with others and read signs of empathy-like behavior. They compared behavior with and without lurasidone. The aim was to see if the drug restores social function, not just calms symptoms. Work like this may point to care that helps people rejoin daily life.
pmc-13557328:
Molotla-Torres and four colleagues fine-tuned a chemical colitis model in BALB/c mice to be reproducible without killing the animals. Dextran sulfate sodium in drinking water inflames the colon and mimics human colitis mechanisms. Dose decides whether the model is informative or lethal. Mice drank two or three percent solutions for seven days, then plain water for seven more. Disease activity and survival were tracked daily for fourteen days.

Both doses raised disease scores, inflammation, and gut permeability while shortening colons and cutting body weight. The stronger dose shifted mucus-producing cell patterns further. Permeability was measured with a dye assay, and colon tissue was stained three ways. The twenty twenty-six optimization gives colitis researchers a calibrated protocol: enough disease to study, with survival high enough to study it humanely.
pmc-13557628:
Xiaohao Hu and twelve colleagues engineered in 2026 a wound gel that pairs a plant compound with fat-derived stem cells to heal diabetic wounds. Such wounds stall because inflammation persists and new blood vessels form poorly. Their gel blends silk fibroin with a synthetic polymer, loads it with berberine, and carries living stem cells, and the team tuned the blend before testing it in cells and diabetic rats.

A seven-to-three silk-to-polymer ratio gave the best pore size, strength, and slow drug release. Loaded stem cells secreted more growth factors, skin cells multiplied and migrated faster, and vessel-forming cells built more tubes. Immune cells in the wound shifted from an inflammatory state to a healing one. In rats, treated wounds closed faster with better skin regrowth, collagen, and blood supply. The authors present the combined gel as a strong candidate therapy.
pmc-13557928:
Essi Heinonen and eight colleagues chart prescription drug use in pregnancy and after birth in Sweden, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They linked birth and drug registers for pregnancies from twenty oh seven to twenty twenty-two. Use was counted from three months before conception to three months after delivery. More than a million women took at least one drug in pregnancy.

The share of pregnant women with a dispensed drug rose from about fifty-seven to sixty-eight percent over the period. The rise was steepest in women over forty. Use of five or more drugs also grew, while risky bone-shaping drugs stayed rare. Antibiotic and pain drug use fell, while several long-term drug classes rose.
pmc-13558728:
Priyankaa V and four colleagues pooled in 2026 quality of life scores for women with cervical cancer, using the EQ-5D scale that health economists feed into cost-effectiveness models. Their systematic review, registered in advance and run to current reporting standards, searched four databases to July 2025 and gathered twenty-four studies covering two hundred eighty-two thousand participants in fifteen countries.

Seventeen studies supplied utility scores, which averaged under four fifths of full health, though studies disagreed with each other almost completely, so the average hides wide local variation. A companion self-rating averaged about seventy-two on a hundred-point scale. Pain and discomfort plus anxiety and depression were the most frequently damaged life domains. Stage-by-stage estimates wobbled, especially for the most advanced disease, where tiny samples and survivor bias cloud the numbers. Reference values, the authors say, are useful yet must be handled with care.
pmc-13560028:
Haizhen Chen and five co-authors published a 2026 study of machine learning models that stage liver scarring from a blood protein, without biopsy. They enrolled 1,011 follow-up patients and staged their fibrosis with an elasticity scan. From 23 lab values, 15 were picked to build models around the protein CHI3L1. One model staged fibrosis in five grades with strong accuracy.

Sharper versions followed: a seven-marker model scored near 0.98 on the accuracy curve, and simpler two- and three-grade models kept scores around 0.94 to 0.95. The final model beat two standard blood scores by a wide margin. The authors say such models fit many clinic scenarios, including spotting reversible scarring early. The approach promises cheaper, needle-free staging.
pmc-13560128:
Gayeon Kim and colleagues review nanomedicine designs that attack glioblastoma in stages, arguing that single-trick particles keep failing in trials. Their 2026 review organizes recent work into a three-step delivery framework for this lethal brain tumor. Any injected therapy must cross the blood-brain barrier, then find the tumor, then release its payload on site.

Step one covers barrier crossing through natural transport routes, engineered protein coatings, cell-mimicking carriers, and techniques that briefly open the barrier, such as focused ultrasound. Step two adds tumor homing through decorated surfaces, penetrating peptides, and magnetic guidance. Step three triggers release with tumor cues like acidity or with outside signals like light. The authors weigh preclinical promise against manufacturing, regulatory, and immune-clearance hurdles. Their verdict: only platforms integrating at least two stages stand a realistic chance.
pmc-13560328:
Katharina Ecsy and colleagues gather patient and carer perspectives on how chronic graft-versus-host disease wears down quality of life after stem cell transplantation. Their 2026 two-part study interviews ten adults who had passed through more than two lines of therapy, then surveys twenty-seven more, including a standard quality-of-life questionnaire. Data on this heavily treated group had been thin.

Patients described a profound drag across daily life: treatment side effects, the sheer burden of regimens, constant appointments, and hits to finances, education, and mental health. Many felt unprepared for how severe and how long the symptoms would run. They asked for better communication among the several professionals treating the same person. The authors call for fuller education at the outset, treatment plans shaped to the individual, and stronger support services to soften the emotional and financial weight of the disease.
pmc-13560628:
Chebotar and colleagues published a 2026 genome note on a bacterium living inside a hardy weed. The strain, Pseudomonas Can09R, was lifted from roots of Chenopodium album in Russia. Bacteria inside drought-tough plants may one day help crops face dry spells. The team read the strain's full genome with a high-throughput machine.

The genome spans about six million DNA letters in its assembled form. Its gene count came to 5,281 predicted protein-building genes overall. The host plants came from the Stavropol region in southern Russia. Roots were surface-cleaned so only inside dwellers made the culture plates. The sequence gives trait hunters a base for testing farm uses. Such root dwellers are prized leads for drought-helping farm products.
pmc-13562328:
Gavin M. Joynt and Gabriele Leonie Schwarz examine whether intensive care admission for the very old, patients eighty and above, should be a shared decision. Their 2026 essay weighs shrunken odds of functional recovery, fewer remaining years, and often diminished quality of life after discharge against a patient's right to choose. Prognosis in this group resists confident prediction.

Very old patients face opposite harms: over-servicing with aggressive treatment they may not want, and under-servicing driven by ageism. Shared decision-making can align the team's knowledge with the patient's values, and a time-limited trial of intensive care can support it when the answer is unclear. The authors set limits honestly: triage under scarcity and genuinely futile admission fall outside shared decision-making, because fairness and appropriateness override autonomy there. Untangling chronological from biological age in those calls, they argue, is where fairness is won or lost.
pmc-13562528:
Putta Priyanka and two colleagues work on cutting Waspaloy, a tough nickel alloy used in jet engines, with electrical sparks instead of blades. Spark machining suits hard alloys, but slow cutting, worn tools, and rough surfaces limit it. The 2026 study made electrodes from copper mixed with 5 percent graphite and ran trials across current, pulse timing, and gap settings. Some runs used sunflower oil as the insulating fluid instead of standard oils. Removal speed, tool wear, and surface finish were scored together.

Current and pulse length drove cutting speed most, peaking near 0.43 cubic millimetres per minute. The gentlest tool wear came at low current. Sunflower oil gave the smoothest finish, with roughness near one micrometre and a thinner damaged layer. A ranking method picked a best compromise setting across all goals. The authors present the mix of composite tool, plant oil, and structured tuning as a cleaner route for alloy work.
pmc-13562628:
Mustafa Farahat and colleagues asked how much trust drug teams should place in computer models of drug spread through the body. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic models, known as PBPK models, predict how a drug moves into tissues from its chemical traits. Such models now guide early drug screening, but input errors and untested guesses can quietly widen the doubt. Their 2026 study tested four models against 1,854 lab data points.

Once plausible input errors were added, drug levels forecast by the models swung widely, from nearly exact to off by thirtyfold, for drugs and models of different kinds. Models clashed most for fatty molecules with a positive charge. The authors trace which traits and guesses drive the spread, and warn that virtual screening needs honest error ranges before its forecasts steer real choices.
pmc-13562828:
Mirta Aguado and co-authors present a 2026 hunt for peptoid compounds that block parasite enzymes. The targets are metal-using aminopeptidases from the germs of malaria, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis. Such enzymes do work the parasites need inside the human host. Two compound libraries, seventy-four peptoids in all, were built by a mix-and-match reaction that swaps parts freely. One library then grew amino acid tails for more range.

Each enzyme met the full shelf, and blockers from mild to strong turned up for all three. Docking sims point to greasy grips as the main hold. With drug proofing spreading among parasites, fresh blocker families matter. Peptoids shrug off the body's own cutting enzymes, a bonus for drug life.
pmc-13563728:
Shu-Yi Li and five colleagues follow older adults to see which eating patterns guard against sarcopenic obesity, the double burden of weak muscle plus excess fat. Evidence on diet and this condition has been scarce. Their 2026 cohort held 3,398 Chinese elders free of it at the start. A 280-item food questionnaire fed four diet scores, covering quality, a brain-health pattern, an Okinawa-style pattern, and an inflammation index, while factor analysis pulled patterns from the data. Four years of follow-up recorded who developed the condition.

Cases numbered 266, and 80 percent arose in people who began with obesity alone. Higher quality, brain-health, and Okinawa scores each cut risk by roughly 14 percent per standard step, while a more inflammatory diet raised it by about 16 percent. The protective links showed in the group starting with obesity. Eating for low inflammation and antioxidants, the authors conclude, may slow that slide.
pmc-13564628:
Xiuge Zhang and three co-authors mapped where a leaf pest of a prized tree can live in China as the climate shifts, in a study published in 2026. The moth eats just one tree, grown for wood and medicine. Their fitted model joins pest locations with weather facts to grade each place. Cold month lows and dry month rain drove the grade most.

Suitable ground now spans about a fifth of the land, with the best in the center and southwest. Maps for the next century move the rim zones while the core holds. One path gave the widest growth by the 2090s, with the heart of suitable ground slid south. The authors present the maps for watch posts and pest plans that bend with the climate.
pmc-13565728:
Yuanyuan Yu and eleven co-authors published a cattle genomics study in twenty twenty-six on carcass traits in crossbred Angus herds. Weight and dressing percentage decide beef value, but their genetics in mixed populations are murky. The team compared single-population genome scans against meta-analysis of subgroups for both gene hunting and prediction accuracy.

Two hundred seventy-nine animals were genotyped on a dense marker chip and measured for carcass weight, live weight, and dressing percentage. Candidate genes near significant markers included STRIT1, SEL1L3, NOC4L, and ANK1. Prediction accuracy depended on context: adjusting for subpopulation structure helped in some settings, meta-analysis in others. The comparison tells breeders which strategy suits herds built from mixed Angus sources.
pmc-13567028:
Zepeng Wang and seven co-authors present a 2026 paper on recovering phosphorus from wastewater by growing a fertilizer mineral in place. The element is both a pollutant in waterways and a finite farm resource. Struvite crystallization captures it, but standard recipes need bought magnesium salts and alkaline chemicals. The team instead dissolved natural magnesite rock with electric current: the current freed magnesium ions while the cathode made its surroundings alkaline, so the mineral could form.

Under tuned settings, about fifty-eight percent of the phosphorus was recovered and the solid reached roughly sixty-three percent purity by their estimate. They note some nitrogen loss may be ammonia escaping near the cathode rather than entering the mineral. Imaging and diffraction confirmed struvite in the product. The authors pitch the reagent-saving route for greener recycling of the element.
pmc-13568028:
Shu-Yuan Wu and Theodore Brown present a 2026 journal article on a self-organizing way to cluster wireless sensors for area coverage. Randomly scattered sensors must choose cluster heads and sleep rotations without coordinates or central orders. Their method, EARDC, borrows reaction-diffusion math from pattern formation, scaled by each node's leftover energy, and works from one-hop neighbor chatter alone.

Simulations at three densities tested lifetime, coverage, and redundancy against three classic protocols. EARDC ran networks longer with fewer awake nodes than all three, though one rival trimmed redundancy better. The authors stress that lifetime and unbroken coverage are separate goals to balance.
pmc-13569428:
Katherine Fodder and co-authors search, in a 2026 study across human and mouse brain data sets, for early signs of trouble in oligodendrocytes in Alzheimer's disease. These are the cells that wrap nerve fibers in insulation. Network analysis combined chemical tags on DNA from four brain regions with gene activity data from single cells and from mice.

A DNA-tag signature enriched for oligodendrocyte genes appeared across regions covering early and late disease and matched altered gene activity in those cells. The same signature showed up in mice with early amyloid changes and even in other degenerative diseases without amyloid. Support cells, not only neurons, may falter early in Alzheimer's, widening the search for early markers.
pmc-13569528:
Cao and colleagues compared in 2026 the three main endothelin blocker drugs for pulmonary arterial hypertension, using a structured scoring framework built with nineteen experts. The disease raises pressure in the lung arteries. The drugs differ in benefit, side effects, blood-test burden, interactions, and price, which complicates pharmacy and formulary choices in China.

Twelve trials supplied the hard numbers. All three drugs improved walking distance and blood flow measures, with ambrisentan showing the largest walking gains and a trend to fewer drug harms. Yearly drug costs in China ran lowest for bosentan and far highest for macitentan, and the cost per meter of walking gained was lowest for ambrisentan. After weighting all six domains, from safety to access, ambrisentan scored highest overall. The authors offer the framework as a transparent tool for hospital drug decisions.
pmc-13571128:
Katherine Embleton, Sophie Bennett, James H MacCabe, and Alice Egerton report a two thousand twenty-six study of inflammation markers during six months of clozapine treatment. Clozapine uniquely helps schizophrenia that resists other drugs. It may stir and calm inflammation at once, possibly explaining its power.

Blood cytokines and C-reactive protein were measured before treatment and at three and six months. Symptom scores tracked alongside. After statistical correction, two signals rose over time: an anti-inflammatory interleukin and a pro-inflammatory factor. Immune changes did not simply mirror symptom improvement. Longer immune profiling may clarify how clozapine works.
pmc-13571228:
Ming Y. Lim and co-authors model, in a 2026 cost-effectiveness analysis, adding the antibody drug emicizumab up front for hospitalized older patients with acquired hemophilia A. This is a rare autoimmune bleeding disorder where the body attacks its own clotting factor. Standard hospital care leans on bypassing agents that need frequent infusions and carry clot risks until immune treatment removes the antibody.

Despite its high price, adding emicizumab to the standard agent produced lower total direct costs and better health states in the model. Fewer bleeds and hospital days offset the drug bill. The drug remains underused in hospitals largely over cost fears. The analysis gives hospital pharmacy committees a counterintuitive case worth checking against their own prices.
pmc-13571328:
Qin and colleagues reported in 2026 a leadless pacemaker implant in a woman with complex congenital heart disease. The patient, aged 29, had Ebstein anomaly, a small right ventricle, a prior Glenn shunt, several defect repairs, and a replaced lung valve. She developed symptomatic heart block, where electrical signals between heart chambers fail.

Standard wire-based pacing was risky given her distorted anatomy and displaced tricuspid valve leaflet. The team chose a Micra AV leadless device, which keeps the chambers in sync. Guidance combined ultrasound imaging through the oesophagus, three-dimensional electrical mapping, and X-ray fluoroscopy. The device was placed on the front-septal wall of the right ventricle without touching the displaced valve leaflet. The authors conclude leadless pacing is feasible in such complex hearts with careful planning and multi-method imaging.
pmc-13572328:
Sofía Rincón-López and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 71-year-old woman with heavily pretreated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma who developed a deadly immune complication six months after CAR-T cell therapy. The complication, a hemophagocytic syndrome tied to the infused cells, involves runaway immune activation that consumes blood cells.

Most CAR-T toxicities strike early, so a fatal event at six months stretches the danger window. The authors point to lingering CAR-T cells sustaining disordered immune firing. Teams following CAR-T patients are urged to keep watching for this syndrome long after the expected risk period and to treat late fevers and falling blood counts with suspicion.
pmc-13572928: Rowena de Berker wrote a 2026 case report about a young man with a sudden inflammation of the pancreas. Scans confirmed the illness, yet his blood level of lipase, an enzyme doctors rely on to spot this condition, stayed normal throughout. Tests also showed he carries one copy of the gene change linked to cystic fibrosis. The author reviews how a normal lipase can mislead, and how damage to the gland's enzyme-making cells, tied to that gene, may explain the flat reading.
pmc-13573328:
Karla Fernanda Garcia-Ravelo, with nine colleagues, presents a 2026 pooled review of whether felt stress tracks with body metabolism. Metabolic syndrome, a cluster of waist, pressure, sugar, and fat risks, raises heart disease and diabetes odds. Stress is often blamed, yet past studies that used a standard stress scale disagreed.

The team gathered 30 studies with 12,491 adults who took the Perceived Stress Scale and had metabolic measures. Most measures, from body mass and waist size to pressure, fasting sugar, and blood fats, showed no clear link to stress scores. One stood out: insulin resistance, gauged by a standard index, rose with higher stress. The authors call that link early and shaky, since it hinged on single studies. They suggest stress checks may aid prevention once firmer data arrive.
pmc-13573428:
Guo-Wang Li and co-authors published a 2026 review comparing robot-assisted and standard keyhole surgery for removing parts of the liver with benign disease. Both methods avoid a big open incision. Robotic arms give surgeons steadier, more flexible instruments, but cost more. Whether robots do better for non-cancerous liver disease was unclear.

The authors searched eight databases for studies comparing the two methods head to head. Nine studies with 790 patients qualified. Robotic surgery took less operating time once setup was excluded. Patients lost less blood during the operation. Far fewer robotic cases had to switch to open surgery mid-operation. Hospital stays after surgery were also a bit shorter. A blood protein tied to recovery ran higher after robotic operations. Subgroup checks by disease type added detail. The review favors robots on these measures, within the limits of past-looking data.
pmc-13573728:
Preminger and Lannigan reviewed a 2026 patent survey of RSK inhibitors as cancer drugs, covering filings from 2020 to the present. RSK is a family of four kinases, enzymes that relay growth signals, and two members promote tumours while two can suppress them. Runaway RSK activity is implicated in inflammation linked cancers.

Patents were gathered from international, United States, and Derwent patent databases for compounds that reduce RSK activity. Preminger notes the disclosed compounds lack isoform specificity, hitting all family members at once rather than the harmful ones alone. Information on selectivity and target engagement in the patents is limited or missing throughout the set. One broad inhibitor, PMD-026, has reached phase two trials for metastatic breast cancer. The authors suggest degrader drugs exploiting side pockets could finally separate the isoforms.
pmc-13575028:
Miguel Martin leads a 2026 narrative review of abemaciclib, a targeted drug for the most common form of breast cancer. The cancer type is hormone receptor positive and HER2 negative, making up roughly 70 percent of cases. Abemaciclib blocks CDK4 and CDK6, two proteins that help cancer cells divide.

The review gathers trial results across early and advanced disease. Adding the drug to hormone therapy lowered recurrence risk in high-risk early cancer and lengthened control in advanced disease. It worked alongside several hormone partners and as a single drug, across many patient subgroups. Side effects stayed consistent across trials, and dose cuts helped patients stay on treatment for long periods when needed.
pmc-13575228:
Omolara Jemimah Ojezele and Matthew Obaineh Ojezele measure heavy metals in shop-bought hair dyes in a 2026 study from Ibadan, Nigeria. Dyes can carry trace metal contaminants from pigments, raw materials, or packaging. Repeated use may add up to low-level exposure for users and the environment.

Levels varied by colour: chromium peaked in blue dyes, while copper varied most and peaked in red dyes. Nickel also ran higher in blue dyes. Statistical grouping hinted that some metals share sources in the formulations. Most levels sat within available guidance ranges. The authors frame the work as screening data that supports routine monitoring.
pmc-13575628:
Ayesha Johar led a team studying blood pigment levels and bleeding stroke outcomes in Pakistan in a 2026 paper. The pigment carries oxygen, so levels that are too low or too high could affect brain recovery after a bleed. Evidence so far is mixed. Their multi-centre study gathered adults admitted with acute bleeding stroke and grouped them by pigment level measured within a day of arrival.

Stroke severity was scored on a standard scale, and function at discharge on another. The analysis adjusted for age, sex, severity, and other illnesses, and tested which factors predicted a good outcome or death. The study design and measures are set out in detail, aiming at recovery and prognosis in this setting.
pmc-13576128:
Yaqing Lin leads a 2026 report of a new HIV variant found in Guangdong, southern China. When several HIV strains circulate together, they can swap gene segments and create recombinant forms. Surveillance for drug resistance before treatment picked up unusual strains among men who have sex with men.

Most used the CXCR4 entry route into cells. The authors call for stronger molecular surveillance in this population.
pmc-13576328:
Yaxian Shi, Guiling Huang, and Jeannette M Beasley survey where health workers in China get nutrition information, in a 2026 study. They also ask how those sources link to how competent staff feel giving nutrition advice. Patients trust clinicians on food questions, yet many staff had little nutrition training. The survey covered 450 professionals, two-thirds of them nurses.

Colleagues were the most used source, followed by social media, then professional websites. Median self-rated competence sat at 120 on the scale used. Checking colleagues more often, asking friends or family, and joining webinars or continuing courses each linked to higher self-ratings. The link for informal sources caught the authors' attention, since confidence drawn from weak sources may mislead. They frame the work as a prompt to improve access to solid nutrition guidance.
pmc-13576528:
Yujia Zhai and colleagues tested a cell-depleting anti-PD-1 antibody in mouse models of type 1 diabetes at two stages of pancreatic inflammation. Early inflammation was delayed in its progress toward high blood sugar, while late inflammation was made worse by the same treatment. Islets from late-stage mice carried heavier immune infiltration and a sharper imbalance between effector and regulatory T cells.

One macrophage group, called Mac3, gathered in islets and raised receptors that bind antibody, and removing macrophages cancelled the harmful late effect. The work warns that the local immune setting can flip an immune therapy from helpful to harmful.
pmc-13578128:
Jodi Warman-Chardon, Bernard Jasmin, Rashmi Kothary, and Robin Parks report on the seventh Ottawa International Conference on Neuromuscular Disease and Biology, in a two thousand twenty-six conference report. The meeting convened in Ottawa in mid-September two thousand twenty-five.

Sessions covered novel disease gene identification and characterization, muscle, motor neuron, and stem cell biology, and the pathogenesis of neuromuscular conditions. Current standards of care were reviewed alongside recent advances in therapy development. The short report serves as the published record of the meeting's scope and themes for the wider community.
pmc-13578328:
Abdirisak Mohamed Yousuf, Deepa Krishnan, and Zubeda Ukundimana link shifting rain to failing water quality in the Mubuku River basin of western Uganda, in a 2026 study. The team tracked ten years of rain records, from 2014 to 2024, and paired a standard drought index with mapped lab tests of river water.

Both dry years and heavy runoff years left the water worse, through two routes. Dry spells let minerals build up in slow flow, while wet spells washed farm and town waste into the river. Dissolved solids climbed by about a third, hardness rose, and germ counts passed safe limits at several sites. Three sampling spots ran far dirtier than the basin average. The authors urge action aimed at those hotspots, timed to the seasons.
pmc-13578428:
Amit Kumar and Sujata Jadhav model how reliably a sensor run hydroponic farm keeps working, in a 2026 study. Soil free farms stack sensors, controllers, and pumps, and a failure in any part can kill a crop. Steady uptime matters most where water and land are scarce. Their math model walks the system through working, worn, and failed states over time.

Two nature inspired search methods then tuned the setup for uptime. A swarm method and a gene based method each pushed availability near ninety eight percent in their runs, with small gaps set by tuning choices. The authors offer the pair of tools as a planning aid, helping growers set repair schedules and pick settings before breakdowns bite.
pmc-13578628:
Hamdaoui published in twenty twenty-six a modeling study of sound-driven breakdown of pollutants in water. Ultrasound creates tiny collapsing bubbles that generate strong oxidants. The author models how contaminant loading near those bubbles governs breakdown speed. Two chemically different pollutants served as test cases. Experiments varied starting concentration across a wide range. Breakdown sped up at first with more pollutant, then removal efficiency fell. A four-parameter version of the model fit all profiles for each compound.

Validation that held out whole concentrations still predicted well. Simpler models sometimes matched or beat the full one, the author notes frankly. Fitted values are best read as condition-specific descriptors, not direct physical measures. The framework is offered as a tool for interpolation and timing within tested settings. Other reactors or waters would need fresh calibration.
pmc-13578828:
Gabriel Reis Alves Carneiro and colleagues build a lab test for retatrutide, a new long acting hormone drug, aimed at anti-doping work. The drug acts on three gut hormone switches at once and reshapes body weight and metabolism, which draws off label use among active people. Four users who dosed themselves under the skin twice gave blood and urine samples over set times for the study.

The method, built on precise mass reading of liquid samples, passed sport authority checks for reliability. In urine the intact drug never showed up, despite several extraction tries. Blood levels rose and fell in waves, hinting at slow release from the injection depot. Traces stayed findable in blood for about eight weeks after the first dose, so the authors urge blood based testing for this drug class.
pmc-13579828:
Sebastian Sanchez-Lopez and colleagues draw lessons from a Lassa fever case that surfaced in the Midwest of the United States, in a 2026 review. Lassa is a rodent borne viral fever rooted in West Africa, where models now project millions of infections a year, most mild yet some deadly. A traveler case far from that region exposed how slowly rich health systems can spot a rare, high stakes fever.

Early signs mimic common ills, and skipping the travel history delays the call. Lab confirmation leans on gene tests whose reach bends with viral variety and timing. The standard drug rests on thin, mixed proof, while vaccines and antibody drugs remain out of reach for routine care. The authors map gaps in spotting, testing, and treating such imports, and urge rehearsed readiness before the next one lands.
pmc-13580428:
Badawy and co-authors systematically review the skin injuries caused by radiation during brain and spine catheter procedures, in this 2026 paper. Long fluoroscopy runs can concentrate high doses on one patch of skin. Following PRISMA 2020 methods across four databases, they gathered case reports, case series, and other studies that reported a skin reaction, a relevant dose, or both.

Twenty-five studies covering roughly 686 patients in eleven countries qualified. Hair loss dominated the reports, appearing in 21 studies, while dermatitis and redness appeared in four and ulceration or tissue death in two. Cohort incidence ranged from about 5 to 56 percent, climbing with dose and complexity. Temporary hair loss clustered near the known threshold of roughly 3 gray, appearing two to five weeks post-procedure, whereas ulcers surfaced months to years later. The authors demand standard peak skin dose reporting.
pmc-13581828:
Kerim Mutig, Prim Singh, and Svetlana Lebedeva published a review in two thousand twenty-six on the kidney protein uromodulin and ageing. Uromodulin is the most plentiful protein in urine. It guards against urinary infections and stones and helps tune salt handling in the kidney.

Levels of the protein in blood and urine fall with age. That decline may explain part of the older kidney's weaker defence and concentrating power. Gene variants in the protein link to kidney and heart disease, and its levels are emerging as risk markers. The review gathers what is known about hormone control of the protein in healthy and sick ageing. It weighs whether targeting it could help older patients.
pmc-13583828:
Kimberly Lovell Donnelly and seven co-authors check, in a 2026 study, how often cardiac sarcoidosis patients carry antibodies to a common virus. Sarcoidosis grows clusters of immune cells, and its heart form can kill yet hide from plain tests. A virus called coxsackievirus B has been eyed as a possible trigger for the disease. The team read files from one Kansas health system, 2011 to 2025.

Of 56 definite heart cases, more than nine in ten held virus antibodies in their blood. Eight in ten held mid-to-high levels. In past population groups, the rate ran near one in seven. Heart scans in the group showed the scars and inflamed spots the disease is known for. Plain heart tests, by contrast, caught signs in only a small share. The authors pitch the cheap blood test as a screen to pick who needs deep heart scans.
pmc-13584428:
Arghavan Zebardast and Kasra Javadi review what Epstein-Barr virus does to the body's microbial communities in this 2026 paper. The virus infects most people for life and links to several cancers and immune diseases. Whether it also reshapes the bacteria living in the mouth, gut, and other niches was far less clear, so the pair searched three large databases for human studies.

Nine studies from 2017 to 2025 fit, covering the mouth, nose passage, gut, stomach tissue, and gum pockets. Where the virus or its linked diseases were present, microbial mixes differed in ways that changed from niche to niche. Measures of community variety, though, pointed in mixed directions across studies. The authors warn that all the work was watch-only and small, so no cause can be claimed yet.
pmc-13584928:
Wang, Wu, and Yu review epigenetic strategies against kidney fibrosis in twenty twenty-six. Fibrosis, or scarring, is the core irreversible process in chronic kidney disease. Current treatments slow the disease but cannot cure it. Epigenetic controls, which tune gene activity without changing DNA code, offer new angles.
